AR, SAC, and VC are currently being edited by Horst Lasic (VC) and myself. These files are not reproductions of the text as printed in JNA, but already incorporate a number of corrections based on the manuscripts. Due to technical difficulties, these corrections have not yet been marked—the footnotes have not yet been added to the files.

More useful files will be provided once the critical editions are completed. *KBhAṭxt* was originally produced by Tadashi Tani and kindly converted to ASCII by Kyō Kanō. I have subsequently converted this file—which utilized the Kyoto-Harvard convention for encoding diacritics—to conform with the @-convention used consistently across all other files.

The file contains several footnotes within the text that include abbreviations for textual editions; some of these abbreviations may have been erroneously converted and currently appear anomalous (e.g., RNA > r@n@a@). In any case, this serves as proof of the limitations of Kyoto-Harvard.

With the exception of this file, wherein the use of brackets and other formatting devices is as yet inconsistent (I shall attend to this in the near future), all other files adhere to the following standard:
page and line numbers are given in square brackets [ ],
while the folio numbers of the manuscript are given in round brackets ( ).

Notes from the editor or from the typist are given in fuzzy brackets { }. Pointed brackets are used to indicate emendations to the text. NOTE: A more comprehensive list of specifications that should be observed in Sanskrit e-texts is provided on my home-page, http://www.ipcṛiroshima-u.ac.jp/~kellner/etextṛtm. These specifications are subjective and have grown out of my personal experience.

I hope that these files prove useful, despite their current limitations. Any suggestions on how to improve their utility would be greatly appreciated. Birgit Kellner, 01-06-1997. I have revised this electronic text in order to make it useful for Word users.
Notes from the editor or from the typist are excluded for practical use.

Jñānaśrīmitra’s Collection of Treatises 1:
The Chapter on Momentary Destruction (Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya)
The First Section: The Topic of the Property of the Subject (Pakṣadharma)
[1b] ||Homage to the Buddha||

While this world, which lasts but a moment, is being stretched out by the rays of the Sun’s kinsman as if by other [forces], awaken from this sleep—do not lament over what is undesirable—as if awakened by a blow upon the chest. ||1||
Whatever exists is momentary, like a rain-cloud; for these entities exist.
Here, existence is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), which is established through valid cognition (*miti*) regarding those things proven to exist.
That capacity is not a single uniform kind, for otherwise [if it were always the same], there would be no production of something else, nor would there be any action at all.
In both ways, the connection with momentary destruction follows from this and comes to rest upon the probandum. ||2||

Here, the reason presented in the first quarter-verse is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason). This is not, first of all, unestablished (*asiddha*). For although there may indeed be a difference in the definition of existence (*sattva*) according to each philosophical system, nevertheless, it is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) that is intended here as "existence" and adopted as the reason. And this [capacity] is not impossible; it can by no means be denied, nor is it something that could be accepted by anyone.

For if those who cannot tolerate such definitions were to state our critique as being at most over-pervasive (*ativyāpta*), there would be no suspicion of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*)—either in its own nature or by way of its locus—because precisely those entities which have their specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) established by valid cognition are what constitute the subject (*pakṣa*).

Furthermore, regarding those things which, despite the possibility of their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), have not been ascertained in reality to possess that nature: even if they are excluded from the present subject (*pakṣa*), if a causal efficiency is perceived later by one who investigates them, then another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) will certainly arise. But in the absence of such efficiency, the non-apprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) is precisely what is intended, just as in the case of other logical marks (*liṅga*).

If it is argued that, in this way, the proof of momentariness would not be established—no; for we intend to prove the state of being [momentary] for everything whatsoever that is at any time or in any place useful for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), since it is only that which is useful in some instance that is fit to be the subject of an investigation into its specific nature. Therefore, [the proof] does not fail by avoiding an undesired form, nor is there an incapacity to determine the logical reason (*hetu*).

Nor is there a "locality" (prādeśikatva) of the proof of the probandum caused by the absence of a single simultaneous application of inference across all subjects possessing the property to be proven, as is the case with the inference of God and so forth. By this, it is shown that the various entities whose capacity for causal efficiency is certain are the subjects (dharmin), while the general property of causal efficiency is the logical reason (hetu).

Alternatively, all these entities that fall within the scope of perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the subjects (*dharmin*). The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is the logical reason (*hetu*). This is because it is impossible to establish any subject whatsoever in an inference that proves a positive entity if it is not an object of a *pramāṇa*, and because an inference operates everywhere only with respect to what is an object of a *pramāṇa*. What further pervasion (*vyāpti*) could there be for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*)? Thus, since the subject is within the range of a *pramāṇa*, the reason does not suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

Nor is there a lack of establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), because regarding those things where the attainment of external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is undisputed, there is no need for further deliberation. Even in cases where that [efficiency] is not directly ascertained, the determination of the capacity for causal efficiency is nonetheless certain, simply because it produces a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this occurs directly in the case of perception and indirectly in the case of inference.

On this point, some say: how is the existence of that very cause established, which is defined by its capacity to produce an effect? If that [capacity] is not established, then the primary [cause] itself lacks causal efficacy (*arthasāmarthya*). Alternatively, just as the seed has efficacy in relation to the sprout, so too let the sprout have efficacy in relation to the leaf, the stalk, and so forth; and likewise, let cognition have efficacy in relation to another cognition, memory, verbal expression, purposeful activity, and so on, or in relation to benefiting oneself and others.

It might be argued as follows: if there were no finality in the pursuit of a mere succession of effects, then the proof of momentariness—which relies on perceiving even a single thing that performs some causal function—would not be possible. Furthermore, if the very effect that terminates the series is itself devoid of causal efficacy, then by the same logic applied to its predecessors, not even a single thing capable of causal efficacy could be established; thus, the objection of "unestablished reason" (asiddhi) would remain unrefuted.

Furthermore, as for the claim that even if existence (*sattā*) is not established because the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are different, there is no impairment of the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), that too is incorrect. For even if existence is established despite a difference in exclusion, how can "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) be established? For producedness is indeed "coming into being after not having existed," and for you, coming into being is nothing other than the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Therefore, as long as there is doubt regarding the capacity for causal efficiency, it is impossible even to say "it comes into being."

The state of depending on the operation of another for the completion of its own nature is what constitutes "being produced"; this, too, is not a property of a non-existent thing. Furthermore, existence (*sattā*) is nothing other than causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Thus, properties such as being differentiated when conditions differ are properties of existent things; they cannot be predicated in order to determine the existence of something that is non-existent. [p. 3]

To this it is replied: First of all, sprouts and the like cannot be said to be non-existent when they manifest clearly in a perceptual consciousness that has attained proficiency through specific practice, even if there is a suspicion of error regarding their being surrounded by an illusion; for even if the result [of their existence] is not seen, otherwise there would be no confidence even in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and due to the absence of the conventional distinction between the real and the unreal, the world would become motionless.

Now, if you argue that for you [Buddhists], the very capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is the definition of existence (*sattvalakṣaṇa*), then must the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) now be stated by means of a definition established by mere convention? If you also wish to state a defect in your own definition through this same sequence, then let it be stated. For us, however, there is no preparation to establish that definition; rather, our purpose is to prove momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) by means of that definition.

Therefore, the failure to ascertain that characteristic would only create an obstacle to the proof of momentary destruction regarding the effect. However, when another effect is observed, who could prevent the subsequent inference of that [destruction] there as well, occurring sequentially? Now, since only that which is capable of causal efficiency is made the subject (*pakṣa*), it has already been stated that there is no fault whatsoever even if the probandum and the probans are unestablished with respect to what lies outside the subject.

Therefore, even in the case of a conventional definition, how much less could there be a contradiction of the property of being an effect—a property of the thing—in a real entity such as a sprout, which is supported by the force of a more acute perception and whose reality is not merely uncertain? In relation to that [perception], the seed and so forth are indeed capable of sustaining the proof of their capacity for causal efficiency; how, then, can it be unestablished?

Now, it may be asked: "How can sensory perception, which does not touch upon the definition of a real entity—whether that be the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) or something else—establish its status as a real entity? This objection is trivial, because once there is direct experience (*anubhava*), there is no room for deliberating about other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it is observed that even without the mention of a technical definition from the treatises, activity directed toward an object becomes non-contradictory simply through the arising of a perception conditioned by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*); so what can be done in this matter? It would be thus: [the establishment of reality occurs].

If, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), being a real entity (*vastutva*) consists precisely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), then when perception delineates a real entity as the locus of production—such that "this arises from that"—it is indeed the capacity for causal efficiency itself that is delineated. However, if the definition of a real entity is something else entirely, then it is that [other thing] which is delineated.

Just as blue, which is not distinct from that [cognition] because it does not exclude its being composed of the three *guṇas* or anything else, is indeed apprehended by the perception that grasps the blue, so too—despite the lack of observation of other effects even when there is a correspondence regarding the effectivity of sprouts and the like—it establishes the causal efficiency (*arthasāmarthya*) of the cause, such as the seed, through that very perception. This is established even in the absence of seeing another effect.

If it is argued that, like an effect, even a seed and so forth should be considered a real entity (*vastu*) simply because it gives rise to perception—what is the use of investigating causal efficiency?—we reply: no, for in the conventional usage of "real entity," we do not disregard the capacity of the object while relying solely on the acuity of perception; rather, we follow causal efficiency precisely because that too is dependent upon perception. However, our purpose is to establish momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

For the conventional usage of real entities (*vastu-vyavahāra*) established through perception, being common to both that which possesses the aforementioned characteristics and that which does not, is not invariably capable of proving momentariness. Although causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is the defining characteristic of a real entity, even if it is not present [in all cases], wherever it does exist of its own accord, it necessarily does not enter into its own essential existence without bringing that [momentariness] along with it. Therefore, it is established that this [causal efficiency] is introduced here as a means of proof (*sādhana*), and not as the defining characteristic of a real entity.

The same applies to cognition (*jñāna*): self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) is invariably concomitant with existence, as in all previous cases. Therefore, it should be understood that by this [self-awareness] as well, the establishment of the object through its own causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) remains unimpeded. For when one thing is known by another, there is room for the suspicion of error; but in the case of self-awareness, such suspicion is entirely absent.

Now, if one were to object regarding self-awareness, [we reply]: if awareness is admitted even by a cognition that inheres in the same object, then—just as in the case of a sprout and so forth—there is no fault whatsoever, since the other [cognition] also contributes to the constitution of its own nature. Otherwise, the loss of all empirical activity regarding perceived objects would inevitably follow in every respect.

But how indeed is the causal relationship between the object and its cognition to be understood, given that the object is not perceived prior to its perception? We reply: it is through the evidence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, only when an external object exists can there be an undertaking to determine whether it is stable or otherwise. Therefore, just as in the case of taking a collection of things that perform causal functions (*arthakriyā*) as the subject of proof, so too in taking the entire range of objects within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the subject, the two-fold unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the reason "because of instability" does not arise by way of the nature of the locus (*āśraya-svarūpa*).

[Page 5] Now, if it is thought that momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*), being endowed with the power of conventional entities, must itself be conventional and not ultimate (*pāramārthika*), to that also it is replied: Here, the practice of reality (*tattvābhyāsa*) is the cause for the fruits of higher status (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); therefore, the wise undertake an investigation into permanence, impermanence, and so forth, because such practice is impossible without certainty regarding those matters.

And as for that practice, whether it has assistance provided by a permanent deity and so forth, or is independent of such, it must be the cause of its fruit; in such a context, the examination of the means of valid cognition leads to the introduction of the momentary destruction of the sense faculties. Here, if this conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)—which is the means to the supreme human goal and is inseparable from the persistence of capacity through the avoidance of the undesired—is indeed conventional, then let momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) also be merely conventional, since one applies oneself to momentariness precisely for the sake of attaining the supreme human goal.

Of what nature is that which, when one reflects upon the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), is devoid of any distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of cognition (*prameya*), or any conventional practice of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)? Now, if such [distinctions] were possible even in the ultimate reality, then the existence of causal power (*śakti*) drawn from that [reality], or momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) as its concomitant, would not fail to be ultimately real.

But when there is an absence of the distinction between means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, whether through the total cessation of consciousness or through its establishment as mere self-consciousness (*svacinmātra*), the non-establishment of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)—just as when one is certain of the absence of the property of being a subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—does not cause any distress. In that regard, why does one who is terrified by the thought that the non-establishment of momentariness is unreal (*atāttvikī*) not likewise fear that the attainment of the fruits of heaven and liberation is unreal?

Therefore, as long as there is the conventional usage of the relationship between the probandum and the probans, so long does that which is capable of withstanding investigation possess ultimate reality; for, in the face of a fundamental refutation, any further subtle analysis is as good as non-existent. Enough of this excessive detail.

By this, it has been demonstrated that everything which the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, who is obsessed with irrelevant matters, has described—having raised a series of refutations against the Bhāṣyakāra’s account of the causal relation—is entirely useless. For instance, if the utility of such great effort lies solely in pointing out a lack of proof (*asiddhi*), what is to be gained by this? Furthermore, the lack of proof has already been refuted; for one who is engaged in determining the true nature of reality through the pursuit of human goals, the establishment of causal capacity (*śaktisiddhi*) is an inseparable concomitant of that activity.

Therefore, the claim that the production of an effect [from a permanent cause] is impossible—whether by way of succession or simultaneity—and that this [objection] is likewise unestablished, is rendered without foundation. Furthermore, whatever was suspected by him [the opponent] and answered out of pride in his own position, culminating in the point that conventional reality results in causal efficiency—namely:
"That which is capable of causal efficiency is here the ultimately real" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.3 = Pratyakṣa 3).

Having raised the objection that such a statement is redundant, [the author] writes: If it is argued that whatever is capable of conventional causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), then why is existence not likewise accepted for universals (*sāmānya*), wholes (*avayavin*), conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), and so forth? If it is argued that these lack even conventional efficiency—no, for the appearance of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is equal in both cases.

For instance, wherever the eye operates, there the appearance of a pillar or the like does not occur in the manner of the hair-visions of one suffering from ophthalmia; thus, the capacity of the pillar and so forth is understood. Likewise, the cognition of the continuity of "cow-ness" and so forth does not occur in relation to buffalo and the like. Furthermore, the cognition of the conjunction of a composite whole does not occur in relation to mere atoms, which are devoid of conjunction; thus, the capacity of universals and the like is also understood. That too is without substance.

For it is not the case that mere conventionality entails either acceptance or rejection; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting even the conventions of the ignorant. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of rejecting the conventions of the wise, which are intent upon accomplishing the supreme human goal. For conventionality is a cognition that is agreeable so long as it is not subjected to critical analysis. Now, the ignorant person possesses a grasp of things—such as a reflection in a mirror or a mirage—as being real, which is devoid of analysis. Likewise, the wise possess a grasp of the means for accomplishing the human goal, which is not subverted by your [critique of] analysis, and this too must not be abandoned. For if that were abandoned, one would find no need for the investigation into momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Now, if you argue: "This analysis belongs to the Buddhist; for me, however, there is simply no acceptance [of it]. Therefore, this results in a contradiction of the Buddhist's own tenet (*siddhāntavirodha*) and the fault of the probans being unestablished for the proponent (*vādyasiddhi*)," then we ask: Is this analysis a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is a valid means of knowledge, then the distinction that "this is yours alone and not mine" is untenable. On the contrary, if you accept its exclusion from the category of valid means of knowledge, it follows that you likewise have no standing (*anadhikāra*) even in the counter-argument (*prativāda*).

Now, if it is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then even if some point established in a portion of scripture is not valid, there is no harm to the subject at hand. This follows: "If something in a certain treatise is not logical, it is refuted; yet one who speaks of another thing as being logical—this is the established practice of the royal court" (PV 4.63, *Parārthānumāna*).

Thus, for one established in the Sautrāntika tenet who is proving momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the contradiction with another state of duration is not a subverting factor. Otherwise, it would contradict the [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya] statement: "Space and the two cessations—these three unconditioned phenomena are eternal" (AKBh 1.5).

What is new stated by this? Furthermore, for the Naiyāyika who accepts comparison (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how is there no contradiction with his own tenets (*siddhānta*) when compared to the Vaiśeṣika? However, the fact that they have different primary focuses is the same [in both cases]. Moreover, the reliance on causal capacity (*śakti*) does not overstep the system of the Sautrāntikas. If, however, even in that [comparison] there were no establishment of capacity, then one would merely be describing one's own mental appearance and would not be abiding in the Buddhist tenets.

Therefore, even when there is a contradiction with another system (*nayāntara*), there is no possibility of contradicting the established tenet (*siddhānta*), nor is there a failure of the proponent’s proof (*vādyasiddhi*). Furthermore, in an inference that functions by the force of the real object (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*), there is no conformity whatsoever to scripture. However, regarding the validity of the investigation into that [object], since the capacity of the object must necessarily be admitted even if it is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), any conceptualization of universals, inherence, and so forth—which are held to be eternal—is sublated by the proof of momentary destruction brought about by that [capacity]. Thus, such conceptualizations are not to be accepted as having causal efficiency, because they belong to an inferior conventionality, like the conventionality of children.

Since it is impossible for that which is incapable of producing cognition of its own object to be admitted as existing, let it be a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*); however, there must be the certainty that each subsequent level is even more inferior than the one below it. For this very reason, in relation to each progressively lower conventional reality, those established at each higher level must necessarily be accepted as being the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Thus, a conventional reality is called "ultimately real" only because its causal efficacy is unsurpassed.

For instance, when a child perceives a face in the surface of a mirror, it is said that "the ultimate reality" (paramārtha) is that the face appearing here is actually non-existent in relation to [the actual face]. And in relation to that, the ultimate reality is that the rays of the eyes, having turned back by reflecting off the mirror, perceive one's own face. Thus, as successive conceptualizations become more powerful, each preceding one is the conventional (saṃvṛti) and each succeeding one is the ultimate reality, until the stability of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is reached.

For if that [causal efficiency] were transgressed, the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender would collapse, resulting in the establishment of mere appearance; in such a case, what talk could there be of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)? Therefore, it is precisely the capacity for ultimate purposeful action (*arthakriyāśakti*) that is denoted by the term "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*); thus, conventionalities such as universals (*sāmānya*) and the like do not approach even a fraction of that [capacity], merely by virtue of being conventional.

Disregarding the validity of such investigations by way of "closing one's eyes like an elephant," it is stated in various places that power (*śakti*) alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), while universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth are merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Likewise, the whole (*avayavin*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so on, should be understood in both ways; for while power is accepted as the ultimate reality, [the former] are subject to the nature of momentary existence.

For indeed, it may be that atoms themselves, when produced in a specific state, or two substances devoid of conjunction, serve as the basis for those respective cognitions; what then is the use of a "whole" (*avayavin*) and so forth? How then can the inclusion of universals (*sāmānya*) and the like be equated with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) on the grounds that they are mere conventionalities (*saṃvṛtimātra*)? And if their equality were established by that alone, what would be the point of proclaiming logical arguments? Let there be no status of being a lower-order conventionality—this is the introduction of a restriction. And that [status] is difficult to avoid, given the connection with momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of that which possesses capacity or its substratum.

As was stated previously, if there is an absence of the connection with causal capacity (*śakti*), then since even its substratum would possess only conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisattva*), how could one avoid the consequence that its properties, such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, would also lack the status of being conventional? Therefore, the similarity lies precisely in their being mere conventionality; and the fault regarding that has already been stated. Furthermore, this argument known as "the distinction from cognition" will also be examined in the discussion on *apoha*.

Furthermore, as for what was said: "If conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is a cognition whose true nature is not investigated, and if it is precisely from that [conventional reality] that the determination of cause and effect is accepted, then, such being the case, the causal relation of non-momentary things alone—well-known among all worldly practitioners—should be understood as having its name according to its meaning; so what is the use of subtle analysis there?"—that too is incorrect.

For instance, when the Sautrāntika puts forward a proof to establish, in reality, the portion of entities that are momentary by nature, his threefold capacity—which is to be apprehended through perception and non-perception—is indeed real, because there is an absence of application for either proof or refutation once one is established in one's own pure consciousness alone.

How can this [objection] be countered? How is he able to remain if he must avoid another [position] established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) concerning an external object? And to that extent, the establishment of real momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) merely demonstrates that non-momentary things possess a conventional causal relationship; so what is the point of the effort to accept [this objection]? Furthermore, an objection cannot be avoided simply by its appearing during an investigation, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of disregarding [the arguments] regarding the negation of shadow as a substance, the proof of God (*īśvara*), and so forth.

For one who speaks of what is undesirable, even an investigation that is already established is rendered superfluous by its subtlety; therefore, enough now with this arduous labor of the succession of treatises. Consequently, what is the use of subtle investigation in that regard? Abandoning such investigation, it would be more appropriate to say, "This [argument] is not beautiful," rather than saying, "It is a rejection of non-momentariness. And that [rejection] is not established by mere assertion alone. We, however, have presented a proof for the purpose of transcending permanence, and there is no fault therein.

Furthermore, if one is intent on the aforementioned subtle investigation, it is indeed a fault that another subtle investigation would also find scope; as he said: "By means of subtle scrutiny, there would indeed be a distinction [between cause and effect] based on their causal relationship, according to the logic you have stated. This too is only fitting for one who is dull-witted with blind faith. For as long as we do not tolerate the abandonment of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) of entities, our acceptance of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) remains unassailed and our refutation of permanence stands firm.

But when the mind proceeds toward a powerful investigation into the analysis of capacity (*śakti*), then it will be unable to escape [the doctrine of] momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) as well, for the force [of the argument] is the same. Nor can the acceptance of capacity revive either permanence or impermanence, because it is not common [to both]. For indeed, it is not the case that something called "capacity" exists somewhere at some time while being devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is no escape [from momentariness].

Rather, this [seed] and so forth is capable of producing the sprout and so forth; it is in this very form that it is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And just as that direct perception is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too is it [a means of cognition] regarding the difference between the action and other factors of effects. By such a method of reasoning, causal capacity (*śakti*)—resting upon momentariness—is not common to permanent entities. How, then, could there be a revival of both [the seed and the sprout]? Thus, when there is a powerful investigation suggesting the collapse of the relation between cause and effect, causal capacity is established.

Momentariness alone exists; that is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Permanence, however, is merely an inferior conventionality, and thus it should be understood as being like a universal (*sāmānya*). When that [permanence] is subjected to analysis, there is no room for any doubt; thus, causal capacity (*śakti*) is indeed established. So why is it said: "Even so, because it is unestablished, momentariness is not established by means of existence, nor is the pervasion of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by succession and simultaneity established"? For it has already been shown that [the argument] holds even on the view that capacity is conventional.

Now, one might object: just as for one who, within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), seeks the supreme human goal and engages in the search for its means, there is no possibility of remaining without relying on the efficacy of the object (*artha-śakti*), so too, from the search for means with the thought "I must become a possessor of that fruit," the grasping at permanence (*nityatā-graha*) necessarily follows. Thus, even if that [grasping] is conventional, how could it not be an object of a lower convention (*adhara-saṃvṛti*)? Surely, the permanent self deserves a separate consideration.

Nor is it appropriate to accept [the self] on that basis alone, because it would then have as its object a specific conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Let it be granted that the apprehension of capacity (*śaktigraha*) is the motivator for investigation. One may indeed say, "What is to be done with this capacity? However, by these words, the transgression of capacity is not shattered, since the apprehension of capacity is accepted as the cause for seeking the means [to knowledge]. But this cannot be maintained regarding the self. If it is argued that even the apprehension of capacity is a motivator only through conventional reality, let it be so—whether by way of convention or by way of ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Furthermore, since the proof of causal capacity (*śakti*) establishes that the apprehension of a self (*ātmagraha*) is also a motivating factor, it does not necessarily entail the proof of a self. It has already been stated that if there were a requirement for a definitive determination, the proof of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would subvert that [notion of a self]. However, the argument for the establishment of a fixed synthesizer (*pratisandhātṛ*) during the apprehension of cause and effect will be introduced in the *Anekāntacintā*.

This has also been stated: even by means of subtle analysis, according to your own view, the apprehension of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is lost, because you do not admit the apprehension of one thing by another that is not connected to it. Furthermore, since a connection (*pratibandha*) resides in two things, it cannot be grasped by perception, which grasps only non-dual [simultaneous] objects; thus, inference does not apply there. In our view, however, there is no impossibility of apprehending the causal relation either, because we do not accept the restriction that perception has only a single moment as its object.

And likewise, in the context of establishing the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it was argued that even the perception of persons such as ourselves sometimes operates with respect to objects past, future, and so forth, by the power of causes such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); for otherwise, the understanding of causality would not be possible. [p.10] All of that, too, is fruitless. To explain: first of all, the cognition of one thing by another is accepted by both proponents—both those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness and those who do not.

And in that case, if there were indeed a perception of non-duality by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this would contradict logic; for it is only logical that there be a perception of duality. This being so, there is no contradiction in the perception of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Even a proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*) who accepts this [perception of duality] would suffer what kind of loss? For it is not as if he has never seen or accepted such a thing before. Previously too, he adopted his own philosophical tenet simply according to his own will; why should he not be allowed to adopt another one now? (PV 4.74)

Now, if it is somehow argued that only the apprehension of non-duality is logical, then its opposite—the apprehension of the relation between cause and effect, which is inclined toward [establishing] causal efficiency—is merely a matter of your own preference; where would it be useful?

Or, if your intention is that even the apprehension of the relation between cause and effect is impossible under the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), then let the contradiction be pointed out by stating that "the relation between cause and effect exists," rather than claiming "it is unestablished" (*asiddhi*). And we shall explain this in that context.

As for what was said—"If it is argued that this cognition arises solely from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), we say no; for here too there is a lack of valid evidence"—in that case as well, one might be able to present a proof establishing that there is a substance called the "self" (*ātman*) distinct from body and mind, in which [the cognition] inheres, and that there are qualities characterized by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) as separate entities; but to establish that "karma" is simply a particular power of the mind (*cetaḥ-śakti-viśeṣa*) is a matter of great faith! For it is the very power of the mind that is designated as "latent impression."

Therefore, for one who maintains that there is only the perception of unconnected moments, conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is beginningless; from that comes mental impression (*vāsanā*); and from that comes false cognition (*mithyā-pratīti*). One should consider that the claim that "all this is without authority (*apramāṇaka*), like a succession of blind men," is merely the play of the dull-witted. For the proponent under discussion is the Sautrāntika, who asserts the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga-vādin*); to say that his cognition of the relation between cause and effect is a false cognition is a great delusion.

However, it is more appropriate to say that the Yogācāra is one who denies the relation of cause and effect and maintains the doctrine of the cognition of mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvinmātra*). And nothing follows for the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*) from the refutation of that [Yogācāra]. If there is a logical possibility for the denial of that [momentariness] even by one who denies cause and effect, then that too is not far off; so what is the point of this insistence? This remains established: whether the capacity for causal efficiency (*kāryakriyāśakti*) is real or otherwise, in either case, the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhi*) does not apply.
The first chapter, titled "The Section on the Property of the Subject," is concluded.
[Chapter 11, Section 1] [In the Chapter on Momentary Destruction] [Section 2:

The Section on Positive Concomitance] [11.3] Nor is this reason contradictory (*viruddha*), because it is observed in the "cloud," which has been established as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*); for a contradictory reason, characterized by a pervasion with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), cannot possibly be observed in that which possesses the probandum. [Objection: But this is a rash assertion, since the capacity of cognition to take momentary destruction as its object is not perceived anywhere, and there is no such determination. Furthermore, the proof of momentary destruction in a cloud does not arise from relying on the force of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For the recognition "this is that very same cloud" presents its persistence over a period of time through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Because [the inference] is sublated by this, there is no room for inference. Nor is there any other inference [that could apply]. Furthermore, if one were to seek another instance for the inference based on existence (*sattva*), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, because [the reason] is not observed in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), the contradiction is not avoided.

Furthermore, because [the reason] exists in the cloud, which is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is indeed no contradiction; rather, there is the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the non-existence [of permanence]. Moreover, regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), the thesis of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*). As Śaṅkara said: "Because by direct perception itself the absence of the reversal of stability is established. Nor is this apprehension of oneness (*ekatāgraha*) regarding earlier and later times unauthoritative, for it is reliable (*saṃvāditva*).

And likewise, Nyāyabhūṣaṇa [states]: "Just as the validity of the cognition 'this is its effect' is accepted solely because of the absence of contradiction, so too the validity of the cognition 'these were performed by him in succession and not simultaneously,' as well as that of recognition such as 'I am that very same person' and 'this is that very same crystal,' must be accepted solely because of the absence of contradiction, since they share an identical status regarding their logical security. This, however, is inconsistent.

For a conceptual construction that lacks a real objective correlate (*aliṅga*), what is called "non-discrepancy" would have to consist either in the attainment of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) or in its correspondence with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In this case, since there is no occurrence of another means of valid cognition here beyond the mere determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "it is that very thing," [non-discrepancy cannot be established].

Furthermore, no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) whatsoever is established as being tied to a single [cause], because there is no contradiction in such an efficiency being produced even by something different, provided it possesses an equivalent capacity. To illustrate: just as one jar holds water, yet another jar existing at that same time does not hold water, so too, if another jar were to hold water in the second moment, what fault would there be? As for a dissimilar action, there is no need for consideration at all.
Therefore, just as the actions of cooking and so forth are established and experienced as being tied to fire and the like—

[12] One attains corroboration regarding the cognition of burning; however, no action that is perceived as being within the range of experience is found to be connected with the identity of the initial and final moments in such a way that even the apprehension of a single entity would be corroborated.

If it is argued that because there is always a uniformity of single determination for all [cognizers], what need is there for dependence on further corroboration? We say no, because this is unproven (*asiddhatvāt*). For even if unity is to be determined by those of equal capacity, it cannot be established by "all" if one is not omniscient. There is no contradiction if among the gods, sages, and yogis who perceive supersensible objects, someone might at some time be a perceiver of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Furthermore, the observation of ever-increasing capacities is the seed of such a possibility.

If, however, this [momentary destruction] called *kṣaṇabhaṅga* were not an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then it would be correct that there is no apprehension of it by those [means of knowledge]. And that has begun to be examined. Therefore, as long as its establishment as an intrinsic nature is not achieved, so long is the determination of the negation of momentary destruction for all things not established. For those who hate the perception of supersensible objects are not virtuous in asserting a negation based on mere non-apprehension alone, because of the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

However, let it be for now that non-apprehension of a suitable object is incapable [of establishing absence] when the object is remote in terms of place and so forth. Furthermore, even in the case of hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia, a partial consensus is possible, yet it cannot establish a correspondence with reality. And this is stated with reference to perception.

But since those who perceive a difference in entities based on a difference in moments [establish this] through inference, how can they be refuted even in this assembly, given that the practice of proving that [inference] is not barred in some cases? Therefore, for all people, there is no single determination—whether perceptual or inferential in nature—that necessarily negates the determination of difference; thus, its validity is not confirmed by correspondence (*saṃvāda*) in the same way as other means of valid cognition, because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of things such as hair that has been cut and grown back again, or blades of grass, plantain leaves, and thorns.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by this one who is conceited regarding his specific argument: "Now, recognition is seen even when it is non-concordant (*visaṃvādin*); is the cognition of the relation between cause and effect not also seen to be non-concordant? If you say, "That which is non-concordant is not indeed a cognition of cause and effect, because it lacks validity," then the same applies here as well: that which is non-concordant is not indeed recognition, because it is a mere semblance (*tad-ābhāsa*) thereof.

It might be argued as follows: if the distinction between definitions could be established just like the cognition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). For instance, even in the cognition of the causal relation, if one were to apprehend the production of smoke and so forth by the mere entity [fire], one would have to abandon all caution regarding fire due to the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of donkeys and the like. In the same way, it should be understood accordingly whether there is merely positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or merely negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Furthermore, when the cognition of the causal relation—which consists in perception and non-perception directed toward the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance—is brought forward, as we have established in our investigation of the "threefold" and "fivefold" [criteria], [then it is understood that]:
"It does not abide therein, nor is it born from another, nor has it come from elsewhere;
for if an effect were to exist upon the presence of something, it would belong to that [thing] alone, and not to anything else."

"In the case of establishing the relation of cause and effect," it is then that there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Thus, if even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) a difference in characteristics were shown—or could be shown—to be relevant to deviation and non-deviation, then this would be correct. But this is not the case, because in all instances of objects that are absolutely similar, the recognition of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) is of a single uniform nature.

If there were a temporal restriction such that the cessation of the delusion necessarily occurs after this much time, then this would be appropriate. However, even in the case of a mass of hair that has been cut and regrown, the cessation of the delusion of identity does not necessarily occur for one who exerts effort even upon the exhaustion of a human lifespan. If you argue [that it must occur], we say no; for even in that case, there is no such certainty. For even for one who strives, a mere word is not authoritative, and another logical proof is difficult to find.

If another argument were to subvert the unity established by recognition, why is such a thing not likewise maintained in the present case? It is a great power of discernment that while the wretched inference, based on recognition, was previously incapable [of proving anything], now even your mere word is capable regarding hair and the like.

If it is argued that since one observes the determination of non-difference even when hair and the like are distinct, let there be some way or another an awareness of difference in those cases; [we reply: no, for such is observed extensively elsewhere as well. For indeed, when one pillar has been removed and another similar pillar is placed in its stead, recognition does not fail to occur. This principle applies likewise to jars, cloths, crystals, and so forth, as long as an absolutely similar instance is obtained. And this rule holds even when the observation occurs at different times.

However, even when two iron balls are perceived simultaneously, there certainly occurs a determination of their difference. Therefore, regarding a pillar or the like—which is intended to be one despite a difference in time—is this determination of oneness truly distinct from it, just as [the determination] is from another pillar? Or is it non-distinct? How can such a doubt, which subverts the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), be refuted? If it is argued that there is no doubt because a non-difference across moments has never been observed before, this too is not correct.

For it cannot be said that something does not exist simply because it is unperceived, since even an existing thing may go unnoticed due to its subtlety—just as the arising and passing away that occurs moment by moment is not perceived despite the growth and decay of the body. Therefore, even when [the difference] is not perceived, a doubt characterized by the inclusion of the factor of existence regarding the distinction is unavoidable. However, in the absence of such reflection, there would be a firm, singular conviction for ordinary people; yet even that, as previously stated, is merely a form of doubt. Furthermore, even through the difference of moments, difference is indeed "seen," because it is observed by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[14] Just as, in the case of a stream and so forth, even though water falls in one spot after another within a certain portion of space, there occurs both the determination that "this is that very same water" and the possibility of its opposite.

If it is argued that the apprehension of identity occurs in cases where there has been no repeated observation (*anabhyāsa*), whereas in the case of a pillar and the like, it occurs even for one who possesses such repeated observation—well, it has already been established that in every instance, this lack of repeated observation applies to the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) that arise from momentary difference. However, in the case of water, a pillar, and so forth, there is indeed repeated observation everywhere regarding a coarse object (*sthūlaviṣaya*) which takes as its support the general property (*sāmānya*) consisting of the efficacy of those functions. Therefore, it is not possible to accept that perception performs the function of proving non-difference between two moments.
Even if a mere determination of oneness (*ekāvasāya*) exists, it is incapable [of proving identity] because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

[Objection: Surely, in every case regarding blue and so forth, the operation of perception, being followed by a subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), confers upon it validity. Therefore, let the determination of identity also illuminate the validity of this [perception] as having precisely one object. [Response: Indeed, the sense-cognition does not possess validity with respect to the object of every subsequent conceptual construction. For if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a cognition whose object is a mirage would possess validity with respect to water, since it is determined as water.

The principle is that validity depends upon conceptual determination (*vikalpa*); thus, when such determination does not arise, there is no validity. But when it does arise, that validity depends precisely upon corroboration (*saṃvāda*). And it has already been explained that this [corroboration] is not the same as the conceptual determination of a single [object]. Now, one might object: "In cases where there is sublation (*bādha*), there is invalidity; where there is no sublation, there is validity—is this not sufficient? This approach, however, applies even to the appearance of a sky that seems to be slanting, as it can extend across different places, times, and persons; yet, when scrutinized, it falls apart—and this is equally true for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as well.

Furthermore, regarding this so-called "non-sublation" (*abādha*), there are two alternatives: is it the absence of sublation, or the non-perception of sublation? In these two options, respectively, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), which are difficult to refute. This is because negation is not established by mere non-perception, and because a sublatant inference (*anumāna*) will be stated [later].

Now, if this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is called "equal to perception" (*pratyakṣasama*), how can it be sublated by inference? Moreover, by the very assertion that it is not subject to sublation, one has granted the opportunity for the existence of a sublatant; thus, the scope for inference is provided by oneself alone.

If it is argued that since validity alone is the subject of both proof and refutation, perception itself must be its sublater—then what can even a hundred perceptions do to this [validity] when its firmness is established through corroboration? Therefore, even by means of perception, a refutation of this [validity] brings to mind an inference that conceives of a weakening of corroboration.

Furthermore, have you not observed that the recognition—"the magician is pulling out the ball submerged in his head with his mouth"—is sublated by an inference based on the contingency of there being a hole in his head? Let it be granted that what is sublated is not perception, even in the case at hand. Therefore, the claim of its being perception here is merely a borrowed ornament and offers no protection.

Just as the appearance of a downward-sloping sky, despite being universally perceived, is certainly not non-sublated, so too it is clear that it is not non-contradictory either. In the same way, the apprehension of oneness, despite being universally perceived, is not non-contradictory. For, apart from the arising of a subsequent determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [oneness], no further corroboration—whether in the form of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) or otherwise—is possible in the cognition "this is that very same thing" regarding the perception of the slanted sky.

Therefore, even in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is impossible to establish the conventional designation of non-validity. Likewise, for one who maintains that validity is established through correspondence (*saṃvāda*), how can there be a conventional designation of validity for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the absence of such correspondence? And when both [validity and non-validity] are unascertained, doubt—which depends upon both—is established. Furthermore, since its definition is seen to deviate in cases such as the plantain stalk, and because its constituent parts are both desired and undesired, how then could it possess validity?

Furthermore, one who says that a non-concordant [cognition] is not recognition at all because it is a mere semblance of it, must also necessarily say: "That 'knowability' (*prameyatva*) which, when used as a reason for sound and so forth, deviates from the probandum, is not actually knowability at all, because it is a mere semblance of it."

Now, if being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) consists merely in being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that status is not lacking even in the case of that which is errant (*vyabhicārin*). If that is so, then the purpose of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is merely the non-separation from what was previously perceived; and that [status] exists even for that which is errant. Whether recognition is called an action or not, one must simply state that it is not a means of valid cognition at all. You should also say that whatever possesses the status of being an object of knowledge while being errant is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) at all.

Since deviation in one case is not prevented even when it occurs elsewhere due to the fact that [the object] has a single characteristic, it is likewise impossible [to prevent it] in the case of recognition as well.

Furthermore, as for one who says: "That which is non-concordant is not indeed a recognition, because it is a mere semblance of it"—by that same logic, one must also say: "When the property of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is employed as a reason for sound and so forth, and that *prameyatva* which deviates from the probandum is [adduced], that very *prameyatva* is not actually *prameyatva* at all, because it is a mere semblance of it."

Now, if "knowability" (*prameyatva*) consists merely in being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that property is not lacking even in the case of that which is fallacious (*vyabhicārin*). If this is so, then the purpose of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is merely the non-identification [of the present with the past] as before; and that [non-identification] exists even for a fallacious [cognition]. Whether recognition is called an action or not, one must simply state that it is not a means of valid cognition at all. Furthermore, you should also say that whatever is knowable yet fallacious is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) at all.

Since deviation is possible elsewhere just as it is in one case due to the fact that [all things] have a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇatā*), it cannot be ruled out; thus, even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), it is not impossible. [Objection: But surely, when there is a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), the inference "there is fire here" and what is not an inference have the same form. So how is it that confidence occurs in one case and not in the other? [Response: Because of the distinction made by way of the reason (*hetu*).

For just as one [cognition] is produced by the ascertainment of a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics while another is otherwise, and just as it has been shown that some cognition of the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is perfectly pure—being established through perception and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)—while others are otherwise; so too, since their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinct, there is no confusion between what is reliable (*āśvāsa*) and what is unreliable (*anāśvāsa*). Likewise, this cannot be maintained regarding recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), because even when the object is deceptive, such knowledge—or the operation of the senses of one whose faculties are unimpaired—still functions.
Nor is there any other distinction pointed out by others. However, the mere persistence over a long period of time is abundant...

[16] Even when there is a delay in the convergence of the causal complex for error due to delusion or the influence of causes such as the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), it is still logically possible, as was stated previously. Alternatively, if one accepts inference as the cognition of an imperceptible object based on whatever [mark] it may be, then that which is subject to deviation cannot truly be a logical mark (*liṅga*) or an inference. Thus, maintaining the cessation [of error], for what purpose would one state the definition of a logical mark—such as its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—and the inference produced from it?

Furthermore, even if one observes deviation [in some cases], it is impossible to fail to observe deviation [in all cases]; for if a thing were considered a logical mark (*liṅga*) merely because deviation is not observed due to a delay in obtaining the necessary causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then a definition must indeed be stated—that by the observation of which certainty arises and by the non-observation of which lack of confidence is produced. Otherwise, a prudent person would not undertake an action consistent with that [mark].

For there certainly exist proofs for those who maintain opposing views—proofs that, through long-term habituation, have become manifest by the power of balanced meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet whose objects of perception are subject to deviation, just like the proofs for momentariness and so forth. Therefore, should one now, on account of such deviation and the mere non-observation [of the probandum], conclude that the proofs are indeed invalid because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) will not function? Or should a discerning person, by engaging in practices corresponding to those [opposing views], enter into a fruitless delusion?

However, regarding the definition [of a valid reason] such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, when one examines that definition and finds it not to apply, one abandons it at that very moment and does not enter into a state of exhaustion; or, if that definition is found to apply, one would simply adopt it. Therefore, resorting to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not sound, because the undertaking of the investigation was precisely for the sake of excluding [the possibility of] negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

If it is asked how its definition can be inexpressible, consider this: even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), as long as you do not perceive a difference in the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), you—failing to observe any deviation in one instance—should not, merely because of that non-observation of deviation, place absolute confidence in the other. Therefore, if a sublation (*bādhā*) were possible for that which possesses the defining characteristic, then that very characteristic would be invalidated; thus, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases.

Therefore, let this recognition dispel the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for, tainted by that [suspicion], it is neither able to establish the persistence of an object over time, nor is it able to preclude inference. So how can the thesis be said to be sublated by perception in view of that [recognition]? Or how could there be an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), namely, the cloud?

Now, let it be that recognition lacks validity, or that the certainty of stability following from it does not exist; however, how can the determination of momentariness be established in the "similar instance" (sapakṣa), since the presence of the reason (hetu) in the similar instance would otherwise be impossible? It is replied: here, the capacity of a rain-cloud for the act of holding water necessarily entails a single functional nature (ekārthasvabhāva) that cannot be avoided.

And in another moment, such as the second and so forth, since that action has already been performed, it is impossible to perform it again; therefore, one would either perform an action of the same kind or of a different kind, or else one would not perform any action at all—this is the position. Thus, even prior to the moment of performing that action...

[17] It must be stated: in that case, if the cloud has a nature capable of producing that [effect], then why would there ever be an interruption of its activity even at another moment, just as it is at that [first] moment? Or, if its nature were such that it is capable of producing an activity to be brought about at another moment, then—just as in that other moment—it would follow that it would produce both similar and dissimilar activities even at that [first] moment. For since that capacity exists even at the other moment, production would occur; and that [capacity] is not diminished at other times either. Indeed, effects are delayed only due to the absence of their causes.

"When the efficient cause is present, what causes their delay? (TS 395). By this, the position that [the cause] does not act is also refuted. When even a delay is intolerable, then non-action is cast far away. Or, if there were incapacity, it would follow that there would be no action even at the desired time, because of having a single, constant nature. And if there were a loss of that nature, the moment-by-moment destruction of the cloud is established. In this regard, the formal argument is: whatever is capable of producing something at a certain time, it necessarily produces that thing at that time.

Just as the final causal complex [produces] its own effect, or that very cloud while holding water performs the function of being a festival for the eyes of farmers and so forth, or at the time of discharging water performs that action—since this [cloud] is capable of accomplishing both effects in both states, it follows by way of a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) that [the capacity must exist prior to the action]. If capacity were established without actual production, there would follow the absurdity of attributing the conventional usage of "capacity" to everything in every respect. Yet, this conventional usage is recognized as being restricted [to specific instances].

Furthermore, no cause other than its production is possible for this [capacity]. Therefore, since it is necessarily absent from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) where there is no production, it is deprived of its own existence by being separated from that which pervades its definition; thus, it must rest in production itself. Consequently, the state of being a producer is established as being invariably concomitant with the mere fact of being the object of the conventional usage "capable"; such is the establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Thus, whenever something is capable of performing a certain action, it necessarily performs that action at that time; for example, the final causal complex. And this [agent] is capable even at a time when all actions are bypassed. This [reasoning] should be applied to the alternative position that [the agent] never acts at any other time.

But if its nature were incapable, then whatever is incapable of a certain action does not perform that action, just as *kodrava* grain does not produce a rice sprout. And this cloud is incapable in the subsequent moment just as it is in the moment of non-action; thus, because of the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*), it would never act—this is the meaning of the logical reason (*hetu*). The formulation by contrapositive (*viparyaya-prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not perform an action is not capable of it, just as *kodrava* grain, when not producing a rice sprout, lacks the capacity for it. And [the cloud] does not perform the action accomplished in the first moment during the second and subsequent moments, nor does it perform the action accomplished in the second and subsequent moments during the first moment.

Or, regarding the first moment: this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Since a rain-cloud possesses a nature that is both capable and incapable with respect to its various actions, it produces a distinction [of its nature] at every moment. Thus, in every respect, with regard to non-action: whatever does not perform an action in a certain case is not capable of it, just as *kodrava* grain, when not producing a rice sprout, is not capable of it; and likewise, at the time of non-action, [the cloud] does not perform the action which is the effect of the time of action. This is with regard to capability (*sāmarthya*).

Whatever performs an action is not incapable in that regard, just like the final causal complex (*antyasāmagrī*). And this cloud performs the act of holding water; thus, the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) distinguishes that which is capable of acting from the moment that is incapable.

For just as the capacity for effective existence is pervaded by production, so too is production pervaded by that [capacity]. That capacity which is the opposite of incapacity pervades the causal efficiency; thus, it renders nugatory the observed capacity [of the cloud] by means of that [capacity]. Therefore, due to its nature of being both capable and incapable, a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) is established for the rain-cloud. So how can it be said that there is no inference other than [that based on] existence (*sattva*)?

In this context, the objection raised by some—that the reason (*hetu*) is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*) because "fitness for the operation of causal efficiency" and "the production [of that fitness]" possess distinct exclusions (*bhinnavyāvṛtti*)—should be understood as having no basis. Therefore, since a momentary entity performing a single function possesses a nature that is either capable or otherwise relative to subsequent moments, there is indeed a difference; thus, by virtue of its momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitā*), it attains the status of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Consequently, the establishment of existence (*sattva*) in a cloud is not contradictory.

Now, one might object: even for an entity that persists through different moments, its performing or not performing an action is possible depending on its conjunction with auxiliary causes; how, then, can this establish a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)? Consequently, the fundamental reasons stated in the aforementioned reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, what could be done by the auxiliaries for this [entity] which possesses a capable nature, such that it would not undertake activity toward its own effect without depending on them? For dependence upon that which provides no assistance is illogical.

It is logical that one who is himself incapable, yet desires capability, must depend upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). However, it is contradictory to claim that auxiliary causes are both ineffective and yet objects of dependence. Regarding this, Śaṅkara says: "The absence of auxiliaries is indeed called its incapacity. And that [incapacity] is removed by the causes of the totality of auxiliaries (*sākalya*), because there is a contradiction between those two [incapacity and totality] existing together in a single locus. Furthermore, from the causes of totality, there is the exclusion of deficiency (*vaikalya*) itself, not of that which possesses it [the cause]; for the totality consists in the very exclusion of the absence of auxiliaries."

Nor is the existence of that which possesses [the auxiliary causes] established by the appearance and disappearance of the completeness or incompleteness of those auxiliaries, because it is distinct from them. For this very reason, the disappearance of that which possesses [the auxiliaries] is not established by the cause that is the exclusion of the absence of auxiliaries.

The author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* has said exactly this: "If it is asked what assistance the auxiliaries provide to that [cause], such that it does not act without them, [the answer is: they produce the very effect itself. For if they were to provide assistance to something other [than the effect], they would not truly be auxiliaries. To explain: if they produced that [other thing] alone, then they would be its producers, not its auxiliaries. Indeed, those who produce a single effect together with it are designated as its auxiliaries."

One might object: "Granted that even something unhelpful may be a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*), if its capacity exists already beforehand, why does it not act? If it does not exist, how can that which is later incapable act? And if it becomes capable later on, how is there no difference between the capable and the incapable states? For the superimposition of contradictory properties is the mark of difference. Anticipating this, [the author] replies: "Indeed, its capacity consists in the completeness of the cooperative causes; its incapacity consists in their deficiency. Therefore, due to the deficiency of the cooperative causes, it is said to be incapable beforehand."

Furthermore, [the cause] is capable of producing the whole; moreover, the distinction between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) has been established. Therefore, even when the capacity arises, it does not necessarily follow that the [substratum] arises; and even upon the cessation of incapacity, there is no necessary cessation of that which possesses it, because there is no necessary connection (pratibandha).

All of this should be understood as already refuted in the discussion on *apoha* by the demonstration of the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*), since the property-bearer itself exists in such a state through the manifestation or disappearance of its completeness or incompleteness. Or, let there indeed be a difference between the property and the property-bearer; nor do we dispute that auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are of no consequence [in themselves]. We maintain only that it is not these auxiliaries alone that produce the effect.

Nor does it produce the effect in its entirety; rather, that entity itself [produces it]. Since effort is exerted by those very [causes] for the sake of that [effect], there is no utility in a detailed [explanation of other factors]. And if the nature of that entity—which possesses the property of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā*) in its final moment—is exactly the same as it was in the first moment, then being compelled to act at that very time, it cannot be warded off even by the curse of the gods.

But what is the use of this mere distressed outcry born from the affliction of your vital point? For just as, in order to avoid the consequence of [the entity's] being either capable or incapable, capacity and incapacity are conceived as distinct natures characterized by completeness and deficiency respectively, so too that nature which possesses the property of non-delayed action cannot be said to be distinct from the entity itself, because it would follow that the entity is a non-agent.

Now, just as we maintain that capacity (*śakti*) and incapacity (*aśakti*) are two distinct properties (*dharma*), and yet the entity (*bhāva*) is not affected in any way by the arising or passing away of those two, so too, the property of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā-dharmatva*) and the property of delayed action (*kṣepakriyā-dharmatva*) are themselves merely other properties. These [properties] arise and pass away according to the presence of conditions consisting in the proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). It is said that in this very same way, there is no change whatsoever to the entity itself.

Let it be said: let there simply be no production of an effect at this time, because that which is considered the cause remains in its original state. For it is not the case that the auxiliary factors alone are the producer, nor is it the case that the totality alone is the producer; thus, while the totality exists—

[20,1] Even the state of having the property of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā-dharmatva*) once it has arisen does not produce the entity in question independently; for even if it were a producer, one would have to admit that the entity itself is the producer. However, the entity in question must also be accepted as the agent. And since its form is not distinct from its prior state, if it performs the action now, it should have performed it previously; or, if it does not perform it now, it would not perform it later either—thus the same predicament remains.

If, however, some other distinct entity such as "completeness" (*sākalya*) is the occasional cause, then it is logical that the effect, depending upon that [entity], should also be occasional. Thus, for every further conceptualization of a distinct property (*dharmāntara*), the entity remains indifferent [to the production of the effect]. Now, if the nature of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā-dharmatva*) has arisen, what logic is there in saying that the effect is nevertheless not produced from it? Therefore, the effect must necessarily be produced by it.

Furthermore, since that property of non-delayed action did not previously exist, there would be no occasion for the arising of the effect. If that were the case, then non-delayed action would be inseparable from the production of the effect, and the production of the effect would be inseparable from non-delayed action; thus, mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident. Otherwise, if non-delayed action were not inseparable from the production of the effect, then the production of the effect would not be necessitated by non-delayed action.

Furthermore, if the production of the effect were not invariably concomitant with non-delayed activity, then it would have to occur even prior to that non-delayed activity. However, if they share a single essence, then once completeness (*sākalya*) has arisen, a distinct property (*dharmāntara*), namely non-delayed activity, has come into being; what, then, has been stated by this terminology other than that "the effect has arisen"? And such being the case, there is no avoidance of the original fault. For there is no dispute regarding the birth of the effect itself; rather, the point to be considered is how the occasional nature (*kadācitkatā*) of the effect's emergence—which depends upon its own specific nature (*svarūpa*)—can be explained, given that that nature remains constant at all times.

Therefore, if this designation "that which has the property of non-delayed action" or "that which produces" is applied by virtue of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), how could it ever fail to produce [the effect] if it existed even previously? Or, if the prior entity—which possesses a nature opposed to that which has the property of non-delayed action—were to persist later, how could the effect ever possibly arise? Now, if that very [entity] alone were the producer, this would be logical; however, it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer, and in the absence of its other auxiliary factors, [the effect does not arise] even for one that is powerful.

What is contradictory here in the claim that "the effect is produced"? It has been stated that they are "cooperative" (*sahakārin*) because they perform a single purpose, not because of some [external] assistance.

To this it is replied: If they perform the effect while being conjoined, then let them have this "cooperativity" characterized by performing a single purpose; who would deny it?
