But from where is it obtained that that effect must be performed by them *only* when conjoined? For as long as there is identity between the prior and posterior effects, the consequence that the entity must be subject to one of the two—either always producing or never producing—is unavoidable.

Therefore, it is the totality (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer, not a single entity; thus, the desire of those who maintain the doctrine of permanence has a different object. If it is argued, "It is indeed observed to be so," we reply: for this very reason, the position of permanence is untenable. For every reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) culminates in its opposite. Consequently, if the producer were eternal, the produced effect would either exist at all times or never at all. But this is not the case; since the production of an effect occurs only occasionally despite the presence of the totality of conditions, there is a violation of the [alleged] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Now, if a permanent cause were ever observed anywhere at all times, then the consequence that it would always possess agency upon the admission of its permanence in some case would be logical. However, since such a thing is never present at all times, how can such a consequence be leveled against it?

(9b) This too is vulgar. For instance, regarding the phrase "given that it is eternal," this is its meaning: if the very nature of an entity which exists at a later time and is productive were itself to exist at an earlier time; or if the very nature which exists at an earlier time and is non-productive were itself to exist at a later time—then that [nature] would be perceived precisely as either producing or not producing. And that being the case, by superimposing unity upon two established states, it would follow that what is already established is either production or non-production.
Since the identity of the prior and posterior intrinsic natures is impossible, it is stated that "if [the thing] were eternal"; what contradiction is there in this?

Now, one might ask: "If the identity of the preceding and succeeding states has not been perceived, how can it be superimposed? If this were so, there should likewise be no superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl; for mother-of-pearl in its true nature as silver has never been within the range of perception. However, it is your own established conclusion that the silver being superimposed must have been perceived at some time or other, otherwise superimposition would be impossible. Likewise, even when such a case occurs, I do not perceive any identity between the natures of the preceding and succeeding states.

However, the prior and posterior natures being superimposed upon one another are already established; thus, the performance or non-performance of that superimposition is entirely consistent, just as there is burning when fire is superimposed upon a cluster of *guñjā* seeds. This reveals an extreme lack of subtlety on the part of Śaṅkara. Therefore, this negation by the Buddhists—who assert that "non-momentary things do not exist"—is as irrelevant as the denial of blue and other colors to those born blind.

Therefore, it is established that if there were a permanent self-nature, the restriction of cause and effect could only exist through their conjunction; yet this [position] merely nourishes the daydreams of the unfortunate, for it serves only to delude others by stating something irrelevant and useless. For the proponent of momentariness—who, by superimposing a distinction based on the contradiction between the capacities and incapacities of things, intends to establish such a capacity or incapacity—has not thought to provide a refutation of that very point. Instead of setting that aside, he has himself composed [this work].

[22,1] To construct a rebuttal by means of convention (*saṅketa*) demonstrates the great skill of this preeminent Naiyāyika. For even when one says, "Because of smoke, there must be fire here," if someone were to apply the convention of the word "smoke" to a donkey or similar object and thereby deny the presence of fire, there would be no fault. Indeed, the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) states that whatever is called a "producer" is capable by virtue of its own nature as the effect that arises immediately thereafter. And this is not merely a novel convention.

For even in the world, the conventional usage of "capacity" (śakti) is based solely on the act of producing. Although production occurs only when there is completeness [of conditions], one does not call something "capable" by virtue of that completeness; rather, it is called so because of its production. This is because, even when completeness is delayed, the direct conventional usage of "capacity" is absent; furthermore, since we observe production even when the completeness of specific auxiliary factors has not been definitively determined, the convention "this is capable in this respect" arises. And such an essential nature (svarūpa) is what is called "capacity."

Even though there is a designation of difference by saying "its power," it is nonetheless non-different from the entity, just like its "own nature" (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, since that generative nature exists even prior [to the production of the effect], yet it does not produce [the effect], it follows as a certainty that the mother is also a barren woman. In this context, even if you have employed the term "power" (*śakti*) in some instances, there is nothing whatsoever in the manifestation or concealment of a thing that affects the entity itself.

What follows from that which has been set forth? Since the nature of the producer is indeed non-different from the produced, if there were no arising and passing away for those two, how could the effect be occasional? Or, if it possesses arising and passing away, its difference in intrinsic nature remains as before.

If, however, even that [non-producer] is indeed distinct from the form of the producer, then by its own arising and passing away, there would be a rupture of the entity; thus, the entity would be merely non-productive, which results in the destruction of its very root. Therefore, you must say: for one who produces something at some time, there is indeed a difference [between the two states], because of the superimposition of contradictory properties—the capacities and incapacities—due to the distinction between the times of cause and effect.

For this very reason, as the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* has said: "Because there is no contradiction due to the difference in time; for example, a crystal is inactive prior to the arising of an action, and that same [crystal] is active afterwards. If it is argued that this is not a valid example because it is something yet to be proven (*sādhya*), we say no, because what is established by valid cognition cannot be considered "to be proven.

For if one were to argue that even the distinction [between entities] is unestablished due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), how could such a person be refuted? Therefore, in whatever manner a contradiction between two properties is observed, they must be accepted in exactly that way.

Just as that very same cause is capable with respect to its own effect but incapable with respect to another effect—so that the capacity and incapacity of a single entity toward different objects are not contradictory—likewise, even if there is a difference in capacity due to a difference in time, there is no distinction between the two cases because the non-difference of the possessor of the power (*śaktimat*) is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This too is without substance; for by this [argument], one merely mocks the grand display of a heap of *hiṇṭīra* flowers.

For indeed, it is certainly not possible to assert the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while disregarding perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). And among these, what is called "perception" is nothing other than conceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); and that has already been refuted. As for the inference stated by Śaṅkara in his *Sthirasiddhi*: "An entity does not perish immediately after its arising, because it is an object of cognition (*prameya*), like the exclusion of a thing (*vastuvyāvṛtti*)," this reason is purely positive (*anvayin*) because there exists no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

If it is argued that there is a "doubtful negative concomitance" (*sandigdhavyatireka*) because there is no contradiction between being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), we say: no, for indeed, the status of being an object of cognition cannot be established for anything that is momentary. This is because that which has the property of existing for only a single moment (*kṣaṇasthitidharmin*) has already passed away by the time of its apprehension through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); moreover, if the past were perceptible, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). That [objection] is merely a pious wish. For instance: let there be no apprehension of the past; the apprehension of the present, which is momentary, will occur through a momentary cognition. Therefore, there is indeed no contradiction between being an object of cognition and momentariness.

Now, if it is argued that because the object is the cause [of cognition], an entity whose existence is required prior to the knowledge [of it] would not be graspable at all if it did not persist into the subsequent moment; or, if it were to persist through the subsequent moment, it would necessarily be non-momentary—[we reply: Is this some royal decree that an object of apprehension must not be non-productive [of knowledge]? If you say, "This is simply his established convention (*samaya*)," [we reply: This is an occasion for logic (*nyāya*), not for a mere convention. Therefore, one who is addicted to debate should instruct the opponent by presenting logic, without relying on conventions.
For if convention (*samaya*) were the means of proof, there would be no such thing as "logic" (*nyāya*) for the sake of establishing everything.
But how could logic, which exists precisely to refute convention, take refuge in that very convention?

If it is argued that there can be no apprehension by what has not been produced, and that such a view leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), then how is there apprehension even by what has been produced? For a cognition arises while experiencing its object; and that [apprehension] would be either caused by the production [of the cognition] itself or caused by something else—what is the difference? As for the charge of over-extension, it applies equally [to both views], since the cognition is also produced by the eyes and other sense organs.

If it is argued that this is because it lacks the nature of being an object (*aviṣayasvabhāvatvāt*), [we reply]: surely only that which is actually perceived is designated as an "object"; there is no such thing as an "object" restricted by its genus (*jāti*). Therefore, since the argument "because it is not an object" means "because it is not being perceived," how can this response be relevant? For if you say that the sense organ is not perceived precisely because of its own nature (*svabhāvāt*), we say no, because the perception of it by yogins is accepted. If you argue that this restriction applies only from the perspective of ordinary people (*pṛthag-jana*), then even subtle things and so forth would be perceived by their very nature from the perspective of ordinary people; thus, there is no over-extension of the argument. Alternatively, [the following may be said].

Rather, it is the very same preceding causal complex that produces the object-moment together with its cognition— just as [the complex] produces color along with light— by which there is a simultaneous perception of both.

Alternatively, the cognition produced by that [object], being restricted to its own specific object, grasps only that; or, it is produced as restricted to that by the totality of its causes. Thus, there is no difference. Therefore, how could those two—the object and the cognition—be subject to the over-extension of having a fixed birth in the relationship of grasped and grasper?

Now, for those who maintain that cognition possesses an aspect (*sākāravādin*), it is held that the arising of the awareness of an object’s own nature occurs from the object itself. In that case, if there were an apprehension of what is past, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); and if [the cognition] were to persist through the moment of apprehension, the establishment of stability (*sthirasiddhi*) would follow—this is what is intended. Is this, then, a *prasaṅga-hetu* (a reason leading to an undesirable consequence) which does not occur without depending on the opponent’s admission? Since that is so, because it results in a contrary conclusion (*viparyayaparyavasāna*), either the establishment of stability or the apprehension of the past [would follow]; thus, the cognition of the object’s own nature would not arise from the apprehended object.

This being the case, the maxim "one thing is eaten and another is vomited" is clearly applicable; for while he has begun to establish a stable [view], he subverts the cognition of forms by its very opposite.

Now, if it is merely said that for the Sautrāntika both of these [positions] are inconsistent, that too is not the case. For when one stands on the position that cognition arises with a form (*sākāra*), even if there is persistence into a second moment, the manifestation of the object is untenable because of its entanglement; thus, the cognition of the object is simply the self-cognition of a nature that has a form similar to the opposite [of the object]. And in this way, there is no adherence to the present, since the proximity to that [past object] is not lost even regarding the past.

Nor is there an over-extension [of the argument], because similarity is established by means of another object; nor is the establishment of that [opponent's] view the subject at hand. For you, however, even by resorting to that view, the reason "being an object of cognition" (prameyatva) is not capable of proving stability, because it fails to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).

Consequently, since it is impossible for a stable entity to be established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even a diamond (*vajra*) is included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*); how much more so the wretched crystal? Therefore, how can this [diamond], which undergoes change between its states of being with and without function, serve as an example when there is no contradiction due to a difference in capacity? Furthermore, the attempt to demonstrate that there is no contradiction between capacity and incapacity through a difference in time, just as there is through a difference in object, is also ineffective; for in all cases, it is the counter-correlative property (*pratiyogin*) that constitutes the contradiction.

Furthermore, the non-performance of its own function is not the opposite of the performance of another's function; rather, it is simply the non-performance of its own function. Likewise, the performance of another's function is the opposite of the non-performance of another's function, not the performance of its own function. For it is precisely to exclude the non-performance of its own function that one says "it performs its own function. Moreover, the operation of perception establishes the distinction between two entities: that which performs its own function and that which performs another's function.

However, perception is not an absolute determiner regarding the difference in time, because recognition has already been refuted. Consequently, the performance of its own effect—which remains as the only alternative—is not sufficient to resolve the contradiction. If it is argued that "the performance of its own effect in dependence upon the multiplicity of moments is contradictory," this might be so if there were a functioning means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing non-difference for that which possesses successive parts, just as there is for the distinction between objects; however, this has essentially been stated before. If you ask, "What is the proof for your position that it exists without depending on that [recognition]? [we reply: [This is established by the very fact that] otherwise, the production of effects would be impossible.

It has already been stated that whatever is capable of producing something at a particular time must necessarily produce it at that time, and so forth; furthermore, the dependence upon auxiliary causes has been refuted by the consequence that the effect would either never arise or would arise regardless of the presence or absence of those auxiliaries. Therefore, for the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*), power is intended to be nothing other than the very nature of producing. And if there were a difference in that [nature], how could there not be a loss of the entity itself?

Furthermore, as for what has been prattled by Nyāyabhūṣaṇa: "Even if a power distinct from the possessor of power is admitted, nevertheless, a difference between the potent and the non-potent is not necessarily established. Why? Because even in your own system, the rule that a difference in properties necessitates a difference in the substratum is unproven. And likewise, while demonstrating the separate utility of auxiliary causes even when the effect is distinct, he wrote in the *Hetubindu*: "From the clay-lump and so forth, [the effect arises] from the essential natures of the clay," and so on.

And just as in that case there is no difference in the effect despite the difference in the nature of clay, the self, and so forth, so too there will be non-difference despite the difference in the nature of being capable or incapable, because the uncontradicted determination is the same.

That too has been refuted by this [argument]: for there are indeed phenomena (*dharmas*) that are mutually contradictory and those that are not; however, contradiction or non-contradiction does not follow from the mere fact that something is a phenomenon. For it cannot be asserted that being a Brahmin is not contradicted by being a grammarian, and yet is contradicted by being a Caṇḍāla. Furthermore, in this case, being a Caṇḍāla is not pervaded by being a Brahmin, nor is it contradicted by being a grammarian.

And just as in this case, it is "otherness" (*anyatva*) with respect to its own counter-correlative, Brahman, that constitutes the contradiction, and not [the property of] being a grammarian; likewise, the nature of "producing" is contradictory precisely by virtue of "not producing," and not by way of a difference in the continuum of the entity (*vastu-santāna*). Let "blueness," "quadrangularity," and so forth, encounter contradiction with "whiteness," "circularity," and so forth, but they do not [encounter contradiction] anywhere with [their respective] causes, effects, and the like.

Therefore, if—due to the impossibility of even a scent of contradiction—the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and the clay-nature must exist as non-different from the same substratum (*dharmin*), then what conscious person could conceive that this would also apply to two things that are absolutely opposed, such as that which produces a certain effect and its opposite? How, moreover, is it to be understood whether something is contradictory or not?

When there is the affirmation of one thing through the exclusion of another, or the exclusion of one thing through the affirmation of another, those two are contradictory. Nor is there even the possibility of suspecting that the affirmation "made of clay" excludes "having a large belly. By the mention of its being the producer of that [effect], its not being the producer of that is indeed excluded; and by its not being the producer of that, its being the producer of that is excluded. For even the sentence of the negative compound *na-taj-janakam* ("not the producer of that")—meaning "that which does not produce that"—is forgotten [if this distinction is not understood].

Therefore, the contradiction between two phenomena must be accepted exactly as it is observed; it is appropriate only with this specific qualification in mind, and not with reference to a single point in time, because [contradiction] does not apply to two things that possess equal means of valid cognition.

For it is reasonable to accept that by means of a difference in time, even a single entity can be endowed with activity and inactivity, or blueness and non-blueness, and so forth; or, for one who has applied a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) toward its own nature, there may be no contradiction regarding a difference in time when a dispute arises in some respect. This is logical. However, it is clear that neither of these two cases exists here. Therefore, the qualification "having an uncontradicted object" for the determination of oneness (*ekatvādhyavasāya*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, the mere determination of oneness is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it depends entirely upon a subverting proof (*bādhaka*).

Otherwise, one would not require a subverting proof even in the case of [illusory] hair and the like; yet such a subverting proof has been stated. Furthermore, if this [subject] were to undergo a distortion as if dreaming, and if no difference in nature is admitted for anything that is of a non-different essence, then the statement regarding the distinct utility of the cause and the effect would be the prattle of a child or a madman. Therefore, if it is intended merely to establish a difference between property and property-bearer by disregarding their identity (*tādātmya*), then that is not useful for the present context.

For instance, let properties be either distinct from the substratum or not. At any rate, there exist certain mutually contradictory properties which, according to the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), cannot even subsist without splitting their own substratum; this is what he intends to say. In that case, it is only logical for him to state either that such properties do not exist at all, or that even if they do exist, they establish difference only in dependence on conditions (*upādhi*) such as time. What is the point of saying that "because auxiliary causes function separately, these [properties] are indeed separate from the substratum"? What does this accomplish?

If, however, his position were that only those possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are differentiators, while those lacking it are not, then this would be logical. But since even forces (*bala*) and the like are observed to be differentiators of what lacks force, and these are indeed distinct because they consist of the nature of action (*kriyā*) and so forth; therefore, whether according to the Buddhist view or your own view, let distinctions be merely constructed by conceptualization—why then is there not an absolute distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) in reality? For that is a separate topic.

However, it is established that the probandum is proven by those properties which, being difficult to avoid, exist in a state of contradiction while differentiating the possessor of those properties (*dharmin*). Now, if you merely point out the inconsistency of the opponent’s position—that there is non-difference from the effect regarding intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), yet there is a distinct range of utility for the collection of auxiliary causes—is this of any consequence, since it does not undermine the subject at hand? Furthermore, because properties possess the capacity to differentiate even among things that are themselves differentiated, the appearance of inconsistency arises when they stand in mutual relation across countless instances within different contexts.
It occurs in various contexts; however, what that reality (*tattva*) is like will become clear upon the examination of each respective context.

[27,1] In this regard, if you intend that one must remain by elaborating on whatever happens to be at hand even if it is irrelevant to the subject under discussion, then this is possible for anyone. Moreover, the debate concerning the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is not concluded by this much alone. Therefore, why this persistence in offering a disparaging remark against one who is no more than a mere infant in the womb? Furthermore, if that were the case, his concluding statement—that "the substratum does not differ merely because of a difference in properties"—would also be untenable.

It is said that the Buddhist does not assert a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*) merely on the basis of a difference in properties (*dharma*), but rather on the basis of contradiction. Otherwise, he would have to declare a difference in the substratum even for such things as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*). By this very point, the words "due to the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties" (*viruddhadharmādhyāsāt*) have been brought forth. If one does not perceive any distinction between contradiction and mere difference, then it is appropriate that he has said this; what else remains to be said?

Furthermore, he himself has said this: "How could that which has the nature of performing a subsequent effect perform that effect at the outset? If it were to perform it, then it would not have the nature of performing a subsequent effect. For that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth. Nor does the possessor of those natures differ because of the difference between the natures of producing the first and subsequent effects, since it has been stated that a difference in nature is subject to deviation."

That too is devoid of substance. For if by the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) one intends the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then when there is a difference in that [nature], there is indeed a difference among things; where, then, is there any talk of deviation? Therefore, the phrase "difference in intrinsic nature" is properly understood as the multiplicity of imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*). And the opponent does not establish a difference between the substrata (*dharmin*) by that alone, but rather through contradiction (*virodha*). Nor is there any deviation regarding the difference between substrata even when there is such contradiction. For contradiction never deviates from difference; it has already been stated that difference, however, may deviate from contradiction.

If it is asked: "But if those phenomena (*dharmas*) are merely imagined (*kalpita*), where is there contradiction, or where is there difference?"—here, the referent of the word "imagined" (*kalpita*) is twofold. First, when a thing exists as excluded from this or that [other thing], mere difference appears through conceptual construction; that too is imagined, like the blueness of a lotus. Second, that which resides in mere conceptual construction is imagined, like the horns of a donkey or the three qualities (*triguṇa*) of a woman's hair. In that regard, if the latter type of imagined object were intended, it would not be logical to say "because of the cessation of difference."

In the case of a past [moment], however, since it is the very nature of the entity (*vastu-svabhāva*) that is determined (*adhyavasāna*) with respect to the imagined object, the distinction or contradiction being established exists only by taking recourse to correspondence; thus, there is no fault.
And as for this [objection]: "How could that which is its nature to perform a certain effect in a subsequent moment perform it in the first moment?"

To say that otherwise the production of a subsequent effect would not be its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is also stated without due consideration. For if an entity possesses a stable intrinsic nature, why is it that this effect occurs only at a later time and not at an earlier time? And since that [earlier occurrence] is absent, how can the cause be said to have the intrinsic nature of producing a subsequent effect? Indeed, words are beautiful when they conform to the facts; the state of affairs does not conform to the words, as is the case with kings.
If you ask, "What can we do? Let its birth simply be subsequent," then so be it.

If, however, it were stable, then that [activity] being impossible would indicate its instability. If you argue that even if it were stable, this very nature belongs to it—namely, that it acts only in the subsequent moment—then all hope for valid cognition is destroyed, because one escapes the contradiction by resorting to "nature" even when it is subverted by valid cognition.

For even when it is stated, "There is fire here because of smoke," or "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire," it is possible to assert: "This is simply its nature that now there is smoke here even though it is without fire. Therefore, one relies upon a nature that is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the destruction of the means of valid cognition does not occur through reliance on a nature. And the determination by means of valid cognition has indeed been provided. Furthermore, to say that "that which has the nature of producing blue does not produce yellow and so forth" is an unexamined statement.

For the negation of its being a cause refers to it as a material cause (*upādāna*), but not even as a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); for its utility there even as a cooperative cause cannot be refuted in some way or another. Nor is there a negation of one letter-sound being the material cause of another letter-sound. For it is observed that turmeric, which is yellow, becomes the material cause of red when assisted by a powder; thus, the illustrative example is inconsistent. And if, just as blue does not produce yellow, so too the preceding [letter] does not produce the subsequent one?

Therefore, enough with this persistence in such idle chatter. This is established: because of the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties, there is indeed a difference between that which has the nature of being a producer and that which does not, just as there is a difference in space, so too in time.

By this, that which the author of the *Nyāyamañjarī* also said is refuted: "Now, those whose proximity is required as the cause for the production of an effect are indeed 'those whose proximity is required' (*apekṣitasannidhi*); what do these auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) do for it? Nothing at all."

Those whose presence and absence follow solely the presence and absence of the effect, and who assemble with their proximity required by that very effect, perform that intended effect together with the cause; thus they are called "cooperators" (*sahakārin*). However, they do not deserve to be called cooperators merely by being the agents of that [cause] with which they act.

(12b) Therefore, for that which is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), there is a twofold capacity (*sāmarthya*) in the production of its own effect: one is its innate capacity (*nija-sāmarthya*), and the second is an adventitious auxiliary cause (*āgantuka-sahakāry-antara*). This is because, in the absence of these two, that effect would not arise; for it is accepted that the production of the effect results precisely from this twofold capacity. Thus, those others who, having grasped only the single non-momentary [entity], imagine that the production of the effect occurs from that alone, are ignorant of the very nature of causal capacities.

Because even for that which is non-momentary, when those various successive causal activities are to be performed, we admit that its capacity resides solely in successive auxiliary factors. And thus, since the multiplicity of successive effects is established through the multiplicity of successive auxiliaries, it is impossible to demonstrate that entities undergo change at every moment.

That too has been refuted. Even if the capacity imagined through another cause is unknown to us, nevertheless, that essential nature which has entered the sphere of conventional usage—namely, "that which produces"—must necessarily be admitted; for in our system, the capacity of an entity is reckoned as what is called its *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic). Why then have you raised this objection by means of the dichotomy: "Does it exist before [the effect], or only after?"?

In this regard, what has been stated by him [the opponent] is explained as follows: as for the refinement that "they [the auxiliary causes] have their presence required solely by the effect," that too is useless. For if the effect itself were independent in its own production, then this would be logical; however, if this were the case, the postulation of the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the auxiliaries would be fruitless. Thus, why would the effect sometimes occur and sometimes not occur due to the independence of the cause alone, without depending on the capacity of the cause?

Through the failure to establish the efficacy of the cause, or by taking "efficacy" to be a mere conventional designation, it follows that nothing whatsoever is efficacious anywhere. If you ask, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—then the intellect would be purified [of error] by the view that real causes are entirely inefficacious, while the non-existent effect is independent. But consider this: if the effect already exists in its own form at the time of production, for what purpose does it depend on another thing?

Therefore, by the statement "the effect depends upon the totality," the meaning is simply that the totality itself is capable of producing the effect; nor is that [totality] distinct from the constituent members. Consequently, it is the members themselves that are the producers. Or, even if there were a distinction, since completeness would be a cooperative factor just like any other external object, there would be no difference [in the logical outcome].

Therefore, since as many auxiliary factors as there are are each individually capable, how could there be a failure of activity on the part of those that already exist? For it is your established doctrine (*samaya*) that completeness alone is what subsequently makes production possible; yet even that [completeness] must have its origin from those very auxiliaries. If they were non-existent previously, how could there ever be a state of being devoid of existence—as long as even one of them is absent? If you argue: "This is merely the fault of the effect, in that it is sometimes not produced while these [causes] are incapable," [we reply]:
if the effect does not arise even when the cause remains identical in all its states, then the cause is not a cause at all.

"In that case, the effect would be independent; but if that were so, it would not be an effect. Do you not see this? It might be argued: "A thing is called an effect not because it necessarily exists when [the cause] exists, but rather because it certainly does not exist when that [cause] is absent; thus, it is due to the predominance of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)."
If it does not exist even when that [cause] exists, how can it have existence when that is absent?
Since its non-existence is contingent upon the non-existence of that [cause], how can it be said that "it is that [non-existence]"? (PVA II 411)

For if the cause were indeed producing the effect itself, then one could also say that its non-existence is necessitated by the effect's non-existence. But when the effect has not come into being despite the cause being ready to produce it—due to the cause’s very independence—how can there be the cognition that "its non-existence is necessitated by the effect's non-existence"? Therefore, if there is a causal relationship, then it must necessarily be the case that just as the effect invariably does not occur in the absence of the cause, so too it would invariably occur in the presence of the cause.

And it does not tolerate [the claim] that the self is its cause. Therefore, this connection of the arising and passing away characterized by capacity and incapacity among causes—even through a succession of efforts—cannot be concealed from the four types of intellects, just as the offspring of an adulterer cannot be hidden.

[30,9] Furthermore, Maṅkara has said: "Nor is the distinction of a cause established merely from the distinction of effects due to a difference in auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). Just as a lamp, despite its unity, produces various flames—the modifications of the consciousness-wick—due to a difference in auxiliaries, yet it does not itself become distinct, because its non-distinction is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is a novel attempt at deception on his part.

If one raises the objection by considering the alternative—whether this nature, which consists of unimpeded activity and is denoted by the term "capacity" (*śakti*), existed previously as well, or only now—the proponent replies: "What I call 'capacity' is simply the totality of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-sākalya*). He then resolves the issue by asserting that there is a distinction [between the two states] due to the imposition of contradictory properties characterized as capacity and incapacity, on the grounds that a difference in the cause follows from a difference in the effect. But who, indeed, has set out to state that a difference in the cause follows from a difference in the effect, such that this would have to be said?

The difference in effects resulting from a difference in auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) does not constitute a difference in the cause; rather, whatever has the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) to produce something at a certain time, it necessarily produces that very thing. For instance, it is not the case that a lamp alone is capable of producing effects such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) all at once and thus generates them simultaneously. Or else, why does it not produce its homogeneous and heterogeneous effects—which occur sequentially—at that very same moment? Therefore, it is logical that for those [sequential effects], the lamp is indeed a different agent. This same principle applies elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the cognition of the persistence of a crystal and the like is non-erroneous because no cause for its production or destruction is perceived in each instance—just as with manifest entities such as lamps—that too is like shooting an arrow in the dark; for even in the case of a lamp, no cause for the production of one [lamp] after another is perceived. Indeed, the causes of a lamp are the wick, the oil, and so forth, and since these change from moment to moment or from instant to instant, how could there be any determination [of identity]?

Otherwise, even in the case of a crystal, why would one not accept that each preceding moment is a distinct cause for each succeeding moment, following the pattern of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? Furthermore, although there is a perception of difference due to temporal change in the case of a lamp, this is not so for the oil and the wick; how then can it be said that the cause of the production of individual instances of lamps and the like is perceived, while such is not the case for the crystal? As for the cause of destruction, we shall consider it later.

Nor is it tenable to say that the destruction of its cause follows from the fragility of the lamp itself, for since the cause is not distinct, it would follow that the effect—the lamp—is likewise non-distinct [from that destruction].

[31,7] Now, if it is argued that the exhaustion of the wick and the oil is perceived—since even the lamp is deprived of its pervasion of the space being consumed, and that very [deprivation] constitutes exhaustion—[we reply: the oil was abundant before, but now it remains little; the wick is likewise. The lamp too, by relinquishing successive portions of oil and wick, pervades successive other portions of them. But how can cessation be determined in every respect, given that recognition remains in that same state?

If it is argued that at the time of the disintegration of the wick and so forth, an action arises in a part; from that, a disjunction arises; from that, the destruction of the conjunction; from that, the destruction of the substance composed of those parts; then again an action [arises], and from conjunction, the arising of another substance—thus, the persistence of a single substance is not established.

Even if this [subject] were to attend to the manifold world while descending into the realm of experience, how could even a Buddhist—who likewise proclaims his own system—be prevented from doing so? From previous homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), when another auxiliary object is encountered—such as wind, sunlight, or darkness—there arises from them another [effect] of equal magnitude, whether less or more than that, according to the convention of the power of the auxiliaries; thus it is not the case for things such as the hundred-pointed crystal.

The establishment of oneness is accomplished through its own internal consistency. However, when this [oneness] is presented merely as a proof, it is not established by its own process, nor is it sublated by your process.

[31,18] If it is argued that wind and other factors either augment or diminish [the qualities] in crystal and so forth—by virtue of which they are postulated as cooperative causes—since there would otherwise be an over-extension if causality were based merely on prior existence; [we reply: No gross augmentation or diminution whatsoever is produced in it by them. For this very reason, there is an arising of something absolutely similar. However, because a subtle change is impossible to perceive, it is unfit to be designated as "this" or "that," and likewise, it is equally unfit to be denied.

Thus, when there is a confusion of many entities, if at some time a certain one is utilized, no single entity would be a cooperative cause for the production of the subject at hand; therefore, the meaning of the argument is that one must not understand the production of a single thing to be possible simply because of the total absence of other cooperative causes. However, if you are able to maintain your own system once the stability [of the entity] is established, then you may do so. For the present, this is an investigation into the Buddhist proofs.

And in this context under discussion, by whom was it whispered into your ear that because there are multiple effects, there must be multiple [causes], such that your employment of the lamp as an analogy would be appropriate? This is what is being said: "The disease is one thing, and the medicine is another."

As for what was also said—that the very same proof which establishes the non-difference of a lamp when there is a difference in its effects due to a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), serves as the proof for the non-sequential [lamp] as well when there is a difference in its effects due to a difference in sequential auxiliary causes—that too is utterly incoherent. For it is precisely sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*) in the form of non-duality that expects the disappearance of difference in the case of the lamp; for a lamp, being characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), cannot occupy a single location.

Furthermore, the perception of difference in an object located in a different place—even if it is extremely similar—is unavoidable, as in the case of a ball of illusory magic (*māyāgola*). Therefore, sensory cognition of a single form establishes the lamp’s unity alone. For it is observed that even when an object is different due to a difference in time, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) arises toward things that are extremely similar; and there is no means of proving unity other than recognition.

Therefore, how can it not follow that this very thing is the means of proof? Nor does recognition, due to similarity despite a difference in time, constitute a factor of doubt, because deviation is observed and there is no absence of its defining characteristics. Even in a perception that manifests non-difference at once, there is no lack of trust; for such is seen in some cases. Indeed, even when two objects are perceived in succession by sensory cognition, they do not obstruct one another as long as they are apprehended as having become one. So how can there be distrust in all cases?

Therefore, the objection raised by means of the example of the lamp is useless. Even in the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, having taken this very form as the example, [the author] spoke thus while illuminating another underlying intention:

Furthermore, by whatever intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) form (*rūpa*) produces another form, it does not produce taste (*rasa*) and so forth by that same nature, because it would follow that taste and the rest would also possess the intrinsic nature of form. Consequently, every effect of form would be perceived by the eye; and this is not accepted. Therefore, just as form produces another form by its nature of producing another form, it produces consciousness (*vijñāna*) by its nature of producing consciousness, and not form and the like.

And by its nature of producing taste, it produces taste alone; likewise, by its two natures of producing smell and touch, it produces those two alone. Similarly, although non-momentary, that which has the nature of producing the first effect performs only that [first effect] by means of its nature of producing the first effect; it produces only the subsequent [effect] by means of its nature of producing the subsequent effect, but not the first or the successive ones. In this way, even regarding subsequent effects occurring over an infinite duration of time, specific natures are to be understood.

It is also incorrect to say that only the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are causes and not the thing possessing those natures (*svabhāvī*), for this would entail the consequence that form (*rūpa*) is not a cause, since it is only the intrinsic natures that function as causes. Now, if you do not admit a difference in the intrinsic natures of form, but rather maintain that there is only a single such intrinsic nature by which it produces effects that are distinct in form and distinct in location—then how can you explain that there is a difference in its intrinsic natures in accordance with the production of those effects of distinct intrinsic natures?

But surely, in this way, another [opponent] might also not deserve censure, for by postulating the nature of an entity as being non-momentary and indeed of a single, undifferentiated nature, they would do so out of necessity to account for the production of multiple effects that possess distinct natures occurring in succession.

[33,3] This too is merely an attempt to confuse those whose minds have been stained by envy. For instance, if you intend to say only this much—that even though its nature is non-different, a single entity performs multiple functions such as destroying darkness like a lamp because of an imagined distinction in its nature—then alas, who is there to forbid it? There is indeed the possibility that one might produce many things. Likewise, if the past and future moments, being of a single nature, were to produce many effects, there would be no dispute.

It is not logical to claim that there is merely a delay in the production of an effect in some cases, while in others there is non-delayed action; for if it were possible for a single entity to produce many effects simultaneously like a lamp, then the example of the lamp would be pointless. Now, if you intend to say that multiple things to be produced by an agent constitute a single effect of a single self-nature, then [the example] is valid. Indeed, even now, the lamp cannot be used as an illustration. Even when such an illustration is being made, this must be said:

Nor does this follow logically: that whatever is manifold must be produced by many [causes], like the effect of a lamp; for it cannot be established that a manifold effect occurring at different times is the effect of a single cause alone, nor can it be maintained that if a single agent were absent, the birth of the manifold would simply not occur. This is because we observe that a manifold result, such as burning or immersion, is produced by many factors, such as fire and water respectively. If it is argued that what is intended is a single entity undivided by time, [we reply: ...

[33,13] You do not observe that which is manifold being produced by a single self that is separated by many intervals of time. However, you might say: "Whether one or many, whether at different times or at the same time, it arises from that which is eternal. But that is merely the presentation of a thesis; it neither establishes any desired point for yourself nor does it refute a proof employed by another—so what is the use of this? Even so, there is nothing gained by the example of the form of a lamp.

Moreover, even if the proponent of existence (*astitvavādī*) were to differentiate existence through the differentiation of its effects, you should nevertheless remain composed after raising the objection of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) on these grounds: "How can form itself, which is undifferentiated, produce both color and taste, which are differentiated? Furthermore, what is the use of proving the unity of form once again? For it is already established.

Furthermore, even regarding Śaṅkara, he appears not to have reflected at all when he asserts that "it cannot be the case that by the very same nature which is the cause of the modification of the wick, there is also the perception of the flame," for this would entail that those two also possess that same nature; this is because there is no contradiction in a single thing performing multiple functions.

Now, just as the Buddhist has asserted: "If the very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity persists even at another moment, then it would follow that it must produce [its effect] just as it does now; yet it does not produce it. Therefore, there is a difference in the intrinsic nature of the entity. For instance, if a lamp were to produce the transformation of the wick by means of the very same form that produces cognition, then it would follow that the lamp itself is that [cognition]. But it is not that [cognition]. Therefore, must not the lamp also possess a different intrinsic nature?

Just as there is no difference in the cause even when effects lack identity (*tādātmya*), so too it is intended that there is no difference in the cause even when effects exist at different times. Even then, the Buddhist, relying on the force of his own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), has superimposed a difference in the nature of the entity between its causal and non-causal states. If you find this intolerable, then it is only appropriate to state the refutation, such as "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) and so forth; with just that much, he will be defeated—what is the use of this elaborate argument?

Now, suppose that very proof is indeed faulty; nevertheless, whatever is established by it remains established for the time being. Let there be a difference in the nature of the lamp, or let there not be; even so, what is the use of adducing it?

Furthermore, as for the argument called "the absence of identity among effects" which is intended to prove a difference in the nature of the lamp—if that [argument] also possesses an established necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum, then if it could establish difference for anyone even simultaneously, what would be the use of this Buddhist argument? One should abandon the effort to establish one's own probandum through it, like a second bridegroom from Karṇāṭa who has come and gone at Prayāga and the Vaṭa tree.

Otherwise, once difference has been established by this [reason], why would one even proceed to establish the difference of lamps? Or rather, no proof whatsoever would proceed to establish its probandum, having observed that proofs such as smoke establish their own respective probanda.

[34,14] Now, if this proof for the difference in the nature of the lamp is either sublated by perception (*adhyakṣa*) or devoid of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum (*svasādhya*), then let that very proof perish. In that case, there is no damage to the Buddhist argument. Nevertheless, what is the point of its presentation? If, in rivalry with the Buddhist, this other comparison has been brought forward merely to render that investigation worthless, then this position—that there is a difference in the nature of the lamp—is untenable.
If it is argued that, such being the case, there is only a single specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*) which is the producer of those [effects], then...

This [position], being devoid of both scripture and reasoning, does not please those whose character is rooted in logic, even if it is accepted out of mere rivalry. This is because, in the absence of a specific material cause for their own nature, their arising everywhere has never been observed; and likewise, if there were no distinction in the nature of the cause, the absence of a distinction in the effect would entail its being accidental (*ākasmikatva*).

And thus, by stating that "the entire universe would otherwise be of a single nature," how could he possibly reinforce the very distinction between intrinsic natures through his own words? Nor is this logical. For instance, as for what was said: if the lamp were to be the cause of the modification of the wick by the same intrinsic nature by which it is the cause of the flame and so forth, then it would follow that the flame and so forth are also modifications of the wick; but such is not the case.

Therefore, the lamp proceeds by means of a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the modification of the wick, and by a distinct one in the flame and so forth; this is the meaning of the counter-argument. And in that case, there is indeed a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), because the lamp and such appear there as being partless. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of its appearing as surrounded by an infinite number of intrinsic natures, like a *kadamba* flower-bud. Nor can it be maintained that these [parts] are unperceived, because if they possessed the nature of the lamp, their non-perception would be a contradiction.

And if you maintain that invisibility is contradictory even to the nature of a lamp, then why do you not also conceive that it can be the cause of the wick’s transformation and the cause of the flame and so forth, since you are so preoccupied with postulating a mass of intrinsic natures? Therefore, that which is not perceived cannot have the nature of a lamp. And if it were perceptible, there would be no way to avoid the refutation by direct perception. To claim that some other entity—whether visible or invisible—distinct from the lamp itself is the nature of the lamp is the language of the Nāga world.

For the terms *svabhāva*, *svarūpa*, and *svalakṣaṇa* are well-established as denoting that which is non-different in nature. However, regarding a property (*dharma*) presented by conceptual construction—which, although appearing as if distinct, is apprehended precisely through its identification with the thing itself—the term *svabhāva* is employed; for example, "eternality is the *svabhāva* of sound. Therefore, even if the term *svabhāva* is used in some cases for something distinct—just as the word "power" (*śakti*) is used for an auxiliary cause—it nonetheless means "it acts by means of another *svabhāva*," that is to say, it acts by means of an auxiliary cause which is a different entity.

Nor is the prevention of causal efficiency intended for that which possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the word "intrinsic nature" refers to an external object. It follows from this that [the cause] produces diverse effects by means of that very same undifferentiated intrinsic nature; the only distinction is that it is surrounded by a multitude of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). And who would not accept this? Furthermore, the auxiliary factors are not to be imagined according to one's own fancy, but rather they are exactly as many as there are operations of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, since that causal operation does not exist apart from the fire, the oil, the wick, and so forth, what is the point of this additional formulation? On the contrary, by postulating entities denoted by the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and attempting to include them within the six categories (*ṣaḍ-padārtha*), why do you labor in vain?

And when it has been thus established at the end of the argument that the single intrinsic nature denoted by its own term is the cause of multiple effects, then the pervasion—that "whatever is produced by a single form must be one"—is not proven.

That being the case, just as in the original consequence, there is likewise no avoidance of the inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) regarding the reverse [argument] either. Furthermore, their having a restricted nature as their material cause does not proceed from the lamp alone possessing a plurality of real natures; rather, it is through the method of abstraction (*apoddhāra*) within that causal complex (*sāmagrī*), by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that one [assigns] oil to one [factor], the wick to another, and the lamp to yet another. How, then, could the production of all these [factors] be perceived everywhere?

As for the claim that there is a difference [in cognition] due to a difference in causes, in that case, one accepts that the difference in the effect is caused by the heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) of the cause characterized as the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), since this is precisely how it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, it has been explained in the very treatise (*śāstra*) itself that the multiplicity of causes contained within the causal totality does not constitute a manifold nature (*aneka-svabhāvatā*) for a single [effect]. Therefore, enough with this insistence on conceptual constructions based merely on their own imagination, independent of valid cognition. Furthermore, it has already been stated that even if these various distinctions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) were real, they would not result in any actual establishment of an object; thus, this notion is entirely fruitless.

[36,3] In that case, let the intention of these two also be determined in accordance with how Trilocana conducts himself. And so it is stated in the *Nyāyamañjarī*: "Even existence (*sattva*), though uncommon, can be brought forward by the Mādhyamika method. For instance, even in the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇavāda*), by whatever nature a preceding form-moment produces the immediately succeeding moment, does it produce the taste-moment by that very same nature or by a different nature? If it were by that very same [nature], it would follow that taste also possesses the nature of form."

For we do not observe a diversity of effects arising from a cause that possesses a single nature, as that would entail the consequence of the entire universe being without a cause. Suppose, then, that it acts by means of a different nature. If this were so, it would follow that a single entity possesses two contradictory natures. Indeed, the nature that produces form is non-deviant from the nature that produces taste; therefore, if there were a different nature therein, there would be both existence and non-existence of that very same thing in that very place. Existence and non-existence are directly contradictory and would thus divide the prior characteristic of form. Yet, such a divided [entity] is not observed.

[36,12] It might be argued as follows: when the preceding moment of form produces taste, it is simply another nature within that very same preceding moment of taste; and there is no contradictory other nature. If this were so, then even for a non-momentary entity, when producing successive manifestations of effects, there would likewise be successive other auxiliary causes consisting of other natures. Thus, everything is the same, except for your dogmatic attachment.

Therefore, for one who accepts [the reason] as being uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), existence (*sattva*)—which would have to exclude itself from momentary things due to the resulting difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)—does not exclude non-momentary things. This is because the manner in which the difference in intrinsic nature is refuted applies equally even to the case of non-momentariness. Consequently, since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established.

[36,18] In this regard, without considering the finality of the Yogācāra system, this person—who possesses pride in his knowledge of the Buddhist tenets—speaks according to the logic of the Madhyamaka, claiming that "both [schools] agree on the denial of cause and effect in reality. However, having refuted such a lower-level proof, we have already demonstrated in the *Sākārasiddhi* that our investigation into momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is based on the established existence of the causal relationship. And that establishment [of causality] occurs only when the reality of the subject-object relationship (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) is apprehended.

And in that case, let whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something be its effect and its cause, as in the case of the seed and the sprout. Just as a single observed effect is seen to follow the positive and negative concomitance of a certain [cause], so too, if multiple effects are perceived to follow the positive and negative concomitance of a single [cause], then why should there not be a single effect even from multiple [causes]? For if one denies the experience of another, then even a single thing would not be the effect of a single [cause].

In the case of one who is not subject to refutation, even a manifold effect is prevented from belonging to a single [cause]. Therefore, there is nothing gained by introducing the views of those who deny the perception of others. However, when the existence of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject is established, the principle that a manifold [cause] can produce a single effect is the same as for a single [cause]. Thus, it follows that what is produced by a single essence must indeed have a single form.

As for what was said—that we do not observe a diversity of effects arising from a cause that possesses a single nature—that is an extreme rashness. Or rather, does one not see a single lamp producing various transformations and removing darkness? Or does one not see the sun bringing about the destruction of darkness and the blooming of lotuses? Or, being perpetually immersed in darkness, do you perhaps fail to see the thousand-rayed sun performing its thousands of functions?

The meaning is that because the cause has a single nature, there can be no difference in the effects; thus, from a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no heterogeneity among the effects. For this very reason, it is not the case that the entire universe is without cause. Therefore, the production of multiple effects from a single [cause] is not contradictory. However, by way of its effects, one may conventionally designate two natures—such as "form is the cause of form" and "form is the cause of taste"—through a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Precisely for this reason, there is no talk of contradiction; for when a conjunction is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is not even a trace of contradiction, just as in the case of wind and sunlight in a single location of space.

As for what was said—that the nature of producing form is indeed non-deviant from the nature of producing taste—even by that much, only a mere difference is established, not a contradiction, as in the case of "produced" and "impermanent. For just as yellow, which is non-deviant from the absence of blue, cannot be blue, yet there is no contradiction based on that alone; for it is impossible to state that whatever differs from something is, without qualification, contradictory to it.

As for contradiction (*virodha*), although it is the rule that two impossibilities cannot coexist in a single substratum (*dharmī*), this occurs sometimes because the presence of one thing excludes the other, as in the case of fire and snow; and sometimes because, by their very nature, one property cannot exist where another resides in the same locus, as in the case of existence and non-existence, or blue and non-blue. In that regard, if the presence of one substance—such as blue or yellow—were to entail the exclusion of the other, then there would indeed be a contradiction known as "incompatibility through non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*).

But it is not by the mere fact of non-deviation from its absence [that contradiction is established]; rather, there is merely a difference [between the two] on that basis alone. Likewise, even in the case of blueness and yellowness, there is merely a difference due to their non-deviation from their respective absences, but there is no contradiction. Contradiction, however, exists because when a substratum (dharmin) has accepted blueness, yellowness—which is itself the exclusion of non-blueness—is absent therein. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of contradiction even for such properties as "producedness" and "impermanence" merely on the grounds of their non-deviation from their absences.

[37,25] Now, how is there here the non-deviation from its absence? For there is no logical justification for the claim that "whatever is produced must necessarily be impermanent. If this were so, what would be the justification for the claim that "whatever is a producer of color must not be a producer of taste"? If you say, "Because it is a producer of color," [we reply: No, because such a justification is exhausted by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) when qualifying [the term], since the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is unestablished. To explain: does "producer of color" mean that it is *only* a producer of color, or that it is the producer *of color alone*? [In either case, the reason is insufficient.]

In that regard, according to the first position, there is merely the exclusion of the non-production of form, and not the exclusion or affirmation of the production of something else; for since there is a contradiction with that very [non-production] in dependence upon another means of proof, the exclusion itself remains unestablished. But in the second position, the exclusion of the production of something else is established beyond doubt; it is simply that no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required therein.

For if, just as one [cause] possesses an invariable concomitance (*tan-nāntarīyakatva*) with that [effect], the second [cause] were likewise to possess it, there would be no fault, as in the case of a lamp. However, the mere fact that something is a producer of color (*rūpa*) does not entail the exclusion of its being a producer of taste (*rasa*), because the status of being a producer of color is already fulfilled by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Thus, there is no valid argument here either.

In the conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanā-buddhi*), the capacity to produce color appears as if it were a distinct entity; likewise, the capacity to produce taste—which is invariably concomitant with the absence of that [color]—is determined to be entirely separate. This is because a distinct operation of the means of knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*) is required, and by that alone one determines the contradiction. Such a cognition is not determined by anyone even in the case of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*); nor is there any utility in asserting a contradiction therein.

For contradiction (*virodha*) is established precisely for the sake of mutual exclusion within a single substratum (*dharmī*). Therefore, if there were contact with a single substratum even in the case of contradiction, what would be the point of considering contradiction at all? However, in the case of blue and non-blue and so forth, contradiction consisting of mutual exclusion is indeed applied.

[Objection: But surely, since there is no difference in their being invariably concomitant with mutual absence, why is it that for some properties there is a contradiction consisting of non-coexistence within a single substratum, while for others there is merely a distinction and not contradiction?

It has been stated here: when the affirmation of one thing occurs through the exclusion of another, or the exclusion of one thing occurs through the affirmation of another, necessarily, those two are contradictory by virtue of being contraries (*pratiyogin*). Where this condition does not apply, they are non-contradictory; therefore, enough with further exertion. Thus, it is established that although the production of color and the production of taste do not deviate from each other’s absence, there is merely a difference between them—like "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*)—which draws upon different means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but there is no contradiction.

As for what was said—namely, "if there were another intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvāntara*) and so forth—is that reasoning afraid of producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*)? If you say, "let that same *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) apply there as well," we reply: surely a *prasaṅga* proceeds by means of the opponent's own admission. And I have not admitted this—that contradiction, consisting merely in the non-deviation from mutual exclusion, is the cause for the impossibility of coexistence in a single locus. Is this your own admission, or is it the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? In either case, it is not my fault.

Furthermore, the contradiction between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), and so forth, is much more clearly established; this is not the case [with identity]. Therefore, because the function of mutual non-deviation lies in the negation of identity, "being produced" itself is not "impermanence. If there were no negation, then upon the existence of one—namely, being produced—there would have to be both its existence and its non-existence. It is said that this would be like accepting both the existence and the non-existence of a thing, such as blue, when its non-blue exclusion is not distinguished. For "blue" is indeed its existence.

Furthermore, "non-blue" is an absence; the presence of "non-blue," which is pervaded by that absence, is not capable of remaining without drawing along its pervader—that absence—since the contradiction between existence and non-existence has already been established. Thus, there can be no coexistence within a single substratum (*ekadharmī*). Therefore, whatever is blue is not non-blue, such as yellow or other objects; likewise, regarding a property (*dharma*), whatever is "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is not "unproducedness," such as impermanence and so forth; and whatever is the production of color is not the production of non-color, such as the production of taste and so forth.

Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that once the means of knowledge called verbal testimony has operated in one case regarding the production of the nature of being produced and so forth, it would not require any other means of knowledge in another case regarding the production of impermanence, essence, and so forth.

Therefore, the fault would be that existence and non-existence would occur in one and the same place if there were identity (*tādātmya*); it is not so if they have a common substratum (*tad-ādhāratva*). For if those two properties, which are mutually distinct, were to exist in one place, what kind of fault would there be? This is because the fault regarding existence and non-existence is already resolved by the very proof of their difference. Moreover, even in the treatises, the superimposition of contradictory properties is said to be "difference" (*bheda*), not "contradiction" (*virodha*). The definition of contradiction, however, is well known to be something else entirely.

The negation of identity is also stated on the basis of the non-perception of an intrinsic nature that does not depend on qualifiers, and not from the perception of a contradiction. Thus, because of the connection with contradictory properties characterized as existence and non-existence, the two properties themselves—which appear as having that [subject] as their locus—become distinct; it is not the case that even for those two underlying entities there is any talk of difference merely through their association with various properties.

When, however, two properties are thus divided such that they stand in the aforementioned relationship of mutual opposition, then there is also a division of their substratum (*dharmin*), just as in the case of the properties of "blueness" and "non-blueness," or existence and non-existence; and it is also like the production and non-production with respect to a single effect. Therefore, existence and non-existence, being directly contradictory, divide [the substratum] precisely as the properties of "producing form" and so forth, appearing as the very nature of their own substrata. They do not, however, divide the support of those two—which is characterized by a prior heterogeneous state—because there is no contradiction in that [support] itself.

For this very reason, it is not perceived as distinct; moreover, the capacity and incapacity to produce a single effect inherently differentiate their own substratum by way of mutual opposition. Since the perception of non-difference is contradicted by the determination of such opposition, the operation of inference is thus entirely faultless.

[39, 22] But this [opponent] himself says, "Indeed, we do not see a difference in effects arising from a single nature, nor is that [difference] observed to be distinct. Speaking thus, he is simply unwell and is not fit for serious debate. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that a diversity of effects arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that does not possess a single nature, but rather from one devoid of a succession of natures. Thus, by dispelling the doubt regarding the nature [of things], that which was stated—namely, that existence (*sattva*) being excluded from momentary things would result in an uncommon [property] and entail a difference in the nature of the material cause (*upādāna*)—is refuted.

The appearance of difference is merely conceptual; it is not a real difference. Furthermore, even if a real difference in intrinsic nature were to occur, one must simply accept that existence (*sattva*) remains non-common (*asādhāraṇa*). For existence does not become excluded from momentary things any more than it is excluded from eternal ones by virtue of exceeding their magnitude, such that it could be determined as non-common. If it is argued that within the abundance of intrinsic natures, something might also be eternal, [we reply:]...

In that case, let it be suspected that the entity which follows [the reason] is common (*sādhāraṇa*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); and this must be considered, because there is the possibility of subverting [reasons] with gaping mouths.

Now, if it is argued that since a succession of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) is possible, one must specify which entity among them possesses momentariness—and thus [momentariness] is said to be excluded even from the [intrinsic nature] itself—that too is not the case. For by establishing the activity of the substratum (*svabhāvī*) as distinct from its own intrinsic natures, its preservation is secured. Furthermore, even if a distinction between intrinsic natures were impossible, the destruction of the root [substratum] would not be logical; for even when infinite adventitious attributes (*upādhi*) occur, the loss of the possessor of those attributes is not admitted.

Even in our own system, if indeed there is the emergence of a mass of other entities, it is nonetheless clear what kind of destruction could possibly occur for the entity under discussion. One must consider whether that mass conforms to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not. Or, let us grant the denial of the root [entity]. As for those intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) which are observed to be real, because they are submerged within the essence of that [root], let the one root not be momentary while existing separately;
however, since many [intrinsic natures] are indeed momentary, this is merely an accumulation of momentariness. How, then, could there be an exclusion of existence from momentariness?

Thus, such ravings, which produce pride only in the minds of vulgar folk, are fitting for them alone, but not for Buddhists whose intellects are sharp as a needle-point and hardened by logic. As for this "instruction" beginning with "this would be so" and so forth, intended to prove a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), let that belong to these very people; for one who is sound-minded is unable to say that "one thing has the intrinsic nature of another. Moreover, a difference in intrinsic nature is already refuted because proof is impossible and because it is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, even your position does not touch upon the fault under discussion. Nor can reasons that establish a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) by means of "teeth-pulling" (i.e., by extracting the very root) regarding the claim that "an auxiliary cause is itself a different intrinsic nature" be overturned. For a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), seeing the auxiliaries themselves, presents a proof to establish a well-known difference in intrinsic nature; he cannot be deceived by such words in any way whatsoever.

Therefore, that [alleged] means is not a means at all; it is better to call it such because it contradicts the establishment of the undesired [consequence] which was stated as the [proponent's] position. And regarding this, we have already said: "Nor is this effort of the opponent merely for the sake of establishing auxiliary causes (sahakārin). For since the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with the effect has been experienced, the auxiliary causes are established by perception and other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) themselves; what remains to be proven here?"
