Therefore, when the proof of the distinction between intrinsic natures (*svalakṣaṇabheda*) has been presented for those things regarded as non-momentary in relation to their successive manifestations of effects, if one were to offer the rejoinder—without stating a refutation—that "the very presence of another auxiliary cause is itself the difference in intrinsic nature," let that person take it as a source of satisfaction for his own heart; however, this does not invalidate the opponent's thesis. Consequently, it is established that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by impermanence (*asthairya*).

Furthermore, as for what was said by him: first, this proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) should be questioned. When the preceding moment is to produce the subsequent moment within a single continuum (*ekasantāna*), there is nothing else whatsoever that must be depended upon. Consequently, because it is independent with respect to the arising of another, the subsequent [moment] must also exist while that [preceding moment] is still present, being necessarily bound to it alone. Or, if it were not so, it would not be bound to that alone; rather, it would be understood as depending on some other cause.

However, in the case of the arising of a dissimilar [moment], since there is no distinction in their being included within the same single continuum—namely, that they previously existed in a similar continuum—they would be either capable or incapable [of producing an effect]. But this is not the case regarding the arising of a restricted moment of a similar type. For if that were so, because there would be no distinction in their being invariably connected to the mere existence of the preceding moment, each subsequent moment would arise simultaneously, abandoning the sequence of priority and posteriority. Consequently, the continuum of those moments occurring at the time of the effect-moment—which depends upon such a continuity—would be severed.
Furthermore, because the continuity of all things existing throughout the three worlds would be severed by this very process, it would follow that the entire triple world is mutually crushed.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no relationship of cause and effect between the two horns of a cow—right and left—because they arise simultaneously (samaya-samaya-bhāvitvāt), then, in this case, an entirely unprecedented method of following positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) would be required: namely, that an effect might arise from a different entity in a preceding past moment, yet fail to arise when that entity is present. By this reasoning as well, the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva) of momentary things remains untenable.

[41,21] All of that, too, is incoherent. For instance, as for the claim that when the subsequent [moment] is to be produced, there is no dependence on anything else whatsoever: in that case, you intend by "subsequent" all moments [of the series]. Otherwise, the consequence that all [moments] would occur simultaneously would be untenable. In that regard, if the refutation applies to your own intended position, then there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*) at all.

Then the follower of the Sugata himself must be questioned: if it is claimed that the former [moment] is independent when the subsequent moment is to be produced in the immediately following instant, but not independent regarding the later moment, then that very nature which produces it does not exist [in the first moment]. Therefore, since it would be dependent upon its own nature, how could it be independent? If it is argued that "that nature will perhaps occur for it at some time," then what is the meaning of the statement "it is dependent upon that" if it will not occur?

This is the meaning: when it is said that Devadatta is capable of this task in dependence upon Yajñadatta, two things are understood there—namely, that he is himself incapable and that he is capable together with Yajñadatta. Furthermore, not all conventional usage conforms to ultimate reality; rather, in some cases something is true. Thus, even here, the portion stating that he is himself incapable cannot be denied, because it is agreed upon by both parties.

The dispute here concerns the claim that "that very [entity] is subsequently capable in conjunction with another. For this very reason, a sublation (*bādhana*) occurs regarding the proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, because that part is unestablished (*aṃśāsiddhi*), even the word "itself" (*svayam*)—which depends on that [part]—is removed. In some cases, the meaning is simply that it is "incapable" (*asamartha*) because it is dependent. Consequently, what is the meaning of saying it is "dependent" when the subsequent effect to be produced is impossible, despite its nature being one of producing it? [The meaning is: it is capable of producing each subsequent effect. Thus, let whatever refutation there is of this point be stated.

It might be argued as follows: each subsequent [moment] is not distinct from the nature of its predecessor; therefore, just as the preceding [moment] is capable with respect to the subsequent one, so too is it capable with respect to the subsequent-subsequent one. If it were incapable with respect to the subsequent-subsequent one, how could it be capable with respect to the subsequent one? For the two possess an identical nature.

That too is untenable, because a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāvatva*) is not established. If it is argued that a single intrinsic nature is established in relation to a succession of homogeneous moments (*sabhāgakṣaṇaparamparā*), we say no, because homogeneity is not established in every respect. For the meaning of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) is the meaning of "belonging to the same class" (*sajātīya*). And being of the same class is threefold: by way of form (*rūpa*), by way of capacity (*śakti*), and by way of both. In that regard, although there may be a state of being of the same class based on form alone between each subsequent moment and the one following it, nevertheless, there is no such state based on capacity.

Consequently, a state of heterogeneity is indeed established. For this very reason, the production of the effect, the sprout, occurs from seeds and so forth through a certain succession of transformations of their own nature (*svabhāva-pariṇāma*). For in that process, the power (*śakti*) to produce the sprout resides in the final momentary seed; furthermore, in the final [moment], it resides in the penultimate, and in the penultimate, in the one preceding it, and so on back to the occurrence of the first seed. In this way, it should be understood that the causal complex (*sahakāri-sāmagrī*) there also becomes increasingly distinct at each successive stage.

For this very reason, although the formative forces (*saṃskāras*), which possess distinct powers at every moment due to their connection with successive conditions and continue in a stream, may be perceived as similar on account of some degree of uniformity, nevertheless their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed different. Consequently, it is the logical principle that only a specific thing can be the cause or the effect of another specific thing. (18a) Therefore, because they are entirely devoid of homogeneity (*sabhāgatva*), even though the preceding moment possesses the capacity to produce the subsequent one, there is no production of each succeeding [moment] from it, because of the distinction [in their] specific capacities (*śaktiviśeṣa*).

Likewise, for that [moment] as well, there is an increase or decrease of power from another; indeed, a distinction is stated for both, in that it "is distinguished from another. Therefore, how can there be any room for the objection regarding the simultaneous occurrence of all moments considered to be homogeneous (*sabhāga*) within a single moment? Furthermore, the final [objection] concerning the production [of effects] through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is merely a misdeed. For, in establishing the capacity to prove momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), positive concomitance is precisely that which one thing arises immediately after another.

And since that cause was previously non-existent, the effect itself is necessarily non-existent at another time or place; this very fact constitutes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). What can be done about this, even by one who does not wish to accept it? For even for the proponent of eternalism, the cause and the effect do not arise simultaneously; rather, the effect arises immediately after the arising of the cause. And if the effect were to come into being from a moment other than that of the cause—whether before or after it—what benefit would the cause provide to the effect?

Since the effect has its purpose fulfilled by that much alone—namely, that its birth occurs immediately after that [moment]—there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by that much alone, as well as negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), in the sense that "in the absence of that, there is an absence [of the effect]. The only distinction for the proponent of eternalism is this: that even after that moment, the existence of what is considered the cause can be ruled out merely on the grounds that it is no longer conducive to the effect, as established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that [distinction] has already been examined. It remains settled, however, that positive and negative concomitance consist of nothing more than what has been stated.

Furthermore, having asserted the uniqueness of the sentient being (*sattva*), and after deliberating on whether one thing arises from one, many, or many arise from one or many, Vācaspati adopted the position that many arise from many and stated: "Are the preceding moments the producers of the subsequent moments while being entirely independent of one another, or are they dependent?"

But has it not been stated that those [causal moments] which have reached their final moment produce effects independently of one another? Why then this elaborate fabrication of what is not accepted? Is it now the case that even the seed-moment that produces a capable seed-moment is itself independent in producing that [capable moment]? We say: "Yes. Well then, in this manner all seed-moments would be independent in producing their effects; thus, there is no need for auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).

But was it not said that these [seeds] are not discerning beings; rather, their presence is restricted by being dependent on their own causes, such that they cannot endure even for a moment through any obstruction? Well then, is even this farmer not discerning, who, having removed the seed from the granary, sows it in the ploughed earth, because the seed possesses the capacity to produce a sprout through a succession of excellence generated by its coexistence with the soil and other factors? For if it were sown where it remains in the granary, that [sprout] would not be seen even after a hundred years. If you say this, [we reply: no.

Now, why is it that this seed-moment is not capable of arising solely from its own continuum? If that were the case, how could it not depend upon another continuum as a cooperative cause for the production of the effect?

[44,1] But surely it does indeed depend [on something] for its own production, yet not for its own effect; it is said that it is independent in that regard [the effect], but not with respect to its own arising. [Objection: Even regarding its own arising, its very preceding moment existing within its own continuum remains independent and active. In this way, each preceding moment falling within its own continuum would remain independent and active in producing [the next]; thus, the farmer who has placed the seed in the granary would alone be successful. There would be no need for this discerning person to perform the labor of farming, which is a source of suffering.

[44,11] If one should think that there are two kinds of effects here: first, that which has the nature of producing a succession of specific excellences (*atiśaya*) imparted by auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); and second, that which produces its effect independently of the excellence of auxiliary causes. In this regard, the sprout is born in dependence upon a succession of specific excellences; however, the initial excellence is produced without depending on a succession of excellences created by auxiliaries. Yet neither of these two kinds of effects can possibly arise from the seed’s own continuum alone.

It is postulated that the seed, whether residing in its own continuum or in a different continuum such as earth and so forth, produces an occasional effect only in dependence upon another continuum; thus is the work of agriculture conceived. As for those other continua which are the auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) for the production of the occasional effect, they alone are the causes for awakening the capacity of the seed in the production of the sprout. Sometimes, even those very causes that produce earth and the like become the causes of that capacity, just as follows:

The "approaching conditions" (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*) are the causes for awakening the capacity [of seeds and the like] to produce their initial excellence. A seed that has not had any excellence imparted to it by other continua cannot, under any circumstances, produce a specific effect that occurs only occasionally. Furthermore, the causes for awakening this capacity consist of both auxiliary conditions (*sahakāripratyaya*) and approaching conditions. This is untenable. To explain: let it be granted that the effect is of two kinds, and let it be granted that, because of its occasional occurrence, it depends upon another continuum. However, the meaning of this "dependence" must be stated. If you say it means "the awakening of the cause's own capacity," [we respond:]...

Is it not the case that since capacity and its awakening are not distinct from the reality of the capable state, it has been stated that the arising of the cognition of capability [occurs] through this? And thus, the very admission—that the cause required for its own production exists by virtue of a cooperative condition—is urged as a fault.

Now, whether this moment is capable of producing a sprout or is the first excellence (*atiśaya*), is it produced by a preceding moment born solely from its own continuum without dependence [on anything else], and not rather by one born solely from its own continuum, since even this [moment] arises from the very same prior aggregate (*puñja*)?

[45,1] But surely, among the series of seed-moments arising from a granary which possess equal power, why does only one particular seed-moment produce, through a succession, a seed-moment that is conducive to the production of a sprout, and not other seed-moments belonging to different series? Indeed, prior to the advent of the auxiliary condition (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*), there is no mutual distinction whatsoever among these seed-moments residing in either similar or dissimilar series.

Due to the condition of the approach [of the auxiliary factors], the moments of the series do not produce, even through a succession, a seed-moment conducive to the production of a sprout, because they produce only seeds. For a certain seed-moment, however, there is the production of an initial excellence co-arising with the condition of the approach. Alas! In that case, even if it has arisen in the absence of that [approach], it would certainly produce [the sprout].

Nor is there a rule of coexistence with the condition of approach (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*), because seeds existing in a granary—which do not belong to that same continuum and share the same fate as [the seed under consideration]—lack coexistence with that condition of approach; and because it is impossible to determine a causal relationship between one moment and another distinct moment. For the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) regarding production, which have a general category as their object, are established only in that very [context].

And thus, since deviation is possible for individual factors alone, even one who does not wish it must admit that for the production of the first excellence or the sprout, the very nature of seeds and other factors is to produce them through mutual dependence.

This too has been largely refuted by the ancient masters. For instance, even if it were established that the capacity to produce belongs only to those things that are mutually dependent, what does this prove regarding the matter at hand? Or, if it is argued that mutual dependence is observed among things that exist simultaneously—

Thus, even for that which is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), if it were to abandon its auxiliary causes when they provide no assistance, there might arise the possibility of some action at some time; in such a case, the exclusion of the permanent from the real would be a mere laborious assumption. This is the intended meaning. If this is so, how can the commitment to its "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) be maintained? It would be more appropriate to state that its exclusion from the heterologous class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

[45,19] Now, it has been established that for a momentary entity there is no dependence upon auxiliary causes, nor is such dependence logical; and this intention will be explained further on. Therefore, since the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by both dependence and independence, it is excluded from the impermanent because of the absence of those two; and it is also excluded from the permanent because of the lack of successive or simultaneous action according to your own view. Thus, it is clearly an uncommon [inconclusive reason].

And thus, for that which is momentary, there can be no dependence upon auxiliary causes because of the absence of any benefit [conferred by them], nor can there be non-dependence, because in the absence of such dependence there would be an absence of causality; therefore, the absence of the pervader is established.

[45,24] That too is trivial. For what kind of object of dependence (*apekṣārtha*) is being taken up when this is said? If, first of all, "it depends on an auxiliary cause" means that it must be assisted by an auxiliary cause, then since such assistance is absent, how can there be a dual exclusion for the momentary entity, given that it is indeed independent? As for the impossibility of its acting without a distinction of auxiliary causes, that follows simply from its own non-existence at another moment.

If it is argued that there is no distinction whether it was "this" or "that," and therefore, even though such a nature is possible, its non-production [at times] is not tenable for those who are independent of auxiliary causes;

This is incoherent, because that which is not an agent lacks such an intrinsic nature. (42b) If the very nature of a thing—which produces an immediate effect while situated amidst all auxiliary causes whose potencies are unimpeded—is the same even at another time and place, then alas, it must likewise possess the capacity for action then as well. Furthermore, similarity in color and shape alone cannot entail the identity of other seeds.

For indeed, even when there is a similarity of form, entities are established as distinct due to differences such as the presence or absence of their effects; likewise, they may also differ through a difference in potency (*śakti*), as in the case of *harītakī* fruits in the process of ripening. To the question of how that difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arises among them despite their commonality in being seeds, the only recourse is the difference in the potency of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). This has been demonstrated in the discussion beginning with "by various successive conditions" (*aparāpara-pratyaya*), even though some degree of similarity is perceived.

[46,12] Therefore, what was said—namely, "But surely [in the case of] those born from the same granary," and so forth—is refuted. For it is the seed, whose differentiation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) has been brought about through the transformation of the totality of causes (*sāmagrī*), both seen and unseen, which—having the soil as its basis and being assisted by the cooperative condition of the impulse (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*)—produces, through a succession of transformations, either the initial excellence (*atiśaya*) or the sprout. Other moments of the seed do not do so, because they lack such a causal succession and thus lack that specific intrinsic nature.

Now, one might object: when all seeds have been produced, harvested, and so forth in a single field, and are subsequently brought and cast into a granary, they are perceived as being of a common nature. Therefore, from where could this specific quality arising from such-and-such a seed come, which is not present in the others? And since this is so—because the touch of the hand for the purpose of harvesting the field belongs to that [specific seed] alone as its own nature, yet is seen later even when other [seeds] are being carried—how can it be possible to deny that this [seed] possesses a common nature?

To this it is replied: Indeed, the cause in all cases is twofold—namely, the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). This is established for all those who maintain the existence of all things (*sarvāstika*). Among these, the unseen has the nature of karma, produced in another birth, determined solely by its non-perception, and possessing a variety inferred from the observation of the variety of effects. The seen, moreover, is of two kinds: that which has a nature pertaining to this world, and that which is both visible and invisible.

And each of these is either inherent in a conscious entity or inherent in an unconscious entity; thus, there are four types. Therefore, in this way, the entire causal complex (*hetu-sāmagrī*) is not perceptible in every respect to an ordinary person. As Trilocana has said: "Some auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) are perceptible, while others are imperceptible. Consequently, the totality of perceptible and imperceptible auxiliary conditions cannot be established through direct perception by one who is not omniscient."

Even in cases where that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is partially perceptible, an ordinary person (*pṛthag-jana*), due to their coarse vision, is incapable of enumerating its internal subtle distinctions. Consequently, there may indeed exist such a difference in nature among certain seeds—those whose functional capacities have been brought forth by the hands of experienced artisans—which, through a continuous succession, is powerful enough to produce the intended effect, whereas other seeds do not possess it even when situated in the same single granary; yet the world would not perceive this distinction.

Nor does its non-existence follow from mere non-perception; rather, there would be doubt. And that doubt is not set aside by you through the effect, namely the sensation of touch. Thus, among the parts of a single body which arise from a common causal complex such as the undivided union of mother and father, certain moles, freckles, and the like appear—whether innate or acquired in succession—and are observed [only in specific locations]. Furthermore, there is an equality of skin, flesh, and so forth even in other parts of the body.

Therefore, how can these [marks] such as the *tilaka* and so forth—which, being distinct, manifest even without being perceived the differentiation of the transformation resulting from a collection of causes both seen and unseen—be denied? The same applies to external entities as well; for the learned accept that the entire aggregate of effects arises from both common and uncommon karma.

[47,11] Furthermore, it might be argued: "In the case of the body, since moles and the like appearing on various parts—whether right or left, concealed or exposed—necessarily bring about pleasure, pain, and so forth, the restriction of their location is appropriate due to the predominance of karma conducive to such results (*satsaṃvartanīyakarma*). However, when seeds are scattered into a granary, or when they are sown in ground prepared by other means, there is no such distinction; therefore, because of this disparity, one should not postulate the efficacy of karma. If this is your objection:

Ah! Thus, since the direct observation or non-observation of utility determines whether one postulates or does not postulate the causal capacity of factors such as karma, one must admit that some effect in the world is produced by karma or accomplished by a Lord (Īśvara) and so forth. For you do not perceive any purpose in the rounding of the dung of goats and the like, merely by excluding what is common to [other] specific animals such as children.

In the case of the unenjoyed and withered fruits, flowers, and sprouts of forest trees, those very men who possess [the marks] such as the *tilaka* are seen to have their own *tilaka* marks and so forth unrecognized; or even when they are recognized, they are observed approaching death without having manifested suffering, mental distress, or the like—so what utility is there in that [mark] either?

Furthermore, since there exist many locations—whether on the left, the right, or other hidden places—that are large enough to be suitable for the occurrence of *tilaka*s and the like, how can there be a fixed rule regarding the location of their manifestation? Moreover, in the case of deer and other animals, where there is merely a change in color in a certain limb, it is sufficient to suspect it might be due to mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and so forth; what need is there to describe such things as being "useful" (*upayoga*)? How much more could one possibly demonstrate in this manner?

Or how much more must you yourself understand? Why then will you come in vain? Even in the absence of any logical inference, the observation of differences in effects among entities that possess specific locations, times, and natures is everywhere permeated by differences in capacities—such as those produced by imperceptible actions and so forth—which are brought about by intermediate distinctions.

Whether directly or indirectly, that [nature] invariably establishes, in a general sense, that which is useful for the purposeful activity of visible and invisible, conscious and unconscious objects—even if it cannot be precisely delimited even by intermediate yogis; thus, a seeker of logic must be made to accept this, even by force, by one who knows logic.

And this being the case, the nature of a certain seed alone is rendered harsh through contact with the conditions for its germination, whereas the nature of others remains unpolished due to the absence of that specific [condition]. Thus, by virtue of these internal and further internal distinctions, that very momentary seed (*bījakṣaṇa*) is, through a causal series, conducive to the intended effect, while other moments of the seed are not. Furthermore, this internal distinction, which is inferred from the touch of the hand, cannot be rejected on the grounds of failing to conceive of a specific capacity for the means such as action (*karman*), or on the grounds of failing to conceive of a specific utility.

Just as a specific part of the body arises from [the application of] a *tilaka* and so forth, or a specific part of a tree from some slight trace of localized modification; for even there, having encountered this visible or invisible cause at the location of the particle of modification, this particular difference in nature—through a succession of specific constituent parts—is capable of performing a function that cannot be accomplished by other parts. Thus, even when the specific distinction is not determined, there exists some particular cause or efficacy that is otherwise impossible; such is the general [principle].

The determination of a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a member [of a causal series] arises from its connection with a cause of transformation. Likewise, in this case as well, there exists a difference in the intrinsic nature of the seed due to contact with the hand prompted by human cognition; thus, it is generally difficult to deny the certainty that it partakes in a subtle distinction between the husk and the fruit. Therefore, because such a difference in intrinsic nature is possible, it is established that only that specific seed is utilized—through a succession of moments—to produce a particularity conducive to the generation of the sprout, and not other seed-moments.

As for what was said regarding "not indeed approaching," and so forth—that refers to the operation of which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It cannot be that of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because even when there is an ascertainment of a gross, single generic nature through the similarity of form, the internal difference—which remains unperceived due to its subtlety—cannot be negated. Moreover, it is observed that in the case of bitter and other flowers, although they possess a similar form and a gross generic distinction, perception falters by generating a single determinative judgment.

Therefore, the establishment of reality does not follow from mere singularity alone, because an invalidator has been shown regarding that aspect. However, when there is a concordant cognition thoroughly cultivated through extreme habituation, the establishment of oneness is not contradictory due to the absence of an invalidator; thus, in the present case, a mutual exclusion of excellence has not been perceived through direct perception. Nor can it be established through inference.

If it should be argued that when earth and so forth are to be produced, that material cause (*upādāna*) is already the very form of the seed itself as earth and so forth, then the seed would not be the producer of earth and so forth independently of them. For if it were independent of them, their distinction from the sprout would be untenable. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that things do not depend on what provides no assistance; nor is assistance possible for a momentary entity other than its production, because such a moment is indivisible.

And likewise, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by the dependence on or independence from unity and plurality—since there is no third possibility—and because the negation of one of these two is inseparable from the affirmation of the other; and since, in the case of a non-momentary entity, those two modes of dependence and independence—which pervade unity and plurality—are absent, existence is excluded by the aforementioned sequence. Thus, [the reason] is not an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), but rather a non-deviant one.

[49,6] Because no indicative mark (*liṅga*) is shown, and because it is impossible to show one, and because a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) indeed exists; therefore, nothing is achieved merely by shouting what is undesirable. [49,8] By this, it is shown that "assistance" is not the meaning of "dependence," and thus for a momentary entity, there is indeed no dependence on its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); nor is there the exclusion of both [dependence and non-dependence]. Now, if "acting together" is the meaning of dependence, even then, if "dependence" requires the qualification "of that which was previously situated," then for a momentary entity there is still no such thing at all; thus, non-dependence remains unrefuted.

Now, if [the term] "of that which was previously situated" does not imply dependence, but rather the meaning of dependence is merely the state of being combined, then there is indeed dependence and not independence. Even so, there is no exclusion of both [possibilities]. Alternatively, if dependence is established according to our own system, then we have already established that what is dependent is precisely incapable. Thus, the formal rule is: that which is incapable with respect to an effect is dependent, whereas that which is capable is independent.
And at that time, because the affirmation of one follows from the negation of the other, incapacity itself becomes capable; for it has been said:
"It is indeed capable," and thus there is no exclusion of both in the case of momentariness.

And as for what you said: "Furthermore, does the seed, having reached its final moment, produce the sprout, earth, wind, water, and fire independently? Does it produce those others by the very same form by which it produces the sprout, or by a different form? It cannot be by that same form, because then the earth and the other elements would also have to possess the nature of the sprout. Indeed, when there is no difference in the cause, the effect cannot be differentiated, for that would entail the absurd consequence of the causelessness of the distinction between effects."

As it has been said: "This indeed is the distinction, or the cause of distinction, namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) and the difference in causes (*kāraṇabheda*)" (SV 20,21). Nor is there a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because that too is a single unity; otherwise, there would be no necessity for their coexistence. A thing produces others through a different form: for instance, when a seed produces a sprout, it acts as the material cause (*upādāna*), since the sprout arises from the transformation of that seed.

If it is argued that, in the case of the other [elements], these [earth and so forth] serve as its auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), whereas for those [auxiliaries], the preceding wind and so forth are their respective material causes (*upādāna*), because they arise through the transformation of those [causes].

Now, are the nature of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritā*) and the nature of being the material cause (*upādānatā*) one reality or many? If they are one, how can it be a producer by means of a different form? If they are many, is there a difference or non-difference between these two and the seed? If there is a difference, how can the seed be the producer, since the sprout and so forth would be accounted for by those two alone? Or, if there is non-difference, why does the seed not possess multiplicity, given its identity with what is distinct? Furthermore, the oneness of these two [forms] follows from their identity with the one [seed].

If it were argued that when earth and so forth are to be produced, that material cause (*upādāna*) is already the very form of the seed itself as earth and so forth—then the seed would not be the producer of earth and so forth independently of them. For if it were independent of them, the distinction of those [products] from the sprout would be untenable. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that things do not depend on what provides no assistance; nor is assistance possible for a momentary entity other than its production, because such a moment is indivisible.

And likewise, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by the dependence on or independence from unity and plurality—since there is no third possibility—and because the negation of one of these two is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other; and since, in the case of momentary things, the two pervading modes of dependence and independence from unity and plurality are absent, existence (*sattva*) is excluded according to the stated sequence. Thus, [the reason] is an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) one, like "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*).

[50,15] If it should be thought that even those which provide no assistance are auxiliary causes and are to be depended upon, because their presence or absence conforms to the presence or absence of the effect, and because they do not perform the function of an auxiliary cause;

But surely, even in the case of a non-momentary entity, by this same sequence, it might depend upon successive auxiliary causes—even though they provide no assistance—since its positive and negative concomitance with the effect would be replicated; and it might produce effects sequentially through the power of the conjunction with successive auxiliaries. Thus, since the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished, existence (*sattva*) is inconclusive due to a doubtful negative concomitance in the proof of momentariness.

[50,19] That too has already been refuted. Furthermore, as for what he says additionally: "Nor is there a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because that too is a unity"—to this we reply: just as there is no difference in the causal complex, so too, since effects are not different, why would they not conform to the non-difference of their cause?

[50,22] But surely, what kind of verbal artifice is this, that effects which have distinct and manifold forms should be non-different? If that were so, then indeed no entity distinct from the collection as a whole would ever fall within the range of perception. And this must be considered according to the Buddhist view. Therefore, since the collection is non-different [from its parts], the claim that the very members of the collection—those with distinct and manifold forms—are themselves non-different: what kind of verbal artifice is this?

For one who suspects that the difference or non-difference of the effect follows from the difference or non-difference of the causes characterized as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), this doctrine of a non-distinct complex (*abhinnasāmagrīvāda*) is appropriate for Vācaspati. Otherwise, it is understood by this much alone: how could a single seed produce a sprout, a lake, a mountain, a house, and so forth?

And this is not a valid objection; for if the intended refutation of the production of the manifold from the single were based on following the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then direct perception (*adhyakṣa*)—which apprehends multiple effects such as the transformation of the wick arising even from a single lamp—would undermine confidence in all those views contrary to it.

If it is asked, "How so?"—surely, when an investigation is conducted by prioritizing the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one begins with perception and then enumerates the remaining ones; thus, once something has been established or sublated by that [perception], there is no further authority for others to either sublate or establish it. As for those who transgress the path of valid cognition, the same response should be given to them; let this matter rest for now.

Now, how can that which produces a sprout be the cause of the moment of the earth? For even here, it is not logical to assert a contradiction by means of perception, because the moment transcends the range of that [perception]. Furthermore, if there were an invariable concomitance (vyāpti) such that "whatever is the producer of one thing cannot be the producer of another," then there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) by the case of a lamp.

If, on the other hand, the producer of the sprout is not the cause of the earth, then there is an inconclusive reason due to lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇānekānta*). If it is argued, "How can that which is the cause of the sprout be the cause of something else?", [we reply: is it the cause of the sprout alone, or of the sprout and others, or does it first belong to the sprout while its status regarding others remains uncertain? In all three of these positions, the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) are respectively difficult to avoid. Therefore, no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates here.

The formulation of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) also occurs by means of the opponent's own admission; however, it is not the admission of those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness that "one [cause] does not produce many [effects]. Therefore, it is not the work of a fool to deduce the unity of the effect from the unity of the individual entities contained within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Furthermore, when dependence upon a cause characterized as a causal complex is admitted, it is established that even distinct things such as sprouts and the like conform to the difference or non-difference of their causes. Thus, there is no necessity for sprouts and the like to become one simply out of conformity with non-difference.

For just as sprouts and so forth, despite being individual effects, possess both distinct and non-distinct natures, so too the seeds and other factors denoted by the term "assemblage," while each acting as a cause, are indeed both distinct and non-distinct; thus, it is established that difference arises from the difference of causes.

[51,20] Now, even though seeds and the like are distinct in nature, they are made the objects of a single conventional designation by virtue of some proximity; likewise, it is so for sprouts and the like. Thus, even when there is no difference in the cause, non-difference is established. In that regard, the fact that the causes each produce a single effect is the basis for the single convention; as for the effects, however, it is the fact that they are each produced from a single [cause], which is the same [principle].

Why, then, must [the cause] become one with the sprout and so forth? For even when there is dependence upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that much alone is sufficient for the effect to conform to the difference or non-difference of the causes. Furthermore, this is stated merely in accordance with conventional cognition (*buddhi*) for the sake of the opponent who understands the term "cause" as referring to the causal complex;

in reality, however, it has already been shown that just as the causal complex is intended by the word "cause," so too are difference and non-difference intended as heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) and homogeneity (*avaijātya*).

[52,3] But surely, since even now a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not something other than its constituent members, it follows that the similarity or dissimilarity of effects depends precisely on the similarity or dissimilarity of those very constituents. This is indeed so; however, this does not refer to a mutual determination of similarity and so forth among the members situated within that same aggregate. Rather, it refers to their similarity or otherwise with respect to their own genus (*svajāti*) in relation to members situated in another aggregate, just as one army is determined to be similar or otherwise to another army.

In this context, however many and of whatever nature objects are considered causes when they fall within the scope of a single designated causal complex (*sāmagrī*), if that same number and those same types of objects exist in another place or time, then that is a similar complex, and its effect is also similar; thus, by the term "effect" (*kārya*), a mere aggregate (*puñja*) is meant. The meaning is that however many and of whatever nature effects have arisen in one instance, exactly that many and of those same types arise elsewhere as well.

But when there is dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*), which is differentiated by degrees of difference, the effect (*kārya*) is also differentiated by degrees of difference; thus the meaning is that the dissimilarity belongs precisely to the aggregate of effects by way of their varying degrees. This same principle applies even when one intends to express mere difference: when there is a disagreement, a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces a distinct effect. It is precisely such conformity of the effect to the difference in its causes that accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And if that [rule] were transgressed, the consequence would follow that the entire universe is without cause; for there is no transgression of a restriction to a single cause producing a single effect when such a rule is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, this talk of the Naiyāyikas regarding the imitation of difference and non-difference resembles the report of the desire for milk-rice from the mouth of a cowherd.

Therefore, a single seed produces many things such as the sprout and so forth; likewise, each factor such as the earth and so forth does the same. Consequently, there is no exclusion of either the "one" or the "many," since this is another non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). This is further presented for the purpose of making the position of momentariness incompatible with causal activity through its existence (*sattā*). As for the position that [the cause] produces by means of a different form (*rūpāntara*), we have already rejected it; thus, there is no need to exert effort in providing a series of refutations against that.

And this is stated with reference to reality (*tattva*). In the play of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-vilāsa*), however, that which is the production of a sprout is not the production of the earth; likewise, being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) is not itself being the material cause (*upādānatva*). Thus, even though such a proliferation of categories may occur, there is no deficiency whatsoever in the entity characterized by the absence of activity, because everything is accounted for precisely through its real nature.

For this very reason, why should we state that when earth and so forth are to be produced, their material cause (*upādāna*) is already a transformation of the form of the seed of the earth and so forth—such that the subsequent argumentation would be sound? Furthermore, since it has been established that [the cause] is independent even regarding its auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), the conclusion of the entire section by one of confused intellect is utterly muddled.

Furthermore, those who inquire: "By the very same nature (*rūpa*) that the seed produces the sprout, does it also produce the moment of the earth?"—they too are to be questioned: "What is intended here by the word 'nature' (*rūpa*)? First of all, do you mean those factors (*dharma*) such as being produced, impermanence, and so forth—which, like being the producer of the sprout or its opposite, appear as if distinct while resting upon the bed of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and which have already acquired their conventional usage even under the term "essential nature" (*svarūpa*)?

Now, regarding "form" (*rūpa*), its own nature (*svarūpa*), or its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): since there is no other distinction of the entity apart from that [nature], it is spoken of with reference to that. If that which is initially the very nature of the entity were to not produce [its effect] later as well—just as it did before—and so forth.

Alternatively, it has been stated that "form" refers to the cooperative cause itself, being designated by the word "own-nature" (*svarūpa*), just as the Naiyāyikas employ the term "brother" for one who does not know the name of the husband. In that regard, first of all, in the case of the former position, there is no logical consistency in the objection.

For phenomena (dharma) constructed by conceptualization (kalpanā), although they appear as if existing in relation to one another and to their substrata (dharmin), cannot function as instruments in any activity whatsoever, because they lack existence according to their appearance and thus cannot withstand valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For indeed, although the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone—which has been made the object of direct perception—is devoid of parts, and although the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nevertheless, due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*anādi-vāsanā*), there arises in the conceptualizing mind a mere linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). This convention is projected by relying on the force of the determination (*vyavasāya*) of things as excluded from this or that [other thing], within confirmations (*saṃvāda*) regarding properties (*dharma*) that are abstracted [from the whole]; it functions thus: "In this or that activity, this or that property is useful."

However, these [qualities] do not possess the status of being instruments (karaṇa) in any respect, because they themselves lack existence. Yet, that which is produced by intention (*vivakṣā*) is not denied. Just as in the case of a lamp whose nature is light and which, in its very form, effects the destruction of darkness and makes the space yellowish-pink, so too, when it is ascertained that this lamp is of the nature of light, it follows from that that it removes darkness like the moon; and because of its yellowness, it is conventionally treated as a cause of making things yellowish-pink, like turmeric and the like.

And in that case, the luminosity and the orange color are not distinct; however, in the conceptualizing mind, they appear as if distinct, and having extracted each one separately, they are intended—though not actually established—as being the performers of distinct functions. Yet, by mere intention, the lamp does not become a non-agent or a distinct entity.

[53,20] Likewise, regarding a seed as well, its production of a sprout occurs through an imagined form that generates the sprout, and its production of that [sprout] occurs through the earth which generates it. Thus, even in conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), in reality (*tattvataḥ*), there is neither a negation of a single [entity] performing multiple actions, nor the establishment of a distinction [between them], nor indeed a state of non-action. Therefore, with respect to forms mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpārūḍha-rūpa*), the performance of multiple actions by means of multiple forms is merely conventional discourse (*vyavahāramātra*) and not a real entity (*vastu*). And this investigation is based on what is real (*vāstavī*).

So what is the use of this conceptualization—whether it be by that form or another? Even if one does engage in conceptualization, the response is made by means of only one [form], merely as a matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); and there is no fault whatsoever. As for the second position, however, it is tenable only when there is a perception of multiple particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, even the particular characteristics of seeds are not the object of a simultaneous observation under a single number. For indeed, when the full extent of a person is not perceived, the question "Is this man to be employed in this task, or is that one? does not arise.

In the third alternative, however, the meaning would be this: "Is it by the very same form that it produces the sprout that it [produces] the soil? or "Is it by the very same auxiliary cause with which it generates the sprout that it [produces] the earth? And when would this be said? Only if, when the seed's production of the sprout is established, there were some fixed-form auxiliary factor determined to be active in one production while its activity in another production remained doubtful. But such a thing cannot be demonstrated.

Now, this being the case, the meaning of the dilemma is as follows: if earth, water, and so forth are the auxiliary causes for the seed’s production of a sprout, are they the same [causes] for its production of earth? Even by that [line of reasoning], there is no utility; for since it is well-established that all things everywhere stand in a mutual relationship of auxiliary causality, what is the point of this question? Furthermore, the subsequent argument is not appropriate here; for even then, there is no coherent connection to the claim that "the difference or non-difference of the effect follows from the difference or non-difference of the cause."
Therefore, those who consider themselves experts in logic merely wish to agitate others with senseless ravings tormented by the thorn of envy; enough of this persistence on this matter.

Moreover, this manner of proclaiming an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) is unprecedented. For an existent entity whose positive and negative concomitance with both the probandum and its opposite are uncertain is rightly considered uncommon, such as the property of possessing odor (*gandhavattva*). However, by the force of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) under discussion, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) itself is entirely non-existent; how then could that [reason] be an uncommon inconclusive one? It would be more appropriate to state the refutation of "unestablished" (*asiddhi*); and that has already been stated therein.

Now, if it is argued that [the reason] "absence of pervasion" was stated regarding momentariness, and therefore [the subject] is not entirely existent; then, in that case, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), while indeed existing, is excluded from the momentary alone. Consequently, by necessity, it rests in the non-momentary and is thus pervaded by it. Let there also be contradiction (*viruddhatā*).

If it is argued that there is doubt because there is no direct perception of either a sublater or a prover of non-momentariness, [we reply]: if its existence is established, then its exclusion from momentary things alone constitutes the proof, which leaves no room for doubt. Furthermore, if there is doubt regarding its existence, the very fault of "unestablished due to doubt" (sandigdhāsiddhi) applies.

Furthermore, since the non-perception of the pervader of the subject (*prakṛtavyāpakānupalambha*) possesses its full efficacy with regard to the non-momentary just as it does with regard to the momentary, how can there be the establishment of a subverting proof? Thus, non-establishment (*asiddhi*) follows in every respect. For it is possible to say regarding even a permanent entity: "It does not act while dependent on auxiliary factors, because there is no benefit [conferred by them]; nor does it act independently, because it acts even without them."

Furthermore, regarding the objection that a stable seed produces the soil either by its very nature as a producer of the sprout or by a different nature, and so forth—when there is the critique of the production of dissimilar things such as the soil—and likewise that for you [Buddhists], even a lamp is non-momentary; in that case, it is the same: would the transformation of the wick and the exhaustion of the oil be produced by one and the same nature or by a different one?

As for the claim that "the distinction in the nature of a particular meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consists simply in its auxiliary conditions being distinct"—by asserting this, one must now abandon any hope of conveying specific, determined meanings through words such as "self" (*ātman*) and "other" (*para*), since it would follow that "the other is the self" and "the self is the other. Nor is it appropriate to say, even when engaged in a single activity, that "Yajñadatta is the nature of Devadatta," or that "blue is the nature of white.
Thus, this argument, devoid of both scripture and logic, being propounded out of mere rivalry, will certainly become an object of ridicule.

[55,9] Furthermore, disregarding the auxiliary factors, it is evident that a stable entity (*sthira-bhāva*) does not produce an effect—whether by its own nature or by any other state—even though that which is denoted by the term "own-nature" is present. Thus, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is necessarily admitted. For even in the case of another [entity], that very same self is the producer, and not the entity itself; thus, nothing whatsoever is a producer. Therefore, this logical principle, which establishes the negation of activity, applies equally to both stable and unstable entities.

If that [reason] were established, there would be no action whatsoever, and thus the reason would simply be unestablished (*asiddhi*); for even the fault characterized by the absence of both succession and simultaneity could not ultimately be avoided. Even in the case of a permanent entity, the cessation of action must necessarily be admitted. Otherwise, how could the mere statement of the negation of action in the case of a momentary entity result in the removal of the charge of being "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇatā*)? For being uniquely inconclusive does not consist merely in the exclusion from the probandum (*sādhya*).
Otherwise, why would one not say that the mere exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) constitutes being uniquely inconclusive—what is the point of such great effort?

[55,17] If it is argued that a reason (*hetu*) must indeed be a valid reason because it is restricted to the probandum (*sādhya*) by its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), then it is equally the case that it would be a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) because it is restricted to the counter-example by its exclusion from the probandum. Therefore, even when there is a mere thesis regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is simply no proof. Now, if by some other means it is shown that there is merely a lack of certainty regarding both [the presence and absence of existence], and thus existence is made known, then in that case, non-commonality (*asādhāraṇatā*) is indeed logical.

That is incorrect. For the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) necessarily brings about the ascertainment of absence; how then could there be no ascertainment? In this regard, even if the strength of the non-perception of succession and so forth—which excludes existence from a permanent entity—is considered inconsistent, nevertheless, the firmness of the present [reasoning] which sublates permanence in the momentary is indeed intended, since otherwise its presentation would be illogical. Consequently, the absolute exclusion of action from that which is subject to momentary destruction is itself the exclusion [of the reason] from the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatā*).

For it is not possible to ascertain that the possession of odor is excluded from anything with absolute certainty. Thus, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), even when depending on the non-perception of the pervader in the case of a stable entity, is not valid for proving uncommonness (*asādhāraṇatā*). Since it uproots action entirely, there is simply a lack of proof (*asiddhi*), and no relationship of probandum and probans exists.

Therefore, in the course of a debate, relying on external sensation, an external cognizer established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and real causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), one who asserts the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) of a reason need not demonstrate—either for the probandum or its opposite—the coexistence, identity, or exclusion [of the reason] in a single locus; rather, there is merely doubt regarding both. Furthermore, such [coexistence or exclusion] is impossible when the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is not perceived. Thus, it is established that the presentation of uniqueness is not sound.

It might be argued as follows: If there is a difference in the nature of the producer when producing effects at different times, then this same consequence would apply to the production of effects in different locations. Therefore, the spatial separation of effects must necessarily depend upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). And since an auxiliary cause is defined as that which performs some function, temporal separation—which likewise depends upon auxiliary causes—must also be considered non-functional (i.e., irrelevant) for them. Alternatively, one might claim that spatial separation arises from a difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), whereas such a claim cannot be made regarding temporal separation.

If it is argued that for things produced at different times, the distinction in time for the effect is based solely on the distinction in the nature of the causes—since, according to the view of permanence (*sthirapakṣa*), the material cause (*apādāna*) would still be present even at those later times—that too is not the case. This is because the distinction between the material and auxiliary causes (*upādāna-sahakārin*) is neither real nor even conventionally true. Even if it were real, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a lamp or similar object would possess multiple natures, due to the distinction between its material and auxiliary causes arising from the distinction between the effects and their auxiliaries.

Therefore, how could this difference of the cause—consisting of an imputed nature and arising from a distinction in the state of its auxiliary conditions—be capable of producing a spatial difference in the effect? If even an imputed difference of the cause were indeed capable of producing a spatial difference in the effect, then an imputed difference of the cause alone would suffice for a temporal difference; thus, one should abandon all hope for a real (tāttvika) difference.

Nor should it be said that while there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*)—such as "whatever is a producer at a particular time is so at that time"—which applies to a difference in time, such a subverting argument does not apply to a difference in place; for it is possible to state a similar subverting argument even regarding a difference in place: namely, "whatever is an effect is located in a particular place, just like that which is intended to be its material cause (*upādāna*), and this [other] effect is likewise an effect. Furthermore, as for what is stated [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*], "even when all conditions are equal," etc.
(PVA I 396a), it is indeed possible to recite [the response] in that case as follows: [the same logic applies].

"Even though the cause is identical in all locations, if there is no effect," and so forth. (PVA II 396ab) Now, this fault would indeed arise if one were to admit that the cause possesses a pervasive nature (*vaibhava*). But if it lacks that [pervasiveness], what is the basis for its being identical in all locations? In that case, it should not produce an effect in another location either, since it does not itself operate there. If, however, it produces the effect there by virtue of mere capacity (*yogyatā*) without depending on its presence in that specific location, then its location is the same [in both cases], because no assistance is obtained from either side.

Therefore, when one says "he produces it in that place," the status of the place as a substratum is not from its own perspective, but rather in relation to the effect; and its production therein is by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of producing an effect located in another place. If that were so, then when one says "he produces it at that time," that time would necessarily be the substratum of the effect alone, whereas for the cause, it would be both present and absent. However, by way of excluding non-connection, the production of an effect at a single time does not contradict the production of an effect even if it exists at other times.

Therefore, it is logical that even for a thing whose intrinsic nature remains identical across all states, such as being in a granary and so forth, there is the production of effects at those specific times and not at others, just as there is the production of multiple effects in different locations.

[57,12] This is not tenable, because there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). As for that "being its effect" which was put forward to prove its being in the same location—that is no proof at all, because there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to subvert its opposite. Furthermore, the causal relation is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); and just as these two are observed when an effect arises in the same location as [the cause], so too are they observed when an effect arises in a different location.

Nor is it correct to say that even when the cause remains constant, the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an effect produced at that same time or an effect produced at another time are identical; for there is no means of valid cognition other than recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) to show that the very same cause persists at a different time, and since that recognition has been refuted, how could there be a grasp of the concomitance of effects that occur at different times with a permanent cause? Thus, this logic is not the same [as the case of non-momentary entities].

Therefore, if—due to the absence of a subverting counter-argument (*viparyayabādhaka*)—the reason that establishes difference based on spatial distinction is capable of proving its own thesis, what follows from that for the powerful reason that establishes difference based on temporal distinction? For it is not logical to say that because a bull is unfit for milking, a cow must likewise be so.

Or, even if we grant that the proof of difference through spatial distinction possesses the strength of a subverting counter-argument, one might ask: "What fault is established by this much against the proof of difference through temporal distinction—is it the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?
If you ask this, is this merely the recitation of a mantra?

If it is argued that the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is considered doubtful because one observes the non-production of something capable of producing at certain times, even so, what is the point of this labor? For its establishment is achieved simply by the fact that "it would be capable, yet it does not produce. If it is argued that the example of place serves to reinforce the doubt:

[58,1] If the sublation by the contrary (*viparyayabādhā*) is its strength, then even if it is fully developed, it accomplishes nothing unless it transcends doubt. However, if there is an absence of sublation by the contrary, the reason is overturned by mere doubt; what, then, is the use of its "development"? And if that [absence of sublation] alone is intended here, then once this has been refuted by the sublater of the contrary, what is the point of restating it? Now, if it is argued that because the same logic is observed everywhere regarding time and place, they share a common fate (*ekayogakṣema*), and thus—just as with a difference of place—there is no difference in the reason even when accompanied by a difference of time.

That too is incorrect. For instance, proponents of eternalism do not maintain that the spatial pervasion of an atom is similar to its temporal pervasion; nor is the temporal pervasion of a flash of lightning similar to its spatial pervasion, and this applies equally to a jar and other such things. How, then, can there be a uniform principle of reasoning (*samānanyāyatā*) in all cases? Furthermore, even if a uniform principle is not observed elsewhere, it does not follow that it must exist everywhere; for in the case at hand, there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the possibility of the opposite being true.

[58,11] Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*) and the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) when there is a difference in location—that this constitutes a "subordinate" [distinction]—that too is incorrect. Even though those two states of being the material cause and the auxiliary cause, appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), are not real entities despite appearing as if they were distinct, nevertheless, because it is possible for a real entity to possess various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), there is no establishment of unreality; and because they are mutually dependent, there is no contradiction. Just as, for example, the status of being both father and son for a single person is not unreal in relation to another, nor is there any contradiction.

Nor is there the production of two effects by means of two forms, such that—because the two forms appearing in conceptual construction (kalpanā) are unreal—there would be no production of the two. And just as there is no production of two by means of a single form, so too [the cause] produces its own effect in its own location and the effect of another in the location of another; thus, although a difference in location is logically established through the difference in the material causes (upādāna), the difference in the location of the effect does not arise merely from an imputed difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāva), but rather from those [causes] which, while producing their own respective effects in their own respective locations, necessarily produce [other effects] in different locations.

The principle is that an action must be performed by means of cooperation (*sahakāryaṃ kāryam*). Therefore, it is not merely due to a difference in an imagined intrinsic nature (*vikalpita-svabhāva-bheda*) that a non-different [cause] produces effects at different times; for such a difference is established through the force of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). For this very reason, the cause does not possess identity across all locations.

For its status as a cooperative factor (*sahakāritā*) consists in its acting upon the material cause (*upādāna*) of its own cooperators, and since that effect can only arise in the very location of its own material cause, its capacity for cooperative action exists only there and not in another location. Thus, how could it have the same location everywhere, especially in the absence of any assistance from anything else?

As for what was said—that time is necessarily the locus of the effect alone, whereas it is both the locus and non-existent for the cause—that too is refuted by the same logic applied to space. For just as a cause located in one place produces effects in different places without reaching them, so too a cause existing at one time produces effects at different times without reaching the time of the effect.

Consequently, even if it has perished immediately after arising, it may produce all its effects throughout the duration of time by depending on auxiliary factors; thus, the promise to perform a single purpose by coming together in one place is fulfilled.

[59,4] Now, if it is argued that even in the case of location (*deśa*), since the effect is produced only after reaching [the location], the example of location is not established; we say no. For knowledge, which exists within the person, there is no reaching of a location. Even when the lamp—which is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) of knowledge—is in contact with the light, there is no opportunity for the radiance to enter inside the body at the place where knowledge, pleasure, and so forth arise. Thus, this [argument] is a mere grasping at straws (*kāśakuśāvalambana*).

Furthermore, this reason (*hetu*) of "being an effect of that" (*tat-kāryatva*), which was proposed as a proof for [the object's] being located in that same place, is not independent (*svatantra*), because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Even if such a connection were to exist, we have already stated that it does not establish our position. Nor can it constitute a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), because the fact of being its effect is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thus lacks the status of being a mere concession by the opponent, and because it lacks the property of leading to the opposite conclusion (*viparyayaparyavasāyitā*).

For in that case, since it would not occupy that same location, it would follow that it is also not its effect; yet this cannot be maintained. Even if it were possible [to maintain], there would be no damage to our fundamental arguments (*mūlaprasaṅga*). Nor is the aforementioned fault applicable, because the capacity to produce [an effect] exists at another time merely by way of its being propagated, and not through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And in the case of the opposite, there is the absence of non-production; the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) excludes the capacity for that effect in another moment, thereby proving the momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) of the cloud in both positions—whether it performs another action or does not perform any action at all. Thus, because the reason "existence" (sattva) is present in the similar class (sapakṣa), it is not contradictory.
The second chapter, titled "The Section on Positive Concomitance" (*anvayādhikāra*).
[60,1] [The Chapter on Momentary Destruction] [60,2] The third chapter, "The Section on Negative Concomitance" (*vyatirekādhikāra*).

Nor is there any suspicion of the reason being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established as encompassing all cases. But surely, the establishment of pervasion occurs through the force of a means of valid cognition that sublates the opposite (*viparyaya-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and there is no mention of such a [cognition] being adduced here. So how can it be said that pervasion has been established? This is merely the play of an extremely flickering and unsteady intellect. For it has already been stated: "That action does not belong to an agent at any other time; rather, it would be either the action of another or non-action itself."

Therefore, in both modes, the concomitance of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) with existence is necessarily established; that is to say, it is an invariable connection (*tanmātrānubandha*), and this has already been proven. Consequently, that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) is indeed pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*). [Objection: But if this is so, let there be mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*); however, how can one obtain the absolute exclusion (*vyatireka*) from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)? [Reply: Precisely because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established. [Objection: But how is the establishment of pervasion itself obtained in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?

No; for pervasion (*vyāpti*) is of two kinds: that which is positive (*anvaya-rūpā*) and is a property of the agent (*kartṛ-dharma*), consisting in the necessary presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*dharmin*) possessing the probans (*sādhana*); and that which is negative (*vyatireka-rūpā*) and is a property of the object (*karma-dharma*), consisting in the necessary absence of the probans where the probandum is absent. This is according to the principle that "pervasion is the existence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) only where [the pervaded] exists, or the existence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only where [the pervader] exists. And the establishment of one of these two necessarily implies the cognition of the second, because otherwise not even one of them would be established.

It is merely that in one case the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is direct, while in the other it occurs through necessary implication (*nāntarīyakatayā*); by this much alone there is a single designation. And this being so, although doubt regarding the other [object] may arise before the means of valid cognition has operated upon the first, it is subsequently dispelled by that [cognition].

Just as for those who maintain the proof that sublates the contrary, the positive concomitance (anvaya), even if doubted, results in the removal of doubt through the force of its absolute exclusion from the heterologue (vipakṣa)—namely, that "this existence, which is in every way impossible in a non-momentary entity, is necessarily restricted to momentary destruction"—so too, because the possession of existence necessitates the presentation of a distinct nature at every moment, the moment of doubt regarding existence, though previously active even in the absence of that [certainty], dissolves of its own accord.

If that which possesses activity must necessarily be momentary, then existence is invariably absent in the absence of momentariness. However, if it were to exist even in the absence of that [momentariness], then how could there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) such that momentariness is necessarily present when existence is present? Therefore, there is no difference in meaning between the absolute exclusion (*ekāntiko vyatirekaḥ*) of the probans in the absence of the probandum, and the necessary positive concomitance (*avaśyam anvayaḥ*) of the probandum when the probans is present.

The operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), however, is twofold in its conventional usage: primarily and by implication. For this very reason, wherever there is a search for a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), it should be understood that when the probans (*sādhana*) exists, there is also an investigation for a proving proof (*sādhakapramāṇa*) for the concomitance with the probandum, as indicated by that [subversion]. Furthermore, by the term "subverting the opposite" (*viparyayabādhaka*), both [the proving proof and the subverting proof] are indeed included.

For in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the probans when the probandum is reversed; whereas in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there is a subverting proof against the reversal of the probandum when the probans is present. Thus, the meaning is that in the absence of both [types of concomitance], the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probans and the probandum is untenable.

Otherwise, even if the means of valid cognition that ascertains the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not directly obtained, if one were to demonstrate the means of valid cognition that establishes the necessary rule of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between the probans and the probandum, what obstacle would there be to the establishment of the probandum? For the negative concomitance implies the force of the positive concomitance as well. Otherwise, the application of the method of agreement (*sādharmya-prayoga*) would be entirely useless, since the negative concomitance would not be demonstrated directly.

Therefore, even if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not explicitly grasped through its own form but is instead understood through implication, nevertheless, by the mere fact that "wherever there is the probans (*sādhana*), there is the probandum (*sādhya*)," one who acts motivated by the expectation of the probandum achieves their goal when the probans is present. For even though the probans might be absent when the probandum is absent, if the probandum is necessarily present whenever the probans is present, then the undertaking of the probans has borne fruit.

Therefore, both aspects must be investigated through conceptual analysis by the proponent of the proof; furthermore, the proponent must demonstrate at least one mode that is established by valid cognition. It should be understood that in the arguments of others, just as with negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that possesses a necessary rule is likewise extremely difficult to find.
