In our own primary proof, however, we have already demonstrated through the two preceding [arguments] a necessary positive concomitance (*anvaya*) characterized by the absence of both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*). Although those two operate with respect to the cloud, which has been taken as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), they nevertheless proceed in this manner: "Whatever has the nature of producing something necessarily produces it; whatever does not produce something does not have the nature of producing it. Thus proceeding, they demonstrate that everything endowed with causal efficiency is necessarily restricted to momentariness; therefore, there is a universal application (*sarvopasaṃhāra*).

The seed for implying the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is like that of smoke and so forth. Just as perception, while cognizing the pervasion of smoke by fire, does not apprehend the existence of fire in the kitchen due to non-inclusion (*anupasaṃhāra*), so too the aforementioned inference, while cognizing momentariness in a water-bearing cloud, extends the pervasion of momentariness to whatever possesses activity in general, by way of a common principle.

As for what was stated previously—that there is no inference other than existence by which an endless regress would not occur—that has been refuted, because the aforementioned reductio ad absurdum and its contrapositive also establish that very point.

If it is argued that the adducing of the reason "existence" (sattva) is thus useless, we reply: Is the other proof (sādhana) redundant merely because of the existence of another reason? Or is it because that [other reason] is also adduced regarding the subject under consideration (pakṣa)? Or is it because it is possible to adduce it? Or is it because it must necessarily be adduced? Or is it because, once the pervasion (vyāpti)—that "whatever performs a purposeful action is necessarily momentary"—is established, the proof of momentary destruction for mountains and the like, which also perform purposeful actions, follows by way of the example of the rain-cloud? These are the alternatives.

In this regard, first of all, [the objection that the reason is] "unfit" is not tenable; for even when many means of proof are possible, only that which is brought forward by the speaker's intention (vivakṣā) is of use to the opponent. For this very reason, "being capable of being adduced" (*śakyopanyāsatva*) is also not a cause of futility (*anarthakya*), because even such a [reason] was unobtainable prior to its being adduced. Furthermore, the adducing [of the reason] in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is distinct from its adducing in the mere subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

Therefore, the requirement of necessarily adducing [the reason] in the *pakṣa* is also unestablished; for once pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by the force of that [adducing], the probandum is established by this much alone: "this is a *capalacāmara*."

The final objection, however, is that when the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which must include all instances—is unestablished, it leaves room for doubt; moreover, in that case, there is no distinction even regarding the counter-evidence (*bādhaka*) against the opposite. For even if the pervasion of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitā*) with activity is established in general, one who desires to act toward a particular instance must necessarily present the evidence, thinking "this is that"; so what is the point of insisting on this?

Now, even so, one must necessarily rely upon that inference with respect to the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) in order to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*); and that very same proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgasādhana*) applies to its own subject. This being the case, one might as well achieve the goal by presenting it with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) itself; what is the point of this much effort to introduce those inferences separately? For, having cognized existence as being pervaded by that [momentariness], one would conclude that there is momentary destruction in the subject because of its existence.

[62,19] If this is so, then the same objection applies even to the proponent of the valid cognition that sublates the contrary, because he too must rely on the establishment of pervasion for such formal arguments as "whatever has the nature of producing something at a certain time," and because its efficacy regarding the subject of the thesis remains intact.

Therefore, a distinction must be made here based on the difference in the practitioner's engagement: for one who, introducing [the analysis] such as "whatever is capable of producing whatever in each respective object," is capable of examining momentariness, the proof of the destruction of moments (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) follows from that very [analysis]; what is the use of another reason? Likewise, in the case of instructing another, for one who establishes [the point] in the same way with respect to each individual object, there is no need to put forward another reason.

However, one whose intellect is awakened by comparison with that [awakened person] understands—through the application of the means of proof for that [momentariness] in a single case—that this very same process applies to everything possessing activity. Thus, while not yet ascertaining its pervasion (*vyāpti*) through momentariness, and without undertaking the effort of applying that logic to each individual case, he establishes whatever object he perceives to be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as being non-enduring. This is the utility of the reason "existence" (*sattva*); and it is the same in the case of demonstrating it to another.

There is no fault, for it is existence (*sattva*) alone—possessing a pervasion established by logic—that performs the operation. Thus, the effort to introduce that logic for every individual object here would indeed be unbearable; however, out of necessity, the first cognizer must resort to that very [existence].

The second [type of opponent], however, by means of the same reasoning applied to a single instance through its possession of cognition, immediately determines that mere activity is dependent on instability; he thus establishes the other [subject] as being existent (*sattva*) alone. Yet, there is no obstruction to the capacity of that reasoning to prove momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) in any instance possessing activity, nor is there a total failure of the proof based on existence and so forth, because the reasoning has not been presented against the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). Enough of this prolixity.

[63,10] Thus, since pervasion (vyāpti) consists in the necessary presence of the pervader (vyāpaka) wherever the pervaded (vyāpya) exists, the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) from the reason of existence (*sattva*) is unimpeded by the very power produced through the pervasion in the form of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the property of the subject (*kartṛdharma*). Therefore, it has been established: what is the need here for adducing a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary? For this very reason, even the impossibility of adducing such a proof does not cause any pressure, because the probandum is already established by the subverting proof of the contrary itself.

In the treatise as well, in the first rule, pervasion in the form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been established in detail under the pretext of avoiding inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), using the example of seeds and so forth. However, because [the negative concomitance] is not more clearly understood, people merely attribute this "preparatory equipment" (*parikara*) to it, which is characterized by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

[63,16] Here too, there is a curiosity regarding the refutation of the statements of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) concerning pervasion (*vyāpti*) in its form of exclusion (*vyatireka*). Even then, it is not merely one mode; rather, would that which is intended to be permanent act at another time—either before or after? This is the indication of sequence. Or else, it would not act at all at another time; this is the restriction, and thus not before.

Nor is there an action after [the sequence]; thus, there is a teaching of non-sequentiality (*akrama*). However, if the action were to occur either before or after at some time, then there would indeed be a sequence; in this way, the definitions of these two are declared to be unmixed. And although simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is relative to a single action occurring at the same time, while sequence (*krama*) is relative to different times, nevertheless, due to the difference in what is being relied upon, there is no confusion between them, just as in the case of father and son.

And by the mention of "non-action" (*akriyā*), there may be, according to different views, either the total absence of the entity itself in every respect, or its essential nature (*svarūpa*) remaining as devoid of action; there is no insistence on this point. Furthermore, in that context, the term "genus" (*jāti*) is used with the intention of expressing only the identity between the prior and the posterior—whether the action be prior, posterior, or both one and many. At any given time, both [the prior and posterior] in relation to the action do not fall outside the denotation of the word "simultaneous" (*akrama*).

Even there, only multiple actions are real, because the production of a new aggregate from a previous aggregate is what constitutes reality. The mention of a single action is due to mere suspicion or logical impossibility [of multiple actions]. Therefore, since even that [single action] is indicated by the term "simultaneity" (*yaugapadya*), the meaning subsumed under non-sequential order should be understood in the word "simultaneity" as well in the treatise.

And since this two-fold mode pertaining to the effect is compatible only with a creator who is subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), its exclusion from what is eternal is stated by way of a function that determines absolute non-existence. However, the word "primarily" (*pradhānyena*) in the phrase "compatibility with momentary destruction" is capable of indicating an exclusion from the momentary as well, just as it does from the eternal. Alternatively, it may be for the purpose of following the rule that "the pervaded exists only there [where the pervader exists]."

By this, it is stated that because for a permanent entity there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—their existence, which is defined by that [causal efficiency], is lost; therefore, it rests solely in momentariness and is pervaded by it. Thus, through the non-perception of the pervader characterized by succession and simultaneity, and because of the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposite case, the pervasion of existence—defined as the capacity for causal efficiency—by momentariness is established.

In this context, when "causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*) is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*), then the conventional expression "the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā-śakti*) has the same meaning. One might raise the objection: "If the property of the object (*karmadharma*) is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, how can there be a conventional usage of pervasion regarding the property of the agent? To this, we reply: even in that case, the causal capacity—which is itself being pervaded by way of having successive and non-successive effects—is said to be "pervaded by succession and non-succession" for the sake of brevity in conventional discourse.

By this, having established the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and relying upon the sequence [of causal efficiency], the objection of Trilocana—that this sequence cannot be excluded from that which is momentary—is refuted as a worthless argument. Furthermore, in the phrase "due to the contradiction with causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā-virodhāt*), causal efficiency must be understood as a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*) alone, because of the statement that "existence is defined by that [causal efficiency]."

Alternatively, if "characteristic" (*lak�șaṇa*) is taken as an "indirect indicator" (*upalakṣaṇa*) rather than an "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), then even the property of an action may be included. In that case, the meaning is that for an eternal entity, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as indicated by succession and simultaneity is contradictory. In the first position, however, the meaning is that for an eternal entity, the capacity for causal activity as indicated by succession and non-succession is contradictory. By using the qualification "by means of succession and simultaneity," there is no suspicion of permitting other [modes], since these are employed for the purpose of establishing the reason (*hetu*).

Since causal efficiency occurs only through succession or simultaneity, it is therefore contradictory to the notion of permanence; this is because permanence entails the transcendence of both succession and simultaneity.

[65,3] What, then, is the contradiction here? First of all, it is not "incompatible coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*), because both would attain the status of real entities (*vastu*) and thus would necessarily be eternally existent. Nor is it the second [type of contradiction]. For if it were argued that the eternal is contradicted by its opposite, the non-eternal;

Because its absolute sublation in [the case of] the eternal is established by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is indeed a contradiction, as stated in the words: "or because of sublation by another valid cognition. In reality, however, the conclusion will rest on mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*) alone. If it is asked: "What, then, is the valid cognition that sublates causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the non-momentary?"—[the answer is: whatever is not employed in causal efficiency characterized by succession or simultaneity is not capable of causal efficiency, just like a lotus in the sky (*hari-padāravinda*). And the entity postulated as eternal is not employed in an action possessing the properties of succession or non-succession; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

Indeed, there is no other mode besides succession and simultaneity by which the possibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) might not be pervaded by those two. Therefore, because [causal efficiency] is invariably concomitant with causal efficiency in general, and because it is absent when either of those two modes is absent, its pervasion by them is established. Thus, since the absence of the capacity for causal efficiency is established in the subject (*pakṣa*) through the absence of those two modes, there is at least no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

In this regard, what Śaṅkara said—while attempting to conceive of an alternative possibility when the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is negated through both successive and simultaneous modes—namely, "Nor is the non-existence of a third alternative established, because the negation of a specific case implies the admission of the remainder," has been refuted.

However, by the statement regarding the meaning of being a cause, it is argued that if [an object] has a perceivable nature (*upalabhyasvabhāvatva*), its absolute non-existence cannot be established precisely because of that very perceivable nature, as in the case of a cloth or similar objects; whereas if it has an imperceivable nature (*anupalabhyasvabhāvatva*), there is no certainty of its non-existence regarding remote things. Thus, how can there be a certainty of the absence of other modes [of existence], since the grounds for such [certainty] are impossible? So they object.

In that case, if one were to insist on such a restriction, alas, it would destroy the very basis for establishing reality through the delimitation of the number of categories—the distinction between the paths to heaven and liberation. For when a third category is suspected beyond two, a fourth beyond three, a fifth and so on beyond four, then since there would be an infinite number of categories in every instance, how could there be an established order of reality based on restrictions such as "there are only two" or "only three," as in the cases of "the four means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇas*) or "the six categories" (*padārthas*)?

And when even hundreds of other types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are possible, then that which is not established by the four [means] might be established by another, and that which is established by the four might be sublated by another; how, then, could there be a determination of reality (*tattva-vyavasthiti*) on that basis?

Thus, when a thousand [other] objects are established as distinct from substance and so forth, what remains to be practiced for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), since the final determination of reality has been subverted? Furthermore, how could he have refuted the two positions regarding whether the impermanent [self] possesses the capacity to produce cognition or not, having himself already ceased [the inquiry] in this manner, because it is impossible to negate even a hundred such modes?

Furthermore, even animals do not immediately act upon what they perceive as improper; how then could this rash deed have been committed by him? Having restricted the two-fold division [of causes] into sequential and simultaneous based on the non-perception [of a third alternative] and the requirement of a specific qualification of the perceptible, the refutation of duality through [the exclusion of] sequence and simultaneity is indeed impossible for proponents of duality, because it is impossible to demonstrate any other mode [of causal operation].
Therefore, let this one strive for the nourishment of the great ocean of chatter; for when one thing is negated and another is affirmed, the possibility of a third mode is impossible to express.

Furthermore, if a second action occurs immediately after an action at the same time, there is the conventional usage of "succession" (*krama*); if it does not occur, there is "non-succession" (*akrama*). To suspect a third alternative even between existence and non-existence is the height of sophistry! Enough of this persistence. It is established, therefore, that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) is indeed pervaded by succession and non-succession.

Furthermore, Trilocana [argues] that some auxiliary conditions are perceptible, while others are imperceptible. Consequently, the totality of perceptible and imperceptible auxiliary conditions cannot be apprehended through direct perception by one who is not omniscient.

If that were the case, since succession and simultaneity are entirely imperceptible for that which possesses the totality of similar auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), existence (*sattva*)—which is pervaded by them—would likewise be imperceptible; how then could the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) be established through perception? To this he replies: "That too is useless. For it has been demonstrated that succession and non-succession are properties of the effect. Therefore, even in the absence of certainty regarding the completeness or incompleteness of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), the restriction of effects to either succession or simultaneity is indeed within the range of direct perception.

How could it be that the production of an effect occurs at one time and not at another, if this were beyond the scope of perception? For even then, the effect must be either single or manifold; and it is indeed perceived as such by direct perception. Even if multiple [causes] are possible, let it be that only one is perceived; in any case, it is established that the accomplishment of an effect is pervaded exclusively by succession and simultaneity.

[66,21] But surely, on the view of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), there is no cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), nor is there any cognition of succession or simultaneity; so how can pervasion (*vyāpti*) be established? And thus Śaṅkara [says]: "If things were momentary, then because all cognitions would be restricted by their own nature, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the essential forms of cause and effect would not be established; consequently, it would be impossible to ascertain the existence of that [effect] in every case. For the existence of the cause is not perceived through the cognition of the effect, since at that time the cause has already passed away."

Nor is the existence of the effect determined by the cognition of the cause when that [effect] is present, because at that time it has not yet arisen; nor is there an establishment of the past and future through the present, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Nor can the cognition of the cause’s nature be established by the cognition of the effect alone, because it would follow that one could ascertain that smoke is produced by fire even without having observed positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). By this, the cognition of the effect through the mere cognition of the cause is also refuted. Furthermore, for a proponent of self-cognition (*svasaṃvittivādin*), the absence of the effect when the cause is absent is beyond even the reach of their imagination, since there is no possible means for them to apprehend the non-existence of the effect in the absence of the cause.

For it is not logical to claim that something does not exist and yet there is a cognition of it by means of that [cause]. Thus, one who perceives the presence of the effect when the cause is present and its absence when the cause is absent, establishes a persisting synthesizer [of experience].

And thus, if an enduring agent were established, then the fundamental reason of "existence" (*sattva*) would indeed be inconclusive due to commonality (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*); what, then, would the presentation of a proof that subverts the opposite (*viparyayabādhakapramāṇa*) accomplish here? But if that [enduring agent] is not accepted, then because the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible, both [reasons] possess a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṇṛttikatva*). Just as it is impossible to perceive successive causes and effects, so too it is impossible to perceive them in the case of simultaneous effects; thus there is no perception of succession, nor of simultaneity.

As he himself has said: "Nor can simultaneity [be established], because it is impossible to prove the simultaneity of determinate forms by means of a cognition that possesses a different form. Simultaneity cannot be apprehended by that very same number of cognitions, for since they are not mutually cognizable, their simultaneous existence is unproven—just as in the case of distinct mental continua. Nor can a single [cognition] possess multiple forms, because if there is a difference in the forms that constitute its very nature, a difference [in the cognition itself] necessarily follows.

Furthermore, if there were a difference [between the cognition and its forms], it would entail that the cognition is something other than its forms; in that case, the fact that the object possesses those forms could not be established."

To this it is replied: because the cognitions intended to be linked together cannot withstand the conceptual alternatives of being either different or non-different. For if there were non-difference, it would have to be either that very same [self] or the cognitions themselves. In the first case, since there is no action; and in the other case, since there is no agent, what would be the purpose of the linking? Even if there were difference, what would be the purpose of the linking for the person (*jaṭa*) who is distinct from the cognitions? If it is argued that he is the linker because of his connection with the cognitions, like a seer (*draṣṭṛ*); [we reply:]...

In that case, since it is necessarily accepted that cognition alone is the seer and the unifier, what is the point of this borrowed ornament—the claim that another [entity] becomes such through its connection with that [cognition]? If you argue that this is because cognitions lack agency, then it follows that the conventional designation of that self as the "seer" and so forth is untenable even by way of those [cognitions].

For if the intellect (*buddhi*) were the seer of either the cause or the effect, and the synthesizer and conceptualizer of their immediate succession and specific determination, then—by virtue of that connection—it might indeed be said that it possesses the status of a seer and a synthesizer. However, as long as the intellect has not acquired distinction with respect to each particular object, even its connection [to them] is not capable of establishing a distinction in practical discourse, such as: "now it is the cognizer of the cause," "now of the effect," or "now it is the synthesizer."

If, however, one accepts a specific distinction residing within such a cognition, what else remains to be done? For practical discourse is fully accomplished by that alone. If it is argued that without a stable self, that very cognition would not exist, [we reply: so be it.

[68,5] By whom have you been thus deceived? Oh, the greatness of delusion, that it brings even such as these under its power! For instance, when it is said that "this does not exist without that," this is indeed appropriate only when the causal capacity has been determined elsewhere through perception and non-perception, as in the case of fire with respect to smoke; or, as in the case of the eyes and other [senses], when the collection of visible causes is present, if the effect is not seen and is later seen, one concludes in a general manner that something else must be required.

The first position is clearly untenable. The second is also not possible. For when the cognition of the effect arises immediately after the cognition of the cause, there is no previously unobserved synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) occurring in one who has engaged in a determination—such as "this was seen by me immediately after that"—on account of which one might postulate the causal capacity of something else. Likewise, memory also [arises] from experience either through some indirect transformation of potentiality, or through the force of its maturation.
If that is so, why is there no memory in one person of what was experienced by another?
Since the relation of "belonging to another" is not established, why such an objection?

In the context of a debate concerning the establishment of a distinct related entity [the self] as different from experience and so forth, to raise an objection by relying on that very [self] which is already established is irrelevant. For once that [self] is established, the debate comes to an end; what further dependence could there be? Therefore, having removed "of another" because it is the subject of dispute, the remaining question—"Why is there no memory in experience?"—is not useful for the matter at hand. However, the following is a fitting formulation of the objection:

If experience is bound to a particular body, why does memory not arise in relation to another body? By saying this, it is as if one were asking: "Why does a seed belonging to one field not produce a sprout in another field? And what logic is there for such a claim?

[68,21] But surely there is no other proximity between experience and recollection than the mere relation of cause and effect; nor is there this restriction regarding the causal relation, namely that the effect must have the same locus as its cause, since we observe the effect of cognition even when it occurs at a place extremely remote from its object. If that were so, then for a sprout as well, there would be no proximity other than the mere fact of being an effect; thus, like cognition, the seed would produce the sprout even when located at a distance.

Now, one might object: "If certain atoms that initiate the seed are established as the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of the sprout, how can they produce a sprout in another field? For you, such a proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is absent. Furthermore, since this [sprout] shares the property of being an effect with consciousness and so forth, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would be produced even at a great distance remains unavoidable. If this is argued:

Why, then, do the atoms of the seed function as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) specifically for the effect that is the sprout, and not for cognition and so forth? Because all things are of the same nature insofar as they are effects. Consequently, like the sprout, cognition would have to exist in that very same location; or else, like cognition and the rest, the sprout would also be produced at a distance. This is because there is no distinction between them in their status as effects, and because the seed functions as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the sprout in exactly the same way as it does for those other things.

[69,6] But surely, that very sprout in which the seed-atoms attain the status of inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is the sprout; so how can it be urged that their inherent causality pertains elsewhere than in the sprout? If this is the case, then since inherent causality—being of a single nature as an effect—is difficult to avoid, it follows by necessity that all [atoms] possess the same form as the sprout and occupy the same location. Thus, your hope for a solution has borne fruit in the most appropriate place!

Furthermore, if all effects are indistinguishable by virtue of being effects, then all causes must likewise be indistinguishable by virtue of being causes; thus, the diversity of the universe would be left without a basis for explanation. Therefore, even though they share the common property of being effects, it is not the case that there is only one single mode for all of them.

Just as, according to you, due to natural diversity, a certain thing functions in some cases as an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), in others as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and in yet others as an efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), so too for us: one effect produces its cause in the very same location, while another produces it in a separated location; furthermore, one effect is by necessity characterized by arising in the location of its cause, while another is otherwise.

Likewise, the possibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) occurs with respect to a single effect and not elsewhere, despite the lack of distinction in their being effects—just as in the case of different lamps or cognitions. Furthermore, regarding such effects, where you establish the status of an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), for us that is the conventional usage of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) in the case of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, but not in other cases.

Furthermore, within such a succession of causes and effects, in one case there is the establishment of a single continuum (*santāna*), while in another there is merely the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*). Thus, despite this difference in process, the duality of effects is established by nature in such a way that even you cannot transcend it; this is settled. And when such a distinction is possible, how could that which possesses the property of arising in the very locus of its own action and instrument arise elsewhere?

Or how could a cause, which is capable of producing its effect only within its own locus (*svādhikaraṇa*), produce that effect elsewhere? Therefore, even in the case of experience, how could it produce a memory—which is generated in the very locus of the experience—elsewhere, like a sprout from a seed? Or else, since memory necessarily arises in the same locus as the experience, just like a sprout, how could it arise elsewhere, such that the objection regarding the undesirable consequence of memory occurring in another body would find any ground?

But in the theory of a self (*ātmavāda*), this difficulty is unavoidable: since that [self] is all-pervading, it would reside in another body by virtue of its very nature of producing memory. Furthermore, the recourse to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) applies only to something eternal. If it is asked, "How is it to be understood that the principle governing experience and memory is like that of the seed and the sprout, and not like anything else?"—[we reply:

even in the case of the seed and the sprout, that principle is determined solely from such observation; and likewise, there is an observed regularity between experience and memory, for when one person possesses an experience in one body, another form [of being] does not possess the resulting memory.

[70,3] But how can the body possess experience? There is no fault, for there is an intention to express a relationship [between the body and experience] by virtue of the body being its substratum, its cause, or having the same cause as it. Furthermore, how does the self possess experience? If you say "by the force of inherence" (samavāya), [we reply:]...

But surely, even *samavāya* (inherence), when accepted as the cause of the cognition "it is here," is merely a conceptual construction based on that very cognition "it is here. And since there is the cognition "here" with respect to the body, why is *samavāya* not also postulated? If it is argued that this is because there is no state of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhatva*) between the body and consciousness, since they are perceived as entirely distinct; ... [the response follows] ... [The text continues: If it is argued that this is because there is no state of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhatva*) between the body and consciousness, since they are perceived as entirely distinct; then [we reply]: No, for the same reason that *samavāya* is postulated—namely, the presence of the cognition "it is here"—there must also be a postulation of *samavāya* between the body and consciousness. For just as the cognition "the cloth is here in the threads" arises due to *samavāya*, so too does the cognition "consciousness is here in the body" arise. Therefore, since the cognition "it is here" exists, *samavāya* must necessarily be postulated. Furthermore, if one were to say that the cognition "it is here" occurs even without *samavāya*—as in the case of a pot on the ground—then why would it not also occur in the case of consciousness in the body? Thus, the postulation of *samavāya* is unavoidable. If it is argued that the cognition "it is here" is based on spatial proximity (*saṃyoga*), then that is incorrect, for such a cognition does not occur in the case of a pot in the sky. Therefore, the cognition "it is here" must indeed be based on *samavāya*. Consequently, since the cognition "consciousness is here in the body" exists, *samavāya* must be postulated. If it is argued that the cognition "it is here" is based on the relation of part and whole (*avayavāvayavin*), then that is also incorrect, for that relation does not exist between the body and consciousness. Therefore, the postulation of *samavāya* remains necessary.
