Now, it may be argued that the rule of cognition as "this is here" applies only to two entities perceived separately; for when two entities are observed in an upper-lower relationship, the use of the locative and nominative cases is appropriate because they are not intermingled. But when there is no separate perception at all, how can one who designates them with the distinction of "this is here" not lose their status as a discerning person? This is so because, in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), no difference is ever observed anywhere. If this is your objection:

For this very reason, having produced by one's own will the cognition "it is here" as being merely a conceptual construction (vikalpamātra) capable of being brought about at will, the so-called inherence (samavāya) is postulated. The establishment of inherence depends upon the cognition "it is here," and the cognition "it is here" would occur only upon the perception of two things. Yet, in no case is there a perception of those two objects; it is merely one's own imagination. Therefore, this [postulation] is merely a means [to an end].

Thus, to apply the designation "possessing intelligence" to a self that does not exist at all is like the story of a barren woman’s son fashioning a horn from a donkey. For when something is postulated for a certain purpose, its non-existence is established by the fact that such a purpose is accomplished by something else; and since the functions of memory and so forth are established as belonging to something other than the self, experience residing in one body is not capable of producing remembrance in another body.

[70,19] But surely, if [the self] were momentary, since memory arises only in another body, how can this be resolved? Or, if one accepts [rebirth in] another life, why would the same undesirable consequence not apply even to a body intended to be a different continuum, given that their distinctness (*anyatva*) is no different? If this is asked, [we reply: such production of memory in another body is difficult to avoid for the self as well; therefore, the consequence applies elsewhere too because distinctness is no different—this is the same [for both positions].

Even if the momentariness of the body is not accepted, its rapid perishability is certainly accepted by them; therefore, the fault is the same, from which fear they accept the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*). Now, if it is argued that in the doctrine of a self there is no fault because memory is produced in the very body conditioned by the karma of that self, then in the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), whose is that karma? For apart from the body, only a momentary cognition (*buddhi*) is possible.

For this very reason, the pleasure, pain, and so forth resulting from that action cannot belong to the momentary agent, because that [agentive] moment lacks the experience thereof. And since the moment that experiences is not the agent, the fault of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) remains as an additional problem; yet, for you, there is no establishment of any [single] karma from which these original faults might be avoided. Furthermore, even the "continuum" (*santāna*), though spoken of, is nothing distinct [from the moments]. Nor do you admit any distinct karma. Thus, it is like painting a picture without a wall.

To this it is replied: First of all, the moment of the agent does not admit of being denied, even in the absence of that action or the enjoyment of its fruit; for a man is not thereby deprived of fire simply because that fire, while producing burning and so forth, is not currently present. Even the final moment is connected [to the result] by way of a causal series (*paramparā*) through its assistance toward that action, precisely because it participates in the enjoyment [of the fruit]. Furthermore, simultaneity is impossible even for cause and effect, yet it is possible for Mount Meru and Mount Mandara.

Therefore, the connection expressed as "this belongs to that" regarding a distinct entity occurs solely by way of benefit (*upakāra*). And such a benefit exists in its full magnitude for the final [moment], which is produced by that [action]; and for the intermediate moments belonging to that same continuum, there exists—either directly or through a succession—the capacity to produce a final moment of that same kind. Thus, since this arises from that very action, their connection to it also occurs solely by way of benefit.

And thus, when the established relation of all [beings] to their respective karma is fixed, it is only in a body brought forth by the sovereign power (*adhipatya*) of that karma that there arises the emergence of moments of intellect and body produced by that karma; not elsewhere, because of the absence of such proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Furthermore, while karma is certainly not distinct [from the person], the designation as if it were separate is merely for the sake of conventional usage.

However, that moment which is said to be connected with prior karma arises as a specific transformation such that, in the end, there occurs a continuum capable of producing a moment that experiences its fruit, as well as the occurrence of a succession of bodies corresponding to that.

In that process, from the first distinguished [moment], those two moments of intellect and body which have arisen as possessing the slightest degree of distinction, acting together, produce subsequent moments possessing a lesser degree of distinction; and those, in turn, produce further subsequent moments with even lesser distinctions. In this manner, the excellence of the specific quality characterized by capacity increases through a progression of degrees—such as "more" and "most"—until the arising of that which is capable of producing the final [result]; that is called the "final."

Because the intellect and the body are mutually bound by their dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), they are distinct from one another; thus, there is no room for the suspicion of duality apart from this specific relationship. Even when assuming another birth, once the impressions of that life's lifespan are exhausted, another body corresponding to it is produced by a moment of mind (*manas*) acting as a cooperative cause alongside the final moment of the decaying physical form; as before, this body provides assistance to the mind, so there is no room for concern regarding memory or the status of being an enjoyer in another body.

And here, there is nothing distinct by way of what is called a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*), because even with respect to the continuum, its establishment is unimpeded precisely through the establishment of the connection of the moments (*kṣaṇa*) with their actions; for that [continuum] is distinct from them. Nor is the presentation of the tenet (*siddhānta*) primarily by way of the continuum, but rather by way of the moments; thus everything is clear once the root has been thoroughly purified. As it has been said: "In whichever very continuum the impression of action (*karmavāsanā*) is deposited, therein alone it bears fruit, just as [the dye] in cotton."
Thus, that [is established] upon the proof of the characteristic of one's own intended continuum.

As for what the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* said while refuting this—namely, "No, because proof and refutation are impossible: there is no proof because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth; for a positive concomitance such as 'memory [arises] from the causal relation, like the redness in cotton' is not possible; nor is there a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) such as 'wherever there is no memory, there is no causal relation'; and there is no refutation because fallacies such as unestablishedness (*asiddhatva*) have not been raised"—[that is rejected].

For subsequent cognitions cannot arise with respect to an object already experienced by a preceding cognition, because they are distinct from it, just like the cognitions of another continuum; thus, no fault whatsoever is established by the example "like the redness in cotton" (29b).

[72,12] That is an unconsidered statement, due to a failure to understand the intended meaning of the proof (*sādhana*). For in this verse, it is not perceived that the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is presented as the reason for memory. What then? It is the latent impression of action (*karmavāsanā*). For a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is indeed the formative influence (*abhisaṃskāra*) produced by action; for that which is infused (*vasita*) is said to be "formatively influenced" (*abhisaṃskṛta*). The bond of results such as experience occurs only in that very continuum (*saṃtāna*) wherein the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) produced by the action has arisen, and not elsewhere.

Having asserted the proposition that "there is no such distinction [between them]," for one who says "just as [dye] is red on a *karpāsa* [cotton] plant," either the difference in the continuum of formations (*saṃskāra-santāna-bheda*) is intended as the reason, and the probandum here is the negation of results such as experience; yet, the suitability for those results is perceived within that very continuum. Thus, this is the formal argument (*prayoga*):

Whatever formation (*saṃskāra*) is deposited within a particular continuum is capable of yielding its fruit only therein and not elsewhere; just as in the continuum of a cotton plant, that which is produced by the application of a dyeing substance in the state of the seed is capable of manifesting the fruit of color in the states of the flower or the fruit, but not in another continuum.
And this formation is the mental continuum generated by actions such as giving.

Thus, with respect to the probandum as a collective whole, it is indeed a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason). For, within that specific continuum, there is a capacity for yielding fruit accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), whereas in any other continuum, there is an absolute incapacity for such; this is because no other cause is required. However, when each [individual] is the probandum, the first is a *svabhāvahetu*.

In the second case, however, there is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). This is because the nature of being a latent impression (*saṃskāratva*), which is pervaded by the giving of its fruit within its own substratum—contrary to the giving of fruit in another continuum—is perceived [to exist] in its own substratum alone. In that regard, if, even when a latent impression exists, the capacity for the giving of fruit in that continuum were to depend upon another cause, then the production of the latent impression through effort would be purposeless. Furthermore, if it possessed the power to give fruit even in another continuum, then a second effort would be redundant.

Nor is it the case that because one *āmalaka* fruit is sprinkled with milk, all *āmalaka* fruits will yield sweet fruit. Therefore, the cultivation (*saṃskāra*) is pervaded by the yielding of its fruit only within its own continuum; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, since it is established by scripture (*āgama*)—and accepted as such—that the cultivation is a specific quality of the mind produced by karma, the response is just as valid as the objection; hence, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*). Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no contradiction, nor is there a failure to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Alternatively, whatever continuum there may be, it is capable of yielding its fruit only when the respective conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*) has been rendered sweet; just as in the case of a cotton continuum, this is a mental continuum—as explained previously.

[73,9] This same principle applies even with respect to the results such as memory (*smṛti*) and so forth. If this [establishment of the relationship between agent and experiencer] were based on the continuum (*saṃtāna*), then it would follow [absurdly] even for a continuum well-known to be connected by way of knowledge or blood (*vidyā-yoni*). Consequently, a disciple would have memory and so forth regarding what was experienced by the teacher, and likewise, a son would have [memory] regarding the experience of the father. Such a continuum is not intended here; rather, it is of the nature of a succession of cause and effect consisting of the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*). What, then, is the definition of the material cause and its product?

The restriction of having a single substratum applies when there is no cause for investigation; even when there is investigation, the restriction of its suitability [to that substratum] remains. For the diverse succession of causes and effects has already been established previously, and it was also indicated therein that such a succession characterized by these features is called a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*). Furthermore, this is not the case for the minds of teacher and student, or the minds of father and son; thus, the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) alleged by the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* does not apply. Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) regarding the determination of the continuum and the determination of the material cause (*upādāna*), because it has been demonstrated that the determination of the material cause does not depend upon that [determination of the continuum].

Alternatively, the consensus of those who are free from error regarding the single [continuum] is that both the original nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformation (*vikṛti*) constitute the characteristic of cause and effect as the material cause (*upādāna*) and the product (*upādeya*). Within the continuum of cause and effect, this should be understood as being characterized by the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which discerns: "this is the material cause" and "this is the product. However, in the case of the arising of something dissimilar (*visabhāga*), the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) itself constitutes the characteristic of the material cause as the original nature and the product as the transformation.

Alternatively, the definition is "the state of being both a material cause and an effect"; this is an expression where the abstract quality (*bhāva*) is the primary referent, as in the cases of "wood as a sacrificial post" (*kāṣṭhayūpa*) and "wood as charcoal" (*kāṣṭhāṅgāra*). Even when multiple [effects] arise, only the distinct parts are the material cause, just as in the case of smoke, heat, and so forth, the embers are the cause. Furthermore, even in the case of cognition (*buddhi*), there is a single conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) and a single determination (*avasāya*) regarding a person. And indeed, for one who discerns the coloring by objects and reflects upon pure consciousness alone, there arises the determination within that continuum accepted as a single person: "This is that very same cognition."

Furthermore, because they do not reproduce the entire nature [of the cause] here, or even if reproduction were possible, the determination of them as one—as in the case of a different tree—is erroneous; thus, there is no established relation of material cause and so forth between father and son. Therefore, if one establishes the relation of material cause and so forth in such a continuum without depending on the definition of material cause and so forth, then when the question arises as to what kind of continuum the karmic impression (*vāsanā*) is deposited in, there is no fault in stating that it is "in that wherein the relation of material cause and so forth exists."

Furthermore, he says this: No, for in the absence of a specific relation, a distinction between material cause (*upādāna*) and other causes cannot be established based merely on a difference in the nature of the cause. Just as in our view, although there is no difference in their status as producers (*janakatva*), there is a distinction between inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes due to a specific relation, we do not see such a distinction between material and other causes in your system.

This too is indeed refuted, because even with respect to the general nature of causality, a distinction has been shown in relation to the effect. For if cause and effect were not dependent upon each other's specificities, the difficulty of establishing their relationship—even by way of a connection—has already been pointed out. Furthermore, it has been indicated at least in part that inherence (*samavāya*) is not capable [of serving as such a connection]. Therefore, there is no refutation whatsoever of either the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) or the continuum (*santāna*).

[74,11] Even though the term "karmavāsanā" (karmic impression) is employed here in this verse, its meaning does not follow that of cotton; nevertheless, since the meaning of "vāsanā" as "abhisaṃskāra" (formative activity) does indeed follow, it is that very [activity] which should be understood as the indicated cause. Alternatively, by the word "karman" (action), "kriyā" (activity) is also meant; the sense is that whatever formative activity has been produced by any kind of activity within a continuum. By this, the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is shown; the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), however, is to be understood from the context.

Therefore, having taken up that which was stated—namely, that memory establishes the relationship between cause and effect directly—all of that is undermined; however, the position that memory conforms to the specific particulars that serve as the basis for the causal relationship is faultless.

Furthermore, regarding the argument that there can be no recollection by subsequent cognitions of an object experienced by a preceding cognition because they are distinct, like the cognitions of a different mental continuum (*santānāntara*): in this case, is it being denied that the subsequent cognitions—which are the subjects (*dharmin*)—have a connection with a cognition whose nature is recollection? Or is it that their very nature as recollection is being excluded? Or is it being established that they do not result in the fruit of recollection? First of all, the first position is untenable.

For we do not maintain that memory is one thing and the cognition possessing memory another, such that there would be a negation [of the latter]; rather, that cognition is of the very nature of memory itself.

If it is argued that at the time of looking at a cow while remembering a horse, that perception becomes "possessing memory," then is it intended to negate memory only in that specific state? If memory exists as such in its own right, let it be so. If this is not the case, then what is the point of this reference to concomitance regarding subsequent cognitions?

If it is argued that the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) is solely for the sake of inference (*anumāna*), we say no; for once the intended entirety of the matter has been established, it is desired at all times thereafter that there be a negation of memory. Consequently, the means of proof (*sādhana*) would suffer from the fallacy of being unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhi*). Alternatively, if you maintain that negation is not intended at the time of mere memory when incapacity is observed, then what fault has the time associated with another cognition committed, such that—given the possibility of memory occurring at a later time even without a self—negation should apply only to that specific instance? Furthermore, there is no subverting argument whatsoever regarding the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In the second case, however, regarding the denial of the status of memory for subsequent cognitions, does this mean that experience itself is denied the status of memory, or rather that previous cognitions are? If it is a denial in all respects, then what is the point of specifying a particular distinction, as was the case before?

Regarding the third alternative, the futility of specifying such a distinction must be established in exactly the same way. Now, if it is intended that because the specification of a distinction is merely illustrative, no cognition other than experience itself has the nature of memory, nor does it produce memory—then the fact that experience possesses such a nature (i.e., being of the nature of memory) has not been refuted; consequently, both [positions]—that experience is of the nature of memory and that it produces memory—are undesired consequences that follow.

Otherwise, the qualification "as something other than experience" would be meaningless. Let it be meaningless; even so, if "being other than experience" were the reason for all cognitions, it would be unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*), because experience itself is not "other than that."

Furthermore, the mention of "subsequent" (*uttara*) is intended as a subject of dispute (*vivādapada*), and not for the purpose of excluding others; for even the Buddhist does not accept that other cognitions possess the nature of memory. Nevertheless, this is not a valid response under the third alternative, because experience (*anubhava*) itself is also a subject of dispute. For, under the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), it is precisely what you do not accept that experience produces memory directly; whereas for the Buddhist, this is accepted. Thus, this [opponent] is unable to accept that experience generates memory because it is undesirable, yet he cannot reject it either, because the reason [he offers] is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhi*).

[75,16] Let it be so; nevertheless, pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be established even in either of the two positions. For instance, regarding that subsequent cognition which is intended to possess the nature of memory or the capacity to produce memory—if its difference from experience were to be established upon the attainment of both [properties], such that its non-difference from them could not be maintained, then pervasion would fail because its difference from them would be negated by those two properties. And this is not possible.

If its distinctness from experience were abandoned, it would simply be experience; and how could that be called "recollection"? Furthermore, if it is said to be the producer of recollection, then that [status] does not rest without presupposing that experience is the cause of recollection. For a reductio (*prasaṅga*) is applicable only when a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been established. Likewise, [arguments] such as "occurring at a later time" and so forth should not even be suspected, for they can be countered in the same manner. However, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, if you are intent on raising objections, you should speak in this way.

If it is argued that remembrance, experience, and so forth are produced from mere experience or mere karma alone, then it would follow that they could arise even in a different continuum (*santāna*), which is not accepted. Whatever possesses identical capacity or incapacity with respect to something else must possess identical fruitfulness or fruitlessness with respect to that thing, just as the two sets of causal conditions consisting of seed, earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth [produce the same fruit]. Furthermore, the two continua possess identical capacity and incapacity with respect to experience as well; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

And the proof for this has already been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "yasminn eva hi... and so forth, since the specific nature of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) was clearly stated [in the verse] beginning with "karmavāsanā... (31a), just as we previously explained. Likewise, the principle that memory arises from experience follows the same logic.

Alternatively, this objection concerns the reason stated previously: namely, that this principle—that there is no production because of difference—applies only to experience, memory, and so forth, which are considered cause and effect in a continuous series, but not to other things. If it applies only to the case at hand, then some logical justification must be provided for this principle obtained as a specific instance; otherwise, this particularity would have to be understood here by overriding the sequence established in general. If you argue that it is because such a thing is not observed in the case of a different continuum (*santānāntara*), [we reply:]...

If production occurs through a succession of specific qualities, then in the absence of those [qualities], that [production] would not be observed, just as redness is not observed in cotton seeds that lack the dyeing process. However, it cannot be claimed on that basis alone that there is no production whatsoever in all cases.

In the second case, however, this is merely an objection raised on the grounds of non-establishment (*asiddhi*). For when a seed is red, one observes that the flowers or fruits produced in its continuum are also colored by that same hue. As for the argument that memory cannot be explained by the relation of cause and effect because of the lack of deception regarding their distinctness (*nānātva*), here too the poor woman "shame" (*trapā*) has been cast aside by that very statement; if the effect were excluded from the cultivated cotton, everything would be fine. Thus, this is a general logical principle established by common consensus.

Even if they are distinct, the restriction that a result occurs in one continuum and not in another—due to dependence on other specific conditions—is impossible to prevent even in the present case. Whether this verse establishes a proof or provides a refutation, let that be for now. Thus it is established: even in the absence of a single, permanent entity, recollection occurs through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced in a continuum by experience. Furthermore, perception has never been observed to have the same substratum as recollection.

[76,19] As for what was said here—that it is not so, because it is observed: for one determines that the experience and the recollection have a single substratum, thinking, "I now remember that very object which I previously experienced; I who was the experiencer am the same I who am the rememberer. This determination does not depend on the recollection of a connection with a logical mark (*liṅga*), nor does it depend on the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*). Nor is this a delusion, because there is no contradiction [with reality]. Furthermore, one who denies the perceptibility of pleasure and so forth need not be instructed by means of sensory perception.

Likewise, the fact that even the desire for recollection, aversion, and so forth, have a single cause is apprehended through perception: "I see that which I previously saw"; "Having seen it, I desire it or I feel aversion toward it"; "Desiring it or feeling aversion, I exert effort"; "Exerting effort, having attained that object, I have become happy or miserable."

Thus, since memory, synthesis, desire, and so forth—which have as their locus that object which appears in the cognition "I"—manifest through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the self is apprehended by direct perception. For the cognition "I" is neither doubtful nor erroneous; nor is it inferential or verbal. That [objection] too is merely a false satisfaction. To explain: this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) first exists in the form, "I alone am the seer and the rememberer."
Furthermore, not every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is an object of trust. Thus, it has been shown by Trilocana that it is fourfold.

Among these, it cannot first of all be one that arises subsequent to perception (*pratyakṣapṛṣṭhabhāvī*), because you yourself do not admit the existence of another perception that could grasp it, such that this [conceptualization] could be described as its "subsequent" state. Its status as being based on inference (*laukikatva*) has also been refuted by yourself. Therefore, if you accept as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) something that is either without a real basis (*avastuka*) or whose basis is doubtful, what limit is there to your concessions?

Now, if this fifth [type of] perception is asserted as distinct from these, then this same logic would easily apply to every object that one personally favors but lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, there would be no obstruction to the establishment [of such objects].
If it is argued that [perception] is distinguished by its being a conscious experience (*saṃvedana*), [the response follows:]

Furthermore, it has already been largely established that this "corroboration" (*saṃvāda*) must consist either in the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-prāpti*) or in the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara-vṛtti*). And if another means of valid cognition exists, let that alone suffice; what is the use of this [corroboration]? Moreover, no purposeful action is ascertained that is to be accomplished by something enduring, since everything is established through the intellect and the body. Nor is the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) directed toward anything beyond those two.

For just as in the case of the recognition "This is that Caitra," where Caitra’s body alone is recognized as a single entity across prior and subsequent times by disregarding the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and states, so too is it with this cognition: "I myself am the seer and the rememberer. This is merely a conventional designation based on the intellect (*buddhi*), such as when one says, "He who was a fool is now a wise man."

Furthermore, some designation is made by way of the body, as in "I am fair" or "I am fat," because it is well known that a designation for a whole is made through a part. Yet another is by way of both, as in "the kingdom was ruled by me" or "my misfortune," and so forth; these should be inferred according to their respective cases.

Even the designations based on pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*) are merely designations for the intellect (*buddhi*), because there is no difference between them and the intellect—as seen in such expressions as "I am happy" up to "I am righteous. Even the designation of distinction, such as "the face belongs to him" or "the body belongs to him," is intended to express a distinction between a whole and a part, just as one says "the branch of the tree. For this very reason, the expression "I am the face" does not occur.

[77,22] How then is it that "my intellect and body" are spoken of? It is just as one says "the body of a stone-son" (*śilā-putraka*). In that case, one might also say "intellect-body"; for have we not also seen such expressions as "the body of a stone-son" or "the head of Rāhu"? And just as in that very case there is the conventional usage "my self" even though a second self does not exist, so too is it the same when a first self does not exist, in the expression "my intellect and body. And just as it is not the case that "I am the self," so too it is not the case that "I am the intellect and body."

If it is argued that because the meaning has already been stated by the expression "I am the self," it is not fit for further application, [we reply: the same applies to the expressions "I am the intellect" and "I am the body," as their meaning has likewise already been stated. Furthermore, wise men do not insist upon words that depend solely upon mere whim; so let this matter rest for now.

Therefore, this word "I" (aham) of the speaker is intent upon the negation of another, but it does not refer to any other entity apart from the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body (*vigraha*). And because of the identification (*ekādhyavasāya*) of those two—the intellect and the body—even when they are past or future—with the present [self], one employs such expressions as, "It was seen by me alone," "It was touched by me alone," and "It was remembered by me. Consequently, just as in the case of "This is that Caitra," this is merely a superimposition of unity upon the two aggregates across earlier and later times; it is not a reference to a distinct entity.
If it is argued that Caitra himself is the very self being recognized (*pratyabhijñāyate*), [we reply:]...

No, because there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of what has not been perceived; for it is only the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body (*vigraha*) that are perceived. And although the intellect of another is inferable, nevertheless, due to extreme habituation, one observes its functioning as if it were directly perceived (*adhyakṣavat*), so there is no fault. For it is observed that from the mere sight of a friend or an enemy, one carries out actions corresponding to them; and in that case, there is no delay in following the form of an inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Nor is such performance [of religious rites] possible through the apprehension of the body alone, for that would entail the absurd consequence [of efficacy] even in the case of a dead corpse. Furthermore, because it is the motivator of all bodily activity, the very perception of the self by the intellect from birth onwards remains constantly present as the seed for the practice of association with it in future lives as well. However, there is no such perception of the self to serve as a seed for practice, since all activity is exhausted within the body and consciousness alone.

Therefore, it is the mind and body alone, which are the objects of the word "Caitra," that are recognized as "this is that very same one. Likewise, regarding those two which have sound as their object, this is merely a recognition: "This was seen by me," "This was remembered by me," or even "This was done by me," "This will be experienced by me"—all of which are merely determinations of oneness belonging to those two alone.

Therefore, in this position, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which follows immediately upon perception has for its object a state of reassurance; however, if it refers to mere existence or unity across preceding and succeeding moments, it is devoid of a real entity (*avastuka*). But if its object is something distinct [from the momentary], then—even though the object appears—because of the confusion between doubts as to whether it is unreal or real, it is of a doubtful nature (*sandigdhavastuka*); how, then, could it establish for itself the status of being established by perception?

Furthermore, that which he proclaims—the inference that "the various states such as desire and so forth belong to a single related entity, because they are the objects of the unifying cognition 'mine,' just as spectators are the objects of the unifying cognition of a single dancer"—that too merely reveals his extreme lack of intelligence. For there is no dancer who is in reality a single entity, since she is nothing more than a collection of atoms presided over by consciousness.

If it is argued that, having relied upon a unity established by conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) for the sake of establishing the example, who can prevent that which is established by conventional usage from applying to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well? And if it is claimed that the example is not [identical] in every respect;

This is true. However, by whose power could a real identity (*tāttvikam ekatvam*) be established, given that its concomitance is not observed in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and thus pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not proven? For pervasion, which relies on the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is established even when it is seen in an example; but regarding what is not seen, there is not even the possibility of such establishment. Therefore, while it is said that an example need not be common in every respect, it must at least necessarily be common with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).

Indeed, there is no purpose for an example other than the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*); nor does the demonstration of pervasion become shown by means of a probandum that has not been exhibited in the example. Furthermore, the removal of the charge of being devoid of the probandum is not achieved by establishing [the subject] as a single composite whole (*avayavin*), because the dancer lacks the status of a composite whole insofar as she is a collection of body, intellect, and so forth. On the contrary, with respect to the body, the refutation of the composite whole remains very much alive.

But with respect to the self, that [self] remains unestablished even today; and because there is no sublation of the contrary, there is no peace from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). For the recognition "this is mine" may indeed occur—like a memory—due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādy-avidyā*) as a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); how then could it be accepted as being dependent upon a single underlying relation?

Thus, just as for the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), the entirety of the connection between memory and the fruit of action and so forth does not fail even in the absence of a persisting entity (*avasthātṛ*), so too is the cognition of the relation of cause and effect; therefore, there is no stain of doubt regarding a non-exclusive inconclusiveness (*asādhāraṇānekānta*).

Maṅkara, however, because of his loquacity, performs some sort of dramatic gesture. For instance: sometimes the cognition of smoke, preceded by the perception [of fire], produces a certain determination that "this object, grey like the neck of a pigeon, is an effect of fire"; sometimes there is a non-perception preceded by the perception of both [the fire and the smoke]. Furthermore, since non-perception has the nature of perceiving the counter-positive object, it is indeed of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moreover, since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established in the context of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), it must be determined in that very same place.
The method for apprehending positive and negative concomitance through perception and non-perception has also been demonstrated in the investigation of the triad and pentad; let that suffice for now.

We shall, however, speak of the matter at hand. In both cases, among cognitions occurring in succession, because each preceding one deposits a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the final cognition succeeds—just as before—in producing the thought, "this is the effect of that," without requiring the persistence of a persisting entity on the part of the synthesizer.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that "the exclusion [of one thing from another] is not even within the scope of a mental wish"—that is an extreme absurdity. For it is not claimed that the very same perception which apprehends a real object also apprehends the exclusion of two objects upon the cessation of those two objects; rather, it is simply another perception whose nature is the apprehension of a distinct counter-positive object. Therefore, where does the argument—"that [exclusion] does not exist, and thus there can be no cognition of it"—serve? It is not logical.

And in this way, there is no consistency with the doctrine of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) regarding perception. If it is argued that there are two cognitions in the preceding and succeeding moments, that from those two arises a latent impression (*vāsanā*), and from that [impression] arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines cause and effect—[we reply: no.

[80,1] Now, do you follow this rule: "Whatever might be suspected must be stated"? For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would have to be either a synthesis of what has been perceived or a superimposition of a form that does not belong to the object. It cannot be the former position, because for a person who has not observed positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there can be no grasping of the causal relation; consequently, a specific latent impression (*vāsanā-viśeṣa*), which is the cause of the cognition of synthesis, is impossible. Furthermore, if there were synthesis of what has not been grasped, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

This consideration is not correct; for, since the preceding and succeeding moments, which stand in the relation of cause and effect, are directly perceived through sequential experience, their status as cause and effect is indeed grasped. It is simply that, because the effect is absent at the time of the cause, even though the capacity regarding that object is grasped, the determination [of the causal relationship] does not yet proceed due to the non-perception of the effect; it only proceeds upon the observation of the effect.

Likewise, even when observing the effect, its status as an effect is apprehended and subsequently synthesized by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*); thus, this conceptual thought consists precisely in the synthesis of what has already been apprehended. Furthermore, the grasping of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been established through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*); therefore, this [objection] is trivial. By this, that which was said is also refuted: namely, that for one who has not observed positive and negative concomitance, the causal relation between a latent impression (*vāsanā*) and the cause of that impression is not established; and since the same objection applies there as well, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

[80,13] Indeed, the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the subject at hand has already been established. The proof of the positive and negative concomitance between latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows from the final instance of perceptual non-apprehension (*adhyakṣānupalambha*), because activity does not occur based on a solitary perception or non-apprehension; for since a latent impression is by nature a capacity (*śakti-svabhāva*), its establishment is impossible without an effect.

Furthermore, for that [cognition] which is thus established, its positive and negative concomitance with its own cause—namely, experience—is proven precisely through the positive and negative concomitance of the effect. Nor does the first objection hold: as long as there is no conceptual construction of synthesis (*anusandhāna-vikalpa*), there is no proof of positive and negative concomitance regarding the latent impression (*vāsanā*) or the cause of the latent impression; and as long as there is no proof of positive and negative concomitance regarding the latent impression or its cause, there is no conceptual construction of synthesis.

For the conceptual construction of synthesis (*anusandhāna-vikalpa*) does not depend upon a determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-niścaya*) regarding the latent impression (*vāsanā*) or the cause of the latent impression; rather, it depends merely on the existence within one’s own continuum of those two—synthesis and latent impression—which possess positive and negative concomitance. However, the determination of their positive and negative concomitance does indeed depend upon the conceptual construction of synthesis. In this regard, just as smoke—which is dependent [on fire]—does not involve mutual dependence because it does not depend on the determination of the positive and negative concomitance of the modifications of fire and fuel, so it is in the case at hand as well. Enough with excessive talk.

As for the position that superimposes a nature not belonging to it, we have already set it aside by disregarding it, since the resulting refutation pertains to an irrelevant matter. Therefore, it is established that the cognition of the causal relation is unconfused and [the object] is indeed impermanent.

Furthermore, when those two are established, the perception of sequence is unavoidable, because the cognition that "this being present, this arises from that" is inseparable from the determination of sequence. Otherwise, the application of distinct grammatical case-endings to denote the cause and the effect would be untenable, as there would be no restriction regarding their respective objects. For there is no difference in terms of the requirement for sequence, whether the perception of sequence pertains to the cause and the effect, or to two effects.

There is not even a suspicion of simultaneity, because immediately after the observation of several [objects] at one time, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises—just as a sprout emerges from a seed—that "these have arisen all at once. Indeed, there is no fault or contradiction regarding momentariness caused by the apprehension of the arising of those multiple effects. For while in the case of sequential perception, there might be a superficial synthesis based on a stable [entity], in the case of simultaneous perception, what need is there for a stable entity?

It might be argued that in the case of simultaneous perception, it would follow that there must be another cognizer immediately following; however, that has already been refuted previously. Or rather, let that very point be stated; what is the use of this belching out a refutation of cognition with forms (*sākāra*), which is like scratching an itch where there is no wound, since it is irrelevant to the topic? If you mean "apprehension," then let there be apprehension of multiple things simultaneously by means of either a cognition with form or one without form; why then insist at this moment on the practice of reaching the ultimate limit of all reality?

If, however, it is intended that there is simply no simultaneous apprehension of multiple [objects], then let it be the same as the refutation of the theory of forms (*sākāra*); for otherwise, apprehension by that very [single cognition] would be suspected. Furthermore, how is the absence of the apprehension of multiple [objects] simultaneously intended? Is it because multiple [objects] do not exist at once, or because the mode of apprehension is impossible?

[81,15] First, in the case of the initial eon, how is it that the transformation of the wick, the destruction of darkness, and so forth, are produced by the lamp itself? For us, however, this being the case, there is only a simplification of effort and no harm; for the proof of the thesis is established precisely through the refutation of succession in the case of the eternal.

But in the second case, on what basis is the conventional usage of "many" established? Let it be established by inference. If, when asked "What is that inference?", you provide an explanation, then let simultaneity—accompanied by succession and pervading purposeful action (arthakriyā)—be established by inference; how then can there be the fault of being devoid of an inherent nature (*prakṛti*)? If, however, you do not provide an explanation, you are defeated by that alone. Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous grasping or non-grasping of many [objects], it would be better to accept simply that the internal organ, the mind (*manas*), is incapable of functioning toward many objects simultaneously; what is the use of this [other argument]?

[81,23] Now, if it is thought that a single synthesizer of multiple forms and multiple cognitions must be postulated, then what of it? For our current position is undermined by the admission of a permanent [synthesizer], since that would involve succession; otherwise, however, this would merely be an entry into another [competing] theory. If it is argued that, in the same way, a synthesizer is established even in the case of succession—

Even that [cognition] would be established only if it were proven by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that its apprehension is invariably concomitant with having a form (*sākāra*); otherwise, since mere assertion is easily made, the opponent could simply maintain that [cognition] is formless and thus resolve the matter. Furthermore, there is no effort to prove the existence of forms; rather, it is the object itself that has been established as possessing that form. Therefore, how could one state that [cognition] is independent of that [object], or even that it is imperishable?

And in this case, even if one accepts a synthesizer that is not incompatible with instability, there is no necessity to accept [its] succession, just as one who desires an entity of non-different nature to produce effects in different locations does not necessarily desire it to do so at different times. Therefore, for the sake of accepting a synthesizer in relation to succession, another mode must be resorted to; what is the use of this [present argument]? Consequently, he has followed this method [thinking]: "In some way, a solution to the knot must be made. This is not being refuted here because it is not the occasion for a rebuttal of the criticism regarding the form [of the argument].
Now, even so, if cognition possesses a form, and there is no mutual perception of distinct [objects] because this manifestation is one and the same, then no contradiction arises here.

Therefore, the objection that [the whole] is either capable or incapable [of action] is refuted; likewise, the fault regarding momentariness does not apply to the composite whole, nor is there any contradiction with its possessing a form.

Indeed, for this very reason it was said: "This is not the occasion for a refutation of that. For neither the non-establishment of that [the whole] nor the establishment of the composite (avayavin) is a subverter for us. Furthermore, even the Sautrāntika tenet regarding the quality of being desired, which follows from the three [qualities] being eternal, is not subverted in its partial aspect.
If not, then by denying the person (pudgala), one commits an offense precisely by contradicting the established tenets of the Buddha.
Therefore,
if this doctrine of mine— that cognition possesses a form—
should be faulty, how could it possibly be sublated by means of valid cognition?

If that [external object] is established by valid cognition, let it be so; however, this convention belongs only to the mind—that there is a single persistence even within a variegated external [object]—and thus the external is indeed abolished.

For among entities, a difference in form is invariably concomitant with a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). In that case, if there were no difference in causal efficiency despite a difference in form, then—alas!—since nothing would exist beyond a mere difference in appearance, the consequence would be the total denial of external objects. Therefore, this [proponent] must necessarily admit that for an external thing, a difference in form entails a difference [in the object itself], whether or not the cognition differs; for even if they were of equal status, the cognition alone is not capable of being apprehended [as the object].

Otherwise, the consequences of self-awareness and the illumination of another would also apply to external objects, which would utterly subvert the very relationship between the grasped and the grasper. Therefore, if the unity of cognition is established by valid means of knowledge, let it belong to that very cognition which possesses manifold forms; but the external object, having distinct forms, must indeed be distinct.

If it is asked, "How can even the external world, which has diverse forms, be [considered] non-different?", let the three worlds be but a single entity; what is lost to us? However, it has been stated that in the absence of distinct purposes, functions, and applications, this [external world] would not exceed the status of being a mere appearance, like a city of Gandharvas. Furthermore, there is no occasion here for a distinction such as "unity in some cases and difference in others."

[83,10] Now, if even the unity of cognition (*buddhi*) is merely a conventional agreement (*samaya*) and not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then let that very convention—which is subject to sublation and contradiction—be faulty. But how can this present distinction between entities, brought forth by valid means of knowledge, be abandoned simply because of mutual contradiction? [83,13] Furthermore, if the reason (*hetu*) is defeated by the speaker’s reliance on convention, then [it is defeated] within that convention.

Let this [objection] be yours; however, for a proponent, there is no consideration of a formal agreement (*samaya*). Indeed, it is not the agreement of the speaker that "one must speak while remaining within the treatise" when establishing the validity of a statement.
For in the process of inferring through various forms [of evidence], scripture (*āgama*) possesses no quality as a means of proof.

Moreover, for us, difference is not merely contradiction, but rather [the distinction] between being capable and incapable. And this must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, since the debate would terminate due to the dispersal of the pursuit of that which is capable of establishing or refuting, what would be the point of anything else? Therefore, difference by way of capacity and incapacity is difficult to avoid.

Consequently, even if contradiction alone deviates from difference, there is no deviation for the specific feature under discussion, just as smoke, though it may deviate from fire, does not deviate from the entity characterized as smoke.

If it is argued that there is indeed a distinction based on being capable or incapable [of producing an effect], and that this distinction arises precisely from contradiction (*virodha*), and that such [contradiction] is fallible (*vyabhicārī*); [we reply: smoke too is a probans (*hetu*) and a signifier (*gamaka*) precisely because it is a real entity (*vastutva*), and yet "being a real entity" is fallible—this is the same [in both cases]. Therefore, the meaning is that smoke is a signifier of fire precisely because it is a real entity, not by setting aside its being a real entity. But it is not the case that everything that is a real entity is a signifier. Likewise, the meaning is that the distinction between being capable and incapable is established precisely through contradiction; thus, it is not by discarding contradiction [that the distinction is made].

However, it is not the case that as long as there is contradiction, so long does it prove difference. And it has been said: "If contradiction were to deviate from difference, then this specific [contradiction] intended for the cognition of difference would prevail by way of its capacity and otherness;
yet if it were powerful even in a powerless generality, then one would have no hope for fire from smoke—that thing which never deviates from the crested one."

If, due to contradiction alone, the stronger or weaker status [of two things] is established without abandoning their common nature as entities, then even that smoke would be strong in relation to fire;
or else, let smoke deviate from the entity fire, yet its difference [from it] remains powerful.
This same principle applies even to the subject at hand: the occurrence [of a result] is established by valid cognition.

For if there were no difference between that which is capable and that which is incapable, the entire triple world would be thrown into total confusion, being stuck in a state of neither activity nor cessation; therefore, the contradiction between capacity and its opposite must necessarily be accepted as proving their difference, whether this occurs through the medium of form or not. But surely, even the difference in form is inseparable from the difference in capacity—so what constitutes the distinction? True; this is exactly so in the case of external things, for water, fire, and so forth are perceived in precisely that way.

Otherwise, there would be no such thing as an "external" object at all, since nothing remains but mere appearance. As for the forms (*ākāra*) of cognition, they are not useful in acts such as burning or immersing, because those functions pertain to external things. Furthermore, even regarding effects such as determination (*avasāya*), that too is subject to the dispute over whether it is identical to or different from another form; so how can a single operation be demonstrated in one and the same place?

Or let there be some single effect; even in that case, it must be considered whether one assumes a single uniform operation by means of abstraction (*apoddhāra*), or whether it arises precisely from diversity. Furthermore, we have no compulsion in proving the unity or multiplicity of variegated cognition (*citrabuddhi*); our intention concerns only its having a form (*sākāratā*). As for the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), we have no insistence on that either. And when an object that is not invariably concomitant (*anāntarīyaka*) is sublated, what harm is done to another? (PV IV 47cd)

According to this principle, therefore, the determination of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) regarding the capacity of an object and its sequential or non-sequential nature is not established by mere non-perception.

Furthermore, as for what is said: "If it is pervaded successively, then how can it be pervaded non-successively? Or if it is pervaded non-successively, then it is not pervaded successively. By one who asserts that it is pervaded by both succession and non-succession, the very absence of pervasion is demonstrated. For pervasion consists in this form: the existence of the pervaded only where the pervader exists. Thus, by asserting both, the essential nature of the pervader is abandoned. Indeed, fire is not said to be pervaded by both smoke and the absence of smoke.

What indeed can be said against such a speaker? For he has, by this sequence, offered a final libation of water to the mass of objections raised through various conceptualizations—both by those who follow the path of all logicians and by himself.

One might argue that by refuting these various modes [of proof], their non-existence is established, and thus the object of knowledge (*prameya*) would be non-existent; having thus conceptualized this, they offer refutations. However, if the object of knowledge to be refuted is not pervaded by those modes, then even in their absence, there is no necessary rule (*niyama*) regarding its own absence. Thus, even when refutations are stated, doubt remains just as before; therefore, enough with such arguments. Alternatively, if there were a necessary rule that its absence follows from the absence of those modes, then that very rule would constitute the meaning of pervasion (*vyāpti*); so what is there to be negated?

And so, one who does not accept the substantiality (*vastutva*) of the continuum (*santāna*) begins his refutation by considering the alternatives of whether it is distinct or non-distinct; and since he would find satisfaction only in demonstrating the absence of both, he cannot succeed without accepting that substance is pervaded by both difference and non-difference. This remains the case even for the alternatives of three and so forth. Therefore, the logical principle is this: there is no pervasion by each individual alternative, but there is indeed pervasion by their totality. Just as, for example, if someone is none of Yudhiṣṭhira or the others, he cannot be a Pāṇḍava at all.

For when one [instance] is excluded, reality existed by relying on another mode; but when there is an absence of all modes, where could it be? Therefore, a restricted exclusion is indeed a pervasion (*vyāpti*).

As for what was said—that fire is not pervaded by both smoke and the absence of smoke—that too is most wretched. For the pervasion proposed belongs to those who maintain that the arising of an effect is pervaded by succession and non-succession, and it is characterized by the absence of any third category; how, then, is this relevant here? Indeed, smoke and the absence of smoke are not properties of fire in the same way that succession and non-succession are properties of effects. Rather, it is the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*) that is intended here by the term "property" (*dharma*).

If, by the phrase "by means of smoke and the absence of smoke," what is intended is "by means of possessing smoke and not possessing smoke," then what is the connection for the cognition of that connection? For fire is never found anywhere existing devoid of those two states.

Now, if it is argued that just as the aforementioned property [of fire] is invariably concomitant with smoke, so too is it certain in the case of smoke as a distinct entity and in that which is denoted by the term "absence of smoke"—and therefore how could there not be pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this [fire] by those two as well, since the definition of a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) remains intact; for indeed, wherever there is an absence of both smoke and the absence of smoke, there is also an absence of fire, and wherever there is fire, there is the possibility of one or the other of those two, just as when smoke exists, there is the possibility of one or another of the various types of fire— [Response: This is not so. For the absence of smoke is not invariably concomitant with the absence of fire, because smoke is observed even in the absence of fire, such as in the case of a mirage. Nor is the absence of the absence of smoke invariably concomitant with the presence of fire, because the absence of the absence of smoke is established even where fire is absent, namely, in the very presence of smoke itself. Furthermore, the absence of smoke is not invariably concomitant with the absence of the absence of smoke, because the absence of smoke is observed even where the absence of the absence of smoke is present, such as in the case of a mirage. Likewise, the absence of the absence of smoke is not invariably concomitant with the presence of fire, because the absence of the absence of smoke is established even where fire is absent, namely, in the very presence of smoke itself. [86,3] If this is your insistence, what fault is there in that? For mere non-desire (*aniṣṭi-mātra*) is not a constituent part [of a valid argument]. Indeed, pervasion (*vyāpti*)—when sought for the purpose of the necessary exclusion of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) by means of the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), so that when the pervaded is present, one of the specific varieties of the pervader must also be present—is only defective when there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the operation of both of those [factors]. And that is not the case here; so what is the point of your mere non-desire?

Because it lacks a specific defining characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of fire by smoke and its absence is not stated directly. For instance, since there is a difference between fire and smoke, they do not possess identity (*tādātmya*); and since this [fire] does not arise from the presence or absence of smoke and so forth, there is no causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Therefore, the pervasion of the locus (*āśrayabhuj*) is established directly only through the properties residing within itself, namely "possessing smoke" and its opposite.

However, when expressed by means of smoke and its absence through the door of accepting that [objective] referent, it does not entail any fault. Therefore, if such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not desired by you, or if its opposite is desired, let it be so.

For our part, this very sequence of pervasion is what we intend to express; and it alone is useful for the present context, since the discussion proceeds on the basis of the pervasion of the causal capacity of an object by way of succession or non-succession, with the aim of completely excluding the reason from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). And since that is established precisely in this manner, enough of this insistence on such a minor slip.

Thus, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by succession and simultaneity is established, the pervasion of the absence of succession and simultaneity by the absence of causal efficiency is likewise established. For there is no other means to establish the pervasion of the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) by the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) apart from establishing that very relationship between the pervaded and the pervader; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*). Furthermore, there is not even a scent of contradiction in the establishment of the pervasion for the non-perception of the pervader under discussion, because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Nor is there a lack of proof, because the contradiction regarding the absence of succession and simultaneity in a permanent subject (*sādhyadharmin*) is established. On this point, Nyāyabhūṣaṇa says: "If it is intended to establish the non-existence of non-momentary things, then what here possesses the status of the subject (*dharmin*)? If that very thing itself is the subject, it is illogical to prove its own non-existence. For when the subject is absent, the reason lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). And without the property of being a predicate of the subject, there is no capacity for proof."

Therefore, the proposition that non-momentary things are non-existent is untenable. Alternatively, if the meaning of the proposition is that existent things are not non-momentary, even so, since there is a contradiction between succession and simultaneity, how can this [reason] possess the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? Furthermore, the contradiction of causal efficiency with a permanent entity is understood precisely through the non-perception of its pervader; but how could this apply to succession and simultaneity, which are themselves the pervaders? Moreover, in this way, existence itself would follow for the permanent; and thus, every effort [to prove its non-existence] would be fruitless.

As Śaṅkara said: "One who pursues the establishment of a contradiction must also admit its contradictory, because the establishment of the contradiction is inseparable from the cognition of that [contradictory]. This is as in the case of fire and snow, or of dependent and independent entities. But how can a non-momentary entity, being perceived as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), abandon its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) due to the obstruction of a subverting factor? For it possesses causal efficiency in the form of being an object of cognition. If it did not possess that efficiency, how could it be perceived? Since that which does not produce [an effect] is not an object of knowledge (*aprameya*). Thus has this been written according to the essence regarding external objects.

And likewise, Nyāyabhūṣaṇa says: "Because contradiction cannot be apprehended when the contradictories are not apprehended; for indeed, there is no apprehension of contradiction between fire and snow if one of the two is not apprehended. If the non-momentary is apprehended due to its contradiction with succession and simultaneity, then how could it be non-existent? Because it performs causal efficiency in the form of cognition. If it did not perform that [efficiency], how could it be cognized? For you do not accept that something which produces nothing else can be an object of cognition."

Now, if that which is non-momentary is not perceived at all, how can its contradiction with both succession and simultaneity be understood? Thus, since a permanent entity is non-existent in every respect and is therefore not an object of perception, there is a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). Likewise, there is also a lack of the essential nature of the subject (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

As Śaṅkara said: "Now, if the non-existence of non-momentary things is established because of the impossibility of successive or simultaneous action, and thus momentariness follows from existence—then, since that [existence] produces the cognition [of it], the inconclusiveness of the capacity for causal efficiency remains as before, because [that capacity] exists even in its absence."

For when the absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*) is established, the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*) must be understood as something else, just as the absence of smoke—such as water and so forth—is understood in the absence of fire, or the absence of a *śiṃśapā* tree—a place devoid of it—is understood in the absence of trees. Likewise, in the absence of succession and simultaneity (*kramayaugapadyābhāva*), the absence of capacity (*sāmarthyābhāva*) must be understood as something else; for if that were not established, it would be impossible to establish the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a reason whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is uncertain. But if it is established, then the relationship of pervader and pervaded consists in the performance of a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in the form of cognition, and thus the [absurd] consequence (*prasaṅga*) is unavoidable.

For this very reason, its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is also impossible to state; for there is no cognition of the absence of successive and non-successive activity, nor of the absence of causal efficiency, in a sky-lotus. If such were cognized, it would follow that all things, by virtue of being real entities, would be included within both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar class.

[87,22] If it is argued that its capacity to convey [the probandum] is due solely to the power of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), we say no; for even a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is absent. If it is argued that a rabbit’s horn and the like serve as the instance, we say no; because such a thing is not an object of cognition. For it is impossible to cognize something as being devoid of the properties of the probandum and the probans if it is not cognized even in its own nature (*svarūpa*); and it is not logical for that which is not cognized to function as an instance.

Furthermore, this proof for the absence of causal efficiency in an eternal entity—which is a proof for its non-existence—does not escape the threefold class of fallacies, just like a proof for existence.
For, according to the sequence already stated:
"A property of an existent does not exist if [the subject] is unestablished; that which depends on both is inconclusive."
"How can that existence, which is a property contradictory to non-existence, be established?

Thus do Maṅkha and Nyāyabhūṣaṇa demonstrate. Trilocana also, refining that very same set of objects of cognition, says: "Does the subverting proof—that the absence of succession and simultaneity—establish the non-momentariness [of things], or rather does it establish the negative concomitance (vyatireka) consisting of a necessary connection with the object? It cannot be the first alternative, because since the nature [of existence] is unestablished in the case of space, time, direction, self, mind, and atoms, the reason would be unestablished due to the unestablishedness of its locus (āśrayāsiddhi)."

That non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) likewise does not escape the three types of fallacy. In this regard, it has been stated that the property of being devoid of succession and simultaneity (*kramayaugapadyarahitatva*) is not established as a property of the non-existent (*abhāvadharma*), because its locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*). For wise people do not accept that being devoid of succession and simultaneity is a property of a rabbit’s horn.

Furthermore, as long as their non-existence is not apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their status as a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*) is not established. Otherwise, there would be an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the establishment of their non-existence would depend upon the establishment of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and the establishment of the property of being a feature of non-existence would depend upon the establishment of their non-existence. Moreover, if this were a property of existence (*bhāvadharma*), it would be contradictory; if it were a property of both, it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This same logical consequence applies equally to non-existence as it does to existence.

Nor is the second alternative tenable; for even there, the meaning of the term "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*) is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) accompanied by the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). And since that absence must necessarily be apprehended as a constituent part of the means of cognition, if it is apprehended through experience, it would have experience itself as its cause; and because that which lacks a cause cannot be apprehended, the reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since—given that negative concomitance is of a positive nature due to being produced by experience—it would be included within the category of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Because of the absence of both positive and negative concomitance, an uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇahetu*) is non-probative. Therefore, negative concomitance must necessarily be admitted and necessarily known; and regarding its necessity of being known, the undesirable consequence of knowing that [entire class] has been demonstrated.

It might be argued as follows: "Exclusion (*vyatireka*) is not intended to be grasped by a direct-perceiving cognition (*sākṣātkāri-vijñāna*), because [if it were], it would have to be the producer of that direct-perceiving cognition; rather, it must be conceptualized (*vikalpya*). And an object being conceptualized cannot logically be the cause of a conceptualization whose production depends upon its own immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). So why is it said that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*")?

That too is untenable, because every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not transcend these four possibilities: namely, some conceptual construction of blue and so forth which follows upon direct experience; another whose object is doubtful, such as the conceptual construction of a *piśāca* and so forth; another whose object is non-existent, such as the conceptual construction of a hare's horn and so forth; and furthermore, in this context, some conceptual construction is born from a logical mark (*liṅga*).

In this context, by stating that every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—beginning with those arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*)—has a non-real appearance, it is described as resembling perception (*pratyakṣābha*). This is because perception has the manifestation of a real entity (*vastu*), whereas in the absence of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that manifestation is lost. Conceptual construction is not like this, because its manifestation does not conform to the real entity. Therefore, conceptual construction resembles perception. However, that which arises from a logical mark is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it causes one to attain the object exactly as it is determined.

Furthermore, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*) does not construct a distinctness (*vyatireka*) that is being conceptualized, because such a mark is absent. Moreover, even though a conceptual construction preceded by experience arises from a real entity through a traditional lineage, it lacks authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding that entity, because only the direct experience is authoritative.

And since the experience that would serve as the basis for distinctness has just been refuted, it follows by elimination that a conceptual construction—whether its object be non-existent or its objective reality doubtful—is what brings about certainty; thus, existence characterized by a non-existent or a doubtful distinctness is insufficient to prove momentariness.

Nor is the third alternative possible; for it is understood that the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—which is preceded by the establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—occurs when succession and simultaneity, being excluded from non-momentary existence, are established in momentariness along with their own pervader. And yet, the negative concomitance has already been refuted by the previously mentioned method.
Thus, in this way, the permanent does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition; therefore, the reason suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
Therefore, because of the reason and one's own experience, there is no impairment [of the thesis], yet one's own position is also rejected.
Furthermore, emptiness is not established by a duality, nor is non-existence established in the same way as existence;
for it is impossible to establish a contradiction with the eternal through that which is non-existent, even in the case of succession and so forth.

In this regard, these very [opponents] are questioned as follows: "Does there exist here, with respect to some dharma, a conventional practice of negation or affirmation established by the mind regarding a non-entity, or not?"
If it exists somewhere, how can there not be so many objections?
And if it does not exist at all, then the contradiction with one's own words is established.

[90,1] Indeed, the linguistic practice of affirmation and negation regarding any phenomenon is not one that corresponds to reality and is restricted solely to real entities; rather, it applies even to non-entities (*avastu*). If you maintain the position that such practice does not exist at all regarding non-entities, then when questioned as to how this is so, if you should resort to the king’s decree as your authority, how could you avoid the fallacy of the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddhi*) if you were to offer some reason?

It is not appropriate to remain silent when one possesses the capacity for speech; thus, one who utters whatever comes to mind has no rival. Nor is he established by the authority of another. Furthermore, by one who asserts that "there is no conventional practice of affirmation or negation regarding a non-entity," the very practice of negation regarding a non-entity is accepted; however, the opponent is merely deceived. For there is no possibility of a meaning for the negative particle (*nañ*) other than negation, and if that negation is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can it be respected?

Furthermore, what is the point of his statement?
