And if one accepts the establishment of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perception itself cannot be the proof for the negation of non-existent things, because perception is in contradiction with such an object, as it depends upon the causal efficacy of a real thing (*arthasāmarthya*). If, however, inference is relied upon, the "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) fallacy is unavoidable. Therefore, when dealing with non-existent things, one is reduced to silence; there is not even room for a mere thesis (*pratijñā*). Nor can this be possible unless the discussion of non-existent things is prevented by royal decree.

In the context of a discussion, however, the statement of what is possible for an existent entity necessarily follows, because the possibility of an inquiry arises; and for a statement, there is no function other than affirmation or negation. Therefore, one enters a great and painful dilemma: neither speech nor non-speech.

And so, at this very moment, since there is an absence of both successive and simultaneous action—just like a lotus in the intermediate space within a permanent entity—there is no causal efficacy (*arthasāmarthya*). Thus, given this premise that no property whatsoever can be affirmed or denied regarding a non-entity, even you, a learned man, cannot remain silent; rather, a negation has indeed been established, because for that which is non-existent according to the Buddhist view, causal efficacy ceases due to the absence of succession and simultaneity.
"But the absence of cessation is a positive injunction, a real entity even though it is non-existent;
yet its own absence is said to be 'non-existent'—behold the manifestation of such audacity!
This is an intermediate verse (antaraśloka).

Now, if it is argued that because the eternal [entity] is a real thing by virtue of its internal purity (*koṣṭhaśuddhi*), there is no contradiction with the means of valid cognition regarding the negation of any property whatsoever, then does it follow that even a sky-lotus must be a real thing by virtue of its internal purity? Or, if it were a real thing, how could a conceptual construction devoid of a basis (*nirvastuka*) ever be conceived?

Therefore, regarding a non-entity such as a sky-lotus, let there be an absence of causal efficacy due to the lack of succession and so forth, or let there not; in either case, the fulfillment of this thesis—that neither affirmation nor negation applies to a non-entity—is impossible. Furthermore, when seeking the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish how this is so, if perception is absent, any inference relied upon is entirely consumed by the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Moreover, a mere statement lacking a means of valid cognition is disregarded by any discerning person.

Nor can the absence of both be asserted, because affirmation and negation have the nature of existence and non-existence respectively; for by the negation of one, there is the affirmation of the other. Indeed, affirmation is negation and negation is affirmation—so what else could it be? Furthermore, let it be granted that the thesis of the negation of both avoids the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the reason being presented.

As for what was said—that because the internal organ (*koṣṭha*) is pure, the entity itself is eternal—what follows from that? For that [entity] is not the subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of being a real entity (*vastu*), since that would entail the consequence that the fault of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) would have no scope. If it is argued that this is stated with reference to the opponent's own admission, then the meaning is that the reason in the *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*) is unestablished in its eternal locus because it is a non-entity; thus, the absence of succession and so forth is not a valid reason.

This being the case, one must state that a reason (*hetu*) with respect to a non-existent entity (*avastu*) is pervaded by the fault of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*); for no reason exists without an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*). While a *prasaṅga* (reductio) may be stated based on the mere property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in reliance upon what the opponent accepts, this acceptance does not extend to the pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself. If it is argued that "this might sometimes be the case," even so, the opponent has not accepted that a reason with respect to a non-existent entity is pervaded by the fault of having an unestablished locus, because they have formulated their reasons precisely regarding a non-existent entity that is eternal.

Furthermore, precisely where the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) of a reason is brought forward because of the [proponent's] treating a non-entity as an entity, it is there that the proposition (*pratijñā*) is defeated by the principle that "there is neither affirmation nor negation regarding a non-entity.

And if you maintain that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is intended solely on the basis of what is accepted by the opponent, such that the reason is not "governed by the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) because it is a non-entity in a non-entity, then this is not acceptable to you; nevertheless, the claim that "there is neither affirmation nor negation regarding a non-entity" is contradictory, because a negation is being accepted by yourself, and since the negative particle (*nañ*) has no meaning other than negation.

Furthermore, according to the logical principle that every reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) must culminate in its opposite, if a non-entity were eternal, then there would be a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for that [reason]. Yet, there is no lack of a locus; therefore, what is intended by the claim that "a non-entity is not eternal"? Even then, since the fault of *āśrayāsiddhi* has been introduced, and the eternality of the subject (*dharmin*)—the non-entity—is not established, how does the statement "a non-entity is not eternal" not fall into contradiction?

Therefore, since this [subject] is itself independent and non-existent, the "unestablishedness of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) pertains to the reason when it is applied to a non-entity; thus, for one engaged in refuting the reason, this is the primary issue. Consequently, the claim that "there can be neither affirmation nor negation regarding a non-entity" has been set aside. Furthermore, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is employed as an essential nature (*svabhāva*), based on the misconception that being a locus is pervaded by being an entity. And that misconception arises from a failure to understand the contradiction with one's own words.

Indeed, for one who considers it a contradiction of their own words to hold that the status of being a locus for affirmation and negation does not belong to a non-entity, the conceit of pervasion regarding "entity-ness" (vastutva) as the property-possessor (dharmin) cannot touch the mind; rather, it serves only to belittle oneself—this is the general rule. Furthermore, what kind of logic is this, wherein these [opponents] themselves extend the conventional usage of affirmation and negation toward a non-entity, yet reject the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) as a means of valid cognition when refuting another?

For the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, by stating that "there can be no property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) for a reason when the subject (*dharmin*) does not exist," has clearly expressed a denial of the property-of-the-subject status of a reason with respect to a non-existent entity. When investigating the reasoning behind how this is so, he intends the reason "because the subject is non-existent. Otherwise, what regard would there be for mere words?

Furthermore, one who asserts that "the non-momentary is not perceived at all; how then can its contradiction with succession and simultaneity be understood? clearly states that there is no apprehension of contradiction because [the non-momentary] is not an object of cognition. And this property, which is common to other non-entities (*avastu*), is attributed even to that which is considered eternal as a non-entity; otherwise, if this principle did not apply elsewhere to a non-entity, how could it be asserted even in the case of the eternal?
Maṅkha also clarifies this very point: since a non-entity is not an object of cognition through dependence, the contradiction is not established; otherwise, the treatise would be purposeless.

If it is argued that there is no fault because—given the absence of a genitive or locative indication—the non-existent does not contradict the existent, and this is the intended meaning; [we reply: since even now the non-existent remains unperceived, the reason you yourself have manifested must still be required. How, then, can there be a dismissal of the non-existent as the subject (*dharmin*) and of the two [logical reasons], namely non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and pervasion (*vyāpaka*)? For, when contradiction with it is not established, the reason is simply its lack of being an object of cognition.

And if you accept the avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) by means of the indication of the instrumental case, then there is no harm: since both succession and simultaneity lack connection with the eternal, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) also lacks connection with the eternal. In this way, we shall explain the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) of the reason as follows: its presence in the subject (*pakṣa*), its presence only in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and its absolute absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Let there be peace regarding the blow of the unestablished locus. Therefore, there is merely a difference in intended expression and not a difference in reality; so what is the use of this ascetic practice?

Furthermore, let it be granted that there is indeed a contradiction and sublation with respect to what is non-existent. However, when there is a question as to whether there can be a contradiction between two existing things, if one accepts this [question], then the Buddhist tenet is already established, and the presentation [of the argument] is redundant. If, on the other hand, one accepts that there is no such contradiction, then one must rely upon that very reason [adduced by the opponent], namely "because it is not perceived"; thus, the negation of contradiction regarding a non-entity occurs through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), and the Buddhist tenet is once again established. Likewise:
"A property of an existent does not exist in what is unestablished" (PV I.191a).
In this case as well, this very principle is our refuge.

And thus Trilocana clarifies with his own words: "The property of non-existence—namely, the state of being devoid of succession and simultaneity—is not established, because its locus is not perceived. For here it is clear that non-existence is the subject (*dharmin*), and its property—the state of being devoid of succession and so forth—is what is negated, on the grounds of the reason "because its locus is not perceived."

Thus, one who asserts that a non-existent thing can possess the status of a subject (dharmin), yet immediately thereafter claims that wise people accept the property of being like a rabbit’s horn—which is devoid of both succession and simultaneity—is a great reckless person who does not laugh at himself by his own hand. For it is precisely because of its non-existence that the status of a subject for a rabbit’s horn must be negated; yet, since you have admitted that even a non-existent thing can be a subject, what contradiction could there be regarding the horns of horses and the like?

Now, if the status of being a subject (*dharmitā*) for non-existence is accepted by means of the negation of its being devoid of succession and so forth, why should it not simply be [accepted] as being devoid of succession and so forth? Oh, what a display of intellectual power! One considers the hare’s horn, which is non-existent, to have the status of a subject through the negation of its being devoid of succession and so forth, but not by virtue of its actually being devoid of succession and so forth.

Since the conventional practice of affirmation and negation regarding a non-entity is accepted in both cases, the Buddhist conclusion is difficult to avoid; therefore, it would be better for the subjecthood (*dharmitva*) to reside in both [the universal and the particular] simply by virtue of being devoid of succession and so forth. Why, then, resort to the story of the one who enters the Northern Road (*uttarā-patha*), abandons his horse for that price alone, and yet undergoes the labor of pregnancy?

Alternatively, what can be done here if the extremely subtle intellect does not perceive such a gross and incongruous distinction? Nevertheless, close your eyes for a moment and consider this: does the horn of a hare possess a sequence of stages and so forth, or not? If you say that it does, then what more is there for us to say? The members of the assembly and others are the authority in this matter.

Now, if the position is "no," then how can you, while that [object] is devoid of sequence and so forth, establish it as a subject (*dharmin*) by negating its lack of sequence and so forth? Having interrogated the reason in both ways, I shall certainly state that it is because of its being a non-entity (*avastutva*); enough with this elaboration.

[93,17] Even in such a context as "Is the son of a barren woman a speaker or not?", one cannot remain without asserting a negation; nor can one do so without presenting a proof such as "because of insentience" or "because of being a non-entity. If you ask, "Why does no one entertain such a doubt? or "If it is said that this must be answered in such a way, why so?"—the answer is: "Because its status as a non-entity is well-established. If you say this:

Once again, the same point arises: the negation of the possibility of doubt regarding the speakerhood of the son of Bandhula, who possesses the property [of being a speaker], is based on the reason that he is not a subject of praise (*astuta*) because he is well-known (*suprasiddha*). However, even if one is well-known, there is no absolute absence of doubt; for the power of delusion is boundless. Indeed, even among the authors of treatises, a delusion of this kind is observed, such as the negation of the absence of sequence and so forth in the case of a hare’s horn.

Therefore, just as one who conceives of sound as impermanent because it possesses visibility is not refuted on the grounds that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), so too here there may be both doubt and its refutation; there is no contradiction. Consequently, just as with a real entity (*vastu*), the conventional practice of affirming or negating some property even with respect to a non-entity (*avastu*) is unavoidable, since even those authors of treatises who are directly opposed [to this view] accept it precisely through their own statements of negation.

In this regard, how can things that are non-entities—extending even to the son of a barren woman—possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*)? In the absence of any cognition of them, how can there be conventional discourse? And if they do generate a cognition, how is it that they do not possess the status of real entities? Furthermore, since one cannot accept mere words as a valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*), whatever reason (*hetu*) is adduced, how is it not all "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*)? Thus, it follows that "the fault which is equal for both," and so forth.

And if these faults do not apply even to things whose existence is determined to be non-existent, then why would they not apply to an eternal entity whose existence is unestablished prior to the proof? What, then, is the ultimate truth here? For it is impossible for an authoritative person to avoid the conventional practice of affirming or negating any property whatsoever regarding a non-entity.

If it is argued that these faults do not follow as consequences, it is replied: first of all, there is no absence of the status of being a subject (*dharmin*) for a non-entity. For wherever there is a reflective awareness (*prāmārśa*) in the form "this is thus," that very thing is the subject by way of this mode of "this is this. The phrase "thus" denotes its connection with a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*). Just as in the case of "the jar is blue," the blueness of the jar is perceived as a property, so too in the case of "the son of a barren woman does not speak," the capacity to speak is perceived as a property of the son of a barren woman. Thus, there is no absence of the status of being a subject even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*).

Only some properties belong to a real entity (*vastu*), such as blueness and so forth; some belong to a non-entity (*avastu*), such as the absence of all designations and so forth; and some are common to both, being merely non-apprehension (*anupalambhamātra*). In that context, it is logical to negate the status of being a property of a non-entity in relation to a real entity as its locus (*dharmin*). However, this does not apply to properties in general, because self-contradiction (*svavacanavirodha*) acts as a subverting factor. Furthermore, it is also incorrect to claim that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) occurs despite the absence of cognition.

Furthermore, it is not the case that a cognition of one and the same kind for both [real and unreal objects] is a factor for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). For the cognition of a real entity arises through its own inherent capacity (*svasāmarthya*); conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), moreover, is an indirect effect of perception and inference. However, in the case of an unreal entity, or of something whose status as a real entity is doubtful, there is merely conceptual construction. Indeed, if—due to the absence of capacity—the cognition of those two were not established even as mere conceptual construction, then [the object] would be entirely beyond conventional discourse.

And since conventional usage is accepted, cognition in that case consists merely of conceptual construction (*vikalpana*); and the nature of those two [the object and its cognition] is precisely what is presented by that construction, and nothing else. Just as the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) is only that which is brought forward by perception or inference, so too the essence of a non-entity or of something whose status as an entity is doubtful is only that which is presented by conceptual construction, and not otherwise. Therefore, those who are wise ought not to be considered "good" [logicians] when they draw in a factor [of the reason] based on mere convention. As it is said: "Those who know the logic [of reasons] understand that the state of being a reason is simply the state of being a graspable object" (PV III 247).

Thus it has been stated; that was said with reference to the apprehended object as being distinct from the apprehending subject in the context of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). For it is established that this same principle does not apply even to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

And thus Nyāyabhūṣaṇa himself says: "For you do not accept that a non-producer is an object of cognition as a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). Nor is a non-entity (*avastu*) a distinct entity; for it is only an entity (*artha*) that is called a 'distinct entity' in relation to another entity, but not a non-entity. That [non-entity] is merely the negation of its existence. Therefore, because there is no such thing as being a distinct entity, there is no dependence on a cognition produced by itself for a non-entity. Consequently, mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) is the only refuge here."

Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that its nature is precisely that which is delineated by that [cognition's] aspect, and nothing else; otherwise, the non-articulation of words such as "hare's horn" would result, and how then could linguistic usage proceed? For instance, having referred to an object denoted by a word such as "donkey's horn," something must necessarily be predicated of it—such as the property of being devoid of succession and so forth, or being possessed of such [properties], or else the cognition of a contradiction with nothing at all, or that it does not possess the properties of a real entity (*vastu*).

In that case, if the intended object is not conveyed by words such as "hare's horn" or "non-existent entity," and instead a different object altogether is the referent of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) generated by the sound, then for what would the negation of succession and non-succession and so forth—which are being predicated—be perceived? And in the absence of such perception, the utterance of the word would result in being meaningless. Yet, there is indeed the conventional usage of words such as "tortoise-hair"; therefore, that [usage] itself is its meaning, and the determination of the object is likewise that very same thing.

Even when there is perception (*dṛṣṭa*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*) alone is the ascertainment (*niścaya*). If that is so, then let conceptualization alone be relied upon in all cases; what is the use of perception? It is not so, because when an object is excluded by perception, since only the mental image (*ākāra*) flashes forth in the conceptual mind, one must rely on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the purpose of establishing its reality or for the purpose of subverting it. However, when an object has been made the objective domain by perception, conceptualization is an ascertainment to the same extent as the form [of the object] within that [perception], provided there is no deception due to similarity.

Therefore, even with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), conceptual construction alone is not the refuge; rather, it is that very [construction] which is the refuge for what is unreal (*avastu*). For in that case, one requires a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external form that depends upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and that is established by conceptual construction itself. However, in the operation of a [direct] means of valid cognition, there is no dependence on another means of valid cognition.

Therefore, when wise persons, through the reflective awareness of that very nature delineated by that conceptual construction, establish—by virtue of its fitness—the negation of being devoid of succession and simultaneity and so forth, what kind of fault could there be in establishing a state of contradiction with a form that is the opposite of that nature?

Or, just as the negation of beauty and so forth in the case of the son of a barren woman is appropriate, what contradiction could there be with the contradiction of substantiality? Furthermore, if the obstruction of contradiction is due to the absence of experience, then let the negation of beauty also not occur simply because of that same absence of experience; consequently, the consequence remains unavoidable that there would be no utterance of words expressing non-existence when some property to be predicated is absent, and it has already been pointed out that this is not possible.

[96,1] Now, since the son of a barren woman and the like lack any other form distinct from the form that is to be conceptualized, and since they are made objects of conceptualization as mere suchness, there is no harm to the corresponding conventional usage. This being the case, what harm could there be to the corresponding conventional usage of contradiction? Just as there is a contradiction of the son of a barren woman by way of his being a real entity, so too, why would there not be a contradiction with that property which can be established as an opponent even for the eternal?

In that case, how could the mere absence of experience be a valid means of establishing contradiction and sublation if it were not explicitly stated? If, however, even in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that object did not exist, or if there were no reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of its contrary form, then contradiction—defined as "incompatible coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*)—would have to be what is intended to be proven; only then would the establishment of contradiction occur, for the determination of incompatible coexistence arises because one thing does not exist when the other exists.

And since existence is within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could it be possible for one thing to have another as its cause? Furthermore, the characteristic of existing through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇatva*) is established merely by the conceptual reflection (*parāmarśa*) of opposing forms; even when made an object by mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is not necessarily dependent upon a real entity (*vastu*) as the basis for its established arrangement. Otherwise, how could there be a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence themselves?

And regarding that contradiction, those same two [examples] serve as the primary illustrations. Even if one accepts that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a real entity (*vastutva*), there is no "existence" of an existent within the entity designated as "non-existence," nor is there an "existence" of a non-existent in what is called "non-existence. Thus, it is impossible to maintain a succession of non-existent entities. If one maintains that a non-entity has as its sole nature the mere cessation of itself and is to be treated as such, how can that which is contradictory to it be established?

Furthermore, if there were no established distinction between contradiction and non-contradiction, then in that case a single entity—namely, its own self and its own exclusion—would both exist and not exist by its very nature; yet this is not the case as a rule. This is precisely what constitutes the meaning of contradiction, just as in the case of the momentary and the non-momentary: for just as one thing is not non-momentary, so too another is not momentary. Therefore, it is established that there is no sublation of the contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between an entity and a non-entity.

[96,19] But surely, if contradiction (*virodha*) is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) by means of it would also be unreal; for a contradiction cannot be ultimately real if its substratum is not ultimately real.

As Śaṅkara said: "In that case, even the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) constructed through the conceptualization of contradiction does not establish a real exclusion (*vyatireka*), because the contradiction itself is merely imagined. Since existence (*sattā*) thus possesses an unreal exclusion, momentariness—which is dependent upon it—is likewise unreal."

Nyāyabhūṣaṇa also, refining that very point, says: "If it is argued that the establishment of contradiction is with respect to a non-momentary entity established by conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), then even that which is conventionally established must be either real (*vāstava*) or conceptual (*kālpnika*). If it is real, how can it be non-existent? Or how could there be a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? For that which performs causal efficiency is called real. If, on the other hand, it is conceptual, then is the contradiction with it real or conceptual?"

First of all, [the contradiction] is not real, because it is a contradiction between two imagined entities, like the contradiction between a barren woman’s son [and his absence]. Now, if the contradiction itself is merely conceptual, then there is no ultimate contradiction between the non-momentary and causal efficiency by way of succession or simultaneity; therefore, the establishment of the exclusion of existence from the non-momentary is also not ultimately real. Since existence thus has an unreal exclusion, momentariness—which depends upon that [existence]—is likewise unreal.

[97,6] This is an incoherent prattle. For we do not maintain that "contradiction" (*virodha*) is some distinct entity (*vastv-antara*) that stands as a foot upon both sides and is designated as a relation (*sambandha*), such that it would become non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*) in the absence of reality in one of the two related terms. Nor is such a thing logically tenable. Rather, according to how it is maintained, contradiction is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*). The meaning of contradiction between two things regarded as opposed is simply the mutual exclusion of their respective intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*).

And that [contradiction] between existence and non-existence is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*). For existence does not enter into the nature of non-existence, nor does non-existence enter into the nature of existence; this very rule of their non-confusion is what constitutes contradiction. And that rule establishes even the contradiction itself within the sphere of the ultimate. Likewise, the rule that the eternal does not enter into the nature of succession or simultaneity, nor do succession and simultaneity enter into the nature of the eternal—this very rule is the contradiction between those two.

And since it is never otherwise, the very establishment by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitutes ultimate reality; so how can it be said that because contradiction is not ultimately real, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "existence" is also unreal?

Furthermore, since everything has been established precisely by accepting that the permanent lacks ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*), there is no fault whatsoever. As for what was stated—that the contradiction of an imagined contradictory is denied its reality because it is a contradiction of an imagined contradictory, like the contradiction of the son of a barren woman—let us for now set aside exposing this wretched man’s failure to perceive even such a gross fallacy as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

[97,19] And this is considered: Is it the very state of being opposed to what is opposed to the imagined that is contradicted by reality? If, first of all, it is not contradicted, then there would also be opposition to what is not opposed to the imagined, and reality itself would also exist; how then could the presentation of that [opposition] be exclusively effective for its refutation? For from the affirmation of something non-contradictory, the establishment of a negation of anything does not follow.

Now, if it is contradictory, is that contradiction real or unreal? In that regard, an unreal contradiction is ineffective because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of indirect existence (*paraṃparābhava*). On the view that it is real, even the contradiction with an imagined contradictory is itself accepted as real; and yet you claim that for us alone it expresses the negation of its own contradictory—behold the manifestation of such audacity!

For just as there is a contradiction between permanence and succession or simultaneity—a contradiction consisting in the opposition of the imagined to the real—because the permanent is [itself] imagined; likewise, in the case of a contradiction between the real and the imagined, there exists a contradiction between two contradictions, namely a contradiction consisting in the opposition of the imagined to the imagined. This is because the "opponent" (virodhin) is imagined, or because it belongs to that [imagined thing]. Indeed, we observe that what you are attempting to prove through your own effort is this: that the contradiction of an imagined opponent is itself merely imagined and not real.

Therefore, the contradiction that exists between that imagined contradiction (or its contradictory) and reality is itself established as a "contradiction with an imagined contradictory. If that [imagined contradiction] were real, it would result in a contradiction with one's own words; if it were unreal, the refutation has already been stated.

Furthermore, what is called "contradiction" (virodha) is sought for the purpose of prohibiting the coexistence of two things in a single locus; however, the establishment of the reality of both is not the result of contradiction. But where there is the establishment of the reality of both, then by implication, because one thing excludes another thing in a certain location—as was stated previously regarding non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*)—the present contradiction has as its result the negation of the existence of two properties in a single substratum (*dharmin*).

In this regard, just as two properties that both exist are negated—where there is blueness, there is no non-blueness; therefore, blue and non-blue are not one—likewise, even two contradictory properties in the form of existence and non-existence, when superimposed upon a single substratum (*dharmin*), are indeed negated. For it is not the case that the status of being the son of a barren woman, though superimposed upon the son of a mother, need not be negated because it is factually non-existent.

Or, in the case of the son of a barren woman, who is the exclusive object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the status of being a "mother's son" is superimposed [upon him] and cannot be denied. For the mother’s son and the barren woman’s son are not one and the same entity; the contradiction is exhausted by that much alone. What is the use of another so-called "contradiction" which does not attain its own existence without depending on the actual properties of things? Thus, where there is permanence, there is no possession of succession or simultaneity; where there is possession of succession or simultaneity, there is no permanence; therefore, it is not permanent.

In ultimate reality, [existence] is not endowed with either succession or simultaneity; consequently, even that which is associated with existence is not necessarily so in ultimate reality. Therefore, existence must find its rest in the momentary alone, for existence itself is dependent upon that [momentariness]. Thus, there is no contradiction in the proof of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) from the fact of existence.

And if, even so, you wish to enter the hollows of mountain caves and proclaim [your view] by grasping at contradictions and absences through the process of "mother-candy" (mātṛ-modaka), then do so; yet you will not be of the slightest use in obstructing the success of our undertaking. Therefore, enough of this obsession! It is best simply to accept that these contradictions and so forth are indeed real.

If it is argued: "Is there not no contradiction other than the two contradictory properties of permanence and possessing succession or simultaneity? Of what, then, would there be reality?"—that too is trivial. For we do not assert that contradiction is ultimately real merely because another property is possible; rather, since two things are contradictory, even if another property were possible, if they were not contradictory, then contradiction would not be ultimately real.

[99,1] If those two are contradictory, then by that much alone there is the conventional designation of "real contradiction"; what is the use of another property? As for what was said regarding the contradiction like that of a barren woman’s son, is this contradiction being cited as an example as one having a single locus, or as depending on a second term? Even if it depends on a second, is that second a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) or merely something else? First of all, the first position is untenable, for no one maintains that contradiction has a single locus.

Therefore, if the contradiction between the son of a barren woman and [his opposite] is unreal because they share a non-distinct locus (*abhinnadharmī*), then by what logic could it be that the two loci themselves do not possess a real contradiction? Thus, there is no contradiction merely by being "other," as in the case of "produced" and "impermanent. However, in that case too, a contradiction with the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is indeed accepted; for the son of a barren woman does indeed have a contradiction with the son of a non-barren woman. And the negation within a single identity is precisely what is intended.

[99,9] But is it not the case that when two properties (dharma) are contradictory, the negation of the identity of their substrates (dharmin) is logical? For the contradiction between "the son of a barren woman" and "the son of a non-barren woman" resides in the property and the property-bearer. This is not a fault. For substrates are indeed designated only by means of their properties; likewise, in some cases, the designation of two substrates may be made with the emphasis on the state of being (bhāva).

Furthermore, the presentation of fire and frost by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is also incorrect, because what is intended is their mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*). As for the dependence and necessary occurrence (*dhruvabhāva*) mentioned as being the objects of that [exclusion], there too, dependence implies occasional occurrence, which is non-eternality (*anityatva*). If "necessary occurrence" means the necessity of its existence, then that is precisely eternality (*nityatva*).

Therefore, how can this presentation of the state of contradiction between the eternal and the non-eternal, being based on experience, not provoke laughter? For the very point at issue is precisely how there can be a cognition of contradiction with that which is eternal. Furthermore, if it is argued that "certainty" (*dhruvabhāva*) must necessarily exist, even that is not an object of anyone's experience; thus, the same fault applies as in the case of the eternal.

[99,18] This might be argued: "This is said with reference to that which has been observed to have necessarily occurred at some time. In that case, however, there is no contradiction at all, for that [object] is both dependent and permanent. Alternatively, if it is argued that at that time there is no dependence because it is already established (*siddha*), then at other times there is even less; for it is precisely because it is not yet established (*asiddha*) that there is no dependence. If it is claimed that dependence belongs only to an unestablished property (*dharma*), then the fault remains the same: there can be no determination of contradiction regarding what has never been experienced.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with that which has been experienced precisely because of its dependence on the time of its establishment (*siddhi-kāla*), then it is correct to say that if one accepts such dependence on the time of establishment, there is no contradiction at all. By this, when the non-existence of a contradiction due to the absence of experience is to be proven, the intended example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhya-avyatirekin*); whereas in the case of attributing a contradiction to what is non-existent, it lacks the probans (*sādhana-avyatirekin*). Furthermore, if "inevitability" (*dhruva-bhāva*) is taken to mean "permanence," then it is simply included within the category of the property to be proven.

Let it be that difference, non-difference, and so forth serve as the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Nevertheless, there is no rule that contradiction between two things exists only between non-momentary entities, for this has been established even in other cases. As for the claim that "a property of an existent does not exist when [the subject] is unestablished" (PV I 191a;

PVin III 63a), that too is refuted because the objection regarding the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) has been set far aside. Since even a non-existent thing can be established as a subject (*dharmin*), and since the establishment of the conventional status of conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) with respect to a non-entity is proven, the objection that space and the like cannot be cognized in their own nature is also avoided.

It might be argued: "If the avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) by relying on a cognition in the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) applies equally even when proving existence (*sattā*), then why is it said that 'there is no property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) in what is unestablished,' and so forth? And how is the proof of the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the self (*ātman*)—namely, the fact that its qualities are perceived everywhere—cited as an example of the unestablished locus? [Response: Because of the requirements of the proof (*sādhana*), in both cases only a property of an entity is employed as the reason (*hetu*) and is what is suspected [to be the case]. Thus, although the avoidance of the unestablished locus is achieved through conceptual cognition, the reason remains a property of an entity. Therefore, the aforementioned critique regarding the non-existence of properties of entities in the unestablished remains valid. Furthermore, in the case of the self, since the reason is a property of an entity, the charge of the unestablished locus cannot be avoided by resorting to conceptual cognition. Consequently, the example cited for the self is indeed an instance of the unestablished locus. Thus, the argument stands.

Furthermore, a property of an entity cannot have a non-entity as its locus (*dharmin*). For smoke, *śiṃśapā*-ness, and so forth do not reside in a non-entity. Therefore, wherever a property of an entity serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*), there the locus must necessarily be an entity itself. Nor can there be confidence in the reality of that which is merely the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because mere conceptual construction does not cease even with respect to a non-entity. Consequently, one who treats an entity as the locus must state its establishment in the form of either perception or inference.

If, however, that [subject] is not explicitly stated, then an object that has become the domain of mere conceptual construction—whether its existence is doubtful or its existence is denied—and which is being made the subject (*dharmin*), how could it be established as certain by way of its reality? And this being the case, whatever property of a real entity serves as a reason (*hetu*) would all suffer from the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because there is doubt in one instance and error in the other.

Therefore, it is correct that in the proof of existence (*sattā-sādhana*), a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) cannot be a logical reason because its locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhatva*), since [the locus] is not established by either perception or inference, which have real entities as their objects. However, in the proof of non-existence (*asattā-sādhana*), a property of a non-entity (*avastudharma*)—which is established for a non-entity through mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*)—cannot be refuted by the fault of an unestablished locus. For such a [property] does not depend on a real entity as its locus, precisely because it is a property of a non-entity; nor does its substratum depend on perception or inference, precisely because it is a non-entity.

But when existence (*bhāva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the real entity (*vastu*) itself is the locus (*āśraya*), because it is a property of a real entity. Furthermore, the ascertainment of a real entity occurs only through perception and inference; therefore, in their absence, there is necessarily a failure of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus, how can the same fault apply to proofs for both existence and non-existence?

As for what Trilocana stated—that in establishing the non-existence of eternal things, the fact that the absence of succession and so forth is a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatā*) is not established—that is a statement difficult even for a child to maintain. For the eternal things are the subject (*dharmin*); non-existence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*); and the absence of succession and so forth is the logical reason (*hetu*). Its being a "property of non-existence" means it is said to be invariably concomitant with its own probandum, on the grounds that this is a property of non-existent things such as a rabbit's horn and the like, and not a property of existent things.

By this statement, it is meant that as long as the probandum is not established in the subject by another means of valid cognition, the pervasion of the reason is not established; yet we do not know where this [pervasion] was perceived by him with respect to which reason.

Just as elsewhere, the invariable concomitance (*sādhyanāntarīyakatā*) with the probandum—which was established at another time by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) currently operating—is recalled by means of an example and employed for the sake of establishing the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*), yet it does not depend on any other [means] for the establishment of the probandum; so too, in the absence of succession and simultaneity, the property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatā*)—which is essentially the nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—is established at a different time from the establishment of existence (*sattva*) through succession and simultaneity.

At the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the example of a sky-lotus—established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that has already functioned—is employed as a reminder for the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*); it does not depend on any other proof of the probandum. Otherwise, all inference would be useless. For, once the pervasion of existence (*sattva*) by succession and simultaneity is established, the absence of the pervader (succession and simultaneity) is proven to be pervaded by the absence of the pervaded (existence); thus, the nature of non-existence has succession and simultaneity as its object.

Just as the nature of pervasion was already determined previously, so too the property of being absent where the probandum is absent (*sādhyābhāvadharmatva*) is not established in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of another instrument of knowledge through the establishment of the probandum; likewise, our position is that the probandum is established and settled by the absence of both succession and simultaneity. Since this has been settled previously, how can there be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)?

Furthermore, a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is likewise applicable here: the establishment of the absence of sequence and so forth as a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharma*) results in the establishment of their non-existence; and the establishment of their non-existence results in the establishment of the absence of sequence and so forth as a property of non-existence. However, by one with a biased view, it was not stated that there is no causal efficacy (*prayojakatva*) because the property of non-existence is unestablished, but rather because the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmanā*) is unestablished. What kind of circularity is that?

Nor is the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) itself the property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatā*), because the property of non-existence consists in its being inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāva*). Now, if the property of non-existence were to belong to the absence of succession and so forth, then it would be a property of those eternal things that have been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*); it is with this intention that the non-operation of that [property] was shown by way of the operation of the property of the subject. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to state a circular argument (*cakraka*). That too has already been examined in the ancient discussion.

Furthermore, if the nature of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*) constitutes the form of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) does not follow this logic common to other reasons. Nor is it the case for this reason alone; for whether the nature of non-existence constitutes pervasion or not, by what means is the absence of succession and so forth negated in the eternal?

Nor are these [reasons] subjects (*dharmin*) by way of being non-existent; rather, they are so by virtue of possessing doubt regarding existence and non-existence. Therefore, this objection—that the property of being a positive entity (*bhāvadharma*) and the property of being both [positive and negative] are not intended for this reason of "absence of succession" and so forth—is of no consequence. Nor is there a fault in the second alternative, because it has been established that even though the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is of the nature of a non-entity, it is nonetheless cognized through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For there is no cognition or non-cognition of things that are of the nature of non-existence other than conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); otherwise, in either case, it would follow that the conventional usage of "non-existence" would be lost. Therefore, since there is no dependence on direct experience (*anubhava*), there is no room for fault regarding the consequence of its production. However, lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) is appropriate to be addressed; that too is eliminated by the fact that it is born from a logical mark (*liṅga*), namely the non-perception of a pervader characterized by the absence of both succession and simultaneity.

For indeed, this very purification of the three-fold mark (trairūpya) was undertaken precisely for that purpose; why then is its established nature forgotten, such that it is said "because of the absence of a logical mark" (liṅga)? Therefore, how can there be a lack of confidence regarding the conceptual alternative of the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of existence from what is pervaded by succession and so forth? For the doubt concerning non-exclusion is the object of that lack of confidence. And since this [doubt] has no place once the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is ascertained, existence—which is invariably excluded from eternal things—is established as being pervaded by momentariness; thus, there is no fault.

Since the certainty of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been firmly established even in the third alternative, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), while establishing the absence of succession and so forth in its own permanent substratum, necessarily establishes the exclusion of existence from that [substratum] and establishes its necessary connection with momentariness; thus, it possesses three functions which are subsumed within a single operation, and it is not tainted by even a trace of fault.

And since the threefold nature [of the object] consists in the power of the object being characterized by existence (*sattā*), whereas when it is merely a cause it serves only to establish exclusion (*vyatireka*) for the purpose of establishing non-existence (*asattā*), it is established that there is indeed a duality of function.

[102,14] But surely, since the absence of a pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*) is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāvarūpa*), even if the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is avoided by its being a property of a real thing (*vastudharmatā*), how can that non-entity be the cognition of something, or the cause of its cognition? Or how is the cognition of that [non-entity] itself possible? Why is this not seen? Furthermore, it has been stated that the conceptual construction of exclusion (*vyatirekavikalpa*), which arises from that logical mark (*liṅga*), does not at this very moment harbor any suspicion of non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*).

Furthermore, one who establishes the cognition of a probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a proof (*sādhana*) must necessarily accept the linguistic convention of existence (*bhāvavyavahāra*); otherwise, everything would be contradicted if that proof were of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvarūpa*). Even regarding the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), if it is merely non-perception, that same fault applies; nor can the non-perception of something else be designated as the "non-perception of the pervader," since that would simply mean the non-perception of some other thing.

That too is of little consequence, because non-perception elsewhere is established precisely through the perception of the locus (*dharmin*). For instance, in the case of the statement "there is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees," there is the perception of the locus as a bare spot in relation to the tree, which is the non-perception of the tree; and the mere cognition of the bare spot in relation to the *śiṃśapā* is itself the cognition of the absence of the *śiṃśapā*. Thus, the operation of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) culminates in the essential nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

Likewise, regarding a permanent subject appearing in conceptual cognition, the mere appearance [of it] independently of succession and so forth is the non-perception of succession and so forth; and with respect to causal efficiency, the mere perception [of it] is the perception of its dissociation from causal efficiency—this is the distinction.

Furthermore, with respect to conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), just as there is the expression of non-existence (*abhāva*) by means of the fifth case of the cause—as in "there is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees"—so too is there the conventional usage that "existence (*bhāva*) is the means of proof" (*sādhana*). However, non-existence is never exclusively the means of proof. And that conventional usage cannot be set aside, because it is non-contradictory with respect to the object as it has been determined.

Indeed, that which is devoid of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is necessarily devoid of the pervaded (*vyāpya*); since this very point is consistent with the facts, it is established by that same method. And if this principle applies when the locus (*dharmin*) is real, why should there be any difference when it is unreal? [Objection: But surely this is a great difference! For when the locus is real, that very locus is associated with the pervader within a single cognition; thus, its perception constitutes the non-perception of the pervader. However, when the locus is unreal, it is not associated with anything within a single cognition. [Response: If you say this, then...

By that very property belonging to itself which is accepted as the pervader; for in this case, the single cognition is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Since that conceptual construction grasps the eternal, it might—by way of possibility—represent even the form of succession and so forth for the eternal, just as it represents another internal form, in its connection with the properties of succession and simultaneity. Thus, the coexistence within a single cognition of both [succession and eternity] is unavoidable.

If the eternal [nature] were not perceived as being in the range of cognition together with another property—such as the state of being incapable of having anything added to it—then simultaneity or non-simultaneity would indeed not be an object of cognition along with the real substratum; yet this is not the case. Furthermore, without the possibility of the thing to be negated, a co-occurrence within a single cognition could never be attained at that time.

In this regard, just as a horn was perceived in the head of Hariṇa as being associated with that same single cognition, and thus its association is denied even in the body of Hari by means of the very possibility of such a connection, so too, since the status of permanence or impermanence is not yet established for blue and other qualities, succession and simultaneity— being observed as associated with their own substratum in a single cognition— are introduced into the negation solely through the door of association in a single cognition based on the possibility that they might occur even in a permanent entity, being grasped by a cognition apprehending the permanent together with its own substratum, which is impermanent.

[103,18] But how is it that succession and the like do not manifest in eternal cognition? For we conceptualize the eternal precisely as being characterized by the extremes of succession and non-succession. If this is argued, then it is for this very reason that the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) applies; for without introducing a contrary form, that [argument] would be purposeless. While this superimposition of succession and non-succession upon the nature of the eternal may indeed necessitate the presentation of a subverting argument, it is not capable of including succession and non-succession within the eternal, because of their contradiction.

For permanence (*nityatva*) consists in having a single uniform nature throughout different times, whereas succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*akrama*) consist in having distinct natures even in two moments. Consequently, since the capacity for successive and simultaneous causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) in a permanent entity is of a nature mutually contradictory to permanence, their opposition is unavoidable; how, then, could succession and so forth be included within the permanent? And because they are not included therein, how could there be any mention of succession or simultaneity by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a pure permanence that has eliminated all superimposition (*samāropa*), given that everything [in this context] is within the domain of mere conceptualization?

The establishment of contradictory properties—whether determinate or indeterminate—is made in relation to forms superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For example, in the case of the triad of qualities (*triguṇya*), unity is a contradictory property; [furthermore], the activities of serenity, distress, and dejection are determinate, while the connection with either selflessness (*nairātmya*) or its opposite is indeterminate. Similarly here as well, if [the agent] is non-agential due to having a single nature across prior and subsequent times, then it is eternally non-agential; and if it is agential at all times, then it is eternally agential. However, succession and simultaneity are sometimes the very nature of the capacity for action; for if there were simultaneity, [the result] would indeed be manifest.

“Functioning at one time only” means that its activity is occasional (*kādācitka*). Even in the case of a succession [of moments], because it functions having already functioned and will function again, its activity is indeed occasional; for the dependence upon auxiliary causes has already been refuted. Therefore, since “occasional activity” and “non-occasional activity” are characterized by mutual exclusion, their contradiction is established.

This being the case, when the counter-positive is conceived as eternal, the non-perception of the incompatible—namely, succession and simultaneity—which would otherwise meet the condition of occurring in the same cognition, is itself the non-perception [of the eternal]. Or rather, that very [non-perception] is the non-perception of the pervader of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*). Therefore, because it consists in the perception of the locus of the pervader (*vyāpaka-dharmin*), it is not distinct from other types of non-perception of the pervader.

Furthermore, if for you, who are unfortunate, the distinction between what is real and what is unreal remains poorly established even now despite [the fact that] they share the status of being subjects (*dharmin*), then even regarding a real subject, who could prevent one from searching for distinctions such as "in one place there is a solid part, while in another there is liquid water" and so forth? Therefore, what use is the consideration of a distinction based on reality and unreality?

[104,14] But surely its utility is great! For, in the case of a real entity (*vastu*) as the locus (*dharmin*), inference characterized by the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), which is indirectly connected to that [non-existence], becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the establishment of valid means of knowledge has the real entity as its foundation. And it cannot be so in the case of a non-entity (*avastu*). If this is argued:

[104,16] First of all, if "being based on a real entity" (vastv-adhiṣṭhānatva) means simply that [the property] has come from the real entity even through a succession [of conceptualizations], then its dependence upon a real entity—which is the object of the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding both successive and non-successive causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*)—is not lost; nor is its dependence upon the real entity that is the object of the conceptualization of the locus (*dharmin*) lost.

Now, is the fact that something serves as a cause for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) in some respect its "having a real entity as its basis" (*vastv-adhiṣṭhānatva*)? That too is established merely as a means for proving an entity that is subject to momentary destruction; or rather, since this conceptualization of a subject (*dharmin-vikalpa*) itself is the cause for the linguistic convention regarding a non-entity being based upon an entity, what is the point of this [separate] "having a real entity as its basis" on the part of the subject-entity itself? And if this [conceptualization] were indeed grasping [the object], then would it be only inference (*anumāna*) that possesses "having a real entity as its basis" or validity (*prāmāṇya*)? No.

In the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is precisely the reliance upon linguistic expression (*loka-āśrayaṇa*) that allows for the consideration of a subject (*dharmin*). However, perception, when not relying on such [expression], arises from the object itself and functions as a conventional designation based on the object; thus, it has the object as its basis. Let it be understood that inference (*anumāna*) likewise has the object as its basis in exactly the same way. For even in the case of perception, while its very birth is direct through a lineage [of causes], its practical application (*vyavahāraṇa*) occurs only through the mediation of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, for inference as well, both [the object and its cognition] are mediated through a succession; even practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is mediated by memory, desire, and so forth. Thus, the fact that inference has a real entity as its basis is indeed a defect due to this mediation. However, it is merely a delusion of the intellect to think that this requirement of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is an additional burden compared to the mediation already present in inference in other cases with respect to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Moreover, this property is not common to all other types of inference.

For in the cases of the non-perception of cause, effect, and pervader, the capacity to indicate [the probandum] exists through the pervasion of the opposite, having set aside the direct connection with one's own probandum.

In the same way, if the fact of having a real entity (*vastu*) as its basis were to occur in a particular object through the aforementioned mediation, what kind of fault would there be? For there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*). However, with respect to the conceptualization of the subject (*dharmin*), even that much mediation is not possible; moreover, the proximity is unique, because the subject is unified with the form of the conceptualization. This is because, even in the position that [cognition] is formless (*nirākārapakṣa*), the subject—which possesses an unreal and eternal form—has its manifestation dependent upon conceptualization.

Therefore, since the investigation into the substratum of the real entity within the locus (the *dharmin*) fulfills its purpose by relying on a specific proximity even through the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no fault whatsoever. This very principle should be applied in such cases as: "The son of a barren woman is not a speaker because he lacks consciousness," or "A donkey’s horn is not a substance because it is devoid of substantiality"; and it serves as the refuge in such cases as: "There is no contradiction regarding a non-entity because it is not an object of cognition."

If the state of not being an object of cognition were intended with respect to mere cognition, then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddhi*); if it were intended with respect to experience, then the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, there is the capacity to avoid such types of refutations; however, there is no counting of any multitude of refutations such as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and so forth.

By this, the [objection] that "in the case of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*) must be understood as something distinct" is easily set aside; for it has been established that the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*) itself is the object of cognition, just as the absence of *śiṃśapā*-ness follows from the absence of tree-ness in a *gaṇṭśala* (a type of tree). Thus, there is no lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) regarding the non-perception of the pervader under discussion, because the contradiction between permanence and [the alternatives of] succession and simultaneity has been demonstrated.

As for what was said—that there is a contradiction between succession and simultaneity—that is stated again by way of its pervader as "contradiction with causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*). Nor is there a lack of establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because even a non-entity can be established as a subject (*dharmin*), and because its cognition is established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For this very reason, in the treatise, its establishment and ascertainment in the subject occurs either through perception or through inference.

Thus, it should be understood that this is clearly an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule (*utsarga*), wherein the proponents of other systems claim that even in a non-entity (*avastu*), such as a fingernail and so forth—which possesses an unproduced and unprecedented nature (*anutpādyāpūrvarūpa*)—there exists the establishment of a probandum and a probans based on its simultaneous non-causality with respect to sound and other phenomena.

[106] In this way, the objection regarding the non-establishment of the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is also avoided. Furthermore, the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is indeed established, because there is no disagreement regarding them, just as there is none regarding "permanence. Consequently, the denial of the reason's presence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is also destroyed. Now, if it is argued that the reason has fallen into the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), [we reply: by this very [argument], because of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the established probandum (*siddhasādhya*), the acceptance of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) for the subjects of the probandum is established through the reason of existence (*sattva*).
The third quarter, titled "The Section on Negation."
[Chapter on Momentary Destruction] [Section 107.2] [The Fourth Quarter:

The Topic of Causeless Destruction] By means of perception, which discerns positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— just as in the case of smoke and fire— [one perceives that destruction is causeless].
The state of cause and effect consisting of the visible and the invisible is established for the two factors of destruction and its constituent parts.

Prior to the presence of the cause, the non-existent fruit—namely destruction—extends over that period while [the entity] remains; yet even this is false, for destruction is the non-perception of its own nature.

For the very nature of destruction is not within the range of perception such that—through the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance—one could establish the stability of an entity over the time during which the effect called "destruction" did not exist prior to the presence of the hammer or other factors considered its causes; for, since the nature of the destructible object is not perceived, this [notion of a cause] is merely a false imagination. Thus, how can stability be established through the non-perception of a cause?

If it is argued: "But surely jars, hammers, and so forth are indeed seen; therefore, there is some thing called 'destruction' among those very objects, and thus the non-perception of the nature of destruction is unestablished (asiddha)."

This jar has been seen, and its falling here was likewise seen; the collection of shards has been seen, but no further non-existence has been seen. Therefore, where is this term "non-existence" applied? What indeed is its cause here? This mere series of potsherds is seen independently of any other obstacle.

First, this jar is seen; here its falling is likewise seen; the collection of shards is seen; but nothing further is seen that could be called "non-existence. Therefore, where has the expression "non-existence" been placed? Furthermore, what is the cause here? Only this series of potsherds is seen, belonging solely to the jar [and not to non-existence]. [As it is said: "Of the obstacle..."

Even though we examine most skillfully with our physical eyes, we do not perceive any other category of entity here that could be made the object of the scriptural statement regarding non-existence (*abhāva*). And because such a thing is not seen, what cause for it can we ascertain, by whose absence it would follow that each preceding [entity] is non-existent and destroyed? Furthermore, as for the "stick" imagined to be its cause, we observe only a series of potsherds that conform to its presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and nothing else whatsoever.

This has been presented once again as an example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*): just as this [pot], by manifesting positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) through perception and non-perception, is established as the effect of the stick because it is visible; so too, if the entity called "destruction" were visible, its status as the effect of that very stick would be unavoidable, provided it could be distinguished from things that do not possess its nature. But this is not the case. Therefore, this is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). It might be argued as follows:
"Let alone the row of shards; this destruction of the jar did not exist previously.
Therefore, let stability be established by that [prior non-existence]; what is the use of a subsequent destruction?
To this, the reply is:

If that very destruction is said to be [the absence], then how is it that when another jar is placed there, the designation "absence" occurs? Therefore, even in our view, the existence of absence is established.

This is the meaning: just as it is possible for you to demonstrate that there is no destruction of the jar prior to the blow of a swift hammer—because the series of potsherds, which constitute its very nature, is not perceived—likewise, it is also impossible to maintain that there is no familiarity with a succession of absences. For even in the case of absence, it is not the series of potsherds itself that is being spoken of, such that the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) would serve as a basis in exactly the same manner.

Now, if it is argued that even non-existence (*abhāva*) is nothing other than the series of potsherds, like destruction (*nāśa*), then how could there be the conventional usage of "non-existence" when one jar has been removed from a certain place and another jar is placed there—given that the series of potsherds is absent? Yet, for someone who perceives some degree of difference, there is indeed the conventional usage of "non-existence" even in that case, because of the delusion caused by the similarity of one [jar] to another, despite the determination of its former state. Therefore, how can the series of potsherds alone be non-existence? If, for one who applies the term "destruction" to this [series],...

It may indeed be said that prior destruction (*pūrva-dhvaṃsa*) does not exist because of the absence of the state of shards; however, it cannot be said that non-existence (*abhāva*) does not exist, for it is difficult to perceive due to the presence of other similar things. Therefore, since the prior non-existence of the jar is possible even before the blow [of the hammer], our desired point is established. This is simply the failure to apply the perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*); hence, there is no utility in applying the designation "destruction" to the shards.

Furthermore, nothing else is observed that follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the hammer; thus, destruction is merely a matter of conventional usage and does not exist as a real entity.
If destruction is not determined by its own cause, why is there a restriction in cognition such that "the jar has been destroyed" at a specific place and time? Therefore, it must be an effect.
Nor indeed is there any other cause, for otherwise, it would have occurred differently even before the swift stroke of the staff.
Who can prevent the stubborn cognition of a destroyed jar that arises from its destruction?

In that case, the boastful assertion—made with puffed-up cheeks—that the destruction (dhvaṃsa) follows the positive and negative concomitance of its cause just like any other effect, is refuted; for, unlike other effects, it is not experienced as such.

Having established destruction through mere reasoning, you sought to prove that it is dependent upon a substrate intended by us; but that reasoning has been exhausted, since we observe a series of potsherds produced by a hammer and so forth when the water-bearing jar is seen [to have vanished].
First, the cognition of a destroyed jar arises through the following convention:

"In this causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no factor whatsoever named 'destruction'; nor does such [destruction] exist within it, neither now nor ever before; and yet, this complete state [of the complex] persists."

By the first half [of the verse], the causal complex for the arising of the cognition of a "destroyed pot" is shown; by the second half, it is demonstrated that there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for something called "destruction," whereas both are observed for the causal complex of its discernment (*tad-viveka*). In this regard, positive concomitance is rejected because there is no factor named "destruction" present in this causal complex as a cause; furthermore, the reliance on negative concomitance—that the cognition would not arise even when this causal complex is present—is also cast aside.

In that case, why was this cognition not [produced] previously? [The answer is: by means of the remainder, there is the destruction of the notion of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). If this causal complex (*sāmagrī*) had existed previously, this cognition, necessarily arising, would have indicated a dependence upon another object. But this causal complex did not exist previously either, because it was absent due to the deficiency of the series of potsherds and the absence of causes such as the falling of a crossbar. Therefore, how could there even be a question of negative concomitance?

However, regarding the aforementioned causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) expressed by the two negations: "this [cognition] would not exist even in this [complex], nor ever. The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is made explicit by the remainder [of the statement]. The meaning is that because the absence of the causal complex itself is established at the time of the absence of cognition, that absence of the causal complex is pervaded by the absence of cognition.

However, for one of biased vision who maintains that every causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is indeed "indirect" (*parokṣa*) by virtue of its being a totality of factors other than perception, and who consequently asserts that because of this indirectness there can be no determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for it—alas, even the connection between smoke and the causal complex of fire, fuel, and so forth would vanish, resulting in the absurd consequence that the world would be devoid of both purposeful engagement and withdrawal. Therefore, since the acceptance of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) does not obstruct the observed capacity of the means [of accomplishment], enough with this elaboration.
Thus, it is established that for one who has the cognition of the jar, the very experience of the potsherds is the means for determining the destruction of the jar.
Therefore, this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is exhausted; it is not capable of establishing destruction.

If it is argued that "there can be no cognition of a qualified object without a qualifier," we say no; because destruction exists at a different time from the [jar], its status as a qualifier is unestablished.
That by which something is qualified through one's own cognition is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Because there is no existence of destruction at two different times—namely, at the prior and subsequent moments—who could be qualified by whom? [If it is argued that it] is made an object of cognition in some instance: yet destruction is not a property of duration residing in the entity itself, but rather resides in a location. And what resides elsewhere cannot be a qualifier of another, just as a staff [qualifies a person]. If it is argued that this could still be the case because of their difference [from the entity]:

Now, only that qualifier which appears at this moment through its distinction from all other forms can make the qualified object the focus of a cognition colored by itself, and not one that does not appear in its own form, just like a staff. If it is argued that there is an inconclusive case because the cognition of a "staff-bearer" arises even with a staff established only through inference, we say no; for our intention is [to exclude] that whose own form does not manifest in any way whatsoever.

Furthermore, although the staff does not appear at the time of inference, it certainly has a manifestation of its own nature at the time of grasping its relation with the mark (liṅga) intended as the determiner.
