Therefore, through the recollection of that [manifestation], the staff may also produce at the time of inference a cognition colored by its own form. However, for one who has never before seen a staff, even the staff was never previously seen to be an object of inference or a cause for a cognition colored by its own nature.

In this way, how could the meaning of "destruction" also be such [as you claim], since it is in every respect unperceived? Furthermore, the cognition of "the man with a staff" (daṇḍin) is not distinct from the inference of the staff; for there is no difference in meaning between the expressions "there is a staff here," "this belongs to him," and "this man possesses a staff."

Furthermore, this [non-apprehension] cannot be an inference merely by virtue of being a thesis (*pratijñāmātra*) when the inferential mark (*liṅga*) has been abandoned; for how could that which, even when its cognition has perished, requires a certainty that establishes the object named "destruction," be itself designated as the means of proof? Nor is there any other inferential mark, because since it is entirely imperceptible, no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) can be established for anyone with respect to it. For this very reason, every form of cognition is resorted to as a refuge for establishing it. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) on account of what is established through inference.

Since the cognition of the qualifier in an inference is inseparable from and immediately follows the manifestation of the qualifier's own nature, and since the inference and the cognition of its qualifier are not established as distinct, [we state the following]:

that which does not have a manifestation of its own nature cannot be the cause of a cognition colored by itself, just like a donkey’s mane. And since there is no manifestation of its own nature for destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

[110,19] Being the cause of a cognition colored by itself, [the object] is pervaded by the very state of appearing, since its existence when the manifestation has ceased is sublated by the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the consequence]. Nor is this unestablished (*asiddhi*), because there is no conventional usage of "appearing" for an external object that cannot be shown as "this," and because there is no dispute regarding that which can be designated as "this. For even a staff is not to be established by the cognition of the person carrying the staff, since it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Even when establishing conventional usage for a fool, there is no designation as "this," especially in the case of what is within the range of the eyes.

[110,24] Now, if every object appears by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) and not by way of another’s nature (*pararūpa*), just as existence itself does not appear in the form of non-existence, so too non-existence, even while not appearing in the form of existence, certainly appears by way of its own nature. If it is argued that appearing as "this" (*idantayā*) belongs only to an existent thing that is an object of the eye, and therefore, even in the absence of appearance as "this," there is no total non-appearance at all;

An appearance in the form of another is not sought at all, since its non-existence is already established. Furthermore, when we examine what its own nature (*svarūpa*) is that appears, we find nothing. As for the designation "this-ness" (*idantā*), even if it applies to some entities, it is certainly not a royal decree.

If one were to say that the designation "this-ness" applies only to certain entities that come before the eyes and not to all, then what could be said regarding the *ṭaṅka*, *vaka*, and so forth, which likewise appear but can ultimately not be designated as "this"? What more is there to say here?

Therefore, the logical principle is this: as long as an object moves within the range of the eye, it appears as a designation by way of "this-ness" (idantā); however, that which is devoid of designation by way of "this-ness" does not appear at all as something graspable by the eyes.

Now, if it is argued that the manifestation itself must be established by means of the cognition of a particular [quality], just as the cognition of a "man with a staff" does not occur without the cognition of the staff, so too it does not occur without the manifestation of the staff; and likewise, since the cognition of destruction is also a cognition of a particular, it cannot occur without destruction and the manifestation of destruction—how then can there be a claim of non-manifestation? [We reply: There is indeed a transformation, but it is not of such a kind.

"The appearance residing in one's own continuum must also be apprehended by us through inference"; thus, this same [principle] now applies even to the appearance of a jar and so forth. Consequently, would a physician not have accomplished his purpose even without acting upon the meaning—that "I see something" must be understood through inference, even by means of the word of a reliable person for one who is not reliable? In the end, one might even resort to cessation [of doubt] by means of an oath. For these modes of cognition find their scope regarding objects that are beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), but not regarding consciousness itself.

Furthermore, when one who does not see [an object] is made to grasp that "you indeed see it while perceiving yourself," this is clearly the "science of buffoons" (bhaṇṭavidyā), which causes even one who sees to fail to perceive. And he who, though not seeing, grasps "I see" by virtue of that person's word—he is truly a beast among beasts. For even in the doctrine that knowledge is imperceptible (*jñānaparokṣatāvāda*), that which does not appear is established by the appearance of something else; one cannot establish "this has an appearance" or "this has no appearance" through logical arguments.

Therefore, the claim that even the appearance (pratibhāsa) is what is to be proven is incoherent. If, however, destruction (nāśa) itself—which does not appear [directly]—is being proven, let it be proven; but certainly not by means of the cognition of a destroyed jar. This is established:
either there is destruction, but it is not the producer of the cognition, just as the cognition of a destroyed jar is not produced by the jar [itself].

Even granting this for the sake of argument, we say: let there be such a thing as "destruction," yet it cannot necessarily be maintained that the hammer or other such instruments are its perceived producers. Just as the experience of the shards is not accepted as the cause of the cognition of a destroyed jar, so too, even for destruction, there might be some other unobserved cause entirely, distinct from the hammer and so forth; therefore, the prior non-perception of a cause is not established.

Just as an unseen entity called "destruction" (nāśa), established by its own acceptance, is the basis for the cognition of something destroyed, so too there must be some unseen cause of destruction itself, and not the mallet or other such instruments. How then could the cessation of destruction be necessarily tied to their absence? However, this distinction holds: while the efficacy of the mallet with respect to the potsherd, and the efficacy of the experience of the potsherd with respect to the cognition of destruction, are established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the same is not the case for the mallet with respect to destruction, nor for the object to be destroyed with respect to the cognition of destruction; this point must be accepted only out of deference to your position.

If it is argued that from the experience of the potsherds there would only be the conceptualization of the potsherds, and not the cognition of a destroyed jar—this is like pulling out the fangs of a living tiger. For the arising of the cognition of a destroyed jar, which is directly experienced immediately upon seeing the circle of potsherds following the perception of the jar, is being denied. If that were so, then the denial of every object established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) would follow as a consequence.

Furthermore, when emptiness is [perceived] by a person through the non-apprehension of a jar due to a lack of interest and so forth, then from the observation of the potsherds, only the conceptualization of the potsherds arises, because a difference in causal conditions (sāmagrī) is what produces a difference in cognition. Even if those [potsherds] were to conform to your own intention, such would not necessarily be the case; and even if you should desire that the cognition of destruction arise solely from the experience of the potsherds, it would indeed occur in that way—thus, destruction itself is not the causal factor.

Therefore, enough with this reliance on mere personal speculation; the perception of the potsherd alone is the basis for the cognition [of destruction]. However, when it requires the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the jar, it likewise requires the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); thus, there is no over-extension of the principle. Furthermore, a convention cannot be established by pointing out actual destruction, precisely because that [destruction] is not perceptible; rather, by pointing out a transformation consisting in the production of a heterogeneous state, one applies the term "perishes" to such a condition.
By this, those who imagine that the very perception of non-existence constitutes the non-apprehension of an entity are refuted.

[112,18] Precisely because one does not perceive a form consisting of non-existence, there is therefore no such thing as "destruction" that occurs subsequently. Furthermore, if this world is established as having a different nature at every moment, then by the force of sound reasoning, its death would either be delayed or not; what of it?
It might be argued as follows:
"If that [otherness] were to exist together with existence, it could not exist without destruction.
Since it would then be both existent and non-existent, what kind of entity could it possibly be? Therefore, this [otherness] must necessarily follow from the nature of the entity itself."

Because it exists, and because it is impossible for that [effect] to have a cause distinct from its own cause, the "otherness" produced by that [cause] also vanishes; how then could there be destruction at every moment?

It was stated that "if there were a similarity with existence" (*bhāvena sādharmyaṃ sa cet*), this refers to the description of the arising of non-existence from the presence of an existent cause. In this regard, what is the meaning of "other than destruction" (*dhvaṃsād anyatā*)? Does one and the same existent thing become shattered into pieces by it? Or is it merely the production of another existent from this [destruction]? Or is it both the cessation of the prior and the production of another existent? Or finally, is it merely the cessation of the prior?

In this regard, destruction does not cause a single entity to attain multiplicity, because of the contradiction between those two—oneness and multiplicity. If it is argued that even a single thing becomes multiple through a difference in time and thus incurs no fault, [we reply]: what does it matter if there is a difference in time when there is an absence of internal difference within the entity itself?

For if a difference in time were to entail a difference in the entity, then this might be so. However, since the entity remains in its very same state (*tādavasthya*), such a resort to the straw of *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass is appropriate only for those like you; thus, the first position is refuted.

If it is broken, there is no shattering of that [pot]; this is the second fault. For if another object is produced, the previous [pot] is not shattered; thus, even when shards and so forth are present, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving the pot.
What is the use of its shattering by means of something distinct?

If it is argued that there is no utility in the perception of that pot by means of another object such as the shards, and that its utility lies in the production of that very other object called "destruction" (nāśa); [we reply:]...
But since you arise from a different birth, why is it not the cause of destruction?

Let the birth of the potsherd arise from that very same cause from which the destruction by the hammer and so forth arises; why then postulate a destruction as the probandum? By this, the portion concerning the production of another in the third alternative is also refuted; thus, only the fourth remains: "its cessation is brought about by destruction. Even then:

If it is held that the birth of destruction occurs through [another] destruction, then by that [second] destruction another destruction would have to be produced, resulting in a series of destructions; thus, that entity would never cease to exist.
If it is argued that there is no cessation other than destruction, then how can there be mutual annihilation? [The answer is:
It is not so, because when that [annihilation] is observed as a real entity, its appearance is explained as being due to the perception of destruction.

For destruction cannot transcend the status of being a real entity (*vastutā*) or the status of being an existent (*bhāvatā*), because it possesses the capacity to produce an experience and because it is established through other means of proof. How, then, can one thing be called the "destruction" of another? As for the reply that "because the object is no longer perceived when this [destruction] exists," that is not correct; since it has been demonstrated that there is no perception of destruction, how then can it be said that "when this is absent"?
Furthermore, if it is claimed that the cessation of the entity called "destruction" occurs because the object is not perceived when that [destruction] exists, then—

Let destruction be the mallet itself, or perhaps the fragments; for in either case, the intended meaning of "while that exists" is untenable, because the mallet exists prior [to the destruction], whereas the fragments are simultaneous with it—just as in the expressions "while the seed exists, the sprout [arises]" or "while the cows are being milked, he has gone. Here, "destruction" (*nāśa*) means cessation (*nivṛtti*), specifically that which is called annihilation (*dhvaṃsa*). Let this annihilation also be nothing other than the mallet and so forth. There is no need for a separate conceptualization of annihilation, since by that much alone it is established that the entity was stable prior to its absence. To this, it is replied: [114,15]
That pair [of existence and non-existence] does not obstruct existence by virtue of being an entity;
for an entity itself cannot possibly be the opponent of an entity. And if there is no opposition, how could there be the cessation or the non-perception of another? To this, the reply is:
for you, the very nature of an entity is its difference from other entities.

In this matter, there is no capacity on the part of entities (*bhāva*); rather, it is you yourself who possess the nature of being an entity or a non-entity. For instance, "an entity" (*bhāva*) is that which "comes into being" (*bhavati*); and "coming into being" is first of all accepted as its origination (*utpatti*). Even when "an entity" is understood as "that which exists" (*asti*), the meaning of "being an entity" is still existence; and that too is accepted as characterized by the reality of its own nature (*svarūpasattva*), adorned with permanence for as long as it lasts. Furthermore, that which does not come into being—i.e., does not exist—how could it be connected with the act of originating, like the son of a barren woman or a sprout?

[115,1] Now, if it is argued that even capacity (*śakti*) is admitted to be existence because the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs only in the absence of any description of functional capacity, then that capacity is indeed already accepted as being produced by its own cognition; and walking without hesitation and so forth are precisely its effects. There is, however, no inherence of existence (*sattva-samavāya*) or inherence in its own cause (*svakāraṇa-samavāya*) as you yourself have asserted. Furthermore, it is not necessary for every property of an entity to be present in every entity, nor does the absence of every property of an entity imply that another entity cannot exist.

This being the case, it follows that universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) would also be non-existent. Furthermore, the very production of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) from those [categories] is a fault. Moreover, since a real entity (*vastu*) necessarily possesses destruction—meaning that "destruction" resides in it because of its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—it cannot be a positive existence (*bhāva*). Alas, what a painful and perverse obsession with a dogmatic tenet! Therefore, you have full autonomy in this matter. If you say that even destruction must be a positive existence, then the hammer and other such tools would also be the non-existence of the jar.

If it is argued that no one indeed designates a thing such as a hammer as either an entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*), [we reply]: Well then, if even destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) were perceived by someone as arising in some form—specifically, as something persisting eternally—who would designate it as a non-entity? For we see that things such as smoke from the body, whose forms are unperceived due to obstruction, lack of attention, and so forth, become recipients of the designation "entity" when they are perceived again.

Therefore, the cessation of the conventional usage of "existence" is personally experienced precisely through non-perception, because its very nature consists in the perception of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). And that non-perception, if one accepts it as an experience, is itself an existence; however, if it were unperceivable, then to speak of its "arising" and so forth would be like painting a picture in the sky. But if the essential nature and the arising [of non-perception] are themselves perceived, then the conventional usage of "existence" follows by force; how, then, could this [non-perception] also be contradictory?

Nor is it the case that the term "non-existence" (*abhāva*) does not apply even to the hammer and so forth, for its establishment occurs through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of other positive entities (*bhāva*). Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). For by whatever relation the very entity called destruction is said to be the cessation of the jar, that same relation is not obstructed by the shards or the iron bar. Furthermore, their opposition (*virodhitva*) is most fitting, since they excel one another even by the slightest part, namely, by the act of being perceived.

Because the statement "the conventional usage of the absence of a jar occurs when those two exist" would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the grounds for its refutation are well-established. Furthermore, it is not the case that one positive entity does not at all contradict another positive entity; otherwise, how could "cowness" contradict "non-cowness," or fire contradict cold?

Furthermore, contradiction (*virodha*) is also known to be of two kinds. Among these, if contradiction were simultaneous coexistence (*sahāsthiti*), then it would belong only to two positive entities (*bhāva*), like fire and snow. For the determination of non-coexistence (*sahānasthāna*) occurs when one thing exists while another, whose causes are unimpaired, is absent. And it is clear that this [mode of] operation is not possible for existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva*).
[This is because] there is no exclusion of one by the other when their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) consist in mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*).

Indeed, it is not the case that contradiction characterized by incompatible definitions (*alākṣaṇika-virodha*) has the function of subverting an existent entity; rather, it is only [contradiction] characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). For [in the latter case], there is a restriction solely to two properties (*dharma*), whereas in the former, when an entity is already established, there is a negation of the confusion or intermixture of its own nature (*svarūpa-saṃkara-vyatikara*) with either another entity or a non-entity. Therefore, just as blue is not non-blue because the two possess mutually exclusive intrinsic natures, so too would it be for a jar and its destruction. Yet, this much does not establish our desired conclusion, because the jar’s persistence remains intact even when the mere proximity of a hammer occurs.

[116,7] But surely, in the case of a jar and a thunderbolt and so forth, it is only because of the contradiction between two properties that there is a mere difference in what they inhere in; however, since the destruction of the jar and [the jar itself] are themselves contradictory by virtue of being of the nature of existence and non-existence, how could they coexist?

No; for it is only between two properties (*dharma*)—existence and non-existence—which consist respectively of being and non-being, that there is mutual exclusion. This is because there is no non-existence of that which is superposed as existing, nor existence of that which is established as non-existent; or else, because there is no identity between a jar, space, water, or a lotus. What is not precluded, however, is mere contradiction, provided that one existing thing overcomes another existing thing. And by that much alone, the operation of "non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*) is fulfilled. Therefore, mutual exclusion belongs only to two properties.

If it is asked, "How [is there contradiction] between blue and non-blue?"—the meaning is simply that because blue and non-blue are mutually exclusive, there is no identity (*ekatva*) between them. Thus, even by this method, it is precisely the contradiction of properties (*dharmavirodha*) that is revealed. Otherwise, just as in the case of snow and fire, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even one wearing blue and non-blue garments could not coexist when joined together. Yet, even then, there is certainly no identity (*tādātmya*).

If it is argued that the location (*deśa*) of the blue and the non-blue is indeed distinct, let it be distinct; however, there is no contradiction between the two entities (*vastu*) merely by virtue of that difference in location. Otherwise, it would follow that even water and fire could exist in a continuous state when combined in that same way, since the efficacy of contradiction depends on their exclusion from a subtle location (*sūkṣmadeśa*). For this very reason, in the perception of a contradiction (*viruddhopalabdhi*), the locus (*dharmin*) is the gross location itself, conceived as a single entity.
Thus, the statement "the blue is contradicted by the non-blue" means simply that the blue does not become the non-blue.

If, however, there were a direct contradiction even between the subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*), then wherever non-blue-ness exists in a subject, blue-ness would not exist there. Yet this is the case, as for example with gold (*tapanīya*) alone among other jewels; likewise, even though destruction is merely a property consisting of non-existence, the pot—which possesses the property of existence—is not non-existent, and that which possesses the property of non-existence is not existent. This is the meaning. Therefore...

By means of the established property of non-existence, a jar that is indeed non-existent is conventionally designated as "non-existent," but it is not the case that an existent thing is being negated. Rather, it is existence (*sattā*) that is excluded; this exclusion functions everywhere through the principle of incompatible coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). But how can the non-existence of a jar be a property (*dharma*)? To what, then, could it belong as a property? If you argue that because it is accepted as a property, it necessarily implies a substratum (*dharmin*), and therefore let it belong to the surface of the ground itself—then does it follow that the non-existence intended is that of the ground alone?

[117,5] If it is argued: "Is it not the case that the absence (abhāva) of a jar, which is related to it through the relation of the sublated and the sublator, is said to be a mere property (dharmamātra) of the ground, and not the sublator of the ground itself?

Let it be so; let that property of the ground simply not be its sublator. Just as the presence of a blue object is not contradicted on a ground that possesses non-blueness—which is the opposite of blue—so too, even on a ground possessed by an absence that is considered the opposite of a jar, there would be no contradiction in the presence of the jar. Therefore, their status as the sublated and the sublator is established merely through conceptual presumption (abhimāna).

Therefore, it is logical that the conceptual cognition—which manifests the absence of the jar by way of its relation to the locus, namely the ground—treats that absence as a property (*dharma*) of that [locus]. However, with respect to what has been determined (*adhyavasita*), there is correspondence or otherwise; thus, a property that is contradictory through mutual exclusion brings about the non-existence of its own opposite—which is indeed non-existent—within its own substratum (*ātmadharmi*). But it does not remove [the opposite]; rather, it is precisely the cause for the conventional treatment of difference within the substratum.

Likewise, in the case of water, fire, and so forth, the quality of touch—whether hot or otherwise—is made the object of the conventional usage of "contradiction" through the mere examination of their own nature, even at a distance, by virtue of possessing mutually opposing forms, without depending on their mutual removal. However, non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is established only through the observation that the existence of one results in the cessation of the other. Therefore, if contradiction is intended to mean non-coexistence, then let it be established as the cessation of both existence and perception in the case of entities;
however, this applies only to two positive entities (*bhāva*), not to an entity and its absence (*abhāva*).

[117,17] If it is argued: "Is not contradiction intended here as 'incompatibility through non-coexistence' (sahānavasthāna), defined merely by the fact that when one exists, the other ceases? And since this is obtainable even between an absence and a presence, the restriction that it applies only to two presences is not logical."

It has been stated here that the phrase "only when this exists" is difficult to establish in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, what is the use of establishing such a nature of non-existence, since the contradiction between two existents (*bhāva*) is not thereby resolved? Moreover, since the contradiction [of the pot] is established by the hammer and so forth alone, destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is of no use. If, on the other hand, a figurative contradiction is intended, then because its purpose is fulfilled simply by the non-confusion of essential natures (*svarūpa*), the persistence of the existent is unavoidable.

Furthermore, according to the position that contradiction is characterized by non-coexistence, an opposing factor cannot obstruct another unless it has itself arisen; like cold and fire. First there is its own arising, then its operation, and then, depending on the degree of proficiency in that operation, the obstruction of the other occurs after some small number of moments. Thus, for that duration prior to the obstruction, it would have to coexist with the prior non-existence of the object to be obstructed.

Now, even if the operation occurs at the very moment of origination, such that an entity, acting as a cooperative cause with the destruction that is simultaneously arising, would bestow its own bondage upon its own effect, then cessation would follow; thus, simultaneous existence is unavoidable. Even if one disregards the bestowing of the moment of bondage, since destruction occurs immediately after the subsequent moment of its own continuum, simultaneous existence is established for even a single moment. And how can this be tolerated by one possessing consciousness—that an entity both exists and does not exist in one and the same moment?

Furthermore, since you accept non-coexistence, just as cold is destroyed by fire by producing another destruction, so too must the substratum (nipātin) be removed by that destruction; and since that [destruction] would likewise have to produce another destruction to counteract its own counter-positive (pratiyogin), there would be an infinite regress. Consequently, even in a hundred lifetimes, no one could ever achieve the conventional usage of "non-existence" for anything.

Now, as for the second contradiction: where there is existence, there is no room at all for non-existence. For this is the very nature of contradiction according to its defining characteristic (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*), namely that when two contradictory properties reside in a single substratum (*dharmin*), there is no room for the other; thus, destruction simply does not arise.

Now, if it is argued that because of the efficacy of a cause, how could [an entity] exist after having been non-existent—therefore, destruction must necessarily occur—we say: no. For it is impossible to postulate the efficacy of a cause regarding an object that is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Indeed, as long as the breath of an entity moves, there is not even a scent of non-existence. Otherwise, if two properties considered to be contradictory were to coexist in a single substratum for even a single moment, where would the contradiction of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāravirodha*) be?

For indeed, even if existence [of the cause] occurs by the power of its cause, coexistence (*sahabhāva*)—the simultaneous presence and absence of two things in one locus—is difficult to avoid in reality. That entity (*bhāva*), being previously established, does not cease simply because it is exhausted by the effort of coming into being. Furthermore, the function (*vyāpāra*) of the hammer and so forth consists precisely in destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Even if there were a function in both cases, what need would there be for destruction? Nor is it to be ceased by destruction alone, since destruction has no function prior to its own arising.
Therefore, the persistence of the entity and the production of non-existence are established as coexistent, like a mountain and the lion (*kāśariṇa*) being produced upon it.

If you argue that the existence will be refuted later by the destruction of the fuel, as in the case of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), then this is merely the lamentation of one who, fearing the refutation of the coexistence of existence and non-existence, persists in his long-practiced fallacious reasoning. Whether the entity is subsequently refuted by destruction or not, the flaw in your position has already arrived in the form of the consequence that existence and non-existence must coexist. What is the use of further searching?

And if an established entity were to be destroyed by that destruction, then it would be evident that this is an operation of the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*); thus, there would be a loss of the subject matter at hand. For it was the contradiction of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra-virodha*) that was intended to be investigated. Therefore, if one who still considers this to be the contradiction of mutual exclusion were to deviate due to forgetting the context, then the operation of removing an established state should not be touched upon; thus, the non-coexistence would be far more extensive.

[119,2] Now, since existence and non-existence—which depend respectively on the power of their own causes—are brought together and long maintained within a single substratum (*dharmin*), the discussion of contradiction is concluded. If it is argued that there is no such fault because the entity (*bhāva*), being constrained by its own destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), ceases to exist even before its own arising, and destruction subsequently proceeds immediately after; and if it is further claimed that this operation does not constitute "incompatibility through non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*); we reply:
this is not possible. For [this would require] the entity to be already established...
Even though it occurs later, destruction is merely a scar upon that [entity];
for while it has not yet occurred, the entity itself is far more powerful.

It has already been explained that this operation [of a cause] applies not only to non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) but also to mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*). Nor does a future entity possess any causal capacity. In that case, let it cease by itself; if this is so, what is the use here of another destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), such as a mallet? Furthermore, if there is a dependence upon its proximity, the meaning of the word "itself" (*svayam*) becomes empty. Just as when one says, "the sprout arises by itself depending on the seed," the fact that it is produced by that [seed] is not thereby avoided.

Now, if it is simply a case of avoidance (*parihāra*), then one should not say "in dependence upon that" (*tad-apekṣya*). And since the probandum would already be established by that much alone, what is to be done here with this [argument]? [For then] the cessation of an entity would be established even prior [to its destruction], because the entity would cease of its own accord without depending on the hammer or other causes of destruction. Furthermore, since destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*) and independent of any other cause, [it follows that they cannot coexist]. "If for you the contradiction between two things consists in their not abiding together, then how could there be even a moment's coexistence of cold and fire? [119,16]

Destruction, by bringing about another destruction, would itself become contradictory at that very moment; since that too would lead to yet another dissolution, there can be no annihilation whatsoever.

[119,20] Now, if the object exists by virtue of having mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), then there would be an absence of its very destruction; or let it coexist through the power of causes.
By this destruction, there is an annihilation of its intrinsic nature, yet it does not arise [again].
If an object is already powerful in itself, what need is there for another factor here to cause its diminution?
Thus are the two summary verses.

By this, it has been shown that the statement made by Śaṅkara— asking how there can be a negation of an entity through the production of its non-existence, since the production of non-existence itself constitutes the negation of the entity due to its inherent contradiction with coexistence— is characterized by a lack of understanding regarding that contradiction.

Therefore, one who asserts that "the claim that the production of non-existence results in the persistence of the entity in its very same state is the talk of a fool" is clearly this wretched man who, like dust blown by a contrary wind, only cuts himself; he should be understood as an object of pity for the great ones due to being submerged in profound delusion. If, in your view as well, non-existence is conventionally employed, is it an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? If it is not a real thing (*vastu*), then there is no contradiction whatsoever with its being existent through [conventional] existence.

Or how is the establishment of the two types of contradiction [to be understood]? Or what is its cause? If a thing is occasional or non-occasional, why is it not designated as "time"? Or how is it that, as before, there is no subsequent production of a succession of moments? And if there were such production, the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) would not exist.

If it is argued that even the mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*) between existence and non-existence is unreal because non-existence is not a real entity, then this very position of the opponent is incapable of withstanding analysis.

Therefore, it follows that mere cessation is the object of conventional usage; however, the repeated naming [of it] as a "thing" is contradicted, for its birth does not [re-occur]. What need is there for a cause?

Because of obstruction alone, there is no such conventional usage at once; nor is there arising when the cause is exhausted, for obstruction is real, since the destruction of the mutual intrinsic nature of two real entities is established.

The definition of its essential nature is that it is merely the falling away of an entity, designated as a non-affirming negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). In that context, since they maintain that in a negation there is only negation and no real entity, it is described as "merely a falling away. When the doubt arises as to what this "falling away" might be—a third kind of negation of an entity—it is stated to be called "non-affirming" (*prasajya*); furthermore, that is an object of mere conventional usage and not an object of direct experience, for otherwise it would be a real entity itself.

Furthermore, not everything that is conventionally expressed by a conceptualizing mind (*vikalpabuddhi*) is a real entity (*vastu*), for otherwise even things such as a donkey’s horn would entail the status of being a real entity; moreover, it is impossible to establish a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that lacks a real basis (*nirvastuka*). And since that [non-existence] is indeed contradicted by existence (*bhūti*) as its property (*dharma*), this answers the second question. Existence (*bhūti*) means either the capacity for effective action (*arthasāmarthya*) or abiding in its own nature (*svarūpeṇāvasthāna*).

In both cases, because they are mutually opposed in form, they are contradictory merely by their very departure [from one another]; thus, the definition of contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇa*) has been stated.

[121,1] Is it not the case that mere cessation (*pracyuti-mātra*) is nothing at all, and how could that be contradicted by anything? Precisely because mere cessation is nothing, whereas an entity (*bhāva*) is the opposite of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is for that very reason contradicted. Furthermore, this contradiction is not a mutual obstruction (*anyonyapratighāta*), as in the case of existence and non-existence; rather, it is merely the non-penetration of their respective forms. And since that [non-penetration] exists even between the conceptualized and the experienced, there is no fault. As for the question "What is the purpose of the cause?"—since mere cessation is never an entity—it is answered in the fourth [section].

For a cause could only be postulated if [the effect] were to emerge in some form; yet that which is non-occasional must either always exist or never exist. Since the position that it always exists has been rejected, it must therefore never exist at all. However, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is occasional, because that [usage] does not occur at the time when the entity exists. How so? Precisely because of contradiction. For non-existence (*abhāva*) is the opposite of existence; having the nature of a departure and existing as a conceptual inversion, how could it be conventionally designated at the time when the entity exists?

For an existent entity (*bhāva*)—whether it be causeless, produced by the cause of its own existence, or created by another cause—might indeed exist even at the time of its non-existence, and it would thereby acquire a conventional designation (*vyavahāra*) that follows from its existence. However, when there is no existence of this [entity], then there can be no conventional designation following from its existence. As for the contradiction that follows from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how could it proceed for one who possesses certainty upon seeing the reality, given the absence of the awakening of latent impressions?

[121,13] For this very reason, as long as there is the determination that "this very thing exists as a real entity," there is simply no room for the conventional usage of its non-existence, even though momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) actually occurs in reality. However, when one determines through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the nature of an entity is indeed a property that lasts for only a single moment, then at the second moment—simultaneously with the moment that is the effect (*upādeya*) of that entity—one conventionally designates the non-existence of that entity.

But when that means of valid cognition is not obtained, the linguistic usage of "non-existence" occurs only in dependence upon the perception of transformations such as potsherds; this is the resolution in the fifth [chapter]. In the sixth [chapter] as well, it is stated that there is no arising from the exhaustion of causes, but rather a continuity of homogeneous moments.

This has been stated: in the case of sounds that perish by their own nature, because of the dissimilarity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in each preceding moment due to the presence of the hammer as a cooperative cause, a sterile moment is produced; thus, the material cause (*upādāna*) is exhausted, and there is no further production. Furthermore, that entity which, upon its occurrence, brings about the placement of a sterile moment and prevents the reconnection with subsequent moments of the same kind, is established as the "opposer" (*virodhin*) of that entity; this constitutes the determination of opposition as non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*).

By that very same fourth quarter of the seventh [verse], even if there is indeed a contradiction consisting of mutual exclusion between the real (*vastu*) and the unreal (*avastu*), nevertheless, there is no loss of their ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*). For there is never any confusion of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-sāṅkarya*); this alone is the meaning of the contradiction between properties (*dharma-virodha*). Therefore, the mention of "abiding" (*sthiti*) is intended to indicate a necessary rule (*niyama*). By this, the third alternative (*vikalpa*) is also refuted.

Consequently, it is established that what is called "destruction" (*nāśa*) is neither of the nature of a negation (*prasajya-ātman*)—which would require a cause—nor does it entail these aforementioned faults. Thus it stands.

Furthermore, regarding whether an object is perishable or otherwise, what is the use of causes for its destruction? If it arises with a perishable nature, causes that are not the cause of its purpose are useless; if it has a non-perishable nature, they are incapable. Likewise, then, regarding whether it is destined to come into being or otherwise, what is the use of causes for its birth?
For one could say: if the object is destined to come into being, the causes of its birth are useless; if it is not destined to come into being, they are incapable.

And thus says the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*: "That is not so, because it would follow that the discourse on reasons (*hetu*) is cut off, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is possible in all cases. For instance, regarding a reason: does the thing to be produced have the nature of existence, or rather the nature of non-existence? If the first position is held, then it exists by itself, because it has that very nature; thus, the reason is redundant."

In the second case, however, [the effect] is incapable [of being produced], for it is impossible for anything to produce the nature of a non-entity, such as a rabbit’s horn. Likewise, causes such as cutting or burning must be seen as untenable—due to their futility and incapacity—under both the positions that [the effect] has that nature or does not have that nature. And thus, since all causal efficiency would be excluded in this way, any effort toward liberation and so forth, as well as the study of the scriptures and the like, would be in vain.

[122,13] Here, this objection is raised: "Why resort to this method of striking at the root with an axe? It is said that in no case whatsoever, when something is presented as a reason, should a refutation characterized by incapacity or futility even be mentioned. This is first of all untenable; for indeed, the futility of an axe is observed in the case of what can be cut by a fingernail, and the incapacity of a fingernail is observed in the case of what can be cut by an axe.

Likewise, when a task is to be accomplished by Devadatta alone, the operation of Yajñadatta acting as his assistant is redundant; yet, without him, Devadatta lacks the capacity. When the causal complex of fire and fuel is present, the donkey's contribution to the smoke is redundant; when it is absent, he lacks the capacity. Alternatively, where there is the bolstering of what is already established, there is redundancy; and where any one of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacies is present, there is a lack of capacity.

As for those who maintain that even the "proving of what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) is included among these [fallacies], their effort yields no fruit; for the fault of futility (*vaiyarthya*) cannot be denied as a refutation of the reason in any way whatsoever, and because even a probative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*) acts as a causal factor (*kāraka*) toward cognition. Furthermore, if futility and incapacity were not defects of a reason—since there would be no other defect of the reason—then everything would be established by anything at all.

Now, if it is argued that the refutation based on the distinction between having that nature or not having that nature is invalid, that too is incorrect. For whatever reason is adduced regarding a lamp—whether for its producing illumination or for its causing darkness—is it not defeated by either futility or incapacity?

Furthermore, he himself says that even the example of light and so forth is untenable. For, in our view, it is not established that the lamp and its light are one, nor that they have a single cause. Our established doctrine is that immediately after the substance arises, qualities such as light arise from a different collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*).

That too is irrelevant. For even if the quality of luminosity (*prakāśa*) arises after the substance has arisen, nevertheless, that very substance, once arisen, does not depend on any other cause for the perfection of its own form; nor does the subsequent quality of luminosity depend on anything else for its nature as the quality of luminosity. Thus, there is no deficiency in the example. [Objection: Suppose it is argued that even the form of the substance, prior to its connection with the universal "substanceness" (*dravyatva-sāmānya*), is neither a substance nor a non-substance because of its inherence (*samavāya*) in that [universal].

In that case, the position is that the substance-form is known from the generality of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva-sāmānya*), or else it becomes the object of the conceptual thought and the verbal expression "it is a substance. Regarding the first alternative, there is no fault. For it is the very subject under discussion that a substance should arise from the generality itself—by whatever nature it arises—and that once so arisen, it does not require any other cause for its existence.

Even in the second case, there is certainly no fault; for that which has the nature of a substance is indeed already produced even prior [to its manifestation], since the cognition and verbal expression of the substance arise precisely from the universal (*sāmānya*). Nor does this require any other cause for its existence. Indeed, when the effect brings about the causal factor’s functional capacity regarding its own object, it is not the case that the capacity was previously unestablished, nor is that capacity itself the cause for the existence of the effect, such that the effect would have to depend on another cause.

Furthermore, even if a distinct quality of illumination were to arise later, once the lamp has already become endowed with that quality of illumination, why would it require any other cause for its existence such that the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) would be undermined? Therefore, one who relies on what is not authoritative cannot defend or bolster their own system. However, in accordance with experience, the example may be exactly as one intends.

For there is no perception of a distinction between the first and second moments based on the presence or absence of connection with a universal (*sāmānya*); nor is there an experience of a difference between the substance and the universal. Since the matter at hand is established even otherwise, there is no insistence here [on that view]. Therefore, it is established that manifestation (*prakāśa*), being produced from its own cause as having the nature of manifestation, does not depend on another cause for its existence, because that would be redundant; and it is likewise incapable of being rendered dark.

[124,1] Now, it is observed that white cloth (*śuklam ambaraṃ*) is being colored through contact with a dyeing substance; in that case, why is the objection regarding the dyeing substance—not its uselessness or incapacity—when the cloth is either of a red nature or not of a red nature—not raised?

Indeed, it is not intended that this conceptual alternative applies in all cases; rather, the point is that there exists, for the time being, a refutation of the reason by way of the two alternatives—whether it has that nature or does not have that nature—and thus an absolute negation of its impossibility is undertaken. Consequently, wherever this refutation can be established, it enters into the state of being a valid refutation. What is the use of further deliberation if there is a difference in reasoning? And so, what is called perishability is either momentariness or existence for a shorter duration of time.

Imperishability, moreover, consists in persisting for an exceedingly long time or in persisting forever. In every respect, if an entity that was produced by its own cause with a certain duration of existence were to be destroyed by something else within that interval, then it would not have been produced with that very duration of existence. For it is not tenable for this [entity] to possess two mutually contradictory natures, such as persisting for a year and yet being destroyed in a single day.

[124,10] But surely, what contradiction is there in this: that [an entity] persists for a year in the absence of a cause of destruction, yet undergoes intermediate destruction when an intermediate cause of destruction occurs?

For if the certainty [of the nature of a thing] pertains only to its contradiction [with another], and not to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then there would be no entry into the object's reality. For example, if one thinks, "If smoke were possible upon the falling of leaves here, it must certainly be embers; otherwise, however, it is a cluster of *guñjā* seeds," this does not constitute a difference in intrinsic nature. Likewise, if something perishes during the day, let it be produced by a cause limited to that very time; but if it perishes at the end of a year, let it be limited to that duration. However, there can be no conjunction of two mutually contradictory natures in a single place.

For on that day, it is not possible for that which is perishing to endure for a year, nor can both [perishing and enduring] exist by way of alternating halves. Alternation, however, belongs to knowledge itself as it is of a doubting nature; it is not a property of the object. Therefore, an object possesses only a single nature and cannot be associated with another contradictory nature. Furthermore, this endurance throughout the day and so forth must be examined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine whether it is real or not.

However, having accepted this [position], it is considered as follows: because it is difficult to rely on the efficacy of a cause when that [efficacy] is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, even if there were non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatā*), it is established that for as long as the duration of its persistence lasts, another cause is incapable [of acting] within that interval, and beyond that, it is useless.

Even in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), it is clear that in that very moment nothing can be done by a cause of destruction; yet since it ceases of its own accord in the subsequent moment, there is no purpose in a cause of destruction. But in the case of something eternal, this [cause] is simply incapable.

Therefore, when destruction is to be produced, no cause whatsoever escapes the refutation of incapacity and futility. However, when it acts upon a different object, such as a potsherd, that very hammer is not tainted by those two defects; for the potsherd comes into existence immediately after its operation. Likewise, in the case of a dyeing substance acting upon a cloth that is already red and undergoing change immediately after its operation, there is neither incapacity nor futility.

Furthermore, when a white cloth is being dyed, what is it that prevents it from becoming [red]? Even when there is only a single substance—the cloth—throughout both states, there is still no escape from this fault. For it cannot be maintained that even in its state of being red, it remains purely white. Therefore, if that substance remains purely white even then, there is no room for the red; thus, the dyeing substance is ineffective. On the other hand, if it were already previously red, then the expectation of a dye corresponding only to that [pre-existing] color would be redundant.

Therefore, because a defect arises only in dependence upon stability, such a transgression of the convention pertains to the [conventional] state and not to the entity itself. For when the previous [state] is naturally ceased, by depending on its material cause, the removal of that defect is established through the production of a newly dyed cloth by means of a dye-substance.

If it is argued that the state of things (*vastu-sthiti*) is not thus, then surely it is precisely this that must be considered: what is the state of things? Why should the opponent be made to believe by means of a "drinking from the bowl" (*kośapāna*—an oath)? Why then is it stated so abruptly that such is the state of things, given that the reliance on the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has already been refuted?
But how can it be called a violation of convention (*samayāparādha*), since one accepts the manifestation and disappearance of two qualities within a substrate (*dharmin*) that remains established?

If this is so, then even though the operation of the dyeing substance would be rendered purposeless and ineffective by the removal of the previous qualities, it fulfills its function precisely through the production of a previously non-existent red quality; thus, how could it be touched by the aforementioned refutation? For the consideration of futility and incapacity was initiated with reference to the form already established, not with reference to something new.

For even when something new is to be produced, there is no room for the determination that "if it has arisen from its own causes in such a form, then [the cause] is useless," or "if it has arisen in this way, then [the cause] lacks the capacity. Moreover, every entity that is to be destroyed is already established as prior. And since that entity, whether perishable or otherwise, cannot transcend the nature of one of these two alternatives—due to the exclusion of any other possibility—it is impossible for a postulated cause of destruction to remain either ineffective or purposeless.

Nor is it logical that this would lead to the consequence of the total abolition of the theory of causes (*hetuvāda*). For one resorts to a cause only when the effect is not yet established; once it is established, this [present] inquiry arises. And if at that very moment the cause were already produced in such a form, then the debate would proceed precisely by prioritizing the cause. Yet, it has been stated that this is not possible when the effect is unestablished. Therefore, how can our aforementioned alternative (*vikalpa*) apply in all cases?
Even if a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) were possible everywhere regarding what is accepted as cause and effect, this does not constitute an admission of fault in our reasoning.

If, however, it were possible to demonstrate that even when a thing is established, [the reason] still requires another reason—despite the fact that the two pervading natures have been introduced and there is neither incapacity nor futility—then there would be a fault. But this is not the case. Therefore, if the fault lies merely in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no fault in the qualified [reason]; thus, as in the case of non-perception (*anupalambha*), the presentation of that alone is useless.

(50b) Now, if the fault lies solely in the fact that mere non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) lacks the capacity to establish its own probandum, then it is a flawed argument to claim that mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is characterized by the mere mention of incapacity and futility, does not lack the power to refute the doctrine of causality. Oh, what human effort this one adorned with ashes possesses! For, by thus denying cause and effect in every respect, he effectively establishes that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) possesses a cause; thus, he clearly mocks himself by his own hand.

Therefore, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities and so forth—though its power is established by mental construction (*saṃkalpa*)—must be abandoned with respect to the object by one who maintains the determination of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); otherwise, the very foundation of the engagement with the present topic would be destroyed. However, a conceptual construction based on an established limiting condition (*siddhopādhi*) devours only the destroyer, not the cause itself. It is indeed correct that you, fearing the collapse of the [logical] consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), do not take this into account. Therefore, this effort to destroy cause and effect is fruitless; rather, having established them in a general sense—
Reality is nowhere else than in the very act of reflective awareness directed toward an object, as it is conceived at its inception.

*Prārambha*, *upakrama*, and *prastāva* (commencement, introduction, or prelude) refer to that by which something is brought forth or honored. Having established in a general sense the existence of the relation between cause and effect, this inquiry of ours—which considers whether or not the existence of a cause might possibly apply to a specific object such as destruction—is appropriate to the present context. However, any effort to uproot the very notion of cause and effect is fruitless, since the treatise proceeds precisely after establishing them in a general sense.

Furthermore, this conceptual alternative is not capable of refuting the relationship between cause and effect—namely, that "that which has the nature of arising" or "that which has the nature of non-arising" arises from a cause. For instance, first, regarding that which has the property of non-arising, such as the offspring of a barren woman, and that which has the nature of arising—for you, the latter never lacks existence while the former never possesses it—the operation of a cause toward these two would be either ineffective or futile.

Speak of an occasional entity, whether it be of the nature of existing or of the nature of non-existing; however, this [entity] cannot possibly be occasional while remaining independent of anything else. That object which is depended upon for the restriction of time, place, and intrinsic nature is itself the cause. Now, if by "having the nature of existing" you intend not the property of being existent (*sattā-dharma*), but rather the property of arising (*utpatti-dharma*), even then, since "arising" is nothing other than the acquisition of selfhood by that which was previously non-existent, the answer remains the same. Furthermore, the denial of the occasionality of destruction has already been stated.

[126,21] Now, regarding the alternative that it exists by way of a cause: does that which exists as a produced phenomenon exist as something other [than its cause] or not? This is the sense of the dilemma. In that case, the argument comes to rest in the very first alternative. For it is said that it arises from a cause and not previously; thus there is no pointlessness. Since it arises from a cause and does not arise from anything else, how could there be a lack of capacity? And any insistence on this matter is futile; therefore, only a mere indication is stated here, because both [positions] are established and because the relationship of cause and effect has not been introduced.

Since this conceptualization, which possesses an established adjunct (*siddhopādhika*), subverts only the cause of the destruction of what exists and not the production of what is non-existent—because the underlying logic is dissimilar as previously stated—therefore, causes such as cutting or burning are indeed possible, just like the cause for a red silk garment; and since it is also the cause for the specific state called liberation (*mokṣa*), effort directed toward it is fruitful. Consequently, there is no cause whatsoever for the destruction of what exists; rather, its production as a temporal entity, just like its spatial form, occurs solely from its own cause.
Furthermore,

whether this destruction exists by the force of an affirmation like a door-bolt, or whether it is an entity like a pebble, it remains in that very same state; for those [conditions] are incapable of doing anything to it.

Therefore, there is no cessation of its activity; having given [the result] within three moments, how could its time—like its place and form—be restricted by causes such that it is not fruitless? For this reason, time is also held to be determined for it.

For just as it might be thought that a hammer or a heap of gravel [causes destruction], it has been stated that there is no production of destruction because a cause for destruction is impossible. Or, let there be a distinct entity called "destruction" arising through the power of a cause; like a staff, let it remain presiding over the destruction of the gravel or the redness by occupying another locus. Let entities remain in that very state, for [the alleged cause] does nothing to them.

For just as a mallet or a heap of sugar is incapable of acting upon it [the pot], because otherwise it would follow that the very admission of its destruction would be purposeless, so too, how could destruction—which arises from its own causes while the entity remains—be unable to do anything to it? For just as its total destruction is impossible for that which exists by the power of its causes (due to the aforementioned futility and incapacity), so too is destruction impossible with respect to its corresponding parts.

Even in that case, since there is no way to prevent the introduction of the alternative between "perishable" and "non-perishable" as before when there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this is stated merely in accordance with conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), even regarding an impartite (*niraṃśa*) entity. In reality, however, even if there is the destruction of parts, there is nonetheless total destruction; and since that [total destruction] is impossible, it has been established that something previously non-existent is produced. But in fact, [that production] is what is being prevented.

Therefore, let there be another unprecedented entity—just like the previous one—which remains hidden within another storehouse for an eon, or let there be yet another distinct entity called "destruction" produced by that [entity], just as [the former was]. However, it cannot be maintained that "nothing happens to the entity," for otherwise the consequence would be unavoidable: that the entity’s activities, such as generating its own cognition or maintaining its own continuity, would never cease.

By this, that which Vācaspati said is refuted: "Now, even when this [non-existence] has arisen with a distinct form, what has happened to the entity? Nothing has happened; let this venerable entity remain. Since its non-existence—which depends on its own causes, is characterized by the absence of its own nature, possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and brings about practical activity corresponding to the object—has dispelled all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), what is lost to us? [128,1] By this, that which Vācaspati said is refuted: "Now, even when this [non-existence] has arisen with a distinct form, what has happened to the entity? Nothing has happened; let this venerable entity remain. Since its non-existence—which depends on its own causes, is characterized by the absence of its own nature, possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and brings about practical activity corresponding to the object—has dispelled all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), what is lost to us?"

That has been refuted, because when it is in that state, it is impossible to accomplish the very negation of all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). If you argue that the persistence of that state is destroyed precisely by the absence of that [efficiency], we reply:

Well then, if it were a positive entity, being in that very state due to the influence of its own causes, it would have to turn away from non-existence and perform that destruction; thus the aforementioned difficulty regarding their simultaneous occurrence remains unavoidable. And this being the case, the claim that [destruction] is characterized by the absence of its own nature is untenable, for if it consists in the absence of that nature, its existence at that time is impossible.

Therefore, if one applies the designation "non-existence" to something that is common to other objects such as a mallet and so forth, there is no proof of the manifestation of the intended possession of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); for if it were asserted that this brings about the engagement in corresponding linguistic usage, it would be untenable. Furthermore, since the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) remain unchanged [in the presence of the non-existent], there arises the undesirable consequence of mutual attraction leading to the production of yet another destruction.

If it is argued that because its nature is self-cessation (*svayaṃ-nivṛtti-rūpatā*), there is no room for another destruction (*nāśāntara*), we say: no. For the nature of self-cessation occurring at the same time [as the entity] has already been refuted; rather, only a form excluded (*paryudasta*) remains, just like any other distinct thing (*padārthāntara*). And by means of that destruction, there is necessarily the production of a separate entity called "destruction," just as by a mallet. What indeed is the difference between this [self-destruction] and a mallet, given that its form is merely excluded from that [entity]? Therefore, this [destruction] destroys [the entity] while itself remaining independent of anything else.

The mallet, however, being independent [of the object], would be "destruction"; yet there would be the acquisition of the designation "destruction. Without that [designation], even for the mallet, there would be no distinction [from the object], since a mere difference in form exists even in the case of gems and the like.

[128,19] If perception and non-perception were restricted to a single [object] as the means of establishing causal capacity, then there would be a distinction; but it has been demonstrated that such is not the case. Therefore, in the case of absolute negation (*prasajya-pakṣa*), there is no simultaneity; nor, in the case of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), is there the exclusion of the destruction of another.
If there were something other than that which exists elsewhere, it would necessarily exist simultaneously, in accordance with its nature as a different moment.
This is the summary.
[129,9] If it does not arise even when the cause is present at one time, what is the purpose [of that presence], since momentary destruction is possible?
What fruit could be produced by that which remains in space for an equal duration, such that its destruction by that fruit might even be perceived?
This is an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*).

If, however, the effect called "destruction" is not the remover of that [entity], but rather something else entirely such as a staff and so forth, then it would follow that existence ceases and non-existence begins; thus there would be a difference in time. However, this serves no purpose, nor can it be said that by its absence all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is eliminated. Furthermore, the issues of incapacity and futility have already been raised. Therefore, this verbal formulation is utterly hollow.

Furthermore, regarding what was conjectured here—that as it has been stated, an entity arises from its own cause either perishable or imperishable—it is said in reply: we do not know [entities] as being perishable or imperishable; rather, existing things arise from their own causes and perish due to other causes whose presence is dependent upon their own conditions. Moreover, destruction is distinct from that which is being destroyed, both because of the difference in causes and because of the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). To this, it is further replied:

If you have spoken thus while being ignorant of the nature of that which is perishable and that which is imperishable, then where indeed is the category of "destruction"? Or from what exclusion could it be established as something distinct from that which is currently perishing—something which was just now asserted? Since it is being established through such ignorance of the nature of the perishable and the imperishable, why is it not likewise established in the case of space and other such things?

If it is argued that "destruction is not observed in those [entities]," well, is it not the case that destruction is indeed observed elsewhere? This is something that can only be settled by an oath! Therefore, you are forced to admit that there exists a nature other than that which is perishable; what need is there for an oath in this matter? Furthermore, even while seeing that the production of various forms from their own causes occurs with necessary regularity—and thus observing the refutation of [the need for] incapacity or redundancy—how is it that you still assert the existence of another cause? Even we do not know how this can be so.

Now, this is the underlying intention [of the author]: how can the production from something and the destruction from something else—which are perceived directly through the speech of Vaidarbhī’s son—be set aside by the conceptual alternatives of "perishable" or "non-perishable"? For that which is established by direct perception cannot be sublated even by a hundred conceptual constructions, since the operation of all means of valid cognition finds its final rest in direct perception alone.

In that case as well, if "destruction" is said to be a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*) established by its own technical system—that entity which, being produced by a hammer or similar cause, renders objects such as a jar useless—it has already been demonstrated that it is a great audacity to claim that its birth and its operation fall within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, how can there be no room for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?

Now, if what is intended by "destruction" is that which appears as if distinct—though it is not actually so—when its own form is being sought in isolation by excluding other differences, even as it is perishing of its own accord; and if, in that case, one says "they perish from other causes" without fear [of contradiction], then, when the established doctrine (siddhānta) maintains that blunt instruments like hammers cause things like axes to perish rather than [the objects] perishing of their own accord, the claim that "destruction is the cessation of all causal efficacy" is nothing more than a dream-conception.

Therefore, we do not know what Vācaspati intends by this. If that is so, how can there be a denial even of that much which falls within the scope of perception? And to what extent does this scope of perception extend? It is established that when an entity is arising from one cause and ceasing from another cause, the cause of its production is distinct from the cause of its destruction.

Nor is there such a thing as "destruction" that is distinct [from the entity itself], from which it would follow that there is room for the objection regarding its being an object of perception. Shame on this! If destruction were non-different from the entity, then the cause of destruction would simply be the cause of the entity; and if it is the cause of the entity, it cannot be the cause of the entity's arising. Therefore, how could there be a cause of destruction other than the cause of arising? And how could there be a cause for something already produced at a later time? Furthermore, this relation of priority and posteriority is indeed established by direct perception.

[130,17] Furthermore, is the entity that is arising and ceasing one or many? First of all, its being one is untenable because of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). If it is argued, "What can we do? For it is established as such by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)," [we reply: if two properties residing in a single substratum are perceived simultaneously by a single direct perception, then non-contradiction is correct, as in the case of blue and squareness. However, when two distinct perceptions occurring at different times each grasp a single form, then it is mere recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) alone that conflates them.

And that has been stated to be invalid. Therefore, due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, there is indeed a distinction [between moments]. However, since there is no division within a single moment, there is no contradiction, because existence occurs in one place through the mere difference of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). For instance, that very same moment of an entity is called "arising" when it emerges from prior non-existence, and it is called "ceasing" when it follows upon subsequent non-existence.

No, for contradiction itself is established by way of pervasion: even at the first moment, an entity as it arises is pervaded by the non-abiding of other prior moments of existence and does not touch its former state for even a single moment; and when it is ceasing at the final moment, it is pervaded by the non-abiding of other subsequent moments of existence and does not touch its future state for even a single moment—thus, there is indeed contradiction.

Furthermore, since this distinction occurs within a single moment, it is merely a difference of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and not a contradiction. Therefore, even regarding two moments, when one intends to speak of their duration, there can be no identity because of the contradiction between the properties of arising and perishing. And in the case of multiplicity, the preceding entity—while perishing even in the absence of any enumerated causes of destruction such as a hammer—is merely manifesting the capacity of its own cause to grant a fixed duration; thus, there is no separate cause of destruction whatsoever.

Now, if the causes of destruction are indeed uncountable, then what is improper about the thought that some cause, difficult to perceive and remaining unrecognized, might bring about its own basis—the destruction? If this is so, then since the possibility of destruction exists at every moment without ceasing, the formal establishment of a "cause of destruction" is useless.

For, lest the determination of destruction—which is characterized by the well-known cessation [of existence]—be precluded by the certainty of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) regarding a cause whose characteristics have already been enumerated, the author has begun to establish that destruction possesses a cause. However, since the acceptance of a cause that is difficult to perceive due to its subtlety would result in the futility of effort, enough with this false conceptualization!

Therefore, since it has been demonstrated that everything is incapable of affecting an entity that possesses stability, the meaning of this statement is that existing things are born from their own causes and perish due to other causes. How then could this magical illusion of jewels, mantras, and medicines have been learned by an existent thing, such that it is sometimes perceived and sometimes unperceived while remaining in that very same state, with the causal conditions for its perception being entirely unchanged?

[131,17] But surely this fault has already been stated and is appropriate within the doctrine of momentariness itself. As Śaṅkara said: "For there is no loss of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of an entity after its cessation, as there was before; for if that were so, it would not be an object of non-perception at that time, nor would it have existed previously. Or, if there were a loss [of nature] later, that very thing would be the production of its cessation. This is incorrect. For on the view of momentariness, to say that there is no loss of essential nature even later, just as there was before, is sheer audacity.
If you argue that even if the loss of essential nature is accepted, it is incoherent unless it occurs through the production of a cessation—[we reply: so be it.

[131,21] Whether or not there arises another distinct entity (padārthāntara) designated by names such as "cessation" (nivṛtti), precisely because this object is restricted to abiding for only a single moment, it is said that "it does not exist in the subsequent moment," since it does not extend into that other moment. It is by this very statement that it is expressed: "destruction has occurred for that same object in the subsequent moment. No production of a previously non-existent thing is being enjoined.
