For the employment of words follows from linguistic convention; however, the actual state of affairs (artha) must be investigated.

In that case, if the determination of the existence of a thing in another moment is established by its dependence on a single moment, then the doctrine of destruction has achieved its purpose by that much alone; what is the point of searching for the production of anything here? For there is no such principle as: "Because Devadatta exists only in his house, it follows that in every other place there is a cessation of the designation of some other entity.
If it is argued that even in that case, there is a positive injunction of non-existence in other locations, [we reply:]...

Let it be so, for that very purpose the particle *eva* is employed as a restrictive conjunction. It is simply that some existing or arising entity does not enter the path of cognition, since only a negation is perceived. And by that much alone, one who is pursuing Devadatta attains proficiency in both engagement and withdrawal.

For even when the cognition of another object has been established, as long as one does not—by means of a restrictive rule—settle Devadatta’s own negation by excluding him from elsewhere than the house, [the argument] remains unstable. Therefore, a mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*), whose nature is untouched by the form of a positive entity, must necessarily be communicated.

Nor does the cognition "it is not elsewhere" establish some positive entity-form (*vastu-rūpa*) and then lead to a sequential realization that "only this exists, not Devadatta," as in the case of "it exists only in the house, not elsewhere. Let it be so; nevertheless, the final rest (*viśrāma*) occurs precisely through the subsequent cognition of mere non-existence. Otherwise, if one were to engage in the comprehension of another positive entity-form, a human lifespan would be exhausted, and the accomplishment of the intended understanding of negation would not occur.

Therefore, just as in this case a mere negation of Devadatta’s presence elsewhere than in the house is conventionally expressed, and that alone—the non-existence of Devadatta elsewhere—is the object of cognition, so too is the meaning of such conventional usage: "Existence is in one moment alone; it does not exist in another moment. In another moment, its non-existence is cognized; thus, a mere negation is indicated regarding the other moment, not a contact with the actual nature of a real entity.

Nor is it for the sake of establishing a negation dependent upon that [intrinsic nature]. Thus, even the claim that "there is a loss of intrinsic nature" is merely a conventional expression of negation. And since nothing there serves any purpose through arising or existence, how can it be said that "the loss of intrinsic nature occurs without an arising of cessation"? For this very reason, if one were to say that "upon its loss, that itself is the arising of its cessation," such a fallacy must be avoided like a sin, as it leads to an infinite regress.

Furthermore, the claim that "there is a loss of its own nature" later is merely a subsequent conventional usage of negation; it is not the arising of any real entity. And that conventional usage of negation is inconsistent, because Devadatta’s presence elsewhere is restricted by his necessary existence in one particular place.

By this, it is refuted what Nyāyabhūṣaṇa also said: "For who would believe that an entity exists only in its present state and is non-existent later, yet does not perish later? To that, we ask: who indeed says that it does not perish later? If it perishes later, then one has accepted the arising of destruction later. If you alone are the master over the meanings of words!

This might be the case: the status of an object is twofold—following valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and following convention (*samaya*). In the first case, the meaning is established as follows: "it perishes later" means that it is designated as "non-existent later. Therefore, how could one who relies on valid cognition be able to assert both "it is non-existent later" and "it does not perish later"? However, in the second case, there is no contradiction.

For one who maintains that "it perishes later" thus intending the arising of a subsequent destruction, [the entity] is non-existent later; it cannot be treated as existent, nor does it perish later, nor does there arise for it a thing called "subsequent destruction. How, then, can this be a matter beyond belief?

[133,6] Alas! This is a mere delusion of speech regarding a reality that is never fully established, a desire to sustain one's own philosophical system (samaya) through that which only charms the minds of common folk. Therefore, an entity arises from its own cause with a duration fixed to a single moment; thus, it exists only at that time and not otherwise. If you think, "But is such a capacity of a cause for production even within the scope of possibility?"—even then, if there is a capacity for production, it must necessarily produce an effect in some form.

What could form (*rūpa*) not produce, even by abiding for only a single moment? But for whom would it be a matter of faith that a cause could perform its function without touching its entire effect? Therefore, just as this entity arises from its own cause with a restricted location and a specific form such as the shape of a particular object, so too is it restricted in time; what is impossible here? Nor should it be said that the restriction of place and so forth brings about the very non-existence of the entity through a contraction of its own nature.

For non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot either contract an entity that has already arisen, nor can it produce something contracted by coming together with the cause. In this regard, if even non-existence—which is devoid of independent human agency and included within the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*)—could somehow be established as a producer of an entity, what would be lost for us? Whether the causal complex be of such a kind or another, it may well bring about its effect.

We ask: if it is capable of producing [an effect] with a restricted place and form, what power could possibly obstruct it from doing so at a restricted time as well, such that another subsequent production would be required for that purpose? Even regarding the first alternative, we must consider these options: is that entity produced by its own causes as possessing all forms (*viśvarūpa*) and then rendered restricted by non-existence; or is it produced in no form at all; or is it indeed produced in some form, but not with respect to place, form, and time?

First of all, the final [position] is untenable. For that very form in which [an entity] is produced is its own aspect (*ākāra*), and that [aspect] does not exist anywhere without an entity; nor is there ever an entity that has not existed [previously]. Thus, how can there be an avoidance of aspects and so forth? Let it not be so; however, for one who is capable of producing [an effect] in some form, what is the point of indolence or envy toward anything other than its own cause, since the restriction of capacity in one place cannot be established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? As for the middle position, on what basis is its status as a cause established—whether by royal favor or otherwise?

Even in the first case, when the effect is merely the cessation of existence for a single subsequent moment—a process subtler than the simultaneous cutting away of the forms of the entire three worlds—there is not even the slightest consideration [of a cause]. Therefore, since the limitation of time is already established by that which is called "non-existence" (abhāva), which effects a contraction of space and so forth and is already proven, what reason is there to seek another enduring entity existing at a different time that depends on other causes? This has essentially been stated already.

If it is argued that non-existence has a distinction for each respective object, this is a mere act of audacity, since its nature is entirely unperceivable. Therefore, why is it not accepted that space and so forth are excluded from everything, just as all phenomena are excluded? Furthermore, experience does not tolerate the claim that the aforementioned operation exists in such a manner.

Therefore, since from its own cause it is produced as restricted by space and so forth, it is likewise restricted by time; thus, the undesirable consequence of [continued] seeing and so on does not apply to the theory of momentariness as it does to the theory of stability, because the entity itself no longer exists. On the theory of stability, however, that state still persists, so the undesirable consequence is not averted; for even if another entity were to arise, the original entity would have nothing to do with it. Furthermore, this is an irrelevant statement, because while the cessation of the entity is the subject at hand, you are avoiding the emergence of a different thing.

[134,12] But surely, while the cessation of an entity is the subject at hand, it is the arising of that cessation which is being taught; so why is this irrelevant here? Indeed, as long as there is no teaching of an arising, cessation must be understood as having a non-existent nature (*prasajyātmā*). However, when there is an arising, because another thing excluded by that [cessation] is being enjoined, cessation is again drawn in by implication (*arthāpatti*), but it is not that very same cessation, precisely because it would then be a real entity (*vastu*); otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for what Śaṅkara says: "If it is asked, 'Since there is no difference in being a distinct entity [from the thing itself], how can that very thing be the cessation of that very thing?'—to this, the answer must be given by the inherent natures of things (*vastu-svabhāva*), namely that some things arise from their own causes with the very property of existing in contradiction to coexistence. For there is no rule that because two things are distinct entities, and there is no contradiction to their coexistence, the absence of one must constitute the non-existence of the other; rather, the contradiction between the coexistence of those two is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

For it is not the case that something is a non-cause of other things simply because it is a different entity; likewise, let this [non-existence] also not be such [a non-cause] of its own effect. This very point has also been refuted by Nyāyabhūṣaṇa on the grounds that both types of contradiction are applicable there. Furthermore, it has been shown that if exclusion occurs due to contradiction even for a different entity, it would be better for the exclusion to belong to the hammer itself. Moreover, neither perception nor inference is operative regarding [the existence of] cessation. And since a contradiction established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily be stated, [your position] is quite elegant! [It is not.]

In the case of fire, smoke, and so forth, however, the causal relationship between cause and effect is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, even when describing the arising of a different entity, there is no appearance of the cessation of that [cause]. Consequently:
"If a different entity were produced from the fire, the wood would still be seen;
nothing at all would happen to it—it would simply not exist."
Thus, this principle is difficult to circumvent.

As for what Nyāyabhūṣaṇa says—that if nothing belongs to it, then even its negation does not belong to it, and therefore, since its nature remains unnegated and in that same state as before, it would be perceived just as it was previously—this has already been refuted.

For if the meaning is that even a negation does not occur for it—that is, if even the category of reality called "negation" is not produced—then this is true; however, the object's nature is not thereby un-negated, because its state of being negated at another moment is established by its own causes alone. Alternatively, if a verbal negation is intended, then who would set that aside?

In this view, it is incoherent to claim that [the object] would be perceived as before; for that which does not exist at a certain time cannot be perceived at that time. Otherwise, one residing in Kānyakubja would be seen in Pāṭaliputra, or even Māndhātṛ would be perceived today.

[135,15] But surely, today there is the non-existence of Māndhātṛ; therefore, it is not perceived by him. Who indeed has said otherwise? Even though a distinction is concluded from the mere mention of the genitive case, no distinct entity is thereby enjoined. Whatever is the meaning of "Māndhātṛ does not exist today," precisely that much is the non-existence of Māndhātṛ today, because its existence is restricted to that specific time. Surely this too is the same: whatever is the meaning of "the non-existence of Māndhātṛ today," precisely that much is "Māndhātṛ does not exist today."

As for what is also said—that it is because of its existence being restricted to that specific time—even there, by stating "it exists only at that time," one is merely demonstrating its non-existence at other times; so what more has been stated here? This has already been explained. Nevertheless, it is further said: in reality, the referents of the designations "difference" and "non-difference" are one and the same. If the establishment of a distinct entity were based on the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even for the sentence "the first does not exist," the meaning would be precisely this: "the non-existence of the first exists."

Now, let it be granted that the sublation of a distinct entity itself is what follows from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that "its absence exists. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement "the absence has arisen today" should be understood simply as "it does not exist today. And when searching for a means of valid cognition, it is said that for that which is accepted as being perceptible, non-perception alone is the sublater; thus, it is also said that "there is neither any prover nor any [sublater]."

It has been established that even if there is no current perception, the existence [of an object] at another time is proven merely by its absence at that [present] time, provided that this absence does not touch upon the nature of any other entity. Nor, however, can one hope for actual reality based on the mere mention of "absence" as an instrument (in the phrase *virahamātreṇa*), because the conventional usage of action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka*) is dependent upon the speaker's intention. For example:
"This son of a barren woman goes from a city of the Gandharvas, having bathed in the waters of a mirage, to offer handfuls of water to his father."
If it is argued that this [dream-object] is entirely false because it lacks substantiality despite possessing the capacity for all causal factors (*kāraka*), we reply: no,
because it was cited as an example merely by virtue of its dependence upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

If it is asked, "Who could speak in such a way as that?"—let no one speak; for there is no contradiction to the point at hand being established. Nor is it impossible for even a correct word (*sādhu*) to have this reading; for when someone who has heard it asks, "Why would a correct word not express that [meaning]? its correctness is not impaired by that mere reading. Furthermore, even if the falsity of "tortoise-hair" is accepted, must that too necessarily be expressed by an incorrect word? Nor is this [statement] entirely false.

Likewise, in the case of "Māndhātā does not exist" or "one does not dwell here as Māndhātā," the manifest capacity of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*) does not restore its status as a real entity (*vastutā*). If it is argued that there is merely a negation of it, for that very reason the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is independent and free from doubt. Therefore, the hope for establishing the reality of a thing through the designation of causal capacities (*kāraka-śakti*) resembles the desire to cross water by means of a mass of foam.

Thus, since the reality of the object does not depend on its designation, but rather this designation depends on the nature of the object, the specific indication of a difference—such as "today its non-existence has arisen"—should be established in the sense of a mere non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) that merely indicates "this is not here today," as if perceiving the arising of a distinct entity; it should not be taken in the opposite sense, because this distinction lacks any basis in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the statement that there is an absence at another time due to the restriction of its presence to that specific time is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For it is only the arising of another entity at a later time that is being negated, and not merely the conventional usage of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Thus, even when demonstrating the refutation of this [position], no other ultimately real category is established.
Therefore, having set aside [the opponent's view], the author of the *Vārttika* verse and Nyāyabhūṣaṇa composed the following verse:
"If there is no entity later, why is its absence desired?"
Even that [negation] is not a negation; why then is it accepted as the absence [of something]?

Thus, this is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we merely accept that the conventional usage of "non-existence" (*abhāvavyavahāra*) is subsequently initiated by a certainty of sublation (*bādhāniścaya*), since it is precisely the arising of a real entity that is being negated. But what kind of verbal artifice is this—to say that only the conventional usage of non-existence is accepted later, yet there is no actual non-existence? For if this were so, it would follow that the conventional usage of non-existence is deceptive; and if non-existence is false, then the very thing to be negated would be a real entity (*bhāva*).
And what other kind of negation could there be than the negation of a negation, which is nothing other than an affirmation (*vidhāna*)? (PV IV 221cd)

Because this principle is asserted by [the opponent] himself: that non-existence (abhāva) occurs only subsequently. Thus, since its occurrence is clearly occasional (*kādācitkatva*), it must possess a cause and be a real entity (*vastutva*). And so he says: "The very non-existence of a thing that occurs later is called destruction (*nāśa*). How could any destruction of a thing other than this be perceived? Now, if it is said that there is a "destruction of a thing," but it is not said that "it comes into being" (*bhavati*), what is the fault in stating that it "comes into being"?

If you argue that it must indeed be an entity (*bhāva*), then does the nature of an object undergo a transformation simply through its designation? And if such a transformation were to occur, then one should say that it "is born. If you ask how there can be birth for that which is non-existent (*abhāva*), it is because it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatvāt*). For if it were not occasional, then non-existence would have to persist even in the present state.

To this it is replied: First of all, by the term "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*), we intend both certainty and speech; and speech has precisely the same object as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, the object of conceptual construction is twofold, distinguished by the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). Among these, that which appears to the conceptual cognition as it arises is called the apprehended.

However, that upon which activity and cessation depend is the determined, such as the arising of a different entity [in the case of the thought]: "later, the non-existence of the very thing has arisen. This is the object of that very conceptual construction.

That which appears directly as the apprehended object (*grāhya*) is the basis for the withdrawal of one who seeks the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of that [apprehended] state; it is also the object determined (*adhyavaseya*) as a thing possessing a nature distinct from that [apprehended object], at that same time and place. For, when that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises, one who is averse to the mental engagement with the production of a thing called "destruction" and who seeks the causal efficiency of the absence of the object to be negated does not act toward the thing existing at that place and time, but rather withdraws from it. Therefore, it is said to be determined as a thing possessing that specific place, time, and state.

In this context, what is called "mere conventional usage" (*vyavahāramātra*) is stated with reference to another object that appears [in cognition]; for even with a thousand eyes and through diligent investigation, no other entity is perceived apart from that which arises. Therefore, even when there is a discrepancy regarding that [appearance], there is neither non-discrepancy nor discrepancy with respect to the object of determination (*adhyavaseya-viṣaya*), wherein conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) completes its function through engagement or withdrawal. And it is concerning the object of determination that one considers whether there is discrepancy or its opposite, not concerning the appearing object (*pratibhāsī*).

Therefore, even if this is a universal principle, in the present case we shall determine consistency solely through correspondence with the object to be known (*avaseya*). As for the appearance itself, if its inconsistency is established only when the probandum (*sādhya*) is established—if the deities are pleased—what is the point of your indignation in this matter?

Therefore, even though the form of the effect appearing as a conceptual construction of non-existence is false, the conventional usage of "non-existence" is not deceptive, because the reality of the object as it is determined exists. And although that constructed form is false, there is no falsity in the mere exclusion—which is the opposite of existence—and which is the sole form to be conventionally expressed; thus, when a thing is negated, there is no consequence of its becoming a positive entity. Nor is that [negation] negated in its nature as mere exclusion; rather, it is negated only in its status as a constructed form of a real entity.

[138,9] But is it not the case that "the thing does not exist" is itself a negation? And thus, regarding the question of whether that cessation exists or not: if it exists, how can it not be a thing? If it does not exist, how can there be no negation? It is said in reply: the negation is merely the attribution of "thing-ness" to the mere absence of a thing; it is not a negation of "thing-ness" itself that constitutes its negation.

Therefore, the statement "there is falling away" means that there is no falling away from the very nature of falling away; however, there is no affirmation by mere verbal usage of even something imagined, such as its consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). Just as it is correct to say "the jar does not exist" when one has no expectation of a form distinct from the negated form of the jar—whether in terms of permanence or momentariness—so too, it is correct to say "there is no falling away" when one has no expectation of it as a real entity.

However, there is a non-conditioned (nirupādhi) falling away; thus, it does not entail a fault regarding the non-falling away from its own nature. As long as the state of the negandum has not occurred, so long is there falling away and non-falling away from its own nature, because these two are mutually exclusive by their very nature.
For this very reason:
"If there is no cessation in that [locus], why is the presence of the reason (hetu) not desired?"

"This too is not a negation; what is being negated is the cessation? (PV IV 224 = PVin III 15)—this principle is difficult to bypass. Thus, if one suspects that by the phrase "if there is no [existence] later," there is an absence of what is called non-existence later, then why is existence desired for that?

If it is said thus, then there is no fault. For when the negation of "it exists" for something at a certain time—which is the opposite of "it does not exist," being a mere absence consisting of a non-entity and revolving within conceptual construction—is refuted, then that thing necessarily attains a presence within the internal sense-faculty (*antar-mātrā*) in the form of "it exists."

But when, after not having rejected mere absence (*virahamātra*), there subsequently occurs or arises—by virtue of the transformation of conceptual construction (*vikalpavivarta*)—the negation of an imagined entity-form (*vasturūpa*) that is deep-rooted in latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), then how could there be the consequence of existence (*bhāvaprasaṅga*) arising from the rejection of mere absence? For what "existence" is desired for that [negation]?

Thus it is said: for a jar does not undergo a fall from its own nature when a superimposed form is negated, because that would entail the consequence of its being devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as the holding of water. Nor does the mention of a fall from its own nature fulfill the expectation of its being a real entity (*vastutva*), just as in the case of "the son of a barren woman has the nature of non-existence" and so forth; for even if one were to posit the persistence of its own nature, that [fall] would still be impossible. Or it is like [the argument] "the reason is unestablished" (*asiddho hetuḥ*) and so on.

Therefore, the claim that "destruction occurs later, arising from such things as a hammer" is merely a conventional expression of the ignorant being denied; for we say that the nature of the thing itself—which was previously described as having occasional occurrence and so forth—does not exist.

Nor can it be maintained that everything as far as it is presented by conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is the reality (*vastu-tattva*) of things, for that would entail the absurdity of making the composition of treatises (*śāstra-praṇayana*) pointless. Furthermore, if one were to demonstrate that conventional usage is false, it would not be easy to distinguish between what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected on the basis of their fundamental strength or weakness. And it has been shown that the "basis" (*mūla*) is that which is to be determined (*adhyavaseya*). Therefore, in the investigation of reality (*tattva-cintā*), it is said that "it does not become an entity" (*bhāva*), and likewise, "it becomes a non-entity" (*abhāva*);
or rather, subsequently, it becomes a non-entity, or the entity itself remains unchanging. (PV I 278cd)

And thus, it is stated that an entity does not exist later [as something else], being restricted solely to its own time; therefore, there is no production of a different object. Consequently, under the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), perception and so forth are possible because of the persistence of the same state (*tādavasthyāt*); however, it is established that this is only the case under the doctrine of stability (*sthirapakṣa*).
First of all, the object does not cease by itself; nor is it destroyed by a cause of destruction, because such a cause is purposeless since [the object] has already perished.
Nor is it destroyed by the operation of a club or similar instrument, for that is said [to act] upon what is still existing.
Furthermore, it cannot be due to annihilation, because that would entail the consequence of a separate destruction, like a physical barrier.
Why does this not quiver? What is this that has occurred at the time of the sparrow?
This is an intermediate verse. But if [things] are momentary,
then just as an entity arises from its own cause with a form distinct from other forms,
why does it not likewise arise from its own cause as something existing in a distinct and separate moment?
Thus it has been said.
If there were a sublation [of existence] by means of non-existence as a distinct entity, then another non-existence would have to be observed there as well.
Regarding this, he says: "Some say that there is no such state, like aversion and illumination. To that, it is replied:
The view that the lamp serves as an illustration is not acceptable, because it lacks the demonstration of its own nature.

For a lamp is observed to possess the power to illuminate other things; how could it be denied? But for non-existence (*abhāva*), however, even the cognition of its own nature is difficult to find even in a dream. In that regard, who would be so audacious as to act like a painter in the sky, saying: "This is its distinction when there is existence, and this is not there when it is non-existent; and being differentiated by this very form itself, it does not depend on anything else"? How, then, can it be comparable to a lamp? Furthermore: "If this non-existence were like a lamp, it would both differentiate existence and be differentiated [by it]."
That very entity, having arisen from its own cause, differentiates both the entity itself and that which is to be differentiated.

For a face does not become crooked when it is spoken to in this manner; for there is no observation of the absence of other human agency. Nor is the probandum established by a mere example; since no reason (*hetu*) is being adduced to prove that [absence], what could there be that is not unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*)?

Furthermore, as for what was said: "But we do observe this. In that regard, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is not accepted where some observed fact would be contradicted by that infinite regress; yet here, no observed fact is contradicted. To the extent that there is the exclusion of a jar from things such as cloth, by that very exclusion it is established as being excluded from the jar and so forth. In that case, there is no disruption whatsoever by an infinite regress of further exclusions.

If it is argued that the object is not established as excluded because its capacity is exhausted by the apprehension of a succession of exclusions (vyāvṛtti-vyāvṛtti), we say no; for it is admitted that even those [objects] inverted by qualifiers are apprehended. To this also it is replied:
let that admission stand; however, in this case, the entity is reached through a succession by means of that very succession of its apprehension.
If it is claimed that the cognition of a qualifier’s qualifier is not desired, then the logic is the same, and thus there is no distinction between the two cases.

It is claimed that even an unperceived eye causes the perception of form; thus, for one who believes that a qualifier, though itself unperceived, causes its own qualifier to be perceived, it would follow that the primary qualifier itself—remaining unperceived—would cause the qualified object to be perceived, rendering the perception of that [primary qualifier] unnecessary. Moreover, this is not the actual sequence of qualifiers.

Therefore, just as the particularized object (*viśeṣya*) cannot be characterized at the very first moment without depending on the apprehension of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), so too it cannot be characterized by the second and subsequent moments; how then can this division be considered tenable? For just as there is a fear of apprehending a confused [object] without the apprehension of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of non-existence, so too, if that adjunct itself is not apprehended as distinct, how can it be called a differentiator of another, being like a solid mass of matter (*viṣṭambhi-dravya*)? Thus, in this mutual dependence, since there would be no apprehension of the excluded entity even after many eons, its disappearance is unavoidable.

If, moreover, non-existence were the qualifier, then since distinct entities can arise from their own causes alone, and since the perception and conceptualization of difference would be established through presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*), what is the use of non-existence? For a distinct thing is not to be experienced as non-distinct by a non-erroneous cognition, nor is a distinct thing that has been experienced contradictory to a distinct conceptual construction. If, on the other hand, there is neither distinct nor non-distinct without non-existence, then where indeed would the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) take place? Thus, non-existence itself becomes accepted as a causal factor.
Nevertheless, since everything is consistent insofar as distinct entities arise from their own respective causes, the doctrine of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not a subject of agreement.
And as for what he said: "Alternatively, even the infinity of exclusions and the excluded is grasped by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*),"—in that case as well:
He shamelessly asserts in his heart that this very appearance is present even in non-conceptual [cognition], thereby failing to abandon the veil of the owl-like [insight].
Where even a single thing is unperceivable and manifests under the name of non-existence as all-pervasive, there [arises] the traditional succession.
If false speech has been initiated, what is the point of this secrecy? This is entirely appropriate for Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, who writes as follows:

"Is the cognition [of an object] by its own nature excluded or non-excluded? If it is excluded, then that exclusion is purposeless. If it is not excluded, there follows the undesirable consequence of the confusion of entities (*vastu-saṅkara*). What is the meaning of 'by its own nature'? Does it mean without exclusion, or by a form distinct from exclusion? It is not tenable to say 'without exclusion,' because exclusion is an eternal property (*nityadharma*) of the object."

For a substratum (dharmin) is designated even in the absence of a particular property (dharma) that occurs only occasionally; for example, a man is "without curls" when he lacks curls, or is "undesirable" prior to his destruction. However, a thing is never devoid of its exclusion from other things (vastv-antara-vyāvṛtti), just as there is no cow devoid of cowness (gotva), nor fire devoid of heat (auṣnya).

Now, if it is intended that [an entity] is "excluded" by way of a form that is distinct from exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), then that is exactly what we accept, since difference (*bheda*) is admitted. Nor is exclusion thus rendered purposeless. If a person is wealthy by virtue of wealth that is distinct [from him], does the wealth thereby become useless? Therefore, even mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is indeed a separate entity from existence (*bhāva*).

That too has been refuted. For this objection is certainly not directed at something else that is distinct from a real entity (*vastu-sat*) and accepted as such; rather, its meaning is as follows: because it is useless and ineffective in producing the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-pratyaya*), exclusion is not established by means of that [real entity]. Among these, in the first position, uselessness (*vaiyarthya*) was stated; in the second, however, ineffectiveness (*asāmarthya*) is intended.

[142,19] Now, this is the meaning: if an entity possesses an excluded nature (*vyāvṛttasvabhāva*) and arises from its own cause, then it must be cognized as being indeed excluded by that cognition which arises in dependence upon it. For there is no such obsession regarding the object—nor is it determined by any means of valid cognition—that even when all other conditions are present, I must not produce my own cognition in the absence of that [exclusion], despite the fact that the object lacks any distinct entity characterized as exclusion.

Nor can there be a grasping of that cognition produced by it as being "without that [exclusion]" when it is actually not so grasped; thus, this exclusion is purposeless, and since the cognition of an exclusion can arise otherwise, it should not be postulated.

[143,1] Now, if an entity has not arisen as excluded from its own cause, and yet has arisen, then how could the exclusion of that which has arisen with a mixed nature—which is itself non-existent—produce a cognition of exclusion? Thus, it is incapable. And while proceeding with this objection, having merely established the exclusion as already proven, what is the use of [discussing] the eternality of the property of exclusion and so forth? For by this, the point regarding the avoidance of the futility mentioned in the first position is not addressed.

For instance, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is postulated by virtue of the power of the cognition of exclusion; yet, since that cognition of exclusion is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*), what is the point of this postulation? To such an objection, the respondent might say: "Exclusion is an eternal property (*dharma*); therefore, without it, [the cognition] is not possible. But how is this relevant?

For as long as one maintains that the cognition of exclusion is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*) except through exclusion itself, there is no occasion for this argument. What is the use here of setting aside that [point] to engage in mere talk of a philosophical tenet (*siddhānta*)?

Nor is it appropriate to illustrate that "it is not unperished prior to destruction," because a distinction in destruction itself is unestablished. Furthermore, regarding the claim that "an entity is not devoid of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), if there is no real difference from the exclusion, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is because a distinction is unestablished; for even in the case of the example, it is impossible to demonstrate the difference between the cow and the fire by means of "cow-ness" and "heat"—which are themselves of the nature of the exclusion of non-cow and non-heat—by way of their being distinct from the cow and the fire.

Furthermore, regarding the second alternative within this very position—namely, whether exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) occurs through a distinct operation or not—that is already resolved by its non-acceptance, because what is intended to be expressed is the meaning that "it is cognized as excluded by its own nature" or "it is cognized as having a form excluded from everything. Nor has the avoidance of the first [alternative's] futility been addressed; this has already been stated.

Nor is the establishment of a distinct exclusion achieved through the example of wealth, because there is no restrictive cause [for such a relation]. Alternatively, like wealth, it would not depend on conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*); consequently, other qualifiers such as "having a staff" or "being white" would also have to be treated as having a [substantive] relationship. Therefore, there is no such thing as "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*), since things arise from their own causes as mutually excluded.
This applies equally to what is excluded by another time. Thus, nothing at all is done by a cause of destruction. As it is said:
"If some effect were to exist, then another [cause] might depend upon it" (PV I 279ab).
Thus the principle is established. What is the point of this useless grinding?
[The statement] "destruction has arisen today" does not mean that existence is the referent of another word; rather, existence is restricted to its own time and does not exist at any other time.

For one who holds that even the claim "it does not exist at another time" is merely the arising of something else, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) regarding the cessation of the object of negation.

Furthermore, as for the distinction he established—by way of being the object of the linguistic usage of "non-existence" and "existence"—in order to prove the difference between the non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and the exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), that was already refuted in the passage: "For you, the non-existence of an entity is merely its [linguistic] designation. Indeed, it is not correct to subvert what is established by reason (logic) through mere convention. To explain: those things which are perceived as arising, which perform a function, and which the wise designate as having the nature of an entity (*bhāva*), these alone are real. This [distinction] does not depend on convention; if it were subject to change, there would be no stability regarding entities, and this would not be an exclusionary negation.

For when someone, by the power of their own whim, might assert the existence or non-existence of something among various categories—such as the material and the immaterial, the resistant and the non-resistant, the invisible and the visible, the distant and the near, or the gross and the subtle—or might assert the existence or non-existence of things like the Vindhya mountains or the son of a barren woman, then an instability of the entity would result. Yet there is no such harm, because different designations are possible in accordance with one's own conventional system (*svasamaya*).

[57b] What, then, could possibly be designated as the excluded entity? Therefore, even if the word "non-existence" does not apply due to conventional usage, one must state that another entity of the same kind—whether it be something possessing a potentiality dependent on causes or something that is perceived—is what is excluded.

How, then, can there be a rejection of the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) based merely on the conventional designation of the word "non-existence"? If, however, it is argued that even the possibility of perception regarding that which is considered non-existent is dependent solely upon convention, then this is indeed a real *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation) and not a *paryudāsa*; thus, there is no fault. But by this person who fancies himself a knower of logic, having transgressed that very method established by reason, he must accept that the capacities for existence, perception, and causal efficiency belong to non-existence as its actual reality.
And as for this [distinction] between exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), what further calamity or endless trouble could there be beyond this?

Furthermore, regarding what he said: "For origination is not the defining characteristic of an entity (*bhāva*), such that cessation, being an occurrence, would constitute an entity; for even space and the like, which are unoriginated, exist. To that also [we reply]:
according to Pāṇini, the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers are not "rivers" when they are dry land (*sthalī*).
Even if it were non-existent, it would not be an entity for him; even if it were existent, it would not be an entity for him.
A person who has attained independence does whatever he desires;
this principle applies equally in both cases, according to the opinion of those who know the law.
Even when the designation "river" is negated, there is no sublation of the act of immersion;
even when the designation "existence" is negated, the exclusion (paryudāsa) is not sublated.

For everything that has the capacity for the object of perception and whose birth depends upon causes is excluded [from being the ultimate reality], since it exists only in dependence upon another entity.
In the absence of the notion of non-existence, the establishment of relative negation (paryudāsa) would not be possible anywhere, because the notion [of existence] is easily found everywhere.

Furthermore, regarding this claim that origination is held to be characterized by the cessation of its own nature (*svarūpa*) in the case of destruction, rather than being characterized by a relation to existence (*sattā*) for what was previously non-existent, or by inherence (*samavāya*) in a cause— even in that case,
it is simply the cessation of the very nature itself that is called "origination" everywhere. By introducing the concept of inherence, however, the deluded have lost sight of even that.

Since inherence (*samavāya*) itself does not exist, where could there be a relation with existence (*sattā*) and so forth? Or, let us grant that it exists; even so, "origination" (*utpatti*) is simply the acquisition of a previously non-existent nature. However, the presence or absence of other factors such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are neither proving nor subverting [this definition]. Furthermore, even for an effect that is a non-entity (*abhāva*), there can be no relation with existence for that which was previously non-existent—what is the meaning of this? Does it mean that what was previously non-existent does not exist at all? Or does it mean that it lacks existence even later on? In either case, how can it have the status of an "effect," being like the sky-flower? Let there be the existence of what was previously non-existent later on, but not a connection with the category of existence (*sattā*).

Now, one might object: "Is this not the case that *sattva* (the state of being) and *sattā* (existence) are not different in meaning? And *yoga* is a relation. In that regard, there is some principle here according to which there is a connection with *sattva*, but not a connection with *sattā*. Therefore, *sattā* is called the 'Great Universal' (*mahāsāmānya*), and even in its absence, a thing is later said to 'exist' by virtue of its mere existence as its own nature (*svarūpasattvamātra*)? If this is argued:

In that case, if that intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattva*) were real, then by that alone [the thing] would be an effect; what further function would there be for another [cause] regarding any other effect? Or, if it is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), then how can even destruction possess the status of being an effect? For indeed, even if the subsequent existence of the son of a barren woman is figuratively attributed, its status as an effect is certainly not real.

As for what is said—that even cessation (*nivṛtti*) has a beginning—that too does not add anything further. We cannot accept that this cessation possesses a beginning by way of being a non-entity (*abhāva*), because it has been established that it shares the same nature as other effects. This mere assertion is fitting only for kings. The argument that its form is not perceived at the time when the entity is perceived also gains some plausibility only when the form is subsequently perceived; yet that [subsequent perception] does not exist. It has been shown that there is nothing more than the conceptual construction of the non-existence of a jar, which follows conventional usage.

One who desires the purposeful action of a jar does not proceed toward it when the jar is not perceived; thus, there exists [the non-perception] of something other than the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) as seen by another.
Therefore, enough of examining this mere heap of analytical procedures, for they are open to faults that one may discern for oneself.

As for his claim that "there is no consequence of [non-existence] being an entity merely by virtue of being a cause of causal efficiency, because the definition of an entity as stated by you is not accepted," even in that case, it has been said that it does not transcend the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*). Consequently, non-existence is not something other than existence.

Furthermore, as for what you said—that you have also stated a distinction in the characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) of existence and non-existence—how then can there be identity? For the establishment of difference among all things occurs precisely through a distinction in their characteristics; if, on that account, no establishment of difference were possible, then the difference of anything from anything else could not be proven, which would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-duality (*advaita*).

That too is the result of a lack of careful consideration. For when one says "destruction itself, being of a perishable nature, destroys," the suffix *ghañ* is used in the active sense according to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*), or it is designated by that term through the conceptualization of it as having that property (*taddharmatā*). We maintain that this destruction is the very nature of the entity;
and relying on that very [nature], because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence (*sattāmātrānubandhitvāt*), sound is impermanent. (PV I 269ab)

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, this very [author] has raised the point that "destruction" (*nāśa*) is simply an entity (*bhāva*) characterized by the property of momentary duration; therefore, we maintain its non-difference [from the entity]. The term "destruction" (*nāśa*), derived from the root *naś* (to perish), must be explained in two ways according to its nature: first, in reality (*tattvataḥ*), because it lacks substantiality (*vastutva*), this [destruction] is an entity devoid of both identity and difference; thus, it is merely a locus for the negation of an entity, like the horn of a donkey.

However, just as in conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*) it appears to be occasional when conceptualized through temporal distinctions, so too, because its nature is the absence of all designations (*sarvopākhyā-viraha*), it appears as if distinct from existence; thus, there is no contradiction in describing a difference in characteristics even though it is not a real entity. This being the case, since a distinction between existence and non-existence is accepted through conventional reality due to a difference in characteristics, and since in ultimate reality (*tattva*) the unity of an entity is denied in the absence of a single characteristic, how can one level the charge that this leads to the consequence of monism (*advaita*)?

As for the claim that "destruction" (*nāśa*) means perishing—how could that which has a perishable nature avoid being of the same essence as the entity itself? Furthermore, it must have a cause, and that cause is none other than the cause of the entity itself; there can be no other cause for it, because [that other cause] would possess the very nature of the entity. Thus:
"For this conceptual distinction regarding an entity would exist only due to the affirmation [of its existence], in accordance with the reality of the thing" (PV I 278ab).

To this he says: that too is untenable because it contradicts your own words. For you have asserted the identity (*tādātmya*) of existence and non-existence; yet that is contradicted if one does not admit their essential nature (*tattva*). Even if one admits their essential nature, the distinction of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is contradicted. For how can something whose difference is stated by way of a distinction in defining characteristics be said to be "indefinable" as either identical or different in its essential nature?

Nourished by that pleasure, due to its playful nature, it causes whatever has been done to be done again and again. Indeed, we do not assert that there is identity between an entity and a non-entity whose very nature is the cessation of that entity. As for the non-entity which "does not exist" in relation to a subsequent moment, what contradiction could there be regarding identity with it? This has already been addressed in the investigation of destruction (*nāśavimarśa*). In this same way, other [objections] as well should be understood as having been set aside without further elaboration.

As for what he also said: "But surely, since non-existence has the characteristic of being the separation from all phenomena, its arising is not logical; for that [arising] belongs only to the nature of existence"—this is not so, because even in the absence of the nature of existence such as knowability and so forth, [non-existence] still exists—and so on. That too is without substance.

For it is not the case that merely by virtue of possessing a common property there is room for properties that are mutually exclusive; otherwise, it would follow that even fire possesses coldness, or that non-existence itself exists everywhere, since even [properties such as] knowability (*jñeyatva*) and so forth would be negated. Furthermore, it has already been established that origination, being of the nature of coming into being after not having existed, is indeed a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*).

As for the statement that "it does not exist by itself," what is its meaning? Does it mean that this non-existence is itself? Or does it mean that it brings about its own non-existence? Or that it does not bring about existence? Or that it does nothing at all? Or that it itself is nothing? Having raised these alternatives, you have begun your refutation; yet even that is merely like the piteous cries produced when one’s vital organs are being cut.

For in that case, the meaning is indeed made manifest: "by itself" means it was produced by its own cause with a duration fixed for a single moment, independent of any other cause; therefore, nothing [of that nature] exists in any subsequent moment. Consequently, how could this thing, which does not possess that nature, arise later?

For that entity, by virtue of its own cause, arises as having that very nature (svabhāva) and as excluded from what does not have that nature. How could it later become something that does not have that nature? For a stone, being excluded from lightness by its own nature, can never become light. That [entity] indeed floats [as expected]. Just as it arises excluded from staying in another location, so too, being excluded from staying for another moment, how could there be room for it to stay for another moment? This has already been explained.

Now, the term "non-existent" does not denote that very same entity, because it is the object of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, you do not accept that anything else denoted by the word "absence" can enter the range of cognition; therefore, a negation that lacks an object would be non-veridical, and thus the entity would remain unrefuted.

It is not so; since even passing away (*pracyuti*) is what is being established, how can there be a lack of objective referent? Nor is there any contradiction, for a contradiction would occur if the negation applied while the entity remained existent. But that is not the case, because passing away has been established. Furthermore, it has already been stated that it is not impossible for a non-entity to be an object of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*).
As for the objection: "Even if the negation has another thing as its object, how can it negate the entity? [the answer follows].

It was asked how that which expresses the absence of something could not be a negation; that too has already been effectively answered. For that absence is not of the nature of a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), since another positive entity is admitted. If it were merely an implicative negation (*paryudāsa*), the exclusion of one thing does not necessarily entail the manifestation of another positive entity. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there is no contradiction [between them]. Or, even if there were a contradiction, what is the point of resorting to the medium of the contradictory? Let the absence be established directly.

It might be argued: "When the non-existence of something is established by means of speech, there remains room for doubt; however, certainty arises through the door of a contradictory [statement]. This is incorrect. For even the presentation of a contradiction occurs solely by means of speech. Just as, regarding fire which is to be understood by mere speech, the statement "there is no cold here" is appropriate, but not "there is no cold here because of fire"—so too is this case.
Now, another point is considered:

[the opponent argues] that the apprehension of one thing is not sufficient for the purpose of negation; if it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), how can the apprehension of one thing be a negator of the other?
Or how does the form of your conceptual construction, "that jar is destroyed," effect the negation of the jar?
To this, the reply is:
for one who is intent on the conceptual construction that "this does not exist here," there is no rule of negation other than that [construction], nor is there any other cognition for the time being.
Even for the cognition that conceptualizes non-existence, its status as a negator is not set aside when there is no doubt regarding its being a constituent part of the proof.
It has been stated that the destruction of an existing thing is not tenable;
for there is no power to produce what is non-existent, since an entity is by nature existent.

Therefore, there is no inconsistency here in the view that the experience of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the absence of other counter-correlates. Nor does the operation of negation by the experience consist of anything other than that alone. Furthermore, even for a conceptual construction such as "the jar is destroyed," which serves as a cause during states of purposeful activity—such as walking without hesitation—or during states of withdrawal from activity due to its connection with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it does not have the function of negating anything else.
In the same way, it should be understood that even the status of a verbal statement as a means of establishing negation occurs solely through the production of such a conceptual construction.

By this, the removal of such objections as "In that case, non-apprehension is simply the cognition 'it does not exist'; how then could that, being itself a real entity, be the object for the negation of another entity? is established.

For us, non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is not the cognition "it does not exist"; rather, it is simply the non-conceptual apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). The cognition "it does not exist," however, is merely a mental conventional expression (*mano-vyavahāra-rūpa*) which is the result of that [non-apprehension]. Furthermore, such a persistent insistence is useless when investigating the nature of reality (*vastu-cintā*). As for the definition of the object of the cognition "it does not exist," that too is already covered by the definition of it as "unreal" (*asad*).

As for the objection raised concerning the possibility that the ground and so forth, as distinct from the jar, might be the object [of the cognition], it was stated: "No, because the ground and so forth are a different entity; and when one entity is presented or cognized, another entity such as the jar is not thereby presented or cognized as non-existent.
For in this way, the refutation that was stated against the view that "destruction is indeed a different entity" would be automatically avoided by you yourself.

That too is incoherent; for if the object of this [cognition] is merely the bare ground, how is there no cognition of the non-existence of the jar and so forth? Indeed, that very state of isolation of the location which exists in relation to the jar and so forth is itself the absence of the jar. Likewise, when the bare location is communicated even by speech and other means, how could it not be a communication of the absence in relation to the jar and so forth under discussion?

Thus, if there were a perception of mere destruction—as in the case of a potsherd and so forth—then let the cognition of the negation of the jar occur; but by what means was the negation of the jar itself produced? For the pre-existing absence of the jar must be apprehended through that [perception of the locus]; indeed, the absence of the jar is not produced by the location, but rather the already existing absence of the jar is to be ascertained through it. For if the jar were also non-existent, there would be no cognition restricted to the single form of the location.

[150,1] Thus, just as if a jar were still present today, there would be no cognition restricted solely to the form of a potsherd, so too there would be no cognition restricted solely to the form of its destruction; let it be that by this force there is a certainty of the jar’s absence. However, if the jar’s absence had existed previously, that is not the case. Even if that [absence] were present, what would be the use of destruction? For the matter would already be established by the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) itself, namely the potsherd.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no cognition of destruction either; therefore, since the refutation of the destruction of an existent was stated in terms of its being either existent or non-existent in nature, how could there be a determination of an existent as either existent or non-existent in nature? Thus, the rebuttal is not equivalent. As for what he said—that "if there is no cognition of the distinction (*viveka*) from that [the jar], there can be no apprehension of the [surface] as distinct from it; and that distinction is not merely the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the ground and so forth, because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)," that is outside the bounds of logic. Even the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists only in a form established by conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*). And that—

It perceives a differentiated entity as non-differentiated; clearly, that which is victorious through another's nature renders the partless universe—like a vast cluster of *kadamba* blossoms—into its own parts.
Moreover, it is capable of producing the intense delusion regarding objects within the mere form of itself.
Volition is like a supreme magician who has shaken off the stability of all existing things.

For just as [a cognition] arises by unifying a differentiated entity, so too is there the sense that it perceives an undifferentiated entity as differentiated—just as in the cases of "the body of a stone statue," "hands and feet in the body," or "long-eared Devadatta. Therefore, since the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is dependent upon conceptual construction, how can this linguistic usage—which, even regarding an undifferentiated entity, depends on the intention to express differentiation—extend itself into the nature of a fixed distinction?

If it is argued that this is merely a figurative designation, such as "the head of Rāhu," when his movement is faltering; if this were true, then it would be precisely because the distinct [entity] is not directly perceived. Furthermore, this mode of expression exists even with reference to another category of entity called the "separation from a jar" (*ghaṭaviveka*); nevertheless, the drinking from the vessel [of ordeal] is the proof that it is not so. Therefore, this is simply the location where the jar is absent, which is distinct from the jar; it is not, however, qualified by a separate "separation from the jar."

Therefore, although some qualifiers such as "oxen" (*vāha*) are indeed seen to be distinct, this is not an absolute rule, because the opposite is also observed and because there is no evidence to sublate the possibility [of non-distinction]. Furthermore, dependence upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is the seed for the possibility of such an example. Thus, it should not be said that the qualifier and the qualified are different entities because they are distinct, like oxen and so forth. Moreover, if difference were pervaded by the state of being a qualifier and a qualified, then in the absence of difference, that state of being a qualifier and a qualified would necessarily be absent.
Just as there is no such thing as a "distinguished location," so too this is the case here: whether the perceived object exists or does not exist depends on the difference in one's mode of seeing.

Nor is there a sublation [of the argument] by means of the non-perception of the perceptible—a form of valid cognition—on the basis of a mere conventional distinction such as "that [space] is other than the jar," which is grounded in the object itself; rather, it is simply "of this [space] in that very way.

And as for what was said—that even if there were non-difference, no proof whatsoever exists—that applies only to one whose eyes are not yet opened, because otherwise it would be impossible to prevent the arising of direct perception.

Furthermore, if the object of both this cognition and its expression, "the jar does not exist," is the bare ground itself and not some "absence of the jar" distinct from it, then the object of the cognition "the jar exists here" would likewise have to be the bare ground itself. One need not postulate a "jar" distinct from that; let the bare ground, characterized by the presence of the jar, suffice for both cases.

And this is not tenable; for just as there is a positive manifestation of a jar, so too in the absence of a jar, something other than the elements appears. In this way, indeed, the employment of affirmation and negation would be meaningful. It would be better to be blind from birth than to have an intellect scorched by such fallacious reasoning. For if it is claimed that even a jar, like non-existence, is merely an object of conceptual construction and not within the range of the eyes, what can we say to that?

If one says that the ground has arisen together with the jar (*sakumbham udbhūtaṃ bhūtalam*), this would entail simultaneous production; yet there is no confusion of their forms, because the perception of their difference and the restriction of their distinct causal functions (*arthakriyā*) cannot be denied. Likewise, it has already been considered that non-existence (*abhāva*) does not appear as something distinct from the ground, the potsherds, and so forth.

Furthermore, let people who have forgotten the conventions [of language] declare whether the destruction of the jar is here perceived or not, turning away from critical reflection on their own vision.

Furthermore, regarding what specific objects you perceive here in this world— if the Supreme Lord points them out to the earth and other elements, then you alone are the true assembly members (sabhya), and we are not.

Therefore, what inconsistency could there be even in the application of affirmation and negation, since both states are demonstrated? For instance, how can the absence of light entering through a lattice window—which is itself appearing—be denied? It is merely that, being distinct and characterized by a vivid blue luster, it persists in that location; yet because its object is determined to be different [from the light], it is known by another name, "darkness.
Just as with light, so too the absence of other things serves to clarify the essential nature of the self; whether it be a jar or a distinction within sunlight, what a great marvel this is!

For even when one examines minutely, the subtle distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) in the mass of entities—which is extremely diverse—is not within the range of perception, like darkness, unless one employs a metaphorical distinction based on the differences among the related things. Therefore, it would be better to maintain that even the differentiation of light is simply non-perception, just like the differentiation of all other things; rather, grasp that darkness is indeed a real entity (*vastu*). Why, for heaven's sake, do you involve yourself in such a painful dilemma?

[Objection: "But surely, even for one with eyes closed, such an appearance of blue is possible, yet it does not present the object 'blue' [to consciousness]. [Response: That is incorrect, because it would follow that all other things of black color would likewise be non-existent.
[Objection: "This other black is of a different kind, even by a fraction, from what appears to one with eyes closed."

In that case, darkness (*andhakāra*) as well, appearing again in a limited space with various shapes, is experienced as having a distinct form from the appearance when the eyes are closed, because it appears much more clearly; whereas the appearance when the eyes are closed is of a single uniform taste (*ekarasa*). Furthermore, darkness is sometimes thin in form at times when there is a mixture of a multitude of light-ray atoms, while at other times it is dense or even denser; so how can there be any similarity? Moreover, mere blackness is common elsewhere as well.
If it is argued that in another case, regarding an object of blue color, there must necessarily be a concomitance with other types of tangibles (*sparśa*), [we reply: so be it.

No, because that [tactile sensation] is absent in a lattice of sapphire and other jewels. The hypothesis that the tactile sensation there is imperceptible does not fear the darkness. Therefore, let both be mere form (*rūpa*); for indeed, nothing that is perceived can be called "impossible. And if a substratum must necessarily be sought, there certainly exist things such as jeweled walls. Furthermore, in the determination of reality, no wise person is pleased by the assertion of error based on a distortion of appearance, merely because one relies upon the appearance of direct perception.

Otherwise, because things such as a flaming pillar are perceived due to disturbances of wind, bile, and so forth, even a real flaming pillar would be unreal. However, just as there is an absence of that appearance when one returns to one's natural state, so too is there an absence of the delusion regarding the non-existence of blue at the time of opening the eyes. As for the non-perception of darkness, it depends precisely on the healthy state of the senses, according to the specific distinction already described.

Furthermore, the cessation of that appearance upon the disruption of the causal complex for the possibility of perception is indeed a merit, not a fault, since its nature as a direct perception is what is intended.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that because it is impossible to perceive a black form without light—surely yellow, white, and other colors are also not perceived independently of light; thus, lamps, the moon, sunlight, and so forth would likewise require another illuminator. However, the diverse natures of entities, as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), do not deserve such critical questioning.
Moreover, Śaṅkara and Nyāyabhūṣaṇa maintain that just as with light, the eye is independent of any further light even when perceiving the absence of light.

That too is nothing; for visual consciousness, which is the determiner, does not apprehend non-existence because it is not a real entity, and it is already established that it does not depend on another light.

Nor should it be said: "Whatever entity is apprehended by a certain set of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), its absence is also apprehended by that same set; therefore, darkness, being apprehended by the set of conditions for apprehending light, is simply the absence of that [light]. This is because such an argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that light itself—when apprehended by the set of conditions for apprehending darkness—is the absence of that [darkness]. Furthermore, it would entail the consequence that a jar and a cloth, having the same set of conditions for their apprehension, would stand in a relationship of mutual absence.

Therefore, darkness—which appears in perception as distinct from other objects by way of its specific form—is indeed a real entity that is opposed to light. As for the objection that "if it is opposed, then at some time darkness might even overcome light," this is not a valid criticism, because the theory of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) still stands, just as in the case of a tuft of cotton and fire.

By this, it is established that the perception of darkness itself—the very thing that serves as the counter-positive—is capable of immediately bringing about the conventional usage of "absence," even when there is merely the cessation of light in the dark. Thus, the hope held by Śaṅkara and others—that just as there is the perception of the absence of light here, so it is everywhere else—should be understood as refuted.

Furthermore, it has been shown that when the focus is on non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the establishment of absence occurs even when the counter-positive is a form of cognition; and no fault whatsoever attaches to this, so let it rest for now. Therefore, it remains settled that there is no such thing as "absence" wherein the operation of a cause could take place.

By this, Trilocana is also refuted, who said: "For those who do not accept a cessation distinct from the entity itself, it is impossible to establish the cessation of its own nature. For if that very state of the entity which was previously observed by you to be capable of performing causal efficiency were to persist even at a later time, then how could the entity be established as having ceased in its own nature?
At that time, this entity would be destroyed; it is not the case that some state, distinct from the nature acquired from its own causes, should suddenly arise for it."

[154,1] At the time of its arising, that very thing has another nature born within it; thus, there is a change of state (*atādavasthya*). We call this very change of state its destruction. If there were no change of state, there would be identity. We do not understand the true meaning of the expression "the entity has ceased in its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa nivṛtto bhāvaḥ*). For this cessation of its own nature, when occurring, must be either the entity itself or something other than the entity.

In reality, for that which has been produced from its own causes, since it cannot arise otherwise [than as it is], the consequence of its being eternal follows from its very production; and if there were any change, then that very thing would be something other than its cessation—thus the beloved has simply done what is pleasing to himself! Therefore, casting aside this delusion, one must accept that "perishedness" is nothing other than the occurrence of destruction. Why, then, is it said that "there is no perception of the perished, nor does anything happen to it"? For the non-perception of the perished is simply the perception of its non-existence.

We accept that the destruction of the self is indeed the arising of non-existence; thus, everything is faultless. Existing things are non-momentary because they possess causes. Whatever possesses a cause is non-momentary, just like the destruction of an entity. And these existing things possess causes; therefore, they are non-momentary.

[154,10] However, since this [entity] possesses a cause, the suspicion that it might persist even when the opposite of the probandum occurs is removed by the very fact that it possesses a cause for its destruction. Thus, because its non-momentariness is established through the possession of a cause—whose pervasion is well-known—it has been demonstrated that the cessation of its own nature is possible even without the cessation of something distinct. Consequently, after a moment, how could there be the persistence of the previous state of capacity? And even if there were the production of something distinct, how could [the entity] be said to have "perished"?

The statement that "it has come into a state of non-identity with its previous condition and non-self-identity" means, in its very literal sense, that this [entity] has arisen from its own cause precisely as something devoid of any change in state or nature. The subsequent conventional usage of terms such as "non-identity with its previous state" is rooted in that [initial arising]; it is not a separate entity appearing as a conceptual construction. Therefore, there is no room for the conceptual alternatives of identity or difference. Consequently, casting aside delusion, let the conventional usage of "destruction" remain; however, nothing other than that [original entity] arises.
And since non-perception is precisely the perception of non-existence, this has just now been refuted; thus, everything is beyond reproach.

Therefore, for non-existence—which is of the nature of a mere negation (prasajya) and termed "destruction"—there is no cause whatsoever. However, in the case of that which has a perishable nature, since its capacity is established by its own causes alone—having set aside the power of any other cause—it perishes immediately upon arising and does not persist into another moment; thus, the [opponent's] argument is established. Furthermore, the pervasion of "possessing a cause" by "non-momentariness" is unproven, and thus the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika). Moreover, there is a contradiction if one accepts that produced things must necessarily perish even at the end.

It is established that if that which is within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the thesis is sublated by inference; whereas if it is not within its scope, there is a lack of proof regarding both the locus (*āśraya*) and the nature of the property itself. Furthermore, this [opponent], failing to comprehend the momentariness established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which has been proven by the Blessed Master Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) from the standpoint of direct perception—indulges in the negligence of nonsensical speech, desiring at length to offer a refutation based merely on the superficiality of pointing out the absence of a corresponding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, this should be understood as merely a manifestation of ignorance regarding the self, easily accessible to one who is fickle and immature. For instance, although momentariness is established by perception, it is not conventionally expressed through perception, because a corresponding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise; rather, it is grasped by perception, since its conventional expression is established through inference.

Furthermore, if that inference, having established [the object] for itself from some logical mark (*liṅga*), were to effect the conventional usage of grasping momentary destruction through perception by its own force, then there would be no distinction [between it and other inferences] such as that of existence (*sattva*). For in that case, the grasping of momentary destruction being established by perception only through the force of the matter (*artha*), and lacking any touch of its own human agency, it does not nourish the well-known establishment of momentary destruction as a result of perception.

However, when inference—which relies on the apprehension of a momentary duration by perception as established by other means of knowledge—arises to establish mere conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) alone, illuminating only that human agency which is indistinguishable from the subsequent conceptualization (*vikalpa*), then it is said that the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is primary through perception. This is the meaning: momentariness does not fall within the range of the falling [of] perceptual cognition; rather, it is only its conventional usage that is established by the means of establishing the apprehension of what is present.
