If momentary destruction were not established by another means, its apprehension would have to be through perception;
yet, it is from its apprehension by perception that the establishment of its momentary destruction follows.
For instance, whatever manifests in whatever manner, all that is exactly so— just as the water of the Gaṅgā is white;
otherwise, there would be no restriction of power for each individual object in the case of their being mixed together.

If conditioned phenomena appear to the senses and the intellect as persisting for a single moment, that would be due to their being perceived in a single moment; otherwise, what is seen would be a composite of the three times.

This application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is interspersed with the proof of the form of the *liṅga*. Furthermore, because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there is no fault of contradiction. By the second quarter [of the verse], the exclusion of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) is established.

To explain: "manifestation" (*pratibhāna*) is said to be the appearance in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, if an entity, while possessing a certain specific distinction by which it attains manifestation in direct perception, were to partake in the persistence of its own nature while disregarding that restriction, then its form would be entirely intermingled; consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that everything would be useful for everything everywhere.

Therefore, when there is a need for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine the essential nature [of an object], that which appears to this person’s perception in a certain way regarding engagement or withdrawal must exist exactly in that manner and not otherwise.

By this, it is shown that the appearance in perception is pervaded by non-falsity; for if the object were to exist otherwise—in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—the pervader would be absent, and thus [the appearance] would not occur, being thereby pervaded by existing in that very manner.

The third quarter [of the verse] summarizes the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), while the fourth provides the refutation of its non-establishment (*asiddhi*). For if an entity were identical across prior and subsequent times, then because it would lack any other form than the form perceived, the form belonging even to another location—which is permeated by every fraction of time—would necessarily manifest; thus, there would be no occasion for seeking another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its state in another place or time.

Furthermore, there is an inquiry as to how that object exists in another place or time at the present moment, wondering whether it has been moistened by a latent trace of passion (*rāga-rasa*) that has not yet manifested; for such an investigation is observed during the interval when the manifestation of that [object] is possible. And such a possibility does not exist once the object has already become an object of perception. Nor can it be asserted that there is no determination even when something is seen, because in the case of a desired form such as redness, there is no lack of familiarity, just as there is none regarding momentariness. Otherwise, even upon seeing it later, no ascertainment would arise. Therefore, the absence of such ascertainment is due solely to the non-appearance of that [ascertaining cognition].

[156,11] But surely, even if there is an appearance of an object as pervading the three times, the non-appearance of its specific related particulars—namely, other times, places, and states—is not a sublation; for this is the same as the case where, even when a moment is apprehended, there is a similar non-appearance of other objects related to it, such as causes, effects, or conjoined things. Therefore, it is entirely reasonable to seek further means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to those other related entities, if one should so desire. Thus it may be argued.

This is not so, because since place, time, action, qualities, and so forth exist, difference is not established [between the moments]. However, let it be that even for a distinct related entity there is no appearance when that [object] does not appear. Therefore, having set aside all states belonging to other moments, it is established that every object appears with a form that encompasses only the single moment. Thus, as long as a dissimilar state such as redness is not present, let there be a perception of them as unified for that duration of time.

That too is not the case; for immediately after the perception characterized by the ten moments, when the eye suddenly moves, there arises a suspicion of error regarding even those moments that are actually similar, because such a suspicion cannot occur with respect to things directly perceived. Therefore, the perception of that [object] which follows the movement of the eye is not momentary, since the suspicion of error in the determination cannot be established for an ordinary person unless that perception necessarily persists for two or three moments. Thus, it is only while arising over several moments that such a perception is useful for that purpose.

If it is asked: "How can there be a loss of appearance (*pratibhāsabhraṃśa*) for a form that persists for two or three moments during its very first moment, by means of which the distinction of the second and subsequent moments would be established?"—then for one whose visual consciousness wavers immediately after the moment of perceiving the first moment, the arising of conceptualization regarding the object allows no room for reflection on the non-occurrence of all other moments; this is unavoidable. If it is argued: "This cannot possibly happen to anyone," what is the refutation (*bādhaka*) here? And if it is asked: "What is the proof (*sādhaka*) here either? [we reply: it is the very fact that such a thing is observed.

It is said: if the search for the means of proof occurs immediately after the moment of perception (*īkṣaṇakṣaṇa*) when the determinative cognition (*avasāya*) arises, then there are two kinds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following perception: the conceptualization of the mere seen, and the conceptualization of the specific nature (*svarūpaviśeṣa*), such as "this is a cloth" or "this is a genuine or artificial gem," and so forth. In that regard, the error of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of dull intellect, which is removable by similarity regarding its object, is dispelled by [the conceptualization] arising from the excellence of practice established through generalization (*utsarga*).

Therefore, when the limit of the gradation of brevity in time is reached through the gradation of excellence in arising, this [arising] attains its manifestation even immediately after the moment of perception; thus, its negation is impossible to conceive. However, in the case of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has been merely perceived, its birth—which is established as occurring immediately after perception—is set aside by means of a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

For instance, since conceptual constructions have become habitual through the beginningless continuum of *saṃsāra* by their very nature, all beings—even regarding an object directly perceived—act or refrain from acting only in dependence upon conceptual construction. Especially those who seek the attainment of pleasure and the avoidance of pain, whose mental continua are perfumed by the constant practice of investigating the means to achieve those ends, how could they possibly experience a delay in the arising of conceptual construction when the efficient cause for experiencing that object has already presented itself? They do so only occasionally due to some obstruction.

Since there is no practice of withdrawing conceptual construction, and since at times there is attachment to something else, and at times there is manifestation due to extreme delusion—it is through such a collection of conditions that the arising of conceptual construction occurs with a delayed succession. In the absence of those [conditions], however, the arising of conceptual construction immediately after the moment of perception is indeed established.

Consequently, when all objective moments are deprived of that [initial] perception, why would there be no room for the mind to swing on the pendulum of doubt regarding redness and so forth—even in the second moment, which is made the object of investigation, just as in the series of distant moments? Nor does this occur even in the manifestation of direct perception; therefore, the mass of objects enters into the manifestation of direct perception as if already encompassed by the moment.

This might be the case: [it would be] appropriate [to say this] if perception were momentary; however, since perception extends over multiple moments, there is room for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) when that which extends over multiple moments appears. Therefore, how can the establishment of the apprehension of a single moment be proven?

It is said: First of all, does perception pervade multiple moments because they are useful for the production of its own nature, or because it remains stable once produced in a single moment? Regarding these, the first alternative is impossible; for since cognition lacks the nature of a composite whole, its arising in discrete parts is untenable. And if those parts, which are distinct in each moment, possess the nature of determining [the object] for the perception, then there would be as many perceptions as there are parts; thus, in relation to the first perception, the same difficulty remains.

However, if its nature is one of non-delimitation (*aparicchitti*), then even when aggregated, it is not perceptible. Complete delimitation (*paricchitti*) by means of the aggregate is the determination of the entire objective reality as a whole. Even then, the entire objective reality is merely a delimited fragment determined in the first moment; for that which has not entered into it is distinct from it. Otherwise, the entire universe perceived sequentially would be a single entity, and the entirety of perception would be a single perception.

Even in the second alternative, is it that which has already completed its operation, or is it that which has completed its operation by pervading another moment? In the first case, since its very operation consists in the apprehension of the object, conceptual construction would have no opportunity to arise merely by that much—regardless of whether it itself persists into another moment or not. And if that were so, then while the eye or the object moves, the perception would remain fixed in its inclination toward the apprehension of that object; such a principle is unprecedented!

However, even if there is non-apprehension while remaining in a state of non-momentariness, liberation does not occur merely by that much, because there remains the opportunity for the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Nor can one maintain the position of stability on the grounds that what was previously apprehending no longer apprehends later; for it is utterly incredible that something which does not apprehend its sensory object could still persist. Likewise, the claim that the operation (*vyāpāra*) of cognition persists even when unaccomplished is difficult to believe. For cognition, unlike other effects, possesses no operation distinct from its very arising.

Let it be so; nevertheless, when the sense organ and its object are in proximity, perception arises and—though its object has not yet been fully apprehended—it conceives, during the time of the simultaneous movement of both, that "it exists. This is indeed a well-spoken [objection], as before.

Therefore, enough with these excessively persistent false conceptualizations! For, by the fourth quarter [of the verse], there is an indication—through the reversal of the operation of other means of valid cognition—that at that very moment, a variegated form such as red and so forth appears, whether before or after.
Whatever form is capable of being determined while something is appearing anywhere...
A means of knowledge that has ceased does not desire to manifest there [in the present],

just as taste does not manifest in the appearance of color; likewise, while that [present object] is appearing at this moment, another means of knowledge from the prior state is required for the determination [of its existence].

Thus, by the apprehension of the pervasion of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), it is established that the manifestation of perception reveals the very nature of an entity as persisting for only a single moment. Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated in the section establishing pervasion (*vyāptisamarthana*) that its nature does not exist outside of that manifestation. Therefore, it is proven that fragility (*bhaṅguratva*) is established by perception and is conventionally treated as such by inference, which is brought about by other means of knowledge (*māna*) once that [perceptual establishment] is secured. This is because the direction of the reasoning for the determination of momentariness by perception has been indicated.
For the wise, there is no need for an extensive treatise regarding the rules of linguistic usage established by implication;

yet even that [work] was composed by the eminent teacher Ravi. However, one of small intellect, due to a lack of understanding of reality, being naturally loquacious, has vomited forth what is untrue.
[159] Nor do we depend on the path of the teacher Ravi for our apprehension of momentariness, since its sequence follows from this very point;
and as for the consistency with the statements in the Bhāṣya, that has not been sung here for fear of excessive prolixity.

Therefore, enough with this insistence on incidental discussion. It is established that what is called "destruction" is not some distinct entity, produced by a mallet or similar instrument, other than the iron bar and so forth; for if it were non-existent during the state prior to its impact, it could not fulfill the desire for the stability of an object. [Thus ends] the refutation of the pillars supporting the altar of the ill-conducted school [of the Naiyāyikas], namely those known as Maṅkhuka, Nyāyālaṅkāra, Trilocana, and Vācaspati, performed with ease.
By whatever merit I have acquired through uprooting this momentary flux,
may this person become one who has reached the further shore of the glory of knowledge throughout the three worlds.
The fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Destruction Without Cause," is completed.
And this chapter on momentary destruction is completed.
[161,2–178,6] || An Investigation of Pervasion (Vyāpticarcā) ||
Homage to the Blessed One, who is free from passion!

In this context, it is demonstrated that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and the like by fire and the like—established through perception and non-perception—is characterized by the relation of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*). For our predecessors maintained that the nature of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) consists simply in the observation of smoke where there is fire and its non-observation where that [fire] is absent.

They proceeded to deliberate as follows: "In that regard, even occasional seeing and non-seeing might occur once; therefore, it depends upon repeated occurrence. If it is argued, "But surely, even with repeated occurrence, deviation (vyabhicāra) has been observed in the case of a jar, a woman, and so forth," we reply:
"Does this mean that one should say that inference must also exist in those cases? Or rather, that for that very reason, it should not exist even in the case of smoke and the like?"

The first position is refuted precisely because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The second is also refuted precisely because of non-deviation. For when another thing deviates, it does not matter at all for smoke. Indeed, just because poisoned food is undesirable, other types of food should not be abandoned either;

otherwise, one would have achieved the cessation of all activity by that much alone—so what is the point of seeking its production, or of employing perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) for the sake of ascertaining it?

If "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) were also apprehended solely through observation and non-observation, what fault would there be? Let it be that inference itself occurs through such a distinction; thus, one seeks that distinction. And that distinction is established by way of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and non-deviation. If there is no deviation, then the capacity to convey knowledge (*gamakatva*) is achieved by that alone, making "arising from that" redundant. But in the case of deviation...
Even a hundred of those origins are not capable [of producing it]. Therefore, the search for contact is fulfilled by conjunction alone.
For this very reason, smoke is said to be the cause that is conjoined with fire, and not its effect.

Trilocana, however, says: Since perception and non-perception have particulars (*viśeṣa*) as their objects, how can there be a cognition of a relation between two universals (*sāmānya*) by means of them? If it is argued that the relation is indeed cognized as that which is excluded from non-fire with that which is excluded from non-smoke—well then, of what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is even that the object? It cannot be that of perception, because perception has only particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

Nor can it be established by inference, because that too is preceded by perception. Furthermore, there is no connection whatsoever between two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Now, if it is argued that a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in the wake of perception determines non-difference in what has been seen as different—that itself is the universal (*sāmānya*)—even so, for conceptual constructions, the object is not the real entity itself, but rather the apprehended aspect (*grāhyākāra*). And that is not a real entity; for them, the real entity remains entirely beyond the reach of the senses (*parokṣa*).

[161,23] How, then, is the apprehension of the relation (sambandha) achieved by that [means]? For us, however, the relation among those of that same class is apprehended by the mind aided by repeated observation (bhūyodarśana). Therefore, smoke does not deviate from fire. If it were to deviate from that, smoke would transcend a relation that is devoid of any limiting condition (upādhi); thus, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that removes the suspicion regarding the heterologue (vipakṣa) of the reason is the absence of a limiting condition that meets the criteria for perception (upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta).
The reason is precisely perception known as non-apprehension; from that, the natural relationship is established.

But Vācaspati’s elaboration is as follows: for smoke and the like have an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) with fire and the like, but fire and the like do not have such a relation with smoke and the like; for those [fires] are perceived even without smoke and the like. However, when they experience a connection with moist fuel and so forth, they then become connected with smoke and the like. Therefore, the relation of fire and the like is produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of moist fuel and so forth.

The connection, however, is not intrinsic; therefore, it is not necessary. But the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is intrinsic, because no adventitious condition (*upādhi*) for it is perceived, and because no deviation is observed anywhere. Furthermore, it is impossible to postulate something that is not being perceived, even if it were invisible due to its unobservability.

It is logical that an *upādhi*, which is suspected due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that either establishes or refutes it, obstructs the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of the relationship. For those who do not perceive a restrictive factor, doubt must necessarily arise.
Thus, having been granted this opportunity, the demoness of doubt, by transgressing the boundaries of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), gains a foothold;

she would not allow anyone to proceed anywhere, because there is nowhere where one might not suspect some kind of harm in some way. And for discerning people, the suspicion of harm is a cause for desisting. Ultimately, even regarding the consumption of pleasant food and drink, there is the fear of death.

Because it is seen from experience. Therefore, one who maintains the worldly course according to authoritative tradition should entertain doubt only in accordance with what has been observed, and not regarding that which has never been seen before. For doubt depends upon the recollection of specific features; it does not arise in the absence of such recollection. And recollection cannot occur with respect to something never previously experienced. As it was said by the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika*:
"An apprehension that lacks a basis in valid cognition is not [justified].
Likewise, by that same author, in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*:
"For he who, out of delusion, might imagine an invalidating factor even when one has not arisen..."
"He would meet his end, being full of doubt in all worldly transactions.
Therefore, searching diligently for a limiting condition (*upādhi*) and not perceiving one, we understand that it does not exist and conclude that the relation is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).

It might be argued: "If one thing were related to another without a cause, there would be a relation by way of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*). Then everything would be related to everything by way of its own nature, and everything would be cognized from everything. Or, if one thing is the effect of another, why does everything not arise from everything? Because there is no distinction in their being 'other' (*anyatva*); and consequently, that same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains. If this is said:

The intrinsic natures of entities are not to be questioned; therefore, even though there is no difference in their otherness (*anyatva*), only certain things are causes and only certain things are effects. But is this non-questioning of intrinsic nature not exactly the same even for those things that do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, provided there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*)? Therefore, this [objection] is also of no consequence.

By what means, then, is this essential (svābhāvika) relation apprehended? In the case of relations perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is by means of direct perception. For instance, when one first perceives the relation between fire and smoke as being together with moist fuel, at that time, is the relation of both essentially so, or is it adventitious (*aupādhika*)? Or is it that the relation of smoke is adventitious, while that of fire is not?
[163,8] It is intrinsic. Furthermore, it is impossible to determine that fire is extrinsic while smoke is intrinsic.

[163,9] In this regard, since fire without wet fuel is observed in cases such as a glowing iron ball even in the absence of smoke, it is certain that its connection with smoke is conditioned by the adjunct (upādhi) of wet fuel, and not intrinsic. [163,10] However, because a specific kind of smoke is never perceived without fire, and because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for postulating an unperceived distinction in the adjunct, [the relation of smoke] depends upon the recollection of its specific nature.

Because doubt does not arise regarding that which has never been perceived before, or because if it were to arise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) resulting in the cessation of activity for discerning persons, an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is ascertained. This ascertainment is not mental; for if the mind operated toward external objects independently [of the senses], there would be no such thing as the blind or the deaf.

[This would follow] by way of an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Furthermore, if its operation were dependent upon repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), it would result in the fallacy of [the inference] being another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

For it is not the case that something is "mental" (*mānasa*) simply because the mind (*manas*) is its instrumental cause (*nimitta*); if that were so, nothing at all would fail to be mental, since every cognition (*pratyaya*) has the mind as its instrumental cause.

If, however, the designation of specific means of valid cognition is made in dependence upon their respective uncommon causes (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*), then in this case as well, there is repeated observation.

Since there exists a non-common cause, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) has arisen; therefore, it is logical that the sense faculty itself— assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation— grasps the natural connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) of smoke and the like with fire and the like, just as one grasps the true nature of the distinctions among noble gems.

In this way, regarding those cases where the relationship is known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must be inferred that those very same means of valid cognition—each assisted by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*)—are the authority for grasping the essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*). Furthermore, if reasons (*hetu*) that are essentially connected with their respective probanda were to exist without that probandum, they would fall away from their very nature. Thus, when assisted by reasoning (*tarka*), the probandum is excluded [from the counter-example].

Wherever instances of doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are observed, those [reasons] certainly establish their own probandum (*svasādhya*). Furthermore, in cases such as dark complexion (*śyāmatā*), there is no possibility of an essential connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*) between being Maitra’s son (*maitratanayatva*) and so forth. Since the specific transformation of food and drink (*annapānapariṇatibheda*) exists as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the relationship between dark complexion and being Maitra’s son, being Maitra’s son is not a prover (*agamaka*). By this same principle, [the following is explained]: "His [fruits] are ripe..."

Fruits located at the top of a tree [are known as such] because they originate from that very tree; likewise, relations based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika-sambandha*), such as "having tasted the fruit," have also been explained. Therefore, that whose relation is natural (*svābhāvika*) and necessary (*niyata*) is a constituent of inference (*anumānāṅga*), such as smoke, being produced, and so forth. However, that whose relation is adventitious does not become a constituent of inference, such as "being his son" and the like.
Thus it stands.
To this, it is said: what is called "pervasion" (vyāpti) is either the necessary presence of the pervader (vyāpaka) there, or the presence of the pervaded (vyāpya) only there;

thus, by way of being properties of the agent and the object, it is intended as two-fold through the forms of positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka), according to the requirements of inference.

Otherwise, inference would be useless. For if it were established in a general sense that when the probans exists, the probandum necessarily exists, or that in the absence of the probandum the probans necessarily does not exist, then there would be hope for the probandum where the probans is present, and its absence where the probandum is absent—provided there is a specific designation. But when the aforementioned rule does not hold, then...

If there is the apprehension that "there is a means of proof (*sādhana*) but no object to be proven (*sādhya*)," how can there be any scope for inference? Therefore, by one who desires inference, the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) must necessarily be relied upon; and its establishment does not occur through mere repeated observation alone.
For just as the possibility of a single instance of correspondence might occur by chance, so too could it happen by mere chance even on several occasions.

There is no denial of correspondence. Just as when a concomitance is observed only once, a deviation is perceived, and thus there arises the suspicion that there is no rule of necessary concomitance everywhere and at all times; likewise, even when there is frequent observation, because a deviation is still seen, this suspicion arises and cannot be denied.

As for the claim that inference is invalid because one observes deviation (*vyabhicāra*), that is not tenable. For, whose observation of deviation here serves as the cause for obstructing inference? Is it that of the cognizer alone, or that of the author of the treatise, or that of anyone at all? In the last case, what has happened to the cognizer such that he would not perform an inference?

Otherwise, if another person has already accomplished their purpose by directly perceiving that very object, why would one necessarily seek out inference? Furthermore, it is unworldly to claim that one might infer fire from smoke even without having observed the relationship between them simply by asking the author of a treatise.

For a cognizer, however, even if a deviation exists, it does not necessarily come within the range of perception; for it is not the case that a deviation must exist precisely where it is being perceived.

During that much time or in that much space, it necessarily enters into the realm of cognition. And it is impossible to determine that what is not being cognized simply does not exist; for it may be seen even after an absolute lapse of time, and because its destruction is not perceived even by those whose cognition has not yet been sublated. Therefore, even if there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the non-perception of the perceiver is possible. It occurs.

If one remembers what was taught—that inference occurs when there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and not otherwise—would such a person proceed with an inference based on the certainty of that non-deviation, or would they refrain from it? Since certainty cannot be achieved through mere non-observation, non-deviation remains unestablished; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is either doubtful or unestablished (*asiddha*). In the first case, one might as well perform an inference from a camel. In the second case, however, one could not even do so from smoke. For indeed—

At a time when one does not observe any deviation—whether existing or non-existing—there is no distinction whatsoever. Therefore, if one suspects that the simultaneous perception of a camel and a donkey occurs by chance even though it has happened many times, why should one not suspect the same for smoke and fire?
This is the same. Now, I observe that even when a camel and a donkey are in close proximity, they are perceived as independent of one another.

[165,1] First of all, one who acts with the desire to know whether "when one thing is being removed, does another follow it like a calf follows a cow" does not perceive it in that way. However, when fire is removed, one perceives only the disappearance of smoke; or, when fire is present, one perceives the occurrence of smoke.

If it is argued that, therefore, deviation is possible for a camel at other times but not for smoke, then it follows that only a specific kind of observation and non-observation regarding smoke is the grasper of its production, and not the kind found in the case of the camel. For instance, when in the absence of fire—

One perceives the absence of smoke. At that time, preceded by simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*), the non-perception of smoke when only fire is absent is employed for the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Otherwise, in the absence of simultaneous perception—such as when there is merely the removal of glowing embers and a variegated flame, while smoke is likewise absent—how could there be an understanding of a relationship, given that the absence of a donkey does not imply the absence of a camel? Even if there were simultaneous perception, if it were another entity...

[165,9] When there is the departure of fire accompanied by smoke, at that time it is not certain whether its prior existence was negated by the existence of the fire or by the existence of some other entity. However, if there were merely an absence of fire, it would be easy to conclude that its prior existence was indeed caused by the presence of that [fire]. Even when there is the existence of smoke in the mere proximity of fire, even then, after first not seeing both, there is the perception [of smoke] upon the presentation of the fire alone.

[165,12] The case of smoke has already been addressed. Otherwise, if only fire were brought forth while smoke simply exists [elsewhere], how could a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) be established, as in the case of a camel?
[165,13] Even if fire accompanied by other objects were brought forth, there would be no certainty as to whose absence necessitated the prior absence of smoke.
[165,14] However, when only fire is brought forth, it is logical that its absence necessitated it.

Thus, in this way, the non-perception of one thing preceded by the perception of another is said to be "distinct" (*viśiṣṭa*) in dependence upon that prior perception. Furthermore, that prior perception is also distinct in relation to the two aforementioned types of non-perception occurring at a later time. In the same manner, a distinction should be inferred even in a case where perception is preceded by non-perception—that absence of which causes a lack of confidence regarding a camel and so forth. And it is precisely that distinction between perception and non-perception [which must be understood].

[165,18] Based upon this, there is the conventional usage of perception and non-perception. And that which is their object—the nature of two entities—is called the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

[165,19–20] Furthermore, that which is dependent on another, being not independent, is also said to be "constrained" (*pratibaddha*) therein by way of arising from that; for it is constrained by that alone.

Since even the second concomitance is negated upon its removal, it is evident that the latter depends upon the former. This should be understood to apply equally when only that [the first] is removed; otherwise, there would be a requirement for the removal of the second as well. How, then, is there the removal of only that? It is by the very production [of the effect] that pervasion is stated through the means of perception and non-perception, and not merely by seeing and not seeing while devoid of those specific [causes].

And when there is a requirement for that specific distinction, since cessation is attained through a single occurrence, there is no further need for repeated activity. For just as one does not require another means of cognition beyond the mere perception of concomitance—which is established by a single instance of seeing and not seeing—because it fails to provide certainty; likewise, once the relationship between the two distinct types of cause and effect has been established through a single instance of perception and non-perception, there is nothing further to be cognized by subsequent means of cognition.

Thus, cessation occurs by that much alone. If there is no determination (*adhyavasāya*) by a person of another class [of being] through similarity and so forth, then the cognizer must be one who is discerning. However, when there is mere co-occurrence (*sahacāra*), there is doubt regarding that very same class. Furthermore, the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) elsewhere in cases of mere co-occurrence is a potent seed for this [doubt]. And in this case, the example of poisoned food does not lead to peace.

[166,2] This is because other food is of a different genus (*bhinnajātīyatva*) from poisoned food. However, in this case, since the predominant portion that constitutes the causal factor (*prayojaka*) is characterized by constant concomitance (*sahacāra*), smoke is indeed of the same genus [as fire]. It is not the case that being smeared with poison is a common property (*sādhāraṇa*) of curd-rice and so forth;

thus there is a disparity. Furthermore, since there is no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) at all without [the relation of] "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), there is simply no non-deviation when there is difference.

Because it has the nature of arising from that (*tadutpatti*). With respect to non-deviation, the implication of "arising from that" is indeed untenable. Therefore, smoke is the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) for fire, because it implies non-deviation through arising from that. It is not a reason based on conjunction (*saṃyogin*), since that merely refers to the observation of co-occurrence.

How then is the example of the camel and the donkey given, since there is no conjunction? Let there be satisfaction with the frequent observation of the conjunction between a maidservant and a water-jar.

Nor can it be argued that there is a restriction regarding the coexistence of a camel and a donkey, or of water and a crane, at a particular time and place simply because such is observed; this is of no consequence. Therefore, it is established that when another thing is to be inferred, it is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), and the proof of its existence is based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).

Regarding the objection raised by Trilocana, we reply: "Perception has particulars as its object. Does this mean that particulars are also its objects, or that it has particulars alone? If one adopts the position of *ayogavyavaccheda* (the exclusion of non-connection), there is no contradiction in its having universals as its objects; so why would there be no room for perception and non-perception regarding two universals? Furthermore, why is the position of *anyayogavyavaccheda* (the exclusion of connection with others) stated by resorting to our own established doctrine?

Or from the perspective of the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtti*): for us, both [types of cognition] are indeed valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to both objects, by way of the distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). For that which appears in a cognition is the apprehended; whereas that toward which it proceeds is the determined.

In that regard, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the apprehended object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the universal (*sāmānya*) is its determined object. For inference (*anumāna*), however, the reverse is the case. In this respect:

The direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*) has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object even when one who seeks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) observes a single moment, because it depends upon the continuum (*saṃtāna*).

Furthermore, in the context of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*), even when a single individual instance (*vyakti*) is seen, it has a universal as its object because it has all instances of the same class as its domain. [This is expressed as: "By me, through direct perception, smoke born from fire has been determined," which [implies] the exclusion of all other instances.

[166,20] This is because, having included what has arisen within itself, there is a cognition of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) produced by its power. Just as, through the perception of mere color-form (*rūpa*), there is a determinative judgment regarding a jar—which consists of a specific collection of color-form, taste, smell, and touch—and thus perception has that [jar] as its object.

[166,21–22] Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "universal" (*sāmānya*) that is entirely distinct; rather, it is simply the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves whose mutual differences have not been distinguished.

[166,23] These are called "generalities" (*sāmānya*). However, when distinguishing specific differences, each is treated by its own term as a "particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, [166,24] although all particular characteristics that are distinct from others do not appear [in cognition] and thus lack the status of being objects as apprehended entities (*grāhya*), nevertheless, their status as objects as determined entities (*adhyavaseya*) is difficult to deny; so how can there be an exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)? It has also been said that the object of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) is indeed a non-entity (*avastu*).

This is stated precisely because of a lack of familiarity with the established conclusions of others; for both synthesis (*anusandhāna*) and inference (*anumāna*), by virtue of their dependence on conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), have real entities as their objects.

The rest is a proof of what is already established. Now, suppose the position is that [the object exists] according to the actual mode of being (*vastuvṛtti*). That too is incorrect, because it is impossible to bypass the twofold nature of the object of all cognitions, distinguished as the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). For the very validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is what remains superior.

The duality of objects, however, is established everywhere. In that regard, first of all, in inference, since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the real entity does not appear [directly], it is merely the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavaseya*); the grasped object (*grāhya*), on the other hand, is the form of the cognition itself. Such a point has been thoroughly examined by us in the *Apoha-prakaraṇa* and is therefore not introduced here. Moreover, even if the form of the cognition is not accepted [as the external object], nevertheless, having arrived through the force of the real entity, how could it be excluded?

For there can be no such thing as cognition without an appearance. And since it is established that what appears in inference is not the external object itself, it must necessarily be its own internal form (*svākāra*). If it is argued that this form is false, even so, when it appears, the apprehended and the determinable are both external; thus, once the duality of objects is established, why persist in this insistence? In the same way, in perception as well, only certain individuals appear as the apprehended, while all others—

[At the time of] cognizing the necessary connection, [the object] is determined as being of the same class. For if it were not manifest [to the senses], there would be no determination at all; indeed, even the slightest scent of the establishment of a cognition of the relation through perception would be brushed away.

As for what was said regarding apprehension by means of the mind—assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation—or by the sense organ, in that case, this is [the response]:

[167,10] This is investigated: First of all, there is the repeated sensory perception of individual instances of fire and smoke. And there is the reflective deliberation (*vimarśa*) born from the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [perception]. This [fire] is perceived only in conjunction with this [smoke]. Therefore, is this concomitance between these two eternal? Or is it merely the association of two friends? Even for one whose capacity for reflection is weak, there is the cognition of the necessary connection (*antarīyaka*) through a logical reason.

It occurs, and its performance is accordingly; yet no further manifestation of cognition (*jñānavivarta*) is perceived therein. In that regard, repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) merely acts as an auxiliary by way of generating a mental impression (*saṃskāra*); it cannot be said to be the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, the claim that it has as its object all individual instances (*vyakti*) of a single class without exception is a mere fantasy, because those individuals do not appear [in the cognition].

Doubt, which follows immediately after that, is likewise not determinative of the relationship precisely because it is doubt. And as for the final [cognition], even though it has the form of a certainty, it is devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Therefore, what confidence can there be regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) presented by that [cognition], even if it bears the name of "perception" (*pratyakṣa*)? For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is not born from a logical mark (*aliṅga*) conforms only to the operation of a prior perception that has already occurred, and thus its correspondence with reality—

The arising of an entity does not occur through independence, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, previous perceptions—which bear witness merely to concomitance, like the concomitance of wind and sunlight—do not penetrate any specific distinction; how then could they be capable of establishing its correspondence with reality? Even if it were so, those very [perceptions] would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein, whereas this [present cognition] is a memory. As for its status as a means of valid cognition...

"It is well said that it is being pointed out. It should not be claimed that there is a distinction [between the two cases] because the concomitance of wind and sunlight is subsequently broken; for the intended meaning is non-difference with respect to the period during which no deviation is observed. Furthermore, as has already been stated, even in this case, a certainty regarding non-breaking [of concomitance] is untenable. For as long as the non-arising of smoke prior to the operation of fire remains present in the mind, to that very extent..."

The discernment of a distinction arises from another concomitance; and for that very reason, it is only logical that if there were deviation from that [concomitance], smoke would transcend its relationship with fire as being free from any limiting condition (*upādhi*). Otherwise, when only mere concomitance was previously perceived—just as when fire is seen in the absence of smoke, one postulates a limiting condition for the relationship between fire and smoke in a general sense—the same would apply to smoke in the absence of fire.

If one assumes the existence of an entity, there would have to be the postulation of another limiting condition (*upādhi*); therefore, for what could there be a relation—whether adventitious or essential—with what? For it is not the case that when two friends are perceived through the exclusion of one, the possibility of perceiving the other does not occur even through the exclusion of the first. This is because the existence of Maitra is not contradicted even in the absence of Caitra, as in the case of a cave in a mountain.

Even for that which has entered [into the mind], its fitness for perception does not vanish; however, in the case of smoke, there is certainly no arising at all without fire, and thus there is no possibility [of error]. By that much, the very fact of its being produced from that (tadutpatti) becomes the sole refuge. And it has already been stated that this [production] does not result from repeated observation and non-observation.
For this very reason, it is impossible to assert that the relation between a cow and "cowness" is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).

This is because, in the absence of the perception of their causal origination (*tadutpatti*), there is no distinction from other concomitants (*sahacārin*). Furthermore, even the observation of concomitance does not exist, since neither part is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, what is the point here in casting aside the theories of the intrinsic and the conditional (*aupādhika*)?

By way of distinction: the capacity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) to produce a cognition is due to its being a cause; however, since one cause produces an effect only in dependence upon others, there is no fixed rule regarding the effect.

But the effect itself is restricted by the restriction of the causal complex, such that it is restricted by each individual member. Thus, it is established that only that [effect] is the logical mark (*liṅga*), not the cause.
Now, because smoke is observed when fuel is present along with fire, fuel is established as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) specifically for the sake of specifying the particularity of the smoke.

Furthermore, when there is a connection with fire, that which serves as its limiting condition (*upādhi*) would necessarily be perceptible; however, that which is not perceived is said to be non-existent. Now, is fuel itself the ultimate limiting condition by virtue of which the necessity of perceptibility is intended in the case of the connection? For a limiting condition must be designated as either another object to be depended upon or a specific difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And another object is not necessarily perceptible. Consequently, [the connection remains unestablished].

[168,15] Even in the case of smoke, there might be a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in its connection with fire, yet it is not perceived; how then can it be said that such a condition does not exist simply because it is not seen?
[168,16] For it is from this that the establishment of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) follows.
[168,17] Furthermore, if there were another factor to be depended upon, how could there be a necessary rule for the existence of fire based on smoke alone?
[168,18] If you say this, then surely this very point is being considered: whether fire necessarily occurs when smoke is present, or not.
[168,19] Since at times smoke might exist even without fire by depending on some other factor as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), what is the cause for certainty in this matter?
[168,20] Therefore, how could smoke—which is established as arising in dependence upon fire—be admitted to exist even in the absence of that [fire]? Thus it is.

[168,21] Excellent! This non-perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is unestablished. For just as fire is not connected with smoke without fuel, so too smoke is not connected with that [fire] without fire; thus, the status of being a limiting condition is equal for fuel in both cases. Alternatively, if the presence of smoke is attained through the accompaniment of fuel by means of an established fire, then the status of the limiting condition is settled.

If it is argued that smoke which is not yet established is established as having an intrinsic (svābhāvika) connection because it obtains its very nature through that [fire], and thus does not deviate from it—even so, it follows that this is simply "origination from that" (tadutpatti), and that alone constitutes the intrinsic relationship. Furthermore, such a relationship is not graspable by the aforementioned mental cognition (*mānasa*) and other means of perception; nor can a limiting condition (*upādhi*) be ruled out by the non-perception of what is perceptible. Thus, when there is a suspicion of an extrinsic condition, there is no exclusion of the contrary case (*vipakṣa*).
[168,27] It is established that [this refers] to smoke.

In the treatise of Vācaspati, however, it is stated that in the case of the relation between fire and smoke, fuel is indeed observed as the *upādhi* (limiting condition). But in the case of the relation between smoke and fire, there is an inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*), and its sublation occurs through the mere non-perception of an *upādhi*. And in that regard, the reason is "because no deviation is observed anywhere. On this point, the following is considered: does this reason establish the non-perception of an *upādhi*?

[169,4] Now, even if that very [non-perception] were his proof, it would be a sublater of the [probans] itself due to the suspicion of its lack of firmness, because its intrinsic nature is not perceived as a real entity. [169,5] In the first case, it is useless; for the existence and non-existence of cognition are not to be established by another cause, since they have the nature of being cognized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and another [cognition].
[169,6] And since there is no perception of the limiting condition (*upādhi*), non-perception is indeed established. Thus, even when no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed...

Alternatively, it must be stated that there is no application of a reason (*hetu*). If it is argued that "application" means the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), we say no, because there would be no point of contention (*vimati*);

for the mere non-apprehension (*apratīti*) is already established. The third alternative is also not tenable: if the first [non-apprehension], being devoid of the qualification of being perceptible (*dṛśya-viśeṣaṇa*), lacks the power to establish a negation, what kind of power could the second possess? It is intended that the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) occurs only in the case of the perceptible.

If that were so, then it would not be the case everywhere or at all times; and consequently, since there would be no deviation anywhere, it would be illogical for the relationship to be intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). Furthermore, the mere fact that no deviation has been observed in some instances would lead to the unwarranted conclusion (*prasajyeta*) that fire is also intrinsically related to smoke, or that Caitra and Maitra and others are likewise intrinsically related to one another. And if this were the case, even if a relationship were intrinsic, it would result in a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*).

Therefore, non-deviation must be sought everywhere. Consequently, even in the domain of inference, as long as one does not establish the probandum through perception, one cannot cognize non-deviation; thus, what is the use of inference? Furthermore, the doctrine of essential nature (*svābhāvikavāda*) was resorted to in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) regarding smoke—on account of the fear of inconclusiveness arising from the suspicion of deviation—by means of [theories such as] "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*).

[169,16] Therefore, because it is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), there is no deviation anywhere; and because there is no deviation anywhere, it is intrinsic—thus, there is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). However, for one who holds that the cognition of the production of one kind from another kind occurring even once is itself the cognition of non-deviation everywhere, this undesirable consequence does not apply; for it is logically established that the application of that [intrinsic nature] depends precisely upon repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*).

For just as in one instance, when there is doubt upon seeing, there is dependence on another, so too at other times there is dependence on doubt. In every case, the requirement for perception is indeed mutually induced. However, if one were to demonstrate a restriction regarding the number of repetitions even in that case—just as we do:
"Having previously not seen it, by seeing it in succession, one knows the established relation between cause and effect."

Or, if one does not perceive [the object] sequentially during the observation, there would otherwise be no finality. Thus, regarding the parts, there is a rule of three repetitions for both perception and non-perception; however, regarding the whole, it is sufficient with a single repetition. At that point, one may be well-established. But as for "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), since the number is not fixed, how many times must one who follows the target reach satisfaction?

And if that were impossible, this person would never perform inference; thus, the treatise on defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śāstra*) would be useless. However, in the case of recollection, some degree of observation will proceed for the sake of instilling proficiency in the mind. Therein, nothing is lost without a restriction regarding the measure [of observations], just as there is a restriction regarding the measure of time for a seed to produce a sprout. The same applies to the manifestation of the true nature of a noble gem.

Nor is there a restriction on the number of perceptions, because what is intended to be expressed is merely the manifestation of subtle distinctions in form—like one who has entered a chamber from a luminous space, or like twins. However, in the case of smoke and so forth, it is not a distinction of form that is intended, but rather a distinction of essential nature (*svarūpa*).
For instance, even though the two forms of blue and its opposite are initially more distinct, there are no perceptions [of them] even to the extent of a million.

[They are] capable of determining distinctions. Thus, prior to observing deviation, when two things—one deviating and one non-deviating—are presented as distinct objects, there is no determination of any difference in their forms. In the case of smoke, however, it has been stated that the mind does not even perceive a distinction in its form, but rather perceives it as having an occurrence dependent upon fire. For this very reason, the establishment [of the relation] occurs through perception and non-perception functioning just once.

[170,6] However, with respect to form (*rūpa*), even in the case of smoke, whatever the initial perception is like, even the final [perception] of the limit (*koṭi*) is exactly like that; it does not possess any distinction, unlike a gem.
[170,7] If the cognizer is free from suspicion of deviation regarding such a perception, then there is no need for a second perception.
[170,8] But one who is suspicious would have no conviction even through a hundred perceptions; thus, the word "repeatedly" (*bhūyas*) in your mantra—
[170,9] What is the destiny of the reciter? Therefore, even one who has previously observed a hundredfold non-deviation remains in a state of doubt.
[170,10] As for the claim that "the conceptualization of something unperceived is impossible," this is merely the lamentation of a sleeping person.
[170,11] That is improper even for a child; for it is precisely of that which is unperceived that conceptualization occurs, as in the case of Primordial Matter (prakṛti), God (īśvara), and so forth.

[170,12] However, the distinction is that some imagined [object] conforms to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while others do not. For a pot that is actually being perceived is not called "imagined. Therefore, the conventional usage of imagination applies only to things that are not being perceived. In certain cases, however, there is a firm determination of existence based on the absence of sublation through such means as the testimony of a reliable person (*āptavacana*). But for one who investigates, it remains merely tentative. Therefore, if even smoke—[170,14]...

[170,15] Deviation has indeed been observed; what doubt could there be in that regard? However, when it has not been observed, let there be no determination of its existence as a single part, since we are concerned with what is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). But how can the mention of its existence as a possibility (*pākṣika*) be prevented? Now, if this is the intention: "It is not non-perception in that very place which is intended, but rather, even elsewhere, that which is not perceived cannot be suspected"—well then, fire... [170,17]

[170,18] Furthermore, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is indeed observed in the case of gold and so forth; let there be satisfaction with this. Now, if it is argued that [deviation] is not observed in the case of smoke—well then, is "man-ness" (*puruṣatva*) ever observed in a post (*sthāṇu*), such that one would suspect it in a post? If you say it is observed in what is characterized by verticality (*ūrdhvatā*), then here too, it is observed in another instance precisely where there is frequent co-occurrence (*sahacārin*). Therefore, the argument beginning with "even though it is not being seen" and so forth is refuted. But in whatever case...

[170,21] Regarding that which is doubted: the requirement to observe it in that very same place is unworldly (*alaukika*). Therefore, even if deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is not observed within the class of smoke, they cannot be ruled out simply because they ought to be observed. This doubt, being of the nature of a doubt regarding intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikatva*), necessarily first obstructs the ascertainment of intrinsic connection. [In the case of] an intrinsic relation—

Furthermore, how could smoke be a prover by virtue of its force (*bala*) if that [force] were not ascertained? For a reason is not a prover merely by its existence in the subject (*dharmin*); even when there is doubt regarding its existence, it ought to be a prover. And whatever proceeds despite doubt regarding something will certainly proceed even when that thing is absent. Thus, even setting aside an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*), smoke—and indeed anything else—[would be a prover].

[170,27] There would follow the consequence that [any connection] is a means of proof (*gamaka*). Therefore, in reality, the connection that constitutes certainty is nothing other than a connection based on essential nature (*svābhāvika*). This is because, without certainty, a factor that is supposed to be a means of proof is itself incapable of acting. Therefore: "For those who do not see a restrictive factor, there must necessarily be doubt regarding smoke in the absence of fire" (PV III 324).

Thus, this is difficult to overcome when one does not rely on the production of that [knowledge]. Nor is there, in this way, the reproach of overstepping the boundaries of the world of those who accept valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). For no one asserts uncertainty regarding the domain of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor certainty in the absence of a means of valid cognition—just as you yourself assert the certainty of non-existence despite the absence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the "limitationless" (*anupādhi*). Therefore, there is no room for the demon of doubt (*saṃśayapiśāca*) everywhere; [this applies] in the case of the absence of a means of valid cognition.

Because it has already been accepted as such. If you say that something can be said even regarding the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then let it be said if there is a face. However, if one speaks while accepting the characteristics of a means of valid cognition, then the answer is very easy. But if it is otherwise, then that must be stated by the other party alone; there is no occasion for us, because for one who accepts a means of valid cognition, the result is certainty.

The acceptance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance of certainty regarding its object, which is not subject to dispute. Otherwise, how could the demoness of doubt find an opportunity everywhere? You may simply say that the definition formulated by you is not a valid means of cognition; however, that very point remains to be examined. Furthermore, it would be a violation of the principles of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) to suspect that an unperceived limiting condition (*upādhi*) exists in smoke.

If it is argued that this constitutes a violation of worldly convention (*lokyātrā*), we say no; for those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) have already prohibited the authority to refute through non-perception of the unperceivable (*ayogyānupalabdhi*). Otherwise, the means for achieving heaven and so forth would be as good as discarded. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because [the existence of the omniscient one] is established by the valid means of inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*), we say no; for it has been established in the proof of the omniscient one that once something has been refuted previously by non-perception, inferential and other such means of proof cannot function.

Therefore, this mere non-perception (*anupalabdhi-mātra*), which results from the discernment (*viveka*) through the consideration of what precedes and what follows, is the means for establishing certainty.

Consequently, since there is no room for doubt regarding the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is incoherent to claim that one would not act in any situation whatsoever. Nor is it the case that action does not occur simply because of a suspicion (*śaṅkā*); for action is unavoidable when there is doubt regarding the purpose of an object, just as in the case of pleasant food and drink. However, this [objection] is raised by one who cites an example involving doubt regarding something useless.

[171,19] Even the object of doubt regarding what is beneficial or harmful is itself unknown; what more could be said than this? Nor is this the subject at hand [171,20], because the subject under discussion is whether or not there can be doubt regarding the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*). And that has already been stated therein. Now, this underlying intention is manifold: [171,21] since smoke is observed never to deviate from fire, one might suspect that at some time smoke could exist even in its absence—this is the suspicion of harm (*anarthaśaṅkā*).
And since that [certainty] is a factor for cessation, the meaning is that one should set it aside and instead establish the cognition of an essential relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) alone;

just as, for example, one proceeds toward food and drink only after dispelling the suspicion of death. If this is so, then it is logical that even doubt regarding the object is a factor for engagement. For, through repeated observation of co-occurrence, non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) itself is indeed common, just as [non-deviation] exists between food and drink and life. Now, such...

If it is argued that we speak only of doubt regarding what is not beneficial (*anartha*), then that [doubt] is indeed a motivator (*pravartaka*). How then can it be said that this [person] would never act?

Or how can even doubt regarding what is not beneficial be a factor for desisting (*nivṛttyaṅga*)? This is equally true even when there is occasional deviation (*vyabhicāra*), just as in the case of begging for alms that are sometimes obtained and sometimes not. Thus, the intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) of smoke is established.

[171,28] Proof [is established]. Furthermore, the suspicion regarding what has been observed was already demonstrated previously. For this very reason, the argument beginning with "viśeṣa" (particularity) and so forth is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

[172,1] As for the statement beginning with "tad uktam" (it has been said), this refers to taking a sick person and entering the fire. For indeed, [172,2] as long as a cognition of sublation (*bādhājñāna*) has not arisen, there can be no groundless suspicion.

[172,4] If a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*) has arisen regarding the object being delineated, or if there is a validating means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then what room is there for doubt? For doubt is by nature a state of uncertainty, whereas both a validating and a subverting cognition function as means for reaching a definitive conclusion. [172,5-6] Now, if you intend to mean that no subverting cognition arises regarding the sense faculties due to cataracts and the like, that is irrelevant; for it is not the case that the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of smoke and so forth—
[172,7] Is it not the case that non-establishment (*asiddhi*) was suspected, rather than the lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*)?

[172,8] And what is the meaning of "without proof" (*niṣpramāṇikā*)? If you mean the absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*), then what is the point of the suspicion? [172,9] Or does it refer to the object being delineated by the suspicion? Does that [object] exist in that very place, or elsewhere? Even if elsewhere, would it be in something of the same class (*sajātīya*)?

Or [it may refer to] any other [cognition] whatsoever. First of all, the first position is not consistent with the context. Or let it be so; nevertheless, regarding that other cognition, the means of proof—whether it be mental [perception] inhering in the same object, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—is not exhausted by this [objection]. It has already been stated that the absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the subject under discussion, which is what is being suspected, is itself the prover of that suspicion. As for the [absence of a means of valid cognition] regarding another similar instance...

[172,13] But this is the meaning of "existence" (*bhāva*): that which is suspected to be the independence of smoke from fire is understood by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to belong to that same class (*tajjātīya*). [172,14] In that regard, membership in that class may be considered either with respect to the individual (*vyakti*) or with respect to the genus (*jāti*). [172,15] First, with respect to the individual, another instance of smoke is precisely what belongs to that class. And if its non-dependence on fire is cognized, then, because there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*), [the inference holds].

[172,16] Thus, smoke that is excluded from pervasion becomes a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*). What, then, is the point here of introducing doubt regarding the exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*)? [172,17] If it is argued: "Even though it is not established that [smoke] is independent of fire, since there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*), why introduce doubt? [172,18] [The answer is: Because the absence of deviation is not proven by mere non-observation; rather, absence is established only through the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*).

Because the context concerns proof (*sādhana*), there is room for doubt that, due to frequent co-occurrence alone, something might be neither deviant nor non-deviant as certain. However, with respect to genus (*jāti*), the genus of smoke is indeed distinct from other genera, yet it is of the same class (*sajātīya*) through some proximity such as substantiality (*dravyatva*). Therefore, the observation of deviation in water and so forth—which belong to the intended class—is precisely what has been stated. And this alone is logical.

[172,22] The position is as follows: when considering the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of smoke, because the process of determination proceeds by treating as one even that smoke which is separated by different places and times, it is appropriate to observe the appearance of what is suspected to be a different class (*jātyantara*). For even by that much, there is no loss of the fact that memory is preceded by direct experience (*anubhava*).
[172,24] Otherwise, this syllable would be non-expressive in the first position and useless therein; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

[172,25] For one who does not perceive a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the state of being characterized by doubt is merely the prattle of a child. Indeed, it has been stated that the perception of a subverting factor is contradictory to doubt because it consists of certainty (*niścaya*). Nor is a subverting factor something that results in uncertainty. Therefore, where there is an absence of such [certainty], for us there is doubt; how then could [doubt] constitute the nature of all conventional transactions (*vyavahāra*)? Or rather—

What is intended here is not that one *imagines* (utprekṣate) a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) for smoke’s dependence on non-*uṣarbudha* fire; rather, it should be understood as follows: the very doubt regarding its lack of necessary connection (*vahnyapratibaddhatva*) is called a subverting factor because it contradicts the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Even so, the phrase "one might imagine" (*utprekṣeta*) is contradictory, for the meaning of *utprekṣā* is conceptual construction (*vikalpana*), and it is not the case that the conceptualization of doubt itself—which is already of the nature of conceptual construction—is what is under discussion.

[173,4] But production is indeed logical. Even then, the qualification "unborn" (ajāta) is purposeless, because it is incoherent to speak of the production of that which has already been born. Alternatively, [173,5] if one were to suspect that even something unborn, non-existent, and unreal might be a cognizable object (*prameya*)—such as the dependence on fire and so forth—and might imagine it to subvert its own opposite, [173,6] meaning that one would merely bring it forward by means of one's own conceptualization; even then, if one were to establish that unreality through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and proceed in this manner...

One might say: everything would be acceptable; yet there is no means of proof for this reckless person other than verbal abuse (*ākrośa*). And if one becomes a fit object for such abuse merely by postulating something beyond what is commonly established, then why would reality not belong even to one who, in a debate concerning pervasion based on mere observation and non-observation, attempts to postulate an intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) and so forth in order to dispel the suspicion of the reason's occurrence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)?

Furthermore, for one who asserts that this very relation is perceptible by the senses—which contradicts its being graspable by the mind—or who asserts [objections] against an omniscient being such as "being an object of knowledge" (*jñeyatva*) and so forth; or for one who asserts meanings such as "a vessel" (*pātrī*) which contradict the well-established meanings of words like *urva* and so on; or rather, for this very person who has devised such an invincible weapon of abuse, consisting in the further infliction of wounds upon the gathering of Buddhist doubts.
First, it is appropriate that there be an arrival at cessation (*kṣayagamana*).

If you say that this is desired [only] for that which gives rise to doubt, then surely [the proponent] has failed, because he has given rise to a doubt that had not previously arisen. Consequently, why would he not also be at fault for giving rise to a certainty—which is brought about by either a proof or a refutation—that had likewise not previously arisen? [This applies to] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If you argue that certainty is difficult to overcome because of its strength, then in the absence of that [strength], doubt would likewise be difficult to overcome; enough with this overly prolix discussion. Therefore, how could a non-insane person, through a consideration of what precedes and follows, propose a doubt regarding something other than the object of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) out of delusion? For if certainty, which is bound to a valid cognition, were to occur even in the absence of that [cognition], for what purpose would one exert effort?

The investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) belongs to the discerning person; or rather, the effort of the authors of treatises is for the sake of refuting misconceptions regarding them. Therefore, since doubt necessarily arises when the means of valid cognition are absent, how can it be refuted by mere denial? Even if this is so, nevertheless, because there is no other alternative and because one generally observes concomitance in worldly practice, and because one does not observe [the contrary] even once—
[Regarding] deviation: having rendered what is delineated by conceptual construction—as an unfulfilled doubt—into something as if non-existent, one must proceed with certainty alone, not with doubt.
To this it is replied: Does the causal relationship truly exist as established by valid cognition, or not? If it does exist, it is necessarily...

[173,25] Or else, the object is otherwise. If one takes the position that it is not so, then everything collapses without effort, because there would be no scope for either proof or refutation; this has been analyzed at length in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅga*. Furthermore, even if it were existent, if its object were indeterminate, then it would be as if non-existent; this has been explained extensively in the treatise. Moreover, it cannot be said with certainty that those who seek heaven and the like must follow the Vedas, God, and so forth; for otherwise, it would follow that even the killing of a Brahmin could result in attaining that [heaven].
Therefore, since that [connection] exists, has a restricted object, and is established by the aforementioned means of perception and non-perception, it must necessarily be admitted.

Once this is established, the lack of any other alternative for certainty is proven; for without it, there would be no basis for establishing an essential connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*). As for the statement beginning with "though they are sought with effort," even there, one must search for deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Thus we understand the search for a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it is impossible to establish a limiting condition without deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, as long as smoke is observed, the process of investigation remains incomplete due to the suspicion of deviation; this has already been stated. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of the phrase "being sought with effort"? It refers to non-deviation occurring on several occasions.
For if [the object] is made an object of perception, what kind of cessation could there be in another [state]?

Furthermore, whatever has been prattled about here and there—that too is devoid of essence. For when a form is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is reliance upon its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

However, the determination of the nature of a thing does not occur solely through the force of the doctrine of intrinsic nature. Thus, if [there were] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding a restricted object—

If the causal relationship (*hetuphalabhāva*) is established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the non-perception of the perceiver (*grāhaka-pratyakṣānupalambha*), then what has come of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) regarding an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*)?
