In that case, having cast the totality of conditions for the cognition of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) far from one's heart, when a cognition arises from something else due to the lack of distinction between two co-existent things, the very means of such cognition becomes most remote. And if there is dependence on that totality of conditions, then it is simply "arising from that."

What is the point of this boastful assertion involving the changing of names? In this regard, the process up to the final apprehension by means of the sense organ aided by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation has already been refuted by the previous critique.
Furthermore, as for this [claim] that doubt depends upon the perception of specific characteristics (*viśeṣadarśana*):

"From the perception of commonality, from the non-perception of specific features, and from the recollection of specific features, doubt arises" (VSū 2.2.19). By not accepting this definition of doubt, he raises an objection. In that regard, is it because of fear of violating the definition that one must maintain that a cognition with two aspects cannot occur regarding an object that is not within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Or rather, is it intended that even if there is a dual aspect, this is not doubt?

[174,19] Now, whether there be doubt from the perspective of ultimate reality (tattvataḥ) or not, we nevertheless employ the convention "doubt" because our own defining characteristics have not ceased; such are the positions. First, the initial position is impossible. For when a form is delineated by conceptual construction (vikalpa), and in the absence of either a definitive proof or refutation—such as the news of a beloved’s arrival tomorrow—the conceptual construction that delineates both aspects, namely "Is this true or not? [is what constitutes doubt].

Because even by a king’s command one is unable to prevent [the arising of] birth; for bodily and verbal activities can indeed be forcibly altered otherwise—even when the mind is of a different nature—due to fear and the like. But the manifestation of the mind (*cittavivarta*), which arrives through the gateways of valid and invalid cognition, cannot be so altered. However, this may be the case: because a single portion is perceived more frequently, that limb seems to throb as if fully developed; whereas another [portion], due to absolute incapacity, does not.

[174,25] The portion is as if exhausted. However, in the absence of such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), both [alternatives] are common. Just as in that house, the state of having two aspects—namely, "Is there a crow or is there not?"—does not disappear anywhere. That very thing is the object of doubt;

thus, the second [position] is also untenable. Otherwise, being distinguished from error and correct cognition by way of the forms of non-ascertainment and ascertainment, [the object of doubt would be something else].

If there is no doubt, then why is this a fourth category? Therefore, let this fault belong to the definition itself for failing to grasp it; the object of definition (*lakṣya*) cannot be altered. For this very reason, even the final [category] is not useful. If a cognition that relies on both parts is established as depending upon a one-sided operation, then since the natural relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is not established by that much alone, what is the point of your honor’s [effort]?

[175,4] This is said with regard to the conventional usage of doubt; enough of this talk like that of a child. [175,5] As for the refutation of mental [cognition], let it be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); what is the use of further exertion here? [175,6] Regarding the capacity to indicate [the probandum] through an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), it is indeed *siddhasādhana*. It has been established that this [connection] is characterized solely by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*). And thus:

Because the capacity of repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is undermined, other means of knowledge (*māna*) that rely upon it must be understood as futile for establishing a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) based on the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object of perception. Rather, the inferential means of knowledge (*anumāna*) that sublates the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*) alone is to be inferred;

for in its absence, it is impossible to negate the presence [of the reason] in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), just as in the case of "being the son of that man" [as a reason] for "darkness. Furthermore, regarding what was said here concerning food—

[175,10] The reply—that there is an absence of an essential connection (svābhāvikasambandha) because of the existence of the condition (upādhi) consisting in the specific transformation of drink—is not tenable.

[175,11] This is because there is no certainty that the specific transformation of food constitutes such a condition. For just as smoke does not arise from mere fire without fuel, and thus fuel is said to be the condition for the connection between fire and smoke; so too, if for someone produced by Maitra...

[175,13] If it were determined that he would be dark-skinned due to the absence of the intended dietary transformation, then that limiting condition (*upādhi*) would be established; in that case, what is the use of asserting a limiting condition?

For it would suffice merely to say that "being Maitra’s son" is not a probans because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). But this cannot be so. Therefore, how is this limiting condition certain? Could it be that, due to a vow made by Maitra himself in another life, even seven or eight... [175,14–15]

[175,16] "The sons being seen with dark bodies were not born [that way]; what is the proof here? In that case, one might likewise suspect the mother's or even the sons' own resolve (*praṇidhāna*). And if their merit and resolve are not established, the capacity of a difference in diet is also possible. In that regard, what is the cause for their darkness? Thus, mere suspicion is an inference based on the suspicion of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). [175,18] It is not [valid].
[175,19] He explains: What is the point of this certainty? Now, the matter has been concluded by this final proof of dark complexion:

that which is excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), restricted to the subject (*pakṣa*) and its similar class (*sapakṣa*), whose object is uncontradicted, and which is not a counter-reason—how have you not been afraid, raising the demon of doubt by squeezing your belly to render the reason "being his son" a non-reason? Therefore, regarding the dark complexion resulting from being his son...

[175,22] Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and since non-existence is untenable based on mere non-observation in the case of non-darkness, it is simply correct to say that [the reason] lacks a cause (*ahetutva*). What is the use of this internal talk regarding "limiting conditions" (*upādhi*)?

[175,24] Furthermore, one must accept that the defect of a reason consisting in its doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*) is indeed a real [defect]. It is not...

Otherwise, it would be impossible to remove the status of being a cause for this [diamond], which is beautiful in all its parts. Furthermore, if you do not accept this, then when you seek to prove that a diamond is scratchable by iron by means of the reason "being composed of earth" (*pārthivatva*), what limiting condition (*upādhi*) are you observing that leads you to reject the inference? Now, if you argue that penetration by the tip of an arrow is observed in wood and other materials with loose constituent parts, whereas a diamond is firm; therefore...

If it is argued that this is due to an auxiliary condition (*upādhi*), it is not so. Indeed, we do not perceive any difference between a hundred-edged diamond (*sphaṭika*) and iron on account of their having dense constituent parts (*ghanāvayavatva*), such that what is unimpeded by the sun-gem (*taraṇimaṇi*) would be impeded by iron.
It might be said: "It is observed, at least, that iron is impeded when acted upon by a diamond (*vajra*). But for whom...?

[176,2] A proof that functions either by subverting the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) or by establishing it has not been undertaken against him. However, for one who merely takes the "hundred peaks" as the subject (*pakṣa*), how could he avoid the inference? This has already been largely explained: even if there is an ascertainment of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) due to ignorance of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), [the inference remains unavoidable]. Now, even if no other limiting condition is ascertained in the case of being a product (*pārthivatva*), its own inherent...

If it is argued that there will be some specific quality (*viśeṣa*) or limiting condition (*upādhi*) by virtue of which there is no "scratchability by iron," then, finding its opportunity here, the demoness of doubt (*śaṅkāpiśācī*) will pursue even smoke. There will be some inherent specific quality of smoke itself by which it could exist without fire. Surely, we do not perceive such a thing in smoke, even when searching with great effort.
[176,8] An adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) is characterized by its own specific nature. In the case of a diamond, however, we understand it to be earthen because of its capacity to cut metal.

[176,9] Now, is that capacity to cut metal [known] when an inference has already proceeded for a specific purpose, or is it by chance? Or rather, [176,10] is it through a desire to know (*jijñāsā*)? In the first case, since a great accomplishment of purpose results from inference, another such inference would likewise be required.
[176,11] For you, however, there is no such exertion as that required for the determination of a painting by mere chance. Or, let it be granted that there is no inference of that [specific instance];

how then could there be [inference] of another? Furthermore, the desire to know [the universal concomitance] is entirely without scope; for, among earthen objects—such as clay, wood, stone, and sharp tools—even when one has seen millions of instances where the tip [of a tool] sinks into millions of [other] tips, no deviation is observed, and thus [the relation] is inherent (*svābhāvika*).

[176,14] For one whose doubt regarding deviation has been eliminated by inference—which delineates the certainty of the connection—where is there any room for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) that precedes it?

[176,15] Otherwise, even upon perceiving smoke wafting from a mountain slope from the top of a palace, one who possesses the cognition of an intrinsic connection through repeated observation would have only the desire to know in that case as well, rather than inference. Therefore, in every respect, inference—

This is indeed a mere evasion. For when a correspondence has occurred on a few occasions, an inference from smoke follows at another time due to the ascertainment of an intrinsic connection; it does not require correspondence throughout one's entire life, as would be the case with "earthiness" and the like. Thus says the one of praiseworthy intelligence.
Now, even regarding earthiness, since a gradation of hardness is observed, the possibility of the cessation of "scratchability" in some instances may also be conceived.

Thus, even with further corroboration, there is no inference of "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) and so forth. If it is argued that in the case of smoke, however, no gradation of independence from fire is observed—well, "independence from fire" must indeed be stated as the "cessation of fire. And it is not the case that wherever an absolute cessation is about to occur, there must necessarily be a prior observation of a gradation of cessation, as in the case of a fettered man; for at the end, in just a few moments, [the fire ceases].

[176,23] This will also apply to smoke. It is not merely a conjunction of smoke and fire as two independently established entities, like a man and his fetters. Rather, since smoke is born from fire alone, there is no suspicion of a break in the sequence even at the end. However, if one does not touch upon such specific characteristics, there is indeed suspicion. Therefore, the nature of smoke—which would exclude fire—or the quality of being scratchable by iron in earthy substances, is not observed directly.

Furthermore, since the perception of perversion is common to both, there is no establishment of an essential connection fixed to one side alone; nor is there a determination of adventitious conditions regarding the probandum. Thus, the inference is either equally valid or equally non-inferential.
However, when in the case of smoke it is precisely its origination from that [fire] which establishes the pervasion, then—due to the absence of any distinction—it does not apply to earthy substances.

Nor is there identity [between the two], because it is unestablished that "being scratchable by iron" is its very nature (*tādātmya*), since it is impossible to demonstrate an inference that sublates the opposite [of this claim]. This is just like the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).

Furthermore, perception functions only with respect to specific classes (*jāti*); therefore, "being scratchable by iron" applies only to those instances within the class of earth-substances where it has been observed.

The establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not occur elsewhere. In that case, smoke, being a product (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth, are valid reasons (*hetu*). However, such things as "being made of earth" or "being his son" are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) because their exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. The same applies to "originating from that same branch" and so forth; for, depending on factors such as contact with wind and sunlight intensified by the first sprouting, there is the possibility of doubt regarding the absence of ripening even in something originating from a single branch. Thus, in this way, the pervasion of a certain thing by another object—

If repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) in the presence of the subject (*prakrama*) were the means [of establishing concomitance], then exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) would not be established merely by non-observation;

for such cases are seen to involve deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and thus, because its exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful, smoke and the like do not establish the probandum with certainty. As for the doctrine of "intrinsic nature" (*svābhāvika*) and so forth, it is to be avoided like anointing one's heart with impurity—merely out of a superficial passion for the *ṭiṇṭika* [tree].
It has been established that this is because no additional meaning beyond the mere fact of appropriating another's property is being conveyed.

Therefore, when there is a difference [between cause and effect], the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is simply the cognition of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*). And that [cognition] occurs through perception and non-perception alone.
[Objection: Let it be that the cognition of pervasion is simply the cognition of origination from that when there is a difference; however, it does not occur through perception and non-perception.

Because perception is restricted to the apprehension of the present moment, and because non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) has that same nature; and as for what was stated regarding the sense-cognition’s possession of all homogeneous particulars in dependence upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), even there, what is called "determination" is nothing but the immediately preceding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the claim that perception becomes omniscient by virtue of that [determination] is merely a hollow pretense. It would be better [to say] that smoke [is the mark] of fire.

Thus, let it be accepted that conceptual construction alone—having as its objective support the two types of universals characterized by all individual instances of both [classes]—is the grasper of their existence; or else, let it be considered another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or another form of perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that this is so because it apprehends what was not previously apprehended, and because it exists at the time of the operation of perception, that too is without substance. For even in conceptual construction, the state of having all things as its object is merely a matter of determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), since there is no manifestation of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because it appears as the very form of the object itself, merely by following the shadow of its exclusion from others (*ekavyāvṛtta*), what distinction does this [conceptual cognition] have over direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? It is simply that, with regard to the subsequent continuum beginning with the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) corresponding to itself, the determination of the object is established within the conceptual cognition; whereas in direct perception, even that conceptualization is included—this is the difference. All things...
But contact does not occur even in a single instance; nor is there any other mode of apprehension, as has already been discussed.

Therefore, within the realm of conventional discourse, it is established that the determination of an object—even by means of conceptual ascertainment—is unavoidable, and since this is common to both direct experience and conceptualization, when the relationship between cause and effect is made the object of perception, mental discourse—

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and memory are not valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even through the door of a single part, perception (*adhyakṣa*) establishes the apprehension of all members of a given class by virtue of its contact with the whole; this is not the case for conceptual construction, which by its very nature does not grasp external objects.

Therefore, it is established that the proof of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which is the essential nature of the relation between cause and effect—is possible only through perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
The treatise titled *Vyāpticarcā* is completed.
This work is the composition of the great paṇḍita Jñānaśrīmitra.
[179.2–182.8] || Examination of Difference and Non-difference ||
[179,3] (1b) Homage to the Buddha.
[179,4] With the desire to avoid falling into either of the two individual positions, the position of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), which is resorted to by some, is examined.

[179,5] In that regard, does this have the nature of a conjunction of both, or is it of the form of the absence of those two? If it is an absence, is it a mere negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or is it another entity through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? Is that too a third form opposed to the subject at hand, or—
[179,7] Is it something entirely unrelated?

[179,8] Regarding that, in the first alternative, if those very same differences and non-differences—which are swallowed by the net of various faults—are asserted to reside in a single entity, or are they indeed different from it? If they are identical, then because those faults necessarily persist, the admission [of such a position] is futile.

Even if there were difference, just as that defect [of non-perception] would apply, the quality [of being perceived] would likewise not follow. One might think, "I shall avoid the defect—the consequence of separate cognition—which arises from the position of difference, by accepting non-difference. Thus, you accept non-difference even where there is difference. And if that very same non-difference, which subverts the perception of separateness, is now brought forward, then indeed there would be such an avoidance; however, it is merely a case of sharing the same fate (*ekayogakṣema*).

[179,13] Due to their identity (*samāveśa*), it would also entail the non-occurrence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Therefore, if one were not to entail this by way of its being something else, then for that very reason, one could not even establish the negation of separate perception. Now, if the result of identity is merely the sublation of separate perception and not the inherent nature of the non-occurrence of other words, even so, the admission of duality is fruitless. This should be stated likewise regarding the position of difference (*bheda*) as well.

Now, if it is argued that the sublation of separate apprehension (*pṛthagupalabdhibādha*) alone is the result of non-difference (*abheda*), whereas the occurrence or non-occurrence of other words is the result of difference (*bheda*) itself— for even that [difference], being possible, must necessarily produce its own effect— then likewise, for difference as well, the dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntarāpekṣā*) alone is the result, while the sublation of separate apprehension is the result of non-difference.

It is said: Both are observed to be the effect of both. Furthermore, in the case of difference (*bheda*), there is the fault of the undesirable consequence that it would have to appear separately, whereas its dependence on other words is an advantage. In the case of non-difference (*abheda*) as well, there is the fault of the undesirable consequence that it would depend on other words, whereas its non-separate manifestation is an advantage. Therefore, in this matter, one who maintains that difference merely functions through other words must stand firm. But regarding the second effect—

One must consider the counter-strike of the opponent. Even when producing a manifestation together with that which is non-different, what constitutes the distinction between the counter-strike in one effect and [the other]? It is due to the fact that entities conform to your own intention;

or because of the occurrence of attachment and aversion toward qualities and defects within the things themselves; or because of the occurrence of a difference in time between the two natures and their effects.

In that case as well, is the sequence of qualities and defects fixed or unfixed? Regarding the first alternative, either the position of difference or non-difference, by imparting its own mere quality, will remain untouched by refutation; nor will refutation be brought against it. So why has this adherence to dualism been undertaken by one ignorant of the means of valid cognition for oneself? Furthermore, because entities are devoid of consciousness, there is no intention—
[180,3] Conformity.

[180,4] For this very reason, the second alternative is also not tenable. Granted that there may be affection and so forth toward what is dissimilar, that [affection] would apply to that which benefits or harms oneself; however, nothing has been harmed or benefited by these [words] through their status as signifier and signified, nor by a difference in appearance.

[180,5] By the other [reasoning]. However, the employment of the terms "quality" (*guṇa*) and "defect" (*doṣa*) is made out of deference to you. Therefore, even if that which is devoid of conformity to those [qualities and defects] were to exist in such a state, it would not matter at all. Or, if there is no conformity, consciousness has already been explained [as being impossible].
[180,7] It might be argued: "Like the operation of the collection of instruments that are the causes for the arising of sound, conformity to intention occurs by its very nature."
Nevertheless, the acceptance of duality is nothing but non-apprehension. It has already been stated that why not simply assume such an operation for a single intrinsic nature?
Nor is the proposal of a third alternative tenable; for if there were a difference in time between two intrinsic natures, then at the time when there is no difference...

[180,11] Then there is non-difference; and at the time of non-difference, there is no difference. Thus, there is never an avoidance of the opponent's fault. In that regard, just as in the case of an object—whether distinct or non-distinct—the effects such as synonymy, which arise from absolute difference or non-difference, are not obstructed, [180,13] so too they do not obtain when there is a difference in time between two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), because of the absence of their respective opposites. Nor [is it established] by means of what is yet to be.

[180,14] Negation is not a real entity (*avastu*). Therefore, there is a temporal distinction between that [negation] and the time of its effect; this must be accepted as a refuge. In that regard, as soon as a distinction, having established itself through the operation of another word, begins to bring about a difference in appearance, it is at that very moment obstructed by being subsumed under non-difference. Who, then, being so ignorant of logic, would venture to propose such a matter—which you yourself have grasped with your own hand—as a ground for mere recklessness? You, sir!
[180,17] Without an interval? For there is indeed a difference in time between two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

And for what entity would that [difference] be difficult to find? Indeed, it is not logical for that which arises later to belong to that very same [entity], because even in that case, each [moment] possesses its own temporal distinction, as it is devoid of any consideration of a [permanent] cause. It is not...

For this would be logical only if [the sequence] were bound to a single intrinsic nature; even then, there would be a fixed order for performing desired effects and avoiding defects. Otherwise, however, there would be the consequence of falling into a precipice. Thus, it is clear that one whose heart is captivated by mere whim does not exercise any discernment and deserves to be disregarded. Indeed, we perceive no cause here other than his own desire. Furthermore, when—

If the admission of difference occurs only after [the admission of] non-difference, then who can prevent the second effect of non-difference, which subverts separate perception? If you say "by difference," no; for if it is by another [instance of difference] arising at a later time, then yet another must be sought to remove the causal factor of that [defect], resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it is by the prior [difference], then if it possesses such power...

[180,25] Later on, when it is presented without distinction, how could it not produce a non-distinct appearance? Therefore, if the latter is considered sublated in relation to the former, one must consider why it is not so in relation to what precedes that. Consequently, since each possesses both functions, the claim that either difference or non-difference is restricted to one alone—either as its exclusion or its acceptance—is groundless. Thus, separately...
It would follow that for a single entity, there would simultaneously be appearance and non-appearance, arising and non-arising, and the occurrence and non-occurrence of other words and so forth.

Furthermore, there is not even a trace of experience of the adjunct as distinct from the substratum of the adjunct. Nor is it accepted by others that even a fraction of the individual remains when the individual perishes, in the case of a universal.

If it is argued that it is indeed intended [to exist] in the form of a manifestation (*vyakti*), surely "in the form of a manifestation" is intended to mean "not in its own form" (*nijena rūpeṇa*); otherwise, the qualification would be meaningless. Since this dilemma arises precisely when considering the difference or non-difference of its own form, what has been resolved by this? Furthermore, if no other form of its own is even possible, then to what [does the term refer]?

The investigation into difference and non-difference establishes that dharmas are devoid of limiting conditions (*nirupādhayaḥ*). Now, even if non-difference were possible for that which is different, we recognize the futility of other words; what can be done about this? If one were to say, "In that case, even though the limiting condition is different, the manifestation is not different—what can be done about this?", then there would be no fault even in the doctrine of absolute monism (*ekāntavāda*). Nevertheless, the recourse to the theory of duality is ultimately futile. In the end...
Because the "stretching out of the feet" (the avoidance of the objection) has not been accomplished; rather, only excessive fatigue or mere bravado is being displayed.

Furthermore, it might be argued that when opponents charge one who accepts identity with faults such as the non-exclusion of other words (*śabdāntarāvṛtti*), then the possibility of difference (*bheda*) serves as the rebuttal. And when there is difference, the introduction of non-difference (*abheda*) occurs upon the production of a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsabheda*).

Thus, it is not possible in a doctrine of absolute [identity]; nor is it a case of "stretching out one's legs" (i.e., a lazy evasion), nor does the consequence of both faults follow. For when difference was previously introduced, and once the fault attached to that has been uprooted, non-difference is then introduced.
If it is argued that there is no harm even if there is no finality due to this repeated succession of such turnings?
In that case, it follows that the subverting or proving property being presented by you does not function through its own inherent capacity.

Furthermore, if the application (*upanaya*) were not expressed within the verbal formulation itself, then even fire (*uṣarbudha*) would not be a subverter for you. By this, the argument "because it is not accepted by me" for the sake of a reductio (*prasaṅga*) is also refuted; for it cannot be said that poison being consumed for the sake of survival does not kill.
Therefore, for those of dull intellect who desire to avoid both extremes, this grasping at both sides is like a pair of wooden bolts.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever has a specific cause necessarily occurs when that cause is present, just as, for example, visual perception and so forth.

The arising of cognition has as its cause merely the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and the aforementioned collection of faults depends merely upon difference or non-difference; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Being caused by that alone is pervaded by independence from anything else. Furthermore, even if that [complex] is present, if there were the presence of something else, there would be dependence on another, which is contradictory to it.

Therefore, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), the property of being caused by that alone, which is excluded from the opposite case, resides in that [cognition].

When an entity exists, it is necessarily restricted; thus, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. Nor is there a lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because [the restriction] depends solely upon that [entity]. For no cause for simultaneous arising is logically possible other than mere non-difference (*abheda*). Or, if distinct manifestation were visible, no cause for it other than mere difference (*bheda*) would be possible.

Thus, even though there is a difference between a red-hot iron ball and fire, or between milk and water, the fact that their manifestation does not occur [simultaneously] establishes that the distinction in manifestation is dependent on something else.

If you ask why, it is not so, because non-erroneous sensory cognition (*abhrāntendriyajñāna*) is the subject under discussion. In that case, how can a cognition that presents two distinct entities as one be called non-erroneous? By this, the appearance of two moons is also explained. Now, suppose that single entity were produced by both causes.
When there is the cognition "it has arisen," then it is established that there is no deviation whatsoever, and thus its dependence on that alone is proven. It might be argued:

"Even for that which depends on that alone, there is a necessary occurrence by virtue of being that [cause], just as bile and phlegm necessarily arise from substances that are pungent and sweet respectively. That is incorrect, because substances can produce effects other than those [expected], even when considering their potency (*vīrya*) and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).
[182,7] Because bile and so forth arise from the transgression of disregarding the proper measure of tastes.
The Examination of Difference and Non-difference is completed.
[183–190] || The Secret of Non-apprehension ||
(2b6) In this [work],
a clear compilation is made of such non-perceptions as they appear scattered throughout the established doctrine, specifically those pertaining to the nature of form.

When negation is the probandum, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the third logical mark (*liṅga*). Now, if that [non-apprehension] were merely the absence of apprehension, how could there be the cognition of anything, or how could it be a cause for cognition? Furthermore, how could there even be a cognition of that [absence] itself? Therefore, like [the term] "non-eatable" and so forth, non-apprehension is simply the apprehension of something else by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

In that case as well, if [the negation] were of another thing in general, then upon the perception of any single thing, there would follow the negation of everything. If it is argued, "The negation of identity with everything is indeed intended," then the negation of its location is also unavoidable. This, then, is the distinction.
For when there is a cognition of a certain object, whether that [cognition] necessarily occurs or not,
our intended "non-apprehension" of that [object] is the basis for the establishment of the knowledge of its absence from other things.

When something is being perceived, the thought "it might exist" serves as the negation of those things remote in terms of space, time, or nature. By the word "necessarily," the absence of any deficiency in other conditions for perception is indicated. By this, it is shown that the establishment of the cognition of non-existence applies specifically to that which has attained the status of being perceptible; therefore, there is no consequence of negating everything.

And when something is being perceived, whatever cognition necessarily arises regarding it—that alone is accepted as the "cognition" [of that object], because it is capable of inducing a continuous determination of the non-existence of any second [entity]. By this, it is not merely a negation (*viraha*); rather, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it is stated to be a cognition of another specific thing. And here, the phrase "of that very one alone" follows from the force of the context; otherwise, since the perception of the other would be unprohibited, its non-existence would remain unestablished.

For example: "There is no jar here, because it is not perceived," or "something is somewhere. In this context, the phrase "of that which is perceptible" (*dṛśyasya*) should be understood as referring to a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) and the completeness of all other conditions for perception (*upalambhapratyayāntarasākalya*). The phrase "because of non-perception" (*anupalabdheḥ*) means "because of the perception of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogin*).

And that [locus], having attained the status of a substratum because it is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the negation, is either the ground (*bhūtala*) itself or something else in contact with a single sense-cognition—whether it be something other than that or whatever else it may be, since the general rule states: "When that which is perceived is being cognized, the object to be negated must necessarily be apprehended. In this regard, if the locus is a portion of the earth and the presence of a jar is what is to be proven, then that very ground is the counter-correlate; what need is there for anything else? But when the locus is the sky, even then it is that very thing designated as "light" (*āloka*), or else something else such as a jar whose position is indefinite. However, in the case of the negation of a tangible object, it is precisely this [ground].
By this, the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) that is associated with a single cognition has been explained; however, in some cases, it is otherwise as well.

Now, one might argue that a lamp is not swallowed here [by the mouth], because its taste is not perceived despite being visible; thus, in this case, touch alone is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). For when those two [taste and touch] exist, their cognition is restricted to a single form, as in the case of a beverage (*pānaka*). [Response: But then, how is it that the negation of taste does not occur even when there is the perception of form from a distance? [Answer: Because of the absence of the capacity for apprehension in that which is spatially remote, since the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile faculties function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*). And it has been said: "When X is being experienced, Y is necessarily experienced."

Nor is there a negation of form (*rūpa*) upon the experience of taste (*rasa*), because even then, the definition [of form] does not apply. Likewise, there is no negation of form by the perception of sound (*śabda*). For in darkness, the cognition of sound is not invariably concomitant with the cognition of form, even though form exists. In light, however, there is no negation of that which is actually being seen. As for the negation of a form that is not seen but is capable of being perceived, there is no fault, because its defining characteristics have not been abandoned.

By this it is shown that when a temple or similar structure is perceived, the non-existence of its local drum or other sounds is established without necessarily depending on the simultaneous perception of another sound; for there is no rule that those two must be perceived together. (3a6) This is not the case for a portion of ground and a jar either. However, the absence of a rule regarding the simultaneous perception of both things when they are present is the same for perception in that case as well. There is no distinction whether [the object] is part of a single cognition inseparable from the apprehension of the other, or a separate cognition apprehending the other is inseparable from it.
The same applies whether it is produced by a single sense-faculty or otherwise.

Even in a completely dark room, if there were an absence of light, one would have to follow the doctrine of the opponent by means of another cognition—one devoid of the form of that [light], and ultimately even a conceptual construction. But in reality, it is the darkness itself, as a real entity, that exists in conjunction with a single cognition of the lamp; so what need is there for anything else?

But surely, even though there is a specific nature [of the object], the proximity of other conditions constitutes its fitness for apprehension; and although that [fitness] serves as the cause for cognition by a different sense organ, it is not utilized in the ascertainment of the conditions for cognition by a different sense organ. Consequently, when a negation is made regarding the doubt about the proximity of other conditions for another [object], how could that negation—made ultimately even on the basis of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possessing a determinate form—be established for a perceptible object?

It is said in reply: Indeed, it is not only the cognition by means of the same sense-faculty that is dependent upon the establishment of the presence of other conditions; rather, there is also the perception of a particular state of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) characterized by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). This is so when no further illuminator is required beyond the specific nature of the sense-faculty itself, as is the case with sound, lamps, and the like.

For in those cases, how can anyone prevent the establishment of the absence of a certain object for one who has previously heard or seen it, who knows the application of the sense-faculties to that state, and who possesses a cognition devoid of the respective forms [of the object], regardless of its source?

What, then, is the utility of apprehending another cognition? For the non-existence of that [first cognition] is established simply by the non-arising of a cognition of its state. Or how could there be a negation of something else based on a sensory cognition whose object is different?
It has been stated in this regard that non-existence has no efficacy anywhere.

And so forth. Therefore, another cognition is not relied upon for the sake of ascertaining the excellence of the sense faculty; rather, it is for the purpose of generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the absence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). In this regard, just as a cognition associated with the same sense faculty is capable of ascertaining the non-existence of another, so too is any other [cognition]. There is no distinction whatsoever, since both exist when present and are devoid of the form of a cognition of some other object that is invariably concomitant (*avyabhicārin*).
If one asks, "How so? [the answer follows:]

In this case, desire and non-desire have no causal efficacy. Rather, for whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something else, there is an acceptance of a cause-and-effect relationship between those two. For example, because the cognition of a surface is restricted to a single form [of "bare ground"], its positive and negative concomitance are followed by the conceptual exclusion (*vikalpa*) of other things; likewise, when one thrusts a lamp into the mouth, because the cognition is restricted to the form of touch alone, that cognition [of taste] is followed by the cognition of the absence of taste. Indeed, there is no distinction between mediation and lack of mediation regarding the arising of these two.

Likewise, for one whose nose is applied to pure water and who neither touches nor sees it, even though they do not experience another odor, there arises through the cognition of the absence of odor a mental construction that is empty of that [odor's] form.
If it is argued that this is inferential (*laiṅgika*), [we reply: no.

No, because there is no intervention for one who is in a state of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). For when the very apprehension of X is itself the ascertainment of X, that is neither inferential nor established by perception, as in the case of "blue is not yellow. And in the case of water present before one, for someone whose conceptualization takes the form of merely attending to the nose, there is the ascertainment that "there is no smell. In that case, if the experience of a conceptualization with a restricted form were not the cause for establishing the mere absence of the cognition of smell, then let the experience of blue also not be the cause for the cognition of the absence of yellow.

Alternatively, for one who maintains that [non-apprehension] is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this [objection] is unavoidable even in other cases. And that very same perception is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) with respect to the object to be negated, as has already been stated.

Furthermore, with regard to a deluded cognizer, it is a logical mark (*liṅga*) that determines the absence of a property in a particular locus according to a prior convention. However, for one who is not deluded, since the doubt immediately following [the perception] is absent, this certainty is indeed stable; thus, it is said to be "initiated by perception."

Now, it might be objected that no linguistic usage regarding non-existence (*abhāva*) is produced by perception; nor has perception been said to be fruitful by way of ascertaining the absence of an object, but rather only by way of ascertaining the absence of cognition. However, since it includes the ascertainment of the absence of the object through that very [ascertainment of the absence of cognition], it is said to be "produced by perception."

And although that [cognition] arises from the power of that [object], it is subsequently overridden by doubt; thus, for one who is deluded, it is inferential. For an object does not have the same necessity of being of the nature of illumination as cognition does, since there is no contradiction in its existence even when unperceived. Non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the refuge [for the non-deluded]; but for the non-deluded, it is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because the existence of the perceptible is pervaded by being an object of perception. However, some say that the former person is deluded due to an inability to distinguish between these two.

That is incorrect. For just as cognition is non-luminous and non-abiding, so too is the external [object] invisible; thus, like that very [cognition], its absence—which cannot be precluded by perception—is established. It is merely by its very nature that cognition is visible, whereas the external [object] is visible only in some cases, in some ways, and at some times.

In that regard, for a cognizer possessing specific practice, just as with the generality of another cognition, the establishment of negation regarding a specific external object occurs instantly through perception alone; how can this, being repeatedly experienced, be denied?

If it is argued that inference is possible in reality (*tattvataḥ*), then even the ascertainment of the intended capacity (*yogyatā*) would not be produced by perception; thus, this [objection] is trivial. Furthermore, the aforementioned doubt does not occur solely with respect to external objects. For otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it could not be stated: "This [perception], being either a non-conceptualized vision or the vision of a conceptualized object, precludes the conceptual construction of what was not seen in the perception of the visible aspect within sensory cognition," and so forth. Therefore, even regarding a cognition, there may at times be a reflective inquiry (*vimarśa*) concerning another cognition.

Even regarding an object, certainty (*niścaya*) is a state in which no internal doubt remains unmanifested; thus, the capacity for perception—whether it be sensory or otherwise—is established through a division of states (*daśā*), but not through a division of universals (*jāti*).
Now, [it may be argued] that this follows from the experience of the apprehension of a single [object].

If it is argued that by such statements [as "there is no other cognition"], the capacity for the negation of another cognition is indeed expressed, and experience is likewise [of this nature], we say:

No. For just as "this is not perceived" is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too for one who possesses [mental] cultivation (*abhyāsa*), "this does not exist" occurs instantaneously. However, for one lacking such cultivation, there is first the ascertainment of the absence of cognition; through that, however, comes the ascertainment of the absence of the object. It is with reference to this [process] that it is stated thus in the treatise (*śāstra*). The same should be said regarding effort and so forth, which are associated with a single cognition. For this very reason, those of great intelligence determine all aspects from a mere glance.

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, effort must be exerted at various points regarding those of dull intellect. Therefore, for one of sharp intelligence, just as in the case of distinguishing between a gem and silver, even the conventional usage of its negation is difficult to prevent based on perception alone. Moreover, non-existence is not something corporeal that must be directly perceived through a form distinct from other things; rather, it is something to be conventionally designated. And because it is restricted to a single mode of appearance, it is indeed possible for a sharp-witted person to designate it through direct perception.

Furthermore, one who is not proficient [in perception] and thus doubts even when a determination of absence has occurred at first glance, proceeds with that conventional usage by following the mere non-perception of the perceptible. But one who is even less proficient than that, doubting despite the non-perception of the perceptible, proceeds by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). However, there is no proceeding by this for one who is not deluded; for it is precisely when there is lack of proficiency in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that inference is sought. And that proficiency is established through the generation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Moreover, superior proficiency in that regard arises from the absence of further deliberation (*vimarśa*).

However, it has been shown that perception has no function in negating the Cārvāka, who indeed accepts non-existence as something distinct [from existence], because of the statement regarding the dependence on the capacity of the object (*arthasāmarthya*) and so forth. Furthermore, unlike inference, the determination of apprehension for perception does not depend on ascertainment (*niścaya*), but rather on appearance (*pratibhāsa*). And its very possession of a determinate form (*niyatākāratā*) is the manifestation of the absence of anything other than that [object].

Therefore, it is difficult to avoid the possibility that perception possesses the capacity for the conventional usage of non-existence. As for the statement that "negation occurs everywhere due to non-perception," this is not a rejection of perception itself, but rather refers to another type of logical mark (*liṅga*). Just as it is said that there are only two means of establishing a positive entity, so too this negation of odor in water is produced by perception alone because there is no obstruction; it is not inferential.

Furthermore, what here is the mark (*liṅga*) that is non-deviant from the absence of odor? If it is argued that it is the non-perception of the effect, which is cognition, this would be appropriate when the cognition apprehending [the object] itself serves as the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). But when that [odor] is indeed perceptible, then the cessation of that which is capable of being perceived must be observed; otherwise, if it were not a case of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), then even a jar would not exist [as a non-existent]. Thus, this is merely the fruit of deceiving oneself regarding the nature of the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

If this proponent says this without having ascertained the excellence of the sense faculties, it follows that even a present odor and so forth would not be perceived. On the other hand, if he has ascertained it, one should see that the non-perception of the effect is sufficient; for while he diligently applies the non-perception of the effect to causes and so forth that are suspected to be imperceptible, he now hesitates even when [the cause] is suspected to be perceptible out of fear of even a trace of error—this is incoherent.

Therefore, this is established: when one thing is being perceived, that which is necessarily perceived—whether it be something else grasped by the same sense faculty or something else not grasped by a sense faculty—the cognition of that [latter] is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). And this [non-apprehension] establishes only conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), because otherwise there would be establishment by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For that reason, it was stated that [non-apprehension] is the basis for the stability of the knowledge of absence; however, it is not the basis for the certainty of absence.

Just as for two things that are necessarily perceived together, one cognition serves to exclude the other, so too it is for those that are necessarily not perceived together; thus he says: "Or not. For where there is an object of cognition, the notion of the other would necessarily not occur; this is the meaning. As in the case: "This is blue; it is not non-blue. Here too, what is to be established is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). By this, contradiction characterized by the state of mutual exclusion has been explained.

[Objection: But surely this has already been covered by the statement: "When X is being perceived, it is possible that the cognition of Y must necessarily arise. For even an invisible thing, when being negated through identity, is negated only after having been conceived as visible; otherwise, one would be admitting a distinction between the visible and the invisible by oneself. So what is the point of this separate statement? [Reply: In that case, this absence characterized as destruction (*pradhvaṃsa-lakṣaṇa*) is explained as follows: "Or rather, it would not exist" (4b4).

The meaning is that even though the cognition has arisen, it necessarily ceases when the object of knowledge is present. And this necessity is logically appropriate only as the non-existence [of the cognition] when the existence [of the object] is sublated, as in the case: "There is no cold here because of fire. By this, the opposition characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is explained. If it is argued: "But since there is necessarily no perception in darkness, one does not necessarily have to assume an opposition," we reply: This definition does not depend on a single perceiver, but rather applies generally.

Furthermore, there is indeed the perception of form even in the absence of light by certain individuals; or else, it may be possible [to perceive it] through special ointments and the like. However, regarding the destruction of existence (*sattoccheda*), there is an absolute rule, and thus there is no fault. [Objection: But even in this case, if cold were present, there would be no cognition restricted to the single nature of fire. How, then, is this different from the previous case? [Reply: It is not so, because the negation is intended only with respect to what is accessible through touch. In that case, although the cognition of cold has arisen, it is impossible to ascertain that it has ceased upon the perception of fire, because such ascertainment occurs at another time.

[188] Because it is intended to be so stated. In that case, since its operation is mediated by the recollection of a contradiction previously apprehended, there would be no ascertainment of non-existence from the activity of perception. Let it be; even with such mediation, it is precisely the cognition of the contradictory that is the factor for the ascertainment of non-existence, and not merely any other [cognition]. Thus, there is no damage to the basis for the establishment of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

And it is not accepted here even in this case that [the proof] establishes mere conventional usage; thus he says: "But because there is dependence on another in the case of memory, here non-existence (*abhāva*) is also to be proven. And when that is established, conventional usage—characterized by the stability of the ascertainment of that [non-existence]—is also [established], but not merely that alone. This is the meaning.

Likewise, in the case of the denial of a cause (*hetu*) or a pervader (*vyāpaka*), it follows that "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is also the probandum (*sādhya*). For example: "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire"; "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees. For in these cases, the mere perception of the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*)—namely, fire and the tree—does not produce the ascertainment of the non-existence of smoke and the *śiṃśapā* independently of the recollection of the previously established cognitions of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). Therefore, in these instances as well, the conventional application of the proof of non-existence is established.

(5a1) These are now the reasons for negation: non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Likewise, there are two [reasons] that establish affirmation; thus, five reasons would follow. No, because they are one, being based on the commonality of non-perception (*anupalabdhisāmānya*).

Moreover, non-apprehension is of two kinds: that of itself and that of another. Regarding the cause and the pervader, there is only the non-apprehension of their own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). For the other—namely, the effect or the pervaded—there is what is called the non-apprehension of the cause and the non-apprehension of the pervader. Just as the perception of one thing is indeed the non-apprehension of another, so too, the non-apprehension of the nature of something is called the non-apprehension of the cause or the pervader in relation to the effect or the pervaded; thus, there is no difference in the underlying reality (*vastubheda*) despite the difference in designation.
Therefore, since the negation of everything occurs solely through the non-perception of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), there are only three types of logical mark (*liṅga*).

By this, it should be understood that the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) is indicated by the very non-perception of the intrinsic nature of the efficient cause; or rather, because the word "cause" (*hetu*) is explained as having the meaning of "logical mark. For example: "The causes of smoke, whose capacities are unimpeded, do not exist here, because of the absence of smoke."

How, then, is the statement "there is no touch of frost here because of fire" included within the category of the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*)? Even in this case, there is indeed the non-perception of the nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) consisting in the perception of fire, which is contradictory to cold—the pervader; this is called the "perception of what is contradictory to the pervader" with respect to the touch of frost, which is the pervaded. Thus, there is no fault.

And although that [non-apprehension] could also be described as the non-apprehension of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), it is nonetheless designated as such in order to demonstrate its nature as the cognition of a contradictory counter-correlate (*viruddhapratiyogipratīti*). In this same way, the "apprehension of what is contradictory to the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth are to be explained. In all cases, it is non-existence itself that is to be proven, since it is not established by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*); rather, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is established by means of that [non-existence]. Now, one might ask: how can there be the conventional usage of "non-apprehension" in the case of the "apprehension of the contradictory" and so forth?

It has been stated in this regard that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is simply the apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and that counter-correlate is of two kinds. Among these, when the counter-correlate is contradictory (*viruddha*), the employment of the word "contradictory" establishes that the word "apprehension" itself must be employed. But when the remaining type of counter-correlate is understood, the use of either the word "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) or the word "visible" (*dṛśya*) designates it by the term "non-apprehension" in relation to the object to be negated. Thus, in one case "apprehensibility" is understood, while in the other "non-apprehensibility" is understood; however, since the reality (*tattva*) is one and the same, there is no fault.

And when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is contradictory [to the object] and the second [object] is indeed imperceptible (*parokṣa*), then even for that [imperceptible object], non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is not necessarily only perceptual; rather, it may also be inferential (*anumāna*). For a counter-positive is considered such because, by its own existence, it removes the existence of another. And who can prevent this from occurring even in the case of an imperceptible [counter-positive]? However, when the counter-positive is necessarily perceived together [with the object], the negation applies only to what is capable of being perceived; thus, in that case, there is necessarily a requirement for perception.

For if a jar were present in the location being inferred, it would certainly be perceived; yet, since perception is impossible [there], and because there is no rule governing the commencement of inference, how can there be a negation? If it is argued that, in this way, there is no negation because it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), then [we reply]: [The opponent continues: If it is argued that there is no negation because it is merely a conceptual construction...

Even in that case, it is not said that when the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) is being experienced, one would also experience an external object in the intended location provided the capacity of the sense faculty has not failed. However, it is not possible to say that when an external object is being conceptually constructed, a second [object] would also be experienced. For even when an external object is being conceptually constructed, why should another object in that same location not be perceived? Indeed, the cognition of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogijñāna*) is not the basis for the visibility of another thing;

rather, it is the cause for the arising of the ascertainment of non-existence, because it is an existent entity (*sattvavastu*). And since this is also the case for a conceptual construction, what is the difference?

Now, suppose it is argued that one must conform to the cognizer; that it is correct to conform even to that which is associated with a single cognition. This is not so, because we observe the mere conventional usage of non-existence for the odor in water, or the taste in fire, or even the color in wind, or when only a remnant is perceived. In those cases, since the non-perception of the effect of cognition applies equally elsewhere as well, what is the use of [insisting on] association with a single cognition?
If it is argued that through the non-perception of the effect, only a capable entity is negated— [End of fragment 5b2]

In that case, it is precisely the fruit of great effort in the study of the treatises that [one realizes] even though odors and so forth exist in water and the like, they are not perceived due to a defect in the sense organs; for such a person, even when no cause for the defect is perceived, remains in doubt by imagining that there might be an overpowering [of the odor] by other factors such as suitability. But why does one not remain in doubt regarding the non-perception of a jar on the ground, even when the sense organs are sharp, by imagining that its non-appearance is caused by that same [defect]? Therefore, during the stage of practice, worldly activity proceeds solely on the basis of the persistence of that very state [of doubt].

But for the Master of Logic (Nyāyanātha), there is neither a formal objection nor a dismissal based on following conventional usage; rather, it is out of boldness (*prauḍhi*) to demonstrate that even with such an interpretation, our own definition is not undermined—just as, for example, even though the determination of omniscience applies to every single mind, he alone is called "the Omniscient One."

Furthermore, in common practice, it is observed that when one perceives an object associated with a single cognition, the ascertainment of the absence of another object—the counter-correlate—is likewise seen; this [ascertainment] is common and non-contradictory. Thus, the apprehension of an object associated with a single cognition is not [the sole cause]. Moreover, in the state of relying upon conceptual construction, it is logical that the mere awareness of its own form (*tadākārasamvedana*) is the means for establishing the negation of the other, precisely through such habitual practice.

[190] Because the capacity of perception is observed, thus, even the apprehension of something contradictory that is beyond the senses—consisting of inference—establishes the absence of its opposite. For example, "there is no cold here because of smoke"; in this way, the apprehension of the effect of something contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-kāryopalabdhi*) is to be understood. For instance: "there is no frost here because of smoke. This is the explanation at the time of formal application (*prayoga*), having synthesized these points. In reality, however, there is a single formulation: "there is no cold because of fire. But for the sake of avoiding the charge of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of that [fire], [the following is said]:

And another [inference] is: "There is fire here because of smoke. Likewise: "But there is no frost from fire. For that which is contradictory to the pervader is indeed contradictory. And [the inference] "fire because of smoke" [is established]. The remainder should also be inferred in this way.

If the non-perception of the nature of the cause and so forth is the non-perception of another's cause and so forth in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), then how [does it apply] in the case of non-entities (*nirupākhya*)? For example: "The son of a barren woman is not a speaker because of the absence of consciousness."

In that case as well, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) consists in the cognition of the mental image itself as being devoid of sentience (*caitanya*). Furthermore, the cognition [of the subject] is distinguished by the exclusion of speakerhood (*vaktṛtva*); this is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*).
Since all non-perceptions ultimately resolve into the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), there is no fault in their separate presentation, as they are intended to establish a negation.

If it is asked: "Even so, since negation is directly the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) according to the sequence already stated, why did the venerable Teacher describe it as figurative (*aupacārika*) because it is expressed through a succession? [The answer follows:]...

If the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is intended by the negator as referring only to that which is to be negated, then it is figurative (*aupacārika*). But if it applies to others as well, then it is primary (*mukhya*); what contradiction is there? One might ask: "What is the purpose of speaking only of the figurative? In that case too, the negation is possible only for that which is perceptible, and not for others such as the omniscient, the dispassionate, or the *pradhāna-puruṣa*; thus, they are included therein by way of their effects. In reality, however, the non-perception of that [object] or of anything else as described is the means of proof.
The *Anupalabdhirahasya* is completed.
[191,1–199,7] || An Investigation into the Non-existence of All Words ||

In this context, some provide the non-perception of the effect of cognition (*jñānakāryānupalabdhi*) as the means of proof for establishing the absence of all sounds. For they claim that, due to the absence of association with a single cognition, there is here no occasion for the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

For indeed, three things must necessarily be expressed in this [definition]: the qualification by way of the exclusion of the cognition of jars and so forth, the essential nature (*svabhāva*), and the result. Among these, by virtue of the qualification regarding the object of perception, there is no negation of things such as *piśācas*. By virtue of having the nature of being perceived through association with a single cognition, there is no [negation] of taste from the cognition of visible form. Nor does the fault pertaining to the position of non-existence (*abhāva*) attach here; furthermore, the establishment through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is presented because its result is conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

And that [non-apprehension] is established when there is a basis for the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). That very [basis], by virtue of being inseparable from the non-existence of other counter-positives, possesses the capacity to generate the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of their absence; thus, it serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, it is logical that non-apprehension, which has that [basis] as its essence, is the means for establishing the conventional usage of absence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) for one who is deluded.

Furthermore, when the non-existence of all sounds is to be proven, no single sound is found to be associated with the cognition [of the locus]; thus, there is no scope for that [non-apprehension] here. However, since that mass of sounds existing in the intended location is at that time incapable of initiating the effect of cognition, existence itself is negated without distinction even through the negation of the effect; this is the sense.

On this point, it is considered as follows: It is not the case that sound alone is what is heard, for if it were, the consequence would follow that even a deaf person could hear. Therefore, it is only sound when assisted by the proficiency of the sense organ (*indriya-pāṭava*) that produces the cognition of hearing. And that auditory proficiency is difficult to ascertain in the absence of contact with a single cognition. For this very reason, the negation of a jar depends upon the perception of its location. Thus, calculating the excellence of the sense organ, one determines that the non-perception is due solely to the fault of the jar.

Nor is the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of the sense faculty established in the same way as that of mental attention (*manaskāra*), because the sense faculty is insentient (*jaḍa*). Nor can it be apprehended by another sense faculty, because it is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Its effect, moreover, is simply its perception (*upalabdhi*). And if that [perception] is not established, then the non-perception of the effect is itself unestablished. If it is unestablished, then the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason is proven; for even when an object exists, non-perception—which may occur due to a defect in the sense faculty—is certainly not restricted to the absence of that object. If you argue: "We do not say that the sound is non-existent; rather, we say that there is no [sound] capable of producing the cognition of it."

This is the practice of a quack physician: first, having accepted a desired remedy with bold confidence, one proposes an ineffective means under the guise of a strategic method; then, when the opponent demonstrates the truth of the matter, one subsequently proclaims that the case is incurable. For this non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) is said to be the proof only when the absolute non-existence of the object is what is sought to be known, and not when there is an inquiry into the absence of the capacity to produce cognition. Therefore, if the failure of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is somehow acknowledged, why on earth is the failure of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) not also admitted?

It would be better to seek another means of valid cognition altogether; why, then, is its very non-establishment being proclaimed? For it is not possible for one who does not hear to deny the absence of nearby sounds such as the beating of a drum, since that would lead to the absurd consequence of there being no distinction between the deaf and the non-deaf.

If it is argued that there is a distinction made by hearing—namely, that [the sound] exists before and after [hearing]—it is not so. For if this [sound] were indistinguishable from its prior state in terms of its capacity for being heard, how could there be no hearing when the sound is present? Otherwise, there would have been no hearing even before. If, on the other hand, it is possible that it is in a dissimilar state [even while present], then one should not place trust in hearing either, because such a distortion is possible. In that case, there is no difference between non-hearing and hearing what has not occurred.

If it is asked, "How could there be a reversal of capacity at the beginning?", [we reply that] the same applies to the question, "How could there be its absence in the middle? Therefore, this is simply not a valid position: that although the word exists, it is not heard at that time. When considering what the proof for this might be, it has already been stated that the non-perception of the effect is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the proficiency of hearing is difficult to ascertain.

[192,11] But how can this be difficult to ascertain for one who is engaged in listening and possesses the strength of keen sight, hearing, and memory? For even if there is momentariness, as long as there is an absence of other dissimilar auxiliary conditions, there is no possibility of the occurrence of a dissimilar state. Indeed, those conditions that cause a modification of the sense faculties—such as disturbances of the humors (*dhātu*) or physical blows—whose powers are well-established, are easily discerned as the causes of the agitation of the continuum within one's own stream of being.

But how can those [cognitions] which are unobserved tolerate the suspicion that they arise from a distinct source? For one who suspects that there is a subtle cause for the modification of the senses—such as their being presided over by a powerful being—even upon hearing this, what confidence can there be? Therefore, even when an error of the senses characterized by the confusion of directions is produced by an unobserved cause, the non-alteration of the state of the senses cannot be established simply because the well-known causes are unobserved; otherwise, it would follow that all cognitions other than those [sensory ones] would be erroneous. Why is this not taken into account even now, so that there may be no total collapse of all conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)?

However, the reliance upon the presence of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) and mental application (*sattva*) is common to both cases. For we do not say that there is a certainty of non-existence regarding the hearing of a deaf person, even though he has ascended to the power of hearing through medicinal treatment; this is because there is simply an absence of certainty regarding that power. The same applies to another who has not yet mastered his power.

Indeed, when those who have slept through the entire night and then awakened see no objects, they are observed to engage in unerring practical activity (*vyavahāra*) as those who experienced that state; under such circumstances, what occasion is there for a waking person to suspect that their own nature is otherwise?

Therefore, the negation of that which is not in its original state, or of the persistence of that state, occurs either due to the absence of the well-known causes [of perception] or due to the absence of the defining characteristics thereof.

If, with respect to the state of practice regarding seeing, hearing, and so forth, one who maintains that the basis for being perceptual is the persistence of that state relies—on the conventional level—either on the persistence of the sense faculty, or on the persistence of the cognition awakened by the causal complex, or on self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) with respect to common capacity, then since that very [persistence] exists even during the state of non-hearing, how can there be any inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) regarding the absence of sound?
If it is argued that self-awareness occurs only within the nature of cognition itself, we say no.
[193] When there are objects of a single resolve that are conducive to a single effect and exist as indivisible entities,
a single cognition is established as having all those objects as its domain.

Even regarding the five aggregates, there is a single resolve of "I. There is utility in a single object for speaking and so forth, as well as in mutual dependence. This principle is well-established in the case of form, taste, and so on, which are designated as "pots" and the like; otherwise, conventional usage would be impossible.

[193,5] Is it not the case that the perception of the body does not follow upon the cognition? This is indeed so with respect to their specific individual forms (*prātisvikarūpa*), just like color, taste, and so forth. However, by grasping them in a general sense (*sāmānyena*), they are said to be the object of a single cognition, provided there is no insistence on their analytical distinction (*vivecana*). But when there is such analysis, a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated. Therefore, the two propositions—that Caitra is perceived and yet the cognition is not directly perceived—are not contradictory.
For this very reason, even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "I am in such a state" follows from immediate experience and has everything as its object.

If it is argued that this is an error, we say no; for since there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), the status of being an error is unestablished. Therefore, because it is possible to determine that the auditory faculty remains in its previous state as it was previously perceived, the non-hearing of the sound is due solely to the fault of the sound itself. Thus, even through the absence of cognition, the non-existence of the object is established with certainty; hence, there is no contradiction of the subject matter. If this alone constitutes the causal complex for the definition of "non-perception of the essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), what is the purpose of applying the designation "non-perception of the effect" (*kāryānupalabdhi*)?

For it is only by means of the non-perception of a sound that has attained a specific nature and the completeness of other conditions that its negation is established. Nevertheless, even when a jar is negated under another designation, who is the negator? It is simply said that, like the jar, the negation of the sound is also to be proven through the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*). If it is argued that negation by that [non-perception] is appropriate because of the possibility of the sound's association with a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargin*), [we reply:]...

In that very context, first of all, what is the point of depending on [the object's] association with a single cognition?
