For in the perception of color, taste is not denied [as being present] precisely because it has reached the condition of non-apprehension due to its location in a remote place; this is because the nose, tongue, and body sense-faculties function by reaching their objects. Furthermore, since the stability of the sense-faculties is established by the aforementioned sequence, what is the use of depending on association with a single cognition? It is not so, because light, which is distinct from the sense-faculty, must be depended upon in that case.

For that [object], whose nature consists in arising and ceasing dependent upon external causes easily available, is not something to be established by its own persistence; therefore, the requirement for association with a single cognition will also serve as an auxiliary factor even in the cognition of the excellence of the sense organ.

Thus, it is established that where the capacity for apprehension is independent of illumination, there is no requirement for association with a single cognition. Furthermore, that [association] is required in some cases of proof only when, in its absence, one of the defects—contradiction, non-establishment, or doubt—would necessarily arise. And this [requirement] does not exist when something that has attained the fitness for two kinds of perception is negated by non-perception, such that a correlate would necessarily have to be expected. Even in those cases where it is expected:

In that case as well, it is precisely for the sake of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) when negating an object whose apprehension depends upon light; yet, this does not imply a dependence on it in all instances. For dependence regarding destruction is not the means of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) everywhere, even in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) used to prove momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). And if this [object] were necessarily dependent, what need would there be for the qualification "visible" (*dṛśya*), since visibility is never absent in anything associated with a single cognition? Indeed, a *piśāca* has no association with any single cognition whatsoever.

If it is argued that since the object is one and the same in both cases, there is no need to discuss the purpose of the other formulation when one has already been employed, we say: no, because the distinction [between them] remains unmanifest due to their relationship as general and particular. For a relation (*saṃsarga*) does not deviate from being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), whereas a mere qualifier certainly deviates from it. Therefore, a relation is introduced for the sake of establishing the qualifier, but a qualifier is not capable of drawing forth a relation—otherwise, this would apply even to words. And thus, since the position [of the opponent] is destroyed, what is the point of this exertion?

Therefore, what is called "conjunction within a single cognition" is proclaimed only with reference to the specific example under discussion; it is not to be required in all cases of the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

For when the negation of a jar is under discussion, let that same line of reasoning apply for the sake of establishing the qualification: "that which is capable of being perceived is not perceived"—this indeed is the definition of one's own non-perception (*svānupalabdhi*). Thus, both in the formulation of the definition and in its application, there is merely the presentation of the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions of perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). Furthermore, in the treatise, when demonstrating the sublation of the contrary, it is explained that non-perception is impossible in the presence of other causal conditions for an entity that possesses a specific nature.

Otherwise, one would have to show that in all cases the probans is merely a relation (*saṃsarga*), like a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). However, since identity (*tādātmya*) is negated only after having accepted perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*), there is merely a failure to state the qualifier; it is not a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*), as is the case for a pervasion (*vyāpti*) known by the learned. Or rather, this applies specifically to the statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or [by implication] to negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, even for the Lord of Nyāya (Dignāga), there is no necessary intention to rely on a relation with a single cognition in the case of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

Moreover, one might thus claim that all [non-perceptions] are subsumed under the non-perception of the effect alone, since the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is but a part of it; and one would establish the inclusion of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the inference from effect, with the exception of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).

Therefore, just as the establishment of an inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*) does not apply to the object of sensory perception, so too why should the author of the treatise establish an "inference through non-perception of the effect" (*kāryānupalabdhi*) for that which is not grasped? For just as there is a fear of the collapse of the system of perception in one case, so it is in the other regarding the non-perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). Or rather, just as the effect serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) when [the object] is imperceptible, so too is its non-perception [a mark] only when [the object] is unfit for perception; thus the two cases are equal.

Or, for example, this very Blessed One, through the non-perception of a perceptible object (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), establishes the absence of another cognition within a cognition in conventional discourse. As he said:
"When a conceptualization of a perceptible nature is seen, its non-perception precludes the imputation of conceptuality within sensory cognition."

In that case, what is the correlate within a single cognition? Furthermore, if this is accepted, then even the non-perception of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) would be unestablished; thus, there is indeed an abandonment of the original position. For the absence of the effect of cognition cannot be understood through the non-perception of that very effect, because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), being restricted to a single form, can only imply the certainty of the non-existence of anything else; thus, regarding that which is doubted, if there were another cognition, it would necessarily be experienced. Therefore, in practical discourse, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) alone is the recourse, just as in the case of external objects. However, there might be a failure to state the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), but there is no other way. And since even that [non-perception] does not exist when there is an expectation of association (*saṃsarga*), the reason (*hetu*) is "unproven due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
Consequently, it is impossible for non-perception to function without adhering to the rule of the expectation of association within a single cognition.

If it is argued that there is a restriction based on the external, we say no; for even in that case, there is no underlying basis. For if that capacity which exists internally can still be attained externally even when it is transgressed, why would the situation not be the same? Indeed, the nature of objects is manifold. In that regard, the self requires nothing more than mere fitness for the manifestation of direct perception.

But sound, odor, taste, touch, darkness, and light are indeed specific forms of matter (*rūpa*) residing in configurations such as jars, which generally require a sense faculty distinct from mental attention (*manaskāra*) for their apprehension; likewise, why should the non-apprehension of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the case of negation not likewise depend upon a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*), just as their apprehension does in the case of affirmation?

In that regard, just as in the first case there is no utility in depending on the state of the sense organ (*indriya-tādavasthya*), so too in the middle cases there is no utility in [depending on] that which is associated with a single cognition (*ekajñāna-saṃsargin*). While it might be appropriate for one who requires something additional to depend upon it, it is likewise possible [to argue] as follows: "If the cognition were present, it would certainly be perceived; why then depend on the state of the sense organ? This is the underlying capacity (*sāmarthya*). Similarly, it is indeed possible to say: "If taste and so forth were present, they would certainly be perceived by me through the sense organ in its current state; why then depend on that which is associated with a single cognition?"
Therefore, the possibility of a restriction even outside [the cognition] is extremely remote; or, if it were admitted, one would have to expect it in the cognition as well.

If it is argued that even in that case there exists a connection with a single cognition based on the expectation of a single perception consisting of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), [we reply: surely there is no such thing as a single perception called "self-awareness," because that [awareness] is distinct for each individual property (*dharma*). If you are satisfied with the designation "single cognition" by relying on a generality (*sāmānya*), then the same consequence would apply even to objects grasped by different sense organs, or even to the objects of self-awareness and sensory cognition. If it is argued that this rule applies only to those two things which, when present, do not deviate from one another's perception; [we reply: ...

This rule does not apply even to two forms (*rūpa*), since a *piśāca* is not perceived in a particular location. [If it is argued that] it certainly exists in specific cases, and that a fault in the general case does not infect the specific one—[we reply: even so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding sound and space, or sound and mental attention (*manaskāra*). For the perception of space or the perception of the experience of mental attention does not deviate from the perception of sound when sound exists. If, however, there were such deviation, then the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) would result in the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, the requirement of being apprehended by a single cognition is not all-pervasive, and it is easily available for other things as well; so enough with this dispute.

Furthermore, this connection of two minds within a single cognition is something entirely unprecedented, because a primary [connection] does not exist and a secondary one lacks inclusion within a single sense-base (*ekāyatana*). If you argue that "inclusion within a single sense-base" is merely an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), then why is "connection within a single cognition" not declared to be the indication? However, both of these were stated with reference to the example of the jar under discussion; thus, there should be no dogmatic attachment.

For just as the non-deviation of mutual perception is observed through their inclusion within a single sense-base (*āyatana*), so too it is logical that even through association with a single cognition, there is merely a dependence upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

And what is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of what? It is that pair for which perception, restricted to a single form, is capable of establishing the certainty of the absence of the other. And of which two is there such non-perception? It is of those two for which the perception of one is non-deviant from the non-perception of the other; for when both exist, a cognition restricted to a single form is impossible. Therefore, it is on the basis of specific time, place, state, and continuum that two things are established as being counter-correlatives of one another.

That [object] is visible because their non-connection (ayoga) is characterized by the attainment of consciousness. For this very reason, the cognition of those two as restricted to a single form is able to establish the conceptual exclusion (pratiṣedhavikalpa) of anything else; thus, the absence of such things is said to be established by direct perception (pratyakṣasiddha).

For that very same certainty regarding the deluded person, non-apprehension—which is essentially the apprehension of a counter-correlate—arising as the fitness for apprehension of a simultaneous pair, establishes both the verbal expression and its absence; since the establishment of the nature-reason (*svabhāva*) and the effect-reason (*phala*) is fully accomplished by this alone through the refutation of other views, what is the use of including the requirement of being perceivable by a single sense-organ?

For this counter-argument is common to objects grasped by a single or multiple sense-faculties, as well as to cognitions or to both cognition and object; and it is beyond reproach in establishing non-existence. Therefore, why should one follow that [opposing view]? Just as the perception of a single form regarding the ground and a jar—or regarding two cognitions—is sufficient to produce the ascertainment of their absence because it is not contradicted by any other perception, so too, for one who has perceived both in the act of drinking a beverage and who perceives them to remain in that same state, the perception of touch alone when swallowing a lamp-flame produces the ascertainment of the absence of taste.

Alternatively, the mere self-awareness of the form of one’s own conceptual construction is indeed capable of establishing the determination that there is an absence of a present tactile object. For that awareness of the conceptual construction does not fail to be a perception of the tactile object as it exists at that time. Nor is there any other capacity for producing the certainty of the absence of a second [object] elsewhere than from the non-deviation (invariable concomitance) of their respective perceptions. Furthermore, the so-called "perception of absence" is not a distinct entity from the capacity for producing the certainty of absence;
for absence is not something corporeal that must be directly perceived.

And when, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the counter-positive itself is the absence, then its establishment through perception is indeed primary; thus it is logical that in all cases the result is practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, this counter-positive does not exist for anyone with respect to things remote by nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, such that someone's perception could be capable of manifesting the absence of those things. Nor, in this way, is non-apprehension said to be a mere cessation [of cognition].

The Bhaṭṭa, however, even in the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), takes non-apprehension as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the apprehension of anything other [than the object], without depending on the aforementioned counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Thus, in his view, the rejection of things such as *piśācas* is logical. But for one who perceives color, taste is indeed spatially remote from that location; it does not bring about the aforementioned counter-correlate. However, that which is in contact with the tip of the tongue does not deviate from the non-existence [of the object] in the case of non-apprehension.

[197] Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. For this very reason, it is stated that the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) and so forth, which are incapable of functioning directly, are included within the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) by way of a mediated succession; for such a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) does not exist.

Therefore, the definition of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is simply the non-perception of that which has attained the capacity for perception. And since this [non-perception] exists as the conventional (*vyavahārika*) absence of that which is established by way of the perception of its counterpart as described, there is no contradiction with either the *Nyāya* or the *Śāstra*. It should be understood that the mention of "perceptible by a single sense-faculty" is intended only with reference to examples such as a jar; thus the matter is settled.

In that regard, when one perceives the absence of a drum or similar object in a place such as a temple—which is perceived as a region of space characterized by darkness or light—then either that very [space] as it becomes the object of a cognition colored by the form of that [absence], or the cognition itself, constitutes non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the perceptual occurrence that would necessarily have occurred had the object been present, or the exclusion of the cognition thereof. However, for one whose eyes are not engaged, the exclusion of the object of knowledge consists of taste and so forth, or the cognition thereof, or ultimately the mental attention (*manaskāra*) itself;
and the awareness of that [exclusion] is also an exclusion.

For even that [perception] is not possible for one with acute hearing unless it is accompanied by the arising of auditory perception of sound. However, there is no authority to deny non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*). One must state an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) only so far as the direct perception of sound—connected to its specific location—does not deviate from the direct perception of taste and so forth, or from the experience of a conceptual form; for it is impossible to state, with respect to another [object], a counter-correlate characterized by the non-deviation of mutual direct perceptions.

And thus, as before, the non-existence [of an object] is established by perception; and it is proven that the practical consequence (*vyavahāra*) is the result of the very non-perception of the perceptible, even in the case of verbal expression. This is because, even in the absence of a single cognition [of both the object and its absence], there is no obstruction to the operation of this [non-perception], since the undesired is not drawn in, owing to the reliance upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

Thus: In the case of sounds, lamps, and the like, it has been indicated that for the attainment of their complete manifestation—such as light and so forth—they depend on additional manifestors through birth; yet, for one whose mind has previously heard or seen them, there is a cognition of them as such. However, in other cases, the non-perception of the object itself is indeed the cognition of another [object], which is devoid of the form of its own [perceived] aspect.

If the persistence of the sense organ is established, then the non-perception of the effect is not a capacity [of that organ]. If the persistence of the sense organ is established, then the result is not a non-perception of the effect.

[198] Since the non-perception of intrinsic nature necessarily requires dependence [on other factors], how can the establishment of conjunction be achieved for you, even though you perceive it as the effect of cognition?
If this restriction applies only to external objects, then what causes it even there? For the status of objects is manifold, due to their suitability for occupying specific locations.
Just as the cognition of what is not illuminated does not constitute a sublation merely because it is not stated to be distinct [from it],
so too, in certain cases, there is sublation even while disregarding the associated object.

However, there is no fear for the Bhaṭṭas that the nature of that [non-existence] is simply the cognition of a counter-positive entity; for even that state of being a counter-positive is merely a mutual non-deviation from direct perception.
Therefore, a single cognition is produced by the conceptualization of the absence of others;
it is not an absence that is cognized by perception, because [perception] is nothing other than the certainty produced by that [cognition].
Only when there is the counter-correlativity as previously described is sense-perception capable of determining the absence of that [object]; such is the nature of things.

Is it not the case that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) alone is what is associated with the same cognition, since direct association with a single cognition is intended and the primary form is accepted? Therefore, by implication, the word "one" (*eka*) remains as a mere indicator of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Furthermore, its application as "one" is solely in reference to the single genus (*jāti*) of perception. Nor is this merely a matter of terminology, for such usage is observed through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), just as in the expression: "One grain of rice, when ripened, brings about an abundance of food."

Therefore, even where it is said that "it is seen as associated with a single cognition," the meaning is precisely this: that they are mutually non-deviant in terms of direct perception. However, the state of being within a single sense-base (*ekāyatanabhāva*) should be explained as a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), depending on the context, just as in the case [of the definition of non-perception] where "non-perception is the place and the cognition thereof."

And thus, in the case of the non-apprehension of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), since there is reliance upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it is stated that there is indeed reliance upon the association within a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsarga*). Therefore, how could the so-called "association within a single cognition" not be all-pervasive? True, this is so. If it appears to you that there is a coexistence in a single cognition with something white belonging to every age, what is the harm? Indeed, let the negation of sound itself be the withdrawal of the entire collection [of conditions], even if it is invisible.

[199] Since the non-deviation of mutual perception is possible even in the case of sound for some [perceiver], while for another [perceiver] there is no connection with the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), for one who considers the coexistence in a single cognition to be delimited by the counter-correlate, what further dependence on another could there be regarding the negation of the subject at hand? Therefore, in establishing the absence of sound in a specific suitable location, the non-perception of the effect of cognition need not be resorted to, because the proof is established by the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) alone.

However, since it is easy for darkness and light—which exist by mutually excluding each other's locations—to come into contact within a single cognition produced by the same sense organ, the consideration of other means of proof regarding the establishment of their absence pertains only to those situated at a distance, due to the non-apprehension of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*).
The investigation into the non-existence of all sounds is complete.
[201,2–232,20] || Chapter on Apoha ||
The established position is that exclusion (*apoha*) is revealed by means of words and logical marks;
this is proven for the sake of establishing that all phenomena are inexpressible.

"Stability" (*sthiti*) means "establishment" (*vyavasthā*). By the phrase ending with "is manifested after being established," exclusion (*apoha*) is stated here as the subject to be expressed; by the remainder, its fruit—namely, the establishment of that [exclusion]—is indicated. Alternatively, the meaning is: "This is for the purpose of establishing the system (*vyavasthā*) that exclusion is manifested by words and so forth, as formulated by the Teachers. In either case, the determination of exclusion (*apohavyavasthāpana*) is aimed at demonstrating that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inexpressible.
This is what has been stated.

But is it not the case that this claim—that exclusion (*apoha*) is revealed by words and logical marks—is contradicted by experience? For here, when one understands from a word or a logical mark that "there is fire on the mountain," the cognition is observed to delineate only a positive form.

The statement "it is not the case that it is not fire" merely presents a negation (*nivṛtti*). Furthermore, regarding that which is sublated by experience, there is no consideration of another means of valid cognition (*sādhana*), because the efficacy of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) comes to rest right there—both because they are produced from that [experience] and because that [experience] is their fruit.

Indeed, the arising of another means of valid cognition does not occur independently of the assistance provided by perception (*pratyakṣa*); nor is one's purpose fulfilled merely by the arising of another means of valid cognition.

As long as there is no experience of the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) brought about by that [first] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), another means of valid cognition—being devoid of capacity and seized by futility due to its independence from it—is itself nothing at all. Therefore, it finds no occasion to either establish or subvert what has been established or subverted by it. So how can it be said that exclusion (*apoha*) is the object of words and the like?

[201,17] Now, even if there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form "I cognize cessation," nevertheless, the very mental representation (*ullekha*) of the object "cessation" is what constitutes the representation of cessation. For a cognition that does not include the apprehension of a qualifier is not a cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭa*). Therefore, just as in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*), even in the absence of a conceptual construction such as "I cognize a universal," because of the manifestation of a common form, the conceptualizing cognition is [regarded as] directed toward the universal.

If it is argued that the cognition of others is likewise established as the cognition of exclusion (*nivṛtti*), which, being projected by a causal condition of cessation, extends the conventional usage of the apprehension of exclusion (*apoha*)—well then, if the determination of a universal cognition is based on the manifestation of a common form in the manner of a positive entity (*vidhi-rūpa*), what has been gained for the determination of the cognition of cessation when the mental state does not manifest the form of non-existence? Therefore, "I [cognize] cessation... [is untenable].

If there were a non-manifestation of the aspect of exclusion (*nivṛtti*) even in the absence of such a form as "I cognize," who indeed could deny the established fact of the cognition of exclusion? Otherwise, if the conventional usage of "cognition" were applied to that which merely appears [as such], then let there be the "cognition of a horse" even when the mind has the form of a cow. Now, if it is argued that the cognition of exclusion is included by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), even so—

If the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were of such a form as "not a non-cow," then let there be an entry of that [negation] as a qualifier; however, the cognition is "cow. And since, even though the specific characteristic defined by exclusion (*nivṛtti-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*) exists, it is not projected (*utkalita*) therein, how can that cognition be established?

This follows: if the positive entity (*vidhi*) appears, it cannot be the object of exclusion (*apoha*), yet if the exclusion does not appear, how can this be the rule? Likewise, how can that form which is not determined by determinate cognitions (*niścaya*) be their object? Furthermore, there is no such thing as "determination" of that which does not appear within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As for that positive form which appears within the internal domain (*antarmātrā*), even though it exists, there is also the exclusion of others (*parāpoha*) with respect to it.

That is called "cognition. Even there, it is merely the relation of exclusion (*apoha*); however, since the positive entity (*vidhi*) appears directly, there is no escape from the previously mentioned faults. Moreover, in this way, it is unavoidable that even direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) has exclusion as its object, especially for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which, while delineating the exclusion of one thing, perceives everything else as excluded. Therefore, just like a direct perception that grasps a positive form (*vidhyākāra*), [it would follow].

Even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has only affirmation (*vidhi*) as its object, not the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). As for that which is excluded from another, or that in which another is excluded—it is precisely the external object, distinguished from other classes, that is designated by the term "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) when it appears as a mental image (*buddhyākāra*). Therefore, there is no utility whatsoever in this; under the name of "exclusion," it is simply affirmation itself.

Because it is intended to be expressed, and because changing the name of a thing does not entail a transformation of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), therefore, in accordance with experience, let the external object be understood through words and so forth as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) alone. Furthermore, regarding this, the treatise states: "Of these, two are reasons that establish a positive entity, while one is a reason for negation."
By this [non-apprehension], a negation whose object-part has not been accepted is established;
however, with respect to a real entity (*vastu*), through the two preceding [types of non-apprehension], there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by way of affirmation.
And if, as in the case of the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*), there were a cognition of mere non-existence even from another logical reason (*hetu*), then...

Since there is no distinction based on non-apprehension, the entire system of formal arrangement—which is preceded by the differentiation of logical marks—has fallen into a state of difficulty. How, then, can exclusion (*apoha*) be manifested by words and logical marks? To this he says: "It is established. This is merely a conventional arrangement;
the meaning is that it is not the actual reality (*vastutattva*) that exclusion is the primary object of words and so forth. What, then, is the actual reality here?
If one asks:
first, by words the primary meaning is expressed;
therein, exclusion (apoha) is understood as a subordinate quality of that [meaning].
The object appears as one through superimposition, while another is established as the denotable;
in reality, however, there is not even the slightest thing that exists.
[203,5] Thus is the summary of the meaning of the section.

[203,6] Indeed, a treatise cannot exist by disregarding experience; therefore, it is impossible to deny that a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises precisely upon manifesting the form of certainty (*niścaya*). This is the meaning of the first quarter-verse. Because there is no dispute regarding the application of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is not [discussed] there.

[203,8] Objection: The phrase "by means of words" (*śabdaiḥ*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should also be understood that [the object] is "conveyed by logical marks" (*liṅgaiḥ*) and "made an object of conceptual construction" (*vikalpaiḥ*). This being the case, let alone the fact that exclusion (*apoha*) is the denotable meaning, even its mere establishment is lost. For that establishment is twofold: through proximity (*saṃnikarṣāt*) and through an efficient cause (*prayojakāt*). In this regard, although all phenomena (*dharma*) are inexpressible—

It has been stated that the means of communication (*pratipādana*) is the causal factor (*prayojaka*), and not some form of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that case, there is exclusion (*apoha*). For when a positive entity (*vidhi*) is being communicated as the primary object, exclusion is indeed understood as a subordinate element by virtue of being its qualification.
In that context, the phrase "by way of being its attribute" refers to a connection with the object (*arthasannikarṣa*). Consequently, it is both connected to the object and cognized.

Exclusion (*apoha*), even though it is a positive entity that is primarily cognized, is said to be the principal denotation by setting aside that [positive aspect], because of the stated purpose. Alternatively, it is understood precisely as a subordinate quality and not as the primary [denotation]; thus, those who maintain a literal theory of exclusion (*apohavādin*) are refuted.

Furthermore, although it was stated that there is no verbal mention of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) and so forth, nevertheless, there is certainly no non-cognition of exclusion when it functions as a qualifier.

[203,17] Because the word "cow" and so forth has been applied precisely to the exclusion of non-cows and so forth. For the treatise states: [203,18] "And the application [of a term] is such that one excludes that from which [the object] differs," [203,20] and so on.
For just as when the word *indīvara* (blue lotus) is applied to a blue lotus, its cognition necessarily involves the manifestation of "blue" (*nīla*).

Likewise, when the word "cow" is applied to the exclusion of non-cows (*agav-apoha*), the manifestation of the exclusion of non-cows (*ago'poha*) is unavoidable even when there is a cognition of a cow.

Furthermore, as for those who point out the mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—which they consider a mark of rustic stupidity—in the formulation of the convention (*saṅketa*) of the word "cow" upon the exclusion of non-cows:
how can they, who maintain that the convention applies to either a universal (*sāmānya*) or a possessor of a universal (*sāmānyavat*), escape from this fault?

Do they perceive the self? For indeed, by "universal" (*sāmānya*), one does not mean a mere universal; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying the word "cow" even to a horse. Rather, what is intended is the universal of cowness (*gotvasāmānya*). And if the convention of the word "cow" applies to that universal of cowness, or to the locus possessing it, then when the object is established as the referent, that same fault remains: if the cow is not cognized, the universal of cowness—[is not cognized].

Because of a lack of full comprehension; for if there is no full comprehension of the universal "cowness" (*gotva-sāmānya*), there is no full comprehension of that which is denoted by the word "cow. Now, if the convention were established by such syllables as "the word 'cow' applies to cowness" or "to that which possesses it," then there would be faults. However, when one has pointed out a single individual object standing before one, [the convention is made] with respect to that which abides in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a form common to all individuals scattered across different places and times, on the basis of context and so forth.

If one determines the user and establishes the convention "this is a cow," then, when that person discerns that very common form, he employs that alone by means of the word "cow. Thus, how can there be the fault of mutual dependence? And if it is argued: "This is merely a restatement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of those who explain that the convention applies either to the universal *gotva* or to its locus; it is not the actual sequence of instruction from the originators of the convention (*saṅketakartṛ*) themselves"?
In that case, this fault applies only if the formulation of the convention takes such a form as "the word 'cow' [applies] to non-cows.

However, when the convention "this is a cow" is established for a listener who has determined—through the context—that the intended individuals are the objects of a single unifying conceptual reflection (*ekākārapratyavamarśa*), then what room is there for a fault? For he [the listener], while resting upon the bed of his own conceptual construction, [perceives] all...

[204,11] Without depending on the individual instances excluded from non-cows and so forth, one who understands by himself those individual instances excluded from all heterogeneous instances as being denotable by the word "cow"— and who employs precisely those instances where he understands the exclusion of the heterogeneous—

[204,12-13] does so merely by restating the established doctrine that the word "cow" refers to what is excluded from non-cows; this is not the form of a convention (*saṅketa*), for it is intended [as such].

[204,14] Because when the word "cow" is functioning, the remainder can be denoted by the word "non-cow. Furthermore, that common form excluded from heterogeneous instances—which appears as a universal (*sāmānya*) in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or which is the very self-nature of the individual (*vyakti*)—will be determined later.

[204,15–16] Thus, it is established that there is no circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). And it is established that, just as upon hearing the word "puṇḍarīka," one understands a white lotus, so too [is the understanding of the object].

Even when the word "cow" is heard, although there is no cognition of a non-cow or a camel, the proponent of the universal (jāti-vādin) must necessarily admit that the cognition of the exclusion (apoha) as a qualifier is inseparable from the positive entity (vidhi). Nor is there a difference [between our views] merely because of the presence of a relationship, such that the two are perceived directly in the relation of primary and subordinate; for the word "quality" (guṇa) may also denote a property (dharma), namely, the positive form which has the exclusion of others as its property.
[204,20] Because it is perceived.

[204,21] Regarding that similarity based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) between two superimposed external objects belonging to the third form (*ākāra*), which Vācaspati refutes by saying, "And you do not admit that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is a property of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)," that is indeed flawed. Now, if it were real (*bhāvikī*)...

If it is argued that this is what was intended by the word "therein" (*tatra*), even so, it is of no use, because it is precisely the relationship between subject and predicate (*dharmidharmabhāva*) as established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that is accepted.

Only two points remain: why is there not a designation solely by way of affirmation (*vidhi*), or else, why does the consequence not follow that even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be treated as having the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object?

To this we reply: In this context, a certain systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*)—relying on a mere fraction of reality (*tattvaleśa*) for a specific purpose—is formulated differently even though it exists otherwise, as in the case of "self" and "its arising. For arising is indeed a property (*dharma*) of an existent entity characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); nevertheless, relying on that mere fraction of reality characterized by prior non-existence, it is established as "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*).

[205,2] This is for the purpose of warding off the contraction [of the mind] caused by the suspicion of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*). Or, just as— relying on the designation of a single continuum (*ekasantānaprajñapti*)— one avoids the deception of the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done, thinking "Who else will experience the karma performed by this very person?", so too, even now, the statement regarding the object of the injunction [is made] in order to dispel the suspicion that, in reality, a thing itself might accept a denotability superimposed upon it by another.

The cognition of an inseparable relation (*nāntarīyaka*) is also established as having exclusion (*apoha*) alone as its conceptual object; therefore, linguistic convention does not proceed by way of affirmation alone.
However, when exclusion itself is the primary referent of a word, then affirmation is also brought forward as a superimposition (*āropa*).
As it has been said:
[205,8] First of all, it is by means of words that an object is primarily expressed.

[205,9] However, since there is no dispute regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not correct to establish a rule in that manner. It has already been stated that in that case, there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) in the positive injunction (*vidhi*) qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). For this is the treatise (*śāstra*):
"It determines that [object] and thereby excludes what is other than it," and so forth.

However, with respect to the object of negation, the operation of negation is indeed foregrounded there by the term "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*). Or, for instance, in the case of an affirmative function (*vidhivṛtti*), what is called "non-apprehension" is simply the capacity to produce a conceptual construction of non-existence (*abhāvavikalpa*) based on the experience of a determinate form within the context of the non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

Likewise, in the case of positive conceptualizations (*vidhi-vikalpa*) as well, the capacity for performing the corresponding practice according to the tantra is itself the apprehension of the negation; and there is the capacity for generating the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), such as "fire has been cognized by me. Furthermore, in the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the very perception of a restricted nature constitutes the negation in both cases.

[205,16] Regarding the apprehension: both of these are intended by the author of the treatise. In some instances, in accordance with the context, it is under the heading of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), as in "there is nothing whatsoever of that in form," and so forth.
In some cases, however, statements such as "because they establish the mere thing as excluded from what is not that" rely upon *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation).

Yet, there is no single fixed rule. Therefore, the claim made by the author of the *Ṭīkā*—who was eager to introduce that meaning for the sake of establishing his own theory of *apoha*—and by Trilocana, namely that "the Master is inferred to be a lover of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)," is refuted. Moreover, this is because there is no absence of distinction.

There would be a loss of the linguistic usage of qualification, because—as in the cases of "Rāhu’s head" or "cowness as a universal"—that which is produced by intention does not disappear. Furthermore, even you yourself certainly employ the relationship of qualified and qualifier in such instances as "the absence of a jar in a location" or "the absence of a *piśāca* in a pillar. Therefore, how could this apply to us, who maintain that negation is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?

If this is argued, then the nature of non-existence is not being defined here, but rather its cognition. And that cognition cannot be denied. Even in the case of the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) view, the negation of another is simply the affirmation of that [remaining thing]; thus, there is no loss of cognitive validity.
Nor is there a problem for the status of it being a qualifier, since by this very statement the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of affirmation and negation is demonstrated.

For this very reason, even the objection regarding contradiction is not to be faulted; for there is a contradiction with existence by virtue of its own nature, but not with the absence of another, since they coexist.
Therefore, it is rightly said:
"In that case, exclusion (apoha) is understood as a subordinate quality of that [positive entity]."
Alternatively, this very quality of that expression of meaning is precisely its negation of others; therefore, it should be understood that "it is understood by means of that.

As for the treatise, the injunction regarding words is that they should function by way of excluding what is other; otherwise, their application would be purposeless. By this, the fact that exclusion (*apoha*) is the intended meaning (*tātparya-artha*) has been demonstrated, as well as the avoidance of the charge of being too narrow (*avyāpitva*). This is the path.

In the case of the expression "he approaches Śrughna" (*śrughnam upatiṣṭhate*), this same principle applies with respect to the specific path under discussion; however, with respect to the location intended as the destination of Śrughna, it is Śrughna itself. Because there is no interruption—as in the case of a forest path—he indeed "approaches. By excluding [other possibilities] such as a caravan or a messenger, the restriction that it is "only a path" is easily established. If it is argued that the meaning "it is only a path" is already understood from the pointing gesture of the index finger, [we reply: that would be an exclusion of others (*paravyavaccheda*).

[206,10] For the time being, it is accepted that [the object] exists. Furthermore, in common usage, the employment of a term is indeed observed even when its meaning has already been understood, as in the case of "two Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇau dvau*) and so forth. Just as there is a question such as, "Which path leads to Śrughna?"—intended to exclude [other paths] such as those of a caravan or other people—the answer likewise is "This is the path," for in every instance, an injunction is directed toward that which is marked by doubt regarding what is to be established.

Regarding the two negations: if exclusion of others (*parāpoha*) is not apprehended at the time of hearing the word, how can there be activity by way of avoiding other things? Consequently, one commanded by "Bind the cow" might even bind horses and the like.

As for the claim that, upon the cognition of the cow, its own nature is not the nature of others, and thus exclusion of others is subsequently determined through implication (*sāmarthyāt*), [this is incorrect].

That opinion is untenable, because even for the first-time listener, no sequence of cognition is observed. For one who has mastered the convention at that time, when told "Bring the cow," does not resort to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding the exclusion of others. Nor is it logical to have a certain determination of "cow" from the word "cow" if the cognition were mixed with something else. Or, if such a cognition were indeed produced, how could presumptive testimony arise even subsequently?

For when a cow is perceived, it is indeed accompanied by the exclusion of other forms (*pararūpa-parikara*). How then could it be capable of establishing its own non-mixture with those others? Therefore, the cognition of a cow is said to be the apprehension of the exclusion of the non-cow (*ago’poha*). Consequently, the very time of the cognition of its own object is the time of the cognition of the exclusion of other objects, just as at the time of perceiving the moon during the use of the word "moon," there is also the perception of its whiteness. And just as when whiteness is perceived, what kind of moon—
[The same applies to] cognition; for even when there is a cognition mixed with another form, what kind of cognition of a cow could it be? This is the same [objection].

Nor can an object be apprehended as being neither mixed nor unmixed, because its capacity [to produce such a cognition] is impossible even subsequently. Therefore, relying on the capacity of the object for the sake of understanding a negation is not the best approach.

As for what Vācaspati said— that individual entities possessing a genus (*jāti*) are the domain of conceptual constructions and words, and that since the nature of those individuals is excluded from what does not belong to that genus, one who is instructed, "Bind the cow," binds it and not horses and so forth because of the understanding of that [genus] through the meaning [of the word]— that too is refuted by this very [argument]. For even if a genus were added as something additional, [the cognition would still depend on] the individuals.

If form (*rūpa*) is indeed excluded from what is not of that same class (*atajjātīya*), then how can there be an avoidance of the cognition of exclusion from that [other class] for those [cognitions] which, by means of that very form, become the objects of words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)? Alternatively, if the individual form (*vyaktirūpa*) is not excluded from what is of a different class, nor is it perceived as such, then this is merely the grace of the universal (*jāti*); thus, it has already been stated that there is no understanding of it even through the object itself.

Now, if it is argued that [the exclusion] is already differentiated from others by the very force of its birth, then it must have existed as such even previously; thus, it was not capable [of performing the function] earlier.

How then could it perform it later? For the requirement of the auxiliary factor of remembering the convention pertains only to the application of names (*nāmayojanā*); however, the conceptualization of what is similar and what is dissimilar depends solely upon perception, just as in the case of infants and the like—this argument is therefore trivial.

Alternatively, "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to that which is multiplied or practiced; thus, it denotes an attribute (*dharma*) that is to be adopted. By this, prominence (*prādhānya*) is to be characterized here.

Consequently, in those words for which that very quality—namely, exclusion (*apoha*) itself—is primary, it is exclusion alone that is said to be the object of comprehension in words denoting entities (*bhāvavācin*), and not a positive injunction (*vidhi*), even though it may manifest, as if it were non-prominent. For it is so because it depends upon the non-perception [of the word] in all dissimilar instances.

In some cases, however, the treatise states that "exclusion" (apoha) is connected to the hearing [of a word] when it is of a nature dependent on a [specific] view. Furthermore, even though both [the positive and the negative] appear, because there is no object of cognition corresponding to the appearance, and because the exclusion of others is necessarily a positive entity, exclusion alone is primary. As the treatise says:
[207,13] There might be contact with the form of a real entity when a sound effects a separation [from it], for that [contact] exists there [in that case].
(PV III 132) [207,16] But in the case of words expressing non-existence, [there is no contact] precisely because the entity does not exist. As the treatise says:
"Because non-entities lack form, words that denote forms cannot even be suspected [to apply to them]; they are established as such, making known the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). (PV I 185).
Or rather, when that exclusion (*apoha*)—or the form of what is excluded by way of relative negation (*paryudāsa*)—is the expressed object, the quality consisting in the negation of faults remains.
Regarding those words for which the denotable object is expressed as being excluded (*apoha*) by its very nature, it has been said:
"Because cessation (*nivṛtti*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there is no postulation of another locus.
Furthermore, since the cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) is an error (*upaplava*), it is therefore not a fault. (PV I 169)

Thus, while these reasons for establishing exclusion (*apoha*) as the denotable object are being stated in the treatise, one should infer that in words expressing positive entities (*bhāva*), there is a contradiction with the primary manifestation of exclusion. Furthermore, it has been stated that this alone is the primary distinction within the section concerning words expressive of non-existence (*abhāva*). By contrast, it indicates that in words expressing positive entities, the distinction is secondary and thus not primary. Specifically...

This indeed must be understood: in words expressing non-existence (*abhāva*), the exclusion (*apoha*) is the very object (*padārtha*); in words expressing existence (*bhāva*), however, it is the exclusion of the object from others, as well as the exclusion of others from the object. And the difference between these two is merely one of expression. If the status of exclusion as the denoted meaning is established based on such a connection, yet the actual object itself is declared to be primary, then alas, the ineffability of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanirabhilāpyatā*) [is undermined].

It has been indicated that "this time has arrived, and this undertaking is for that purpose. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the system of denotation is established primarily through *apoha* for the sake of negating the imposition of denotability upon real entities (*vastu*), there too one might suspect: "One accepts the denotability of the object itself, yet teaches it otherwise to the opponent; this is a great lack of discernment. Anticipating this, he says:
"The object is one," and so forth.

This is the meaning: for an object (*artha*) is of two kinds, external and internal, since there is no other. Of these, first, the external one is established as denotable only through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and not through the vivid manifestation of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If it is asked how this is so, it is because of experience itself. For instance, in the case of perceptual consciousness, objects restricted by place, time, and state appear with perfectly clear forms.

Particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) appear and are experienced [in perception], but not so at the time of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). For at the time of conceptualization, some form—which is indeed excluded from those of a different class, yet appears as if intermingled with the forms of others and as if indistinct—is the object of experience, being neither direct perception nor another's mind. As the treatise states:
"Because an object does not appear in the cognition of one whose senses are not engaged by a word, just as it does not appear when the object is being perceived [by the senses].

If it is argued that there is a difference in appearance for the very same [object] due to a difference in means— since in one case the sense organ is the basis for the cognition, while in the other case it is the word and so forth?
Regarding this, it has also been said:
"The basis for the various cognitions of that object is indeed produced one after another.
How can there be a single form appearing as having diverse aspects? (PV III 235)

For two mutually contradictory forms—clear and unclear—cannot belong to a single entity, such that one would appear to sensory cognition and the other to conceptual construction; for if that were the case, there would be a perception of a difference in the entity itself. Indeed, there is no difference in the entity apart from a difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*), nor is there any difference in its own nature apart from a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Otherwise, the three worlds would constitute a single entity.

[209,2] But surely, even though there is a difference in the clear and unclear appearances of a single tree for those situated at distant and near locations, there is no difference in the tree itself, because there is no difference in its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Thus, appearance is a differentiator only when assisted by a difference in causal efficiency. [209,3–4] And since there is no difference in causal efficiency here, how can the cow or other objects—which are the objects of the cognitions produced by the sense organ and the word—be differentiated?

If it is argued that there is a partiality [of the cognition], we do not say that a difference in appearance is necessarily restricted to distinct objects; rather, it is necessarily restricted by the absence of having a single object.
For instance, whatever appearance is contrary to the direct perception of a certain object, that appearance does not have the same object as that [perception];
just as the appearance of a cloth is not the same object as the perception grasping a jar, or as [the appearance of a yellow conch] is not the same object as the perception grasping a white conch.
[It would have] a yellow appearance. And thus, at the time of conceptualization, there is an appearance contrary to the appearance in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the cow;

this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For having a single object is pervaded by the non-difference of appearance, as is seen in the case of what is perceived by the left and right eyes. If, however, there were no such pervasion, then even another direct perception might have a contrary appearance, and the thing—

And it would be of two forms; yet since that duality does not exist, there is indeed a pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, when cognition arising from a difference in its basis is made the subject (*pakṣa*), its opposite is established. Therefore, wherever there is a difference in appearance accompanied by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, there is a difference in the real entity (*vastu*), as in the case of a jar and a cloth. However, when that auxiliary factor is abandoned, [cognition] proceeding [in that way] necessarily possesses a single object.
[209,14] To say that it "excludes" [the other] means that here there is only a single erroneous appearance, like the appearance of yellow in a conch shell.

[209,15] If it is argued that even in that case, the object is simply the conch shell itself? Then it is a very clever assertion to claim that a cognition which does not touch upon whiteness has the conch shell as its object. [209,16] If it is argued that it cognizes the conch shell alone? No, because nothing beyond that appears as the "conch shell alone. [The questioner asks: "Why?"...

If it is argued that the mind manifests as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding a future entity, it is nonetheless established that the non-conceptual appearance of yellow is not the object of the conch-shell. Likewise, the perception of a globular shape from a distance regarding a mountain peak is similar to the case at hand;

it does not have the tree as its object, for it lacks the specific features such as leaves and so forth that would enable the determination of distinctions like *pippala* and other species. This is also because there is an absence of any difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and the like.

If the object is not distinct, then when the state of being erroneous is attributed to one [of two cognitions], we say that if the manifestation in perception is not erroneous, then the manifestation of the other is indeed the error. This same principle applies equally to the appearance of yellow and to the conceptual construction of a cow. Now, one might argue:
"In some cases, the superimposition of something upon another occurs due to some similarity; however, this is not the case with the manifestation in a conceptual construction."

[209,23] If it is argued that some [object] with a distinct form has been perceived even in another birth, [we reply: from where, by what, and upon what superimposition does this delusion arise? This is merely another fault of yours, in that you maintain that the object of conceptual construction is accessible only through direct perception and not through any other means; thus, even if it lacks a real objective basis, it cannot be called a delusion.

For us, however, the proof of the point at hand is established by this much alone: that the object does not extend beyond that [cognition]. If it is argued that "that very thing appears otherwise (anyathākhyāti) and thus remains within its own domain," [we reply: since there is no entity existing apart from the form presented before one's perception, what could possibly be made to appear otherwise? Furthermore, that [object] does not appear at all; so enough with this excessive talk. Therefore, it is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—
The principle is that appearance occurs within conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, what Vācaspati has said—that there is no difference in cognition when both verbal testimony and perception have a real entity as their object, because the distinction between mediacy and immediacy is established through a difference in their causes—is not tenable. For a mediate cognition [does not apprehend] the real entity...

[210,5] Because it cannot be established as an object (*gocara*). However, the distinction of causes based on imperceptibility (*parokṣatā*) is fulfilled simply by the absence of grasping an object within the range of the senses. [210,6] If it is argued: "But you yourself have stated that if [cognition] has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, there would be the consequence of non-difference between cognitions; therefore, by the very refutation of that, it is established that [cognition] has a real entity as its object, and since no other entity exists, it must have that [entity] as its object," [we reply: this is not so, because of the appearance (*pratibhāsa*)— [210,7] ...of the manifestation. (12a)

[210,8] Since the proof of pervasion is established by showing that dissimilarity (*vaijātya*) does not have that as its object, this reductio (*prasaṅga*) is our own. For us, too, this effort is directed precisely toward the disruption of the pervasion. When a dissimilarity in appearance is possible due to a dissimilarity in the causes, how could there be a pervasion by having that as the object? When would even this be appropriate? Or [how could it be so] merely by having that as the object, [regarding] the cause—?

A distinction that is pervading can be demonstrated; however, that does not exist here, because the distinction of causes fulfills its purpose even without the cognition of the object itself. Now, if it is argued that this manifestation of difference is possible even from a difference in causes, despite the two having the same object, then let it be possible for the cognitions of the *gāndhāra* and the *madhura* notes also to have a single object.

Since a difference in causes is possible even there, there is confidence in the identity of the object because both the non-conceptual and the conceptual cognitions have the mere nature of fire as their content. But if it is argued that in those cases there is no mention of either "being a Gandhāra" or "sweetness" in the two respective cognitions—alas, what great rootedness this is! For this is the result of an absolute dissimilarity in causes; [it is not the case that there is] identity of object...

Furthermore, reassurance will arise from the apprehension of a real entity at the end. In the case of doubt regarding a difference in the nature of causes, there is the apprehension of an intermediate property such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*).

But in the case of absolute [non-apprehension], it is of a property common to all; therefore, it does not follow that [the cognition] has something other than that as its object merely on that account.
Moreover, there is a persistence of the unreal property of sweetness even in the *gāndhāra* [note].

If it is argued that its sweetness is of a different kind, then even firehood as posited by conceptual construction would be something else entirely. Furthermore, even when a single form is being delineated, there is no identity of object between the two appearances of intermediate properties, just as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver;
for the appearance of mother-of-pearl does not have silver as its object, nor does the appearance of silver have mother-of-pearl as its object, even though there is a common delineation of whiteness.

Therefore, just as in the conceptualization of fire, even though the thing itself appears, because the intermediate property of "donkey-ness" does not appear, it is not an object of a donkey; so too, although the intermediate property of "fire-ness" appears, because the specific form of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear, there is no appearance of another substance—this is the logical principle, since the particular characteristic alone constitutes the substance of fire. Consequently, there is a difference in the cause of cognition.
[210,26] Let there be a distinction between the two appearances; however, it remains established that neither of these two appearances has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object.

[210,27] Therefore, it is proven that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of words and the like. [211,1] Furthermore, in this way, because affirmation and negation would both be mere exclusions (*apoha*), their very utterance would not even occur; for those two [pertain to] the substratum (*dharmin*).
Or it might concern phenomena (*dharma*), such as whether a tree exists or does not exist, or whether a tree is blue or not blue.
Among these, first of all, the first position is untenable. For a tree, which is determined by its existence or non-existence, is denoted by the word "tree.

Thus, in the position that asserts the determination of existence, the statement "it exists" is redundant, while "it does not exist" is contradictory because it is opposed to existence. However, in the case of defining it through non-existence, the opposite holds true.

Furthermore, since there is an expectation of affirmation and negation upon hearing the word "tree," the logical principle is that this manifestation of a "tree" from the word "tree" is common to both existence and non-existence; it is not an external tree.
As for the fact that the author of the *Tātparyaṭīkā* on the *Nyāyadarśana*, having introduced the view that the individual possessing the universal (*jāti*) is the denotation by his own words—

Immediately following this, it is not the case that the universality of existence and non-existence for the universal (jāti)—which is the referent of the word—is untenable. For although that [universal] is eternal by its own nature, it becomes common to both existence and non-existence by virtue of depending on multiple individuals scattered across space and time; thus, it is capable of being connected with "is" and "is not. Indeed, the existence of a universal consists in its connection with a present individual, while its non-existence consists in its connection with past and future individuals.

And as for the claim that "it does not exist," it has been lamented that because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), common to both existence and non-existence, or else established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*); however, by that much, there is no injury to the subject at hand. For one who places the burden on the universal (*jāti*) has himself admitted that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible.

Furthermore, when the universal (*jāti*) is denoted by a word prior to the employment of terms such as "exists" (*asti*), it must be denoted as being either connected with a present individual, or connected with past and future individuals, or connected with both, or unconnected—these are the possible positions. Not even one among these provides a refuge that can withstand the clever objections raised previously. For in the first position, there would be a restriction to existence.

In the second case, however, there is a restriction to non-existence. In the third case as well, if one’s desire is for the linguistic convention of its existence or non-existence based on its connection with the manifestation of the existent or the non-existent, then the word must likewise denote those very substrata through which its connection with a present manifestation is conventionally expressed, or those through which its connection with past and future manifestations is expressed. For it cannot otherwise be connected to both types of manifestation.
[It] would thus be established; and that being the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of not employing words such as "exists" and so forth.

Now, suppose the following thought occurs: "That form which is related to both individual instances is indeed expressed by this word; however, there is no cognition of the two types of individuals related to it. For the cognition of one related member does not necessarily entail the cognition of the other related member, just as in the case of the cognition of a son and so forth. If this were so, then in the absence of the cognition of the related members, there would be no cognition of the relation itself.
There is also cognition [of the relation], because:
The cognition of a relation residing in two [terms] does not arise from the perception of a single form;
rather, the knowledge of the relation occurs when there is the apprehension of the essential natures of both. (PVA II 3)

[212,1] Therefore, just as in reality even a son, when his connection to a father is not determined, is perceived merely as a person and is independent like a jar, so too an entity designated as a "universal" (sāmānya), being perceived as independent, does not result in a cognition in the form of a universal. This refutes the fourth position. Furthermore, because it does not imply its related entities, there is no employment of words such as "exists" (asti) and so forth.

[212,4] It is established that when that [subject] is being ascertained independently, there must be the application of "exists" and so forth based on its very existence or non-existence, and not that of another. For even in the determination of a relation, the application of words such as "exists" for one [term] does not follow from the existence or non-existence of only one of the two related members. Indeed, Maitra—who is determined to be Caitra’s son—is neither said to exist nor not to exist merely by virtue of Caitra’s existence or non-existence.

The word "or" (*vā*) requires a connection; what kind of connection, then, could there be for a universal that is not perceived? If it is argued that the connection in that case is of a different nature, let it be whatever it may—yet if it is not established through cognition, it is merely a mental construction (*asatkalpa*). Therefore, the application of words such as "exists" (*asti*) does not logically follow with respect to a perceived object that is like a mere wooden tally (*ayaḥśalākākalpa*), based on the existence or non-existence of something else, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, since its own nature has been established as always abiding, the term "exists" (asti) is redundant, and the contradiction with the term "does not exist" (nāsti) remains as before.

Therefore, the commonality of appearing in both existence and non-existence is neither established otherwise nor is it conclusive for proving that the appearance in conceptual cognition has an external object. For the determination of objects is invariably pervaded by the possession of a causal basis.

Nor does any other ground for [establishing the object] arise apart from the proof of the existence or non-existence of the object, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, in the absence of that [ground], since the pervader is absent, the state of possessing an object—which is restricted solely to the proof of existence or non-existence—is itself pervaded by that [proof].

How then could it remain in something contrary to that? Whatever cognition has an appearance common to both the existence and non-existence of a thing, it does not [establish] that thing by means of that [appearance].

[212,16] Having an object, (13a) as in the case of the cognition of a cow [not having the horse as its object]. Furthermore, the conceptual cognition of a tree has an appearance that is common to both existence and non-existence regarding external things; thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For "commonality" (*sādhāraṇya*), which consists in not establishing that [external thing], is incompatible with "the establishment of existence or non-existence," which is the pervader of "having that as its object. Thus, there is indeed the same fault even in the expression "possessing a universal" (*jātimat*) or "denoting an individual" (*vyaktivacana*).

If it is argued that [the universal is perceived] through the individual (*vyakti*), then the establishment of cognition is achieved; whether the genus (*jāti*) is perceived as something additional or not, there is no liberation from those faults.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the followers of Kumārila—that because the entity possesses parts (*sabhāgatva*), there is no fault of commonality, for "treeness" is understood from the word without its existence or non-existence being determined, and it is then connected with one of those two as understood from another word—even in that case:

If "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is intended as a universal (*jāti*), then it is refuted by that very same critique. Alternatively, if "tree-ness" is that which is not apprehended as either distinct or non-distinct [from its instances], then it is necessarily determined by its presence or absence; and since it has been expressed by the word in exactly that way, what further purpose is served by words such as "exists" (*asti*) and so forth?
It might be argued: "Even though it is determined by that [presence or absence], only the aspect of tree-ness is prompted by the word, not the aspects of existence or non-existence."

If this is argued, then is the difference between those two parts conceptual or real? If it is conceptual, how can it be established that this verbal cognition—which appears as if directed toward two distinct things—is actually having a real entity as its object? If it is real, there would be no possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the tree exists," just as in the case of a pot and a cloth; for according to the logical principle, two properties must be restricted to a single entity.

The rejection of the view that [words] possess direct perception (*darśana*) will be stated later. Furthermore, the position of their being either different or non-different has already been refuted elsewhere.

As for the claim that "the manner in which words convey meaning is not like that of direct perception, such that there would be no need for words like *asti* (is) and so forth as if they were seen by it, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess diverse capacities"—that too has been refuted by the critique of the appearance of difference when there is a single referent (*ekārthatva*). Therefore, if...

The presentation of an object through perception by means of a word would appear exactly like that [perception]; and if it does not so appear, it is incapable of making known that object. Therefore, even for this [word], the possession of diverse capacities is caused solely by the determination (*adhyavasāya*) following the experience of the nature of the thing (*vastu*), and not by a difference in the object itself, even when the object is one and the same. This is because, if there were a difference in the appearance while the object remains one, such a state would be contradicted by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, this remains established: it is not [the case that words correspond directly to external objects].
If the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were expressed, affirmation and negation would be impossible for the substratum (*dharmin*); thus, the employment of further words would be redundant.

Nor could they apply to the properties (*dharmas*), because by the word "tree," the substratum is presented in its entirety—just as in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—so what room is there for another word to effect the affirmation or negation of qualities such as blueness, or for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to do so? This is true even in the case of direct perception.

If it is argued that [perception] is observed to depend on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), let it be so; for even that [other means] is non-ascertaining in nature with respect to an object whose specific form has not been familiarized.

However, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is itself of the nature of ascertainment; therefore, regarding that which it grasps, what need is there for another? And yet, there is dependence on words, signs, and other factors.
Consequently, there is no apprehension of the actual nature of the thing, but rather only the experience of the arising of a conceptual construction that mimics the shadow of a single property.
[213,15] It is established. It is not established; for the properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are distinct from one another as well as from the substratum (*dharmin*).
Thus, even when the tree is cognized by means of a single property such as genus, there is no cognition of its possession of other properties.
Therefore, why should the comprehension of other properties—such as being blue, moving, or very high—not depend upon distinct designations?

That is incorrect. For if, despite the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) through its distinction [from its properties], there were no cognition of the properties (*dharma*) by means of words or logical marks (*liṅga*), then let it not be so by means of the sense organs (*indriya*) either. Now, if it is argued that—by the force of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) on the part of the sense organ—the properties, which possess the contact of inherence and so forth, also become objects of cognition when the substratum is in close proximity, then this same [principle] applies to the logical mark as well.

Indeed, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not diminish even by a fraction. Now, although for a word there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) with its denotatum, a proximity characterized as that of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakalakṣaṇā*) is certainly accepted; for in the absence of that, the consequence would be the non-existence of the cognition of the denotatum itself.

Or, if there is such cognition, what need is there for conjunction and the like? And this is so even for those who rely upon an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvikasaṃbandha*), such as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

[213,24] This is equally true regarding the cognition of the object. Nor does the cognition through the medium of the word raise any suspicion of an intervention that would obstruct the cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
