[213,25] For, according to you, the individual (*vyakti*) possessing the universal (*jāti*) is apprehended from the word all at once. But if there were a sequential cognition of each one individually, the cognition of the individual possessing the universal would never occur. Furthermore, no sequence of certain cognitions is observed. Therefore, let the universal be admitted as something additional.

As for the name, the individual (*vyakti*), being perceived as the substratum (*dharmin*), could not attain its own stability without conveying the qualities, actions, and so forth inherent within it.
Otherwise, even in the case of perception, the cognition of other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) would be without a basis.
If it is argued that this being the case, let there simply be the cognition of the individual by means of words—what is the use of accepting their association with limiting adjuncts?
[214,2] In that case, must entities now abandon their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) simply because your own position is rendered futile?

Therefore, let this other fault be yours or not; however, one cannot remain without establishing the cognition of those things related to it by means of the instruments of knowledge (*jñānasādhana*) regarding its object, just like the sense organs (*indriya*). If you argue that it is observed to be so only in the case of the sense organs, and thus there is no such consequence for anything else?

If that is the case, then since a grass fire is observed to be capable of producing smoke that is inseparable from the action of transforming the fuel, a *khadira* fire would not be so. However, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists in both cases by way of generality; thus, there is no distinction. Therefore, if there is an absence of transformation in the *khadira*, then that is not smoke, but rather a mass of dust stirred up by the wind; nor is there a fire (*dhūmadhvaja*) there.

However, if that mass of rays from a heap of radiant ruby jewels were tall, and if furthermore this were smoke and that were fire (*dhūmadhvaja*), then there would necessarily be a modification in the *khadira* wood; likewise, if this were the cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) and the word were its means of proof, then there would certainly be the fault of cognizing a property (*dharma*) that has that as its substratum. If, on the other hand, there is no cognition of a property having that as its substratum, then it is neither a cognition of the locus nor—

[214,11] A word is that which makes known the possessor of properties (dharmin). Whatever is a means of cognition for something is necessarily restricted to being a means of cognizing its properties, just like a sense faculty. And so, the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is this: it follows that the sign (*liṅga*) and the word are occupied with being means of cognizing that which is intended to be beyond perception (*parokṣa*). But this is not the case, because they depend upon other words and signs. For that which is not a means of making known the properties inherent in something is not [a means of cognizing that thing].

That which generates knowledge of its own nature—such as the word "cow" with respect to a horse, or a horse with respect to a donkey—does not cause cognition; nor do smoke and *godhūli* (dust from threshing) [cause cognition] with respect to their own intended objects. Thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) in the case of the contrary: for there is no possibility of seeing a real object even in a dream if it were devoid of genus, quality, action, and so forth, since the perception of a thing occurs through the knowledge of another property that arises solely from the existence of that thing.

"It is pervaded" means that even though both appear as if distinct within the conceptualizing mind (*kalpanābuddhi*), this term refers to their non-separate manifestation. Therefore, it is better that there be simply non-difference (*abheda*) among the properties (*dharma*); for if one accepts the cognition of a real entity in every respect, the objection regarding the cognition of the properties is difficult to avoid. What is the point of accepting a difference that has fallen away from experience? The intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) themselves are the entity.
[214,20] Birth and so forth.

[214,21] As for that which is the ornamentation of the statement—that which is not related to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not that intrinsic nature; if that were so, there would be a lack of relation altogether, for it is not the case that the very same thing is established by itself. That is incorrect; for in the phrase "related to the intrinsic nature," it is precisely that which is the intrinsic nature.

[214,23] It is intended as the nature of some given entity, yet there is no difference between the two; for if there were a difference, it would follow that it possesses a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is contrary to worldly experience. [214,24] How, then, is the objection—that "that very thing is connected with itself"—avoided? For otherwise, the use of the genitive case in the expression "its intrinsic nature" (*asya svabhāvaḥ*) would be untenable. [214,25] Alternatively, if by "intrinsic nature" one means simply a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, then there is no fault, provided that the universal and the rest [are admitted].

[214,26] It is the discernment of the nature of the mere thing (*vastumātra*) after having distinguished it. For it is not the case that this [nature] cannot be stated to be the nature of the thing alone;

rather, it is precisely that which is intended here as being "related to the nature" (*svabhāvasambandhin*), because by the word "related" (*sambandhin*), the universal (*jāti*) and so forth are intended.
[215,1] Therefore, when something, though non-different, is shown as if different through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the conventional usage is that "that is related to this."
It is difficult to avoid.
And as for what Vācaspati said: "When this [object] qualified by one limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) has been apprehended, there is no apprehension of it as qualified by another limiting adjunct;

for while the limiting adjunct qualifies the nature (*svabhāva*) of the substance, neither the limiting adjuncts nor its state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) constitute its nature. That too is indeed floating away. For it was not on the basis of non-difference that the apprehension of another limiting adjunct was raised as a consequence; even in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*), [it is stated that] the beneficiary—

For, by prioritizing the distinction made on the basis of assistance (*upakāra*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that all aspects [of the object] must be apprehended. However, it has been stated that there is no difference between the powers (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*); therefore, even this [objection] does not touch upon our position.

Furthermore, as for the refutation offered there by Bhūṣaṇa—namely, the consequence that when the sun and so forth are apprehended, the entire mass of things assisted by them must also be apprehended—that too is irrelevant.

It has been stated that the result of not fathoming his intention is as follows: this is the underlying motive. Having first established the negation of *samavāya* (inherence) which you yourself will later state, you, the preeminent Naiyāyika, must accept that at the time of perception, when there is a connection with the sense organs (*akṣasaṃbandha*) regarding the substratum (*dharmin*) that experiences it, the properties (*dharmas*) such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are apprehended precisely through their being assisted, because there is no difference in the capacity that assists them, given your admission of their distinction.
For there can be no restriction of one thing by another that provides no assistance, since they would possess distinct natures; thus, by way of establishing the non-difference of capacities, he says:
"If those capacities for the assistance of properties were different from it, what would they be to it?
If they do not assist it, then they would likewise be separate, leading to an infinite regress. (PV I 54)

Thus it is said. As for the claim that what is called "capacity" (*śakti*) is either an innate genus (*jāti*), an adventitious one (*aupādhikī*), or the totality of auxiliary causes (*sahakārisākalya*), and therefore distinct from the entity itself—having refuted that, it was established in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya* that capacity is simply the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) engaged in the performance of an effect. Furthermore, it was also shown in that same work that assistance (*upakāra*), which consists in the nature of producing a common effect, is possible even for that which is not itself an effect.

[215,19] Destroyed. Even between the effect (*kārya*) and that which assists the effect (*upakārin*), there is in reality no distinction at all; however, in conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), when something new arises, it is called an "effect" because of the exclusion (*apoha*) of what was not previously there. But regarding the object of the conceit (*abhimāna*) that [the thing] remained as it was before, it is called "that which is assisted" (*upakārya*) due to the experience of a specific change (*viśeṣa*). Yet, in reality, it is a contradiction for something to both remain as it was before and now be qualified by a change. Therefore, in this case, [the notion of an effect] is advanced by way of a genus (*jāti*) conceived to be stable.

In the case of *cintā* (contemplation), the conventional usage of "being assisted" (*upakārya*) culminates solely in being an effect; whether this is taken in an ultimate sense or as having a single object, there is no fault. Thus, since proximity characterized by assistance must necessarily be admitted, the deviation from experience regarding those things assisted by the sun and so forth—which would otherwise follow—is common to both of us.
As for what Vācaspati says—that the natural relation between an individual and its universal does not depend upon any further assistance—that is not the case.

There is no such thing as a "natural" relation that is something entirely different from those already well-known; rather, it is within the category of relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth that there is a distinction in their occurrence based on whether the related terms are deviant or non-deviant, which is termed "conditional" (*aupādhika*) or "natural" (*svābhāvika*).
The so-called "relation" is merely a conventional designation. An investigation into this matter should be sought in the discussion on pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Just as the relation between an individual and its genus is innate because the former is never found apart from the latter, so too is the relation of the genus with the individual innate for that very same reason of non-deviation.

[216,7] According to the principle that "there can be no universal without a particular, like a rabbit's horn," [216,8] because there is no other proximity between those two, and because inherence (*samavāya*) is merely a conceptual construction,

[216,9] even if the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary does not exist between them— just as it does not exist between the earth and a seed— the rule of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra-niyama*) itself [is what constitutes their connection].

[216,10] For those who are addicted to the acceptance of difference, this is untenable due to the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For if there is assistance, either the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) thereof is invariably concomitant (*tannāntarīyaka*); thus, the meaning of non-deviation applies only here and not elsewhere, so there is no over-extension. [216,12] But in the absence of that [assistance], its avoidance is twofold: by resorting to the doctrine of essential nature (*svabhāvavāda*) or the power of inherence (*samavāya*). Not the first.

[216,13] This is a fallacious position (*pakṣa*), because it would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of overturning the perceived capacity of anything whatsoever. Furthermore, a perceived benefit (*upakāra*)—as in the case of fire, a craftsman, water, and so forth, being the non-deviant cause for smoke, a jar, and a crane—is indeed observed. The only distinction is that [the perception of such a cause] depends upon time, place, and other factors.

Therefore, by asserting that there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) solely due to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and not due to a causal efficacy, one necessarily excludes the existence of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). Second—
[216,16] And the position is untenable, because of the very non-existence of inherence (*samavāya*). For inherence is accepted as being established by the cognition "this is here";

[216,17] yet that cognition is not to be accepted by those whose vision is obscured by the mass of cataracts consisting in the grasping of conventional designations (*saṃketa*), because it would follow that everything would be established for everyone. [216,18] This is because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise under the sole control of mere desire, and so too for other people in the world.

In every case regarding the subject of dispute, that cognition does not exist at all, because of the absence of its cause. For the cause of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which discerns the distinction between the locative and nominative meanings as "this is here"—is the appearance of two objects whose forms are unmixed with one another. This is because, even when water exists in a jar, for one who perceives only the jar, that [cognition] is absent despite the presence of the entire collection of other causes.
Furthermore, such a state [of the jar] subsequently exists when there is the perception of only a second [object]. And yet, this appearance of duality does not occur.

In some cases, even regarding the locus of inherence (*samavāya*), the conceptualization of that [inherence] has as its object precisely the conceptualization of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Where there is no perception of both [relata] by way of excluding what is not their own nature, there is no cognition of "this is here" for one who is not insane, as in the case of a vessel and a jujube fruit when one is not perceived. And since there is no experience of the universal and the possessor of the universal through a distinction in the manifestation of the forms of self and what belongs to the self, this is a non-perception of the cause.

Because the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the two intended [terms] is established—just as in the case of smoke and fire—there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, those who imagine a different meaning by means of the term "self-made" (*svayaṃkṛta*) fall into the same error as the analogy of a horse's weight; this very point he will state [later]:
"And these words, such as 'the cloth is here in the threads' (*paṭas tantuṣv iha*)," and so forth, are themselves self-made. (PV II 149)

[217,3] Thus [it is argued]. But surely it has been stated that even a dual-natured entity (*vastu*) is apprehended by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-bodha*); so how is it that there is no manifestation of two natures (*svarūpa-dvaya-pratibhāsa*)? Therefore, the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is a most wretched argument. For when an object is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), an external instruction is not more authoritative. If you say, "The manifestation is likewise [non-existent]," then this follows: [217,5] ...then this has arrived.
While these five fingers are clearly manifest in direct perception,
he who perceives a sixth finger common to them all is like one who sees a horn upon his own head.

Thus, we who possess only the physical eye, even though we open our eyes as far as possible and examine [the matter] a hundred times, do not perceive anything else; yet for you, despite such an appearance through the grace of an unseen deity, there is no proof of the cognition of anything other than that.
Therefore, one should regard perception alone as that which shows a single object to multiple observers. Thus he speaks.

Trilocana, too, appears to have been wounded by another’s eye; for he says: "Even though a universal (*jāti*) is being perceived, because it does not exist in a location separate from the individual (*vyakti*), it is not seen as distinct from the individual, just like one individual is not seen as distinct from another. In this regard, by saying that the universal is seen but not as something distinct, he has effectively stated that it is necessarily within the scope of perception as non-distinct. And just as it is grasped by perception...

[217,14] For you alone, the object is entirely [particular]; indeed, there is no application of either sublation or proof therein. Consequently, the description of the logical justification—that the universal will differentiate itself from the individual through the recurrence of cognition—is without foundation. Furthermore, it is also incorrect to say that a tactile cognition differentiates touch from smell and so forth; for there is no [cognition] that perceives even smell and touch as non-differentiated.
[217,17] It is perceived directly.
[217,18] In that case, let it be explained that "it is not seen as distinct" means "it is not determined as distinct.
Even then, when it is said "the universal is being seen," is the intention to ask whether it is [seen] as distinct or non-distinct? If it is as non-distinct, then there is determination.

Whether it be through difference or non-difference, what is the point of this inquiry, since non-difference is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Or is it intended that they are seen as different? That, however, is impossible, because the absence of a difference in appearance has already been stated. If you argue that the difference in appearance is established by reasoning (*yukti*), then this is truly shameful; for:
When something that does not appear is established by means of the appearance of something else,
the claim that "this has no appearance" is not within the scope of logical reasoning.
This has been analyzed by us in the section on "Momentary Destruction" (p. 111), in the discussion concerning the non-existence of causeless entities.
Furthermore, if one were to accept that even when there is an appearance of a single form, another appearance must be established through reasoning, then [the fire] would not be hot.
The denotation "fire" is not sublated by perception, because even the appearance of non-heat is possible therein, just as the appearance of a universal is possible in an individual.
If it is argued that there is no parity because there is no proof for the appearance of non-heat in the case of fire (citrabhānu), nevertheless—

[218,6] Let there be doubt; how then can perception be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of that which is not hot, and how can there be an absence of a means of proof (*sādhanābhāva*), given that the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) exists? If it is argued that the logical reason (*hetu*) is non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*), then deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—whether direct or indirect—is also due to perception alone. And it has been stated that in that case, a contrary appearance cannot be negated. Furthermore, if [the reason is] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)...

[218,9] Because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), the non-heat [of fire] is not established; for that reason, due to a fault in the logical reason (*hetudoṣa*), the observation that "fire is not hot" is not a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), since it does not contradict the non-heat [of fire]. Furthermore, the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not perception (*adhyakṣa*). For what is hot is indeed hot; it is not both hot and not hot. Therefore, the awareness of a restricted appearance necessarily sublates the appearance of anything else.
This must be accepted even by one who is unwilling, for otherwise a confusion of activity would result. And thus:
"For this person, not seeing fire... and so forth.
Therefore, as those caught in the current proclaim: when a convention is established regarding individuals that possess a genus (*jāti*), wherever that genus is perceived...

The claim that there is a cognition of being denotable by those respective words in each instance merely mocks the sky with what is not even a thread, because that which is distinct from its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not perceived even in a dream. For this very reason, the validity of conceptual construction—which is held to join the qualifier and the qualified as they are grasped in their mere intrinsic forms—has been refuted, since previously it was shown that the perception of both [the universal and the particular] does not exist at all. Therefore, the non-perception of the cause is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, since there is no establishment of the cognition here, what talk can there be of inherence (*samavāya*)? Moreover, is this claim—that there is an innate connection between the manifestation and the universal—credible? Consequently, even if the doctrine of the difference between the attribute and its possessor is difficult to avoid, then even if proximity is characterized by assistance (*upakāra*), the capacity of that which perceives real entities lies only in the apprehension of what occupies the same location; thus, the avoidance of the deviation regarding subtle things that are assisted remains the same.

Therefore, since the nature of a thing is apprehended through even a single property, and thereby its entire essence is apprehended, where is there room for affirmation or negation by means of another word? Why, then, persist even now with the mere word "tree"? Consequently, where is the established distinction between generality and co-referentiality, or between qualifier and qualified? However, when—

When there is a separation of the connection between a single meaning, either the sound (dhvani) alone functions, or the gender (liṅga), or for you, the expressed object (vācya) is fragmented; in no case is there any real entity.

Because through the denotation of which [word], by the power of the thing itself, there is comprehension of the whole, a word—having a single substratum—becomes thus possessed of various results according to its divisions.

(PV I 129–30) For when a thing is the object of expression, it is impossible to apply affirmation or negation because it is understood in its entirety. However, when [the thing is apprehended] through beginningless false...

[219,5] By the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the habitual practice of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), cognition itself arises from the awakening of certain latent impressions, culminating in the form of the exclusion of one thing (*ekavyāvṛtti*).
In that case, what room is there for the aforementioned faults, which would arise if there were the capacity to grasp a real entity (*vastu*)?

For instance, when "tree" is uttered, by virtue of the appearance of a common form shared by *dhava*, *khadira*, and so forth, the universal (*sāmānya*) has as its ultimate reality the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣāpoha*).

It is established that this form (*rūpa*)—being non-rejected, appropriated, and characterized by distinctions such as existence (*sattā*), substance (*sattva*), and so forth—is dependent upon the employment of other words.

Thus, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "existent," "blue," and "moving" within a single substratum (*dharmin*), as if they were based on different properties. Furthermore, when there is a requirement to indicate a single distinction in accordance with the understanding of the intellect, there is the designation of a distinction, such as "the existence of the tree."

Thus, both types of the relationship between qualifier and qualified are established. This being so, just as in a tree, increase and decrease are observed due to contact with water and fire respectively, and because of the superimposition of identity, there arises the cognition: "This very same tree has become like this";
and although the properties capable of such connection have not arisen, it is determined as if it were connected to them—so too it is in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

[219,14] Even when no other object appears, the form of a tree is perceived as being capable of such [perception]; and in formulations such as "the blue is not fruit-bearing," that very same [form] appears as if undergoing increase and decrease, and is determined to be so. [219,15] However, an external object does not undergo increase and decrease at the time of the utterance of a word, even though it is in contact with water and the like. [219,16] And this [phenomenon] would not be tenable if the object were external, because [it occurs] according to how it appears.

Because it is not the reality, and because it does not appear according to its true nature; for this very reason, even with respect to distinct qualifiers, there is no occasion for the employment of another word, such as "Caitra’s cow," "the owner of cows," or "Maitra is not the owner of horses," since the appearance of increase or decrease produced by those [qualifiers] does not exist externally. Therefore, this is merely a play of the intellect (*buddhivilāsa*). And where this delusion occurs, it is indirectly inseparable from a real entity that excludes others (*anyāpoha*).

In that regard, people whose purpose is fulfilled by the performance of the desired causal function do not exert effort to infer such a specific distinction, nor are they capable of doing so; thus, their practical activity remains uninterrupted. Even in the case of a discrepancy, they do not establish that "this is false. Furthermore, it is not the case that at other times there is no external object as a referent, for even the authors of treatises can conceive of such an inference—so what need is there to mention others? Therefore, it is not [the case].
It is established that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not within the domain of words and the like.

Having apprehended a single substratum as the locus of various mutually exclusive properties, this primary cognition— which appears to involve the presence or absence of each one of those properties— deludes people just as they themselves are deluded.
Having attained fulfillment through the aspect of reality, he does not consider it to be an affliction.
Thus is the summary verse.

Nor does it belong to the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). For instance, in the sentence "Cows are grazing on the northern bank of the river," from the word "cow" (*go*), there appears a form consisting of letters—such as the dewlap, horns, and tail—which, because it does not refer to the distinctions among members of the same class, is for the most part a unified whole; yet that itself is not the universal.
Indeed, "cowness" (*gotva*) is said to be empty of color, shape, syllables, and form;

nor does anything else appear [therein], like space. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the conceptualizations of "cowness" and "horseness" would be indistinguishable. For that very thing—which consists merely of the aspect of blazing radiance—is, despite being utterly distinct from every individual particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), [perceived as such].

That which is being unified is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*). However, that universal is not identical to those [individuals], because it follows after them elsewhere by way of being a mental aspect (*buddhyākāra*). For the treatise states:
"And how could that which is non-different from cognition become a separate object? (PV I 71cd)

Furthermore, in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— such as "this is that," "this is like that," or "this is a cow"— which arises immediately after sensory perception and is considered to be produced by the sense organ and the object, there is no appearance of an external object. Rather, just as one joins an internal, super-sensory,
synthesized form appearing within oneself to an object appearing before one, so too, because that external thing does not exist, this is nothing but an illusion, like [the perception of] hair-tufts.

[220,16] Like light. [220,17] If it is argued that this is so because of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), [we reply: surely there is a discrepancy regarding a mass of hair because of the absence of resistance when a hand is intentionally directed toward it; but in the case at hand, if there is an experiencer, is not that very experience of the manifestation and the manifested the subverting proof? What else could it be?

[220,19] As for the other [point], it has already been stated that people lack the capacity for discernment. Or how is it that even today the absence of resistance (*pratighāta*) and so forth does not constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*)? For those very things, such as horns and the like, though situated in their respective places with indistinct forms and lacking a fixed spatial state, appear even now as if they were being conflated—possessing infinite forms due to differences in place, time, and so on. Regarding them, [the objection of] resistance and so forth—
Since it is fixed, what kind of distinction could there be from hair and the like, such that one might say there is no sublation here?
Therefore, let this be a transformation (*vivarta*) of cognition itself into that form by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); or let that form appear as something non-existent;
or let the individuals themselves appear otherwise through the exclusion of internal differences within their own class, because of the intervention of experience.
Or let it be called a lapse of memory; in any case, this talk of a "universal" (sāmānya) with respect to the external world is nothing but an error.

Moreover, it is logical that it should arise from the experience of the object present before one as "this," since it is produced by the perception of the thing standing in front. Now, the causes of error—such as cataracts, rapid rotation, and so forth—which produce a distortion of the sense faculties, have indeed been enumerated; yet not even one of these is present here.

How can this error be accidental? Or do you think that those are the causes of only non-conceptual error, while this is a mental error? Even that [mental error] is based solely on the perception of similarity between the superimposed object and the locus of superimposition;
since such a distinction does not exist, how can there be even a mental error? Furthermore, all error is based solely on similarity.

Indeed, it cannot possibly occur even in another birth without the perception of something similar. Furthermore, since nothing with a mixed form has ever been seen even in another birth, how could there be a superimposition of that? Oh, what great human prowess! For if, as stated in the preceding sequence, the lack of an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*) cannot be avoided, then whether one engages in the conventional usage of "error" or not, that much alone [is sufficient].
[221,10] Since the point under discussion is already established, why this insistence here?
[221,11] Furthermore, that which was stated regarding its being causeless is incorrect, because you too must necessarily admit a difference in the causal complex (*janakasāmagrī*).
[221,12] Otherwise, how could the sense faculty and the object, which are observed to be restricted to the production of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*), produce conceptualization?

[221,13] Is it produced from that? Therefore, this causal complex (*sāmagrī*), possessing a capacity exceeding [the sum of its parts] through the cooperation of the memory of the previous perception of the lump, produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The meaning is that it produces a cognition devoid of an object (*nirviṣaya*), because the nature of conceptualization is established as being objectless with respect to that [external] part. Thus, it is better [to regard it] as indeed distinct from the experience (*anubhava*) which has a vivid appearance, just like a conceptual construction of a different class (*vijātīya-vikalpa*).

It is better to say that there is also a conceptualization of the similar (*sajātīyavikalpa*); therefore, the establishment of a universal (*jāti*) does not result from direct perception (*adhyakṣa*).

Nor does it result from inference (*anumāna*), because the relation of cause and effect cannot be grasped by anyone through the very domain of direct perception, as is the case with fire and smoke. However, regarding the production of cognition in general, there must be another cause beyond those causes already observed.

That which is to be depended upon might perhaps be established as being like a sense faculty, if it could demonstrate the absence of the intended effect—namely, cognition—at some time, even when all other causes are present. But this is not possible in the case at hand. For if one were to show the absence of the cognition of a cow either within another lump or in the interval between them, then the absence of the cognition of a cow would be logically accounted for by the non-existence of the cow-lump itself.

How could it imply dependence on another entity, such that there might be the expectation that "this very thing is cowness"? But surely, it is precisely because of the universal *gotva* (cowness) that this is a "cow-body" (*gopiṇḍa*); otherwise, even a horse-body would be a cow-body. If that is so, then the universal *gotva* must also arise from the cow-body itself; otherwise, even horseness (*turagatva*) would be cowness. This is the same [in both cases]. It is not so.

Furthermore, it is impossible to ascertain the existence or non-existence of such a universal anywhere, just as one cannot ascertain them for an individual object (*piṇḍa*); therefore, this argument is of no consequence.

Now, it might be argued: "If, due to the absence of a Bāhuleya individual, there is no cognition of 'cow' in a horse, then let there likewise be none in a Śābaleya [cow], since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not persist anywhere. It is true that the particular characteristic does not persist; however, just as it [persists] within its own kind—

In a cognizer who possesses the memory of having seen another individual body, there is the capacity to produce a reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*) of that form in the case of Bāhuleya, and likewise in the case of Śābaleya as well. Therefore, it is not only a single cow-individual (*gopiṇḍa*), but rather all individuals whatsoever that ascend into such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Consequently, there is no cognition of "cow" with respect to a horse.

[222,3] But surely, since capacity (*sāmarthya*) is power (*śakti*), it is simply a genus (*jāti*) that is being spoken of. For is that power distinct or non-distinct [from the individual]? If it were non-distinct, then—like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—it would not be pervasive; thus, no other [individual] would be capable. If, on the other hand, it were distinct and common to others, then it is merely a genus; the dispute is over the name alone. To this it is replied: it is indeed non-distinct.

[222,6] With respect to each individual thing: just as one entity possesses a nature capable [of producing an effect], what kind of fault does another entity, being likewise existent, bring about? For just as in your view, even a single universal (*jāti*) is the cause for the production of identical cognitions and verbal expressions, and another [universal] is also so by its very own nature because it lacks any other universal; so too, in our view, even a particular (*vyakti*), though distinct, is the cause by its very own nature independently [of anything else]. Therefore...
But the nature of manifestation is bound to a succession of causes.

As for what Trilocana says— that the inherence (*samavāya*) of universals and particulars, such as "horseness" and "cowness," in their own substrata is the cause of the designation and cognition "universal"— that is refuted by the very rejection of inherence.

Alternatively, it may be that inherence (*samavāya*) itself, by its very own nature, is the cause; thus, there is no damage to the illustrative example. Nor is there a mutual causal capacity between the universal (*jāti*) and inherence through the postulation of their acting together; for in that case, since even a single entity would possess generative power by its own nature, one would be casting away the very designation of "universal" and the cognition thereof. For it is precisely seeds and the like, which are generative by their own nature, that possess auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

[222,15] Since "completeness" (*sākalya*) is a capacity based on limiting conditions (*aupādhikī śakti*), the fact that [the cause] produces by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) must necessarily be asserted; thus, the reliance upon *samavāya* (inherence) is a deception. [222,16] Furthermore, in the absence of that [cause's] operation, the arising of a cognition bearing that form does not occur from other causes alone; otherwise, why would one not consider that even a cognition with a recurring form (*anuvṛttākāra*) is produced by the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves, rather than by a universal (*jāti*)? [222,17] Thus, even the very notion of a universal is undermined.

It would be as if one were scraping away the very root. Even if [the universal] were accidental (*ākasmika*), that same fault remains; thus, by placing a foot upon the neck of the proponent of the universal, [we ask]:

since the universal must be made to accept its own operation through its own nature within the recurring cognition—out of fear of infinite regress—and since it must be made to accept other universals that have not themselves been superimposed, how can inherence (*samavāya*) serve as a remedy? Furthermore, that [inherence] would require an additional auxiliary factor.
Whether it be so or not, the universal (*jāti*), being independent of the individuals, is capable by its own nature to produce a recurring cognition;

since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be questioned, one cannot state—without the command of kings—that it is the individual (*vyakti*) [that produces it]. By this, it is explained how this recurrence of cognition, which follows a recurring entity, occurs in respect to individuals that are absolutely distinct.

The proposal that [the universal] must exist as following upon the state of being the object of a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*)—which is excluded from those things that follow upon the state of being the object of an exclusive cognition (*vyāvṛttapratyaya*)—is also refuted;
for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of individuals themselves, which are manifested as mutually exclusive yet are grasped by a recurring cognition with respect to their universals.

If it is argued that "since universals are not perceived, where could there be a recurring cognition such that there would be a deviation?", we say no, because this contradicts your own accepted position.

Because it is established by this sequence: for indeed, the recurrence of conditions is adduced to prove the existence of a recurring entity; and if that [recurrence] is inseparable from the absence of a recurring entity, who—other than a fool—is able to point out this contradiction? Furthermore, even regarding imagined universals (*jāti*), the fallacy of deviation remains exactly as it was; what more is there to say here?

[223,4] By means of perception? [223,5] Or is a restriction stated regarding objects currently being perceived? No; for even there, because there is no subverting factor that contradicts the contrary, a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is untenable. Furthermore, since deviation is observed in general, there is a seed of doubt regarding other cases as well. And if...

The exclusion of deviation from the universal (*sāmānya*) is made with respect to a specific visible object; in that case, one should not say: "That recurrence of designation and cognition which occurs among distinct things is caused by a recurring entity, just as the recurrence of designation and cognition regarding 'thread' occurs among flowers, so too the recurrence of designation and cognition as 'cow' occurs among distinct cows. For [the recurrence of] designation [occurs] only when there is a visible cause.

Because there is a pervasion [of the concept] by virtue of its being based on a recurring object due to the recurrence of the conditions (*pratyaya*), there is a necessity for it to find rest [in that object]. And this is logical. For indeed, even in the case of a sutra, there is no recurrence of the sutra’s conditions with respect to things not made objects of vision. Since conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—which possesses a real basis (*savastuka*)—is established as having the perception of a real thing as its effect, when [the concept] is withdrawn through the non-perception of the cause by way of the contrapositive (*viparyaya*), the recurring [conceptualization]...

The pervasion of the recurrence of verbal designations and cognitions by an entity rests solely upon the fact that they have a perceptible object as their cause, provided that they actually have an entity as their object.
However, when there is a dispute regarding whether they have an entity as their object, this rule does not hold.
Furthermore, as for the subverting argument against the contrary position stated by him—that the recurrence of verbal designations and cognitions must cease from something—[it is refuted as follows].

[223,15] “It occurs only in certain instances and possesses a cause; nor is there any other cause,” and so forth. That is not correct. For it has already been established that even without a recurring [universal], there must necessarily be an acceptance of a specific intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) excluded from what is not that [nature], because the recurrence of denotation and cognition occurs [therein]. Therefore, just as a universal such as "cowness" or "horseness" is [recognized] only by excluding particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), [so too is the universal "universal"] recognized.
[223,18] Thus, the recurrence of designations and cognitions occurs due to some kind of proximity; let it be the same in the case of individuals as well.

[223,19] By this, when a recurring entity is to be proven, the recurrence of designations and cognitions serves as the reason, and its pervasion is established by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) which subverts the contrary. Therefore, both [the reason and the example] should be understood as inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, there is no other such thing as "proximity."

Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is distinct [from the universal]. For just as "cowness" is excluded from the generality of horses, so too are "horseness," "substantiality," and so forth; likewise, just as one individual cow is excluded from cowness, so too is another. Regarding the difficulty of considering whether this exclusion is different or non-different, the answer is the same as in the case of causal capacity (*śakti*). Consequently, those objects which, through exclusion of what they are not, are mutually proximate, produce a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*) when another is perceived immediately after the perception of one among them, and no others. And that very thing is causal capacity; it is not...
[The entity] has birth as its nature. Otherwise, since that [nature] would exist even in a single instance, auxiliary causes would be useless.
(PV I 164cd) This point should be understood from the discussion on momentary destruction and auxiliary causes; and that proximity is a causal succession.

It was stated immediately above that [the universal] has arrived. Furthermore, one must necessarily postulate a specific proximity produced by causes, on account of which only certain individuals become the substratum or receptacle for a genus, while others do not. Otherwise, if it were otherwise, the statement that "an effect possessing a restricted genus arises from the restriction of the causal complex" would be a mere triviality for the *Bhūṣaṇa*.
And this being so:

"Since the difference is equal [in all cases], let that very same proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by which a universal (*jāti*) extends to some [individuals] and not others be the basis for words and cognitions. (PV I 162)
[224,9] What is the use of "birth" (jāti) here?

[224,10] Furthermore, regarding what was said by him as another faulty objection: it is not the case that there is no such thing as proximity (pratyāsatti), by which a staff, a thread, and so forth, extend to a certain place and not elsewhere; for that very same proximity [accounts for] the state of being a "staff-bearer" or a "threaded" object in the case of a person, a crystal, and so on.

[224,12] Let there be a basis for conventional usage; what need is there for a staff, a string, and so forth? When would this be appropriate? Only if some capacity established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were denied in some instance. For instance, proximity—which depends on causes such as the impulse to approach—is established by perception and other means of valid cognition as the cause of movement toward a man or a crystal in the case of a staff or a string. Likewise, the experience of the person or the crystal conjoined with those [staffs or strings]—

Furthermore, the basis for the cognition of a "staff-bearer" is established for a cognizer who possesses the recollection of convention; however, this cognition of a "cow" is not observed to follow the presence or absence of the entity "cowness. Rather, it is merely like groping in the dark with one's hands, and someone might think that there must be some such basis for the cognition of a cow. In that case, if one must necessarily accept another alternative mode [of explanation]:

If that [independent existence] is established, there would be no sublation; so why is it said that this is due to a more cumbersome conceptualization? Otherwise, having imagined even that, one could not avoid imagining hundreds of useless things. However, if—as is observed in the case of a person and the like—the proximity of a staff and so forth follows the presence or absence [of the cause] such as the cognition of approach, and if the experience of the proximity of a staff and so forth in a person and the like is indeed observed—

The cognition of "the one who is to be punished" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth follows the presence or absence of the actual object; likewise, the function of the causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*) lies solely in the fact that it possesses a determinate genus (*niyatajātikatā*), not in the unifying reflection (*ekāmarśa*). Furthermore, if there were such a unifying reflection, this very genus would have to be experienced as being currently active; in that case, the fault would belong to the one who denies it. However, this is merely a conventional designation (*samayamātra*), since it has been established that the genus transcends direct experience.

Thus, from where does this objection regarding its futility arise? It would also have to take things such as a staff and so forth as its object. In this manner, a refutation should be inferred for other similar counter-arguments as well. Now, suppose the inference is formulated as follows: "Whatever is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇagrahaṇa*); for example, the cognition of a man with a staff (*daṇḍijñāna*). And this cognition, 'This is a cow,' is a qualified cognition. This is, in effect, a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*). For in the example, the cognition is seen to be the effect of the experience of the qualifier.

[225,3] "The qualified cognition is established"—herein lies the inquiry: is it to be proven that the qualified cognition is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of a distinct qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), or is it to be proven that it is necessarily preceded by the mere experience of the qualifier? In the first case, the thesis is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), which leaves no room for the application of the proof; for in perception, which grasps the actual object, there is no appearance of both [the qualifier and the qualified as separate]. This is because it is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*).

Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) "being a universal" (*sāmānya*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because [the relation] is observed even without the apprehension of distinct qualifiers, as in the cases: "the jar has its own nature" (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*) or "cowness is a universal" (*gotvaṃ sāmānyam*). In the second case, however, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the relationship between qualifier and qualified is accepted by resorting to an imagined distinction—as in "the individual possesses the universal cowness" (*gotvajātimān piṇḍaḥ*)—just like the expression "the jar has its own nature. This is because [the cognition] is an experience excluded from non-cows (*agovyāvṛtta*).

[225,9] Because of its cultivation, there is the conventional usage "this is white. Thus, in verbal and other types of cognition, there is no appearance of either the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) or the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the universal is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) should be considered in the same manner.

[225,12] If this is so, then how is it that the treatise is consistent when it says: [225,13] "First, the primary meaning is expressed by words"? [225,14] For that [primary meaning] is not actually conveyed by it, nor is there a manifestation of it in the cognition of it.
Some say that there is a connection [between the two], [stating]: "it is superimposed.

The conventional usage of objects is twofold: by way of appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and by way of determination (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, in this case, even though there is an absence of appearance, [there is a determination] of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as excluded from others (*parāpoha*).

Objectivity was stated to consist in mere determination (*adhyavasāya*). And thus, because one proceeds toward the very thing (*vastu*) itself by means of that determination even from that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [it is so]. Now, what is this so-called "determination" other than conceptual construction, given that there is no difference in meaning between "that which is conceptually constructed" and "that which is determined"?

Therefore, how can there be a designation of a distinction as "by means of determination from conceptual construction"? Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not [the object] excluded from others (*anyāpoha*).

When conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) manifests, it is determined as "conceptually constructed" (*vikalpita*). What logic is there here by which, depending upon that determination, even that [external object] is established as the object of conceptual construction? Furthermore, if the external is not the object of conceptual construction, yet its apprehension is said to be through association with a word, this is difficult to reconcile. Moreover, since that [association] does not exist within the self, there would be no such thing as conceptual construction at all.

[225,24] For what purpose, then, is there this consideration of an object? If activity were to proceed from a word when the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been apprehended, it would follow without distinction in all cases, because there would be no distinction since everything remains unapprehended. Consequently, even the attainment of the intended object would not occur with certainty; thus, inference (*anumāna*) as well would be subject to error.

To this it is replied: It is true that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) have the same object; however, the term "conceptual construction" is based on the association with words and so forth, whereas determination is based on the capacity for engagement even with respect to what has not been grasped. And although the entire universe is ungrasped, nevertheless, activity is restricted to a specific object because conceptual construction possesses a restricted form. This restriction—

For entities that are capacities have their natures established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and do not admit of the objection regarding the confusion of capacities, just like the arising of what was previously non-existent.

For even though everything is non-existent therein, only a sprout arises from a seed, because its capacity for that [specific effect] has been determined by valid cognition. Likewise, here too, for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form of fire for one who seeks the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of the object "fire," [the capacity is likewise established].

For one who possesses the memory of that [fire], how could the capacity for activity directed toward the object of fire—which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—be subject to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?
Furthermore, through the consideration of proximity, even though the actual fire has a blazing and radiant form, so too does the representation in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

To that extent, the power of the conceptualization of fire to prompt activity resides only in that [fire] and not in water or other things. Nor does it prompt activity through the superimposition of similarity.

We reply: there is no opportunity for the critique that an external form is superimposed upon the external, nor for the critique regarding the form itself. What then? That cognition, arising solely through the maturation of its own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), extends its activity toward the external even though it does not perceive the external;
thus, it is indeed erroneous (*vipluta*).
As for the treatise:
"And the delusion regarding place does not apply equally to cognition, because it arises from the intellect;
for such a [delusion] is not admitted in that case, since the intellect is otherwise. (PV III 13)

Thus, it is not the case that [the cognition] proceeds by way of superimposition (āropa), as in the case of silver and so forth; rather, it is due to the restriction of the power bound to the arising of such a form.

This is just as a rice seed is the material cause (upādāna) for its effect, the rice sprout—even though the latter arises without any persistence of the former—because the stability of the status of "rice-ness" and so forth has been refuted by the critique of permanence. Furthermore, this does not mean that the investigator, while determining [the object], fails to see the thing itself.

The consequence of non-occurrence is consistent; for even in the case of perception, activity is accompanied by purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and the attainment of purposeful action occurs only when there is a necessary restriction to the existence of a real entity (*vastu*). That restriction, just as it is established through perception by way of a direct connection with the entity, is likewise established through a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by way of a causal succession; thus, inference is not without a firm basis. However, in the case of verbal testimony, because there may be doubt regarding the object, even the attainment [of the goal] is uncertain.

In this regard, there is no fixed rule. Therefore, "determined" (*adhyavasitam*) means that even though there is no appearance [of the external object], it has been made the object of activity. Consequently, even if there is no appearance in conceptual cognition, what is determined is not sublated by the external [object]. This very point is the meaning of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, and of the teaching on the apprehension of non-difference. And therefore, that [external object] is not cognized by that [conceptual cognition].

It has been shown that the objection—that there is no appearance of non-difference—is untenable, because the demonstration of its meaning has already been established. Just as the ascertainment "and this is fire here" gives rise to physical activity, so too does it give rise to verbal activity, such as "fire has been perceived by me. It also produces mental activity in the form of a subsequent ascertainment (*anuvyavasāya*) having that very aspect. This being the case, just as by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),...

The certainty that "this object has been apprehended," as well as the thought that it has been "conjoined with a word," occurs because the form of the word flashes forth just like a trace of the form of the object. Therefore, as long as a person possesses the conceit of apprehending an object, they likewise possess the conceit of apprehending it as conjoined with a designation;
thus, the establishment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows merely from the inclination of such a determination, and not from reality.
And it is said:
"Nowhere, whether externally or within the mind, does a contact with words occur; rather, a mere fragment of the form of an object flashes forth, permeated by the shapes of syllables."
Although both "selves" are merely the determinations of the intellect itself, the state of conceptual construction nevertheless posits them as being external and as residing in words.

For this very reason, with respect to the conventional person whose mind is withered by pride regarding that [conceptual nature], the qualification "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is employed in the definition of perception; even according to the Sūtra, there is a distinction indicated by the statement that [perception arises] "from conceptualization through determination" (*adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, in that context, this term "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) is not used as a designation for the conceptual construction itself as the subject (*dharmin*), but rather for the act of determination residing therein.

[227,13] Regarding the characteristic of a phenomenon (*dharma*): this is the meaning. Even when [the object] is not seen, that which is called "fitness for engagement" is a phenomenon; through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is engagement by means of that [fitness].

If the object is known and established through determination (*adhyavasāya*) in terms of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), then the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the object is also obtained; thus, it is logical that being an object consists in mere determination.
Therefore it has been said:
"The object is one, but it is denoted through superimposition.
As the author of the Bhāṣya stated:
[227,19] How is it that it has that as its object? Because it functions toward it.

(PVA***) As for the objection, "How can there be engagement with what is unperceived? and the subsequent lion’s roar stating that engagement occurs everywhere precisely with the unperceived, we have not elaborated upon that here for fear of making the book too voluminous.

Thus, regarding the statement "because one acts through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within one's own appearance," here too, while there is an object within one's own appearance, the "determination" is as previously explained; however, the "object" is said to be the external thing capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). By its negation, the "non-object" (*anartha*) is the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*).
In this way, it should be regarded as both "a real entity" and "non-existent. And this has been clarified by the very words of the *Vārttika*:

In the *Sākārasiddhi*: "The activity of inference is by means of the determination of an object" (*arthādhyavasāyena pravṛttir anumānasya*)—this too has the meaning that inference is the determination of an object (*arthādhyavasāyānumāna*).
However, as for the explanation of the term *ekākāra* (single form) here, one should consult its exposition in the *Svāpohasiddhi*; we have not presented it here for fear of excessive prolixity.

If, then, the external object is the denotable [referent] by way of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), how is it so for the form of the cognition (*buddhyākāra*)? Regarding this, the treatise states: “The referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) is established through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*). It is a threefold property-bearer (*dharmī*), based on existence, non-existence, or both. (PV III 204–205)
And so forth.
It is bound to the conceptual reflections that are based upon those [particulars];
therefore, because it is based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the word is said to effect the exclusion of others.

"That reflection of the object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct [from the cognition itself], even that is not the essence of the object; it is an error arising from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (PV II 164–165) For it is impossible to assert that there is a determinative engagement (*adhyavasāya*) with respect to the form within the cognition itself, because such engagement is established only with respect to the object of purposeful action (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*).
And since that which seeks causal efficacy is indeed external, he says:
"Another object appears as the denotable.

The meaning is that it is the mental aspect (*buddhyākāra*) which is other than the external. This is because in the cognition produced by words and so forth, only the mental aspect appears. Therefore...

Thus, it is said that the object is so called because it is like form being the object of the eye; the point is that it is not [an object] by way of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). And it has been stated:
"This referent of a word is described according to how it is perceived, even though it does not exist" (PV III 83).

It is said to "not exist" because, in accordance with its appearance, it lacks external existence, and because this reflection is considered from the perspective of something directed toward the external.
[228,21] By way of context: this very point is that [the object] is not real according to how it is determined (*adhyavasāya*), and it is not determined according to its actual reality (*tattva*).

[228,22] Since "determination" (*adhyavasāya*) is a synonym for "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), the meaning is that it is established as an object according to the manifestation of conceptual construction. Even in the case of the manifestation of non-existent objects and so forth, the fact that they do not exist externally is precisely what constitutes the object, in accordance with how it is perceived. Furthermore, even its status as an error is only in relation to the external; thus, everything [is explained].

[229,1] It is unconfused. However, it is not correct to assert the non-existence of that which is the object of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) on the grounds that it is of the nature of cognition, as is the case with the appearance of hair and so forth. For this very reason, even though it is expressible, [229,3] neither the aspect (*ākāra*) nor the external object is established by way of affirmation in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).

[229,4] Even conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), it is only external; however, not even conventionally can there be affirmation or negation by means of words and so forth regarding a form (*ākṛti*). [229,6] For there is no application of affirmation or negation by means of words and so forth toward a form that is free from doubt, self-cognized, and [therefore] lacks a [verbalizable] aspect, because such an effort would be futile and incapable [of effecting anything]. Nor [can there be affirmation or negation] regarding an external object that does not appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because if the object is not apprehended, for what [could there be affirmation or negation]?

Would it be an affirmation or a negation? Therefore, just as an external tree is established as the denotable object of the word "tree" through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), so too, through that very conceptual determination, an affirmation or negation regarding the external is conventionally expressed. Even when, due to some particular context, an investigation is conducted by taking up a certain mental form (*buddhyākāra*) through another conceptualization, even then, from that conceptualization—

Affirmation and negation pertain only to the external world; for "it is by discriminating that object that one falls [into error]," so says the treatise. Therefore, in reality, there is neither affirmation nor negation for either [of the two]; for it is only the external that exists conventionally.
And these two [affirmation and negation] are difficult to avoid, for otherwise there would be the consequence of the collapse of conventional discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*).

By this, the claim made by the commentator—that affirmation and negation have as their objects an "external-ness" that is superimposed—is shown to be unworldly, lacking scriptural authority, and contrary to logic; for [such a view] cannot exist without relying upon the two truths: the conventional and the ultimate.

There is a certain established position. In this regard, it is first of all not conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), because that [conventional reality] consists in the conceit of the world (*lokābhimāna*).

And for the world, the meaning of an external word—whether enjoined or prohibited—is a pervasive basis for engagement and withdrawal, occurring without distinction; the world does not touch upon such things as the "externality" of a superimposed object. Nor is this ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), for that which is inexpressible...
Affirmation and negation do not apply to anything in reality; such is the scriptural tradition (*āgama*). Nor is there any other direction for reasoning (*tarka*).

Furthermore, affirmation and negation do not apply to that which is not determinable (*anadhyavaseya*), nor is there determination (*adhyavasāya*) from a word regarding anything other than the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); this is proclaimed by you yourself. Therefore, what follows from this regarding the affirmation and negation of an imputed externality? [It follows only] from appearance and determination—

And through all these gateways, the established order fails to touch reality (*tattva*). In that regard, neither that which is superimposed (*āropita*) nor that which possesses the status of being externally superimposed is the object of appearance (*pratibhāsa*), nor is it the object of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*). To begin with, that which is superimposed does not touch appearance, as he himself has stated: "Superimposition occurs at the same time as the experience of the mental image (*ullekha*); it is non-apparent in form and is a non-entity (*avastu*) that is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)."

Thus, for this very reason, its externality also does not appear, because that is a property of the [external object]. As for the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), since it is restricted solely to the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), it does not belong to these two; so enough of raising this issue.
Even what is called "superimposed" (*āropita*) is merely said to be "imagined" (*kalpita*); and the function of imagining consists in both the appearance and the conceptual determination.

[230,5] There are two [aspects]. Whence then does this other heap called "superimposed" (āropita) arise? Therefore, reflection is appropriate only by means of the external basis for the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*), through both the conventional and the ultimate [truths]. And when there is a desire to express such causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), why resort to a circuitous and difficult path? Enough of this excessive insistence. This is established: [the object exists] through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) as external, but through manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) as the form of cognition.

"It is said that 'the state of being expressible by words' is asserted. Now, if you explain it in this way, you have accepted the expressibility of the entire range of both categories of objects; so how is it that this [verse] was introduced for the purpose of establishing the ineffability of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanirabhilāpyatā*)? To this he says:
"It is established."

This is merely a formal convention established with a specific purpose: that "denotability" consists in mere conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) or mere appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Thus, for one who apprehends the establishment of reality simply by taking external objects as referents, the object is said to be the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), which is intended solely to avoid the accumulation of limiting conditions (*upādhi*); such is the form of the exclusion of others.

The statement that "the object of conceptual construction is its own nature" is intended as the ultimate refutation of all external objects; it does not, however, imply that the status of being an object finds its final rest within itself.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
Why is this so? Because even when the status of being an object is established in various instances, it is not intended that the process should find its final rest therein.
[230,17] However, he states that the intent is the exclusion of other [possibilities]:

[230,18] "In reality, there is no object at all to be expressed" [230,19]. For a manifestation accompanied by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) is, from the perspective of conventional practice, the cognition of an object of knowledge in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*).

It brings [the object] into the state of being an object of perception, just like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For a mere appearance that is devoid of determination (*avasāya*), or whose function is occupied by another determination, cannot establish an object for one who desires to act; it is like the touch of grass to a passing person, or like the superimposition of water upon a mirage. Nor can mere determination, devoid of appearance, suffice—just like the superimposition of water itself. Therefore, [it is] through action...

The determination of an object is pervaded by its fitness; thus, the absence of both [the object and its cognition], being sublated by the absence of the pervader, is necessarily connected to the presence of both. When one [of the two] is admitted to be absent, that [determination] is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). That which does not appear in a cognition, or that which is not determined by it, is not its object—just as a horse is not the object of the cognition of a cow. And [the external object] does not appear in verbal cognition.

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not ascertained by this mental form; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been established, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Even though it is observed that activity and the status of being an object occur through mere appearance even in the case of extreme habituation, nevertheless, that very habituation does not exist without ascertainment; therefore, the agency for that belongs to ascertainment alone. Consequently, that which is not ascertained by something [cannot be its object].
[231,2] The qualification "when there is practice" must be required.

[231,3] But surely even in the case of perception, there is no determination of a grasped moment, but rather of a continuum (*santati*); and since this [continuum] does not appear [in perception], by what means could it have an object? For [the object] is absent in both the moment and the continuum. In the case of inference, however, there is indeed examination (*parīkṣā*).
[231,5] It proceeds; yet there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for which some object exists by way of the possibility of both [means], so this is impossible.
[231,6] Thus, when each one individually establishes [the object], the status of the object as established belongs to the entirety of the external or internal, which is what is to be expressed.

[231,7] To this it is replied: he states the determination of reality (*tattvavyavasthā*); the status of being an object occurs precisely through the possibility of both, but merely in a conventional sense (*sāṃvyavahārika*).

In relation to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), it is designated as "truth" (*tattva*) by depending upon a lower convention; for when one enters into the distinction of moments, conventional discourse would be destroyed, since from the perspective of worldly convention there is no absence of momentary decay. In ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), however, both are absent according to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the apprehension of non-difference between the perceived and the conceptualized is indeed certain.

If it is argued that the fire is thus determined because it has indeed appeared [in perception], we say no; for the delusion regarding that appearance has been dispelled by the recollection of another appearance. Furthermore, just as it is possible to demonstrate that the appearance of a real object (*vastu*) in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) is entirely distinct from its own [conceptual] appearance, so too there is no appearance of a real object other than the appearance in direct perception (*adhyakṣa*); for the appearance of the real object finds its rest in that very [perceptual] appearance.
It would be better to exclude the appearance of an entity that is of a different class from it. Therefore, it is rightly said:
"In reality, nothing at all can be established as expressible.
Alternatively, even if it is not expressible as a distinct entity, exclusion (*apoha*) is understood therein as its qualifier.
[231,17] The status of exclusion (*apoha*) as the denotable object is indeed accepted. Nevertheless, how can there be the ineffability of all phenomena (*sarvadharmānabhilāpyatva*)? To this he says:
[231,18] "In reality, no object whatsoever is denotable.

[231,19] This is the intended meaning: first, according to the position of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), its status as a denotable object is likewise produced merely by cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*), just like the nature of a real entity (*vastu*).

It is not [unreal] because of its appearance, as in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, in the case of the negative position (*prasajyapakṣa*), there is no difference even at other times regarding the mere exclusion of the other;

nevertheless, since this is not the [actual] object, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Alternatively, that which is [stated] in the treatise—therefore, it is established that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have as their object the non-differentiation of all words; this is the summary. He demonstrates its grounding in the [actual] object by means of that very summary.
"In reality, no object whatsoever is expressible.
This is stated because, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), expressibility is shown to exist merely through appearance and conceptual determination;
therefore, he specifies "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*).

This is the meaning: that which was concluded in the treatise as "only exclusion (viveka) is to be expressed" does not have "exclusion" itself as its expressed object; rather, just as the statement "non-existence comes to be" has the meaning "existence does not come to be," so too the expression "the expressibility of exclusion" has the meaning "the exclusion of expressibility. And it has been demonstrated that this very point has been made clear by the treatise itself through the analysis of the three reasons and other means.

Thus, when the question is asked, "In what way is exclusion (*apoha*) the denotation of a word?", the answer is: "By virtue of its being a quality of that [exclusion], according to the meaning as previously stated. Then, when the question is asked, "Why are the mental image (*buddhyākāra*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) not the denotations?", the responses are given in order: "Because of the absence of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those, the appearance (*pratibhāsa*), or both. However, when the inquiry is: "What is it that is denoted by words?"—

In that case, because there is a determination of an object based on a mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*), or alternatively, having conceptualized it as "in reality," the form of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) residing within the conceptual construction is [the object]; since there is no such thing as a particular characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha-svalakṣaṇa*), the responses are given precisely in this sequence.

Therefore, the establishment of the fact that words and logical marks have exclusion (*apoha*) as their objective domain is intended primarily to demonstrate that all phenomena (*dharma*) are inexpressible.
[232,11] Conclusion of the meaning of the first verse.
[232,12] Let there be this proliferation of arguments regarding apoha for the clever; however, the failure of the actual nature of the thing (vastu) to manifest is the vital point.
[232,13-14] In that case, when it is not perceived, everything collapses without effort.
But when it is firmly established, is its excellence not indeed achieved by that much alone?
[232,16] This direction has been elucidated by us in a concise manner;
[232,17] its full elaboration, however, should be sought in the source itself. [232,18]

[243] In the section on the Refutation of the Doctrine of Īśvara, there is a concise refutation for those who fear the composition of a treatise that would require a commentary on the *Vārtikasaptaślokī*.
This is merely a brief discussion of the refutations regarding the doctrine of God.

In this case, although the agent of effort has demonstrated the mere concomitance of the effect for the most part, and has also shown its absence in some instances where that [effort] is absent, nevertheless, because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established, there remains the suspicion that even if something is an effect, it might not be preceded by an intelligent agent.
