Thus, when "effect" is adduced as the reason to prove "intelligent agency," it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) whose exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful, due to the lack of a subverting counter-argument (*bādhaka*).

Nor can the mere observation of the presence [of the probans] in similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the non-observation of its absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) constitute the proof of a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which is denoted by the term "necessary connection" (*pratibandha*)—in the form that "whenever the probans exists, the probandum necessarily exists," or "when the probandum is absent, the probans is absent. This is because such pervasion is observed even in cases where a future deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is known to occur. For one who merely observes coexistence and possesses a reflective mind, it is simply impossible to determine whether this current non-observation of deviation is due to its actual absence, or rather due to the lack of the convergence of the conditions for its observation.

For this very reason, even Vācaspati’s proclamation of an "intrinsic relation" (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is merely a verbal embellishment, as it does not nourish any meaning beyond that [already stated]. For the establishment of an intrinsic relation occurs when, through repeated observation, no deviation is perceived. And the non-perception of deviation is said to be simply the non-observation [of the probans] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

As for the claim that the non-establishment of deviation [of the reason] is due to the non-perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), there exists no such thing as a "limiting condition" that functions like a visible mark, whose non-perception would allow one to establish non-deviation. Rather, its postulation arises solely from the observation of deviation itself.

And because that [invariable concomitance] is not observed, there is no "naturalness" (svābhāvikatva) due to the absence of any distinguishing feature; thus, nothing is gained by the doctrine of naturalness. This is sufficient in itself: that a reason is one that has been repeatedly observed together with the probandum, and that it is not a reason if it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, all of this has been established in the *Vyāpticarcā* after detailed analysis: that in some cases the "obstruction" (*pratibandha*) of one thing by another does not exist except through "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), and that this [obstruction] is established solely by means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). Therefore, that alone should be understood. By this, those who follow the views of Maṅkha and Vācaspati are refuted.

Let it be then that even for one possessing effort (*prayatnavat*), there is a causal connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by the production of the effect from that [effort], just as smoke has with fire. As Vittoka has stated: "For instance, although the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth exist prior to the activity of the potter, the effect called 'jar'—which meets the conditions for perception—is not perceived; yet it is perceived immediately after his activity. Thus, since the relationship of cause and effect is established, how can there be any doubt regarding its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)? This is true in this case.

There is no doubt that [the reason] occurs only in the similar class (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). For here, because the nature [of the objects] is accepted as being suitable for perception and non-perception, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to trees, *vīraṇa* grass, and so forth, which are manifested through the operations of persons who do not perceive them. If it is argued that "grass and the like are themselves made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*), and there can be no deviation by means of what has been made the subject," we say no; for there is no logical principle in making something that has already been refuted the subject. Otherwise, even in cases such as "fire is not hot, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*), making [fire] the subject would be the only refuge. To explain:

"The reason is doubtful because of the statement of the reason; it is set aside as having no basis for the reason"—this is the rule (*nyāya*). Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is said to be the very perception (*adhyakṣa*) [of one counter-positive] with respect to another counter-positive. Therefore, even that which is sublated by non-apprehension is indeed sublated by perception. However, with respect to the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is inference (*anumāna*). And there is no room for anything else even when something is sublated by inference.

In that case, [the argument] would only establish the non-existence of that which has acquired the qualification of being perceptible; however, since intelligence is common to both those whose bodies are perceptible and those whose bodies are imperceptible, it is impossible to establish a rule of perceptibility for the intelligent agent. How, then, can there be a negation of the intelligent agent merely on the basis of non-perception regarding the production of grass and such things? If you argue that it is proper to treat this as the subject of the thesis because of doubt, then this is like "guarding the cow after it has already been sold."

Because it is necessarily entailed that one must accept the object as being perceptible (*dṛśya*) precisely by granting scope to perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), neither perception can serve as the means for establishing positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor can non-perception serve as the means for establishing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with respect to what is imperceptible. Thus, when one arrives at the causal relationship (*hetuphalabhāva*)—characterized by positive and negative concomitance—between two distinct things through perception and non-perception, one is unable to bypass the requirement that the probandum (*sādhya*) be perceptible.
And since there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the fixed presence of grass and the like [in the case of smoke], this constitutes a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).

Now, might one grasp the pervasion through the wonder of non-deviation by means of an effortful agent who is beyond the scope of perception? Let him grasp it; however, for this [pervasion], reliance upon perception and non-perception is not superior. But is it not the case that the grasping of pervasion occurs merely by a prudent person, without depending on the qualification of being "visible" or "invisible"? It is not so; for even by that much, there is simply no room for a pervasion produced by perception.

For since that [universal] is restricted to having the nature of being only visible, how could it have as its object both the visible and the invisible? Indeed, that which is visible and that which is invisible—though they may share common properties such as being cognized by a single cognition—are of entirely distinct classes due to their extreme difference in nature, whether by being remote or not. Therefore, perception, which functions by accepting only the class of the visible and is ignorant of anything else, demonstrates only that specific [visible] universal property as the pervader.

Although that which is remote in space and time is not perceived, it nevertheless belongs to the same class by virtue of its fitness for perception; thus, the exclusion [of the probans] from the contrary is achieved through perception only with respect to what is remote by nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*). For if all other things were excluded, the pervasion would not exist at all—since there would be a reduction to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone—just as in the cases of smoke and fire, or trembling and wind.

For instance, the pervasion established by perception—which operates by taking as its primary object a blazing, radiant form suitable for its own manifestation—is not restricted to a common form shared with the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) in the case of fire (*saptārcis*). Otherwise, one who doubts even the intended form—just as one might doubt the specific nature of grass-fuel and so forth—would not engage in action with a mind focused solely on obtaining the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by that [fire]. Or, for one who reflects that "there is no digestive fire," [the cognition] would be like a deficiency in the necessary connection (*pratibandhavaikalya*).

[245] There would be a functional application [of the inference]. Just as the pervasion established by perception through the swaying of leaves—by way of presenting a form that cannot be touched—results in a conclusion regarding a wind possessing a nature common to still air; otherwise, even now, one who infers the wind from the trembling of a sprout would necessarily act according to the presence or absence of a wind capable of being touched, so too, in the case of the Person (puruṣa), the apprehension of pervasiveness produced by perception occurs only by excluding an invisible form.

Therefore, under the guise of perception, if at most only the mere desired [object] is the means of proof—and not perception itself regarding the generality of both the visible and the invisible—then because of the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is indeed the state of having a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever determination of causality is produced by perception does not terminate in the form of being either visible or invisible, just as in the case of fire, which excludes the common form shared with the digestive heat (*jaṭharaja*) and the sacrificial fire (*jātavedas*). And this determination of causality for an intelligent agent is produced by perception; thus, there is the apprehension of a property pervaded by what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).

For being produced by perception is pervaded by having a visible object as its domain, since perception does not operate with respect to what is invisible; its opposite is having both visible and invisible objects as its domain, which is pervaded by resulting in a form that is both visible and invisible.

Furthermore, if you intend to state a pervasion (vyāpti) by disregarding the qualifiers "visible" and "invisible" and relying merely on "intelligence" (dhīmān), then when one demonstrates the absence of the potter's effect in the absence of an intelligent agent for the sake of establishing negative concomitance (vyatireka), by what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the absence of mere consciousness—devoid of the qualifiers "visible" and "invisible"—established? For the non-perception of the visible (dṛśyānupalabdhi) has jurisdiction only over the negation of that which is visible; otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) due to [the presence of] grass and the like.

Furthermore, non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) directed solely toward a perceptible person cannot serve as a means for establishing the negative concomitance (vyatireka) for mere intelligent agency (buddhimattva), because the absolute difference between their objects is evident. Otherwise, even in the case of the production of grass and the like, non-apprehension directed solely toward a perceptible person would become the cause for establishing the stability of its deviation (vyabhicāra). For there is no such maxim as "entry upon obtaining" and "exit upon cutting."

Therefore, on the view that the qualification "perceptible" is not excluded, since there is no means of apprehending the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the pervasion remains unestablished; consequently, doubt regarding the exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) arises once again. Nor is the observation of the absence of both [the probans and the probandum] in the sky a means for apprehending the negative concomitance, because it is impossible to ascertain that the absence of the effect is necessitated by the absence of the operation of an intelligent agent. For only when all other causes are present can the absence of the effect—occurring solely upon the absence of that specific cause—be understood as being necessitated by that absence.
As was considered in the investigation of the "three and five," in some cases it is easy to find the mere cessation of two things even when they do not stand in a relationship of cause and effect.

Furthermore, what is the definitive criterion: is the absence of "effectness" in the ether due to the absence of the operation of an intelligent cause, or rather due to the mere absence of a cause? If that were the case, all effort [of inference] would be fruitless. For there remains a doubt as to whether the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between effect and cause is grasped by means of a cause in general, or by means of a cause qualified by a person (*puruṣa*). Now, if this specific qualification is indeed observed—as fire is in smoke—how can it be set aside? If it is so, then [the cause] must have the form of a visible body.

[246] Furthermore, this distinction is indeed perceived; how can it be set aside, like the radiant form of the sun? If it is argued that "that distinction is then shown to be inconstant with respect to the effect," let it be inconstant. Even in the case of the effect, let the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—just as in the case of the cause—be restricted solely to those observed distinctions, since such concomitance is seen even in the case of a mansion and so forth, just as it is in the case of a jar; what is the certainty against this? And this mere positive concomitance is stated while disregarding the refutation [offered by others], which is like the closing of an elephant's eyes.

In reality, however, since neither perception nor non-perception can function with respect to even one of the two [terms], there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, while the state of being an effect exists in the case of mountains and the like, positive and negative concomitances do not touch upon a creator who transcends the range of perception. Since there is no third category between being produced by such an intelligent agent and being otherwise—just as in the case of odors and so forth—this is indeed an inconclusive reason due to its being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*). Therefore, it is established that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "mere effect" cannot be grasped through perception.

And thus, these [cognitions] proceed toward the apprehension of the causal relation precisely by delineating a specific class of effects characterized by both perception and non-perception, and not merely by delineating the effect in general. For, immediately following the operation of perception and non-perception, one proceeds by delineating a specific pair of classes—excluding all other types of cause and effect—in this manner: "From such a specific object whose nature is blazing and radiant, there arises such an object which produces a change in the throat and eyes characterized by being smeared with whiteness. In this way, the conventional usage of the causal relation between cause and effect occurs by excluding every other class of cause and effect.

This very principle applies everywhere in the conventional discourse regarding the relationship between cause and effect; however, we observe that this [view] involves a transgression of established logic due to its adherence to [the doctrine of] Īśvara.

What, then, is the fault here, if perception were to apprehend the pervasion of the effect in general by an intelligent agent—even setting aside the distinctions of mountains and the like—just as it apprehends the pervasion of smoke in general by fire, setting aside the distinctions of grass-fire and so forth? Just as the apprehension of pervasion occurs through the inclusion of a mere subtle intermediate genus within the smoke, which is a specific type of effect produced by fire, and not through the contact of something heterogeneous to it, so too let it be with respect to fire and the like by means of an intelligent agent.

Or, just as you desire to grasp a pervasion of everything possessing existence by means of consciousness—even while including within that category effects that are utterly dissimilar—so too should you do so by means of fire. For how could the operation of sensory perception itself assume two different modes of functioning in both cases? If it is argued that this distinction is caused by the observation or non-observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), then such observation and non-observation, failing to enter into conceptual determination (*saṅkalpa*), are as ineffective as the touch of grass; therefore, one must necessarily possess a corresponding reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And yet, such a reflection does not exist.

Indeed, when perception and non-perception—which grasp positive and negative concomitance—are operating with respect to fire, smoke, and so forth, one does not first form the conceptual construction that "every type of effect arises from fire," and then, upon repeatedly observing deviation, or because other effects are perceived even without fire, arrive at the certainty that "this [smoke] alone is produced by this [fire]. Rather, it is immediately through another instance of perception and non-perception that one understands: "This [effect] arises from this [fire], etc."

The synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*), which renders the two specific classes of things—such as smoke and so forth—into objects of the conventional usage of cause and effect, is experienced within the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[247] There is no difference [between this case and that of the causal relation]. And when, for one who is situated within another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there arises suddenly the cognition "pain from a thorn," which—preceded by non-perception—is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and grasps the relation of cause and effect, then the absence of reflection upon the observation of deviation is manifested; for conceptual constructions cannot occur simultaneously. Thus, in this case as well, the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) proceeds by setting aside intermediate subtle distinctions, such as "this effect, characterized by a broad base, belly, and so forth, is produced by this potter."
But when one observes even such things as cloth or carts being produced from a person, then the non-contradictory cognition arises that "this too, and that too, is generated by a person.

Furthermore, does this so-called "deviation" (vyabhicāra) merely undermine inference once the pervasion (vyāpti) has already been established, or does it establish that the pervasion itself is false? Even in this latter case, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that grasps the pervasion remains manifest through its own inherent power.

Or rather, does it bring about the destruction of its own validity regarding all objects or only regarding a restricted one? If it is restricted, is it so by virtue of the [intended] object, or because perception operates only there? First, the initial position is not tenable due to contradiction; for it is not possible that a logical reason possesses a pervasion (*vyāpti*) characterized by inseparable connection with the probandum (*sādhya*), while at the same time there is an absence of inference caused by the possibility of the probandum’s non-existence, especially since this would lead to a lack of confidence in pervasion elsewhere as well.

Thus, it should be understood that while the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) maintains its status as a valid cognition, the attempt to demonstrate the falsity of that pervasion is likewise incoherent. Furthermore, if the validity of the means of cognition grasping the pervasion were to fail in every case, then fire could not even be inferred from smoke, because there would be no other [means] to grasp the pervasion.

What, then, will be the refuge for the inference of a Lord (*īśvara*)? For if a subject is restricted by one's own whim, the wretched means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*) becomes indifferent; thus, in reality, there is neither a reason nor a non-reason, because it would follow that even in the case of smoke, pervasion could be arbitrarily subverted by one's own whim.

But how can perception, even when its object is one of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), have a restricted scope? For just as that which apprehends pervasion (*vyāpti*)—functioning with respect to a restricted class—is held to have all things as its object, so too should that which has deviation as its object have all things as its object, since the capacities of both are neither deficient nor excessive. Thus, if the apprehension of pervasion and the cognition of deviation pertain to the very same object, what now would be a means of proof (*sādhana*) and what a non-means of proof? Or, let it be granted for the sake of your own argument that there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that brings about the cognition of sublation (*bādhā*).

[The opponent claims: "There is a restriction on the object [of the inference]. Even so, it is certainly not the case that those things which possess deviation are perceived as being sublated all at once; rather, it occurs sequentially. And at that time, even for those things that deviate, there is no direct perception of their deviation. Thus, because smoke lacks that distinguishing feature, it would again be a non-reason (*ahetu*), or else anything else might also be a reason.

Nor should it be said that there is no confidence in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding smoke due to the observation of deviation in all other [cases]. For if that were so, immediately after grasping the pervasion in smoke at a previous time, there would be no inference of fire from smoke on the slope of a mountain, rather than an inference of a tiger; this is because one would have to wait for the observation of deviation elsewhere. And this is impossible, given the observations of deviation in other [places] that are intended [as examples].

[248] Regarding the phrase "the resting place of pervasion" (*vyāptiviśrāma*): because even the objects of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) are infinite, and because a human lifespan is shorter compared to the time required to perceive those things situated at a great distance in space and so forth, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*)—like the observation of deviation—is faultless only when restricted to a specific domain, since pure conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) proceeds through differentiation. For this very reason, only an innate conceptual construction (*svābhāvikavikalpa*) has the authority to grasp the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), not one that is adventitious (*aupādhika*).

For there exists a conceptual construction (vikalpa) common to both children and animals that depends solely on the perceptual cognition (*ālocanājñāna*) produced by a pure object. This is called "pure" (*śuddha*) and "natural" (*svābhāvika*). By virtue of this, even animals—ascertaining that the means for allaying hunger, thirst, and so forth are effective only in that specific place—subsequently engage in or desist from it accordingly, based on whether they perceive it as being associated with those means or not.

Furthermore, there exists a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by a perceptual cognition accompanied by the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); for example, when one observes soot from a lamp, the conceptual construction arises: "This is blue, useful for dyeing and so forth. This [conceptualization] is said to be characterized by such conditions (*tādṛgaupādhika*), being cultivated by an experience aided by the recollection of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of an object previously perceived. Yet, no discerning person concludes that, merely because there is then a conceptualization of "blue," all blue things arise from the lamp.

However, it is precisely that object which, being preceded by a conceptual construction corresponding to the mere perception of soot, is fit for the linguistic convention of the word "soot" due to its connection with a universal (*jāti*) or its specific nature (*svarūpa*), that performs the function of a lamp; this has been stated regarding the basis of deviation.

In the same way, even regarding smoke, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following convention—which thinks, "this white object is produced from fire"—only suggests frost and the like through a conditional (*aupādhika*) relation as its effect. However, in a pure conceptual construction, it is only the universal of smoke (*dhūmajāti*) that manifests; therefore, it should be understood that the exclusion of frost and the like from the pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on that [universal] alone is not a valid basis for deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Likewise, every conceptual construction of an effect is purely conditional; for that which is blind to its own production depends upon the operation of another.

Since its production from sensory perception occurs with the assistance of the recollection of the convention that "this is the effect," it is not a factor for the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect. Therefore, although—just as when one sees a jar arising from a person, the conceptual construction "this jar is from him" is easily available—the conceptual construction "this is the effect of him" is likewise easily available, nevertheless, because such a relation lacks intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*), the status of being its effect cannot be established for that which has its identity determined by such [an external relation]. However, let it be so for that which is made the object of an innate conceptual construction (*naisargika-vikalpa*).

[Objection: But surely, even when the object of apprehension is a pure [particular], a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by the recollection of a linguistic convention is observed, as in "this jar is man-made," because of the mention of a name. Therefore, that too would necessarily be adventitious (*aupādhika*). [Reply: No, because in the conceptualization of that [object] alone, recollection is not the operative cause; its capacity lies solely in the mention of the expressive portion [of the word].

And although the arising of an uninterrupted conceptual construction (vikalpa), which is fashioned with the forms of the signified and the signifier, occurs through the assistance of memory, nevertheless, its operation is said to be directed toward that [object] alone by way of abstraction (apoddhāra), just as the potter’s operation is said to be directed toward the mere state of being made of clay. However, the conceptualization of properties such as the inherence of a different genus, the effect, whiteness, and so forth, cannot belong to a pure determinative cognition (śuddhādhyavasāya) without the recollection of previous operations, such as the grasping of the relationship of linguistic convention (saṅketa).

[249] Since its purpose is fulfilled by the mere delineation of that [object] alone, as in the case of infants and others, the pervasion established by perception has that alone as its object; thus, it is faultless. Therefore, it is established that the apprehension of pervasion produced by perception and the cognition of deviation have entirely different objects.

If it is argued that, in that case, the establishment of the "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) fallacy is untenable because of the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), we reply: this is indeed so, provided there is a uniformity of intellectual acuity among all people. However, one of dull intellect, even when perception has occurred regarding a specific class due to similarity and other factors, unifies it with another class and, through the conceit of having grasped a pervasion (*vyāpti*), maintains an inference. When another person of sharp intellect points out the deviation, the dull-witted person is led to conclude that the pervasion is difficult to grasp. Thus, the status of the common inconclusive remains established.

Just as when smoke is present and perceived, one who grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—recalling the pervasion by fire in the case of a rising, dense mass [of smoke]—infers fire from a cloud of dust stirred up by the wind; yet, seeing a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the emergence of steam, which lacks the characteristic of a well-known vapor-cloud, he is dissuaded. For that reason also, it is established that the pervasion is grasped by perception only with respect to a specific class (*jāti-viśeṣa*).

For if perception were to grasp the relation as being restricted to a single class of smoke, then it would be logical for there to be a superimposition of that form upon another object based on similarity, and its exclusion would be justified by the deviation [of smoke] from other similar things.

But when the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs in every case of a class of effects, then what is the need for dependence on similarity? If, then, the cognition of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by perception is restricted solely to a specific class [of objects], how is it that even entirely heterogeneous things such as jars, *kuṭa* vessels, and *kuṇṭhī* tools—which possess a common redness—lead to the inference of the processing of substances like turmeric? Or how is it that the intellect, though itself an entirely heterogeneous entity, leads to the inference of the instrument (*karaṇa*)—which has been observed to have an operative function in the act of cutting—as being an instance of "action" (*kriyātva*)?

If it is argued that even things such as Mount Kailāsa and the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*), though extremely heterogeneous, will lead to the inference of a Person (*puruṣa*) because they possess common properties such as being effects, we say: not so. This is because the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is the means of cognition (*gamaka*); it is only with respect to that [the pervader] that the distinction between homogeneous and heterogeneous is to be considered. Furthermore, the pervaded is twofold—dependent on what is produced (*nirvartya*) or transformed (*vikārya*)—consisting of either the substratum (*dharmin*) or the property (*dharma*). Among these, when there is an entirely new production, the pervasion is stated of the substratum, as in the case of smoke and the like.

And in that case, another smoke is indeed a similar [homogeneous] instance, while any other object is dissimilar. But when there is the determination that a different property has arisen in the very same previously existing substrate, then it is called "pervasion by a property" (*dharmavyāpti*), as in the case of heat and so forth in water; and in that case, another instance of heat is the similar property, such that there is no longer any requirement for the genus of the substrate (*dharmin*).

In the same way, even *rāga* (redness), disregarding the heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) of substances such as jars or cloth, serves as an indicator of the refinement of the substance *rāga* only with respect to its own homogeneous effects. For this very reason, when there is a particularity in that [color], one infers in some cases contact with saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and in others with turmeric (*haridrā*). And it is not the case that, in the instance of pre-existing mountains, clouds, and so forth, a person is intended merely as the producer of properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*); rather, he is intended precisely as a producer of something previously non-existent (*apūrva*), just like a jar. And in that case, properties such as "being an effect" are [inferred] just as whiteness and other qualities are inferred in smoke.

[250] Even properties that are inherent in other classes of entities are incapable of performing any function because they exist outside the scope of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, the apprehension of the pervasion of the factual subject (*dharmin*) does not depend upon proximity to the mere property (*dharma*), nor does it depend upon the homogeneity of the subject with respect to the pervasion of the property. Furthermore, the distinction between "homogeneous" and "heterogeneous" is stated only with reference to a pure, singular conceptual reflection (*vimarśa*). Consequently, even if there is heterogeneity of the subject—as in the case of passion—the properties such as "being an effect" do not possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum].
Otherwise, the undesirable consequence of inferring fire from white smoke would be difficult to avoid, for the rebuttal based on deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is flawed.

However, such an inference applies to the sense faculty as follows: that which occurs only occasionally (*kādācitka*) despite the presence of other causes depends upon yet another cause; for example, a sprout [depends on something else] despite the presence of water and earth. And since cognition occurs only occasionally despite the presence of the object, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and light, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) that if there were no dependence—i.e., in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—occurrence would be impossible because it would be non-sequential (*anavasthāyin*).

The established position is that whatever else is required [for the cognition] is the sense-faculty (*indriya*); therefore, there is no inference of a cause by way of its being an action (*kriyātva*), nor does perception grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, perception must necessarily be held to apprehend a universal (*sāmānya*) only by way of presenting a distinction of genus (*jātibheda*) brought forth by innate conceptualization (*svābhāvikavikalpa*); otherwise, when a convention (*saṅketa*) such as "this is a jar" is made after having shown a single pervasion through perception, would that [convention] then apply to the entire universe as possessing properties such as being an effect?

Is it brought to a state of restricted scope by the observation of deviation? Or does the instructor himself, by negating [the term] in all other classes, establish its restriction to a specific object? Or is this convention not actually concerned with a general object at all?

The same should be understood regarding the distinction between the classes of denoters (*vācaka-jāti*). However, a word for an effect (*kārya-śabda*) is applied merely to that which arises in dependence on another, within the scope of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) without depending on perception; thus, it does not function with reference to a specific [particular]. If, however, even that were applied as "this is an effect" to something existing in perception, then it too would possess other synonyms and would necessarily function with restricted application. Therefore, it is the very nature of perception to take as its object only a specific class of effects (*kārya-jāti-viśeṣa*).

And if perception, even when directed toward a difference in the genus of the effect, takes as its objective basis merely the effect in general, then, when operating upon the cause, it should determine merely the cause as the pervader; why then does it rely on [the cause] as qualified by the cognition of the material cause and so forth? Therefore, unless you comply with our intention, this perception must be either a support for a generality or a support for a particularity in both cases; if it supports a generality, how can there be an inference of the cause from the effect?

[Otherwise, there would be] the attainment of the status of a Lord of News! Furthermore, if one relies on a specific [instance], the pervasion of the mere effect [by the cause] remains unestablished. Therefore, it is logical that perception, based on experience, demonstrates that only a specific class of effects is pervaded by a specific cause. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever perception grasps the relation of causal agency is restricted to a function determined by a specific class [of objects], just as in the case of fire and smoke. And this [perception] which establishes the pervasion of the effect by an intelligent agent is likewise; thus, it is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

There is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to the suspicion of its functioning otherwise, because that is sublated by the non-perception of a cause. For a difference in causes is indeed the cause of a difference in effects; otherwise, it would follow that everything is without a cause. And there is no difference in the cause of this [cognition].

[251] It exists, because it arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by the object, the sense faculty, light, and so forth. Furthermore, when there is a suspicion that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhya-śūnyatā*), the following is stated: whatever is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*) apprehends a generality (*sāmānya*) by means of a specific genus (*viśiṣṭa-jāti*) alone; for instance, the perception that grasps deviation (*vyabhicāra-grāhi-pratyakṣa*), and the perception that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti-grāhi*). This is simply its inherent nature (*svabhāva*). This itself is the avoidance of the inconclusive (*anekānta*). This same formulation applies even to the subject (*dharmin*) that grasps the pervasion between "having an intelligent agent" (*buddhimat-kārya*) and its effect.

Alternatively, in both cases, whatever perception grasps a relation does so by means of a specific universal (viśiṣṭajāti), as in the case of the signified and the signifier; and the perception that grasps the relation between cause and effect is likewise [based on a specific universal], as previously stated.

Therefore, even if this entire range of effects is, in reality, invariably concomitant with an intelligent agent, nevertheless, because the classes of effects are infinitely diverse and extremely distinct, and because one must apprehend the pervasion for each specific class of effect, it is rightly said that the inference of the agent is direct only to the extent that a particular class of effect is determined to be preceded by a person;
thus, whatever kind [of effect] is established...

And so forth. Likewise, regarding effects such as smoke, ash, embers, cooking, the sublimation of mercury, observation, injury, and the like, inference of fire proceeds from that very [perception] which has functioned as the means of establishing the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with respect to each of those effects, and not from anything else.

Thus, even in the case of things such as temples, water-jars, palaces, chariots, and fine silk garments—which are in fact of human origin—we accept the inference of that [human agency] from a product of the same class, provided that human action has been observed in things of that very class. However, regarding the class of clouds, mountains, and the like, since their operation cannot be determined, what talk can there be of inference? For, due to the possibility of an absolute difference in class (*jātivaijātya*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped; and even if the pervasion were grasped, no such product would be observed. As for the inference of knowledge in the case of pillars and the like, it is based on the observation of those who have seen the construction of Mount Kailāsa and other such works.
Nor is it the case that they do not possess iron-like [stability], for their gait is faltering; thus, even that name alone is equal.

Furthermore, if the deeds performed by many similar men are successful, what need is there to speak of a Lord? When the consciousness of the equality of results exists, from what cause could a distinction arise?

Thus there is an intermediate verse. Now, one might ask: what kind of class of effects (*kāryajāti*) is pervaded by an agent possessing effort? Anticipating this, it is stated in brief—since that class is also infinite—that upon seeing which, even for one who observes causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the cognition that "it has been produced" (*kṛtabuddhi*) arises. And in this context, "the cognition that it has been produced" does not mean the cognition of a [specific] means (*sādhana*), nor does it mean the cognition of the specific probandum under discussion, characterized by knowledge of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth; rather, it is the cognition of a probandum whose nature is that of a weaver and the like.

And because of that absence, neither is the non-establishment of your reason (*hetu*) intended here, nor is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) under discussion; rather, this is a demonstration of absolute heterogeneity (*atyantavaijātya*). And by means of that, the non-establishment or the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the reason is precisely what is intended.

For instance, when one perceives a temple or similar structure in an empty city, the notion of a craftsman—such as a potter or the like—arises; this does not occur in the case of a lake, a sea-monster’s abode, or similar places. The intention is that the presence or absence of such a notion of a craftsman cannot occur without an absolute difference in their respective natures (*jāti*). If there were no apprehension of a distinction [between the two], or if the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) for recollection were lost, then even in the case of a temple and so forth, this identical notion of a craftsman would not arise.

Therefore, just as the cognition of fire arising from smoke excludes that of a donkey, thereby necessarily establishing a specific distinction in the genus of the donkey, so too does this [cognition] establish a distinction for Kailāsa, the thunderbolt, and so forth, from those entities whose human origin is definitively ascertained.

If it is asked, "How, then, is the very absence of inference to be understood? [The answer is: because even in a dream there is no suspicion that things such as clouds, rainbows, and lotus-forests could arise from a potter; otherwise, the world would not suffer the hardship of drought caused by the trampling of weavers' feet, nor would one terrified by the invasion of a foreign army seek refuge in the gaps between mountains and oceans and find relief therein.

If it is argued that another factor, standing in the place of the weaver, must indeed be expected there, we say no; for when the production of the same effect occurs, it is illogical to search for a cause of a different genus, since the accomplishment of the goal is achieved by the weaver alone. Indeed, even in the case of another cloth, there is no requirement for anyone other than the weaver.

If it is argued that there is indeed a dependence on a specific artisan regarding a particular type of cloth, this is true only so long as a firm recognition of a single genus (*ekajāti*) is observed in relation to other pieces of cloth; for this very reason, the conceptualization of a weaver as the artisan is possible. In the absence of such a recognition, there is doubt regarding its being a human product. However, Mount Meru, Mandara, and the like are not the objects of a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) for any human agent.

Thus, one who, out of deceit, denies the extreme heterogeneity of these [effects]—which is established by direct perception—and instead accepts them as having a common artisan due to a lack of inference, is refuted. Once the difference in genus (*jāti-bheda*) is established, it is proven that the effects such as jars, which are invariably connected to a person, are not like the effects such as embryos and infants; and since this [latter kind of effect] does not possess the same pervasion (*vyāpti*) by a person, both [the reason and the probandum] are established as being unestablished and non-pervasive. This being the case, the objections—which function by preventing the arising of the cognition of the probandum under discussion—are cast far aside.

For we do not claim that the reason—such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)—is unestablished because of the absence of the cognition of the specific probandum under discussion. What then? We claim that because there is an absence of the artisan's cognition (such as that of a weaver) in the case of Mount Mandara and the like, the fact of being an effect belonging to the same class as cloth and so forth is unestablished. Consequently, there is no distinction [between our position and yours] regarding the deficiency of the cognition of the specific probandum. Furthermore, since it is accepted that there is merely a lapse in the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the recollection of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to what is to be accomplished by a weaver, there is no room for the alternative views proposed by Bhūṣaṇa.

However, the mere cognition of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not what is intended [to be negated]. For those whose memory has not failed, the notion that things such as the earth are "made by a person" certainly does arise; but this is a point far removed from the present context. Indeed, what is proposed to be stated here is the proof of the non-establishment of the Buddhist's own negation of the notion of being produced. And that [negation] cannot be established, because by the term "notion of being produced," the author intends the notion of a craftsman (*śilpibuddhi*). This is because [the opponent's argument] merely demonstrates the existence of the notion that things are made by a person.

[253] Furthermore, this is irrelevant; for this consideration of a refutation applies only when that [subject] is already established. Even there, the phrase "for those whose memory has not failed" is incoherent, because an absolute difference in nature (*atyantavaijātya*) is established, since no pervasion (*vyāpti*) is perceived between the Indus River and other such things, and because the failure of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of memory cannot be avoided. For this very reason, what confidence can there be in the mere babble that "the world was created by someone"? And precisely by refuting the objection regarding the non-establishment of the cognition of the probandum under discussion, the argument beginning with "even in the case of the Vedas" and so forth is also rejected.

If the Mīmāṃsaka were to demonstrate an absolute difference in genus (*vaijātya*) between the Veda and human utterances such as sentences, then why should he be defeated merely by a convention (*samaya*)? For there is no distinction between the two based on their essential nature (*svarūpa*) or their capacity (*śakti*). Thus, having recited both before someone who has not grasped the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), consider this: what kind of distinction could the listener describe regarding which one belongs to which, or do you not see the removal of poison and so forth performed by mantras such as those of Garuḍa? This results in the following: one [the proponent], conceiving a specific effect, [asserts] his own [word] as being distinguished from the cause.
One perceives that the mere effect is pervaded by this [cause], just as one perceives the effect of a fire indicated by its mark;
yet another does not understand that such an effect has that very thing as its cause.
Alas, this is a particular kind of darkness among the learned, even regarding an object of direct perception!
Therefore,
since speech follows the presence and absence of the person and shares its existence with him,
there is no difference between ordinary speech and Vedic words, as both are capable of possessing a nature [of their own].
Furthermore, the Veda indicates supersensible objects that are equal [to those known by other means], and it does not provide certainty regarding a single point;
therefore, it does not rest without reaching the status of being human-authored.

If that were so, what need is there to speak of the human origin of the cognition restricted to those specific classes—such as jars, clouds, and thunderbolts—which are absolutely distinct classes beyond the scope of investigation? Furthermore, that which was censured as a proof for impermanence is also outside the bounds of logic; for such an inquiry into whether something belongs to its own class or another occurs only when one is authorized to understand the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through perception.

Regarding impermanence, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through the mere fact of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) occurs by means of an inference whose nature is a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts the opposite; thus, there is no requirement for a specific class (*jāti*) [of the reason]. However, it must be considered whether that valid cognition is capable or incapable of establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to the mere fact of being produced, unqualified by any specific class. If it is capable, there is no contact with any fault.

Therefore, it is not correct to claim that the pointing out of a difference there by means of the difference between the words "pot" and [the word for] "difference" constitutes a statement of dissimilarity between the example and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). This is because, since the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through two properties (*dharma*) extracted from the nature of the property-possessor (*dharmin*), the property-possessor is in fact nothing other than the reality of the property; thus, the meaning of stating a difference between them is simply a difference in the mere property-possessor.

[254] If it is argued that even here, in the case of effects as the subjects (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is "being produced by a person" (*pauruṣeyatva*) while the reason (*hetu*) is merely "being an effect" (*kāryatvamātra*), and thus there is no distinction whatsoever; it is replied: what is the meaning of this statement that "merely being an effect" is the reason? Is it said because, in a primary sense, the cause—such as saffron and the like—exerts its operation only upon the coloration (*rāga*), which is a mere property (*dharma*)? Or is it because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established for the effect in its entirety, just as "merely being smoke" (*dhūmatvamātra*) is the reason, in the manner that "all smoke" [is pervaded by fire]? Just as all smoke...

[The opponent argues: "It is pervaded by the probandum; for there is the certain conviction that whatever is an effect is entirely produced by human activity. Both of these [arguments] have been refuted. However, the statement regarding the totality—that "the mere fact of being produced is pervaded by impermanence"—is intended precisely to convey the sense of "entirety," meaning: "whatever is produced, all that is impermanent. This is the very meaning [of the definition].

When this point has been established by the convergence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the produced nature of sound is proven, the question "How could sound be [eternal] when only a jar is seen to be produced and impermanent? is entirely without foundation; it is precisely this meaning that is elucidated by the method expressed as "this is merely a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*)."

For just as, in the context of the discussion on the reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) are established as distinct with respect to their forms as they appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpārūḍharūpa*), so too is the subject (*dharmin*), such as sound, [distinct], since there is no other subject possessing those properties. Nor is the impermanence of sound established by proving the impermanence of an entity through the fact of being produced when the subject is something else; for one who, while stating a refutation, brings about a distinction in that subject by means of its existence as a pot or as sound, is defeated by way of the mere distinction of the subject.

In the present case, however, due to the conceit that it is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the mass of effects—which stands in the place of smoke—is distinct from the person to be proven (*sādhya*), just as fire [is distinct from smoke]. It is simply not the case, as with fire, that [the person] exists only at that specific place and time.

However, [the agent] must be determined as being present at the place and time of the production; for instance, by means of the ashes and the pot, the potter—who is present at the location and whose activity is inferred—is determined. Furthermore, the cause is the actual entity (*vastu*). Thus, even when the Person (*puruṣa*) is the probandum, the cause is indeed the entity itself, not the property of "being an effect" (*kāryatva-dharma*). This being so, one who asserts that effects such as mountains and the like are dissimilar to the effect [of a pot] which is pervaded by the Person has pointed out a dissimilarity in the *sādhana* (the reason), not a dissimilarity in the *dharmin* (the subject).

For at that time, the subject (*dharmin*) is precisely the place and time of its own arising; nor has anyone set out to state a dissimilarity between the place and time of a jar or the like and the place and time of Kailāsa or the like, by which a demonstration of dissimilarity in the subject would occur.

Therefore, just as there is an inference of fire from the mere form of heat, this presentation of a dissimilarity in the means of proof (*sādhana*) is intended to demonstrate either a lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) or a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). To say "of the subject" (*dharmiṇaḥ*) is merely a confusion on the part of opponents. This very point is taught by the following direction: "The kind of effect-ness (*kāryatva*) that is perceived in temples and the like, which is pervaded by a person, is not such [a kind] in the case of Mount Yugandhara and the like. The meaning is: that class of things to which temples and the like belong, being pervaded by a person, is not the same class to which Mount Yugandhara and the like belong.

And because of their absolute heterogeneity, it is said that there is a similarity merely in terms of being "words for effects," but there is no deficiency whatsoever in the exclusion of what is not an effect. However, we maintain that [the property of being an effect] is not included within the pervasion (*vyāpti*). For this very reason, similarity based on that alone is not useful, just as [similarity in] corporeality and so forth is not useful for inferring fire.

[255] However, Mañjarī’s objection is misplaced. For by stating that the universal (*jāti*) of jars and so forth is indeed established as pervaded by persons, he intends here merely to express doubt. Furthermore, the notion that [objects] are made by humans such as potters is what was called "the notion of being made" (*kṛtabuddhi*). And the absence of that [notion] has been addressed regarding the difference in universals. Since that [absence] is established for both parties, it does not allow for a dismissal [of the argument]. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that this [absence] is not possible without an absolute difference in universals.

In this way, it should be understood that even for Vācaspati, the search for a distinction is prompted by a failure to fully comprehend the subject matter and the purpose, due to a deficiency in cultivated intellect (*kṛtabuddhi*). For if "the absence of *kṛtabuddhi*" is intended to mean "the absence of the cognition of the probandum under discussion," then one must consider: in this dispute regarding perception, on what basis does that [cognition] exist elsewhere—such as on a mountain—and why is it said not to exist there due to its absence?

But when one has formed the cognition that "it does not exist," the intended meaning is that "the cognition produced by a similar artisan does not exist," and regarding that there is no dispute. Furthermore, the purpose is to demonstrate the absolute heterogeneity (*atyantavaijātya*) of clouds and the like from jars and so forth; yet even that cannot be avoided. Therefore, how can there be a cognition of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtasādhyabuddhi*) from something absolutely distinct from those things from which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped? This is what is intended [by the opponent]. At that point, everything of this kind simply collapses.

Furthermore, since the pervasion (vyāpti) has been refuted for the mere fact of having an origin, alas, the response beginning with "that which has an origin" and so forth is utterly shattered by the "rod of time" (kāladaṇḍa). Therefore, for one who has perceived the pervasion in a jar, only that which is of the same class as the jar is preceded by an intelligent agent. However, it has also been stated that when the apprehension of pervasion occurs even in the case of a palace and the like, then the fact of being preceded by that [intelligent agent] is established for that class as well.

And as for the doubt, "Of what kind [is that]?"—namely, "Of what kind of effect is it?"—the response, "It is not seen to be so," is rendered useless because it establishes through perception the fitness of a universal, which appears in conceptual construction as something intrinsic, for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, even if the conventional usage of "belonging to that class" occurs by way of a form appearing in a conceptual construction based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), it is difficult to avoid; however, since this is rejected in the case of the apprehension of pervasion, there is a great distinction.

For this very reason, even these various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) amount to nothing. To explain: if the question concerns our intended position, then it is only a specific class of effects—characterized by things such as temples and water-jars—that is pervaded by an intelligent agent; for it is from the observation of such [effects] that one infers a craftsman of a similar kind, even when his activity is imperceptible. However, such [a specific class] is not established in the case of the oceans, mountains, and so forth. As for mere "effect-ness" (*kāryatva-mātra*), we ourselves loudly proclaim that it is not so pervaded. Therefore, consider: what is the use of these conceptual constructions?

The claim that "that specific property (*viśeṣa*) by virtue of which a particular class of effects is distinguished is itself of an indeterminate nature" is even more wretched; for it is impossible to deny the mutual dissimilarity among classes of effects established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for whether pervasion (*vyāpti*) resides in a specific class of effects or in the category of effects in general, one may at most entertain this doubt from a superficial standpoint.

Otherwise, how could he himself have avoided the objection regarding the non-production of the "being-a-real-thing" (*vastutva*) as an effect of fire by resorting to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? It has already been demonstrated that there is no dispute regarding the fact that cognitions of deviation have restricted universals (*niyata-jāti*) as their objects. Therefore, since one perceives the capacity for causal efficiency and so forth through various forms, it is better simply to disregard the claim that this person perceives a single, extraordinary form in this world of variegated forms solely by the grace of God.

As for the previous example of the material cause (*upādāna*) offered with the intent of establishing a pervasion (*vyāpti*) over all effects, that too is not applicable; for even there, the operation of perception cannot be established, because it is the object of innate conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and because the material cause possesses both visible and invisible natures.

Now, is it that there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the collection of effects by the material cause at all? Or is it that this [pervasion] must be cognizable through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? There is doubt regarding both [possibilities], because even though a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) might exist, it is possible that no inferential reasoning (*anumāna*) subverting its opposite has been stated, and because at present there is an absence of an exclusive reason (*ekāntahetu*).

Therefore, this universally established tenet—that all arising is accompanied by a material cause—is followed because it is free from contradiction; furthermore, as long as we observe an effect, there is also an undisputed conventional usage that it possesses a material cause. And since the cognition of the full extent of an effect is not possible for an ordinary person, doubt is unavoidable even regarding the slightest contrary portion.

Since it is certain that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Buddha, [the argument] is established because consciousness does not have consciousness as its material cause; thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore, even if one determines that pervasion from the perspective of the established tenet (*siddhānta*), there is no harm whatsoever. However, let it be that this is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); the settled conclusion is simply that in this position, the reason "having a non-conscious material cause" might be suspected of being unestablished in part (*ekadeśāsiddha*).

And that [consequence] has already arrived; what can be done? However, upon obtaining a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts the contrary, even that [consequence] would not hold. This objection—that there is no example at all for the claim that perception is pervaded by its entire effect—is merely [an attempt to avoid] the fact that the restriction of perception’s operation to a specific class [of objects] has been established, and thus arguments such as "due to the absence of a specific cause" are also destroyed.

Furthermore, regarding the human effort involved in presenting another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates [the opponent's] misconception, even there, the first two [means of proof] are indeed sublatives; for just as in the case of smoke, once its production from that [cause] is established, the perception and non-perception that prove it function by way of a specific class [of causes], and thus they are capable of establishing only a specific effect such as a jar.

And thus, if [the world] were to arise even once without an intelligent being, it would not exist at all; or, if there were no fixed cause, there would be no cause whatsoever—not even for a mere effect—because there would be no proof of its production from a person (puruṣa). Consequently, the claim that "this effect is preceded by a person" is also without foundation.

Nor does there follow the undesirable consequence of the non-cessation of effects; for even though that particular state of the cause—which depends on its own causes for its presence and has the transformation of *adṛṣṭa* as its auxiliary—is constantly absent, it is logically possible for effects to be occasional. It is in dependence upon this [state] that the Lord, despite possessing eternal power, does not always act (or exercise his agency). Indeed, if there were a restriction to a single state, one would have to postulate a desire to bring about the engagement or cessation of other causes;
but such [a desire] does not exist, because there is a continuous acquaintance with a series of transformations, just as a seed undergoes states of being more swollen or most swollen.

[257] Because it is impossible to deny them; or, even if there were a restriction to a single state for the Lord, since his will is also eternal, the non-cessation of effects would remain in that same state. But if it is impermanent, and its occurrence at some time depends upon something else, then what fault would there be if the collection of effects were likewise dependent upon that? If one objects: "In the sequence of effects such as jars and so forth, what is the use of the person's will, since it can be said that whatever it depends upon for its own sequence, that very thing also serves as the basis for the sequence of the jar and so forth? That is incorrect.

Because it is impossible to exclude a cause whose causal capacity has been observed through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whereas in the case at hand, due to the absence of such valid means, one merely relies on the occasional nature of the effect; since that [occasional nature] can be accounted for otherwise as well, how could there be a rule that the effect must arise from a person? If it is argued that the occasional occurrence of jars and the like is seen to be dependent upon a person, and therefore other effects are likewise so, then in that case, mere observation and non-observation alone have arrived as the proof for the pervasion (*vyāpti*). What is the use here of the boastful display of adducing a counter-factual refutation (*viparyaya-bādhaka*)? Thus, the third [position] is also refuted.

As for what is said—that certainty depends on the presence of the cause and is subject to the intellect—there too, this very same point must be stated regarding the mere reliance on such observation. Furthermore, no subverting argument against the opposite case has been stated. And if one resorts to perception and non-perception as the basis, then because the causal complex of a lotus seed and so forth is rendered inconclusive by factors such as damage from wind, everything—including the avoidance of dependence—must be understood to be like an effect; the limit of the matter is that only a specific causal complex is fit for pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Therefore, the pervasion of the causal totality by the Person is not established; since its impossibility in the counter-example follows from the non-perception of the pervader, the fourth [argument] is also refuted.

By this much alone, even the hollow prattle of Vācaspati is cast aside. For it has already been stated that the seed of non-origination for extended things is simply the absence of a specific state [of their causes].

Even if it is observed that the meeting of the staff, the wheel, and so forth occurs only through a person, and that the commencement of an effect takes place when they are accompanied by his effort, nevertheless, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish a rule that this is always and everywhere the case, the pervasion is unproven; since the conjunction of causes—which is the pervader of the production of an effect—is itself dependent upon an intelligent agent, the same fault remains.

And just as the occasional existence of effects depends solely upon specific states of other causes, so too is it with specific primordial matter (prakṛti); thus, the fifth [reason] is also rendered redundant.
Furthermore, it is shown in the treatise that this is a proof establishing the occurrence of the mere cause.

By this very [argument], even what was stated by Śaṅkara—that "there is no distinction whatsoever," and so forth—is reduced to mere poetic composition, because all means of valid cognition that could establish a necessary connection have been exhausted. And although there is no difference between the causes of palaces and the like and the causes of mountains and the like insofar as their activity is devoid of intention, nevertheless, if a distinction were to exist through the dependence or non-dependence upon an agent possessing effort, what fault would there be? It is just as there is a distinction between being scratchable by iron and not being scratchable by iron, despite the lack of distinction in their being composed of earth. And this must necessarily be the case, given the lack of distinction in their being devoid of intention.

[258] Furthermore, a specific distinction must be sought here regarding capacity; otherwise, how could there be an absolute difference in the nature of effects? If that capacity were capable of tolerating even an absence of dependence on effort, what harm would there be? Moreover, it is not observed that a corporeal effect is accomplished by the mere volition of an agent without the operation of hands and other limbs; so what need is there to mention mountains and the like, which transcend such [human] volition?

If it is argued that hands and other organs are also set in motion by volition (*samīhā*), we reply: it has already been stated that even volition accomplishes nothing if it lacks the activity of lying down and so forth within a structured body. Therefore, who would believe that the same power—by which causes such as mountains, having cast aside dependence on the activity of hands and other organs, are not obstructed in their causal function despite being devoid of intention—would likewise not transcend volition? For indeed, at the time smoke arises, there is no object manifesting in a dense form [that acts with intent].

Just as that which is conceived as being produced from fire and fuel, when its absence is ascertained, does not lead to any suspicion of its existence even if the other [factors] are absent—this case is exactly like that.

But if one accepts that [the Lord] possesses a body, then because he would be limited, non-eternal, manifold, and non-omniscient, the proponents of the *sudhī* school have effectively proven their point; by this very fact, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth. For, based on the statement beginning with "not being superintended" (*na hy anadhiṣṭhitānām*), [the opponent] touches upon nothing other than mere observation and non-observation as a means to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this [reason], and that has already been answered.

If perception and non-perception alone are the refuge, then just as the performance of an action is observed in one who possesses volition, and thus—in the presence of an effect—the inference of one possessing volition is accepted; so too, since corporeal action is observed only in one who possesses hands and the like, why is it not certain that a person is inactive when the operation of hands and such is impossible? Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever in the validity of the reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

If, however, there were another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) restricted to a single [object], established independently of mere observation and non-observation, then there might be a cognition of a single thing to be proven. But in its absence, there is merely a mutual contradiction between those two, not a sublation (*bādhā*), because they are of equal status; thus, from the perspective of the opponent’s intention, it is a "neutralized reason" (*prakaraṇasama*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not possess the operation of its own parts is not seen to be capable of producing a material object, just as a potter is [incapable] in a state where the operations of his hands and so forth have ceased. And in the case of the person under discussion, there is no operation of his own parts; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

If it is argued that there is no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) because of the reasoning established in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*, then in reality another refutation would be more appropriate; for what room is there for a counter-reason (*pratihetu*)? We reply: No, because this [counter-reason] is presented for the purpose of demonstrating that repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is not a constituent factor in the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). As it has been stated: "If repeated observation were the means, then even this [fallacy] might occur. Thus, it is settled that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the impossibility of the various ways of grasping pervasion.

Or, let it be granted that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs somehow; even so, the hope for the proof of God is not fruitful, because there is no certainty regarding the restriction of the intelligent probandum (*sādhya*) to oneness. For if its oneness were established, then the establishment of its eternality, omnipresence, and omniscience would justify the conventional designation "God. But when the collection of effects, distributed across different places and times, is conceived as being produced by multiple agents exceeding the number one, then neither omnipresence nor eternality is possible; and since only the knowledge of their own respective materials and instruments is established, where is the omniscience?

Now, if it is argued that when many [agents] act with distracted minds, there would be a failure to produce the effect, and furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its destruction and so forth—[we reply: this suspicion might indeed apply to the activity of Lords (īśvara) who possess qualities such as omnipotence individually; however, it is stated here that not even one such [Lord] is established today. Moreover, it is clearly observed that numerous beings of limited power, having begun a single or multiple effect, do indeed bring it to completion.

If it is argued that even in the case of many [agents], there must be one who is predominant or more powerful—like a master builder or a general—and therefore that one alone possesses agency because the others merely follow him, we say no. For even in those cases, there is no such rule; we observe that some independent beings come together for a single purpose, such as the existence of a living being, according to their own respective motives.

Furthermore, there is no requirement that only one among them be the primary instigator, since the longing in the hearts of many may arise simultaneously, and even a lowly person can be an instigator.

Therefore, just as even tiny creatures such as bees, honey-bees, and ants can individually construct things like hives and anthills, what need is there to mention the creation of the universe by a single being? In this regard, the earth, the netherworlds, and so forth—whose origins are not witnessed in this life—are inferred from the fact that they have fulfilled the purposes of conscious beings by their very existence.

And those small creatures would proceed—like ants building an anthill—even while knowing that the material cause is the extremely minute substance such as earth, the instrument is [their own] bodies, the recipient of the pleasure and so forth is the self, and the purpose is the pleasure of their own maintenance and so on. Furthermore, even if [the existence of a creator] were established, the presiding agents need not necessarily be perceived, either because they depend upon actions of diverse potencies or because of the remoteness of their nature. As for trees and the like, which are produced from visible causes and are of human origin, there is no question at all regarding them.

Furthermore, as for those entities existing in the vicinity of the Vindhya, Yugandhara, and other mountains where no human activity is observed, they too must have agents—countless presiding beings such as Piśācas and the like. Who, then, could be all-knowing? Moreover, since space and time are indeed distinct [from one another], how can they possess omnipresence and eternity? Nor is there any subverting inference based on the power of real entities (*vastubala*) that would refute such a doubt.

But surely you yourselves have not accepted this either. And if you argue that between these two extremely difficult hypotheses, the hypothesis of a Lord (Īśvara) alone is better due to its parsimony (*lāghava*), we reply: true, if this were merely a matter of setting aside one hypothesis for another; in that case, we would certainly favor your proposal. However, as long as you do not abandon the guise of inference (*anumāna*), our commitment to a rigorous examination remains unavoidable.

Now, if it pains the mind that the Narmadā and other rivers were created by innumerable minor beings, [we reply that] it would pain it even more if they were created by a single bodiless being. Therefore, valid cognition alone is everywhere more powerful; the status of an object is exactly as it establishes. For this very reason, that [cognition] is firmly determined. And there is no need for any concession regarding minor beings.

[260] Let the arrangement of the world be created by hosts—whether small or large, visible, possessing equal or superior power, independent, or accompanied by individual beings esteemed as primary—consisting of immeasurable multitudes that know only the mere appropriation of their own respective effects, whether gross or subtle, single or manifold, and which are included within the six states of existence; however, let there not be a single creator of this.

Nor is this [the case] for Buddhists, because they do not accept it in that way; thus, there is an exclusion of the reason (*hetu*), since it would follow that [the reason] is excluded from even one [of the two sides]. Furthermore, in an inference that functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta*), there is no dependence on the acceptance of another. For there is no contradiction in abandoning mere acceptance. Thus, when "mere intelligent being" (*buddhimanmātra*) is the probandum, the desired proof is not certain—whether through the necessary connection with the specific characteristic of being cognizant of the material cause and so forth, or through the direct proof of an agent who is cognizant of the material cause and so forth—because it does not establish that all causal activity has a single agent.

Furthermore, if one seeks to prove merely that [the subject] possesses superknowledge such as the power of grasping [objects], it is futile, like the stories of the *Mahābhārata* and so forth. Therefore, since there is no other means of proof, the desired establishment of [the subject] as possessing qualities such as omniscience must be accepted from this very [reasoning]; thus, it is established that the refutation must be stated with reference to that very [subject], characterized by the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*).

Therefore, the phrase "to whatever extent the scope of the object" and so forth is difficult to bypass. Even though the establishment of a particular [property] is drawn forth by the connection with the general property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*), its proof remains dependent upon the means of proof (*sādhana*), because the means of proof is presented solely for that purpose and because there is no other means of proof.
