For even for a Buddhist, the establishment of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is indeed dependent upon the means of proof.

For if the proof of momentary destruction were to achieve its purpose even upon the abandonment of selflessness (*nairātmya*), then what would be the establishment of selflessness through the proof of momentary destruction? On your part, however, having set aside the establishment of omniscience and so forth, another specific distinction characterized by the higher knowledge of appropriation and so on has been established. Therefore, it is irrelevant [to say] that "concomitance preceded by the introduction of a self is not demonstrated in the example."

Even when there is direct observation of its presence in that [subject], the necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*) of the general property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*) must still be demonstrated; and that is impossible because, due to its unity, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the locus of all instances of action.

By this very [argument], Vācaspati’s display of proof for omniscience is also refuted. However, once an omniscient creator is established, our labor in determining the oneness of that creator is useless; therefore, we desist. Furthermore, as for the negative inference (*vyatireki-prayoga*) he has stated, that too is invalidated precisely because oneness is not certain, since it has been demonstrated that even if one possesses non-eternal cognition whose objects are not all-encompassing, it is still possible to have knowledge of the material cause and so forth.

If, however, [the exclusion of non-connection is intended] in the case of establishing fire through smoke—as in the case of the exclusion of non-connection with a mountain (*dharādharāyogavyavaccheda*)—then it would follow by inference that fire also possesses a mass of five-colored flames. If you argue that there is no such capacity here [in the case of smoke], then in that case as well, the capacity lies precisely in the exclusion of non-connection with the subject (*pakṣāyogavyavaccheda*). Even if an effortful agent is established in relation to a mountain, since singularity is not certain, how can the establishment of omniscience be achieved?

But surely, since even a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is an effect, its agent must necessarily be one who perceives its constituent atoms; and those with the eye of flesh cannot possibly be such. Otherwise, what wrong have we done that— [the opponent asks]—[this should be so]?

[261] "If it is asked, 'Do we not exist in that way?'—then one who perceives supersensible objects must necessarily be accepted as the agent, and it is not logical for anyone other than Īśvara to be so. But this too is trivial. For even among those with the fleshly eye, the capacity of the sense organs is not common to all, since we observe an extraordinary excellence of sensory acuity even in vultures and others who are far inferior to us."

Furthermore, some among the most minute beings might even perceive atoms due to a particular capacity for action, just as ants perceive odor-atoms that are beyond our own range. However, by perceiving what is subtle merely in that sense, they cannot perceive other subtle things that are remote in space and time, nor can they perceive all gross objects. Therefore, one cannot hope to establish the existence of God on that basis alone.

If that is so, let there be the possibility of perceiving an atom; but how could there be such a possibility regarding all the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) and the specific merits (*dharma*), demerits (*adharma*), and latent dispositions (*āśaya*) inherent in them? Not at all. For in the example of the potter, the performance of an action is not seen to be pervaded by a complete knowledge of the nature of the *kṣetrajña* and so forth; rather, its accomplishment is held to occur through the cognition of the recipient (*sampradāna*) and the instruments (*upakaraṇa*). And that [cognition] is impossible, because it is logically untenable, and because even according to the aforementioned sequence, the mere cognition of those [atoms] would suffice for the purpose.

Because it is unavoidable that the object (*karman*) would be designated as the recipient (*sampradāna*) due to its being intended by the agent for himself—as in the expression "he builds a temple for himself"—otherwise, there would arise the contingency of a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the requirement of knowledge of the recipient.

If it is argued that another person, who knows the recipient (*sampradāna*), will be inferred in that case, we say no; for since deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed, it is not established that the agent is necessarily concomitant with knowledge of the recipient, and thus there is no basis for inference. Nor does his being an agent imply he is not the recipient; for if that were so, it would follow that even the potter is not the agent, and if he were the agent, one would have to accept that his own self is the recipient.

Nor is he capable of knowing even that which is commonly established in worldly transaction as a recipient (*sampradāna*), such as a field (*kṣetra*), by setting aside the distinctions of latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) and the meanings of words denoting instruments; for just as a potter knows those [instruments] without piercing them through his knowledge of the staff, the wheel, and so forth, so too will living beings, even when merely inferred, eventually come to know their own hands, mouths, and other organs.

Whence, then, comes this thorough knowledge of the distinctions between the nature of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and his respective states of merit and demerit? Furthermore, for one who is bodiless, how can there be any connection with the activity of his own limbs? And what kind of connection with supernatural powers (*siddhi*) could a bodiless being have? For if unity were established, the embodied being would be localized and incapable of all actions; thus, the hope for the proof of a bodiless state arises from such capability, yet it has been stated that unity is difficult to establish.

Furthermore, even in the state of bodilessness (*aśarīratva*), since instruments such as the staff, the wheel, and the like are impossible, it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the culmination of the knowledge of instruments occurs solely through the knowledge of the various latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*). This is for the sake of excellence; for even though space, time, inherence, and so forth are included among the instruments, one achieves the goal merely through the knowledge of them.

But what is this distinction, such that for one in that state, there is knowledge of the instruments only through the knowledge of space and so forth, and not through the knowledge of merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the like? If it is argued that it must be through the knowledge of both, that too has already been addressed. For [the Lord] does not possess every single instrument.

[262] It is observed that an agent must necessarily be known; however, we do not assert a certainty that the cognition of the instruments occurs through the cognition of direction and so forth alone—which would lead to a specific inquiry—rather, it is said here that because other instruments are possible, there is no finality in the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

Therefore, just as in the case of successive makers [of jars], where a state of being known for their use of instruments is observed through a series of external instruments such as the stick, wheel, and so forth, as well as the shuttle, loom, and so forth—[is it] by means of various other instruments such as *dharma* and the like? Or must it be by taking *dharma* and the like themselves? This is precisely the doubt. If, however, there were no other instrument, then an explanation based on the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) would be fitting.

Furthermore, when there is doubt regarding the paths to worldly prosperity and the highest good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*), what could be accomplished by such a maker designated as "God," who is like a man devoid of wealth?

Therefore, even if bodilessness were established, there would be no attraction of knowledge regarding *dharma* and so forth; how much less so when that [bodilessness] is unestablished? Let it be that [God] is not the knower of *dharma* and so forth by virtue of being their instrument; however, he will certainly be their knower by virtue of being their effect. Thus, the claim that "the agent who knows the form and other attributes of the effect is God" is also devoid of substance. For those who perform acts such as giving or violence know them only in their own nature; they do not become gods merely by that. Nor is any other knower of them in their entirety established.

However, the ascertainment that [an agent] is the performer of dharma and adharma does not necessarily follow even for one who performs them, as is the case with a potter. Thus, because there is no ascertainment of the true nature of those who perform such acts, the claim that the ascertainment of the true nature—by virtue of being an effect—would necessitate the presence of a creator in the form of Īśvara is also untenable. For even the ascertainment of dharma and adharma remains one whose existence is itself doubtful.

How can there be hope from that [God]? For one whose nature consists of conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpa*) accompanied by the suspicion of error has not yet been dispelled; rather, it is through the gateway of numerous scriptures and by accepting the recollection of past lives and so forth among the gods that even they possess, albeit in a slight degree, an understanding of the connection between correct actions and their fruits. Yet, this much alone does not suffice for sovereignty.

Thus, since God is unestablished, the auspicious and inauspicious actions of all living beings are not merely instruments, but are themselves the causes of the world's diversity. This is the meaning of the first verse to be accepted by the wise.
The refutation of God is completed.
[265] Explanation of the *Vārttika-saptaślokī* in the Section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*).
I bow with valid means of cognition to him whose teaching is unimpeded, who proclaimed that the world is a manifold creation of karma and is devoid of an independent creator.

When the negation of eternal validity has been established, the skillful one, demonstrating that lack of validity which resides in non-eternal entities, says: "This path removes the portion of delusion regarding that very point."

Even if one has personally refuted the criticisms of others, if there is no satisfaction in merely mentioning the name of the author of the *Vārttika* when there is no further engagement, then it is better to display one's prowess through the very act of describing those [criticisms] once again.

Whatever is an effect is preceded by an intelligent agent, just as a pot; and the earth, mountains, and so forth are effects. Alternatively, whatever is not preceded by an intelligent agent is not an effect, just as space; and trees, mountains, oceans, and so forth are effects. Thus, this is the reason based on the nature of being an effect (*kāryahetu*). Likewise, the following [reasons] should be employed: having non-conscious material causes (*acetanopādānatva*), performing purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), possessing a specific arrangement of constituent parts that initiate themselves (*svārambhakāvayavasanniveśaviśeṣavattva*), performing causal functions after remaining stationary for a time (*sthitvā sthitvā kāryakarmāṇi*), and possessing the property of activity (*pravṛttidharmakatva*). How then can it be said [that these are not valid]?
"Is it not the case that there is no means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*) even for the impermanent?

And this proof is indeed common to both the eternal and the impermanent. However, when the discussion proceeds toward impermanence, the opponent’s search for a means of valid cognition would be set in motion. The mention of the word 'impermanent' is merely for the purpose of introducing that [proof]. We do not, however, maintain that the Blessed One is impermanent. For instance: He is one, all-pervading, omniscient, the locus of a single consciousness, eternal, and is called the Lord (*īśvara*)."
The Creator of the world is accepted as the authoritative source; he is to be petitioned by those who seek heaven and liberation.

To this it is replied: Is the desire to establish the excellence of the Supreme Person—who is the abode of the multitude of qualities taught by these very reasons—accomplished through these reasons alone, or rather by the power of other reasons? In this regard, the first position is not tenable. For, a means of proof (sādhana) establishes only that extent of an object’s nature which it pervades, and no further object. Indeed, the capacity of a means of valid cognition does not extend to whatever object is merely encompassed by one's wish.

Furthermore, to whatever extent the capacity of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) extends, the establishment of an object occurs through that much by virtue of its being the cause; however, even though "being an effect" and so forth are pervaded by "having been preceded by an intelligent agent," they are not capable of producing a cognition restricted to [the agent's] singularity and other such qualities, because no pervasion is perceived with respect to those specific qualifications. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of determining even the opposite nature [of the object]. For having perceived smoke pervaded by the generality of fire (*dahanasāmānya*), no one is able to infer a fire possessing a flickering mass of five-colored crests.

[Objection: Even so, one indeed infers the qualification of specific place and time by the force of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); likewise, for one who has perceived that being an effect depends upon the superintendence of an intelligent agent even in the case of a mountain and the like, the desired conclusion will be established by the logic of a "conclusion-by-implication" (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*). [Reply: No, because the capacity [of the evidence] is not established.

For just as in the inference from smoke and so forth, there is the capacity [of the argument] that what is produced by fire at a certain place and time does not possess that same place and time, we do not likewise perceive—in the absence of a single conscious agent who is omniscient and so on—an impossibility of trees entering into a state of dormancy and the like. Therefore, even if the establishment of the potter’s capacity to produce those [trees] occurs by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), it is not able to support the intended specific quality [of a single creator].

Now, if a perfected being (*siddha*) capable of creating mountains and such were established, what else would be required? Why then is there satisfaction with a mere expressive word whose expressed form remains unestablished? For in this way, the intended subject at hand is not proven. Indeed, the operation of production is nothing more than the state of being invariably antecedent to an effect that is about to arise; and that [operation] is common to insentient things as well, and even for the intellect (*buddhi*), it is not established as being restricted by specific qualities such as omnipresence. Therefore, with respect to the intended probandum, the establishment of a mere statement accomplishes nothing.

But who indeed asserts that mountains and so forth are preceded by an omniscient being? Rather, suspecting that they are caused by an intelligent agent, [the author] says, while internally mocking [the opponent] with a proof:

"In regard to [matters such as] functioning after having remained stationary, specific structures, and purposeful activity, [your argument leads to] the establishment of what is already accepted. (PV II 10ab’c)

Thus [it is argued]: for the entire aggregate of things is held to be produced by both common and uncommon karma. And since karma is insentient by nature, the fact that oceans, mountains, and so forth—which are the causes of all knowledge—fail to be established [as sentient] does not bring anything undesirable upon us; this is the sense. Furthermore, if the intention were that [the world] is to be produced by that [karma] alone, then because the contradiction would be unestablished, there would follow the consequence of the futility of presenting the proof. Therefore, only a qualified [probandum] is to be proven by this [reasoning]. And it has already been stated that the power of the proof does not apply to that [qualified object].

"Let it be, then, that such establishment occurs through another means of proof alone. With this in view, he states "or non-establishment," raising the objection regarding the absence of certainty from the perspective of the second position.

The meaning is that there is neither another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor another logical reason (*hetu*) by which this certainty could arise. Alternatively, since perception is impossible due to [the object's] being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), inference must be invoked; and for that purpose, he speaks with reference to every possible reason.
[267] "Or there is non-establishment.

For, although by the aforementioned inference a conscious agent common to all disputants is established as a mere sentient being, there is no specific property (*viśeṣadharma*) that could serve as a reason (*hetu*) without being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), other than existence (*sattā*) itself; for there is no occasion for inference regarding a property that exceeds mere existence. However, since existence implies momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), he says "or there is non-establishment" with respect to [the opponent's claim of] eternal oneness.

The meaning is that there is a "contradictory proof" (*viparītasiddhi*). For, just as in the case of *adharma* and so forth, even in the case of the eternal (*nitya*), a refutation is intended just like the opponent's proof by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*); this is because the statement of "non-eternal" has as its fruit merely the introduction [of the topic]. Furthermore, he states that there is "inconclusiveness" (*anaikānta*) with respect to the nature of pervasion (*vyāptitva*), or else that the example is "unestablished" (*asiddhi*). What is meant is this: since the nature of pervasion does not exist in reality, and because there is no observation of it in the example, the pervasion of any property (*dharma*) is not established by it. Even if all cognition exists, there is no perception of its being a pervader. Why? He says:

"Or else there is doubt regarding the example," because it is impossible for one of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) to ascertain [the subject] in its specific nature as a real entity. Therefore, for that which possesses the qualities [of the subject] as described, there is no establishment [of the probandum] either directly from the aforementioned means of proof, nor by the logic of a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established incidentally), nor from another means of proof; thus, the absence of any proving instrument (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) is established. However, since the desired [probandum] is established even in that which lacks those specificities, [the argument fails].

Alternatively, when reasons such as "being an effect" have been set forth, there arises a dilemma regarding whether they establish the general property or the specific instance of the probandum—namely, whether there is proof or non-proof. In this regard, since the proponent's position is already established by the fact that [the world] is known to be an object of action (*karmavāditā*), proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*) is evident. Thus, demonstrating the lack of concomitance (*anugamābhāva*) with respect to the specific instance—which serves as the basis for the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*)—he says:
"Or else, there is non-establishment in the example, or else doubt."

Thus, "of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*) is the subject under discussion. In that regard, since [an agent] such as a potter—who possesses qualities contrary to omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth—is established without dispute, there is a lack of proof for the intended [probandum] in the example. Now, if the view is that the intended [attributes] such as omnipresence belong to that portion [of the agent] which is distinct from the body and is by nature difficult to distinguish, even so, let there be doubt; what is the point of this insistence here? This is the sense. As for the phrase "establishing what is already established in the general case" (*sāmānye siddhasādhyatā*):

Therefore, because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalpa*) or because the property to be proven is doubtful (*sandigdhasādhyadharman*), there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" and so forth by the property to be proven in the example. Thus, it is precisely because the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) is unestablished that the logical reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Now, even if smoke is present, there is no concomitance (*anugama*) with respect to the specific characteristic, while with respect to the general characteristic (*sāmānya*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Thus, the logic is the same for both; therefore, their validity or lack thereof must be determined as being uniform. If it is uniform, then what has been considered is not correct. For it is established that inference does not attain the status of valid cognition while disregarding the establishment of a specific distinction.

But that specific qualification—characterized as the mere exclusion of what is unfit for the subject (*pakṣāyogyavyavacchedamātra*)—may exist as something distinct from it, as in "there is fire here because of smoke," or may it be of such a nature [as not being distinct]? In that regard, if the first [type] were denied, there would be a repudiation of inference itself, since the establishment of anything additional is rooted in that [exclusion]. Nor can that [first type] be refuted without following upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For a property that is established as being necessarily connected to the subject (*pakṣadharma*) would, by its very existence as such, be separated from the subject if it did not demonstrate that the subject is inseparable from it; at most, this would exceed the requirement for time and so forth within the context of a valid reason. As for the second type of establishment, however, since it has only that [subject] as its probandum, it does not suffice to deny inference even if it occurs without following a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because its purpose is fulfilled by establishing the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) through a property that lacks those specific [additional] features.

However, there would be a denial of a specific type of inference (*anumānaviśeṣāpalāpa*). For instance, suppose someone intends to infer a peacock with a crest of five colors, and when another person challenges his proof—"There is fire here because of smoke"—on the grounds that it is either a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) or lacks universal concomitance (*ananugama*), he might then say: "In that case, since even mere smoke is excluded, there would be no inference at all here. Such a person might seem plausible; yet, the destruction of inference itself does not follow, because at that very moment he is himself establishing the inference of the generality of fire (*dahanasāmānya*) as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the refutation [of the opponent] is based solely on the distinction of excluding the non-connection with the subject (*pakṣāyogavyavaccheda*).
The refutation applies to those [positions] other than the absence of a positive concomitance with the establishment of the desired [proposition].

These two [fallacies] are not restricted to being either defects or non-defects; rather, it is held that their status as one or the other depends on the difference in the subject matter (*viṣaya*). Likewise here, even if one accepts the exclusion of the impossibility of a conscious controller (*buddhimad-adhiṣṭhāna*) in the case of the ocean, mountains, and so forth, for those who point out these two as defects with respect to some other intended specific qualification, it follows directly that the inference of the "variegated beauty" (*citrakāntiśikhā*) would be destroyed, but not inference in general.
Therefore, validity or invalidity is not restricted to one or the other only in relation to a particular type of inference, but not in a general sense.

[269] But surely, even now, a particular difference is established independently of any commonality; so what prevents it from being another particular difference? Indeed, there is no establishment whatsoever that is devoid of a commonality. For a commonality, by its very nature, cannot remain without drawing in that particularity. Nor can it be claimed that it necessarily possesses this power with respect to every other particularity, as was described previously; otherwise, the inference of the "five-colored crest" (*pañcavarṇaśikha*) and so forth would be impossible to avoid.

In this regard, the objection regarding impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) and so forth applies equally even to a person who possesses a single-mindedness (*ekacittatva*) and other such qualities. A similar inference (*anumāna*) would arise in that case as well. Therefore, one who wishes to assert a specific distinction must necessarily demonstrate a positive concomitance (*anvaya*); since that is absent, the reason is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, it is established that if one were to prove merely "one possessing intelligence" (*buddhimat-mātra*), it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

It might be argued as follows: "Intelligent" does not mean merely possessing consciousness, but rather it is intended to mean one who knows the material cause and so forth, or one who possesses effort. Since such a concomitance is established in the case of effects like jars and the like, the fact that "being an effect" is perceived even in the case of the mountain and so forth brings to mind precisely such an agent; thus, neither of the two faults [previously mentioned] applies.

If it is argued that he is omniscient precisely because he knows their material causes and so forth, and is restricted by place and time, such that a difference between them would not be capable of producing the collection of effects being produced—thereby establishing attributes such as eternality and omnipresence for him as well—then this is like the hope for the enjoyment of fruit from a tree whose roots have been severed.

For if their oneness were established, then the perfection of these qualities would be established; otherwise, when it is possible for an effect existing in different places and times to be produced by many [causes], to whom would such powers as sovereignty belong? And since each would only know its own specific sphere of activity, who could possess omniscience?

If unity were established, the entire probandum would be entailed; yet there is no basis for such a certainty. Nor can the existence of a creator capable of fashioning the earth and so forth be established merely from the occurrence of the singular number [in the word "creator"]; for there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). If such a connection were established, how could an opponent who had realized the unity of the subject overlook this? However, one might allow it in terms of a general class (*jāti*), just as fire is inferred from various successive instances of smoke; thus, we do not insist on a strict necessity.

Nor can the oneness of a single creator be established from the persistence of specific qualities across diverse effects—just as the oneness of a single painter is established in a variegated painting due to the persistence of similar lines and so forth—because no such persisting entity is actually perceived. Furthermore, the perceived properties such as "being an effect" or "being an entity" cannot prove oneness, for they are just like the variegation [of the painting itself].

For even when other qualities are possible, there remains doubt as to whether the agent is one or similar; how much more so, then, when they are absent, can there be certainty regarding oneness? This is certainly like painting a picture on a non-existent wall, that upon the lack of certainty regarding non-difference, omniscience and the like are determined.

The other, however, says: "Unity too must be understood precisely through the production of an effect. How so? If there were many [agents] with conflicting minds acting independently, there would be mutual contradiction; because they would not understand each other's intentions favorable to their own, there would be a non-production of the effect simultaneously, and there would also be the consequence of the destruction of what has already been produced."

[270] Here it is considered by many: regarding the principle that "there is no simultaneous production of effects by multiple causes," the intended meaning is the non-production of effects at different times and in different locations; or else, the position is that it refers to the non-production of a single great composite whole (*mahāvayavin*) such as a mountain and so forth. In this regard, we do not perceive any contradiction to production even when multiple causes act upon a single object. For just as there is activity on one part, so too may there be activity on others, as in the case of an anthill.

If it is asked, "With what purpose in mind do they act?", the answer is no; for since the activities of minds are diverse, it is impossible to determine the specific cause of their engagement. Otherwise, one could not avoid the persistent inquiry as to what even the Lord himself has in mind. Or rather, such a determination might be possible for others who are adept at discerning the sublation of intended objects and so forth, but not for the Lord, whose nature is gentle.

Nor can a rule of mutual coordination among many [agents] be established, since we observe ants constructing a single anthill. If it is argued that such a thing is indeed possible among humans due to their competitive impulse (*ahaṃkāra*), then why do we insist on humans alone when it is possible for one massive object to be constructed sequentially by a vast number of other beings who, though distinct, are discerning and engaged in a single task? Furthermore, no one has ever seen the simultaneous production of objects such as the Yugandhara mountains.

This is merely a possibility, since the capacity for such a thing is conceivable in the case of some single [cause]; nor can a rule of mutual contradiction be established even among persons through a competitive impulse (*ahamahamikā*), because it is impossible for a person to possess two contradictory [capacities] without their mutually contradicting one another. Therefore, this deserves to be presented as a mere hypothesis, not as the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or rather, it is merely a recollection of a conventional tenet that "one [effect], such as Mount Maināka, is not produced by many [causes]."

If it is argued that even in a single undertaking there must be one predominant and powerful agent—like a master builder or a general—and therefore agency belongs to him alone because others merely follow his lead, we say no; for even in those cases there is no such rule, as we observe that some independent individuals, acting according to their own respective purposes, may together construct a single bridge or similar work.

Even in that case, there is no such thing as a single primary instigator, because there is no one to prevent the simultaneous longing in the hearts of many, and because even a non-primary person may possess the capacity to instigate. Merely by that much, one cannot claim primacy, for that would contradict common experience. Furthermore, when there is the possibility of a massive undertaking through countless groups—each consisting of an immeasurable number of individuals acting as architects—what indeed is the lack of success? By this, the argument citing the creatures of an anthill as a primary example is refuted.

Moreover, just as a specific arrangement of parts for comfortable furnishings is perceived in a palace being constructed by many people acting with a single heart, such is not the case even with the great mountains, which are composed of masses of irregularly situated massive rocks; whereby, if these too were preceded by a single primary person, it would have to be so.

Therefore, since multiple operations are incapable of being sublated in the production of each individual Kailāsa and the like, how could they be sublated in the case of entities existing in various distant places and times?

If it is argued that unity is established through scripture (*āgama*), then this ritual for binding a protective amulet with mustard seeds for one who has fallen ill is indeed not a refutation regarding Buddhists, whose minds are uniquely adept at investigating scripture.

For if there is an adherence to the scriptures of investigation (*parīkṣā-āgama*), then since this very moment is the time for investigation, why follow them only now? On the other hand, if it is independent of investigation, then let the establishment of all desired objects proceed from that [scripture] alone; what is the point of this obsession with adducing inference, whose sole essence is laborious effort? Indeed, the exertion to purify a logical reason (*hetu*) is arduous for those whose intellects lack subtle penetration, whereas the attainment of one's desired goal is easy through the mere recitation of a portion of a scripture.

Furthermore, even this very proponent, while establishing the authority of the scriptures, recites the "Pañcālaka" argument as follows: "The *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas] are not non-authoritative, because they are the means for producing concordant knowledge among all those in the stages of life (*āśrama*), just like perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For if they were non-authoritative, there could be no such thing as a consensus among all those in the stages of life; since their non-authoritativeness would allow for the possibility of disagreement through someone's realization of their lack of authority, whereas the rule of consensus is possible only in the case of authoritative means of knowledge such as perception. Thus he argues.

That too is applicable only within the assembly of disciples. For indeed, what is called "corroboration" (*saṃvāda*) must be either the convergence with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or purposeful efficacy (*arthakriyā*); yet neither of these two applies here, as in the [Vedic] passages:
"The Person has a thousand heads" (*Ṛgveda* X.10.1) and "He knows this universe, but there is no knower of him" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.19).

Whether regarding the meaning of such passages as "The one God, generating heaven and earth, has perceived [them]" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.3), or concerning rites such as the Agniṣṭoma which are means for attaining heaven, such a conviction may arise in someone: that just as one member of a religious order possesses the thought that there exists a single, all-pervading, eternal Creator of the universe, so too does another.

If it is argued that there is a practice corresponding to that [knowledge], we reply: this cognition of theirs must arise from that very scripture, or from another such source, or it would have to be of the nature of a mere accidental conceptualization; it cannot, however, be of the nature of perception or inference, for that would entail the possibility of it occurring even for those who do not belong to an *āśrama*, since perception and the like are not subject to error by other persons. Furthermore, knowledge based on scripture would not exist for one who has neither heard nor respected the scriptures; rather, it is logical that it occurs only for someone else through the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from practice in a previous life.

In this regard, this [scripture] is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it arises from the practice of something that is possible whether the object exists or does not exist. Thus, its connection with another means of valid cognition is said to be due to its originating from such [an authority], since that [authority] itself lacks validity. This is the principle: "that which is unestablished cannot be proven by what is unestablished. Therefore:

[272] This is merely a recollection of such a convention, namely that "there exists someone who is like this. Furthermore, we understand that even the term "hermitage" (*āśrama*) is a mere designation; consequently, the qualification "of all those belonging to the hermitages" (*samastāśramiṇām*) is unestablished, because no consensus is established with the Buddhists, the Digambaras, and others. Moreover, since partial consensus exists even among those of contrary views, its presentation is not fruitful. For this very reason, the absolute cessation of disagreement—which would allow for the establishment of validity—is unproven.

As for the claim that this might be possible even for those in the various stages of life (*āśramiṇaḥ*) due to the power of a common delusion persisting from beginningless time—this is trivial. Therefore, even in a single place such as Mount Mandara, who among those possessing effort—who know the portion of the object of activity and the material cause for immeasurable persons—could be considered "all-knowing" (*sarvavedī*)? Furthermore, if such beings were to act in different places and times, how could they possess attributes such as eternality and omnipresence? Nor is there any room for knowledge of unseen portions (*adṛṣṭa-bhāga*), since we observe that even a potter produces the object of his own activity without such [omniscience].

Furthermore, since there is no logical connection whatsoever with the inevitable consequence of destruction and so forth for that which has been produced by many [causes], it follows that upon the loss of unity, the non-existence (anumṛtatva) of omniscience and other such qualities is unavoidable; thus, this [objection] is also entirely groundless, as he said:

Since they would be multiple and omniscient, and because they would possess the capacity to act as creators of all things, there would be no evidence for their simultaneous engagement in effects restricted by specific place and time; thus, the identity of a single substratum for both omniscience and action is not established. For this very reason, the objection that the rejection of a single [omniscient creator] entails the abandonment of many more [such beings] is not a valid refutation. For if it were established that there are many who are both omniscient and all-creators, then the rejection of a single one would be useless, and one would instead be accepting a much greater exertion of effort.

Furthermore, when a multitude of beings—unaffected by the [worldly] qualities under discussion—is encountered, each acting as a producer of a single effect like the insects in an anthill, what loss is there? For in that case, those very beings would not necessarily be the ones sought after by those desiring heaven and liberation.

By this, the view of one who thinks that God must also be manifold, just like your own omniscient being, is rendered untenable; for even a single substratum of all actions has not been established. For us, however, the proof of universal knowledge does not arise from every action, but rather from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

And since that [omniscience] follows from the possibility of inference based on possibility—because the conceptualization of all forms to be directly perceived is possible—the establishment of such omniscience would apply to one person just as it would to another; or, if it is accepted [for one], there is no fault.

If it is argued that, by means of practice alone, the creation of all things will likewise occur, we say no, because it is impossible. For instance, the production of stationary beings or the transformation into a mobile being is not the fruit of practice. Even in the case of imagining the construction of other remaining replicas, one might think, "Something like this could happen"; however, there is no certainty that "this very thing currently perceived, such as a forest and so forth, shall not be otherwise. This is because an inference based on possibility (*saṃbhavānumāna*) does not operate with reference to a specific object. Furthermore, even in that case, [the success] remains dependent on the excellence of rare external implements.

[273] It is the conviction that the cultivation of that [power] is not as easy as the transformation of consciousness (*cittamātra-parāvṛtti*). If one asks, "What is the use of craftsmanship when there is a dependence on extraordinary power?"—it is not the case that it lacks the capacity without that [craftsmanship], for such [a claim] is unproven. If it is argued that this is because it is seen otherwise elsewhere, we say no; for by the observed sequence, the production of a body while still in the womb and so forth would result. Therefore, that [production] must necessarily be other than [dependent on] power. Furthermore, there is no certainty regarding a path for the attainment of such power.

Or let there be the establishment of the craft of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the practice included under the word "and so forth" (*ādi*); nevertheless, he says: regarding the reasons such as "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) and the rest, the proof of the desired non-agency is either established or unestablished; it is indeed unestablished, because of its lack of utility.

For there is no utility for the practitioner of realization in hells and the like; nor is there any purpose in the mere creation of the instruments of pleasure, since one's own highest good (*svaśreyasa*) can be attained through effort, whereas those [instruments] would otherwise exist [only by chance], or else beings will provide the pleasure themselves. At most, for those who do not know that path, the instruction of it alone is beneficial; therefore, for that purpose, the practice of directly realizing the path is superior. Thus, due to futility and lack of resolve, there is no such practice.

If that is so, one might ask: even if there is practice of knowledge regarding every single atom, how is it that there is no impairment [of the capacity for action], as in the case of [ordinary] omniscience? To this he says:

"In the case of the omniscient of all things, there is doubt regarding the example," because the position of the "omniscient of what is useful" (*upayuktasarvajña*) will be primarily discussed later. Alternatively, the meaning is that in that case there is doubt concerning futility and lack of determination, but not a certainty of non-existence. Furthermore, since "mention" (*uddeśa*) is defined elsewhere as "pointing out," there is no equality with the opponent's view. Therefore, even if those possessing effort are established by the reasons under discussion, there is no impairment.

If it is argued: "Is it not indeed undesirable for you that mountains such as Gandhamādana were produced by a multitude of sentient beings possessing effort? Therefore, since no other alternative is possible, an intelligent agent—excluded from multiple instances—is established as the sole creator of all effects, and this, in turn, revives his omniscience and other attributes. This is not so; for a desire lacks a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the actual object, and thus its exclusion from multiple instances does not constitute a valid proof.
And if he should somehow not accept it, then the opponent must be propitiated by means of prostration, such as by becoming invisible, in order to make him accept it;
this is not the proper method, for even a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is not applicable against one who is independent.
For when his unity is forcibly removed, multiplicity is certainly not desired [as a result].
"Because its operation culminates in the opposite [of what is desired].

Now, in either case, it is certainly undesirable for the opponent; for the entire world of sentient beings is not held to be the cause by way of effort, but rather solely through the sovereignty of karma characterized by consciousness (*cetanā*). Therefore, [the world] is invariably concomitant with effort.

[274] If it is argued that the property of being an effect—whether singular or manifold—is a means of proof that places an agent possessing effort in proximity, yet this is only for the sake of what is undesirable [to the opponent], then is this proof now presented merely to establish something undesirable to the opponent, or rather to establish one's own thesis? In that case, whether the opponent’s desired point is established or not, there is no result whatsoever from presenting the proof. To say this, he states:
"In the cases of persistence, activity, and so forth, there is either the establishment of what is desired or its non-establishment."

Thus [it is said]. The sense is that this [objection] is identical for both [parties], based on the statement of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) being devoid of purpose (*anarthakya*). Nor is the proponent of the proof (*sādhanavādī*) alone [at fault], since it would not be fitting for him alone to have an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭa*) imposed upon him in two ways. For even though an undesired consequence has arisen in this context, he has begun to establish the very reality of the universe’s being eternal, unitary, and omniscient, rather than just anything at all. If that is so, then even when the proof is presented, one must state what the basis for its lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) is.
As for what was further stated—that there is a lack of concomitance (*anugama*) with respect to a particular—[that remains to be addressed].

Thus, although there may be non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or doubt regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) due to [the opponent’s view that] the creator is omnipresent and omniscient, as the case may be, nevertheless, let these two not occur by virtue of [the creator] being one. For if a single creator possessing unitary effort is established, the entire probandum (*sādhya*) is established. Furthermore, considering that a single potter is seen to be the maker of many jars, pots, and so forth, [the author], while introducing the positive concomitance even in the case of unity, says: "In the example... (*dṛṣṭānte*).

Thus [it is said]. The term "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) carries over. This is the intended meaning: it is not the case that because one particular effect, such as a jar or a pot, is produced by a single agent, all effects must likewise be so; for in those cases, the activity of multiple potters and others is clearly perceived. Therefore, how can there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a single effortful agent for those observed effects? Alternatively, what is this so-called "potter"? Is he some single entity consisting of a collection of the elements and their derivatives (*bhūta-bhautika*) which is the referent of the designation "pot-maker," or is he merely a collection of hands, feet, and so forth?
In reality, the meaning is: by which single instrument is the production of a jar and so forth brought within the range of perception?

Now, what is the point of this insistence? Whatever kind of single agent is observed to be the object of common worldly usage, such a one—being established as a single creator whose nature is composite and who is cognizant of the material cause and other factors for everything—is established as being indeed omniscient.

Therefore, even if other qualities are set aside, its status as something to be accepted is established by that much alone, and its capacity to bring about both human goals (puruṣārtha) is logically consistent; thus, there is no flaw whatsoever. With this in mind—intending to show that even on this position all these reasons, such as "being an effect" (kāryatva), are inconclusive (vyabhicārin)—he says: [the following].

[275] Thus; the word "of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. For, although there is the state of being an effect due to being a mere aggregate—just like a potter—and the presence of such features as specific arrangement (*saṃniveśa*), there is nevertheless an absence of being preceded by an agent possessing effort; or else, even in the absence of that [effortful agent], such a thing [the state of being an effect] may still exist. Furthermore, if one were to desire another cause for that [agent], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*), and thus no comprehension [of the original point].

But surely, being unconscious by nature, [the body] requires an agent possessing effort for its own production and for producing another; yet since that [agent] is himself the substratum of such a cognition, what need is there for another? For there is no rule that because jars and the like require light, another light must also be required by that light. Therefore, what is this infinite regress?

If that is the case, then how could the collection [of factors] such as the intellect and the sense organs—which possesses effort and is designated as a "potter"—depend upon anything else? Therefore, one must accept that whether conscious or unconscious, a collection arises or produces by its very nature while depending on another conscious entity; thus, there is indeed an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Alternatively, if the group of conscious beings is held to be independent of any other consciousness, then the properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) residing in jars and the like would be established as being invariably concomitant with something other than the intended presiding agent; consequently, they could not maintain their existence without being undermined by the fault of contradiction.

If, however, such a basis [of causal operation] is accepted, then even though there is non-perception due to the remoteness of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*), there remains the possibility of its activity; thus, these [non-perceptions] would not be invariably concomitant with the observation of the opposite. Consequently, because the negative pervasion (*viparyaya-vyāpti*) is absent, the absence of the contradictory conventional usage would follow. Even then, if someone skilled in the analysis of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) does not take care to object for the sake of establishing the relation of cause and effect, let it be—let us leave it at that, as this has not yet been commenced.

So, what is the use of this persistence? For if one persists, there is the risk of introducing gross defects that contradict perception; or else, even so, since the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*), a contrary proof (*viparītasiddhi*) will be applied. Thus, disregarding [the opponent] with a haughty "blindfold" like an elephant, just as he has accepted God as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for the production of all effects, we shall likewise assume him to be such. Then, fearing an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*) if a conscious being were to require another conscious being, and relying on that very [God] because He is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*), he states his doubt.

Now, if a potter, despite possessing effort, does not [exert it] toward his own body but rather toward the jar and so forth, why then would he not depend upon something else for the sake of accomplishing his own body? In that case, why would even the one intended as God—who possesses effort directed toward the subject at hand—not depend upon something else, since there is a contradiction in exerting causal activity toward oneself? Yet he does not depend [on anything else]. Therefore, the rule that "whatever produces an effect, such as a product, must be presided over by one possessing effort" is contradicted by that very instance; thus, the establishment of doubt is achieved.

[Objection: But surely he has no body at all; how then can this [argument] be inconclusive? [Reply: This is the result of forgetting the context. For, with the intent of demonstrating positive concomitance (*anvaya*), you yourself have accepted that the world is created by a single person who is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*)—having admitted a conventional unity in the potter—and thus this is our point. However, if [you argue that the creator] is indeed real...

If oneness that is incompatible with coexistence in a body is being maintained, then one should not introduce conventional oneness as a pervading property of the effect and so forth in the example. Nor is there any fruitful hope for establishing such a state in reality through that [oneness], which is merely nominal, as its pervader. Indeed, no one infers a real fire upon perceiving an effect such as a specific utterance associated with a boy to whom the term "fire" is metaphorically applied.

If it is argued that there is a single, non-erroneous cognition [of] a person as a whole (*avayavin*), who here explicitly asserts that this is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*)? It is said that the application of such a convention to what is not [actually] so is common to both [theories]. Since the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) is sublated by the fact of being a body, the nature of the determination of "oneness" must be understood as an error. Furthermore, even if a whole were to exist, it would be established that the ultimate unreality of the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) is proven—whether one considers the collection of limbs such as the hands to be the whole-body, or the collection of elements (*bhūta*) and so forth, to be the mind (*buddhi*). All these are merely denotable by the single word "one."

It might be argued: "In that case, the person (*puruṣa*) alone is the presiding agent or the creator, and he, being distinct from the body and other such factors, is one and only one. [To this we reply:

Even when the production of an effect is brought about by a collection of visible causes, another unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated; yet even there, having set aside what is seen, that very same thing is [further] imagined. This is a manifold delusion, not limited to a single instance.

First of all, it has been stated that the very existence of the unperceived is difficult to ascertain here because of innate discrepancies in inference. Furthermore, even for that [perceived cause], the status of being a cause is to be established by perception accompanied by the non-perception of the perceived. And that [status] belongs to that very [cause] through the exclusion of what is perceived; otherwise, if activity were possible for hands, feet, and so forth as well, there would follow the undesirable consequence of inferring those too, which would again result in the same fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Otherwise, even the inference of a person [as the agent] would be without a basis.

By this, the conceptualization of the continuum of consciousness (*caitanyasantāna*) as a single person is refuted; for its power is perceived only when accompanied by hands, feet, and so forth, and thus there follows the logical consequence that it must be inferred from its effects in their true nature, just as fire with its fuel is inferred from smoke.

If it is argued that pervasion is apprehended by consciousness alone and not by anything else, we say no; for, by the same logic, it would be impossible to effect a distinction [between them]. Therefore, this person ought to state the causality of that which is non-different from intellect and body precisely through the exclusion of other possibilities (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), since only by doing so could he be able to infer that [causality] through a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and grasp the pervasion based on ultimate identity.

And this being the case, having set aside the observed collection of causal factors whose positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been witnessed, to postulate another cause altogether is a further object of reproach. Furthermore, if that [single cause] were somehow manifold, all effort would be fruitless; thus, it must be postulated as one alone. We perceive this entire [enterprise] to be like the clamor of bees attracted by the fragrance of a sky-lotus.

Therefore, enough with this introduction of [an agent] distinct from the body and so forth. Consequently, the pervasion of an intelligent agent by oneness is not primary, because oneness in reality is impossible for potters and the like, who are denoted as agents. Furthermore, since such a [pervasion] would lead to the same kind of inference based on conventional [reality], there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason—such as "being an effect"—by that very [conventional agent]; thus it was stated that there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).

Now, even so, if such a probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, by what means could there be deviation (*vyabhicāra*); and if it is established, what would deviation accomplish? If you argue that there is non-establishment precisely because of deviation, then, since deviation does not exist when [the subject] is established, on what basis can one determine whether there is non-establishment or establishment? Furthermore, the objection that a real substratum (*dharmin*) must be an actual entity because properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) are real properties of entities is not valid; for this sequence is intended to demonstrate a contradiction with one's own accepted tenets (*abhyupagama-virodha*).

Because it has been initiated in reality; and this [reason] exists in relation to the probandum through the three modes of the means of proof, and in relation to the three-mode means of proof through the intended probandum. In that case, since there is an absence of exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) when the probandum is present, and because it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being established through one's own admission, it is called a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason. In that context, the admission is a constituent part of the effect.

Because of this statement: it is indeed logical that the opponent’s own admission is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since [the argument] proceeds precisely for the purpose of subverting it. For this very reason, it does not serve as a locus (*āśraya*) in an independent syllogism (*svatantra-hetu*). Furthermore, the result of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is its contrapositive (*viparyaya*). However, if one’s own admission were not a valid means of knowledge, there would be no utterance of words at all; and speech is the manifestation of an object perceived by oneself through inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).

Furthermore, since this [statement] does not effect the manifestation of the three aspects as perceived by oneself, it is appropriate that for one who asserts such [a position], the statement of a non-essential part of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). However, for the opponent, it is simply the pointing out of a fault; thus it is established. Alternatively, having raised the objection that the instrument might have been presented by [the proponent] alone for the sake of establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he says:
"Or else, there is doubt regarding the example" (PV II.12).

Thus [it is said]. First of all, there is simply a lack of proof regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*) by means of the example. Or, even if it were proven, there would still be doubt as to what it is for the sake of which the example is adduced; that is to say, for the sake of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases. For indeed, the cognition of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader does not arise for just any object merely because it has been seen in an example, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); rather, it arises from the establishment of an invariable connection (*pratibandha*).

And since there is no evidence whatsoever for this [inference], even if agency and so forth were established in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), they would not entail a self restricted to unity; for there is a lack of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary.

[278] Even properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*), which are restricted to having an agent possessing effort, are merely causes of doubt when used to prove that there is a single agent, because their exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. Thus, Śaṅkara himself stated: "There is no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the property of having a non-conscious material cause (*acetanopādānatva*) with respect to the oneness of the agent," and so forth. As for what he further said—that there is no deviation of the property of having a non-conscious material cause by the mere fact of being presided over by one possessing effort—that alone is of no use in the present context.
Because it was previously established that [the existence of the subject] is dependent upon the establishment of the property that serves as the basis for the dispute.
|| First Section ||

[279] Having thus stated the refutation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to the specific nature of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*), he speaks, reflecting on whether it might also be stated with respect to mere effort (*prayatnavanmātra*): "In the case of the examples regarding the commencement after a pause, specific configuration, purposeful action, and so forth, there is either the establishment of what is already accepted, non-establishment, or doubt."

Thus: the meaning of "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "that which has been seen" (*dṛṣṭo 'ntaḥ*), and the meaning of "established conclusion" (*siddhānta*) is that [the pervasion] is established by mere effortful agency, because a real entity cannot transcend the nature of being either one or many. When [reasons] such as "acting after having remained stationary" have been put forward, the question is: regarding the established conclusion, does there exist the establishment of the proponent's desired [property] in the case of unity, or is there merely non-establishment in the case of plurality; or rather, is there indeed no pervasion at all? Thus, the sense of the question is that there is doubt in both cases.

And here, immediately following, under the section establishing non-difference (*abheda*), the answer has already been given by means of the argument that the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful; therefore, only the third position remains. For we perceive no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) whatsoever when the production of an effect is possible even without the application of effort.

How, then, could there be a restriction regarding the effect and so forth in that case? If it is argued that the undesirable consequence of no restriction in terms of time, place, and so on serves as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), that is incorrect; because even when there is an absence of a particular state of the cause—which possesses restricted power, does not exist at all times, and whose presence depends upon its own causes—the absence of the effect is possible. Therefore, it is not appropriate to assume that [the effect] is invariably concomitant with effort.

If the effect were entirely independent of a cause, then that subverting argument would be applicable and would establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the effect by the cause in general; however, it does not establish it by means of a specific cause such as effort.

Is it not the case that what is called a "cause" everywhere is merely an aggregate, and that this does not exist in a disjoined state? Furthermore, if the conjunction of those [parts] were to occur without an agent possessing effort, it would necessarily be eternal. The same may be said regarding location as well.

And if it is argued that this leads to the very same contingency regarding the restriction of place and time—namely, that because the pervading property of being an effect of the *kalāpa* (the causal complex) is absent due to independence from consciousness, properties such as "being an effect" are impossible and are thus pervaded by dependence on an agent possessing effort (*prayatnavat*)—then, in that case, if that possessor of effort were momentary and localized, the entire collection of effects would be restricted to that single moment and location; therefore, he must be accepted as eternal and all-pervading.

And thus, that very lack of restriction regarding place and time remains applicable even today; so what is the point of accepting this [cause]? Or, if it produces [the effect] by depending on the unseen (adṛṣṭa), would it not produce it invariably? But for matted locks, there is no such thing as an "unseen eye."

If it is argued: "In that case, even without consciousness (*caitanya*), the conditions (*pratyaya*) alone, aided by the ripening of that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), will necessarily produce [the effect]; so what is the use of consciousness?"—for one who speaks thus, it would follow that the potter and others are also useless, for even there the unseen force does not exist as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). But this is not the case; therefore, the opposite is true. Whatever causal complex (*sāmagrī*) there may be, it does not render human effort fruitless without depending on the unseen force, just like the thread, lump of clay, stick, wheel, and so forth. And such is the causal complex here.

[280] The perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) regarding mountains, oceans, and so forth: for the state of being independent of effort (*tadanapekṣatvam*), which is established in the case of space and the like, is what is to be negated. That which is contradictory to this—namely, dependence on effort—is pervaded by the state of being a causal complex (*sāmagrītvam*), because such a complex is produced by effort. To this it is replied: if the causal complex were established as being the product of effort through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), then this would be correct. But it is not so; for even in that case, there is no subverting argument (*bādhakam*) against the contrary.

For just as an effect—because its presence depends upon its own causes—is conceived as not occurring at all times due to its dependence on a specific state of those causes, why should the same not apply to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? Why, then, would the consequence of its being eternal be urged against it? Furthermore, if the causal complex were to be restricted by dependence on effort while still harboring the suspicion of functioning even when its contrary conditions are present, what kind of fault has been committed by "being an immediate effect" and so forth, such that, when these are put forward, the causal complex is invoked as a refuge for one who remains in doubt?

If it is argued that clay and other materials are seen to come together only from a person, why is it not said that an effect is also observed to arise only from one who possesses effort? And just as there might be a suspicion that even if some effect is seen to belong to one who exerts effort, yet another effect—by setting aside the former—will belong to an intelligent being, so too, what purpose does the mere possibility of a causal complex (sāmagrī) serve? Therefore, this argument is equivalent to what has already been stated.

Therefore, even by inserting the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself into the middle [of the argument], one must take the very observation of that complex in jars and the like as the proof. This being the case, it is correct to maintain that the effect itself is established as being invariably concomitant with effort through direct perception and non-perception.

What is the use here of the display of strength in adducing subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*)? Or rather, if—according to the sequence to be explained later—it were possible for perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) to apprehend only a specific class [of things], then it would not be established that "every effect" is pervaded by an agent possessing effort (*prayatnavat*). For that purpose, one resorts to the subversion of the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhā*). If that is so, then even in the case of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) being an effect of an agent possessing effort, those same perceptions and non-perceptions are the refuge; thus, such a collection [of causes] is produced by an agent possessing effort, and a universal conclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) is therefore logical. And so:
Arising never occurs from that which is distracted, nor can it arise from that which is devoid of consciousness;
if this were so, would not this same fault apply equally even to an eternally existing entity?
If you say that its dependence on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) determines the timing, then what is the use of the mind at that time?
Even in the case of a jar and such, the artisan's effort is not fruitless, nor is this a reversal of that [principle].

If, in the case of a jar and so forth, there is pervasion by way of inclusive observation (*abhividhi*), why is there a contradiction in the opposite case? Is it not accepted that pervasion exists precisely through perception and non-perception?
If this is so, then if their object is indeed a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) of such a kind, [the same would apply].
If the array were to arise from consciousness, what certainty would there be regarding anything else?
Thus are the two summary verses.

Nor is it correct to argue that if another causal complex (*sāmagryantara*) were not preceded by that [prior cognition], then this [present cognition] should likewise not be so; for we observe that even all-pervading properties (*dharma*) exist only in certain locations—just as the property of being scratchable by iron exists only in some earthen objects—or just as the property of being preceded by a body is unestablished in the case of certain effects. If you say that [the cognition] does not pervade everything because there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against it, then who can remove the doubt regarding its manifestation elsewhere?

For just as there is no requirement for dependence on an intelligent agent even in other collections of causes or in the production of other effects, so too, for you, there is no proof that such dependence must necessarily exist in every class of things. And just as you observe a dependence on an intelligent agent in some cases, so too the opponent observes the pervasion of a property seen in one instance by a different class of things.

Therefore, the opponent’s failure to demonstrate a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding the case of iron-striking and bodily activity is indeed sufficient to establish doubt; otherwise, it would follow that doubt itself would be without a basis.

Nor is it the case that a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason is now being introduced, such that the opponent’s failure to present a subverting argument here would constitute a subversion [of the probandum]; rather, it is simply the fact that the exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. And this is established, because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not proven by mere observation in the example, since there is no subsequent evidence for it.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: that because the causes of the earth and so forth are insentient, their activity is necessarily directed by an intelligent agent who possesses effort, just as the causes of a palace and the like are; for there is no evidence whatsoever—just as in the case of time and other factors—that proves that even an insentient entity's regulated activity is invariably concomitant with one possessing effort.

Nor does the consequence that there would be no cessation of activity present any logical connection, because the possibility of a single capacity being maintained within entities has been set aside by the fact that their nature is differentiated through the production [of effects] in conjunction with successive conditions (*pratyaya*). Therefore, since the doubt regarding the unity of the agent arises by way of the same logical principle, he says—merely to satisfy his opponent and to refute [the argument] by means of a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason—the following, which brings about an obstruction to the intellect:

"In the cases of acting after having remained stationary, specific configurations, purposeful action, and so forth, either what is desired is established, or it is unestablished in the example. (PV II 10abc’d)

Thus [it is said]. The word "vā" (or) signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*). When these [conditions] are present, the establishment or non-establishment of the desired consciousness—respectively in a subject (*dharmin*) possessing the probans in the example, such as a jar, and in one such as a tree—is as follows. Therefore, the meaning is that these [probans] clearly exhibit occurrence in only a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

By this, the following alternative is also refuted: that if, as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtaka*) and so forth, it is impossible to state a sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhā*), then—just as with smoke and so forth—the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) of effects and the like with effort will be established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). For it has been stated that even in the absence of such [concomitance], because the effect arises [even without effort], there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) itself.

[Objection: But surely, "possessing intelligence" is a property common to both visible and invisible bodies; how then can it be understood that this [property] is not operative in the production of things such as trees, given that non-existence cannot be established by mere non-perception? [Reply: This is correct, provided that pervasion were intended with respect to "intelligence-in-general" (buddhimātra) devoid of the limiting condition (upādhi) of a visible body. If you say, "Exactly so," then, in that case, he states [the following] regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka), just as in the case of smoke: "Or rather, there is doubt."

Thus: when the absence of the jar prior to the potter's activity is to be understood, then the absence [of the jar] caused by the absence of the probandum would not be cognized, because of the doubt regarding the absence of the probandum. For the pervasion was not sought by a mind conditioned by such a physical body, whereby a negation could be established through a specific non-perception; rather, it was sought by means of mere effortful agency.

And just as at the time of the birth of a tree or similar things, it is impossible to negate the possibility [of its absence], so it remains even now; thus, even if that [tree] were possible, the absence of the jar, being merely a possibility, cannot invalidate its own dependence upon the absence of that [tree]. Therefore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful.

If it is argued that it is correct to say "the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful when there is doubt regarding the presence of the probans (*sādhana*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*)," but that the absence of the jar prior to the potter's activity is not doubted, that too has been answered: the proponent of pervasion (*vyāpti*) must demonstrate that the negative concomitance of the probans is necessitated by the negative concomitance of the probandum; and since that [necessity] is not shown here because of the doubt regarding the absence of the probandum, it is likewise not demonstrated.

Or, because there is doubt regarding the essential nature [of the reason] even in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), there is no distinction at all; for in both cases, that [reason] along with its qualification remains doubtful. For this very reason, it is stated that the defect of the two examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) consists in having a subject (*dharmin*) where the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhana*) are themselves doubtful.

If, however, only the absence of the probans were stated, without regard for the absence of the probandum, then this would be correct; yet by that much alone, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not achieved. Otherwise, having established pervasion through perception and non-perception, when a trembling produced by a means of proof for the presence of a wind-stroke is rendered common to trembling caused by rubbing and so forth, then one who attempts to avoid it by suspecting that a still air—which is impossible to negate because it is not perceptible to touch—might exist, would be unable to do so.

If it is argued that because a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) is being established, there is indeed a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), [we ask]: from what, then, is this specific qualification established by that [reason]? If you say, "The word 'obstruction' (*upahati*) will have an object corresponding to it, like the activity of one who is bodiless, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is described through perception and non-perception," then that is equally applicable to you as well. For just as, when avoiding deviation by treating this [reason] as invisible with respect to such mere wind, there is a failure to establish the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) precisely because of its invisibility at the time of grasping the pervasion, so too [is it for you].

For you as well, consciousness exists in that which is devoid of a body; therefore, when there is even a doubt regarding its absence, if one has the conceit of grasping a pervasion merely through the absence of the effect, then likewise, even when there is a doubt regarding the absence of an untouchable wind, the absence of trembling would be established, and thus there would be a pervasion.
