[283] Now, suppose that no one establishes pervasion (vyāpti) by means of the body alone, nor even by means of being devoid of a body, but rather by consciousness alone; and since that [consciousness] exists even at times when there is a body—because a universal must necessarily exist when a particular instance is possible—the apprehension of pervasion, in relation to that [consciousness], remains restricted to the universal itself, just as in the case of fire, because the specific nature of another fire is included within it. This same argument applies equally to the inference of wind.

Furthermore, no conscious person infers the wind from mere trembling alone; for even when there is a determination that [the wind] is omnipresent, the capacity of mere trembling to serve as a probans is not perceived. Indeed, the fact that "sovereignty" is desired does not, merely because it is uttered after being named, validate one who speaks of its means—even if such a statement arises immediately thereafter. Nor does the probans "producedness," though it is in fact a non-member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), establish impermanence when it is presented as a pervader.

Therefore, satisfaction should not be found merely in the purity of the internal organ (*koṣṭhaśuddhi*) through the state of the object of cognition being as it is; rather, the excellence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaguṇa*) must be investigated. Furthermore, in establishing the pervasion of trembling by mere air (*marunmātra*), there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary. It must necessarily be accepted that perception and non-perception can include even that which is remote in terms of nature, place, or time—provided it is capable of becoming an object within their own respective spheres—but they cannot include anything else.

Otherwise, just as the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is restricted to that [consciousness], deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would also necessarily result in being restricted to it. Therefore, just as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which have particulars as their objects, are established as having as their object only consciousness—which is not within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge—why is deviation, which likewise has particulars as its object, not also established as having only that [consciousness] as its object? For it cannot be maintained that "one enters when there is gain, but one retreats when there is a cut."

It is logical that fire, although remote in space and time, being of the same nature [as the smoke], attains an entry into it as if present, by virtue of its suitability for perception despite the remoteness of its own nature; for, due to the single determination of that [nature], everything being ascertained as pervading the smoke is not defective, whereas the gastric fire is not so ascertained because of its unsuitability for such [perception]. For this very reason, the activity of one who is free from doubt toward the intended fire upon seeing smoke is justified.

Otherwise, even if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) were grasped by the perceiver through a fire that is not amenable to perception, the pervasion of smoke would nonetheless be established as having for its object the generality of fire—whether perceptible or imperceptible. Consequently, one who doubts the specific form [of fire], such as that produced from grass (*tārṇa*), would not proceed with a mind focused solely on obtaining the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it. Or else, there would be activity even when one considers "absence of being stomach-fire" (*jāṭharatva*) to be like a deficiency in the necessary connection (*pratibandhavaikalya*).

But this is not the case; therefore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not apprehend a pervasion based on a specific individual essence (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*) by means of a generality (*sāmānya*).

However, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the pervasion of "being produced" by "impermanence" functions by way of the mere fact of "having been and then ceasing to be," without being restricted by any particular [instance]; thus, it apprehends it only as a universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, no one who proceeds from the property of being produced can possibly proceed with a focused cognition directed toward a specific, intended impermanence. Therefore, it is established that even a means of valid cognition which culminates in a universal does not grasp the pervasion through a particular.

And it has been stated by Śaṅkara, who follows the Nyāya, that "whatever means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) extends over whatever range of objects," and so forth. A means of valid cognition whose operation depends upon a particular intrinsic nature cannot establish the pervasion of anything by an intrinsic nature other than that; for example, [the inference] which, being a sublater of the contrary, depends solely upon existence.

[284] By way of a specific instance of impermanence, there is the [inference] of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). Or, for example, there is the apprehension of smoke by means of perception and non-perception (*adhyakṣānupalambha*) which depends upon a specific nature as intended, [namely] fire in its common form as the digestive heat (*jāṭhara*) within the stomach. Furthermore, since the operations of perception and non-perception proceed by depending upon specific natures, there is the grasping of pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding trembling caused by the wind; this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), because, like the lightness of the wind (*mātariśvan*), there is an absence of the operation of perception [regarding such a specific nature].

Nor is there an inconclusiveness [of the reason]. For the apprehension of pervasion by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is pervaded by the fact that it functions in dependence upon the specific nature (*svarūpa*) of that which is intended to be expressed; otherwise, the faults of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and confusion of activity would follow. And its opposite is an activity that depends on a nature other than that. Therefore, the meaning of the proof is this: perception and non-perception, which depend on a specific nature, do not establish the pervasion of trembling by mere wind—that is, by wind in general, whether still or otherwise.
Consequently, there is no inference of wind from trembling in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

Moreover, there is no conceptual construction for establishing your own tenet that does not follow this [same logic], nor is there any basis for its invalidity that is not brought forward against your own inference. Consequently, if, in order to establish the pervasion between an effect and a conscious agent—just as between fire and smoke—one resorts to perception and non-perception as the means of proof, then, with respect to the nature of that which is capable of being perceived, there is an inevitable deviation of the "conscious agent" from the mere "effect," such as grass and the like.

Now, if it is claimed that there is a pervasion by an intelligent agent whose scope includes the marvel of deviation (vyabhicāra), then, just as in the case of the birth of trees and the like, when the operation of an intelligent agent—which cannot be denied even prior to the activity of a craftsman—is present, one must determine for what [effect] the absence of a jar or the like constitutes an "absence caused by the absence" of that agent, such that the pervasion by it could be established. Thus, because its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is doubtful, the reason remains inconclusive (anaikāntika); furthermore, this was previously stated regarding the absence of a subverting proof (bādhaka) in the contrary case, without regard for the distinction between perceptible and imperceptible objects.

The distinction is this: whereas [the pervasion] was previously established by [the proponent] himself demonstrating it, now, by the admission of the proponent alone, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished in relation to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) he accepts. Furthermore, it has been stated that the subverting argument against the counter-example (*vipakṣabādhaka*) should lead one to understand the pervasion through the reason (*hetu*) alone, and not through the cognition of its specific qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), such as "possessing intelligence" (*buddhimat*).

But surely, since trees and the like have been made the subject (*pakṣa*), how can there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of them? For the mass of existing things is threefold: those whose production is doubtful, those produced by an intelligent agent, and those produced by no agent. Among these, having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception and non-perception in the case of jars and the like—which are produced by an intelligent agent—one applies the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) to mountains and the like, which are subjects of doubt, and thereby proves the existence of an agent possessed of effort. This [subject] cannot possibly be a locus of deviation.

As for what was said—that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*)—that is incorrect. For that which is the very object of deviation cannot be the subject (*pakṣa*), because "the statement of the reason applies to what is doubtful; a reason excluded from the subject has no locus" (PV IV 91).

According to this principle, it is therefore appropriate to take only mountains and the like as the subject (*pakṣa*), since their agent is doubtful. However, one must then accept a fourth category: trees and the like, which have non-conscious agents. But how can trees and such be made the subject, given that—by virtue of seeking universal concomitance (*vyāpti*)—they are not perceived to arise from an agent when they are considered capable of being perceived? Let there be no total elimination of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacy common to all [cases].

If an imperceptible agent is postulated to prevent the reason of "being an effect" from occurring in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), how can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) ever be established, since it would be devoid of the proof of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?
Obstruction, however, is restricted solely to the presence of the stated reason; it does not pervade [the probandum] through its distinction.
Furthermore, "non-dharma" (adharma), which resides within the sphere of deviation, is not capable of being made the subject of the thesis.
Thus is the summary verse.

But even so, how can there be no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), given that space (*ākāśa*) is possible as a locus for the apprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? As it has been said: "The existence of production and so forth in things such as jars occurs when an intelligent cause exists, while their non-existence occurs when [such a cause] is absent; and since that [relation], whose invariable concomitance is thus well-established, is perceived precisely in earth and other such things, it generates in those who know it the cognition of an agent capable of fashioning them. The phrase "of production and so forth" means "of being an effect and so forth. To this, it is replied:

The establishment of the probandum does not occur through a mere example—whether by way of similarity or dissimilarity—because such a possibility exists even for that which has arrived by chance. Therefore, what is called an "illustration" (nidarśana) is useful for the logical reason (*hetu*) only by way of recollecting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) once it has been grasped and forgotten; it is not so by its mere presence.

And that invariable concomitance (pratibandha) would either be remembered from having been grasped through another medium while in the sky, or it would be established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whose locus is itself. Of these, the first hypothesis is already discarded, because even in the case of a jar, there is no means for grasping the concomitance of "being an effect" and so forth with the mere intellect, which has the visible body as its limiting adjunct (upādhi). And the latter is impossible.

For instance, even if the cessation of duality were perceived in space, nevertheless, because it is impossible to determine that this is necessitated by the absence of one [of the two], and because the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) does not reside there in the absence of the other, how could there be a cognition of a relationship between anything and anything else? Furthermore, it would follow that one could perceive a causal relationship even between a camel and a donkey. If you argue that such a cognition occurs when accompanied by the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) elsewhere, we reply: surely the very meaning of "concomitance" is co-observation; and since such co-observation sometimes exists even for a camel and so forth, your established rule is flawed.

The meaning of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not simultaneous perception; rather, it is the presence of one thing conditioned by the possibility of another. If it is argued that this [conditioned presence] exists between "intelligent agency" and "being an effect," but not elsewhere, we say no; for the fact that the presence of one is conditioned by the other does not consist in its arising from the operation of that other.

Since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is distinct from the attainment of existence, and since that prior non-existence does not occur without the operation of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), once the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been ascertained through perception and non-perception, what kind of doubt could there be regarding the establishment of the causal relation? Thus, it is merely the recollection of the connection between the cognition of those two that is enjoined "in the sky" (i.e., is utterly baseless); therefore, this is precisely the first position.

Furthermore, what is this? Is this from you merely a display of turning back and forth regarding the Lord, like a prisoner being cross-examined? This same logic applies even to the inference of smoke: having observed the possibility of both [fire and smoke] in one place, one grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) because the absence of the other is observed upon the cessation of the activity of one in the sky.

If this is indeed the logical rule, then for those who desire that [conclusion], their hostility toward the subject at hand is groundless; by merely lamenting in this way, they have lost even the inference of fire, let alone the establishment of the primary point, because—according to the stated sequence—even in the case of a donkey, they would abandon their grasp on the fire when such a contingency arises. But when another possibility exists there that is compatible with the subject at hand, how can "captivity" (i.e., forced adherence) be a refuge?

If you argue: "In that case, the operation of perception and non-perception is resorted to only for fear of such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), but it is not the convention (*samaya*) itself," then, since this is so, you yourself must undergo the ordeal of drinking from the jar (*kośapāna*) to decide whether or not this burden of over-extension has been placed upon you. For, regarding one who—abandoning perception and non-perception—asserts pervasion (*vyāpti*) by taking the cessation of smoke to follow from the cessation of fire's operation in the sky, [the same logic applies] because even the mere entity (*vastumātra*) ceases its operation there. Thus, by that [same reasoning],...

There would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) such that pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be established [by mere non-perception]. Likewise, for one who—setting aside both perception and non-perception—demonstrates the absence of the effect, such as a jar, in space due to the absence of the activity of a specific person capable of producing it, and thereby considers pervasion to exist on that basis: for him, pervasion would also follow from the absence of *any* person whatsoever there; and similarly, it would also follow from the absence of being "another effect. Thus, we see that this is clearly nothing but an over-extension and is not a valid principle (*nyāya*).

It is correct to say that because one observes deviation [of smoke] from donkeys and the like, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) by the mere thing; however, since no deviation is observed in the case of a mere person, this objection will not be a mere frivolous cavil (atiprasaṅga). Not so; for the observation of a sublation in one instance among things governed by the same principle gives rise to doubt regarding other instances as well.

For if the observation of the cessation of both [fire and smoke] in the sky were to establish the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then even in the case of real fire and smoke, that connection would not be sublated; however, since it is sublated there, how could it serve as a means for establishing a definitive conclusion elsewhere? Nor can it be said that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding what has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), because making something the subject is not a magical incantation, but rather the firmness of the grasp of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

And if that [absence] in space were merely the absence of both [the probans and the probandum], then, since a sublation (*bādhaka*) is apprehended there, its reliability is lost; thus, even if it is made the subject of the thesis, the suspicion of deviation does not cease.

If you argue that space exists as the locus of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then why is it that even when smoke arises from fire, that same [space] is not the locus, given that such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would arise?
[287] If this is so, why has the "not over-extension" (nātiprasaṅga) not been set aside by you?
Furthermore, the observation of sublation (bādha) in that case also brings about suspicion here.
This is the summary.

Therefore, the pervasion is not established by the absence of the two [fire and smoke] in space; rather, the observation of their absence in a case where pervasion is already established would serve as the cause for remembering the grasped pervasion. And it has been stated that no means for grasping pervasion is possible. Consequently, even if there is mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is absent, it remains established that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). In reality, however, just like negative concomitance, positive concomitance for this [reason] is likewise difficult to find.

For when it is impossible to cognize that the absence of an effect is necessitated by the non-existence of something because that thing lies beyond the range of perception, its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is certainly cast far away; this is because such a thing must be graspable by perception. Indeed, as has already been stated, perception determines pervasion (*vyāpti*) by including within its own operation even those things remote in space and time, provided they are perceptible, but not those that are remote in their very nature.

Therefore, having disregarded mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of the "elephant's blink" (*gajanimīlita*), the refutation was stated solely on the basis of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In reality, however, there is neither positive nor negative concomitance; thus, he says "or else there is doubt" (*saṃśayo 'thavā*) in order to show that when "merely possessing effort" (*prayatnavanmātra*) is the probandum, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is indeed inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*).

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that, in relation to what is perceptible by the senses and so forth, it is a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason; however, in relation to mere consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), it is an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason. Now, one might object: if an effect produced by the intellect (*buddhi*)—which has the body as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—is established, then an effect produced by the intellect alone is indeed established, just as being produced by a *śiṃśapā* tree entails being produced by a tree, since the general property is not excluded when the particular is present. If this is so, then there would also be a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in relation to that. What loss is there for us, given that the reason "effect" (*kārya-hetu*) resides in the intelligent agent (*buddhimat*)?

Is it because of the acceptance of the existence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? Regarding this, it has been stated: "If one were to thus postulate positive and negative concomitance, then even when inferring fire from smoke based on its form as perceived in a hearth or a painting, one would remain in doubt and would not proceed with the intended one-pointedness of mind," and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not the case that whatever form of an entity is apprehended by perception as pervading its effect is thereby [established] as being impossible there; rather, it is in dependence upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). And since conceptual determination is indeed produced by a person, the [inference] proceeds only with respect to a specific object, such as "by an intelligent being," for it is precisely in such a sense that the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word "person" (*puruṣa*) and so forth occurs.

But it is not by consciousness alone, independent of the activity of the hands and other organs; for although consciousness alone exists, it remains indifferent, because at the time of grasping the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*) proceeds only toward a specific [object]. Or, even though the term is general, it implies the specific context at hand, just as the word "fire" implies its specific pervasion. And that determination, following the operation of perception, would project only that form which is suitable for it externally, and not that which is unsuitable, such as the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) or fuel-wood (*tārṇa*). Likewise, in the case of pervasion by the Person (*puruṣa*) as well, [only the suitable is projected].

[288] There would indeed be a rejection of mere consciousness (buddhi-mātra) when it is devoid of the limiting adjunct of a body (śarīra-upādhi), as it is incapable of that [cognition]; however, there is no rejection of the distinctions such as "dwarf" and so forth. This very logic applies everywhere in the apprehension of positive concomitance (anvaya) through perception.

If it is argued that for one who perceives smoke produced from burning *aguru* wood due to contact with charcoal, there would follow the consequence of its concomitance even in the absence of fuel and so forth—because it is suitable for direct perception—is it then intended that perception, disregarding the restriction of the objects of valid cognition, should establish concomitance with whatever [thing] it happens upon, wherever it occurs? If this were the case, the distinction between a valid reason (*hetu*) and a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) would be destroyed, and since everything would be established by everything, the search for a specific means of proof would be fruitless.

Now, if it is argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended by perception even by transcending what is accessible to it, that is unproven. For when perception, even regarding an object suitable for its own operation, grasps a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) while disregarding the universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to internal distinctions, then what need is there to mention that which is utterly heterogeneous and unsuitable for its own operation? Nor is our position that pervasion is established by everything that is perceptible; rather, our position is that pervasion is established precisely by that which is perceptible.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even donkeys and the like could possess a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with smoke-pots and such. What more could be said than this? But why is it that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) here depends precisely on internal distinctions and not merely on the suitability for perception? For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which requires the proximity of perception and so forth solely for the purpose of awakening latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), is incapable of introducing a specific, restricted feature because its arising form is indeterminate.

True; for this very reason, there is an application of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a means of establishing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In that regard, just as non-apprehension serves as an auxiliary when smoke and a jar are determined to have positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with fire and a person—establishing a threefold negative concomitance consisting of prior existence, production from another, and arrival from another, since otherwise it would be useless—likewise, if it were established through concomitance with a donkey or through concomitance with mere cognition, it would indeed be [established] by those two as well.

Pervasion [is established] in no other way; for it has been determined many times in the treatise—and by us as well in the *Trikapañcakacintā*—that pervasion is not apprehended by perception alone, nor by non-perception alone, but rather by perception and non-perception acting together through positive and negative concomitance.

Furthermore, a donkey or similar animal provides no assistance to that [non-perception]. By this, the absence of the operation of non-perception with respect to a specific instance of smoke is explained; thus, there is no objection whatsoever against one who speaks in this manner. However, for one who describes a pervasion established by that [non-perception] even in the case of what is within the range of perception, his failure to grasp the pervasion regarding that very object results in an unstable position.

This is because, for one who asserts a pervasion established by that [non-perception] even when the object is perceptible, he desires that pervasion despite the absence of the operation of non-perception.

[289] Who would be the objector? For if he were possessed of modesty, how could he describe the operation of that [consciousness], which is by its very nature imperceptible? Or, if the donkey is excluded simply because one who knows the material causes and so forth, being possessed of effort, observes the cause—what is the use here of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)?

In that case, you would be describing pervasion (*vyāpti*) solely through what is actually perceived, and not through that which transcends the path of perception; nor has consciousness alone been perceived anywhere apart from its adjunct, the body.

And if you argue that the establishment [of the pervasion] is based solely on observation—such that a body presided over by mere consciousness is seen to produce jars and the like, and thus there is no contradiction with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding a donkey, and therefore there is no rejection by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)—then how can this be? If you say: "Only general properties residing in the pervader (*vyāpaka*) are the means of proof for pervasion; because others are seen to deviate (*vyabhicāra*), there is no positive concomitance with the donkey due to the possibility of doubt elsewhere," then surely, even in the absence of that [consciousness], there is the observation of deviation.

The statement "the perception of existence" indicates that when there is an absence of the operation of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the lack of proof is brought forward, thereby illuminating the very operation of non-perception in the determination of the probans (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, if you, troubled by the suspicion of an operation regarding a particular (*viśeṣa*), resort to a universal (*sāmānya*), then let [the opponent] state a pervasion (*vyāpti*) even with a mere cause—whether that be a universal such as "mere sentience" (which is common even to donkeys and is fit for proving what is already established) by abandoning the particular who is cognizant of the material cause and so forth, or even something more general than that. For if this were the case, the scope for suspicion would be entirely eliminated.

However, by disregarding this much generality, one remains fixed upon a particularity that is expert in [identifying] the material cause and so forth, yet does not disregard even that [generality], [but rather acts] according to what is observed—what power is there for this other than [the power of] class (*jāti*)? For one who maintains the doctrine of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), there is no doubt regarding whatever generality is within the scope of the operation of perception and non-perception; and where there is room for doubt, there is no such operation. Thus, he does not himself, by his own will, introduce or remove a pervasion (*vyāpti*) anywhere, because it is established solely by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, there is no fault.

But does he not, when asserting that the entire range of effects is produced by causes alone, fail to observe the perception of causal operation even in cases where [the cause] is perceptible? He certainly does observe it, because his own scripture—which serves as a sublater of the contrary—leads him to accept that very point. However, he establishes through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the non-perception of causal operation occurs only with respect to a mind associated with a specific body.

Even in the case of desire (*icchā*), when the activity of the hands and so forth ceases, the effect does not arise; therefore, it is precisely through that [activity] that the aggregate which is the object of the designation "potter" and so on is treated as being perceptible. However, this principle does not apply to mere consciousness accompanied by effort alone. Even then, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) will be understood through inference. Nor is there any requirement for perception itself. The determination of positive and negative concomitance must be made through apprehension and non-apprehension;
and whether that apprehension takes the form of perception or the form of inference—there is no insistence on this point.

Here it is considered: Is that very mind which possesses the body as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and is endowed with effort intended by the term "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), or is it something else? If it were the former, what would be the use of inference, since there would be no dispute regarding what is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Furthermore, by that [perception], positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established; and its deviation from the mere effect is evident. If it were the latter, there is the fault of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

[290] Since the effect, such as speech and so forth, fulfills its purpose through an embodied being alone, pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be accepted even by means of that inferred entity, because—as in the previous case—the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains uncertain. If this is so, then the pervasion of smoke by firewood (*barhis*) is not restricted by place, time, or state, but rather by fire in general; and since that [fire] is distinct from what is actually perceived, the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth is common to both options. Therefore, it must be stated that the pervasion is with a generality (*sāmānya*) devoid of such specific qualifications.

If you argue that the same applies here as well, then smoke would also entail a pervasion by way of its form as it exists in the stomach and so forth. Therefore, it is not the case that only a universal is subject to pervasion, nor is it the case that a particular is rejected outright; for if it were so, the inference from smoke would be utterly destroyed, and there would be doubt regarding the application [of the reason] to the intended flame.

Therefore, if one's own mere whim were not the means for establishing inclusion and exclusion, then, in the process of determining [the nature of things] by investigating the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), some generality must necessarily be sought even by perception—which, though engaged in acceptance—would have rejected it, since its [perception's] application does not extend beyond that particularity. This is just as [perception] cannot apply when the fiery, glowing form [of fire] has passed away, for one who seeks to grasp the pervasion of smoke.
However, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) rejects even that which has been accepted by perception through its inherent capacity, as in the case of a cooking pot and the like.

For that [inference], while establishing the absence of what is intended as the effect in the absence of fire by demonstrating that its presence is necessitated by the presence of fire, proceeds to establish its status as an effect through the exclusion of what is incapable; yet it thereby establishes the causality of something else as well—namely, that in the absence of which it itself does not occur.

However, in the case of perception preceded by non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), when the absence [of a cause] is established through non-apprehension—which functions to sublate prior existence and so forth—due to the absence of the existence of multiple entities; and when, in the presence of the nature of a single entity, its presence is perceived by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) because its prior absence was already manifested as being necessitated by that [single entity's] absence; then, whatever was rejected by direct perception on account of its incapacity for activity, that is indeed rejected. Thus, its status as a cause is established.

Therefore, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the gastric fire and so forth, nor is there a negation of a nature differentiated by differences in time, place, and state; for everything is accepted through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of its own fitness for production. Nor can it be established through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); for it is logical that non-perception, occurring in the absence of a nature not of that kind, negates the causality of something of a different class, but not of that very thing itself—otherwise, its reliance [upon such a negation] would be useless.

Now, one might object: even if there is no nature distinct from place and other factors, this smoke is indeed perceived; for it is unified, through a conceptual recognition of a single form, with that visible aspect which is observed, and not with any other nature that is unfit for perception. For this very reason, that which is denoted by the word "fire-in-general" is precisely that [visible aspect], because even when a distinction is drawn from what is fit for perception, there is still an appearance of non-difference.

But is it not the case that even what is remote in terms of space and so forth is simply incapable of being perceived? True; however, this applies only in certain instances at certain times. But as for that which is remote by nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*), because it is absolutely heterogeneous, its existence does not contradict its functioning through the distinction between acceptance and rejection. Therefore, just as one who maintains the theory of inference must follow after a universal (*sāmānya*) in order to avoid the possibility of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), so too...

[291] Even a universal distinct [from individuals] must be rejected with respect to the specific visible [object], in order to avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This being so, just as it is logical that pervasion and the establishment of unity occur through a subordinate universal that is perceptible, while avoiding a fire-universal that is imperceptible, and not by "mere effort" (*prayatnavanmātra*) alone—since that would be contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—so too [must it be here].

In that case, one who, out of delusion, seeks a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is questioned regarding [the probans'] identity with or difference from [the subject]. However, it has been stated that in the case of fire, the resolution comes through that very same position [of the subject]. Therefore, when there is a desire to grasp pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*), and there is a requirement for a universal (*sāmānya*) suitable for that [pervasion], then regarding jars, trees, and so forth, whether the desired [concomitance] is established or not, the effect (*kārya*) is a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason.

But since neither of the two—positive or negative concomitance—is certain by means of mere consciousness (*caitanya*), which is unsuitable for that [purpose], it is rightly said that its positive and negative concomitances are doubtful (*sandigdha*).
"Or else there is doubt.

This follows from the context of "success or failure. By these two, existence and non-existence are expressed; as it has been said: "Perception itself is existence, and non-perception is non-existence. Consequently, because there is a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of that which is intended as the probandum (sādhya) in a subject (dharmin) possessing the reason (sādhana), such as "being an effect," within the example—due to the uncertainty arising from mere effort—and because all things are subsumed under those two [existence and non-existence], it is logical that there is the inconclusiveness of the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) due to the impossibility of establishing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

But even so, let there be non-exclusivity (anekānta) as well; why is mere positive concomitance (anvaya-mātra) rejected, given that the operation of cognition alone is observed in the production of an effect? In that case, there would be the consequence of positive concomitance of smoke with the common form of "belly-fire" (jāṭhara), because the operation of fire is observed [there too]. Consequently, there would also be negative concomitance (vyatireka) dependent on that, and thus the aforementioned defect remains. Furthermore, the rejection of perception is a common [objection].

If it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because smoke exists even in the absence of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) and so forth—since there is indeed a positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—then why is the production of a jar (*kalaśa*) not likewise cited, even by one devoid of the skill to create Mount Kailāsa? Or, if you claim that here the concomitance is based on the general property of being a "productive instrument" (*karaṇa-kauśala*), then [we reply] that even in that case, it is based merely on the property of being a "burner" (*dāhaka*); thus, there is no point in introducing specific individuals.

If, however, [the concomitance] is considered with respect to the genus (*jāti*), then since that [fire] exists at other times as well, how could there be smoke even in its absence? If, on the other hand, deviation is asserted by relying on a genus distinct from the observed particularity—namely, the mere quality of being a burner—then, in relation to that [genus], how can there be positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? For a genus is apprehended through perception only as something qualified. Or, if there were such a concomitance, deviation would again be impossible.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised regarding the determination of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through perception by means of a similar instance—namely, that not everything of the same class is inferred, because what is perceived is of a different class, and yet the collection of the eyes and other sense organs is inferred from non-perceptible particulars such as color-form (*rūpa*), and likewise the far and near sides of the moon and the earth—it is even more flawed. For inference is never devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and pervasion exists between a universal and a universal.

[292] How could it be that being dissimilar, it could support inference? Furthermore, that [inference] is of only two kinds: either from perception and non-perception, or from the sublation of the contrary. In both cases, the inference is only of that which is of the same class as what is seen in the example. Otherwise, to take a pervasion by means of a property of one class and infer something of another class would be a great lack of discernment.

For even in the case of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*), it is precisely that same commonality of motion which is observed as the cause for reaching another location that is ascertained in another substratum; how, then, can there be an inference of a property belonging to a different class? If it is argued that this is said with reference to a specific internal distinction established by capacity in view of the difference between substrata, then that is equivalent to stating the obvious (*anuktasama*). For no proponent of inference, desiring a particularity for that reason alone, is able to establish a fruitful inference.

If such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) were present even in the inference for God (*īśvara*), then the desired conclusion would be established through the proof of that specific [quality] alone; who then would harbor resentment in that regard? Nor is it reasonable to say that because of the requirement for that specific quality, a similar class is not inferred in all cases; for even when there is an inference of a dissimilar class in some instances, it is stated thus, and that specific quality exists in every inference.

In the case of an inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣato-dṛṣṭa*), although that very same [specific property] is determined even in respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), it should not be said that "on account of that [universal], that very same [property] is inferred everywhere," because the consideration of a common genus (*samānajāti*) is grounded in difference (*bheda*).

But that [point] is indeed irrelevant. For it is not the case that everything which is not perceived is inferred. If you are speaking with reference to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), as in the case of fire, then inference would apply everywhere to perception alone, since no other means of valid cognition operates elsewhere. If, however, you mean this in view of the sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*), then one should not say: "There is no difference between the inference of God and the proof of fire. Rather, it would be more appropriate to say: "[There is no difference] from the proof of impermanence."

If it is argued that this is stated merely on the basis of the nature of being an effect and its cause, then the causal relationship is established solely through perception and non-perception; thus, that same fault remains. Furthermore, it has already been discussed that there is no subverting argument against the contrary. Moreover, the consequence of the lack of restriction regarding place and so forth establishes that [the cause] would be a mere cause [without efficacy]. Therefore, because it does not penetrate the actual object of inquiry, the claim that "not everything perceptible is inferred" is undermined.

However, with respect to the time of inference, everything that is imperceptible is inferred, and there is no disagreement regarding that; thus, [your objection] is equivalent to stating the obvious. But the sense organ cannot be directly inferred from cognition, because the necessary invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is not perceived. Rather, since the effect of cognition—given that certain [other] conditions are present—is sometimes absent and sometimes not, it necessitates dependence upon a cause distinct from those [conditions]; such is the proclamation of the "sense organ."

In that regard, just as the dependence seen in things such as sprouts is established as being of a specific kind, so too are the upper and lower parts [of a jar] in the case of effects such as a jar. Since these are inferred through general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) as being restricted by a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīpratibaddha*), the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnya*); enough of this prolixity. Alternatively, the principle is this: a general effect is pervaded by a general cause, whereas a specific effect is pervaded by a specific cause.

Or rather, there is the common saying that a specific effect arises from a general cause merely through the process of determination (*adhyavasāya*). In this regard, one who asserts that the general class of effects is pervaded by a specific intelligent cause would indeed be overstepping established consensus on the basis of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that means of valid cognition which establishes the pervasion is of only two kinds: either perception and non-perception, or the sublation of the contrary; for these two consist in the nature of perception and inference, as certainty cannot be attained through any other means. Among these, first, regarding the general class of effects in the manner already stated:

There is no pervasion through differentiation because of the force of the sublation of the contrary; nor is there pervasion of the whole [class] through perception and non-perception for one who does not touch upon the distinction between that which belongs to that class and that which does not.

Since the cognition of birth follows—preceded by the negation of prior existence and so forth—just as in the case of smoke and such, in the form "this arises from that," there is thus a twofold distinction of universals.

This is the sequence for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception and non-perception: "This [object], which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, is not perceived; its perception is perceived. Here, "this" refers to smoke and so forth, which appear in a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*) due to their belonging to a single class; "its" means of fire and so forth, by way of excluding other classes of effects and excluding other classes of causes.

Therefore, regarding cause and effect, there must be an activity preceded by a reflective awareness (*paramarśa*) of their mutual difference from each other and from those belonging to their respective classes; otherwise, such activity would be useless due to either incapacity or futility.

For instance, would this [cause] be determined as "conforming to the presence and absence of that [effect]" by way of excluding the mass of non-effects, or by way of excluding other effects? In the first case, the meaning "these things are restricted to this" would be "this is not that thing," because a single uniform reflective awareness (*ekākārapratyavamarśa*) is impossible due to the absence of a single form (*ekākāra*).

If it is argued that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because one is able to say "this is an effect" or "this is a configuration" by means of the general property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth, we reply: here, the cognition that establishes existence or non-existence occurs in two ways—having either the substratum (*dharmin*) as its object or the attribute (*dharma*) as its object—since an effect is twofold, distinguished as that which is produced (*nirvartya*) and that which is modified (*vikārya*).

Among these, the first [type of perception] takes as its object that very substratum (*dharmī*) which, based on the certainty of its arising in its entirety, is delimited by a specific form; even though it is divided by differences of time, place, and so forth, it makes its own nature the object [of cognition] by including it within a single unifying reflection (*ekapratyavamarśa*). Therefore, it is said to have "that as its object. For it sets aside even a possible property (*dharma*) that is not of that form and is incompatible with its particularity, just as whiteness and the like are set aside in the case of smoke and such.

Furthermore, when another property arises in a subject that remains exactly as it was, the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) pertain to the property alone through its causes; thus, it is said to have the property as its object. This [cognition], moreover, setting aside the specific form, takes the mere property as its basis, just like [the cognition of] passion and so forth.

For cloth, blankets, and the like, which experience a distinct difference in form, action, and so forth, and possess a common redness, do not find satisfaction merely by inferring the application of another coloring substance whose capacity has been previously apprehended. Rather, the first [cognition] takes its refuge solely in the form, because it arises in its entirety as such. For just as an object arises from some cause as colored by a specific form, so too is it experienced by sensory cognition produced through the power of that [object], and subsequently brought within the range of worldly discourse by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

[294] How is the exclusion of the specific form (*ākāra*) achieved? Precisely for this reason, when the manifestation of smoke, a jar, and so forth—which has its origin unperceived in one place—is perceived, if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through a particular reasoning at that very moment, the determination of its cause arises in that very instance, and not elsewhere, even if one were to depend upon the observation or non-observation of deviation. Subsequently, however, one may set aside the specific form, for one who perceives only the emergence of a property (*dharma*) within a subject (*dharmin*) already established.

Furthermore, when a jar or similar object is already present, one does not observe the arising of the mere property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), nor is such an arising admitted in the case of mountains and the like, such that—disregarding the form—one could infer a cause for that mere property alone, as in the case of passion (*rāga*). If it is argued that "the configuration (*sanniveśa*) indeed exists within that very substrate [of clay] produced by the potter," we say no; for even immediately after, clay devoid of that specific arrangement is never perceived.

If it is then argued that "such a thing simply did not exist previously, which would otherwise be the object of the designation 'jar'," then it follows that the configuration itself comes from the person (the potter); thus, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) by that much alone.
Nevertheless, if human action were directed toward the general configuration,
then even the application of turmeric powder would be a prescription for color alone.

But even so, does the fact that there is no perception of something already established not indeed contradict the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) being apprehended in another individual? For it was just established immediately prior that, by the force of that [concomitance], there is only inference in that case. And yet, on that basis alone, is it correct to prove that color alone arises from safflower? Is the ground for deviation (*vyabhicāra*), however, weak? What is the conclusion reached here?
Therefore, even in the case of a quality, there is the inclusion of its own kind, just as in the case of a substance;
thus, there is no inference of saffron from color, even when that [color] is previously established.

For if one does not apprehend the specific qualities necessarily associated with that [color], how could one infer saffron even from passion? It is even more remote from inference based on color alone. Just as with color, the manifold distinctness (*vaijātya*) of shape (*saṃsthāna*) is also an object of experience. Therefore, in these two cases, the establishment of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on the restriction of a genus (*jāti*) to a single locus is untenable; or else, if there is no such restriction, there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the individual instance, which is not restricted to one.

Therefore, just like color, even though the reality of the universal (sāmānya) persists within the various shapes consisting of multiple classes, it remains entirely external to the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Likewise, it is impossible to say that causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) previously existed in a non-entity such as a "person" (*puruṣa*); for this would entail the consequence of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) characterized by a total absence of capacity, which would result in its being a newly arisen entity. Thus, it is established that causal efficacy follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the specific person.

Therefore, even when the cognition of pervasion has a property (*dharma*) as its object, it does not pursue a universal (*sāmānya*). However, when it concerns a property-possessor (*dharmī*) by virtue of the context of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), then—just as in the case of splitting [wood], where a perceptual cognition determines pervasiveness by relying on a commonality of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in its observed form through a specific essential nature (*svarūpasāmānya*)—so too in the case of an effect, the perceptual cognition determines pervadedness precisely by means of a specific formal commonality (*pratiniyatākārasāmānya*); thus, there is no doubt.

Otherwise, why would an active cognition, even regarding the cause—just as it does regarding the effect—bring about the intended object by excluding specific qualities such as being intelligent and so forth? Therefore, just as with the cause, one ought to ascertain the effect in this way as possessing precisely such a specific form.

In this regard, even if "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) were to exist in things such as the ground that are external to that form, its mention would be entirely useless; for, with respect to the operation of perception—which grasps the cause and effect within the domain of the property (*dharma*)—the mere similarity of the property is of no consequence. Indeed, it is neither that very form consisting of the object's causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) nor the cause for the manifestation of that similarity. Thus, this similarity serves no purpose whatsoever, except in cases where the term "effect" is used in a non-literal sense.

For he has established a convention regarding an object that exists only as a mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) for the sake of its arising, and which requires the operation of another [sense-organ] alone; thus, there is no contradiction for him. As for a property that is perceived as being pervasive by means of another logical argument, it is precisely in that case—like destruction—that the operation of perception itself depends upon a similarity with the form (*ākāra*) and so forth manifesting at the time of its own arising. However, when there is a difference caused by place and so on, there is the determination of dissimilarity (*vaisadṛśya*); thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, because there is no single [universal] form (*ekakāra*)—that is, no single cause—and since one must rely on individual perception and non-perception, the determination of pervasion must be performed in this very manner: "these entities follow after this cause. However, since even now it is not possible to employ all individual instances in their entirety, the investigation remains restricted to each single object among all types of effects. And that [exhaustive investigation] is impossible, because it is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity.

For instance, there can be no simultaneous positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among them, because when all possible conditions are present, it would follow that the seer himself vanishes from view. Nor can negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) be ascertained, since certain factors—such as the substratum, light, and the body—are impossible to exclude.

Furthermore, this observation of every mode [of existence] is not feasible within the span of a single human lifetime, due to the exhaustion of the object at its end; for how could there be completeness when only a few [conditions] are required?

Indeed, even for a greater portion of this [term], there is no cessation in the understanding of its inclusive sense (*abhividhi*); for it cannot be asserted that "whatever is an effect is necessarily thus," though it may be said that "it is just this much."

Furthermore, as for the claim that an investigation (*vicāra*) which has proceeded with respect to one [object] establishes all entities as being thus, this refers to its operation through a common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*), because it relies on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by excluding [specific qualities] such as "action" (*kriyā*) and so forth. For it was stated that the very function of perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists in the restriction to the apprehension of a single genus (*jāti*). [Objection: But even in that case, since there is the possibility of numerous internal subdivisions, there is a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) because one is unable to designate [the object] as "this is exactly thus."

If it is asked: "Or, here, by disregarding difference and relying on another universal such as 'smoke,' and by resorting to the state of being an effect within conventional usage, what kind of fault would there be even regarding other universals? We do not, by our own will, disregard any particular difference or bring forward any particular universal. Rather, we enter into the conventional usage of the relation between cause and effect exactly as the conceptual construction—preceded by perception—presents objects, whether through difference or non-difference.

But if that [cognition], having encountered a particularity of its own nature (*prakṛtiviśeṣa*), differentiates its activity among the particulars through the presence or absence of the capacity for suppression—whether in a subtle or gross state—then what is there for anyone to do? (The word "some" [*kecid*] appears in the manuscript. However, its transformation (*vivarta*) must be considered. In this regard, just as smoke, even though it possesses internal subdivisions, takes as its object a similarity that excludes other classes, so too should the heart [be applied] to the mere effect.

Regarding the presence or absence of conformity with a single shape and so forth, since these are to be personally experienced by each individual, no further basis for determination is required here; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion in designations, purposeful action, and functional application.

Therefore, it is impossible to establish a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—whether by means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*)—between any single cause and all types of effects, either successively or simultaneously. What, then, is the use of these two [methods]? For this very reason, the claim of those who assert a pervasion of all effects through such a means is merely an expression of their own subjective intention, like the proclamation of a "post" on a path that is not one. This being the case, since the proof would be nothing more than mere wishful thinking, the pointlessness of these two [methods] is evident.

Therefore, the cognition "this [effect] arises from these two" occurs only by way of excluding other possible effects; it does not attain correspondence by taking the mere effect as its object. Consequently, since it dispels the doubt of one who knows the material cause and so forth, he says:
"Or rather, there is no doubt."
The establishment of what is desired by another does not [follow] from the refutation or the proof of that other [person], but rather from the mere cognition and effort [of the proponent].
When there is no positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) in the proof of a specific desired [property], the probans is merely capable of tolerating doubt regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
If the probandum is perceptible, there is indeed deviation; if it is not perceptible, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not established.
Nor is there pervasion (vyāpti), whether through positive concomitance (anvaya) as in the case of negative concomitance, or specifically for one [term] rather than the other.
The Second Chapter.
[297] If it is argued: "This being the case, even if pervasion exists, its ascertainment is impossible; what, then, is appropriate here? Look:

first, the effect possesses multiple classes, yet a single producer is observed; and that which belongs to various distinct types does not possess that [single nature] when there is a cognition restricted to one [class], even though other distinctions exist.

Whatever belongs to a particular genus and is known to have a single cause, that very thing is that specific factor; if it were not so, there would be an over-extension (*atisañjana*), and this method would not be considered valid in the case of the example for the probandum (*sādhyopama*). For it is not the case that the production of various kinds of effects is restricted solely to that which possesses volitional effort (*prayatnavat*); for even fire and other such things, when situated within various collections of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), are seen to perform a variety of effects, such as smoke, ash, charcoal, heat, cooking, melting, clearing away, burning, and wounding.

[This is] because we observe various causal operations, such as producing smoke, ash, charcoal, heating, cooking, casting away mercury, examining, and causing injury. If there is dispute only regarding whether these occur through the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of an agent who exerts effort, then once the rule for one [type of] effect is known, it is not possible to know the rule for other effects, as was stated previously. Therefore, however many modes are determined to have a single cause, that many are appropriate as proofs for that cause, whether it be conscious or otherwise.

Otherwise, by means of fire accompanied by damp fuel, one might infer burning even from ashes and the like—which have never been observed to possess that effect—simply because they are pervaded by smoke. But such is not the case; therefore, the distinction between types of things and the separate apprehension of the pervasion between individuals, when required, uproots inference based on the apprehension of smoke in some instance by means of any [effect] whatsoever.

Who, moreover, says this—that one might infer by means of whatever [mark] in whatever [case] where the pervasion has been grasped—given that in the absence of the recurrence of a single property (*ekadharmānuvṛtti*), there is simply no probans (*hetu*) at all? For in that case, the proof by ashes would not be valid due to lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), nor would smoke be valid due to being unestablished (*asiddhi*). If it is argued that even in the case of a pot, a bell, and so forth, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) alone, despite the non-recurrence of other properties, would serve as the probans when present in the inference, we say no; for the state of being an effect itself was previously established in detail as lacking pervasion.

In this regard, just as a mountain peak (kulagiri) possesses a fixed nature during the time of a potter's activity due to its own inherent deficiencies and so forth, so too, even though "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) exists, there is no difference whatsoever in the absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—just as a donkey is not [the cause] in the production of smoke—due to the occurrence of validity. Therefore, one who has apprehended the pervasion in a specific effect such as a jar cannot infer the pervader from "mere being an effect" in every instance; nor does he transcend the fact that the locus of the apprehension of pervasion and the locus of the means of proof are distinct. Thus, how is the objection regarding the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) avoided?

Therefore, mere conformity with a single property is of no use. Or rather, by whom were the properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*), being a real entity (*vastutva*), and so forth—which arise from smoke—reduced to ashes in the case of ash? If you argue that even though these properties exist, they are deviant (*vyabhicārin*), we reply: surely a deviation occurs precisely because of a lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*), since there is not even a trace of it in the case of actual pervasion. And that absence of pervasion is not avoided even by the property of being an effect; thus, deviation remains difficult to ward off even there. As for the non-observation [of the concomitance] in some cases, that may simply be due to distance.

[298] It does not follow from that alone that the probans is simply non-existent, because the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) which constitutes its very root remains as it was. If, however, the fallacy of deviation (*savyabhicāra*) applies even when there is pervasion, then it applies all the more so when there is no pervasion; therefore, enough with this false obsession. Thus, even if you accept a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) as a probans while disregarding mere pervasion, why not likewise accept a property common to the mountain and other such things? Otherwise, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains exactly as it was.

Nor does this principle apply even to jars and the like, which are treated as being on the same footing as the probandum; for even in those cases, just as we perceive the activity of the potter in the case of the water-jar, the arrow-receptacle, the bowl, and so forth, we likewise recognize that "this too is well-made by him," and thus we determine his operation only from those types of objects whose production has been previously experienced. Otherwise, one would not escape the aforementioned fault.

Therefore, even if from the perspective of ultimate reality this entire collection of effects is invariably concomitant with an agent possessing effort, nevertheless, from the perspective of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it is established that whatever kind of arrangement and so forth follows the presence or absence of a controller, that [arrangement] is what is inferred from it. (PV II 13)

Thus: when one sees something—such as a particular arrangement and so forth—which, even though it is seen by one who perceives no agent, leads to the cognition that it has been "made," like the temples and other structures seen in an empty city; if such a thing were observed in the subjects (dharmin) such as mountains and the like, then it would be logical that from this [reason] there follows the proof of what is intended to be proven.

And that [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*); this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Indeed, for us, there is always the cognition of something being produced (*pauruṣeya-buddhi*). That [cognition] is the cognition of having been made (*kṛta-buddhi*), and the rule is that inference is precisely the cognition of what is to be proven (*sādhya-buddhi*), since in some way, for someone, even in those cases [of mountains, etc.], such a cognition is absent. Furthermore, what is meant by "the cognition of having been made"? Is it the cognition of anything whatsoever being an effect, or the cognition of it being made by a person? If it is the cognition of anything merely being made, then that is established even for the Buddhist in the case of oceans, mountains, and so forth. And because they possess parts, their very state of being composed of those parts constitutes their being "made."

Now, if the cognition of a human agent (*pauruṣeyabuddhi*) is the cognition that [the scripture] was composed (*kṛtabuddhi*), then that is precisely the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*), and it is called inference (*anumāna*). Consequently, how can it not be undermined when it is stated that "because of the absence of that [cognition], there is no inference"? As he said: "Nor does the fault of the unestablished reason (*asiddhatādoṣa*) apply to a reason simply because some person lacks the cognition of the probandum due to delusion; for if it did, that fault would follow in all inferences. Furthermore, as for this which is said: "Such properties as being an effect (*kāryatva*) have been refuted in the case of mountains and the like," [that too is untenable].

[299] Even in that case, we do not perceive any distinction between Mount Kailāsa, a water-jar, and so forth, on the grounds of their being effects (*kāryatva*) or the like. And it has been said: "Nor is there any distinction between the causes of the earth and such things and the causes of palaces and the like, by virtue of which these [latter], while being devoid of intention, would—being independent of effort—possess that [intention] through an activity characterized by specific determination. For we have never observed independence in the performance of actions for instruments whose nature is to be operated, unless they are supervised by one possessing effort; since everywhere, the production of palaces and the like is observed only when they are supervised by an intelligent being."

To this it is replied: this "established cognition" (*kṛtabuddhi*) is not stated with reference to those whose intellects are perfumed by an adherence to philosophical tenets; rather, it is spoken with respect to ordinary persons proficient in worldly convention. And for such a person—who possesses the recollection of a previously perceived invariable concomitance—this kind of cognition indeed arises in a temple and the like when there is no aversion to reflecting on the cause, but not in a place such as a pond filled with fish and crocodiles. Therefore, the presence and absence of this cognition in these two cases cannot be established without positing a difference in genus (*jāti*), for otherwise, the same would follow even upon seeing two types of smoke.

Granted that this is indeed the very notion of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), who has stated that this constitutes the basis for inference for one who possesses it; or, due to its absence, why would there be an absence [of inference] in the case of mountains and the like? Rather, the presentation of its presence and absence is intended merely to indicate a difference in genus (*jātibheda*), with respect to common people, in order to provide an awakening for someone of particularly dull intellect.

For once such a difference in genus is established, one would not be able to claim that perception and non-perception (*adhyakṣānupalambha*) operating in one instance is capable of proving a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) elsewhere.

Therefore, the establishment of the probandum does not follow from a configuration (*sanniveśa*) or the like that lacks a necessary connection (*apratibaddha*); and since that which is connected is unestablished (*asiddha*), how can there be inference? Thus, even when this is introduced as a refutation of inference in general, what is being said is simply that for one [type of inference], its absence [does not entail] the absence of [all] inference. Now, even so, because another [type of inference] would lack the emergence of inference, it too ought not to exist; and how could such a claim be consistent? For it has been stated: "Nor from delusion," and so forth. That, however, is incorrect.

Because, when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of the means is identical, it is impossible for the result to be restricted to one [party] alone. Whatever possesses a specific causal complex with another thing must necessarily have an identical result with that thing; for example, two locations mutually possess the same result from the common collection of causes such as fuel and fire that produce smoke. And the person engaged in worldly transaction (*sāṃvyavahārika*) together with you possesses the same causal complex for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and so forth regarding the means of inference. This is a *prasaṅga* based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

For even for you, the means of establishing the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is indeed direct perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), which operates by way of the authority of temple architects and the like; and this is common to the opponent as well. However, the uncommon [means], namely the proof that sublates the contrary (*viparyayabādhakapramāṇa*), would be difficult to find; and it has already been demonstrated that even for you, such a proof does not exist.

Therefore, if that [reason] does not obscure the mind of one who experiences it merely through attachment to their own view, but rather that very proof is common to others, then for him too—inference regarding human authorship would be unavoidable even in the case of Mount Meru and Mandara, just as in the case of temples and such seen in an empty city. But this is not so. Consequently, when the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for something [is absent],...

For one who possesses the correct recollection, that which arises from seeing something is not an inference when there is no established connection (*pratibandha*) for it; as, for example, when one who remembers the connection between smoke and fire infers fire upon seeing a donkey.

Furthermore, there is no inference of a person on Mount Malaya, the Himalayas, or elsewhere based on the memory of a connection with a temple or similar structure by means of volition; this is the non-perception of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*). It establishes the deficiency in the subject being grasped by the proof that establishes the prior connection, due to the possibility of other cognitions such as the neglect of pursuing the cause of the memory. And that [deficiency] exists even for something possessing internal distinctions, provided there is no excellence of difference in genus, just as smoke [is not a valid mark] for a donkey.

However, this desired conclusion does not follow if there is a failure in either the apprehension or the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). For that purpose, there must be an accurate apprehension. In that regard, if there is a failure of recollection, one would not infer [the presence of fire] even from another temple (*devakula*). Furthermore, a failure of apprehension is impossible from the perspective of perception, because—as it has been stated—it lacks the very capacity for a single unifying conceptualization (*ekapratyavamarśa*). Otherwise, even those seeking water and such things would have to depend upon potters, architects, and the like.

If it is argued that even in that case, another factor standing in the place of a carpenter is required—just as in some instances there is a carpenter standing in the place of a potter—we say no. For when there is no dissimilarity in the nature of the effect produced, it is illogical to require a dissimilarity in the causal capacity. Otherwise, one would not be satisfied even with a mere potter in the production of other jars.

Or, just as a farmer might suffer the hardship of drought that cannot be averted by the efforts of a potter, such a distinction between classes is already established; therefore, because the conceptual determination of a single form is untenable, the pervasion (vyāpti) established through perception—having a specific object—does not incur the fault of being difficult to grasp, since even in the absence of inference, the non-establishment of a superior distinction between classes would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

Furthermore, since the apprehension [of the pervasion] is established exactly as it is, there is no inconclusiveness [in our position], because where there is no inference, there is simply no apprehension of the pervasion. If it is asked: "How can people in such a situation be expected to abandon inference?"—it is precisely for the reasons already stated: because even one seeking water would face the absurdity of trampling on the legs of a potter; or because one terrified by the invasion of a foreign army would desire the protection of great mountains and oceans; we do not perceive a pervasion based on mere sentience.

If it is argued that this undesirable consequence does not apply because [the pervasion] is restricted to the specific state of the potter and so forth, then what fault could there be in grasping the pervasion as being restricted precisely to that state? What is there to say about this? Furthermore, you need have no concern for someone like me whose intellect is stained by the blemish of sectarian bias; rather, the concern is for the world at large. If it is argued that even the world does not understand [the pervasion] through that [specific instance] due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), then in that case, one would not be able to infer [the existence of a jar] from another jar either.

If it is argued, "What fault is there here, since deviation is observed elsewhere?"—this [objection] is not tenable unless there is a dissimilarity of genus (*jāti*). Therefore, why is it not simply stated that perception, which apprehends pervasion (*vyāpti*), operates only with respect to a specific genus, and thus no inference of its operation applies to anything else? Why resort to the introduction of deviation in this case? Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that perception determines a specific genus; otherwise, even a perception that does not have deviation as its object would not [be valid].

If it were of a fixed nature, it might enter another jar as well; and that being the case, the same fault would persist. If you argue that this is because the very cognition grasping the pervasion has already occupied the other jar—surely, when the mind operates with a tendency toward deviation upon an object already occupied by that [pervasion], how could it avoid that very object?

But if both [the general rule and the specific instance] have a restricted scope, this fault does not arise. Now, since perception itself accepts a qualified object, the presentation of an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is no longer fruitful. However, for a person who is confused, the means of valid cognition that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*) are employed to instill the memory of its operation upon a qualified object.
