But pervasion, which extends everywhere, is not made restricted in scope by a deviation merely because it has been grasped; nor is there a mere refutation of inference, precisely because of the reasoning already stated.

Therefore, it is established that pervasion (vyāpti) is apprehended by means of a potter and so forth as having a specific object alone, because perception functions only with respect to a single genus, depending on whether or not deviation is observed.

Thus, even when one desires to grasp a pervasion (vyāpti) by means of mere consciousness alone, no deviation (vyabhicāra) is observed; it is therefore established that whatever genus or individual object the activity of perception (*pratyakṣa*) engages with, that very thing is proven to be pervaded by it. Consequently, how can one who asserts a pervasion in a general sense not deserve censure for merely repeating a convention (*samaya*)? However, if one who desires to grasp a pervasion through a mere person relies on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while rejecting direct perception, then this fault does not apply.

But that has already been examined: if, through the grace of God, this proponent’s perception were to arise everywhere with a single uniform form by abandoning the manifold forms of the world, then that [perception] would be unique and thus not a factor for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Between that which possesses a body and that which does not, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding effort from the perspective of the properties of action when grasping pervasion through perception; for, if one seeking a water-carrier were to fail to follow a potter and thereby lack the inference based on his [the potter's] work, then even if the possibility [of such an inference] existed by another means, since there would be no obstruction [to the inference] other than the specific difference in genus (*jātibheda*), the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) would once again attach itself.
Therefore, the absence of inference in that case—which is brought about by the difference in genus—being established, it demonstrates that inference is restricted to its own specific genus.

Alternatively, if the inference of a human agent restricted to a specific class (*jāti*) is not established, then one who, out of deceit, denies the distinction of classes even though it is established by experience, is forced to admit that distinction by means of a counter-inference. This is done by showing that the absence of the inference of being made by a potter and so forth—which is established by the absence of such activity and which is invariably concomitant with the distinction of classes—would otherwise lead to the emergence of a different inference, thereby resulting in the admission of the distinction of classes. It is said: "If there were such a thing as conjunction distinct from the post and the crow, the world would also perceive this third [entity] as visible."

And likewise, if the kind of arrangement that is observed to be preceded by an intelligent agent were to exist in the case of clouds and so forth as well, then people would also have the cognition that they are made by a person, just like other jars.

And thus it is stated that this distinction is not made by a difference in their genus, because there is no other cause for it. Then, in response to the inquiry, "What kind of arrangement, moreover, is established as being invariably concomitant with a supervisor?"—it is said, "even for one who does not see the action, from seeing [the result]," and so forth. This is for the purpose of avoiding the burden of enumerating various types [of causes] conceptualized through synonyms; for in that context, both are applicable: either the inference of an effortful agent (*prayatnavat-anumāna*), or the inference of the activity of a potter and the like (*kumbhakārādi-vyāpārānumāna*).
Both are consistent.

[302] This follows from the sequence previously stated. The absence of an inference for a potter is itself the logical mark (*liṅga*), because the causal complex for proving it consists merely in the negation of one who possesses effort; or rather, it is the absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as established by those who know that [pervasion]. And this has been elaborated in accordance with the opponent's own views. However, the world follows what it observes: whatever kind of thing it sees to be preceded by a person, it understands that very thing to have been made by a corporeal being alone; it does not even entertain a doubt regarding the cessation of a body. Thus, the cognition of "having been made" remains restricted solely to the inference of a human being.

Even when, by the power of some supernatural accomplishment (*siddhi*), someone perceives a demonic illusion (*māyā*) and a certain mental impression (*ullekha*) arises even regarding an immovable object—thinking, "Could this have been made by someone, or by whomsoever?"—even then, it appears as being utterly colored by hands, feet, and limbs. Certainty, however, remains far off. And that [impression] would not be possible if there were a single genus [of agent], just as smoke, a jar, and so forth [do not arise] from fire, a potter, and so forth [indiscriminately]. Nor is there even a mental impression of something devoid of the activity of hands, feet, and so forth.

Nor can the denial of inference by the proponents of momentariness and the like be established merely on that basis. Rather, we maintain that inference—which relies on the apprehension of pervasion preceded by perception and whose operation depends upon specific universals—is impossible for both the common person and the investigator alike, because it is common to both.

And although the second [type of inference] is also indeed worldly (*laukika*), nevertheless, due to the lack of familiarity with a certain object, there may arise for one of subtle intellect—even for a person engaged in ordinary worldly practice—a need for more intense deliberation (*tīvratarābhyūha*). In that case, even though direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is incapable [of grasping the pervasion], a pervasion already apprehended by means of another inference that sublates contrary instances (*vipakṣabādhaka*) may be employed as an inference by relying solely on worldly consensus; thus there is no fault, just as in cases where the world makes a particular proclamation regarding presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, it is entirely logical that the cognition of "producedness," which takes the form of the cognition of "having been made," establishes a difference in genus through both existence and non-existence. Even when the cognition of "producedness" is understood as the mere cognition of "having been made," there is still no fault. Nevertheless, what is called "producedness" (kṛtakatva) is the state of depending upon the operation of another for its own origination. And this [quality] is certainly not established through direct perception in things such as mountains, in the same way that it is in trees and the like. Furthermore, that which is established merely by the opponent's own admission is simply not a valid factor in an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*).

Then, when relying on that which is established by inference, is it relied upon as being of the same class as what is observed, or in some other way? In the case of the position that there is no end [to the series], if "being an effect" were established as being restricted to a specific location merely by virtue of being a succession of moments characterized by a beginningless stream of causal capacities, then what hope could there be for the intervention of a Person (*puruṣa*) based on such a thing? Rather, it is appropriate that the factor of the same class as what is observed should be the basis for that [inference].

Setting aside the distinction made by the basis of being conscious or unconscious, one might indeed attribute human activity to that which arises from the convergence of a vast multitude of causes, since such a convergence is determined by that [human] agency. However, even the mere fact of having an unconscious material cause is already accounted for by the previous sequence [of causes] and would not necessitate the introduction of the specific factor at issue. This very quality of being an effect is what is known in the world; yet, since this is not established in the case of mountains and the like, how can the charge of "unestablished" (asiddha) be avoided? It is simply not...
This is not a direct proof of non-establishment; rather, it is for the purpose of proving heterogeneity. Nor is it concerned with mere effectness alone, but with everything.

This is the meaning: is it established by the conformity to the presence or absence of a presiding agent, or by the configuration and so forth, that upon seeing which even a person who perceives no action develops the notion that something was "made"? Therefore, if you maintain that the notion of being "made" arises [in the case of mountains], yet it does not arise for the world [in the same way], then their belonging to different categories is established. Otherwise, the world would perceive that even a potter pervades such things as mountains; thus, the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) as before would follow.

Therefore, it is established that due to the difference in their origins, that which is produced by a person is indeed something distinct from [nature], as is known through perception and non-perception.

As for what was said—that there is no distinction in the state of being an effect—even if the property of being an effect is common to all things, if you intend the pervasion to be established by perception, then even though that [property] exists, it is effectively irrelevant; this has already been stated. However, if you intend to express a pervasion by consciousness based merely on the fact of "coming into existence after not having existed," while discarding any specific distinction, then you should likewise discard the operation of perception and take refuge in another means of valid cognition.
In its absence, nothing exists as an effect, even if it were present.

As for what was said—namely, "there is no distinction whatsoever among the causes such as earth," and so forth—that too serves only to bewilder the common folk; it cannot be a means for understanding the intended meaning. It is like someone who, while attempting to prove that diamonds and stones are scratchable by other objects because they are composed of earth, says to one who is in doubt: "There is no distinction between wood, stone, and the like on the one hand, and thunderbolts on the other, by virtue of which these [diamonds], though being composed of earth, would lack the property of being scratchable by iron."

For earthiness has never been observed in things that cannot be scratched by iron; rather, earthiness is observed only in jars, trees, and so forth, which are admitted to be scratchable by iron. Similarly, the present case also appears to be a mere verbal construction. Just as all persons who follow a general rule are perceived to engage in the undertaking of actions dependent upon human intention, so too [all things] possessing earthiness possess the nature of being scratchable by iron. And just as there is no other way [to account for this] than through extensive observation, so it is here as well.

Just as in this case there may be the doubt—even after extensive observation—whether this quality of being scratchable by iron is invariably concomitant with mere earthiness (*pārthivatvamātra*), or whether, despite being earthy, it requires some further specific qualification; similarly, it is the same [logical problem] as to whether the insentient nature of a thing requires the presence of a conscious agent for its causal activities, or whether it depends solely on the specific nature of the activity itself.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no distinction [between causes] because they are all equally capable of being grasped by a single conceptual reflection (*ekapratyavamarśa*), disregarding subtle internal differences as in the case of fire and so forth, then—due to the consequence of there being no distinction even among effects—it would be impossible to avoid the absurdity that a palace could be produced from a mountain just as smoke is produced from fire. If God were accepted [as the cause], perhaps this might not always be the case; however, if the opposite were true [i.e., if everything were caused by God], then it would follow that even a rice seed would be incapable of producing a rice sprout, or else the production of other palaces would be prohibited.
Now, even if there is an absolute difference in genus, [if one were to argue] with respect to the mere property of being devoid of intentionality, that too is an error.

[304] This is so; for indeed, a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not difficult to find anywhere. Nor does that much imply that things possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or an extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), because it would follow that poison and nectar would perform the same function. What undesirable consequence is there? Or rather, having disregarded the fact that the means for constructing palaces and such are themselves indeterminate and lack intentionality—which is a common property—there might also be a negation of the restriction regarding dependence on effort produced by that power which, based on a distinction of intrinsic nature, initiates an absolute difference in effect. If that were the case...
"What kind of fault?"—this is a phrase used for the meaning "there is no distinction whatsoever," and so forth.

Therefore, because there is no means of apprehending a pervasion characterized by various specific features, and because doubt remains unremoved, such a prattle—which is incapable of producing conviction even in one's own heart—is merely a defense of a mere possibility. Consequently, this remains established: with respect to the connection established through perception, that kind of structure and so forth which is proven to be pervaded by an intelligent agent is not found in mountains and the like; and that which *is* found there has not been proven to be so pervaded. Thus, the reason is either unestablished (*asiddhi*) or inconclusive (*anaikānta*).

By this, [the author] addresses what Trilocana said: "Now, what is this 'intellect that has acted' (*kṛtabuddhi*)? Is it the intellect regarding the means of proof (*sādhana*), or the intellect regarding the object to be proven (*sādhya*)? First, the intellect regarding the means of proof is already established for you, since you accept [the principle]: 'What is the source of the world's diversity? If, on the other hand, the latter position is intended, then the meaning becomes this: the 'effectness' (*kāryatva*) perceived in the earth and so forth is not capable of proving the probandum (*sādhya*), but rather something else entirely, because it does not produce the intellect regarding the object to be proven."

And this is not tenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference. For even in the case of smoke and the like, one could just as well say: "This smoke is not capable of producing an inference of fire; rather, it is something else entirely, since it does not generate the cognition of the probandum for one who perceives the probandum. And thus, the means of proof (*sādhana*) is not established as long as the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*) is not established, and the means of proof is not established as long as the cognition of the probandum is not established; therefore, the charge of circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is quite evident. Thus, that [objection] is refuted.

For this is not a direct statement of non-establishment (*asiddhi*); rather, since a person accustomed to worldly usage does not have the cognition of "produced" (*kṛta*) with respect to the ocean and so forth—even while recollecting the pervasion [of the term] with jars and the like—therefore, there is no single genus (*ekajāti*). Thus, this would be a proof merely of a difference in genus. Consequently, it is entirely logical that there is either non-establishment or inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) by way of the pervasion of a specific genus. And in that regard, the absence of the cognition of "produced" means both the absence of the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the absence of the cognition of the probans (*sādhana*), both of which are established.

As for what the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* says: "If it is perceived as being produced, why is there not the cognition that it was made? Even in the case of all palaces and such, the cognition that they were made does not arise; rather, just as in the case of ancient palaces and the like, the cognition that they were made arises only for one who knows the pervasion (*vyāpti*), while for those confused about the pervasion, there is only the cognition that they were not made—so too it is with the earth and other things, and thus there is no distinction."

If you argue that the notion of being created by a person is not possible in the case of the earth and so forth, as it is in the case of palaces and the like, [we ask]: is this regarding those for whom an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is well-known, or those for whom it is not? Even among those for whom it is well-known, is it regarding those who lack the recollection of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), or others? First, for those whose memory has not failed, the notion of being created by a person certainly arises; for even in the world, there is the common perception that "this variegated universe was fashioned by some Creator. This is the case for those who are deluded regarding the apprehension and recollection of pervasion.

Moreover, since the Mīmāṃsakas do not even entertain the notion that the Vedas were created by a person, the reasons such as "being a sentence" (vākyatva) and so forth, which were stated to prove their human origin, would likewise be unestablished (*asiddha*) in that case as well. Furthermore, the proof of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) adduced for the sake of establishing impermanence would also be unestablished; for the kind of "being produced" characterized by imperceptibility to the ear, which is observed in things like jars, does not exist in sound.

Therefore, this dissimilarity between the example and the subject of the inference is common to all inferences and is not a sublation specific to the inference for God alone; thus, that [objection] is also refuted by this very [argument].

Furthermore, regarding what was questioned concerning the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*)—namely, "Is [the inference] based on those things for which the existence of a valid inference is well-known? and so forth—we reply as follows: Consider one who, having once observed the production of a temple pinnacle (*kalasa*) and other such objects through the activity of a master builder (*sūtradhāra*), later infers human agency upon seeing a pinnacle or similar object. How is such a person to be described: as one who possesses the recollection of a well-known invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), or not? In the first case, he would not have the cognition of human agency regarding mountains and the like, because that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring a potter even there.

Thus it has been established. How, then, can there be a necessity for that state among those whose vision has not failed? For that very reason, even the notion that "the world is diverse" and so forth does not arise from the power of recollecting a grasped pervasion (*vyāpti*), but rather from the force of doctrines originating from other observations; for it is absent in those who have not heard such [doctrines], just like a contrary doctrine.

As for the passage beginning with “But for those confused about pervasion,” etc., it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, the example provided is even more flawed, because it merely aims to demonstrate a difference in genus (*jāti*) regarding the absence of the notion of having been produced (*kṛtabuddhi*). Nor has it been stated that the consideration of the presence or absence of that [notion] depends on the proponent and the opponent; for one may, out of personal conviction, conceive of things otherwise. However, this consideration is made from the perspective of perception, within the scope of conventional practice (*vyāvahārika-adhikāra*).

Furthermore, consider this: for one who is ignorant of the conventions of the Vedas and the like, yet hears a Vedic sentence or another work composed in imitation thereof—even if he examines it with great skill—what kind of determination of its specific nature could there possibly be? For, just as in the case of a jar, a thunderbolt, and so forth, all types of objects are seen by men to have human causes; thus, to postulate a perceptual distinction for words that are themselves perceptible would lead to the absurd consequence that smoke and other such things would likewise be [seen to have human causes]. Consequently, those things which exist only when certain persons are present and do not exist when they are absent must be understood to possess the same status as those persons.
There can be no difference between other speech and Vedic words, for both are capable of being produced;
they are equal in their indication of supersensible matters, and there is certainly no assurance in one alone.
Therefore, the Veda does not rest without reaching the status of being human-authored.

If that were so, what room would there be for the existence of that [universal] in mountains and other things that are perceptually distinct? Thus it follows: one who conceives of a specific effect as the unique mark of a cause mistakenly thinks that the mere effect—just like the smoke of fire—is pervaded by this [cause], when in fact it is only a particular kind of effect that is so pervaded.

Alas, it is a particular kind of darkness for the wise that another person does not understand that an effect of such a nature must have that very thing as its cause, even when the object is directly perceived.

Furthermore, since a difference in nature (*vaijātya*) between worldly and Vedic sentences is possible, the Mīmāṃsaka should not be defeated by mere convention (*samaya*). Nor can "the state of being a sentence" (*vākyatva*), whose pervasion is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), serve as a refuge in this matter. As for what was said regarding the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), that has already been examined and will be further considered immediately hereafter.

[Objection: But even so, since the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed in other things as well—even in those pervaded by that [intelligent agent]—just as a jar and the like are invariably concomitant with an intelligent effort (*prayatnavan*), so too might the earth, mountains, and so forth be so. [Reply: Has this not already been stated? Although the property of being an effect exists there [in the mountains, etc.], it remains indifferent because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped. Therefore, despite the fact that these other effects are not different [from a jar] in their nature, not even a touch of an intelligent effort can be obtained from them; only the mere word "effect, effect" remains, undifferentiated.

If that very [reason] has been taken as a refuge by the Venerable One through another door—because no direct refutation was heard there—then he says, demonstrating that even that is for the most part like food for crows:

"It is not proper to infer [the presence of] fire from a word that is identical [in sound] but distinct [in meaning], when that [word] is well-established as having a different referent, just as in the case of a 'white substance' and so forth. (PV II 14)

By this, that which was also stated is rendered without foundation: namely, that "here too, the establishment of the probandum does not occur through the superimposition of having an insentient material cause merely because of a similarity of words; for here too, due to the proximity [between the reason and the property to be proven], there is a real connection, just as in the case of 'producedness' [proving] 'impermanence' and so forth. Nor does a difference in genus (jāti) between the two subjects or the two properties everywhere destroy a real connection, for otherwise it would follow that there is no connection between 'producedness' and 'impermanence' due to the difference in genus between the word and the jar. This [objection] is likewise without merit.

For we do not claim that there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) of insentience (*acetanatva*) and having an insentient material cause (*sopādānatva*) upon mountains and the like; rather, those [attributes] are merely considered non-existent because they fall outside the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). If it is asked: "If one kind of insentient material causality is established as requiring a conscious agent, while another distinct kind is observed in mountains and so forth, on what basis is this distinction made?"—it is made by way of limiting conditions (*upādhi*). If it is asked: "Why does this not apply to two properties belonging to two different substrata (*dharmin*)?"—no, for there is a disparity. Insentient material causality is like smoke [in the context of inference], due to the assumption that it is a logical reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*); and no one says that it differs simply because of a difference in its substratum.

However, when what is intended is that mountains and the like depend upon a conscious agent because they have insentient matter as their material cause (*acetanopādāna*), then the logical state is simply that "smoke possesses fire by virtue of being smoke. This being the case, since a distinction between the two instances of smoke and the two instances of "smokeness" would follow, how can there be parity? If you say, "Let it be exactly so," we reply: no, for a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) that is itself divided [into different instances] necessarily divides the possessor of that attribute (*upādhimat*).

It might indeed cause a division; however, this division—characterized by exclusion from a single unifying conceptual reflection (*ekapratyavamarśa*)—does not touch upon smoke as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), such that it would divide what belongs to its own nature. Therefore, this objection is untenable, just as, for example, the state of being a material cause for insentience does not divide jars, clouds, and so forth.

If it is objected: "But surely, a difference in properties has not been observed based on a difference in the substratum (dharmin)," [we reply]: when a property is presented under a certain form (*yadrūpa*) by which the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) occurs, then even if the class of the substratum (*dharmijāti*) is divided, its appearing as non-different does not constitute a sublation. However, the principle is this: if that [property] is different, then another property residing therein—even if undivided—appearing as if divided, is not a prover. Otherwise, it would follow that one seeking a cloud would have to search for a potter.

If it is argued that [the inference is] not valid because clouds are seen arising in the sky even when that [wind] has ceased, we say no; for why should the projection of that wind by its source not be possible, just as it is with a jar? Furthermore, since only the property of bearing water is observed in both cases, it is logical to establish that here too, as there, there is merely a difference in terminology.

For the ascertainment of an invariable concomitance occurs only when there is a restriction on the nature of the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and commonality consists in the lack of such a restriction, which is contrary to that [ascertainment].

For a certainty is bound to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); if it were to occur even when the essential nature of its object is transgressed, it would have to be established by both a valid and an invalid cognition. But this is not the case; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). Nor is there a lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because [certainty] follows the operation of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). Thus, in this context, since the deviation of whiteness from fire has been observed, this is a refutation of the charge that the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnyatā*). For this very reason, it is not an inference; due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), this results in uncertainty in both cases.

However, there is no deficiency in the probans due to deviation in the case of fire and whiteness, whose pervasion is established; for once pervasion is established, it is impossible to prove an exception to the inference, as deviation itself would be untenable. For pervasion is characterized by universal inclusion; in its absence, how could there be the principle that "when this exists, that exists"?

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as there is no inference of fire from whiteness because the latter lacks an invariable connection (*apratibandha*) with the former, and that [lack of connection] is manifested by way of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Otherwise, one would have remained at ease even while accepting an inference in that case as well. And that deviation demonstrates that every property common to both the nature of the object of valid cognition and its opposite is invariably unconnected; thus, it follows from the aforementioned commonality induced by the lack of connection.

In the same way, it follows that even from the mere fact of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth, there is no inference of an intelligent supervisor (*cetanādhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is indeed beneficial to the opponent. Consequently, it is established that by reflecting upon the actual nature of the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇaviṣaya-svarūpa*), the proof of "being an effect" and so forth leads to intelligence only when accompanied by such a qualifying condition (*upādhi*). And since for such [a qualified entity] there is indeed a real distinction in its proximity (*pratyāsatti-bheda*), it has resulted in nothing but a mere name as one's refuge.

Since it has been established that the distinction between the types of subjects (*dharmijāti*) entails a distinction between their properties (*dharma*), how can there be a denial of this in all cases? If the meaning is that what constitutes a differentiator is denied in all cases, while in some cases it is not a differentiator, then that is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For it has been stated that both [states] exist in relation to the nature of the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And such being the case, the very persistence of difference remains.

[308] Furthermore, the mention of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth is made without the intention of disparaging [the opponent]. For even in that case, pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be established by the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); rather, it is established through an inference that sublates the contrary (*viparyayabādhakānumāna*), because in its absence, the inference would not be accepted.

If, then, the proof of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a mere phenomenon characterized by "having been and not being" through the property of "having been and not being"—which excludes any difference in genus (*jātibheda*) of the subject (*dharmin*), just as the kitchen and so forth exclude it in proving the pervasion of smoke by fire—then what follows for the case at hand, where the method of grasping pervasion is established as residing solely in the exclusion of differences in genus, depending upon the operation of perception? However, if even in the present case, only those properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) that reside in the actual substance of the effect-entity were to be understood as having their pervasion perceived, [then the same would apply].

Therefore, this is not a fault. It has merely been shown that because neither of the two types of means [for establishing pervasion] is applicable, the pervasion itself is untenable. In that regard, the lack of possibility for those [means] consists in the absence of acquaintance with a valid cognition that sublates the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), since such an effort is seen only in certain "Buddha-scented" ones (*bauddhagandhi*). And since it cannot be stated in the present case, one should discard reliance on that [pervasion]. Furthermore, in another passage, [it is said]: "Permanence would mean either existence or non-existence," and so forth (PV II 180).

It should be understood that the venerable Vārttikakāra, while establishing the cessation [of the opponent's view] by indicating—through the force of the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the contrary—that there is a necessary connection between the mere effect and the mere cause by setting aside their specific qualities, observes that the other proponent of pervasion (*vyāpti*), who relies solely on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), is closely dependent upon the power of those two. Therefore, in order to refute him directly, he brings forward a refutation based on the distinction between types of logical fallacies (*jāti*).
Therefore, since the distinction between universals (jāti) established by the operation of perception is extremely clear, it has been stated that even resorting to a mere name is of no avail.

Alternatively, let there be a difference in genus between mountains and the like on the one hand, and jars and the like on the other, for which reason it is said, "Whatever is established as such... (PV II 13), and so forth. But since Mount Kailāsa and others are human-made and thus belong to the same genus as those [jars], why should they not share the same cause as them? Therefore, the meaning is this: whatever is a mountain is entirely human-made, just like Mount Kailāsa, which is a mountain and yet human-made. Anticipating the objection that in this way examples such as small streams, great lakes, rivers, and oceans should also be inferred, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "of that which is established in the distinction of objects," this is the meaning:

since even the cognition of mountains and such things by those who behold the construction of Mount Kṛṭāparvataka and other such works proceeds with faltering movement despite being assisted by logic, it is equal to being a mere name.
Furthermore, if these mountains are established as being built by many similar human beings, what is the point of proving an Īśvara? What has been gained here, and what is completed?

If a difference in genus (*jāti*) were established, one might fulfill this hope by following the principle of a *siddhānta* based on the nature of the locus; however, if there is no difference, even that remains groundless. For, neither through experience nor through admission, does the proof of a creator of something heterogeneous to a jar follow from another jar of the same genus; thus, the genus of these two is indeed distinct and does not bring about a common cause, despite the mere similarity of their names. Anticipating the objection—"What is this restriction that the apprehension of pervasion occurs only in the two ways mentioned and not otherwise?"—he says: "Otherwise, [there would be] a potter for some product of clay..."
If [the existence of] a potter were established because of the production of jars and the like, then the anthill too would be established as his work. (PV II 15)

Thus [it is said]. For even by one who pursues the matter very far, no method for establishing a necessary connection (pratibandha) can be found which—while avoiding the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a potter is pervaded by all earthenware—would establish a pervasion by all effects through effort; this is the sense. Indeed, what contradiction of power (*śaktivyāghāta*) would there be for a potter, who is capable of establishing a pervasion by all effects, to establish that specific instance of earthenware? Or, let it be granted that the apprehension of pervasion occurs only in two ways. As for what was stated: "Not by way of distinction, due to the force of the sublation of the counter-example," and so forth.

Fearing that it might otherwise be the case, and anticipating that one seeking a cloud might— as already stated— be led to search for a potter, he says "otherwise," etc., providing another illustration of this possibility.

For when one establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a general sense even while proceeding with the aim of sublation (*bādha*), how could one then infer a potter from a clay object, since only a cause in general would be established? Even when, in relation to perception, there is a pervasion of a specific effect such as a jar—characterized by a specific operation of production by a specific cause such as a potter—how could that [inference] follow as a consequence? And even when, in relation to mere conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is a pervasion of the particular by the general, then this [objection] is even further removed.

If, however, one were to grasp the pervasion otherwise than according to this established rule—namely, that the universal follows from the particular—then how could the inference of a potter from a clay object not lead to an over-extension (*aprasaṅga*)? For if such an over-extension occurs even from something entirely dissimilar in view of its effect, such as a jar, why would it not also occur from something slightly similar? And likewise, even in the case of a homogeneous object, if there is no inference due to the lack of certainty regarding the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) when considering perceptual determinations that follow internal subdivisions, then what can be said of the case of a heterogeneous object?

The mention of "made of clay" (*mṛnmaya*) is intended to show that this is an instance of the *daṇḍāpūpa* maxim—that is, it applies by extension to one who has observed the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in cases that are absolutely heterogeneous (*atyantavijātīya*).

If it is asked: "Even if both explanations are accepted, there can be no inference because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); so how can this be considered an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?"—we reply: Deviation, according to the sequence already stated, is actually a facilitator for us, not a subverter. For, when there is a transgression of the operation of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or when something falls outside the immediately preceding category, deviation serves precisely to establish the absence of the certainty of the intended necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Furthermore, there are several positions regarding what is called "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*): first, that it brings about the subversion of a pervasion grasped in a general sense with respect to a restricted object; second, that it demonstrates that the apprehension of pervasion itself has not occurred; or third, that even when the pervasion is present, it undermines inference as such. For this very reason, the condition that the subject matter must be uncontradicted (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) is also declared to be a characteristic of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

In that regard, according to the first position, there would be no confidence anywhere; for even elsewhere, the hope for the probandum would depend solely on that [inference], and since that [hope] might be shattered—even if previously certain—somewhere else, doubt would not cease elsewhere either, and for that very reason, its apprehension would be futile. According to the second position, however, there is a distinction in the case of consciousness. For just as the pervasion of the general category of "effect" with respect to a potter is grasped through perception and established as being difficult to grasp due to deviation, so it is also with mere consciousness; for in that case too, there is no difference in the operation of perception.

But in the third case, since pervasion exists only when there is deviation, inference is discarded; thus, this succession of fallacies is truly great. In this position alone, the following absurdity results: that if this probans here does not remain deviating from the probandum, then it establishes the probandum. And no one other than one who perceives all objects directly is capable of establishing such a thing, which is devoid of the probandum.

For he either takes that very subject (*dharmin*) which does not possess such a middle term as the locus of deviation, thereby making it a fit object for inference; or, if no counter-examples are observed at all, he establishes that deviation itself proves the impossibility of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*). Thus, a pervasion consisting merely of the effect is simply impossible with respect to the specific cause under discussion. Once pervasion is grasped, if there is a contradiction, there is a lack of confidence; if there is no grasp [of contradiction], that is not due to the pervasion, provided the wise man perceives no distinction.

When there is a requirement for non-obstruction, there is no perception of all opposing factors except through freedom from fear; therefore, indeed, the method of apprehension does not consist in the mere result alone.
This is the summary.

Furthermore, if it is held that one first grasps a pervasion (*vyāpti*) whose scope encompasses all things, and then establishes its presence within each specific class of objects by means of a sequence of subverting arguments against those classes— why is that [pervasion] not likewise inferred within those classes by means of a sequence of proving arguments?
Why do wise men enter into such a position, which is a ground for the suspicion of being a mere vessel for laborious effort?
This is an intermediate verse.

That which is called "unreckoned" (*aparigaṇita*)—meaning the domain of the operation of things that is most unreckonable—must be without [determinate] scope. In that regard, who, having repeatedly observed that the multitude of classes of effects not belonging to [a specific cause] deviates [from it], would be capable of exerting an infinite effort to restrict the cause solely to its own classes of effects? Such being the case, a cause is capable of indicating [its effect] only at the very moment when deviation is not directly perceived.

If it is argued that [the pervasion] does not hold because doubt arises in that case, we say no; for then this person might achieve certainty regarding some supersensible object. If it is asked, "What doubt could there be regarding that which has been established as having a universal as its object by a perception that functioned with reference to a specific class?"—then, in that case, when one follows the operation of a means of valid cognition that opposes the occurrence of doubt in the same way regarding the higher and lower universals subsumed under those [classes], the point established in the third chapter follows.
Therefore, it is impossible to apprehend the pervasion of all effects by a specific cause characterized by intelligence.
The passage beginning with "siddhaṃ yādṛg" (PV II 13) and so forth constitutes the established tenet (*siddhānta*).

Alternatively, it summarizes what was previously stated: that it is not possible to apprehend a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the effect by mere effort independent of a body, because such [effort] is refuted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), and so on.

"Siddham" means that such a being is the possessor of a body and so forth, and is the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). The rest is easy to understand. The intention is that such a being is the object of defects such as contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*). Now, one might argue: "Since sentience is observed even in that which possesses a body, it is possible elsewhere too; thus, just as the effect and so forth are established as being pervaded by an embodied agent, they could likewise be established by an [agent] according to one's preference. To this, [the author] replies—shattering the desire for proof based on what remains, which is nothing more than a mere name—by means of the previously stated logic, regarding the difference in entities such as a jar: "In the case of a difference in entities, such as a jar..."

If the word "conscious" refers only to well-known agents such as potters and the like, then it is not logical to infer [consciousness] in that which is intended to be non-different from them alone—[an entity] which, by depending on the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), has been set aside [from the scope of common experience]. Thus, regarding the phrase "from a thing considered to be pervaded," whether it is the subject under discussion or implied by the context, he asks "how indeed? and answers:
"like fire from white substances and so forth."

The intention is this: if there were an inference of a distinct thing based merely on a similarity of words, why would one not infer fire from "pāṇṭumna" simply because it shares a similarity of words? Or, if in that case [the inference] depends upon a specific nature of the effect, [then...]

[312] It is argued that perception is not called inference because it excludes the pervasion by another; if that were so, why would perception not also exclude that [inference] by excluding mere consciousness? By this, when even a visible other effect is set aside by perception, what need is there to mention that which is beyond the range of sight, namely mere consciousness? Let there be, for now, a distinction based on the pervaded, since it is perceived as such in the world and otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Anticipating the objection, "What fault would there be if this restriction did not apply with respect to the omnipresent [creator]? he revives the previously stated point by means of another reductio ad absurdum, beginning with the words "Otherwise," etc. "Of the anthill" (*valmīkasya*) means "of the creature that is the anthill. "Its production" (*tatkṛtiḥ*) refers to the production of jars and the like.

This is the meaning: if, having ascertained pervasion even by means of a specific attribute, one were to infer merely consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) as a general property, then since the making of jars and such things is restricted to a potter who is possessed of mere consciousness, it would follow that even an anthill-creature must be inferred as the maker of pots and the like. For just as when the pervasion of a jar with its maker is grasped, the inference of that [maker] occurs because there is no difference in terms of mere consciousness, why should there not be an inference of the inhabitant of the anthill as well, since there is likewise no difference in terms of consciousness? And when...

If the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is by means of an embodied being, then there is the exclusion of any other [embodied being]; at that time, what need is there to mention something entirely dissimilar? Furthermore, plurality is not required here, because even for a single self, such as that of an anthill, the cognition of consciousness exists; thus the term "of an anthill" (*valmīkasya*) is used. By this, it is made clear that the inference of digestive fire from smoke and so forth is also refuted. And regarding the discussion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), everything should be repeated as before.

Regarding what was said—that the "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) and so forth, which are pervaded by an intelligent agent (*prayatnavat*), are not established in the case of oceans, mountains, and the like; and that what *is* established [in those cases] is not pervaded [by such an agent]—to this it may be replied: "Is this not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) arising from the conceptualization of a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*)? For instance, when it has been stated that 'whatever is produced (*kṛtaka*) is impermanent, like a jar,' someone might say: 'If the property of being produced residing in the jar is the reason (*hetu*), then it is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of sound; but if the property of being produced residing in sound were the reason, it would be absent in jars, cloths, and other things that are impermanent aggregates.'"

This is contradictory. Now, if the view is that [the reason] is absent in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) just as it is in the similar instance (sapakṣa), then it is the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) inconclusive (anaikāntika) fallacy. However, by that much, the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not actually incapable of proving impermanence; this case is likewise. For instance, by the statement "that which is established is not pervaded," there is a contradiction with the non-occurrence in the similar instance; or, if one maintains its exclusion even from the dissimilar instance, the "uncommon" nature is thereby implied.

Now, if it is proclaimed that this is not a fault because it conforms to the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtakārya*), then it would follow that even "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and other such reasons would fail to be proofs, and there would be a contradiction with the author of the Sūtras, for he has declared this to be a fault under the name *kāryasama*. As he said:

"The urging of the non-establishment of the probandum based on a mere slight difference in the nature of being an effect is *kāryasama*; this, moreover, is threefold according to the intention of the speaker."

[313] Thus, by virtue of being merely figurative, a slight indication of otherness has been stated, and the threefold nature [of that otherness] has been shown according to the intention of the speaker.

Both of these [positions] are likewise without substance. First, regarding the initial position, it has already been refuted. For it was stated that when the nature [of the pervader] is established by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that proves pervasion, even if the related entities are distinct, they do not constitute a sublation [of the pervasion], appearing as if their distinction were dispelled. However, if that [nature] is distinct, then properties such as "being an effect" (kāryatva), which appear as if distinct even though they are non-different, cannot prove that which pervades them. Furthermore, two methods for grasping pervasion have been shown.

In that case, if—by the force of a counter-inference that sublates the contrary, just as in the case of "being produced" and "destruction"—the invariable concomitance of "having an intelligent agent" with "being an effect" and so forth were also apprehended, then a valid cognition would be operating with respect to mere "coming into being after not having existed" and mere "possessing a specific configuration," etc. Under such circumstances, who could rightly find fault by differentiating the subject (*dharmin*)? Thus, it is appropriate to call this a "fallacy of the genus" (*jātyuttara*).

If, however, by virtue of perception and non-perception, "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) were ascertained to be pervaded [by fire] just like "configuration" (*saṃniveśa*) and so forth, then who could prevent the status of being a probans for sound even in the case of "producedness" and the like? For the operation of perception and non-perception is finalized precisely through the delineation of specific types (*jāti-viśeṣa*). Otherwise, if even properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) residing in smoke were established as invariably concomitant with fire without being delimited by specific types, they would bring about an unavoidable over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), thereby destroying one's own position.

They might indeed encounter it. Furthermore, the objection that another [unestablished] matter introduces an inconsistency is a most trivial counter-argument; for in that case, precisely where no direct perception of inconsistency occurs, that very thing becomes a valid means of proof—so what slightness of burden is there in the weight of the fault?

Furthermore, it has already been explained that for one who has previously grasped the pervasion of smoke by its sole effect, there is no inference of fire from ashes and the like—even in a dream—because such deviation is impossible. Therefore, in view of the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one must admit that the differences among the properties of the subject (*dharmin*) and its class (*jāti*) are indeed differentiators; so how can it be called a "quibble based on genus" (*jātyuttara*)? However, for the author of the Sūtras, who speaks according to logic (*nyāya*), [the following applies]:

"When the effect is used as a probans even in a general sense because it follows upon the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), the fault of asserting a difference [in the probans] due to the difference in its correlates (*saṃbandhin*) is considered 'balancing the effect' (*kāryasama*). (PV II.16)

This is the meaning: when the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) refers exclusively to a specific object, disregarding the operation of perception, then let the statement of difference regarding "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth—based on the difference from other classes (*jāti*) that serve as its relata—be considered a fault, for it is logically established.

Even when the proof (*sādhana*) is employed by relying on a general property (*sāmānya*)—namely, the mere state of "having come into being after not having existed"—which is common to all cases due to the force of the subverting argument (*viparyayabādhaka*) against the opposite [of the probandum] such as destruction, even then the fault of stating a difference based on the difference of relata arises, because it contradicts the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) since [the difference] is observed only in some instances.

[314] It is stated without prior deliberation that this is considered equal to all [other] logical reasons (*kāryasama*) by our teacher; however, at another time, this is merely a fault of the proof (*sādhana*), and thus there is no fault [in the reason itself]. Now, even so, it remains unestablished that pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists as one that encompasses all cases (*sarvopasaṃhāravatī*); yet, for that much alone, the probandum (*sādhya*) is not necessarily unestablished, provided that the apprehension of pervasion has been successfully carried out in accordance with the opponent's own position.

For us, however, it is only the form observed in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that is determined as being pervaded; just as, having determined smoke seen in a kitchen to be dependent on fire (*dhūmadhvaja*), one enters into the universal [of smoke] even though it resides in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), and upon perceiving smoke in that subject, one infers fire—thinking "where there is smoke, there fire has been seen, as in the kitchen"—likewise, although the pervasion is established for the entire class of things such as pots produced by a conscious agent, wherever [that class exists],...

Since it is possible to state that "the status of being an effect is observed there [in the example], and its production by one possessing effort [is likewise observed]," and since the establishment of the probandum is thus not contradicted even in this way, what is the point of insisting on the apprehension of a pervasion that includes all instances? If you argue that this is for the sake of proving the futility of the original proof (*maulasādhana*), then it follows quite clearly that, having taken the pervasion from one class of things, the inference proceeds from that very same class of things.

If [the reason] were based merely on the similarity of names between the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the mark (*liṅga*), then in that case, the actual nature of the mark would not have been stated; there would be nothing more than the mere application of words such as "effect" (*kārya*). Showing that this is incorrect, he says: "Because of the observation of a commonality of words for something well-known to belong to a different class from that which possesses effort, it is not correct to establish [a conclusion], just as [one cannot infer] horns from the word 'cow' when applied to a horse and so forth. (PV II 17)

[Objection: But surely, in the case of [the word] *kārya* and so on, there is no such thing as being "merely a word" (*śabdamātra*), because it is possible to trace the commonality of "having come into being after not having been. However, the word *go* (cow), in the case of [meanings like] heaven and so forth, relies merely upon personal whim (*rucimātra*) and does not function by following any single referent; thus, there is a great difference. [Response: This too is indeed floating [without foundation]. For "coming into being after not having been" (*abhūtvābhāvitva*) alone is not established as being invariably concomitant (*vannāntarīyaka*) with [the word], such that the result would be the reliance on tracing that [concomitance]. [Note: The phrase *nāntaravan nāntarīyakam* appears in the manuscript as *vannāntarīyakaṃ*; it is understood here as *prayatnavannāntarīyakaṃ* (invariably concomitant with effort).]

Furthermore, if that very same [universal] is withdrawn along with its properties (*saroṣa*) upon the establishment [of the proof], what has been either avoided or accepted by this [argument]? Therefore, we observe that even in that case, for one who introduces a distinction based on the difference between the classes of effects, there is no continuity of the real entity (*vastu*); thus, one relies solely on a verbal formulation as the means of proof. Consequently, there is no distinction whatsoever between this [proof] and the proof of horns for speech and so forth by means of "go-ness" (*gotva*).

The same verse applies to the example as well. And in that case, if one wishes to avoid the objection regarding the inclusion of all instances (*sarvopasaṃhāra*), the phrase "in another class" (*jātyantare*) should be construed as "of fire, which is well-known to arise from other smoke. However, when one determines the pervasion by unifying all forms of smoke through the force of a single uniform reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), then there is no mere similarity of words; that very [fire] is what is pervaded.

[315] Since the same point applies here as well, there is no contradiction regarding the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor is it possible to perceive the futility of the fundamental reason (*maulahetu*) in this way. For even though a cognition proceeds in a general manner—namely, that "wherever there is a means of proof (*sādhana*), there is a probandum"—it is not capable of taking as its basis a specific distinction of place, time, and so forth, as intended. Therefore, in order to make a particular instance the object of engagement or withdrawal, one cannot remain without relying upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). So how could the fundamental member [of the syllogism] be fruitless?

Therefore, for one who avoids the inclusion of all instances (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) when grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), even smoke would not be an inferent of fire; thus, in seeking a gain, there is the destruction of the very root. For it is not the case that fire, which was observed to be active in the production of smoke in one place, is likewise [active] in another location; rather, there remains only a similarity of words, namely, "that too is denoted by the word 'smoke' and this too is. This is no different from proving horns for a cow by means of its being a cow. Now, even so, what kind of proof for horns is this for speech? Since it is sublated by perception (*adhyakṣa*), it is indeed self-defeating.

If you say, "The reason is set aside because it lacks a locus," we reply: True, but even such a thing is highly improbable for you; thus, our greed is great! It is strange that as you negate in this manner, the hope for establishing the probandum—even by mere name—dissolves; and it is even more remarkable that, despite your labor in the treatises, you see no proof for the horns of your own words, which are seized by pride.
Why is the accomplishment of what is to be accomplished desired through mere designation?

Since even the cowherd women would not believe it now, he—desiring that they should nevertheless have faith as he strives in this way—uttered a reply in jest suited to that purpose; by means of his inference from horns, he characterized all such improper inferences as mere sophistry.

For when even for things such as fire there is an inference that finds scope even in relation to things such as a donkey, then what is not perceived from what? This is the underlying intention: provided, of course, that there is no direct sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*). [Objection: But surely, in the context of the process where the ascertainment of a pervader follows from the application of a term common to both the pervaded object and [other things], what room is there for an inference of fire from a donkey? For words such as "smoke" or "ash," which are common to objects pervaded by fire, cannot possibly apply to a donkey. [Reply: No, because even by means of a word such as "object" (*vastu*), the identity of the word-form is established; and this is as follows:
Having already refuted this by the very statement "as in the case of white substances and so forth in the fire," he says the following to satisfy [the opponent] by means of an alternative position:
[316] "Because they are dependent upon the speaker's intention, words do not exist anywhere at all."
"But if the object were established through the existence of that [convention], then everything would be established for everyone.

(PV II 18) By this it is meant that even in the case of donkeys and the like, the words "smoke" and so forth are impossible only as long as there is no desire for a convention (*samaya-samīhā*). Therefore, the absence of inference is also limited precisely to the non-application of words such as "smoke. However, once they have been applied, who can obstruct the probandum? This has already been stated. But this is not the case when the entity itself is the means of proof. For indeed: "In the domain of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), the occurrence of a separable connection (*vinābhāva*) is impossible."
Since they are dependent upon the speaker's intention, words do not exist anywhere [independently].
The word "vā" has the sense of "yathā" (just as).
But if the object were established by its mere existence, then everything would be established for everyone.

However, when the establishment of the probandum is intended not merely from the perspective of the state of things as they appear to an awakened person, but in reality, then—as with sound and so forth—the establishment of everything would have as its fruit nothing more than a mere bold assertion; rather, the sense is that the establishment of everything belongs to the pervader precisely in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). Thus, if one speaks of pervasion based solely on what is observed in the example, an establishment that depends merely on the similarity of words results in nothing but non-establishment. Therefore, by one who seeks a real proof of the entity that is the basis for genuine establishment, a pervasion that encompasses all cases (*sarvopasaṃhāriṇī*) must be demonstrated.

And neither of these two [types of evidence] warrants the inference of an intelligent agent from such things as their arrangement; for even if that much were established, the specific feature desired would not be proven—since that is what is sought by those desiring the highest good (*śreyas*), and thus the designation "Lord" (*īśvara*) would not be respected by the learned. This, in brief, is the meaning of the treatise. Therefore, this remains established: that even in the case of something impermanent accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no validity regarding such [an agent].
<Third Section> || The commentary on the Seven Verses of the Vārttika, within the section concerning the Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda), is completed.
[317,2] And this *Īśvaravāda* is completed.
[This concludes] the establishment of the relationship between cause and effect.
Some maintain that the nature of cause and effect is established by three kinds of perception and non-perception, as well as by the fivefold [syllogism]. (1)

The logical principle is that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). In this regard, some maintain that its proof is of three kinds: either two successive perceptions, accompanied by a prior non-perception, having both [cause and effect] as their objects; or two successive non-perceptions, accompanied by a perception that grasps both in a general way. Others, however, [hold a different view].

They say that the fivefold [set of means of knowledge] has a fixed sequence, because the triad exists only when the final two are present. For even when the first three are possible, the cognizer’s cognition does not arise free from doubt; however, once the final two are obtained, it is established. Indeed, the relationship between cause and effect is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); therein, positive concomitance is understood through the triad, and negative concomitance through the dyad.
[317,11] Success is well-established by means of the pentad. The sense is that if either of those two is not ascertained, doubt is difficult to dispel. [317,12] To this it is replied:
[317,13] "If there were a prior non-perception, then from another source [there would be] the meeting and so forth."
It does not negate; what is the use of that negation, and what is the use of a subsequent one? ||2||

Indeed, non-perception is sought precisely for the purpose of establishing a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by means of two types of non-perception. And that [concomitance] must be established by this [non-perception], which subverts the existence of that which is considered an effect when that which is considered the reason is absent. That existence is conceived in three ways:
its persistence in that very same place, its arrival from elsewhere, or its production from a collection of causes devoid of that [reason].

If it is asked: "What is the reason for this [inference] to depend on such an absence of sublation (*bādhā-vaidhurya*)? It has no utility regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Rather, it was already shown that it provides assistance to the perception that grasps the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," [we reply: "Is it not understood by sense-perception (*akṣaja*) that 'when this exists, that comes to be'? For positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is nothing other than the existence of one thing when another exists. And since that is established by perception, what is the use here of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)?"

[Is it] by way of assistance? But in that case, would this not also apply to another thing encountered by chance, since there is the possibility of mere perception? However, if perception is qualified by the apprehension of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), then it grasps that [non-existence], and thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Well then, is that [prior non-existence]—which has the nature of the opposite of an entity divided into three types of distinctions—established as prior non-existence through non-perception, or merely as a general absence (*abhāvamātra*)? In the first case, this consequence follows:
"When this exists, that comes to be;
because otherwise it would be impossible—this is precisely what constitutes the negative concomitance (vyatireka). ||3||
It does not abide therein, nor is it born from another, nor has it come from elsewhere.
If an effect could exist when something is present, it would not exist when that thing is absent; thus, it belongs to nothing at all. //4//

And this is established by perception preceded by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); therefore, nothing is accomplished by the latter two [reasons]. For even that [non-apprehension] is the means of proving negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) precisely because it subverts the persistence of an effect in the absence of its cause, its production from something else, or its movement elsewhere through other effort; it is not merely the latter two [reasons], since [the effect] would not exist even by the hundredth [attempt] in the absence of their operation. And that is the first—
If it is argued that because it was produced by one person, there is no utility for another;
or, if the view is that the first non-apprehension perceives mere non-existence,
then even when mere non-existence is established, the prior [non-apprehension] remains useless.
Prior to this activity of his, what exactly remains? ||5||

If there is the cognition of mere non-existence, first of all, what could have a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with what? Even the cognition of positive concomitance in the form “when this exists, that exists” is merely an incidental occurrence that obstructs utility by leading to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, however, there is a cognition such as “this has non-existence prior to this operation,” then the same threefold path arrives; what remains, then, from which the final non-duality (*advaya*) would not result in futility?

If it is argued that negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is followed because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in positive concomitance (*anvaya*), why is this not likewise asserted regarding the operation of mere perception (*pratyakṣamātra*)? (6)

That for the sake of which one would seek [the cause] previously—namely, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—is indeed called the "relation of cause and effect" (*hetu-phala-bhāva*) precisely because they are each individually subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, the possibility of each [of the two] occurring even when the other is absent does not constitute a refutation; this is the same for both of us.
Thus it is established.
[319,1] Therefore, it is established that the first [moment] has no utility for the last two, nor do the last two have any utility for the first. This is not established.

[319,2] For although one may perceive through the first moment that "prior to its operation, this [effect] did not exist," it is not determined by that [first moment] that "its non-existence is caused by the operation of this [first moment]. However, it is determined by the final [moment]; thus, [your claim] is incorrect, because the lack of utility of the first moment remains exactly as it was.
Furthermore:
Because of the non-existence of that alone, there is a definitive determination by means of the latter.
Since that same logic applies equally, why was it not also accepted by the former? (7)

The statement "it did not exist prior to this activity" also indicates its non-existence solely by means of the absence of that [activity] itself, as has been stated through the implication of the refutation of the threefold nature of existence (*sattā*). Therefore, if there is no certainty by means of that [first], let there be none by the subsequent one either. In that case, for one who perceives that the first [statement] merely establishes the co-presence (*sannidhi*) of the non-existence of both, rather than being the cause (*prayukti*) of the non-existence of the one alone—what confidence can there be in the subsequent one?

If those two were not dependent on that [fire], then the consequence of their arising even in its absence would be the same; thus, the impossibility of the absence of the second [the donkey] remains equal. Now, if it is argued that although smoke arises immediately after the arrival of both fire and a donkey, its absence when the donkey is absent is experienced by the former [the observer], then [one might say] that its absence when both have departed is also experienced by the latter. Thus, one must follow a succession of ever-newer means.

[319,13] There would be the loss of the established fivefold classification. If it is argued that this being so, there are three [factors] and not two, we reply: even by the latter [position], it is not possible;

this much alone is stated. But what is the use of this discussion as to whether there are two or three? If it is argued that there is a utility for the two, because certainty is impossible even in the absence of the other, then at the very moment when non-perception occurs due to the sole absence of the reason (*hetu*), that is precisely when the former [non-perception] occurs.

[319,16] Why is it not accepted that [the cognition] is also capable? If not, it has been stated that this is because it is entirely useless; otherwise, one could just as well say that perception consists of three [factors], not two. Furthermore, for the proponent of five [factors], since there is no distinction due to their occurring at the same time, only the prior non-perception is accepted as one [factor]. And since that exists even when the fire and the donkey have departed, it remains [present] even now in relation to the subsequent non-perception of smoke.
[319,19] It is indeed duality.
[319,20] Moreover, [319,21] having previously not seen it, one perceives it sequentially; thus one understands the status of cause and effect.
Or, if it were seen, one would not see it sequentially; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. ||8||

Because there would be the consequence of having to seek a further and further perception or non-perception of each preceding and succeeding factor in order to refute those respective doubts, one may establish the triad and so forth as desired. However, there is no utility whatsoever in designating the middle member as "perception" for the two types of non-perception; for if there is doubt about another possibility, neither of the two is reliable, and if that distinction is to be made, it is accomplished by one alone.
Therefore,
when the positive and negative concomitances are ascertained through perception and non-perception,
what kind of doubt could there be regarding the established relationship between cause and effect? (9)

[320,7] If they were distinct entities (*arthāntara*), then those two alone would constitute the nature of that [non-existence]. Furthermore, there would be no restriction regarding the cognition of those two, since it would be established in both ways. It might be argued: "This determination is made precisely because of the firmness of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); therefore, for the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) which grasps that [absence], it is entirely appropriate that it transcends the perception whose object is positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For the necessity (*nāntarīyakatva*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is indeed [the basis]."

[320,10] It establishes firmness, not mere frequency, because we observe [the absence of the probandum] even in cases that appear to be valid reasons (*pramāṇābhāsa*). And since the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) alone is sufficient to prove its absolute absence when it is absent, what is the point of running further? For at that time, not even a scent of smoke can be conceived. [Objection: But surely, due to the absence of many [instances], in the absence of what would smoke not have occurred?

If it is argued that there must be a determination (*niścetavyam*), then perception itself, which apprehends positive concomitance (*anvaya-grāhi-pratyakṣa*), is required when the absence of this [effect] is conditioned by the absence of another [cause]. For if this were not the case, one would not take account of its occurrence. Thus, even in a determination preceded by the apprehension of positive concomitance, since many possibilities exist, when the inquiry arises as to "whose presence conditions the presence of this," it is established through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) that: "since the absence of this is conditioned by the absence of X, its presence was also previously conditioned by the presence of X. In that regard, whether in the addition or the removal of each individual factor, [the same logic applies].

Or rather, it is not possible to understand it in that way. And such being the case, there would be the capacity for the establishment of exclusion (*vyatireka*) either in the preceding or the subsequent [instance];
however, it is established that when there are multiple instances of application (*upanaya*) and so forth, there is no capacity for either of the two.
Furthermore, this fivefold classification is not all-encompassing; for it is absent in cases such as ashes and fire, or a potter and his jar, because the latter is missing there.

Likewise, it is established even in the absence of the former in cases such as water and its container. For instance, when someone perceives the stability of a flood of water behind a dam, and observes that the presence of the water follows upon the presence of the dam, the determination of the causal relationship between those two is independent of the aforementioned classification.
It is exactly so. In other cases as well, it should be understood that [the cause] depends on a triad [of conditions].

Now, why is it not imagined that, having previously been unseen, upon the perception of smoke in the presence of fire, [the smoke] produces something else by depending on the fire? Even in this case, the causality would belong to the fire alone, just as it does to the fuel. If that were so, then for any other thing that happens to be present by chance, [the same would apply].

If it is argued that let the donkey and so forth also possess causality, and consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of inferring fire from smoke even in its case—[we reply:

is it because the determination of causality exists for fire that it must likewise exist for the donkey? Or is it because perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*) operate there as well? Since neither of these two is applicable, one does not resort to the three [criteria] for the sake of negating another [cause] in such a manner; rather, [it is for a different reason].

[321,4] For the sake of establishing fire, that [fire] is established; thus, the non-prohibition of anything else is indeed not a sublation (*abādhaka*). Non-inference, however, arises precisely from the lack of certainty regarding causality. The suspicion that "the donkey never acts in dependence upon fire" is itself a certainty, because of the contradiction [otherwise];
