for that suspicion is of the nature of doubt (*saṃśaya*). Its negation also occurs through the investigation of that very [doubt], and not of anything else; therefore, such a thing is simply out of place.

[Regarding] the [objection concerning] idle chatter: "But even so, since the restriction that 'fire is the cause' is untenable, the position remains flawed. For fire alone is not the cause, because other factors have not been excluded, and because fuel also possesses causality from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Nor is it the case that [fire] is only a cause, since smoke is possible even when [fire] has not yet begun; thus, this objection is not valid, because both types of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) [are applicable]."
Because it is established; for thus,
when there is a cutting of another thing in dependence upon a causal complex, it is in dependence upon a substance.
In the case of fitness, there is the non-connection [of the agent]; and in the case of the action, it is established as absolute. ||10||

For when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by that [fire] is denoted in its entirety by the word "fire," then the expression "that very thing" functions as an exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). When, however, it refers specifically to the substance of fire itself, if "causality" means capacity (*yogyatā*), then the expression "it is indeed a cause" functions as an exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*). If, on the other hand, it refers to the action itself, then the expression "it certainly exists" functions as an exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga-vyavaccheda*).
[321,17] This is established. And since this much of an operation is possible only for the threefold direct perception and non-perception, it is correct that regarding this portion,
the explanation of the venerable Bhaṭṭārcaṭa alone [is authoritative],
as is also [the explanation] of the Blessed Vārttikakāra himself.
The production of a jar by a potter, of ash by fire, and of a wound by a weapon and so forth—this is precisely what he asserts when he speaks. (1.11)

But how is it that, despite the lack of distinction in being an effect (*kāryatva*), there is no inference of fire from ash as well? It is not so, because [the inference] is intended with regard to place, time, and so forth. For instance:
every effect, merely by its arising, depends upon a cause.
Furthermore, for the sake of the continuity of the stream, another [cognition] arises depending upon that [previous one], as it knows the time.

In that regard, from things such as a potsherd or ashes, which depend on other factors for their very production—and precisely because they lack a continuity dependent on something else—only the past time of the presence of the cause can be determined with certainty, not the present; thus, there is no confusion regarding activity and so forth. Furthermore, from subsequent signs such as smoke or light, depending on whether they depend on specific conditions or not, and due to the absence of continuity—[the cause is determined through] the material cause (*upādāna*).

[322,4] It is even more deficient for the sake of interrupting the stream, since it does not depend on others while occurring in the present; thus there is no fault. With regard to this, however, the effort to rely on the latter two [definitions] by Master Dharmottara might bear fruit. But the restriction to five [types of non-apprehension] remains subject to criticism even then. Since there is no dependence on anything else in the case of non-apprehension preceded by perception, the first [definition] alone is superior.
The establishment of the causal relationship, preceded by the three types of perception and non-perception, as summarized in the *Ekādaśaślokī*,
the work of the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitrapāda, is hereby completed.
[323,2] || The Chapter on the Determination of the Yogin ||

Whatever is meditated upon becomes vividly apparent at the culmination of the intensity of that meditation, just as the form of a beloved woman appears to a lover. And such real properties of things as momentariness and selflessness are indeed meditated upon by one who seeks the supreme human goal.

Here, this must be considered: let it be granted that through meditation there is a vivid appearance for the mind; however, since this is common to both real and unreal objects, and because a rule of correspondence cannot be established even for that clarity produced by meditation, how can there be validity? How, then, can the cognition of a yogin be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

If it is argued: "Since there is no suspicion of error regarding the cultivation of an object established by inference, how could there be any room for doubt concerning the cognition produced from that [cultivation]?"—let us set aside for a moment the hope for the efficacy of inference; even in the case of perception, after one has apprehended lightning, fire, or the like, there may arise through the culmination of intense cultivation a cognition possessing a much more stable aspect of that object, provided that the application of contrary cultivation has not reached its limit.

And since that object has set, how can there be confidence in its correspondence even when it is within the range of an object brought forward by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Alternatively, even if it has not set, there is no fixed duration for the persistence of fire; the same applies to the ocean and other such things. Furthermore, a dissimilarity (*vaisadṛśya*) is observed in trees and the like over very short periods of time, and in mountains and the like due to fires, thunderbolts, and so forth.

However, since cultivation occurs by becoming fixed upon a certain state, that vivid appearance is restricted to that single state; therefore, with respect to its object, it is an error due to the difference in form, and thus it possesses neither validity nor the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, when even a plowman, having inferred the sacrificial fire, makes it vivid through cultivation, that would not be the cognition of a yogi because it lacks an ultimate object (*paramārtha-viṣaya*); consequently, it would follow that this is yet another kind of direct perception.

To this it is replied: First of all, this immediate objection is not even possible. For would meditation (bhāvanā) arise spontaneously due to the onset of passion, grief, and so forth, or would it be undertaken deliberately by a discerning person out of regard for a purpose? In that regard, since there is an absence of any talk of a supreme purpose, the mere burning or cooking is already accomplished by approaching that location through fire that is merely inferred; furthermore, meditation is futile even in a place where [the object] has not been touched.

Furthermore, when that [object] is cultivated, an error arises in relation to its actual state; the same applies to cultivation brought about by grief and so forth. Therefore, how could there be any connection with the contingency of it being another type of perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

Or, let such cultivation of an object be as it may—like the cultivation of a horn on one's head. Even if it is not an error, it is still included within the knowledge of a yogin (*yogijñāna*). For yoga is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), characterized by one-pointedness of mind; thus, there is no fault. However, when the form of a horn becomes clearly manifest—as in the case of the "earth-totality" (*pṛthvī-kṛtsna*) and so on—it is indeed not perception, because it lacks a real objective basis (*nirālambanatvāt*).
Or rather, that commentary which is authoritative and consistent, like an object previously determined, is accepted as perception born of cultivation; all others are distortions. (PV II 286)

Furthermore, if there is a cultivation that, even when the object has ceased or possesses a different aspect, maintains it as having a stable aspect—and if this [cultivation] is rendered objectless in every respect—that too is appropriate for the position of cultivating the thing-in-itself (*vastu*), but not for the position of cultivating the properties of the thing (*vastudharma*). And the properties of the thing, such as momentariness and so forth, have been undertaken for cultivation because they become manifest through detachment from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-vairāgya*).

Now, one might object: "Since it is observed that there is discrepancy even regarding an object purified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when its clarity is produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), what confidence can there be in any other case? For, apart from purification by a means of valid cognition, this [cultivation] lacks even the cause for confidence, and because it is incapable of being restricted to correspondence (*saṃvāda*). This is not so, because there is a distinction based on whether the object is stable or unstable.

For an unstable entity is swallowed up by destruction and transformation; thus, there is no correspondence [with such an entity]. However, the properties of an entity, such as momentariness and so forth, are never interrupted; therefore, the manifestation regarding them is always indeed possessed of an objective support (*sālambana*).

[324,8] But surely even this is not tenable. For there is no such thing as "momentariness" (kṣaṇikatva) that exists as a real entity; or, if it did exist as a reality, it would itself be eternal and unconditioned, whereby everything would perish without effort. And if it were not a real entity, that itself would be the state of being without an objective support (nirālambanatva). Therefore, even in your own view, what is called "momentariness" refers to the very collection of momentary entities themselves, spoken of as such by disregarding their distinctions and setting aside other differences.

And this being the case, even the "cultivation of momentariness" has the same meaning as the "cultivation of the multitude of momentary entities. To that extent, those very things being cultivated become manifest; thus, the same fault remains. Now, if you argue that although momentariness and so forth are non-different from the objects, they appear as if they were different for the time being—even so, because of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), it is the properties residing in the actual object itself that are being cultivated; therefore, there is no escape from that fault, since it is impossible to cultivate them as something standing apart (*taṭasthatayā*). And thus, the very form "this collection of objects is of a nature that breaks apart in every moment" is what constitutes the cultivation.

[324,21] How, then, is there an avoidance of contact with a real entity even when there is a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the reality of the entity? And if there were such avoidance, there would be only the cultivation of a non-entity, not the cultivation of the Dharma. True. Although the entity is generally implied by the cultivation of the reality of the entity, nevertheless, it does not become manifest (*sphuṭībhāva*), because the intent culminates solely in the reality itself. For it is the cultivation of reality alone, as it becomes manifest, that is the path for departing from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

For it is not the direct perception of a beloved woman’s body that brings about the contraction of passion; rather, it is its very nature as impermanent, suffering, and so forth. Therefore, because the intention (*tātparya*) is directed toward that [nature] alone, it is that very thing which attains clarity through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), not the object itself. But one might object: even if the intention is directed there, how is it consistent to say that the property (*dharma*) of the object becomes manifest while the object itself does not, given that both are encompassed by the cultivation? Or of what sort is the manifestation of a mere property that does not touch the substratum (*dharmin*)? This is merely painting the sky; indeed, it does not produce conviction even for a common plowman.

This is not a fault, because we observe that even though it does not touch upon the manifestation of the substratum (*dharmin*), there is a manifestation of the mere property (*dharma*) alone. It may be argued that there is simply no vivid appearance without depending on proximity to the object. However, its manifestation consists in the sudden flashing forth of its respective form within the cognition of it, without requiring effort when that object is present; yet dependence on proximity to the object is not abolished, precisely because it is a property (*dharma*), just like "dearness" and so forth.

For instance, it is observed that even in the case of the juice of the *nimba* tree and the like, the cultivation of its pleasantness becomes clearly manifest. Yet, that [pleasantness] is not an inherent property of the *nimba* itself; therefore, through the cultivation of that [idea], the *nimba*—whether situated in its own place of origin or present on the tip of the tongue—does not appear clearly until there is an intensification of the application of the cultivation of the opposite [notion].

Nor is it observed that even when dearness has become manifest, it remains neutral; rather, whenever there is an experience of the neem tree or similar objects, at that very moment dearness suddenly becomes the object of experience. It is not experienced as something repulsive as it was before—this alone is the meaning of the manifestation of the property (*dharma*).

For instance, even when an object such as a beloved woman becomes clearly manifest, there is no clear manifestation of the reality (*tattva*) established by convention; likewise, even through the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), there is no clear manifestation of the object, despite the fact that both are mutually non-deviant. What kind of fault is there in this? If it is argued that "belovedness" (*priyatva*) is not an external property because it is unique (*asādhāraṇatva*) and because it is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanādheyatva*), then to what does this property of belovedness and so forth belong? It cannot be denied, since it is personally experienced (*pratyātmavedyatva*). If it belongs to cognition (*jñāna*), then...

What logic is there in the claim that the dearness of an external object becomes manifest through knowledge when it is not being feared? Even the form of the mental cultivation "this neem tree is excellent" does not mean that the knowledge itself is excellent. Furthermore, if the manifestation were due solely to the dearness of the knowledge, no one would ever experience anything unpleasant; for unlike external objects, knowledge is not something whose presence is merely occasional.

If it is argued that even cognition manifests as pleasant only for some [particular individuals], then what is the cause of this distinction? If it is caused by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), then let that practice occur only with respect to external objects. If there is no dependence on such [external] objects, then since there would be no proximity or distance for anything whatsoever, the mind alone would become the locus; thus, there would be no distinction at all.

[325,19] But in the external world, since specific species such as the *nimba* tree and so forth have been made objects of cultivation (*abhyāsa*), there is no over-extension of the principle. In that case, even cognition would be proximate only when it has the cultivated *nimba* as its object; this is the distinction. If this is so, then the following consequence follows: whatever object is cultivated in a certain form, that object is set aside and what is proximate to it becomes manifest. Thus, for one cultivating a beloved woman (*kāminī*), the consequence would be the manifestation of her father or others who are proximate to her, rather than the beloved woman herself.

Now, is there some specific proximity between the object and its perceiver, the cognition? Even so, when the *nimba* tree is repeatedly practiced upon as being dear, the cognition of it flashes forth as dear; yet the *nimba* and such would remain just as unpleasant as before. Therefore, just as in the case of a snake or similar unpleasant thing, the certain determination (*niścaya*) of it—as a means for avoidance—is itself pleasant and not the snake or the like, so it is here too; thus, enough with this cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

[325,26] Now, is it your conception that, by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), a cognition having that object as its domain arises in a pleasant form? If this were so, then since "the bitter neem juice is cultivated as pleasant," it would follow that the cognition of that very object is what is cultivated in a pleasant form. Furthermore, its clarity (*sphuṭābhatā*) consists in the sudden manifestation of the pleasant form by the cognition apprehending it when the object is placed nearby, without depending on effort; it is not the direct presence of the object itself, which remains spatially remote.

In this way, mountains and so forth are also cultivated as being momentary; thus, it is the cognition of those objects itself that is cultivated in the form of momentariness. Its manifestation becomes clear in the presence of the mountain and so forth, arising as the momentary aspect of the cognizer of them, and not as a manifestation of the mountain and so forth when they are absent. This very cultivation of the dharma (dharmabhāvanā) culminates in the word-meaning itself, and thus there is no impairment to the subject matter at hand.

In reality, however, "dearness" (*priyatva*) means the state of producing happiness. In that regard, when there is a cultivation of dearness toward a particular object for someone, that object—by means of its own causal substratum (*upādāna*), which is the mental continuum refined by that cultivation—produces happiness as a cooperative condition (*sahakārī*). Thus, not everything is dear. In this context, the quality of being pleasing (*prīṇakatva*) is a property of that very object; and it is no fault that not everything is a source of joy. Moreover, that [dearness] arises solely from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). This same principle should be applied to mental qualities such as compassion and the like.

The manifestation of the cultivation of "I shall rescue the suffering" is that knowledge which arises instantaneously upon the presence of its object; it is the cause for the production of an undertaking corresponding to that [knowledge]. Likewise, in the case of the cultivation of the skull as pure, the manifestation of "cruelty" (nairghṛṇya) is to be understood as occurring when one approaches the skull-bowl. However, this sudden flash does not occur merely through proximity to a relative, nor through anything other than that.

As it has been stated in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*: "The excellence attained through awakening, compassion, and so forth, does not require such effort when that object is present; rather, it unfolds spontaneously within each individual."

Therefore, even when the practice of the property of momentariness has reached its culmination, for as long as it must be experienced by this [yogin], it remains a form that is fragmenting and distinct from the perception of people like us. Just as our own perception and conceptualization—though directed toward something extremely similar—suddenly manifest as following the most vivid distinctions of different locations, or as an activity corresponding to that, so too are the perception and conceptualization of the yogin directed toward two entities that differ in their moments.

And because his mind is unstained by the blemishes of passion and the like arising from delusions such as stability, its clarity reaches this much; [this is what is meant by] "its state of vivid manifestation. But is this not merely a technical definition—that its degree of excellence extends only this far? To say "because it is seen so" is no answer. Even if it is indeed seen thus, one cannot maintain in the present case that its state is fixed at that extent alone. For perhaps the excellence, as it increases further, might become vivid together with the object itself; thus, the previous defect is not eliminated.

If it is argued that even regarding [the realization of] "dearness" (*priyatva*) and so forth, there might sometimes be a different ultimate state (*niṣṭhā*), we reply: let it be so; yet, by means of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises the apprehension of a clear manifestation (*sphuṭībhāva*) that transcends the merely intended state. For one who acts with foresight and is devoted to cultivation for their own sake or for the sake of others, their purpose is accomplished by that alone; why then would they enter into further exertion, given that it would be useless or even counterproductive? It is just as in the case of food, medicine, and the like, once the desired degree of cooking has been attained.

Just as in this case, even though another degree of cooking might be possible, the conventional usage of the term "culmination of the excellence of cooking" occurs by means of that very [degree] which is intended; so it is also in the present case, and thus there is no fault whatsoever. Therefore, although the manifestation of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*) is accompanied by non-correspondence because of the instability of the object, nevertheless, there is no room for such a suspicion regarding the cultivation whose domain consists of the aforementioned properties (*dharma*); this is established.

If this is so, one should not object that the example of the amorous woman is inappropriate, because what is intended is merely to illustrate the clarity of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). For this very reason, the *Vārttika* says: "like [the clarity of] disgust, detachment, and passion."

In that case, is that yogic cognition distinct from sensory cognition or non-distinct? And what follows from this? On the view of non-distinction, there would be no such thing as a distinct type of perception called "yogic cognition," since it would be subsumed under sensory cognition alone. Nor can its classification as distinct be established on the grounds that it arises in a mental continuum refined by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), for otherwise it would follow that other types of perception—such as those resulting from the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like—would also have to be classified as separate types of perception.

Furthermore, on the view that they are distinct, the claim that the knowledge directly realizing momentariness arises from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) while other [knowledge] does not, is a "virtuous purification" [i.e., a mere pretense]. For if sensory perception itself were to realize instability in that state, what would be the use of yogic knowledge? Moreover, its realization of momentariness is not accidental; rather, that realization occurs when clarity has been intensified by meditative cultivation. And meditative cultivation does not apply to sensory perception, but rather to the mind (*manas*). Furthermore, if direct realization were attained even without such cultivation, then meditative cultivation would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, are those two [the subject and the property] at different times or at the same time? In that regard, being at the same time is untenable. For the momentariness of the subject (*dharmin*) presented by sensory cognition must be directly realized through an experience arising from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Otherwise, for one who would directly realize the subject and the property independently, the refutation based on the subject would be unavoidable. Moreover, it has already been explained that the process of meditative cultivation regarding a property does not result in the direct realization of the thing itself, unlike [the case of] the *nimba* tree and so forth.

Therefore, the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) is indeed superior to the domain of sensory cognition. Consequently, there is a fixed temporal distinction: first, sensory cognition grasps the substratum (*dharmin*); subsequently, mental cognition grasps its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*). If there is a difference in time, then, given that the latter grasps what has already been grasped by the former, it lacks validity (*aprāmāṇya*) with respect to the same object. However, if the objects are different, then mental cognition, proceeding toward something other than the domain of sensory cognition, presents the substratum independently; yet even in this case, there is no escape from the aforementioned defect.

To this we reply: First of all, in the first position, there is no refutation of the entity (*vastu*), because such a specific person (*puruṣaviśeṣa*) as the probandum (*sādhya*) is already established. Nor is there a refutation of the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*), because that particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*), being the very object of proof and possessing a nature that transcends the world, is designated as distinct from the sensory cognitions common to ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) for the purpose of demonstrating the specific means of its realization.

Nor does the treatise achieve its purpose through a mere inclusion under the term "sensory cognition" (indriyajñāna), as if it were like the specific excellence produced by elixirs (rasāyana) and the like resulting from internal purification; for this very reason, there is no mention of a distinction even in comparison with the specific excellence produced by collyrium and such means, because there is an absence of any excellence that transcends the nature of worldly experience.

For, depending on the purpose, it is indeed accepted that even those things which are generally subsumed under a single category may be specified according to their distinct types—just as feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), though both included within the aggregate of formations associated with consciousness (*saṃprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*), are treated separately; or as the afflicted mental cognition (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*), though included within conceptualization (*vikalpa*), is distinguished. Therefore, there is no fault in the position that the sensory cognition and the yogic cognition are not different. That very same [cognition] is "sensory cognition" in relation to its objective substratum (*dharmin*) and "yogic cognition" in relation to its specific property (*dharma*), just as the direct perception of a substratum itself is termed "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) when considered in relation to a negation.

Even on the view that there is a distinction [between perception and conceptualization], the objection based on the appearance of stability versus its opposite does not arise; for even sensory cognition, while grasping an object in its entirety, grasps it only as something whose form is fragmentary. Furthermore, the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) was previously difficult to obtain, but now it has been brought about by the mind, which has attained proficiency by relying on the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); this is the distinction.

But surely, since even the sense faculty at that time acquires an unsurpassed excellence, who can prevent its perception of distant or subtle objects, as in the case of an external yogi? For even in the case of ordinary people, such perception occurs to some slight degree due to the projection of certain karma. Furthermore, among existing moments, a dissimilarity—even if minute—must necessarily exist; otherwise, if there were similarity in every respect, it would follow that they are identical in essence (*tattva*). Therefore, since the goal is accomplished by sensory cognition itself, which is capable of discerning such subtle differences, the knowledge of a yogi is useless.

By this, the direct realization of suffering, selflessness, and so forth, is explained. Furthermore, since it is impossible for a sense faculty to exist without a human body, let it be that the knowledge of a yogi is not to be produced. That too is incorrect; for a discerning person engaged in worldly practice cannot abandon the path that relies upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) merely by resorting to the power of the eye brought about by mere possibility.

Alternatively, it may be that the accomplishment of such sensory power is precisely assisted by that practice; thus, even if sensory cognition is placed on an equal footing with the cognition of a yogi—which is unavoidable—there is no fault whatsoever in the sensory cognition. If it is argued that one of them is redundant, then which of these two, both of which possess the property of being brought about by their own causes, should fear the redundancy of its own operation and thereby cease to function, like seeds and so forth when they have reached their final moment?

If it is argued that one [of two cognitions] must be invalid (*aprāmāṇya*), then let it be that even among seeds and the like, one is not a cause. If it is asked, "Since all possess equal capacity, how can it be possible to designate any single one as the non-cause?", then [we reply]: why should one of the two cognitions—which possess the power of determination—be rendered invalid? If it is argued that, out of mutual dependence, neither should be valid, then it is the same for seeds and the like: let not even one possess causality.

The so-called "apprehension of what has already been apprehended" does not exist at all. If it is argued that this leads to a logical fault (*doṣa*), we say no; for that [fault] is accepted only when there is a difference in time. Indeed, "apprehending what has been apprehended" is said to occur when one grasps what was previously grasped, not when grasping what is currently being grasped. Just as one who performs an action already completed is not considered an agent (*akāraka*), whereas one who performs an action currently being performed is indeed an agent—just like a seed and so forth—it follows that this fault does not apply to the position that [the two cognitions] are simultaneous.

[329,1] If it is objected: "In that case too, does it not follow that there would be the manifestation of two forms? True. First of all, the form of the true cognition is co-spatial [with the object], for otherwise the consequence of its being an error would follow. Therefore, who is capable of determining by what manner those two forms—which are non-obstructive—manifest? As it has been said: "The range of the yogis is inconceivable" (PV III 532).

Thus, since there is no supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is no occasion for either [position]: "What is undesirable? or "What is not a fault? If it is argued that they occur at the same time, how is the fault of independence—previously stated regarding the lack of dependence on sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*)—to be avoided? To say that it will be avoided precisely by depending on the senses is no answer; for in that case, that [cognition] would also be nothing but sensory cognition itself, because it would conform to the operation of those senses. It would not be what is called "yogic cognition" at all.

[329,10] Therefore, it is better to accept only one [of these two positions]; thus, the position of their being distinct is not tenable. It is not so; for let there be no dependence on the sense organs. Just as vision functions to produce its own cognition by depending on the presence of a suitable object in a fit location according to its own capacity, so too will the mind-organ function. This is because non-contact with the object (*aprāpyakāritā*) is common to both, and because at that time, the existence of space (*ākāśa*) is also accepted as being possessed of an object.

However, the mental continuum of an ordinary person does not possess such power; therefore, the mind—unlike the eye and the ear—cannot produce cognition by means of such a spatial restriction upon encountering an object acting as a cooperative condition in a suitable location, and thus there is no over-extension of the principle.

In that state, however, who is capable of determining how far the proximity of the object extends even for the mind, as it does for the ears and eyes? Only this much is said: to whatever extent an auxiliary object capable of imparting its own form can be apprehended by it, to that extent it becomes the range of that [cognition] through a form that is distinct from that of ordinary people and is momentarily fleeting. This being so, the form of the object is produced by the object itself and not generated by mental cultivation; thus, there is no suspicion of non-correspondence.

[329,20] If it is argued that while the capacity of the eye and so forth is indeed observed in making very distant objects their range, the mind, however, does not transcend the senses to have all things as its object—this is not so, because of the possibility of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the like. If it is argued that even this is not accepted by some—that is incorrect, because it is improper to reject something merely on the basis of not having seen it. If it is argued that there is no means (*upāya*) [to achieve such knowledge]—even in the absence of a means, there is no other means than the mere non-perception [of one].

Therefore, the point of this objection is that if it were so, then even on the position that there is a distinction between the sensory cognition and the mental cognition of yogins, there would be no resolution. However, a resolution has indeed been shown in another way. This being the case, there is no fault even on the position that there is a difference in time, provided that [the mental cognition] is the first occurrence of the mental cognition, and its occurrence is by transcending the path of the senses; whereas sensory cognition, even if it lacks validity in comparison to that [mental cognition], does not cause distress—so enough with this elaboration.

Thus, in the case of the yogi’s cognition, because it pertains to the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), its appearance as an object is indeed produced by the object itself. Furthermore, through that cultivation, a certain superior power is imparted to his mental continuum—just as a special ointment is applied to the eye—by which he possesses a vision not shared by other people, as was stated previously. If, then, the yogi’s cognition is produced solely by the object, what is the status of the thorough knowledge of the past and the future? This is the result of failing to penetrate the context of the discussion.

For the introduction to the cultivation of the nature of things was made by way of the authority of the "omniscient one who has attained his purpose" (*upayuktasarvajña*), and not with reference to the position of the "omniscient one of all things" (*sarvasarvajña*). Therefore, even the non-perception of the past and the future does not constitute a contradiction, since the cessation of suffering is established by that much alone, and because it enables the introduction of unshakable teaching for others.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised against the knowledge of the yogin—having first set forth the realization [of reality] by means of cultivating the nature of all things that possess those attributes (the dharmas) through the excellence of meditating on the reality of momentariness and so forth in the *Kaṇikā*, thereby producing a cognition in that form—that objection is indeed to be disregarded, because it falls outside the scope of the arguments found in the *Vārttika*, the *Bhāṣya*, and other such works.

Otherwise, if it were intended that the cultivation of eternal suffering and so forth had been undertaken from the outset, and that this [cultivation] would result in omniscience regarding everything, then how could its refutation have been laboriously set forth in the *Vārttika*?

And why is satisfaction sought in the *Bhāṣya* with the words, "It is not possible for us to know [it]," and so forth? If, however, upon reaching that state, one whose internal organ is free from obscuration—due to an excellence of compassion and a dedication to the prayer for the welfare of others in all its aspects—should attain a particular means such that, while practicing it, there arises a very clear cognition directed toward every object down to each atom, corresponding to each individual state according to its place and time; [then omniscience would be possible].
In that case, there is no lack of correspondence caused by a deviation from the object, nor is there a lack of objective support (*nirālambanatva*), because it is the objects themselves that appear.

[330,19] Now, if the determination of the objective support is established through both [causal] origination and similarity of form, [and if it is asked: "How can something belonging to a different time be the apprehended object?"—the wise know its status as the apprehended object.

Because of the statement, "Those who know the reasoning [declare] that causality alone is capable of imparting a form to the cognition" (PV II 247), similarity [to the object] is thus rendered useless; how, then, can the charge of being without an objective basis (*anālambanatva*) be avoided?

That is incorrect. Indeed, that definition—given in reference to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)—is intended to negate the apprehension of an external object by a cognition that arises simultaneously with it and is not assisted by it, as the context requires. In reality, however, whatever appears in a cognition is said to be its objective support (*ālambana*). As stated in the commentary on the first chapter: "In sensory perception, it is the external object; elsewhere, it is one's own form (*svākāra*); for the apprehension or non-apprehension of perception depends upon what appears."

In this context, the "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*) of an external object is merely the arising of its form (*tadākāra*). For it is simply from the experience of the emergence of a form that appears as if external and distinct that the thought "this has been seen" arises. Indeed, at the time of its conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), no further production is required, because that [production] is determined later either through the attainment of a result or through the absence of both [result and non-result]. And that arising of its form occurs from the object in the case of sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*); in the case of error (*bhrama*), from a distortion; and in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

In that regard, with respect to external objects, there is correspondence when [cognition] is produced by an object, while elsewhere there is error; however, with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is a rule of correspondence everywhere. Therefore, since correspondence with the intended object does not occur in a cognition without its being produced from that [object], nor is there a resemblance to it, one seeks its production from that [object]. For this very reason, having that form (*tadākāratā*) alone is the criterion of validity (*prāmāṇya*); and since both similarity (*sārūpya*) and production from that [object] constitute the definition of the cognizable, the two are not contradictory.

However, in cases where—by the power of a specific cultivation and through the sovereign influence of a deity—there arises a cognition possessing the form of an object that is inseparable from the true nature of that object, as if in a true dream, there is nothing [to be gained] by its production. As the *Vārttika* states:
"Thus, for those of impure intellect, this reflection on the grasped and the grasper [is taught] regarding form and so forth, and the mind; but the state of the yogins is inconceivable. (PV III 532)

Thus, it is said. Therefore, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the persistence of the object of cognition occurs through both similarity and arising with respect to external things; for a yogin, however, it occurs through similarity alone. As for its own nature, the principle is that it occurs through mere capacity (*yogyatā*) alone. If, then, there were a manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-sphuraṇa*) of future and past entities, they would necessarily be present.

[331,16] Now, if it is argued that because the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is not present, cognition itself takes on its form and is therefore necessarily without an objective support (*nirālambana*), that too is not the case. For even when an object is not present, if cognition follows its location and time through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), how could it be without an objective support? This is because, through a specific mode of manifestation, there arises a conceptualization of temporal difference; and since there is a necessity regarding the performance of actions corresponding to that [object], one attains it. As the *Bhāṣya* states: "Just as it was seen as connected with a time such as autumn, so for it there is no sublation" (PVA II 615).

Or rather, having intentionally entered meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*) for the sake of perceiving the nature of objects that possess temporal distinctions, there arises upon emergence from that absorption a determination of those temporal distinctions. As it has been said:
"Whatever he wishes to understand..."

And so forth. However, even effortless (*anābhoga*) cognition is not contradictory [to this] in its gradual sequence. Furthermore, because cognition alone manifests in reality (*tattvataḥ*), there is no consequence of its being present, just as in the theory of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*), where it is the very nature of the object that manifests. And although even in the case of the present, it is only the form of the cognition that manifests, nevertheless, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) therein occurs precisely as "present. The same should be understood regarding the distinctions of distance, proximity, and so on.

In that regard, validity exists when there is a necessary correspondence with the attainment of what was determined; otherwise, there is error, as in the case of a beloved woman in a dream and the like. Furthermore, there is no need for consideration regarding the conceptual construction of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice as a means to attain heaven through intuition (*pratibhā*), because there is simply no manifestation of the future object in its clear form. Nor, in such cases, is there any certainty of a rule regarding attainment for a discerning person engaged in worldly activity.

If it is asked, "Even when the matter is under discussion, what is the certainty?"—well, whose certainty is being considered here: that of the person in question, or someone else? If it is that of the former, then just as for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), once the knowledge of the means of proof has completely eliminated the suspicion of error through repeated practice, why should the appearance of future, past, and so forth, not likewise occur for a yogin through extreme cultivation? If, on the other hand, it is the certainty of someone else, then this follows: as long as another person's realization of its validity has not occurred, it is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As long as something is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so long there can be no non-erroneous cognition of the validity of anything else; thus, nothing at all would be a valid means of knowledge. Therefore, it is not the case that [the opponent] is rendered helpless by mere verbal assertion. Consequently, since the specific distinction of the cultivation [of meditation] accompanied by special methods does not manifest immediately, doubt arises only regarding the establishment of such [a state], but once it is established, it cannot be undermined by defects such as being without a basis (*nirālambanatva*).

Furthermore, having raised the concern that even if an external object is not apprehended by conceptualization, it might nevertheless appear clearly as an object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), [the opponent] says: "That which is apprehended by inference and that which is determined—both are exclusions of others (*anyanivṛtti*) and not real entities (*vastu*), because if they were to penetrate the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression would be impossible. This too is incoherent.

For instance, whether in one way or another, if worldly practice is permeated by the scent of Buddhist tenets—just like the cultivation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a woman’s form—the production of subsequent moments that are pure and desirable, even from a momentary form, is ultimately unavoidable. If, however, you should attempt to establish that such a state of exclusion (*apoha*) does not perceive the conceptualization of a woman and so forth because it rests solely upon the bed of momentary conceptualizations, we shall accept it exactly as you say. Furthermore, the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*) is not merely the negation of a non-entity;
for even in Dharmottara’s view, the established position is that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of determination.

[332,21] Is it not the case that the form of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) is "fire is perceived by me"? And therein, the manifestation of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—this is a rash claim, because conceptualization and conceptual determination have the same object. True; however, it is not said that the particular characteristic is determined merely because it manifests therein. If there is no manifestation, then since there is no cognition, how can there be a determination? Even if there is manifestation, that is merely a presentation (*pratibhāsa*); how then can it be a determination? Furthermore, presentation and determination do not have the same object either.

For *pratibhāsa* (manifestation) is direct flashing forth; even when there is no flashing forth, it is the making of something an object of activity through the power of delineating a single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). According to the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*), this is *adhyavasāya* (determination). Therefore, that which is suitable for execution is the *adhyavaseya* (the determined object), and it is precisely that which has entered into conformity with the form being manifested. And that [determined object] is, in some cases, merely superimposed (*āropita*), while in other cases, it is the nature of a real entity (*vasturūpa*).

But as for the subject at hand, since it accepts the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must be a real entity (*vasturūpa*). How then can it be said that "mere exclusion (*nivṛtti-mātra*), which is a non-entity (*avastu*), is what is determined"? Let us set aside this persistent insistence for now. Furthermore, in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is the appearance of an excluded form, not of mere exclusion itself, provided one follows the dictates of experience; otherwise, anything whatsoever—such as a *rākṣasa*—might appear at all times.

Furthermore, through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is a transformation into the determined aspect (*adhyavasitākāra*) which is uncontradicted; in that case, there is objectlessness (*nirālambanatva*) with respect to the merely superimposed object of determination. However, when it exists, that very [object] is the objective support (*ālambana*), as has just been stated.

As for what you said—that the status of an object as an objective support (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness is pervaded by its dependence upon the sense faculty, and that this [dependence], being excluded from the subject by the perception of its own opposite, also excludes the object's status as an objective support—this is a great display of cleverness to clarify the "perception of the opposite of the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*) without first establishing, through valid cognition, the relationship of pervasion (*vyāpyavyāpaka-bhāva*) between the status of being an objective support and the dependence upon the sense faculty.

If it is argued that [the object exists] because it is seen [in perception], then let us simply abide by the principle of seeing and not seeing; what is the use of this obsession with adducing such a formal proof? Therefore, we see no contradiction if an entity were to assume the status of being an objective support (*ālambana*) even without depending on a sense faculty. Now, as for what was said here: "Indeed, a specific kind of fuel is the cause of smoke; it does not produce smoke even by means of thousands of preparations if fire is absent."

Otherwise, if it were produced by that [object] alone, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the abolition of inference based on the cause of all effects. Therefore, cognition also possesses the property of arising from an object that is dependent upon the sense faculties.

If it is argued: "Since its existence is not present even when all other causes are proximate, provided there is an absence of the operation of the sense faculties, it is established that [the cognition] is dependent upon them; therefore, how can an object that is independent of the sense faculties serve as an objective support (*ālambana*) for its own cognition?"—this too has been refuted by the possibility of knowing another's mind (*paracittajñāna*). Furthermore, those other than the Cārvākas and Mīmāṃsakas accept the existence of those who know the minds of others. Even for the Cārvākas and others, there is no other recourse than to admit this, since they themselves are subject to doubt.

And in the case of doubt, it is impossible for there to be an absolute exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). [Objection: But surely, because the effect that is cognition is necessarily dependent upon the sense faculty, there can be no doubt regarding anything else, just as smoke is dependent upon fire.

If such is the case—that the causal complex required for visual cognition to depend upon sight does not fall short by even a fraction when it comes to the specific movement of footless beings like snakes that depends upon their feet—then why was the example of smoke not capable of negating the movement of those very snakes? Or else, how is it that for some, the task of neutralizing poison and so forth—which involves the activity of hands and other limbs and is accomplished through a succession of forceful incantations—is achieved through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) alone, rather than by another means? Furthermore, smoke is never observed to arise from fuel independently of fire, such that one might suspect the same here as well.

Therefore, external entities, insofar as they are perceived through the relationship of cause and effect, possess a fixed mode of occurrence; however, the manifestation of the mental continuum is indeed diverse due to the power of the formative forces of various karmas. Consequently, it is impossible to restrict the effect based on that [continuum], such that whatever is required in one case must be required in another.

How, then, can there be the total absence of the cognition of another's mind and so forth? Furthermore, if the sense organ does not produce cognition independently—just as fire does not exist without smoke—then even with respect to its own object, [the cognition] would be utterly deficient in cases such as hearing a loud proclamation or seeing something at a distance. For instance, as long as the means for perceiving smoke and so forth—the fire, fuel, and so on—is not perceived within a certain range, it is incapable of extending beyond that range.

In this way, up until the point where it has produced the perception of objects, sense faculties, and so forth within our own location, how could it produce that same perception for vultures and others when they have transcended that location? Or, even if it were to produce it, the causal complex based on the mental continuum would not be capable of the degree of burning required for fuel, nor would cognition be capable of the degree of smoke.

Therefore, why should it not be possible for something to arise from some particular cause even when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary conditions, just as when there is excessive intervention? If it is argued that this distinction is produced by the genus (*jāti*) and not based on the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*), we say no; for the genus itself has the nature of bringing about diverse forms precisely through the sovereign influence of diverse karma, and since karma is not other than the mind, the claim that [the distinction] does not depend on the mind is not avoided.

Now, since the sense faculty functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritā*), it is said that the entire causal complex for the production of consciousness occupies a common location. Nevertheless, why does it sometimes reach as far as a distant place—such as the contact with the rays of light from the eye—and sometimes rest at a nearby point? What can be said here other than the sovereign power of karma (*karmādhipatya*)? Therefore, the capacity of the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*), which is the substratum of that [faculty], is indeed manifold.

For even externally, this is not possible. Otherwise, between two lamps situated in similar locations, one might have a mass of rays extending far away while the other’s would move only nearby. If it is argued that this could happen through the power of a mantra, and that such a mantra also induces dullness in the sight of a reptile, then that is indeed the power of the mental continuum itself. Even in the case of a mantra, its efficacy is produced solely by the greatness of the person.

As established in the *Vārttika*, even though mantras are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), they do not possess efficacy independently of persons; therefore, it follows that the person alone, by means of mantras and other instruments, establishes the capacity of external objects. Given this, what is impossible in the present case? Just as the status of an object as a supporting basis (*ālambana*) is observed to depend on the eye and is thus held to be restricted to it, so too is it observed to depend on light; consequently, owls and the like would not see in the dark.

If it is argued that there is no fault because it is observed to be so, then you are defeated precisely by the fact that it is observed to be so. For instance, although the eye and light are equal in their requirement of auxiliary means for accomplishment, we observe the transcendence of one [the eye] due to the inconceivable power of the mind; this observation casts suspicion upon the other as well. However, such a thing cannot be possible if it were never observed. Now, if it is said that even those effects which possess the common property of being cognitions (*jñānatva*) belong to different classes (*jāti*) and therefore do not arise without depending on a difference in the causal complex (*sādhanasāmagrī*); [we reply:]...

But by what means have you been deceived into thinking that even this extraordinary knowledge under discussion shares the same genus (*ekajāti*) with the knowledge of ordinary persons? If you argue that there is no difference in genus precisely because that [extraordinary knowledge] does not exist at all, then—since there would be no difference in genus due to its non-existence—the possibility of a restriction based on the sense faculties would follow; thus, there is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*).

Therefore, for people like us, who are produced by common karma, the dependence on the sense faculties with respect to the diversity of experience is a pervader of being an objective support (*ālambanatva*); yet, even though it is a pervader, it cannot—by its own cessation—cause the cessation of mere experience, because the establishment of pervasion occurs only with reference to specific [conditions].

Now, if it is claimed that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by unifying mere experience (*anubhavamātra*), then, because there is no subverting evidence for the contrary, pervasion itself is not proven. Furthermore, the basis for the necessity of cause and effect is destroyed, since it is impossible for such a basis to be common to smoke and other such phenomena; for mere experience—arising from a mental continuum possessing inconceivable power due to the impressions of diverse karmas—is not uniform. Moreover, if one relies on a specific [instance], the pervasion does not encompass all cases; thus, that very same fault remains, namely, what is called "possessing particularity" (*viśeṣavattva*).

Furthermore, as he has said: since it is observed that the capacity to produce clear cognition belongs to a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that does not depend on an object precisely because its object is unreal—as in the case of one afflicted by passion and so forth—it follows that even a cultivation whose object is real is capable of producing such cognition independently of it; thus, it is impossible to understand that an external object functions as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

In this regard, what is this "independence from an object"? Is it (1) not having an object as its domain, or (2) not appearing directly as an object, or (3) not having an object as its cause, or (4) deviating from an object? These are the possible positions. Regarding the first position, it is contradictory to claim that [cognition] has a real object while simultaneously being non-objective; for, just like the inference arising from it, it too has that object as its domain insofar as it depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

However, with respect to the appearance (*pratibhāsa*), let it not be that the object of that [appearance] is the external thing, for it is precisely the cognition produced by that [thing] which is desired as its object; thus, the second position is also untenable. The third is impossible, because even that [cognition], by way of the inference arising from itself, has as its effect an object that is real (*bhūtārtha*); therefore, since deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is established for this reason as well, the fourth is not tenable. Consequently, since there is a rule of correspondence (*saṃvāda-niyama*) for the clear cognition produced by that [object], how could the status of the object as the objective support (*ālambanatva*) be impossible to ascertain? Therefore, the objection is sound according to the ancient method, and the refutation has already been stated.

Furthermore, his effort to refute past and future objects by asserting that only those very objective moments existing at the present time can logically be grasped by him—and not those prior to them—is already refuted above. However, regarding the position of the Omniscient One under discussion, the proof of the thesis is established simply by this much: that as many things as produce a cognition and come within the range of one's own knowledge, they are experienced precisely in the form of momentariness, suffering, and selflessness.

Regarding what has been experienced and what has passed, there is recollection; regarding what is yet to come, there is merely a conceptual possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). If it is asked: "If it is indeed recollection regarding the past, how can there be a clear manifestation of the aspects of 'origination' (*samudaya*)?"—the five aggregates themselves are the origination in relation to what follows. In that regard, this very clear manifestation of the aspect of origination is a certain mode of radiance (*sphuraṇarīti*), which, when those [aggregates] have become present, serves as the cause for the immediate production of corresponding conceptualizations, practical applications, and so forth, based on a subsequent reference; by means of this, one becomes distinguished from an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), just as before.

And likewise, regarding past [objects], there arises a very clear recollection. However, the realization of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) occurs by means of its own nature alone, independent of anything else, through momentary and other such aspects. If it is argued: "Since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) cannot arise simultaneously, when there is the determination of the aspects of suffering, there can be no [determination] of the aspects of the Origin (*samudaya*); and subsequently, that determination would be without an object," [we reply: This is true; yet even for each individual Truth, the conceptualization of its four aspects does not occur at one and the same time. And there is no defect whatsoever in this.

For it is precisely a specific mode of apprehension (*grahaṇarīti*), in which all aspects have become manifest, that constitutes direct perception (*sākṣātkāraṇa*). This is because the manifestation of the intended conceptual sequence occurs from seeds interspersed with conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Just as for a person seeing a blue lotus characterized by qualities such as being moving and blooming, there is no obstruction to the direct perception of all its aspects through a conceptual process, so too should it be inferred in the case of [the yogic] flow. Furthermore, moments that are not mutually simultaneous are directly perceived by your very successive experiences.

Furthermore, conceptual constructions proceed according to one's intention, taking the form of a synthesis with what has been previously grasped. And it should be understood that the state of omniscience is established through experience alone. In this same way, regarding the truths of cessation and the path as well, everything should be inferred based on their being known through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Furthermore, as for the objection that seeing all things would follow from seeing even a few—on the grounds that all things are connected to one another in some way, either directly or through a causal chain—that has already been answered by our simply not accepting such a premise. However, if there were a conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) whose object is the totality of all things, mediated by such connections and functioning as a qualifier, we see no fault provided that it occurs at a stage where the recollection of a succession of births is possible.

Just as for one who has practiced [meditation], upon seeing fire and so forth, there immediately arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "this is the effect of fuel" and "this is the cause of the fire," so too may there be clarity (*vaiśadya*) for those things grasped by conceptualization when meditation reaches its peak. However, we do not maintain that the perception of one thing results from the mere relationship [of concomitance] with the perception of another. Or, let there be no clarity at all; for omniscience is fulfilled simply through the conceptualization of all objects, provided it is consistent, even while remaining in that state.

Alternatively, [non-conceptual cognition] has as its object only its own objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), yet it is the cause for the determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) of an object qualified by all things. Therefore, although non-conceptual, it possesses an operation that follows upon such determination and thus has all things as its domain. As it is said:
"Those of great intelligence determine all aspects from perception alone" (PV II 107).

Anticipating this objection, he says: "From where does this power of an experience that relies upon only a few objects derive, such that there is a determination of all things? If it is argued that it is "due to the removal of the veil of passion and so forth," then one would see objects exactly as they are; however, it is not logical for him to possess, on that basis, the skill to produce a determination of all things without exception. For while impurities are easily capable of obscuring reality, they do not constitute an obstacle to the production of conceptual discourse.

In this regard, the inquiry is as follows: when an object is being perceived, is it simply that no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is observed, or is it that such construction is produced by the afflictions (*kleśa*)? Neither of these two cases exists. For nowhere is there a conceptualization of every aspect in the manner of direct experience; nor can the absence of such conceptualization occur without the intervention of the afflictions. Indeed, when an object is seen as pleasant—even though it possesses faults—the non-conceptualization of those faults is then said to have passion (*rāga*) as its cause.

Furthermore, when there is no conceptualization of qualities even toward an unpleasant object that possesses them, that is aversion (*dveṣa*). However, in the absence of practice, the non-conceptualization of all real forms is produced solely by delusion (*moha*). Nor is this an obscuration like that of a blanket or similar objects; rather, it functions by instilling a defect in the mental continuum. Therefore, to the extent that delusion and the rest are overcome, to that same extent, through effort and the removal of defects, when cognitions possess determinate engagement (*vyavasāya*) with respect to those aspects, then—in the end—if they were to occur with respect to all aspects and all things, there would be no contradiction whatsoever.

Because memory is possible even for things previously seen or remembered through a succession of mental acuity, and because a more intense impression of memory is deposited when those things are being perceived, and because birth is without beginning or end, and because a single type of certainty has the nature of determining all things of that same class, there is no fault caused by the non-arising of conceptualizations regarding all objects.

And as for what was said: "That [cognition] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because, while possessing extreme clarity, it is produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); for whatever cognition is produced by meditative cultivation and possesses extreme clarity is not a means of valid cognition, just like the clear cognition of an object cultivated through inference. In that regard, since it has been demonstrated that there is no meditative cultivation at all after one has inferred fire, the example is non-existent.

And as for this poetic flourish of his: "There is here a person whose body and throat are parched by the intense accumulation of cold, and who is engaged in the practice of meditating on fire"—if, in that case, the emergence of the meditation occurs through the obsession of his own mind due to the affliction of indigestion, then what is the talk of inference? For inference is sought as that which possesses the capacity for effective action.

If one is likewise incapable while in that state, what is the use of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? Or rather, let there simply be the manifestation of clarity once again; where then is there room for inference? For it is not possible that a lover would fail to apply himself to cultivation as long as he does not infer his beloved. Therefore, let the example be merely the cognition of fire produced by cultivation in one suffering from indigestion. That too has been answered by the example of the beloved, adorned by its own poetic metaphor.

Furthermore, it is not a logical principle that because one cognition arising from meditative cultivation is non-authoritative due to its being deceptive, another cognition—even one that is consistent—must also be non-authoritative; for otherwise, it would follow that every cognition produced by the sense faculties would be non-authoritative, like the optical illusion of hair-nets and the like.

Furthermore, regarding that which was elaborated to establish the rule of correspondence between the cause—characterized by the excellence of cultivation—and its two effects, namely the example and the illustrated case: even there, do you not perceive that the eye itself is the common cause for both the vision of two moons and the vision of one moon? If you argue that the distinction between the two eyes is caused by the impairment or non-impairment of the cataract (*timira*), then why is there no such distinction between the two types of cultivation based on their having real or unreal objects? Is it not simply some kind of modification produced by the cataract in the eye?

If it is argued that there is some difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the cognition—whether due to the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) or the clarity thereof—even though the object remains the same, we say no. Since a more powerful difference in capacity (*śaktibheda*) can be established on the basis of the causes being either concordant or otherwise, what is the use of anything else? For example, as in the case of food that is either wholesome or otherwise, or of the visual perceptions of color and taste; or as in the case of two cognitions of a probandum arising from a valid reason and a fallacious reason, or the resulting activities induced by them. Furthermore, the mere absence of a physical change in the eye is not itself a defect, even if a change is produced by the application of ointment (*añjana*).

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of establishing faults [in the cognition]. Rather, it is by virtue of being the cause of error; thus, even in that case, the distinction is established solely by way of capacity (*śakti*). Therefore, in this manner, it is only vividness (*sphuṭābhatva*) that is proven through the intensity of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*), not validity (*prāmāṇya*), since [otherwise] there would be room for faults such as the non-establishment of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*). Validity, however, arises from correspondence (*saṃvāda*) due to having a real object (*bhūtārthatva*), and its status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) arises from being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*); by this much alone, one should understand that the entire method corrupted by ignorance (*avidyāduṣṭanaya*) is refuted.

For the author of the *Nyāyaprakīrṇaka* as well, the apprehension of non-existent objects has already been refuted precisely by the proofs for momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth. Furthermore, regarding what he said concerning the conceptual nature (*vikalpatā*) of inference—that everything presented by conceptual constructions is unreal because it is associated with words—[that too is refuted].

And while that [unreality] is being cultivated, once the conceptual construction of yours has been rendered clear through cultivation, the state of being a conceptualizer—which is caused by the apprehension of an object associated with words—is eliminated. And upon its elimination, everything associated with all words regarding the apprehended object ceases. Consequently, it follows that even the non-conceptual cognition of the yogin would be without an object.

In this regard, what is this so-called "objectlessness"? Is it the absence of form (*anākāratā*) due to the disappearance of the apprehended aspect (*grāhyākāra*), or is it having another form (*anyākāratā*), or is it that even while possessing that form, it is not in contact with the nature of that object? First of all, the first position is impossible, because it is untenable for cognition to be devoid of form; for we observe that through meditation on an object such as a beloved woman, it is precisely that form which becomes vivid. For this very reason, the second position is also not tenable.

As for what he himself says—that even for one afflicted by grief whose sensory faculties have ceased their activity, there would follow the appearance of the father and so forth through the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the son—this is merely confused prattle, introduced under the premise that when this [object] is cultivated in conjunction with another, the other form does not clearly appear. For by this [argument], the very manifestation of clarity in every respect is precluded, since cultivation is impossible without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

And since conceptual construction occurs without the association with words, where would its manifestation be evident? Furthermore, for one who argues that the appearance of a father and so forth follows from the mental cultivation of a son, the appearance of the son itself must indeed be admitted; otherwise, he would have to assert that even from the cultivation of a non-son, the appearance of a son would follow. And a mere undesirable consequence is not sufficient to subvert what is observed.

And likewise, Kaṇikā himself demonstrated the clarity of the form of his beloved to the lover through specific words, gestures, and poetic compositions. How else could he have given meaning to such statements as "this very thing, when endowed with cultivation, becomes clear"? Therefore, since the manifestation of one thing does not occur through the cultivation of another, it is correct to establish their difference from the perspective of the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*).

There is no mutual [identity] between the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and that which is intended as the object, because the two are superimposed as one. For even the manifestation of what is intended as external is, in the end, merely the emergence of a clear moment that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of conceptual construction. It is by this much alone that the conventional usage occurs, namely, "that object was directly perceived by him. It has already been largely considered that when an entity exists, the cognition of its form is non-contradictory, whereas it is contradictory when the entity does not exist.

For this very reason, the third alternative as well has been refuted; for it is impossible to define any contact with the nature of a real object by means of cognition other than through correspondence and direct realization. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the cultivation of the son" (*tanayabhāvanā*), what is the meaning of "cultivation of the son"? If you say it is the repeated placing of the son in the mind, even the meaning of "placing in the mind" is nothing other than the conceptualization of its form.

If it is argued that, in this case, what he prattles is that when momentariness is cultivated or superimposed, it is indeed real momentariness that appears in the cognition of the yogi—this is not so; for since truth and untruth are distinct and lack identity, if there were an appearance of the true even while cultivating the untrue, then by the mere similarity of the word "son," it would follow that upon practicing the meditation on the true son, there would likewise appear the essential nature of some other distinct entity called "son" who is non-different from him due to that verbal commonality.

Therefore, the claim that even non-conceptual [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge because it arises from the practice of an unreal object despite being consistent with reality—that too is refuted, since there is no such thing as the cultivation of a superimposed [object].

For just as there is the habitual conceptualization "son, son," so too, if there were the conceptualization "superimposed momentariness, superimposed momentariness," then there would be cultivation of a superimposed momentariness; but it is not so. Rather, [the thought is] "conditioned phenomena are momentary. Therefore, just like the case of a real son, actual momentariness itself is cultivated. Or else, another mode must be stated for the cultivation of a real son.

Since a conceptual cognition of a moment does not touch the momentary particular (svalakṣaṇa), how can that conceptualization or its cultivation [be considered valid]? This is equally true for the conceptualization of a son as well. Furthermore, the determination of it being a conceptualization of that [object] based on the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*) is exactly the same. For even in the conceptualization of a son, nothing other than the superimposed [conceptual image] appears.

Thus, one who desires the clear manifestation of a real son despite the appearance of a conceptual image associated with the superimposed word, while rejecting the subject at hand, is what else but being swallowed by the great demon of delusion?

And this similarity to the cultivation of reality has been stated merely on account of its being external, in relation to that which is superimposed and flashing forth through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, from the perspective of actual externality, the cultivation of a son by one afflicted with grief is indeed a cultivation of the non-existent. For this very reason, that [cultivation] is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because at that time, due to the absence of such a son, it flashes forth in the form of a son that is non-existent. But the cultivation of momentariness, since all phenomena always have that as their nature, has an existent object; therefore, the clarity produced by it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory.

Now, it may be thought that because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has a non-real object as its domain, even when one contemplates a son as a son, the clarity (*vaiśadya*) attained remains distinct [from the reality]; this is not our view—such is the thought held in the heart. Let that too simply perish within the heart. For this *Yoginirṇaya* has been commenced, and there is no harm to it regardless of either position.

Since even for Apoha, when purified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is observed that clarity belongs only to the determined object (*adhyavaseya*); what can be done about this? If it is asked, "Since there is no manifestation of a real entity (*vastu-nirbhāsa*) in inference, how can there be purification by a means of valid cognition in relation to that?", this is a different topic altogether.

Furthermore, this is so: moreover, *abhyāsa* (repeated practice) is the repeated placement of the object to be cultivated within the mind. And that [practice], when practiced with devotion, for a long time, continuously, through celibacy and austerity, is held to be the means for producing the clarity of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) whose form was previously indistinct, once it has reached the stage of direct perception. However, that [practice] cannot be established by one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness and selflessness (*kṣaṇikanairātmyavādin*). For instance, whatever kind of conceptual cognition arises grasping the object to be cultivated, exactly that same kind ceases without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*).

And when that [preceding cognition] has ceased, a condition arising again is produced as something entirely new (*apūrva*) of exactly the same kind.
