Therefore, by this reasoning, since there is no difference in the production of something new even over a thousand eons, a formative impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that—namely, "cultivation" (*abhyāsa*)—does not arise. By this, the production of a distinguished consciousness as "cultivation" is explained. For how could a preceding consciousness, having ceased without leaving any trace (*niranvaya*), produce a subsequent and distinct state that is superior? In every way, it is only a persisting form (*rūpa*) that can be refined by conditions occurring in succession.

This is consistent. For there is no reason for a certain restriction other than the touch of a Caṇḍadevatā that dictates that another cognition exactly like the first—which apprehended an object and ceased without leaving a trace—must arise. If it is argued that this is due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), then surely momentariness is contradicted by permanence, not by the arising of something dissimilar.

For if that preceding [moment], which is characterized by cessation without a causal link (*niranvayanirodhin*), were to produce a subsequent moment that is exactly similar to itself, then what harm would there be if it were to produce a subsequent moment infused with a slight distinction due to even a minute difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? Indeed, there is no hostility toward the momentariness of entities on our part as there is on yours; moreover, in this case too, there exists a slight difference in the causal complex.

For instance, when one applies oneself to meditative cultivation with the desire to exhaust the suffering of saṃsāra, based on the mere restatement that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary," there arises a specific resolve (*saṃkalpa*). That resolve, moreover, produces a specific result that exceeds [the cause] by even an atom's measure, until the final fruit is attained through a gradual sequence of intensification, just like a seed and so forth. However, if they were to remain in an intermediate state due to distraction and the like, there would be only a degree of weakness and so on. As the *Bhāṣya* states:
"When the formative force (*saṃskāra*) is powerful, distraction is removed."

"If distraction is powerful, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would be turned away [from its object]. (PVA II 500). If, then, destruction occurs without any continuity (*niranvayavināśa*), how could the second [moment] acquire a specific quality, given that the previous specific quality cannot be transmitted [to it]? In that case, even in another causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there ought to be such a specific quality, because this [previous quality] does not transmit itself there. Therefore, just as that specific quality arose by the power of the cause even though it was non-existent, so too has this [second moment]. If it is argued that "this is therefore equal to that," we say no; for it is impossible to prevent a specific effect from arising from a specific cause.

For instance, the first particularity arises devoid of such a particularity, whereas this one arises accompanied by such a particularity; how then could they be the same? Furthermore, the principle of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) cannot withstand scrutiny. For regarding that portion which has been transferred from the cause, there is no operation of another cause; and that very operation itself was previously non-existent. Thus, when a factor ceases, it does not persist, and what persists cannot cease.

How, then, can cessation (*nirodha*) and arising (*janman*) be accompanied by a continuum (*sānvaya*)? If it is argued that this is because they occur together with it, then it would follow that even space (*ākāśa*) could be conceived as having a continuum. This is because the meaning of "together" (*saha*) does not exist for something produced merely by persisting through both times [past and future]. Furthermore, that [persistence] is not denied in the interval between the destruction of a jar and the formation of its shards. As for the rest, it is merely a proclamation of one's own philosophical system that stands in opposition to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); so what is the use of it? Moreover, since the Self remains as it is like the word "Hari," the application of the aforementioned excellence [of agency] is impossible; this has been chewed over many times, so let it rest for now.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that practice is undertaken to establish the mind in one-pointedness and to abandon distraction, yet for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*), there is no such thing as a distracted mind because everything is one-pointed by virtue of being restricted to each respective object—that too is incoherent. For it is established by experience that for some, the mind brings a reality (*tattva*) into presence; for others, the opposite occurs; and for another, it is merely a conceptual reflection upon an effect and so forth.

In this context, every state of mind that is turned away from the reality of selflessness and so forth is called "distracted. But is it not sufficient to say that, according to the sequence already stated, a mind fixed solely on reality is "concentrated"? Why must one necessarily seek for a single [mind] alone to possess the capacity to range over various objects?

Nevertheless, prior to the time of the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkriyā*), because the apprehension of a single form as "I" is possible, that [notion of self] is also conventional (*vyāvahārika*). Even so, since the destruction of one's own defects is destined to occur, the engagement in the practice of the path remains unimpeded; for the conceptualization of what is to be attained is the motivator in all cases.

If that is so, even when there is a departure from the actual state of things (*vastutathābhāva*), what prevents one from engaging in activity? If it is argued that activity occurs because momentariness and so forth have been ascertained by such an inference, [we reply: this is not so, because the ascertainment has not yet become second nature (*sātmībhāva*). For the mind, still dominated by the latencies of beginningless ignorance, continues to engage in conventional behavior that is inconsistent with that ascertainment. It is for this very reason that, even when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has been attained, the dependence upon the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is stated; this should be investigated in the *Vārttika*.
Therefore, prior to the attainment of that fruit, practice is accomplished through ignorance alone; and from such practice, one becomes perfected as omniscient.

Furthermore, the refutation of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* from the perspective of the Yogācāra position is irrelevant, because that work proceeds with its proof only after having accepted external objects (*bahir-artha*). Even in that case, the sublation (*bādha*) introduced under the view that everyone is omniscient is already refuted simply by the fact that such a view is not accepted. Moreover, that is not a genuine sublation at all, since it merely establishes a state of doubt.

For instance, as for what was stated to refute the status of past and future objects—the claim that "there is no aspect whatsoever belonging to the non-existent"—this is indeed true for now. Consequently, it is also true that such objects are not apprehended by the cognition produced from them. However, it has been shown that even if they were otherwise [i.e., existent], their possibility cannot be denied, as in the case of veridical dreams and the like. Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no aspect whatsoever for the past and the future at another time simply because there is none now; if that were so, their very status as past and future would not exist, just like the mane of a horse. Moreover, the points regarding non-erroneousness and non-contradiction have already been considered above.

As for what was further stated—that non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*) is not tenable even in your own system, because you intend non-contradiction to consist either in the cognition's being a revealer of an object to be attained, or its indicating the object that is the focus of purposeful action, or the accomplishment of the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) as it appears—this is impossible in the case of cognitions of past objects and the like; nor is it even possible for a cognition of a present object under the view of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). That too is merely the outburst of envy, for it is devoid of logical justification.

If it is argued that [the term "existent"] is applied to the future and the past because of a temporal interval, then this same consequence would apply to spatial separation as well; thus, even in a location suitable for activity, the indicator would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*). If you say, "That [object] at least exists [in its own time]," but another thing—whether future or past—does not exist at that time, we reply: it is the same for something existing in that location, which does not exist [at that time]. Even causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is the same in the presence of that location as it is in the presence of that time; there is no distinction whatsoever.

Even though the present moment is momentary, there is no impairment of its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to conventional reality, because the capacity for the superimposition of unity exists; for it is from that perspective that correspondence is established.

Furthermore, as for the refutation undertaken by the followers of Kumārila—who, having introduced the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) regarding an omniscient being, proposed the alternatives that his cause must be either sensory cognition, mental cognition, or born from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābalaja*), and further argued that even if born from the power of cultivation, it must be either visual or mental—it serves merely to expose the weakness of their own supposition, rather than resulting in the certainty of his non-existence, as was discussed in the investigation concerning the dependence on the senses and the nature of the objective support (*ālambana*).

Nor is the non-perception of a cause the result of uncertainty; for that very reason, even regarding the objects of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), it is impossible to deny the power of that which arises from the force of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Consequently, the inference of the author of the *Kāśikā*—that yogis lack direct perceptual cognition of merit and demerit because of the absence of sense-organ contact, just like ourselves—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it is impossible to establish with certainty its exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣa*).

Furthermore, what is called "knowledge of dharma and adharma" is simply the thorough knowledge of the connection between actions and their fruits. And that is difficult to prevent when the recollection of past births (*jātismaratva*) is possible. Therefore, since such thorough knowledge is possible, once cultivation (*bhāvanā*) reaches its perfection, why would it not be logical that a perception—capable of instantly generating the conceptual construction that "this very gold and so forth, when employed in this way, is the means for achieving that"—should arise? One need only consider the case of the recollection of past births.

In this regard, since mere non-perception is not a valid means of proof (*apramāṇa*), it is not correct to state a total negation [of memory]. For just as, despite the possibility of forgetting what has been practiced due to conditions such as a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*), memory is nonetheless observed in some individuals; likewise, even for one who has endured the suffering of dwelling in a womb, the recollection of a immediately preceding birth (*jātismaraṇa*) can occur due to the sharpness of someone's intellect, the arising of merit, and the mildness of that suffering. Therefore, it is impossible for anyone other than a Cārvāka to deny this categorically.

Furthermore, since it is possible for this [mental cultivation] to take as its object the domains of many successive births, there is no contradiction in the gradual possibility of conceptualizing all objects; thus, the defect consisting in the non-arising of cultivation due to the failure to comprehend the objects is avoided, because cultivation is possible once the arrangement of the world has been correctly grasped from scripture.

Even if scripture (*āgama*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), why should it not be possible for one who possesses faith and perceives its correspondence with other profound means of knowledge? Furthermore, once the non-falsity of its object of cognition is established, the point to be proven is already accomplished. Indeed, the manifestation of even a part is observed through the conceptualization of the whole; thus, there is a gradual manifestation of the subtle and so forth.

By this, that [objection] is also refuted: namely, that one who has mastered a single treatise is incapable of another, or that both are represented in many ways as being manifold; for there is no disagreement on this point. However, this remains: the effort required for the initial mastery of a treatise is not the same as that required for another work with a different subject matter. Thus, in the progression toward the highest degree of proficiency, there may be such excellence in someone regarding what they have not heard that it does not exist in another even regarding what they have heard.

Then, when the recollection of past lives occurs, through further practice, the possibility of *ūha* (inclusion) and *apoha* (exclusion) arises even with respect to objects not previously practiced; thus, one will not remain in a state free from afflictions merely because of that [recollection], as one is capable of acting for the sake of others. Alternatively, because all conceptual constructions are possible, yogins devoted to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) will manifest everything according to their own will.

For this very reason, the objection regarding the futility of cultivation (*bhāvanānarthakya*) in the position that everything is cognizable is also pointless; for it is established that when one who has cultivated the Four Noble Truths—which must necessarily be accomplished—is capable of inferring all objects, it is their own will that is being demonstrated.

[343,10] Now, if one were to perceive that in the direct realization of all things there is indeed another kind of happiness or the accomplishment of the welfare of others, then for one in such a state there would be no weariness from meditative cultivation whatsoever, and the manifestation of everything clearly would be easily accomplished; thus, even the Great Ocean has not said anything more than this. And by saying just this much, the objection has been answered. Therefore, however one reflects upon it, the presentation of objections against the Omniscient One results only in doubt; it is not a definitive refutation.

But the proof for the omniscient being under discussion is absolute. If it is argued that even there, there is no restriction regarding place, time, or person, we say no; for if such restrictions were required, the proof would be ineffective. This proof is indeed directed against one who denies [omniscience] in every respect, and it achieves its purpose even if there is no restriction of place and so forth. And thus, this kind of argument has been set forth by us in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*.
The chapter entitled "The Determination of the Yoginī" is completed.
The Treatise on the Drop of Non-duality (Advaitabinduprakaraṇa)

[345,3] Here, for one who adheres to external objects, the mental conviction is that whatever is perceived in a certain way exists in that way, just as a blue lotus is established as having a blue form. And since jars and the like are perceived as having a nature distinct from consciousness, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (reason based on essential nature). There is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) here, because the forms of jars and the like are encompassed by both appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) as a form that stands before one, capable of being pointed out with the index finger, and separated from the factor of the apprehender (*grāhaka*). Likewise...

For this cognition—"this is a jar" or "this is not a jar"—is personally experienced by all persons, even those who have not mastered linguistic conventions; it is an internal mental state corresponding exactly to that [object], free from the explicit mention of specific names. Even an infant, upon seeing the breast as a means of pleasure, extends its hand and mouth toward it, thereby manifesting itself as accompanied by an external determination (*bahiravasāya*). And thus, by means of that which is distinct...

The cognition of the form of a jar and so forth by means of its color does not set out upon the path of non-establishment (*asiddhi*). Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), because its occurrence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) has been demonstrated; for that which is pervaded by the opposite [of the probandum], being contradictory, cannot occur therein.

For this very reason, there is neither the fault of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) nor the doubt regarding positive concomitance (*sandigdhānvaya*); and because it is not observed in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is not [inconclusive].

This is a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*). Nor should it be argued that even when one with jaundice perceives a yellow conch-shell, or when one with an eye-disease (*taimirika*) perceives falling hairs, there is no such determination [of reality]—and therefore [the reason] is indeed common—because those perceptions are afflicted by subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) and, being erroneous, lack the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, in the case at hand, since there is an absence of subverting evidence and error is not established, the operation of direct perception [remains intact].
Nor could there ever be a sublation even in this case, which would lead to a lack of confidence; for that would entail the consequence of abolishing the operation of perception everywhere. Therefore:
"When there is a sublation due to a difference in place, time, or person, [the cognition] is not born of the senses."
But the cognition of the distinctions such as the jar and so forth is perceptual, because of the absence of that [conceptualization].

In that case, the objection—"What is the use of inference when perception is already operative?"—is not to be raised, because what is intended is the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). For the possibility of dispute regarding the object of perception does not cease merely through the application of inference. In that regard, just as even with respect to a cow perceived by the senses, a fool who, due to some misconception, does not engage in its conventional usage, [is led to it] by way of its being composed of the collection of dewlaps and so forth...

[345,23] It proceeds, or else the conventional usage of non-existence [proceeds] through non-apprehension; likewise, even in the case of perception, the distinction between the grasped and the grasper is conventionally employed by one who follows other scriptures and perceives it accordingly—thus there is no fault. And this conventional usage [345,25] is established solely on the basis of that [distinction], precisely because it is applied all at once. For even in the case of a blue lotus and so forth, the [quality of] blue—

In conventional usage, there is no other or additional cause for [the cognition of difference] than appearance and determination (*pratibhāsa-adhyavasāya*), because it would follow that activity would not occur based on that alone. For even the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) is sought only in the first instance of activity;

such conventional usage is based solely on the appearing object. However, in the case of the present conventional usage of difference, it is everywhere rooted in beginningless habituation (*anādikālika-abhyāsa*).
They are observed to possess proficiency; for it has been said:
"Even a child," and so forth.

Therefore, for one who is proficient in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), such usage is dependent solely upon such a cognition. When that [usage] is the probandum (*sādhya*), being cognized in that manner is pervaded by the state of being independent of anything else. And if, despite there being such a cognition in some case, there were an absence of such usage, then it would be dependent on something else; thus, the probandum—the fitness for that usage—[would not be established].

[346,11] Since "being perceived as such" is excluded from non-existence by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), it is pervaded by the very fitness for being established in that manner within an object free from sublation (*apetabādhaka*). Thus, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, even the charge that the reason (*hetu*) presented has an exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) that is doubtful does not approach it; therefore, it is proven that the distinction between cognition and the cognizable, even regarding the object of direct perception (*adhyakṣaviṣaya*), is established by the aforementioned inference.
[346,14] "The state of being conventionally expressible is inalienable.
[346,15] To this it is replied: What is this so-called "cognition" (*vijñāna*) by virtue of which a distinct apprehension and, likewise, conventional usage would be established?

[346,16] For if it is "cognition" (*jñāna*) because "by means of this one cognizes" (*jñāyate 'nena*) or "it cognizes" (*jānāti*), in either case this definition is dependent upon an object of cognition (*jñeya*). And yet...

[346,17] For those who deny the external world, it must be established that there exists some object of knowledge (*jñeya*), from which cognition could arise as the means for its apprehension. For instance, [346,18] this conventional usage—that "this is cognition" and "this is the object of knowledge"—must be based either on a specific activity (*vyāpāra*) according to the dualist, or on a restriction by genus (*jāti*). [346,19] Regarding the first position, does the activity belong to the cognition with respect to the object, or to the object with respect to the cognition, or to both mutually?

In this case as well, regarding the first position, there are the alternatives of whether [the operation of cognition] is productive (*nirvartaka*) or transformative (*vikāraka*). Among these, first of all, it cannot be asserted that the operation of cognition upon the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is productive, because that would entail the consequence of destroying objects that are not currently being perceived. Nor is such an admission tenable, since at that very moment [the object] is seen by someone through that cognition.
And if one accepts its production, there can be no denial of the persistence of even that which is imperceptible.

Furthermore, if that [object], being perceived later by him, becomes the producer of that very cognition, it would not be the object [of the initial cognition]. If you argue that it is not perceptible to that [cognition], but rather something else produced by that cognition [is the object], then the impossibility of a single location arises. For if it were non-obstructive, how could that which is of the nature of light and is to be known introspectively be [perceived] by another?

[346,26] It would merely be the nature of consciousness itself that is established for the object (*gocara*) by means of another approach. If it is argued that this is not so because it has the form of blue (*nīlarūpa*), [347,1] by whom, moreover, has the production of the blue aspect (*nīlākāra*) in consciousness been proven to be impossible, such that there would be the consequence of failing to apply a proof for its establishment?
[347,2] Therefore, it is not logical for the proponent of duality to claim that what is imperceptible is simply non-existent.

Nor is this an accepted tenet of his; thus, there is no insistence on this point. For even one who maintains that in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there is an absence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), does not intend for that which is imperceptible to be non-existent in every respect; rather, he holds that while it exists, it must necessarily be the object of some means of valid cognition, albeit at a slight distance. Otherwise, it would be impossible to state: "When there is contact with existing objects, the arising of cognition occurs for a person through the sense faculties."

It might be argued that [the object exists] prior to cognition because of its absence [therein]. However, that further assumption is not logical; so what is the use of this? Since only that much was intended to be said, enough with this elaboration.

But regarding the position that [the object] is modified (*vikāryapakṣa*), if one establishes that the object which is modified by a particular cognition is the apprehended (*grāhya*), then in the case of grief and so forth—

If cognition were impaired, would the sense organ also be the object of apprehension, or rather things such as the reflection of a soiled face? If you argue that this impairment is a transformation produced by suffering, we say no; for nothing other than the perception of an impaired form is observed. This has already been thoroughly examined in the treatise, so enough of this effort. Alternatively, if you claim that there is no such excellence in the object of knowledge resulting from cognition, but rather that it is the production of a luminous form [that constitutes apprehension].

If this were the case, even in this position, that which has a single object would have to have all things as its object. Upon the cessation of that person's cognition, because the nature of those objects would cease, it would follow that nothing else could be perceived either.

If it is argued that this is not so because other things also possess the means for their manifestation, then for that person whose cognition has ceased, there would likewise be no manifestation of them.

This leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Even if that cognition ceases while its form does not cease, this same fault remains. For clay that has been removed from the potter’s effort does not become a jar for that very person; nor does a fire, through burning, result in the absence of a jar for one who possesses the fire.
If that were so, then its nature as a benefactor (*upakāritva*) would also be common to all, but it is not so. Therefore, just as in the case of being a jar...

Even if this [cognition] were common [to all], it would not be so by way of its form that produces an effect; likewise, why should there be this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would not be so even by way of its luminous form? Or, if you argue that its capacity to assist specific beneficiaries is what makes it common, then its luminosity—which depends upon specific persons—would likewise be common to all; thus, the two cases are equal.

It is not the same. For what is called "being helpful" (upakāritva) must be intended as either direct assistance or merely the state of being capable of activity. Regarding these, since mere capability is common to all things, there is no dispute over that. However, in the first case—that of direct assistance—why should this thing's status as a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*) in the performance of an effect characterized by assistance not be the same elsewhere as it is in one instance?

This is the meaning of the objection. Nor is this a valid principle, because it depends upon the absence of an interval (*avyavadhāna*) and so forth. Therefore, since assistance belongs to that very [cause] which is in close proximity (*upanidhi*) to the material cause (*upādāna*) existing within its own continuum, how could there be nourishment from something distant and so on? Likewise, if even "illumination" were intended as a conventional usage by way of producing another effect, then this might indeed be the case. As some have said:

[348,1] Its manifestation (*vyaktatva*) consists precisely in its being the producer of the manifestation characterized as cognition (*buddhi*). For in that case, for whatever cognition the material cause (*upādāna*)—reckoned as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)—is present, and no other means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) intervenes, it is not logical for that very [cognition] to be unmanifest due to the absence of the provision of auxiliary causes (*sahakāra*).
[348,2–3] Furthermore, we shall state another refutation regarding that point as well.

And this is not tenable, because we are currently considering the position that the object, which is of the nature of light, arises from cognition. However, if the designation "manifested" is used by way of another effect, then there is no damage to the present argument, namely that it does not arise in that manner [from cognition]. If it were to arise in that manner, the undesirable consequence of its being common [to all perceivers] would be unavoidable; for even the state of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) extends only so far as it is distinct—

To begin with, the capacity to produce pleasure and so forth within a continuous stream (*santāna*) is common (*sādhāraṇa*) from that perspective alone. However, if it were admitted that [the object] is actually of the nature of pleasure and so forth, then who would be able to deny its commonality? If it is argued that even so, "that which is the pleasure of one is not that of another," [we reply: the property of being common or uncommon belongs to the object, whereas [it belongs to] the cognition. Therefore...

It is logical that pleasure and so forth, being restricted to that specific self, are not common to others by virtue of their nature as benefit and so on. However, an external form, even if it is the effect of that [pleasure], is indeed common when it is accepted [as such], because the benefit consists in the form of another moment that is to be appropriated by the cognition of pleasure. If it is argued that, in the same way, there is both commonality and non-commonality?

In this way, there is no such thing as "being the son of Caitra" produced by Caitra that is common to others, like the quality of being fair-skinned; rather, his very state of being produced by him is designated as "his sonship. And that act of procreation belongs to Caitra alone and is not shared with others. Likewise, the designation based on that [act] also arises from the designation of being produced by him. However, the quality of being fair-skinned...

[348,16] Even that which is produced by it is not indeed produced by it alone, because it possesses other qualities; thus, it is rightly considered common [to others]. For this [man] is not white only for his father, but also for others.

[348,17] Likewise, the manifestation (*vyaktatva*) of an object is not merely its being produced by cognition, since its form remains indistinguishable from when it was obstructed and so forth; rather, the accepted position is that there arises a manifestation-form (*prakāśarūpa*) that surpasses that [object]. Otherwise, the object would not be said to be "manifested. Such is the linguistic usage—

That [external object] would be merely the cause for that [cognition], just as whiteness is [the cause] for a person by virtue of being produced from it, or for a Sautrāntika by virtue of its being the producer. And just as there is the consequence of that other producing cognition becoming an object, so too is there [the consequence] for this produced cognition; thus, nothing more than the mere transgression of the convention regarding the causal relationship between cognition and its object is added. As for the avoidance of the charge of commonality, it applies to both cases alike. It is not [the case that one avoids it and the other does not].
[348,22] However, the accomplishment of this [cognition] is established here through the production of an object in the form of a manifestation.
[348,23] When there is the production of illumination, everything has the possibility of being illuminated;
[348,24] but when there is no production and illumination does not exist, not even a single thing is [illuminated].
This is the summary.

For just as one who asserts that the mere fact of being produced by fire constitutes the "manifestness" of both raw and cooked rice— both of which are covered by dense darkness— is not able to truly establish their perceptibility, so too this [proponent] [cannot establish] the production of cognition.

Let it be seen thus: if, however, the production of that which has the nature of illumination is admitted from consciousness just as from a lamp, then its opposite would follow for a pot that is beyond the senses; moreover, the common fault remains difficult to avoid.
If it is argued, "In that case, even a pot manifested by a lamp would be an illumination for everyone," [the answer is: such is the nature of the illumination produced by the lamp.

Luminosity (*prakāśatā*)—which is the state of being free from darkness and consists in the capacity to generate cognition depending on factors such as its location in a suitable place—is indeed common to all. However, that which is restricted and serves as the means for activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth through conceptualization, memory, desire, and the like, is produced solely by cognition.

If even that [restricted luminosity] were manifested as being established in the same way as its brilliance (*bhāsuratā*), alas, it would be common to all, just as the pleasure and other sensations experienced at that time are.
Or rather, it has already been largely stated that [the capacity] to prove anything would belong to everything. Therefore:
"The manifestation of the external mass does not arise from cognition, whether in the mere production [of the object] or in some other excellence."
But if there were the arising of that which has the nature of luminosity,
it would necessarily follow that it is common to all.
Therefore, the operation of cognition is not based on the establishment of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.

If it is argued that, therefore, the status of being an object (*grāhyatva*) belongs to the knowable because of its causal operation (*vyāpāra*) upon cognition, we say no; for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the sense faculty (*indriya*) is also an object. Furthermore, if the status of being an object consists in producing a similar form (*sarūpajanaka*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the specific immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya-viśeṣa*). Moreover, the qualification "provided it is external" (*bāhyatve sati*) is only appropriate for those who maintain that very position; thus, this position too is not tenable. Let it not be so.

[349,16] Let the position that both [cognition and the object] possess causal efficiency be accepted: cognition, arising from an object with a form similar to it, is the apprehender by virtue of its operation of realizing that [object].

[349,17] In that case, because of the object's operation, there is no apprehension of those [objects] that lack such operation; and because of the reliance on the operation of cognition, there is no [apprehension] of the sense faculty either.
[349,18] If it is argued that "the operation of realization does not belong to cognition in that regard," this too is not a valid principle. For that [realization]...

[349,19] Is comprehension (adhigati) identical in nature to the object, or is it a different entity from knowledge, or another instance of knowledge? In the first case, since it is established just like the nature of the object itself, there is an absence of any activity of knowledge. Alternatively, if the object likewise required the activity of knowledge, the aforementioned fault would ensue. In the second case, however, it is contradictory to say that the activity of knowledge resides in itself; for comprehension is nothing other than the activity itself.

In this case as well, the same refutation applies, because the non-difference between the activity and its possessor has been established. In this very manner, the conceptualization of [cognition] as having the nature of both the knower and the known should be understood as rejected.
Furthermore, if the object were something distinct [from cognition], what would happen to the sense faculty? For it is not the case that when blue is perceived, the sense faculty is perceived.

If it is argued that there is the attainment of that [cognition], then what establishes the connection between that [attainment] and the cognition produced by knowledge? If it is argued that this is due to its own activity (*vyāpāra*), then, in that case, since the attainment of both would be established through the activity of both, there would be a mutual relationship of either being the apprehended or the apprehender. And thus, the objection regarding the consequence of the sense organ itself being apprehended is not avoided; for [the attainment does not arise from] the activity of the eye.
[349,28] There is comprehension of form even without [the operation of the sense organ].

[350,1] Now, if it is argued that the function of the sense organ lies only in cognition (*jñāna*) and not in comprehension (*adhigati*), whereas for form it exists even in that [comprehension], who indeed—other than a fool—is capable of making such a distinction? For there is no distinct entity other than cognition and the object of cognition.

Only some form of apprehension (*adhigama*) is perceived, wherein the operation of cognition alone might be postulated; yet in that case, it belongs to the object as well and not to the sense organ—this is merely a desire for something auspicious. If it is argued that the relationship between the apprehended object and the object itself is characterized solely by the state of being object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), then is this very state of being object and subject not itself the operation?

It is examined by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And for one for whom that [construction] is not established in the case of both cognition and the object of cognition, how could it be established even in the case of the realization and its object? Or, if one accepts that the status of being an object belongs to realization based on a single [factor], how could one reject [the same] for cognition? If it is argued, "This conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) certainly exists," then let it exist; however, one must consider what its foundation is—namely, the non-confused...

[350,9] Is it the establishment of their own nature through characteristics, or is it the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) resulting from the habitual practice of beginningless false conceptualization?

[350,10] If one asks, "What is the seed of this?"—what does it matter? For even if the opponent does not understand it, we have thereby demonstrated the unmixed characteristics of these two. By this, the postulation of a distinct cognition for the apprehension [of the object] is refuted.

For that [cognition] as well, its having that [object] as its domain is likewise unestablished. And it is a great absurdity to claim that an object is known by means of a comprehension that does not have that object as its domain. By this, the following conceptual construction is refuted: that at the time of debate, the intellect—neither performing an operation upon the object nor transforming it—is called "having that as its domain" merely because it extends the simple apprehension of it. Therefore, it is not [the case that...].
[350,15] It is established that this conventional usage of "knower" and "known" occurs by way of functional activity (*vyāpāra*).

[350,16] Nor is it restricted by genus (*jāti*), because a thing is established as being known by someone, at some time, and in some place. [350,17] For such a conventional arrangement does not belong to things like "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like, which are fixed by nature (*nisarga-niyata*). Furthermore, this must necessarily be explained even now.

[350,18] Furthermore, a distinction of characteristics is not possible; thus, in the absence of such a distinction, the mere existence of either cognition or the object of cognition would be the cause of reality, whereby it would follow that everyone would possess the cognition of all objects, or else no one at all would, since there would be no distance [between them]. Now, is there not a proximity between the sense organs and their objects, characterized by conjunction, inherence, and so forth? Cognition arising through the power of that [proximity] would [cognize] each respective object—

[350,21] It is established that [the cognition] is restricted and excluded from objects that are distant due to the absence of the sixfold sense-object contact; so how can there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? This too is trivial.
For by this [argument], the restriction regarding its arising would indeed be established, but not the restriction of consciousness as the apprehender with respect to any particular object.
To explain: through the power of sense-object contact such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), cognition is produced by an object, and not by one lacking it.

Let it be that [the cognition arises] from something obstructed and so forth; however, there is no certainty as to what its apprehender is. If you say, "It is that very thing by which it was produced," then the self, the mind, the contact with the sense-faculties, and so on, would also be objects of apprehension; thus, the over-extension [of the definition] is not avoided. For even regarding that which is intended to be the object, no utility of this [cognition] is possible in respect to the sense-faculties and so forth, by which a distinction in apprehension could be established.
[350,27] It was just now considered whether the production of a delimitation is a distinct operation.

[351,1] If it is argued that "therein, there is the manifestation of that very [object], and therefore there is no over-extension [of the definition]," [we reply: although there is a manifestation that cannot be denied in the two parts regarded as the apprehended and the apprehender, if there were anything [else] based on the capacities of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*), then...

Let it be said: mere simultaneous manifestation is not the cause for the appearance of two moons; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that those two [moons] would perceive each other, or that blue and yellow [would perceive each other]. Or, one moon would be false and the second part would be a tangle (*jaṭa*). Furthermore, such arguments as "because the mind cannot function toward two things at once" are appropriate only when one stands upon the position of the Proponent of External Objects (*bāhyārthavāda*); and this investigation has that very [external object] as its subject matter. But when...

Even in the case of two parts, there is no simultaneous manifestation, because it is not accepted that one cognition can be experienced by another simultaneous cognition; thus, this path also does not exist. However, if adherence to ill-conceived tenets is not a subverting factor, then one might consider the following basis: that the forms of internal joy, distress, and so forth, as well as the form of the moon and such, are perceived at the very same time. But this is not the case.
It is established that this is acceptable.

Furthermore, the fact that there is sensory contact with a jar and not with a cloth must be determined from the very experience of that [jar]. And if the status of this [experience] as an experience of that [object] is due to its arising through contact with that [object], then there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Alternatively, if the experience of that [object] is established by some other means, then [contact] would be redundant.

[351,12] Because it would be redundant. Moreover, if [the cognition] were the experience of that object simply because it arises through contact with it, then the experience of the object would have an indistinct appearance established merely by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and not a distinct one; this would result in the loss of what is observed, like [the case of] Maitra’s son being fair-skinned due to being Caitra’s son. Therefore, this portion intended as the object, which appears with distinctness, [is so] because it is free from consideration of the operation of other causal factors.
Just like joy, distress, and so forth, one perceives the self as something known by itself.
As for the one who thinks:
"But that very same prior causal complex [produces] the cognition of the objective moment,"
It would act like a visible form accompanied by light, so that there might be simultaneous cognition.
Thus it is said. Nevertheless:
If the manifest object is produced by the causal complex (sāmagrī), what is the use of cognition?
Furthermore, there would be the fault of commonality; and if the object were not manifest, there could be no appearance of clarity.
Since this is established merely by virtue of dependence on a single causal complex,
it follows that the sense organ as well would possess the quality of illumination.

If stability [of the object] is maintained, how could even a single object be produced by a single causal complex? Furthermore, how could consciousness be perceived simultaneously with the object as it flashes forth?
[351,26] Now, if cognition were non-cognition, then everything would indeed be well-said;
[351,27] but under the view that there is self-awareness, this external world is today difficult to perceive.

If it is argued that the capacity belongs to the causal complex alone, such that the object and the subject are differentiated within it— just as taste and color arise together— who can be questioned regarding their intrinsic nature?
If the form of the object of cognition and the cognizer is determined and characterized, then,
in the search for its production, let it be called the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
When health is established in its excellent form, the power of the physician must be declared;
yet the nature of the object of knowledge and the knower has not even now been definitively determined.
Therefore, when the essential nature [of a thing] is to be stated, there may be either a shift in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
or an irrelevant statement, or indeed the behavior of a *ṭiṇṭika* (a sophist).
Therefore, there is no knower whatsoever, nor an object of knowledge, nor an act of knowing;
rather, this world must be established as self-luminous, independent of those [distinctions].
For blue and other such objects manifest, yet there is nothing else that illuminates them;
thus, their self-luminosity is established, and for us, that alone is consciousness.
Thus are the intermediate verses.

This being the case, there is no such thing as "consciousness" that is established as distinct, by virtue of which the cognition of the form of a jar and so forth could establish its difference from it. Thus, the reason (*hetu*)—characterized by the property of being perceived as distinct—is afflicted by the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*), because its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unproven. Furthermore, the probandum (*sādhya*), namely the conventional usage of difference from that [consciousness], does not serve the purpose at hand precisely because its qualification is unestablished. For even if the jar were of the nature of consciousness, since...

Since difference is established even from some other cognition, it is of no use to establish mere difference. Therefore, since the difference is to be proven with respect to a specific limit (*avadhi*), and you are unable to clarify that limit, your presentation is futile.
[Objection: But surely even for the Proponents of Cognition (*vijñānavādin*) there is the conventional usage of "cognition"; whether it be one way or another, it is the same for us as well.
It will serve as a refuge for establishing those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Furthermore, there exists in the world that which is recognized as "some cognition";

it is precisely from this that we shall state the distinction. There is no need here for our own definition. And if it is argued that in an inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), there is no conformity to convention (*samaya*).
For the Vijñānavādins, consciousness-ness is indeed luminosity;
and that [luminosity] is the same for both parts designated as the grasped and the grasper.
Therefore, the distinction from cognition consists in being manifest;
that distinctness is already excluded in these things such as jars by the very fact of their being perceived.
[353,3] Furthermore, there is a non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), for jars and the like are indeed not unmanifest.
[353,4] But when the subject (*dharmin*) is something other than these, then the non-establishment of the property (*dharmāsiddhi*) is evident.
Furthermore, there is the lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) regarding the fact that it is known through differentiation;
moreover, for one who maintains that it is manifest, there are further issues such as the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).
Therefore, that [argument] is not tenable even from the perspective of the opponent's own view.
Furthermore, in the world, it is said that "this consciousness flashes within.
Consequently, what is the point of establishing its difference from that which is of an unknowable nature?

If the conventional distinction between blue and its cognition is established as being proven through the forms of the object of knowledge and the knower, then that distinction would be a product of human agency.

[353,12] Of those two which have the natures of self-luminosity—consisting of the forms of the non-objectified and the non-apprehending—and which are unique, touching upon internal and external determination respectively; [353,13]
If you are satisfied by the distinction between the "I-maker" (ahaṅkāra) and the body,
why is the distinction between two different mental continua not established for your pleasure?
[353,16] Now, if there is no radiating [of consciousness] toward that which exists in the stream of another,
[353,17] then even if it appears, why is the loss of the state of being the object and the subject not observed?
If no one considers there to be unity between two distinct mental continua,
then even in that case, it would be established by the same means used to prove their difference.
Oh, how great is the prowess displayed by the outsider who speaks in opposition! This is indeed fitting.
But when the Vedāntins and others assert that there is no difference between two cognitions even though their mental continua are distinct,
then there would be no other unity even between the cognition of blue and [the cognition of yellow].
In that case, what is this obsession with calamity?

For even among the proponents of consciousness (vijñānavādins), there are various positions. To this effect: "In the world, the single mind appears as if divided into the portions of the grasped and the grasper;
or else, these two—the self-cognition and the cognition of coldness, pleasure, and so forth—are distinct."

Or else, pleasure and so forth are the supreme object deposited here; or, by the power of ignorance, the single [consciousness], though possessing various forms such as blue and so on, is either with form or indeed without form.

And what is the use now of considering their relative strength or weakness for one who is engaged in proving an external object through such an adherence to a formal proof (*sādhana*)? Therefore, since the form of the jar—which is established as being of the nature of consciousness as previously described and is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*)—is already distinct from that which is accepted as another consciousness, there is no fruit whatsoever in attempting to prove this distinction; thus, the effort is futile. [Objection: But the form of the jar is not personally realized, because it is common to all. Consequently, even though it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it is indeed an external object (*artha*) due to its commonality.

If it is argued that even from that [perception], a cognition of non-difference is employed to establish conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), we say no; for commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) has already been refuted previously. For it has been demonstrated that the manifest form cannot remain without inducing activity or cessation even toward those things that are remote, just as it does toward those whose causes and so forth are complete and present. This being the case, if [the object] is uncommon (*asādhāraṇatve*),...

[354,12] In that case, it would not occur even for those things that are present. It is not that the form of those things that are present is one and the same; rather, it is of that kind. [354,13] If there is indeed a difference, how then can there be a single cognition? This is not a fault, because such a cognition is observed even in the case of distinct things like hairs and so forth.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is not valid because a sublation (*bādhaka*) is observed there, then why is a sublation not perceived here as well, given that there would be the same consequence of activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth even for what is separated [in time]? Even if such a state exists, the cause is simply activity and so forth;
however, when asked what the seed is for the fact that such a manifestation occurs for some and not for others, we say: "It is the latent impression (*vāsanā*). What is this latent impression?

It has been analyzed elsewhere that this mere capacity for appropriation—which has come down through a beginningless succession of preceding cognitions—is undivided, yet appears as if divided depending on certain perspectives. Because such a cognition arises from the transformation of such seeds, it belongs to some and not to others; thus, there is no fault here, owing to the necessity of the continuous succession between the material cause and its effect.

It is like the hair and other objects seen by two people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Or rather, just as in that case, because of its resistance (*pratighatva*), there is also the determination of it as occupying a single location; enough with this elaboration.
Why is it determined as one, even though it is perceived as distinct and different? Because it is determined as such.
If it is argued that there is sublation, then there is no valid cognition; why, then, is sublation not perceived now?
However, similarity is appropriate to manifest due to the equality of the seeds of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
since cognitions lack spatial resistance, even occupying the same location is not a fault.
Thus is the summary.

Therefore, it is established that there is also the state of being personally realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedyatva*). If it is argued that hardness and so forth are nevertheless not properties of cognition (*jñānadharma*), we say no; for all things are cognition by virtue of having the nature of luminosity (*prakāśarūpatā*). Furthermore, one cannot tolerate the notion that even blueness is a property of cognition.

"Hardness," say those of tender intellect. But surely, that very blue which is perceived is experienced as hard; and if it is argued that this is not tenable in the case of consciousness—[we reply: even externally, because of the perception of error, blue is merely color (*rūpa*) and hardness is touch (*sparśa*). Nor is there anything other than these two within the range of perception, since a quality (*guṇa*) is dependent upon a substance (*dravya*).
If this is argued, what is this "nature of quality" (*guṇatattva*)? If it is merely dependence (*pāratantrya*), then the reason (*hetu*) is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*).

Alternatively, if it is something else entirely due to a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), even so, because it is impossible to establish a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka*), the reason suffers from the fallacy of having an uncertain exclusion from the heterologue (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*). As for this [which follows]:
He recites: "Substance is that which subsists in a substance, possesses qualities, and is an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions.
In that regard as well, its status as a quality is established by its subsisting in a substance.
And once the existence of the quality is established, its having that [substance] as its substratum follows;
thus, these two would be mutually dependent.
Therefore, for him, his own system alone is his refuge.

[355,15] It is of no use in debate to treat that [external object] as non-authoritative; enough, then, with chewing what has already been chewed. Or, let there be some other external substratum for the two qualities; even so, if it is luminous (*prakāśa*), then it cannot exist without being included within cognition.

[355,17] If it is not luminous, the reason remains unestablished (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, the simultaneous determination of blue and hardness is nothing but an error. And its sublation consists precisely in their mutual non-inclusion within cognition, according to the sequence already stated. Moreover, the seed of the cognition appearing as blue— [355,18]

Since there is no fixed rule that the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cognition— which appears as solidity— is necessarily dependent upon [the perception of] activity, such jackal-like howlings do not assail the lion of the Yogācāra.
Furthermore, regarding what was said— that there is the cognition "I am not a jar"— in that case too, for those for whom this cognition of "I" has the self (*ātman*) as its object...

If it were said that "pots do not exist for them," this would only negate their status as a self (*ātmatva*), not their status as cognition (*jñānatva*). Even though they are the basis for being objects of consciousness, Maitra does not have the notion of "I" directed toward mere consciousness alone, because that would entail the same notion occurring even with respect to Caitra’s mind. If you argue that Maitra certainly has that notion with respect to his own mind, then in considering why it is not likewise present for him, the answer must be sought in the lack of habituation (*anabhyāsa*) toward other mental continua. That...

Furthermore, the absence of habitual practice (*anabhyāsa*) is indeed present even in the case of forms such as a jar that appear directed toward the external. Thus, this exclusion of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*), being established even otherwise, is not capable of inflicting harm upon the nature of consciousness.
Moreover, it might be argued that whatever is consciousness necessarily becomes the object of either one's own or another's notion of "I"; however, this is not so.

If it is argued that [the cognition] has the form of a jar (*ghaṭākāra*), we say no; for the pervasion of the object by the cognition, which is the subject, is not established. Indeed, the object is held to be distinct [from the cognition]; it is not its effect, though it might be its cause. And since there is no necessary rule that the existence of an effect follows from its cause, there is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to doubt regarding its exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣa*). Thus, this proponent of externalism, having merely invoked the externality of the form— [356,2] If it is argued that [the cognition] has the form of a jar (*ghaṭākāra*), we say no; for the pervasion of the object by the cognition, which is the subject, is not established. Indeed, the object is held to be distinct [from the cognition]; it is not its effect, though it might be its cause. And since there is no necessary rule that the existence of an effect follows from its cause, there is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to doubt regarding its exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣa*). Thus, this proponent of externalism, having merely invoked the externality of the form—(70a) —[is refuted].
The method for proving difference imitates the account of removing gold after it has been fashioned into a knot. Furthermore, it is not mere verbal expression that is to be proven;

rather, what is intended by the context is the distinctness from the illuminator of a jar or similar object that already exists and is illuminated through the operation of the illuminator. Since such proof is not established, the statement of a non-essential part of the proof is a fault for the proponent due to the futility of the means of proof.

[This is] a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Or, even if that were not the case, who can prevent the lack of exclusivity (*anaikāntya*) due to appearances such as those of one who is asleep or suffering from ophthalmia (*taimira*)?
If it is argued: "In all cases, the external object exists as the objective support (*ālambana*), though its nature is different in terms of place and time"?
In all cases, cognition has an object of perception whose nature consists of the alteration of place and form.
In that case, it can also be said:
"How is there a grasping of its own nature? And how is there a grasping of another?
Whether the cognition is identical to or different from itself, the absence of activity is the same."
And just as it appears to be active in other cases, so it appears to be active within itself;
like a lamp, this conventional usage of the intellect cannot be denied.

These are the intermediate verses. Therefore, according to the view that there is "misapprehension as otherwise" (anyathākhyāti), it is thus: "That which is not external appears as having an external form, and that which is not blue appears as having the nature of blue."
If it is determined by oaths that "cognition itself does not appear," [then what?]
What is the cause here for the failure of knowledge, even though its object is real?
This objection is equally applicable to both regarding the cognition of objects restricted to specific locations.
If an internal disturbance associated with a differentiation of capacities is manifested therein,
why can that very thing not be stated as the cause here as well?
Furthermore: "If it is argued that 'the existent appears otherwise,' let that be the case regarding a difference in place;
but how could there be an appearance otherwise through a difference in time, given its non-existence?"
A living actor may indeed appear otherwise, but even so, he is not truly dead;
therefore, it is the mind alone that is capable of appearing otherwise in all circumstances.

Therefore, even under the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (the appearance of something as otherwise), there is no avoidance of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). If it is argued that even when there is a difference in time, the object is not absolutely non-existent because it exists at its own time—what is the use of its mere existence at another time for that which is non-existent at the time of its appearance? That which has no utility through the imposition of its own existence in a particular case cannot be effective there if it is long past, just as a burnt seed or a piece of cloth is not effective toward a sprout or blackness. Furthermore, since an object appears by means of the imposition of its own existence, this is a perception of a contradictory state (*viruddhopalabdhi*), because:

[357,10] Even for that which has perished, there is the possibility of causal capacity; yet, utility through the imposition of its own existence (*svasattopadhānena*) is a contradictory property. Here, even a past seed situated in a granary is utilized for the sprout through a succession, but not by means of the imposition of its own existence; it is for this purpose that the qualification [“by the imposition of its own existence”] is employed. [357,12] Furthermore, an object that is appearing must be said to be utilized within the appearance precisely by the imposition of its own existence, and not through a succession. Appearance—

For that [object], there must be either its nature (*dharmatā*) or its effect (*kārya*). In the case of its being the nature, there is coexistence (*sahabhāva*); in the case of its being the effect, there is the necessity of immediate succession to its own existence (*svasattānantaryaniyama*).

Thus, even a single moment of interval cannot tolerate its existence; therefore, it is established that the object is of use [to cognition] only by way of presenting its own existence (*svasattopadhāna*) in the manifestation. And due to the absence of that [presentation], the past cannot be made manifest.
Therefore, this which is manifesting manifests precisely as non-existent,
because its own existence has been removed by the removal of the substrate due to its having passed away.
Furthermore, even in the absence of that [external object], if there is an appearance, then the appearance of what is non-existent would follow;
for by your own words, you maintain that there is manifestation in the absence of existence.

Therefore, even in the position that external objects exist, the theory of *asatkhyāti* (the appearance of the non-existent) is unavoidable in the case of erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*). Or, let it be *anyathākhyāti* (the appearance of something as otherwise); in either case, it is merely a transformation (*vivarta*) of cognition, because its existence is similar [to the other], and it cannot be refuted by mere dislike. Thus, since there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*), the reason "being perceived as distinct" is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for establishing the conventional usage of distinction.
[It is] established. [Objection: Even if this is the case for those who are mistaken, what follows regarding experience?

If it is argued that there is no inconclusiveness because the qualification "provided it is non-erroneous" is intended, we say no; for the status of being mistaken depends upon a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), and that has been established here as well by the very sequence already stated.
To explain: from consciousness, which is self-luminous and possesses a unique nature...
If there were a difference [between the object and its cognition], the object would be cognizable by another, and likewise, it would be common [to all].
And this restriction is not established in such a way by the reasoning already stated;
therefore, how could a jar be distinct from cognition, like hair and other such [illusory objects]?
Since the establishment of a property does not occur in the absence of that [property],
the positive concomitance (anvaya) of that property thereby excludes its difference [from it].

Therefore, this unique property of self-luminosity—which is the opposite of the common characteristics of externality and non-self-luminosity—is perceived in jars and other objects; thus, by the force of sublation (*bādhaka*), the cognition of them as such is indeed an illusion. Furthermore, this sublation is an established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not merely a product of imagination; therefore, there is no fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in our critique. As for what the Vijñānavādin [has said]:
He provides the proof:
whatever appears is consciousness, like what is seen in a dream;
and the nature of blue and so forth appears—this is the reason.
In that case as well, let this continuity exist for the sake of establishing the necessary connection;
furthermore, any room for doubts regarding the succession of cognitions is far removed.
It is accepted that consciousness is self-luminous and unique;
furthermore, its manifestation is pervaded by that very nature, and by others, it is not produced by anything other than itself.
If blue and so forth manifest by themselves and not by another,
why is it not understood that they manifest themselves and not by something else?
If even a perceived operation of differentiation is deemed inappropriate for the subject at hand,
how can you postulate an unperceived one regarding the difference in the object to be established?
[358,21] But is it not seen that "that which is itself distinct from manifestation," and so forth?
[358,22] Even there, it is not said that the nature is pervaded within the self; rather, it is described as such.
In this way, let it also be understood that cognition manifests itself;
just as emptiness manifests by itself in space, by precluding the activity of anything else.
Likewise, the hearing of another's words serves to eliminate the delusion of one's own mental activity;
for the functioning [of consciousness] is not under the power of such activity, but rather its form is then [perceived] as it truly is.
Just as space is entirely devoid of obstruction and is itself luminous, so too is this [nature];
and this has already been established as being unique.
Therefore, that which is called "manifestness" (prakāśatā), along with its commonality and its action upon others,
is established by having rejected [the opposing view], since the same fault applies everywhere.
Therefore, through reasoning, contradiction with those two is established, and from that, the determination of their identity is obtained;
consequently, due to this very contradiction, there can be no persistence of the reason in its opposite.
Since luminosity is established, cold and other such qualities are of the nature of cognition;
thus, the hope for them to have an external form is merely a vain hope.
If the forms are the very nature of the single cognition, how can there be diversity? Or, if the cognition were distinct for every atom, likewise there would be no mutual awareness [of those parts].
Even if they are mutually cognized in that way, there is a destruction of the definition [of an object], just as in the case of external things.
Even if there is such a difference among those cognitions, how could their connection with illumination be established?

[359,15] Or, if it is precisely in this way that the appearance [arises] through a cognition of one's own mental continuum by means of another cognition, [359,16] then what other external world could there be for this mass of unreal forms?
Furthermore, in the case of false cognition, there is neither manifestation nor anything else.
Therefore, this reason, which possesses the commonality of the opposite side, establishes doubt.
This other exclusion (*vyāvṛttyantara*) is said to be "otherness" (*anyatva*), which is false;
even though it is accompanied by doubt, its status as cognition (*jñānatā*) remains established when it is manifest.
Thus, when it has been established that what appears in this way is cognition, then—
whether in some cases or everywhere— the state of being awareness exists even if it is unreal due to conceptual proliferation (*vāda*).
Therefore, only cognition is real, and not the external object;
whether the external object exists or not, let it be that luminosity is consciousness.
Even the conceptualization of difference and non-difference does not subvert luminosity;
nor is it [subverted] by the pervasion with the aforementioned probandum—so what is the purpose [of such a distinction]?
For one who might imagine that another perceives another, the remaining [objections] might indeed constitute a fault; however, we maintain that this is not the case even in a dream.
Because it is devoid of both unity and plurality, this world is without intrinsic nature;
since it is thus nothing at all, how could there be existence for a single entity?
Whether manifesting as blue or the like, whether aggregated or non-aggregated—
this is the reason stated by us in this treatise for its being a cognition.
In that case, if the absence of being one or many were to impart another property [to the object], what of ours would be lost by that? For blue and so forth do not thereby become non-existent.
[360,11] Once existence itself has been established, whether it be matted hair or its absence—
[360,12] for things such as the horns of a horse, which do not exist, are certainly not inferred in reality.
Nevertheless, this is irrelevant because it is devoid of any inquiry into existence;
for it is only when existence is already established that a specific distinction is considered.
If there is doubt regarding existence, then if it exists, it is indeed cognition;
therefore, non-apprehension is not a fault, because neither the proof nor the sublation of non-existence is established.
Because it possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of its form as a mere conventional reality, it is not without a basis;
otherwise, how could even the reason of "lack of intrinsic nature" have a basis?
If in that case there is not merely existence, but here there is merely the state of being cognition,
then the establishment of external objects is contradicted for both parties.

If you say that what is to be proven here by you is "the state of being an awareness characterized by a real entity," then why is such a qualification introduced when the context concerns awareness in its mere essence?

If the state of being knowledge were not pervaded by substantiality, such that it could exist even in its absence, then where would the fault of "contradictory non-deviation" (viruddhāvyabhicāra) lie? Or rather, let there be substantiality.
Furthermore, is existence intended to be negated by the reason of "lack of intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāvatva) as being either distinct from the nature of mere luminosity or otherwise?

In the negation of something distinct [from the self], there is no exclusion of that which has the nature of luminosity. If this very [luminosity] itself were excluded, by what means could that which appears to direct perception be excluded?
If inference, being a means of valid cognition, sublates something for someone,
why then does perception not also establish something for someone, since it likewise possesses that same status?
[361,7] Ultimately, the validity of perception must necessarily depend upon inference.
[361,8] And that which is produced by the senses, being of the nature of mere manifestation, does not depend upon inference.
Now, if this object of inference is distinct from that of sensory cognition, then since it is of a manifest nature, it is perceptual; how, therefore, could there be occasion for inference?
Now, that which is established by direct perception cannot be refuted;
for if there were some distinction in the exclusions (vyāvṛtti) here, how could it be incapable of withstanding analysis?
Let it be that this property belongs to consciousness alone, while the external object is like the horn of a hare;
or, in the absence of causal efficiency in an object, let that property belong to cognition itself.
The lack of causal efficiency and the inability to withstand analysis belong to cognition alone, not to an external object; what more than this could be required?
This reflection pertains only to manifestation; even its scent does not exist externally.
Since its similarity to a "snake's horn" is thus established, why is the goal not accomplished?
The designation of a "heap of form" occurs among appearances that seem to exist externally;
since feeling and perception are not distinct from mental formations, why are they not considered non-different by you?
The very root of non-manifestation is poorly established, because its existence cannot be maintained;
for that which exists in the nature of manifestation, no other property can be a sublater.
If, due to that same fault, even luminosity is far removed from existence,
then what else will non-luminosity establish regarding non-existence?
Non-existence belongs to that which lacks luminosity, but not to luminosity by its own nature.
Therefore, it is said that this [object] is non-existent; however, this is not tenable with respect to a conceptual construction.
Furthermore, for that which is manifesting, its reality arises precisely from its manifestation;
even in the case of hair, its non-existence is determined by its very appearance as a matted mass.

For this very reason, even in the case of blue and other objects considered to be manifest, it is precisely causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that has been declared to be their reality; without that, there is no distinction between the two.
And because it is followed by mere activity, consciousness also is impermanent;
however, when there is an absence of activity in this [consciousness], its existence is primary, because it appears [as such].
At that time, its momentariness and existence do not deviate from one another;
since existence consists in causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), that proof is not faulty.
Or else, even for that [cognition], there is no other state once its impermanence has been set aside;
it is simply the awareness of that very moment, otherwise there would be no distinction whatsoever.
If it is argued that this causal relationship has therefore arrived [as a reality], then surely there is no negation here of the conventional; its momentariness, too, is merely conventional.
If it were eternal in reality, it would not exist even conventionally;
if you argue that it exists because impermanence is negated, even so, how could there be any understanding of it?

Having placed some entity before oneself, one might speak of difference and non-difference according to distinctions of place, time, and so forth; but what sequence could there be in that which is merely one's own self-awareness?
The intrinsic nature of cognition neither joins with nor is divided from other things;
for the distinction between self and other is merely the empty ornamentation of the intellect.
The so-called "ineffability" of anything else indicates the existence of its own intrinsic nature;
that very form is the reality, and it is established in non-duality.
For the wise person, O learned one, necessarily attains what is certain;
activity and cessation do not occur merely through a mistaken cognition.
First, the aspect of the grasper differentiates itself from the grasped object,
by way of distinctions such as location and form, and likewise from other grasped objects.
Otherwise, non-duality alone would shatter that very absence of difference;
therefore, distinction and non-distinction are restricted to duality, and not so in non-duality.
And as long as one perceives a distinction of time for the sake of awakening from a dream,
this cognition is swallowed by another conceptualization through its exhaustion, just like any other.
Therefore, what is called "permanence" exists neither in reality nor conventionally;
yet, even though it lacks the nature of momentariness, let it be apprehended just as inference is.
