Even the conventional usage of "variegated" and "one" is considered to be directed toward the exclusion of difference;
for here, only the pure manifestation exists, devoid of both unity and plurality.
What is the use of a manifestation that, though existent, is devoid of all causal power?
Since there is no capacity for action, no effect could arise; yet where would its own essential nature go?
If even the nature of illumination is not found upon investigation,
we recognize that investigation as inference (*anumāna*), and it does not invalidate direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If the errors regarding the *guñjā* berry and fire were sublated even though they were produced by the sense organ,
then since the error concerns the form of another object, why would there not be error regarding the sense organ's own nature?
If you claim that a means of valid cognition is not a means of valid cognition, the occasion for investigation is destroyed;
for by speaking thus, you must necessarily be asserting something either to be established or to be refuted.
In that case, what kind of praise could there be for one who speaks unreasonably in an assembly?
There is no reasoning superior to inference; what, then, is established by disregarding it?

If it is argued that because she has been accepted by him, he is therefore awakened by her cognition, then since he accepts her even when she is not sublated, how could he not be awakened by the cognition of her?
If it is argued that there is nothing to be proven, then the sublation itself would also be something to be proven.
To say "that too is not" is a useless statement; what purpose is served by such a mere question?

If the fruit [of speech] were nowhere else than in the awakening [of understanding], then words would be capable of conveying meaning; it is not the case that sense-organs, smoke, and so forth are beautiful [in this regard].
If cause and effect are merely conventional, by what means could their existence be apprehended?
Certainly, the cognition of the cause arises from the effect; otherwise, vows and the like would be futile.
Even one who, tormented by heat, approaches sandalwood and not fire—
without relying on something, it is impossible to speak even a single word of knowledge.
If logical arguments are set forth after having introduced some subject matter, why is there no taking of a position in the treatise? If not, by whom could it be grasped?
When asked about the path to liberation, if one were to explain the cultivation of emptiness,
then while awakening [others] to emptiness, how could one possibly censure the grasping at a position?
Therefore, whether the probandum or the proof depends upon consciousness, it is unavoidable; thus, the acceptance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is unavoidable.
If you claim that measurement is accepted within the conventional, then this very investigation is also conventional.
If you do not accept it even within the conventional, then one who speaks thus is a victor in every way.
Just as the cause and effect are conventional, so too is the corresponding cognition;
for one who accepts inference, there is no such certainty that perception is not [conventional].
If it is argued that there is dispute regarding self-cognition, [we reply] no, because it is established precisely by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Therefore, even if it is not ultimate (*aparamārtha*), cognition as it is grasped is subversive [of opposing claims].

If it is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), where is the extraction [of the ultimate]? Let the ultimate (*paramārtha*) be just that much. And therefore, how could that which is conventional be abandoned within conventional reality itself?
If it is argued that the conventional usage of existence for the mind follows from its luminosity,
how can it be compared to that which possesses neither luminosity nor capacity?
Therefore, without contradicting the fact that it appears while possessing properties such as being unable to withstand analysis,
let that [nature of appearing] belong to the mind alone.
The establishment of the mind is based upon luminosity.
The non-existence that is asserted of that whose nature is luminosity is not a flaw, for it is in reference to an existence imagined by oneself; however,
the other [nature], which is the luminosity itself, is substantially real.
The two are equal in the proof of worldly established entities:
that which has the nature of manifesting what is non-existent is not real, nor is it real in the sense of being other than that;
by one there is not a pair, and by those two there is no non-duality.
If the world were thus devoid of the four peaks,
what would be the distinction between the views of the Commentator and those of the Madhyamaka?
For those for whom even causal efficiency exists only in the ultimate sense,
and for whom even that which has the nature of luminosity is negated—
let there be a distinction between them; however, it is naturally difficult to overcome.
This path for the knower of the self has as its essence the burden of daring.
This has been introduced as a digression in accordance with the opponent’s subsequent argument; enough of this elaboration.
It is established that, by virtue of being manifest, the three worlds are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
[365,17] Thus ends this treatise, the *Advaitabindu*.
The Treatise Establishing Cognitions with Aspects (Sākārasiddhiśāstra)
[Chapter One] Homage to Samantabhadra, whose form is profound and vast, who has shaken off the web of conceptual construction, and whose radiance shines everywhere. (PV I 1)

May he who is the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the *Vārttika* concerning the doctrine of the Lord of Munis, the stage-manager for the drama of the perspective that establishes the existence of mental aspects (*sākārasiddhi*), and the one whose pride first flourishes upon the paths of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa— may he be victorious!
The glory of valor that is difficult for all heroic enemies to overcome.
This entire triple world exists as nothing but representation-only;
herein, the relative strength and weakness of its internal distinctions is now explained.
For it is thus: by means of the sequence beginning with the refutation of external objects,
[it is shown that] this external object does not exist at all, because it is of the nature of manifestation, and because it is necessarily perceived simultaneously [with consciousness].
By reason, nothing else is possible here; even if it were possible, it would not possess the characteristic of being an object of apprehension. Therefore, this is mere cognition.
The world possesses diverse forms, such as white, the notes *gāndhāra* and *madhyama*, fragrant, soft, pleasant, and their opposites. And so says the Sūtra:

"O Sons of the Victor, this triple world is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* has, through a succession of great efforts, illuminated the theory of aspects (*sākāravāda*) specifically regarding external objects. If it is asked, "How then can this be said to be the original discovery of the author of the *Bhāṣya*? [the answer follows].

Because it has been formulated by others according to the direction of the aspectless (nirākāra), it is said that he has established it as if it were merely abiding in existence; however, it is not his own original invention.
Regarding this, others say: "Let white, pleasure, and so forth have the nature of being solely luminosity, yet they are empty of intrinsic nature."

[367,23] However, they are not able to transcend it. If the reasoning characterized by the absence of being one or many is brought forward to conceive of an external object as impossible, [368,1] that reasoning does not fear such things as white and so forth, which possess the nature of consciousness. Therefore, the emptiness of all phenomena alone is superior, as has been proclaimed many times in the Āgamas. Also in the *Vārttika*:
"In whatever way objects are analyzed, they fall apart in that very way" (PV III 209cd).
Thus, the system of consciousness is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti-mātra*).
Regarding this, others offer the following resolution: because it sublates the things produced by you, their unreality is established, whereas mere manifestation is real.

[368,7] There is no such traditional teaching, because the self-cognition of that [light] is perception (*pratyakṣa*), given that it is impossible for it to be erroneous. Since light has light itself as its innate nature (*nijam rūpam*), that nature is not brought about by a distortion (*viplava*); therefore, the cognition of it could not be an error. Blue, however, being a different form, may indeed be brought about by a distortion; thus, the cognition of it could be an error. Consequently, there is no scope for a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) regarding blue and the like.

[368,10] Regarding illumination (*prakāśa*): it should be understood that in all cases, what is negated is the imagined and the unreal. (Cf. *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* 167b8–168a3; Kajiyama 1965) [368,11] Here it is considered: what is this so-called "illumination" that is distinct from blue and other such objects? For if it were not distinct, there would be no cessation of the fear of contradiction. Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for something distinct. First of all, it is not perception, because [perception consists of] those things whose nature is being illuminated...

Because it is impossible to perceive anything other than blue; nor can there be inference, since for that which has never experienced perceptibility at any time, the apprehension of a relation with anything else is untenable.
Furthermore,
Luminosity is cognized within one's own continuum through inference by means of an object that is beyond the senses; what greater insult could there be than this?

It is evident that this view has taken refuge in the system of Śabarasvāmin; what more need be said here? Thus, this perceived self, being unperceived as distinct from jars and other such objects, cannot become the object of the conventional usage of "existence," just like universals and the like.
Otherwise, there would be no negation of those [universals] either.
If it is argued that because permanence is accepted, [the object] is non-existent due to the absence of succession and so forth, we reply:
no, for there is no absence of the pervader of valid cognition when one disregards the non-perception of what is perceptible.

Or how could there be a negation of the qualities, actions, and so forth of a horn? This is merely a triviality. Now, if you argue that when blue is perceived in its nature as consciousness (*bodharūpa*), the perception of both the blue and the conscious self is impossible to deny, and thus non-perception is not established;
then, when a brindled cow is being perceived, how can one who objects on the grounds of perceiving both natures be refuted? For there is no separate perception [of them].

But that [non-difference] is common [to all]. If it is argued that the non-separate mention of light and blue is due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), then the same will apply to qualities (*guṇa*) and substances (*dravya*).

If there is an insistence on the negation of inherence (*samavāya*), then a doubt remains as to whether the non-perception of them as distinct is due to the power of ignorance or simply because of their non-existence;
such a doubt is possible for both cases. It is possible [to say] that the very perception of that [object] is the perception of its action and so forth, even in the case of a blade of grass.
Or, as in the case of a hundred elephants:
if that form which has attained visibility is not seen separately,
how can it exist when blue is scattered in a hundred directions?
Therefore,
universal properties and the like do not exist, just as they do not exist in the case of distinct entities such as white and so forth, which appear as partless.
Likewise, another illumination is also non-existent; therefore, when white and other such things are sublated, how could there be the possibility of non-sublation?
Furthermore:
if the distinction of location were to differ according to each individual self,
then the appearances would likewise differ for two people who perceive the same object with an identical cognition, because they are perceived as such.

For, due to the extreme similarity between a magical illusion and a ball, there is indeed a single cognition even when they exist at different times; however, when they exist at the same time but in different locations, a sharp distinction in appearance occurs, which is necessarily accompanied by the ascertainment of their difference. Therefore, when there is a difference in location, there is an unimpeded difference in manifestation and its subsequent ascertainment.
In a location, there is only a distinct form and not another form, nor is there another location.

If it is argued that there is indeed a difference in intrinsic nature between wind and sunlight even when their location is not different, we say no; for these two arise as the forms of composite wholes (*avayavin*), and thus, being solid and possessing resistance (*sapratigha*), they cannot occupy each other's space. However, a mass of atoms (*paramāṇunikara*) may intermingle.
[It] reaches [it]. And that being so, why is a collection of wind, heat, and dust, which has a distinct nature and occupies a distinct location, not [considered to reach it]?

Therefore, just as there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too is there a difference in location (*deśa*); thus, what is called "location" is not something other than the essential form (*svarūpa*) itself. Consequently, when that [intrinsic nature] is non-different, the manifestation (*prakāśa*) is likewise non-different in its essential form.
Similarly, if one accepts the aggregation of atoms (*aṇu-saṃhati*), the same fault would apply.
Even in the case of a gross resistance, the same fault applies due to the differentiation of location.
Furthermore, pervasion here would otherwise be terminated, because in a fragment there is the occurrence of appearing in a different manner;
therefore, by virtue of that, [the manifestation of] white and so forth persists only as long as the persistence of the illumination.

For as far as the location of a form such as blue extends, if there were an absence of pervasion over that extent, it would follow that blue and so forth would appear as fragmented; this is because of their dependence on that [pervasion], and by virtue of the manifestation of distinct intended aspects. Therefore, for as long as there is the manifestation of white and so forth, there must be the persistence of that which is called "manifestation" over that same extent. Consequently, even for that [manifestation] which pervades that much space, when one considers its nature in terms of parts and atoms—just as in the case of blue—[it follows that it is not a single, partless entity].

Furthermore, there is no liberation because of common defects; therefore, when blue and so forth are negated, nothing remains, because there is an absence of difference itself, due to the absence of any distinction in appearance.

[370,10] Now, even if two moments appear as non-different, their difference is established through a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), and it is the same here as well. For just as the presence and absence of a specific effect—which would otherwise be inexplicable—prove the difference between those two, so too does the occurrence of the subverting argument prove the difference between manifestation (*prakāśa*) and blue. Therefore, if it is argued that manifestation, being unsublated, is indeed distinct from the blue which is sublated, we reply: [370,12] It is said:

Non-sublation (*abādhyatā*) is twofold, distinguished as *paryudāsa* (exclusion) and *prasajya* (absolute negation). Even *paryudāsa*, when its object is the subject at hand—as in the case of "one who is not to be touched" (*aspṛśya*) and so forth—would merely bring about another form of sublation, because it excludes a genus, like "non-Brahmin" which excludes a Kṣatriya.
If this so-called non-sublation is considered to be established by the force of valid cognition (*pramiti*), [then it is indeed non-sublation].
Not even a single valid cognition is capable of establishing a distinction within self-awareness, which is by nature non-dual.
Furthermore, since the absence of sublation is common to both cases when there is no such cognition,
how could it manifest a distinction between the two cognitions that are not perceived as different?

For in the case of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the meaning of "non-sublation" is merely the non-appearance of sublation. And that [non-appearance of sublation] is the same even when the existence [of the object] is doubtful;
how, then, could it establish that the manifestation (*prakāśa*) has the nature of a distinct entity from blue and so forth?
If it is argued: "There is no doubt regarding the establishment of their distinct natures, because blue and so forth are sublatable while the manifestation is unsublatable," we reply: not so.

Because non-sublation consists merely in the non-appearance of a sublater, when there is doubt regarding existence, it is impossible to establish a distinct nature even from a blue object that has been sublated.
For this very reason, it was stated that "there is doubt regarding the term.
However, in the case of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), its avoidance is impossible due to the force of other sublaters; there is no hope for a proof as fragile as this.

And it cannot be argued that the same applies here as well. For in that case, the sequence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) may sometimes be perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in relation to gross time, as in the case of fetching honey or water; yet at other times, even if it is imperceptible in relation to moments (*kṣaṇa*), it would necessarily imply a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) due to its inherent capacity. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of non-existence in a moment where all activity has ceased, for one cannot perform what has already been performed.
Because it is possible.

It is logical that this sequence of effects cannot transcend the sequence of causes; however, here, nothing established by perception or arrived at through functional capacity is found to be accomplished by mere luminosity alone. Nor is there, through analytical abstraction, any establishment of a distinction among effects.

Furthermore, a real differentiation of the self-nature cannot logically exist within that which appears as non-different at once, except insofar as it is situated in mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). This is like the reddish form of light in a lamp, which serves to illuminate and color the darkness, the shadows, and the gaps. And this reflection concerns that which appears as non-different; for there is no appearance of non-difference among moments (*kṣaṇa*), since what is manifested is a form pervading every fraction of time.

[371,8] Because it would follow that everything would be perceived all at once as a totality across the three times. Furthermore, even if such a distinction in effects were not amenable to perceptual convention, it could not serve to differentiate the cause according to its states of existence and non-existence. For if they are grasped as one, then whatever state—whether existence or non-existence—the effect has in one moment, that very same state must persist in the subsequent moment as well.
Because there is no separation [between the object and its cognition].

Therefore, just as its object is a producer by means of a form that lasts for only a single moment, so too this sensory cognition conforms to it and is the grasper by means of that very same form. However, the conceptual determination (avasāya) obscures its [the cognition's] actual operation; in this case, however, it is the appearance [that matters].

Thus, it is experienced even more clearly as being without distinction. Nevertheless, what offense has been committed by a thousand limiting conditions (*upādhi*) if one still postulates a distinction?

Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no other means of exclusion than non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Therefore, this non-sublation (*abādhā*), when asserted while the non-perception of the perceptible is possible, collapses of its own accord and does not require any further argument.
Furthermore, if there were a sublation here and not there, it would have to occur when the two appear as distinct.
If there is no appearance of that constituent part, how can there be a state of non-establishment for it therein?
Even if the reason (hetu) were established therein, it cannot be considered effective.
Surely it is not connected with the probandum; therefore, it is not capable even with respect to the mental image.
An object, by proving its own nature or its cause without deviation,
does not cease from being a nature even when it contradicts someone's argument.
But surely, luminosity indeed appears to embodied beings within blue and other such objects;
why then is it not capable of being established when it is manifest, provided there is no sublation regarding that alone?
What is the point of stating that it does not manifest its own blue nature? For there is no effort here to assert the absence of sublation for that very thing itself.
If it is argued that there is no manifestation of blue, what could be more reckless than this? For if blue were to have a manifestation, what further manifestation could there be beyond that?
Even if its manifestation were to arise from something else, it would still be impossible to prevent.

If its manifestation does not come from anything else, yet its manifestation is something entirely other, then that blue object would not be manifested; for what does it have to do with the manifestation of something else?
And because the relation itself is sublated, there is no coordination expressed by "its";
even if the genitive case were obtained, a confusion of forms would be impossible in any way.
Therefore, its manifestation is undeniable from whatever source it may arise;
and when that is not sublated, there is no result, nor is there anything at all consisting of that alone.
However, let that which is intended and well-established be stated according to your own conviction;
by this very means, the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is eliminated, and for this same reason, the logical reasons (*hetu*) are also established.
If it is argued that objects established as being uncontradicted are those produced by conceptual construction,
then because such an object is equivalent to a mere mental construct, there is no validity in establishing a positive injunction.
If existence is established only by non-contradiction, then that [non-contradiction] would be the reason for existence;
thus a circular argument arises, which dispels this illusion.
Furthermore, even if there is no sublation, it is set aside when a sublation manifests;
but in its absence, such a state of doubt is indeed established.
But if one relies upon the property of being a member of a series (*vargadharma*), it does not escape the fault of circularity (*cakraka*).
Let there be a substratum (*āśraya*); however, let the cause that subverts the subverter be stated.
Furthermore, it has been shown that self-awareness itself does not exist as something distinct.
Nor is it logical for you to maintain that there is even a cognition [of an object] based solely on self-awareness,
since even when there is self-awareness of blue and so forth, sublation may still occur.
If self-awareness does not belong to the blue, why does it not appear? It is impossible to say that "it should be made to appear by another."

Because the cognition of another by means of another has been refuted at length elsewhere. If it is argued that there is no "other" because of its non-existence, let there be no "otherness"; however, by the mere possibility of "selfhood," the establishment of that cognition is achieved through that alone, and nothing further is required, since its nature consists solely in self-cognition (*svavid*).
If it is argued that there is no fault because of an imagined identity (*tādātmya*), this is merely a deception of the ignorant; for [the object] exists only as a manifestation.
For the conceptualization of identity and the appearance produced by it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

If you argue that the conceptualization does not arise from the appearance itself, but rather from the determination (*avasāya*) of the appearance, then that determination of the appearance must also arise from the appearance; thus, let there be a circular argument (*cakraka*): the appearance arises from the conceptualization of identity, and from that [appearance] comes its determination.

[373,5] "Therefore, that is a conceptual construction" (tatkalpanam). If it is argued that even this conceptual construction does not arise from the conceptualization of identity (*tādātmya*), but rather from that identity which has been made the object of conceptual construction, [we reply: no, because that [identity] did not exist prior to the conceptual construction; otherwise, its status as a conceptual construct would be untenable. Furthermore, nothing that is a conceptual construct is ever observed to be effective in any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); were it so, [it would be a real entity].
Because it would follow that [the object] is nothing other than reality itself.
By this, the claim that it has the nature of being unreal (*alīka*) is also refuted, because unreality is untenable if there is some utility [in it].
Otherwise, there would be no insistence on negation regarding an action that is merely nominal; for even that which is manifest may be useful in certain instances.

If it is argued that falsity [of the object] is not contradictory because of sublation (*bādhanāt*), then it is not so; for manifestation (*prakāśa*) cannot be sublated. Furthermore, if the sublater does not even sublate its utility (*upayoga*) in any respect, why must the sublater necessarily be defined as a "sublater"? From where, then, could there be an identity with falsity? Alternatively, if it is argued that it sublates the causal capacity of the object through implication (*sāmarthyāt*) rather than directly, let it be so; what is the point of insistence here regarding the sublation of capacity?
Since it is established that identity is not applicable because it is unreal, this point is settled.

Furthermore, as for the claim that consciousness alone—being of the nature of luminosity—is manifest, yet appears through forms such as blue and so forth due to the affliction of beginningless erroneous predispositions (*vāsanā*), appearing as if deluded like in dreams and the like; that too is refuted by this.
[373,17] It is refuted.

[373,18] Since no entity named "consciousness" is perceived apart from blue and so forth, this is merely a proclamation of a theoretical system. Furthermore, the example of a dream is devoid of the probandum. Moreover, since there is an absence of causal power due to such falsity, in the case of the intention to express something as being "thus"—namely, "blue and so forth"—[the argument fails].

[373,20] Furthermore, since it has been clearly stated that the object is merely a simultaneous manifestation, its lack of being manifest is evident. Therefore, how can there be a transgression of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? If it is argued that "it appears in such a way due to the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), and thus it will indeed be manifest," [373,22] if this were the case, then ignorance itself would be the cause, not the illuminator. For that which is of the nature of illumination cannot [arise] from that [ignorance].

[373,23] Its arising is like that of a lamp from its own cause; how, then, could there be the destruction of its self-illumination? [373,24] Even so, if the state of being illuminated by another were established, it would follow that even experience [is thus]; therefore, nothing at all is called "self-illuminating. [373,25] Nevertheless, because self-cognition is impossible, existence is not established anywhere. Thus, this is not a valid principle.
[373,26] In relation to that which produces the form of illumination, its cessation is self-awareness; thus, it is established that blue and so forth also possess self-awareness.

[373,27] Now, if it is argued that because non-blue is unreal (*alīka*), it cannot be an effect, and therefore there is merely illumination—either by ignorance or by light—and that for experience (*anubhava*), since it is a real entity (*vastu*), it is simply said to be produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)? That too is trivial. Experience, too...

For it is precisely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) that the object is established; therefore, the so-called "unreality" (*alīkatva*) of blue consists in its absence [from that awareness], and its absence follows from its unreality, which acts as an obstacle to its being an effect.

Furthermore, whether blue is unreal or not, how can its status as an effect be denied? For an entity (*bhāva*) whose own nature (*svabhāva*) is established in dependence upon the operation of another is called an "effect" (*kārya*).
Thus, because it occurs only occasionally, this blue is proven to have a cause.
[374,7] A cause must either always exist or never exist, because it does not depend on anything else.

[374,8] In this same way, the lack of restriction regarding place and so forth should also be understood. Furthermore, there is nothing else that serves as the basis for the conventional designation of "being an effect" apart from dependence on another—namely, the state of being established by the restriction of place and time. Otherwise, even experience itself would not exist.

Therefore, regarding this person who, while taking as the object of their mere faith something of that very kind, rejects the postulation of its arising from a certain observed thing because another form is not seen to arise—what can we say to him? By this, the argument that "even in the case of coming into being after non-existence, there is no status as an effect because of the absence of causal capacity" is refuted, since causal capacity is established according to the sequence already stated. As for that which is an object of faith, let it be considered that it is not observed; let there be no such capacity.

[374,13] But what prevents its being an effect (*kāryatva*) by virtue of arising in dependence upon another? For its exclusion from that [other] has not been removed. [374,14] Alternatively, if being an effect is a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*), and there is no such thing as a real entity without causal capacity (*śakti*), then let there be capacity as well; for we observe that being an effect, which is a property of a real entity, is pervaded by that [capacity]. [374,15] If it is argued that because of the absence of capacity, that very [entity] does not exist, we say no, because that is unproven (*asiddha*).

[374,16] But there is no doubt regarding its being an effect, just like any other effect. Therefore, if there is an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) between being an effect and having power (*śakti*), let power be inferred in some instance; it cannot be rejected by mere non-perception (*anūhamātra*). However, in the absence of such a connection, its status as an effect is established. [374,18] Thus, how can it be said that "because blue is not an effect, it is not produced by causes consisting of mere manifestation," since it is not...

[374,19] "Self-cognition" (svasaṃvedana). [374,20] Furthermore, if there were the possibility of another unperceived substratum such that some illumination belongs to someone by means of something else, then—due to the determination of non-difference between preceding and succeeding moments—it might even be said, as in the case of a jar and so forth, that it is [illuminated] by light; but what kind of [illumination] could there be in the case of that which is admitted to be false?
[374,22] Is this a misconception? However, the arising of what was previously non-existent is not contradictory, provided that it occurs through manifestation just as it does through blueness.

Or, let there be no effect-ness (*kāryatva*) in any way; even then, if there were a necessity of dependence on another, there would still be the suspicion of being manifested by another. If there were total independence in every respect, then the absence of self-awareness for all aspects would be beyond doubt. And in that case, when sublation is observed here, it would apply elsewhere as well.
The absence of confidence in existence is established. Alternatively:
if it is held that [the object] is distinct from blue by virtue of being uncontradicted, then from where does the removal of contradiction come?
If it is argued that it comes from the absence of superimposition, then, since this result of non-contradiction depends on mutual existence, there is a circularity.
They say that blue is indeed sublated when it is superimposed. In that case, how could the very result of being sublated—namely, non-superimposition—be capable of establishing non-sublation?
If you argue that this is the very nature of consciousness, then why is it not so for the nature of blue itself?

For just as the very nature of light is illumination itself, and it is not said that this is brought about by an error, so too the very nature of blue is blueness itself; even if it were said that this is not brought about by an error regarding it, that would not cause one's face to contort.
Furthermore, the operation of logic does not function through partiality, such that one thing would be to be accepted and another discarded. Otherwise, apart from illumination—

There is no persistence of blue, nor is there a persistence of manifestation even in the absence of blue. If it is argued that it exists in yellow, let it be so; however, it is not a property of blue.

If you argue that this is because of the commonality of the term "manifestation," then, in view of the manifestation of the property of yellow, the persistence of blue—even when devoid of manifestation—would be a subject for denial.

Therefore, the notion that "this very form belongs to that" is not a conceptual construction restricted solely to manifestation; for it is precisely because of its non-superimposed nature that one gains confidence in its freedom from sublation. In that case, let the distinction between the two be established effortlessly through their mutual deviation. We recall the example of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), since it is impossible to demonstrate [the distinction between] cloth and water. [This applies to] those characterized by persistence and change.
[375,15] "It is precisely because of the non-perception of two contradictory properties residing in a designated substratum that you yourselves are the authority in this matter.

[375,16] Therefore, enough with being under the sway of dogmatic attachment! For that which is to be believed as having that very nature, [375,17] if it appears in such a way to one whose mind is focused solely on conceptual construction, why would it not be so?"

The blue object possesses reality; its sole additional fault in establishing its existence is that it appears as having an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, this is an unprecedented method for dispelling sublation, namely the claim that "its very essence is reality. For even that which is subject to sublation—such as *pradhāna*, *sāmānya*, and so forth—is likewise [subject to this critique].
Whatever appears or is conceptualized in whatever form, that very thing is its reality (*tattva*).
Whether that [reality] exists or otherwise, there is room for sublation (*bādhaka*) in both cases by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This applies whether it concerns blue or a manifestation; if at most there is a distinction in the occurrence of defects such as non-establishment (*asiddhi*), there is a distinction in the operation [of the cognition], but not in the object itself.
[375,24] On the grounds that it is reality (*tattva*).
Furthermore, [375,25] that which is superimposed is merely imagined (*kalpita*) and is sublatable; they say that which possesses manifestation is false and is sublatable.
[375,26] Therefore, reality must reside solely in the imagined; otherwise, how could it not be restricted to the perceived alone?

Being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is spoken of only in conventional usage regarding that which is imagined (*kalpita*) and subject to sublation, just like water [in a mirage]. However, they designate even that which is manifest as false (*alīka*) when it is sublated, like a double moon. Therefore, if you wish to say that even the visible (*dṛśya*) is superimposed, let it be so said. But from where does this [notion] come that the visible itself is superimposed? Consequently, the imagined is not [the object] apart from the removal of superimposition.

[376,4] This is established as distinct from what is proven by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, only that which is established or sublated by valid cognition is fit for investigation. [376,5] However, the emergence of sublation or establishment does not occur merely because such is its reality.
[376,6] Thus, this distinction is also made: blue and so forth are conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), because they are sublated even while being perceived.

However, consciousness whose very body is luminosity (*prakāśa*) and which manifests as blue and so forth is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) and because it possesses powers established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it appears as if it were merely placed in one's hand. For if luminosity were distinct from the blue, then the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), like the blue itself, would not be withdrawn from the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) merely by one’s lack of desire; this and more has already been stated.

[376,10] Furthermore, what kind of sublation could there be for that which is intended as manifest, if it were not manifest? Moreover, it was stated immediately after that capacity (*śakti*) also has only the form (*ākāra*) as its object.

[376,12] And this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) appears to be brought about by mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), like the case of "producedness" and "impermanence," and not directly.

[376,13] It appears as distinct, like a pair of *yāmala* fruits or like two moons. And when the substratum (*dharmin*) appears as divided, it is possible to ascertain that "this property (*dharma*) is possible here, and that is not possible here. This is because, specifically in the case of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), it is only a real property (*vastudharma*) that can be introduced by its opposite. [376,15] Furthermore, every means of establishing difference is merely a means of establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), for nowhere is there [any distinction] without the association of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*).

Because their difference is unestablished. Otherwise, how could there be such a thing as non-difference? Furthermore, two contradictory properties are not differentiated by mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*).

Rather, they must be understood through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as having distinct loci; for if they were perceived as being without a locus or as having the same locus, there would be no operation of either valid or invalid cognition, nor would there be the establishment of contradiction. And if those two are established as having different substrata (*dharmin*), what else remains?

[376,19] Is it the determination that establishes the difference between the substrata (*dharmin*)? [376,20] Precisely for this reason, the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) has as its basis cognition and ascertainment (*nirṇaya*). In that regard, the establishment of the difference between substrata occurs in some cases by way of spatial distinction (*deśabheda*), like two eyeballs (*golaka*); in other cases, by way of temporal distinction (*kālabheda*). It is with reference to this that it is said: "Precisely for this reason, there is a difference in the entity (*vastubheda*) between those two states."

[376,22] "To be determined" means that even there, one cannot point out: "this is the state of being in a granary," or "this is the state of being in a field. Since the difference in time is not demonstrated, the distinction based on performing or not performing an action can be pointed out;
and since the establishment of the distinction is concluded by that much alone, the presentation of action and non-action serves merely as a means for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Where...

[376,25] However, there is no delineation of distinction by way of place or time; in that case, the only recourse is either a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*) or a difference in the sense faculties (*indriya*).

[376,26] This is like the color, taste, and so forth of a beverage, or like the Cārvāka’s own admission regarding the intellect and the body. For he [the Cārvāka], when forming a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a mountain and the like—which is dissimilar to the body with its hands, feet, and other features—by what form could it be a conceptual construction of a mountain and the like in the absence of an example? [376,27]

How could one distinguish them? Where there is not even a trace of a difference in appearance other than from the form of conceptual construction, as in the case of a blue lotus and so forth, there is indeed an ultimate non-difference.
For that which is not thus—namely, where there is no unity in the experience of non-difference—is possessed of distinction.
If it were established that there is no means of proof, on what basis could difference and non-difference depend?
This is an intermediate verse.

Therefore, the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by sublation and non-sublation cannot effect a linguistic convention of difference for a substratum (*dharmin*) without a difference in its appearance. A proof of difference, being merely a form of proving existence, does not incur the threefold class of logical fallacies.
[377,8] It oversteps [the logical bounds]. As for what is also said: "Whatever is neither one nor many in a certain form, that is not real in that form;
for example, suffering in the form of pleasure. And consciousness is neither one nor many in the form of blue and so forth"—this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
[377,9–10] That too is refuted by this very [argument] and is merely a matter of personal satisfaction. For it is not understood, or rather, it does not cognize.
The nature of consciousness is held to be based on its functional activity (*vyāpāra*), because that is excluded elsewhere; however, its essential nature is self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*).

And since that luminosity does not exist in that [non-conscious] form, what is intended is not merely the negation of identity (*tādātmya-niṣedha*), but rather that it simply does not exist by way of its own nature.

By this, the objection that "the fault would likewise apply" is also refuted; otherwise, there would be no establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with respect to the son of a barren woman.

[377,15] This would also lead to the consequence [of proving everything] by mere exclusion (*vyavacchedamātra*). Consequently, since the distinction [between things] is established solely through sublation (*bādhā*) and non-sublation (*abādhā*), no additional object is apprehended by us; thus, this is already understood by that alone. Nevertheless, something will be said here. In this context of proving the manifestation (*prakāśa*) as distinct from the mental form (*ākāra*), manifestation must be established by inference even while it remains unmanifested.

That which is appearing must be established as distinct from the word-form; however, in either case, within the context of establishing a positive proof (*vidhisādhana*), what occasion is there for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)? Even if it exists with a form imparted by that [word], if there is no cessation of the suspicion of its non-existence in its own nature—as in the case of a horn—how can its difference be established?

[377,21] Now, if the non-existence of those two is intended to be of the very nature of another entity, then a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) must always be employed, because the subject of dispute is a positive affirmation (*vidhi*). [377,22] However, when someone might doubt that it could exist even in the absence of that [other entity], then the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is appropriate in relation to that alone. Furthermore, there is no occasion for the suspicion of existence even when [an entity] is devoid of being one or many. It is not so.

And if one intends to state the opposite, it is secure. For in that case, it must be shown that whatever exists in a certain form is either one or many with respect to that form. However, neither an example nor the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) can be successfully established here. Indeed, mere luminosity is not established anywhere because nothing else exists; so how could there be an example, or where could there be an application of the property of the subject, given the absence of any other means of proof?
Or, if it were the means of proving that, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, if one holds the position that "manifestation exists by way of its nature as manifestation," then at the time of formulating the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*), there is no avoidance of the charge of apprehending something irrelevant (*aprakṛtopalambha*).

For there is no dispute regarding unity and plurality in terms of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*); rather, the dispute concerns whether there is difference or non-difference with respect to the aspect (*ākāra*). This is so for those who dispute unity and plurality.

Or how could there be the establishment of existence? If it is argued that blue and so forth are non-existent precisely because of the impossibility [of their being either one or many], then what is the point of the effort to present that [argument]? For even in the absence of that [argument], existence is established through the force of negation (*prasajya-śakti*).
Otherwise, if there were doubt regarding it, how could one establish it? And that will be considered later.
[378,6] Now, if you mean that "the state of being one or many" refers to its own nature (*svarūpa*), and therefore existence is intended to be established by that very nature;

[378,7] even then, when the question is asked, "What is this nature of his by which there is a connection with oneness and manifoldness?"—if it is replied, "It is this very thing which is fit to be pointed out by the forefinger," [378,8] then [the objection remains]: "This is blue"; thus, the claim that "cognition is one or many by virtue of that" is undermined.

If, on the other hand, it is something else, that is not established. Or, if it were established, what would be the point of this [discussion]? Furthermore, that very objection remains in its original state.
For dispute occurs only when a distinct entity is established; but once that is established, there is no occasion for the question: "Does it exist even by way of another form?"

[378,12] Now, suppose it is argued: "This subject (*dharmī*), which is manifestation (*prakāśa*), is indeed established; when its non-existence in the form of blue and so forth is proven, its differentiation is obtained by implication (*sāmarthyalabdha*). Since the intended point is established by that much alone, there is no need to conform to a positive affirmation (*vidhi*); therefore, it is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) alone that is relevant to the present case. [378,14] This is a great display of cleverness! However, if manifestation, even though it is non-existent as blue and so forth due to ignorance (*avidyā*), were [to appear as such]...

In that same way, even by its own nature, what then could be established as a difference? Surely there is no suspicion of its non-existence, because it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), since there can be no error regarding its own nature. For the dispute concerns only difference. If such is the case, how can there be a sublation even of the blue? This has already been stated in such passages as "the nature of manifestation is manifestation itself. And it is possible—

One might say that the very nature of the manifestation of blue is the manifestation of blue itself, and so forth. Therefore, even if one were to reject the distinction [between them], if the self-experience (*svānubhava*)—by not providing an occasion for sublation—were to establish the existence of the manifestation, what does this matter?

Likewise, even if it lacks such power, what does this matter? For, just as in the case of the blue object, the distinction remains unestablished there as well, since the rejection of the "hand-off" (the relinquishing of the burden) has not been avoided.

[378.21] Now, if for the opponent manifestation is established as ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), then the very fact that it is distinct is the point of contention; therefore, the proof of the thesis—that manifestation is indeed existent, but not of the nature of blue—is established. In that case, however, this cleverness (*vaidagdhī*) is merely the exhaustion of all means and the final limit of logic. This deserves to be treated with derision, according to the logic used by the proponent of self (*ātmavādin*) to establish the non-existence of a self (*nairātmyasiddhi*). Furthermore, in this proof, regarding the two things which appear as non-different...

The intended meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) is the distinction between the experience and its form. The reason (*hetu*) is the absence of being one or many in that very nature. Furthermore, it is not possible to demonstrate in an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of this [reason] with the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*). This is because even there, a manifestation distinct from forms such as suffering and so forth is unestablished (*asiddha*). Even if it were established, one could not say "just as the pleasant is by means of the unpleasant," nor "just as the experience of suffering is by means of the form of suffering and so forth."
This is logical.

Otherwise, if the manifestation apprehended by one aspect were shown to be non-existent by means of another aspect, then the distinction would exist only in relation to that [other aspect]. Consequently, at the time of the probandum, the distinction of the blue aspect from the experience of yellow would be established. Therefore, if...

A distinction dependent upon self-luminosity cannot be demonstrated in the example; how then will it be established as the probandum (*sādhya*), given the total absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?
If it is argued that positive concomitance is stated here in a general sense—that "whatever is neither one nor many [is not self-luminous]"—that is incorrect. For:
Even if not explicitly stated, that which is pervaded by inquiry is considered to be the probandum (*sādhya*), like the self (*ātman*) in its own context.

This same principle applies to the proof of the eyes and other faculties being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*). Alternatively, regarding the statement "that which is neither one nor many," if what is intended is that "the object (*yat*) which appears as non-different is manifested by that (*yena*)," then one may analyze this in terms of a generality (*sāmānyena*).
[379,9] There is no concomitance in the case of a particular, and in the case of a universal, it is a proof of what is already established.

[379,11] Just as in the case of pleasure and pain, because the experiences of blue and yellow lack each other's form, their difference—drawn out by their non-existence in that [mutual] nature—is established; however, there is no impairment of perception, which grasps non-difference, in either case. The rest is like our *Bṛhadīśvaravāda*. Moreover, when...
"Furthermore, luminosity is neither one nor many, like blue and so forth"—this is the application (*upanaya*) of the reason to the thesis. In this regard, what is this so-called "luminosity"?

Is it the act of illuminating (*prakāśana*), or that which is illuminated (*prakāśate*)? Or is it some distinct entity denoted by the word "luminosity," established in dependence upon activities such as "it illuminates"?
This latter view has already been refuted.
In the first alternative, this so-called "manifestation" of manifesting blue, yellow, and so forth is merely a property (*dharma*).

Even though it appears as if distinct by way of excluding other differences, it is not capable of remaining indifferent when the conceptualizing intellect analyzes the form of the substratum (*dharmin*).
Therefore, how can a real distinction be established? For nowhere can properties exist apart from the form of the substratum.

[379,19] The existent exists, like qualities, actions, and so forth. However, in the view that it is the agent and the means of accomplishment, only blue and the like are manifested; thus, as before, its emptiness of that very form [is established].

[379,20–21] Furthermore, in the view that it is a distinct entity, if the term "is manifested" is used in a way that implies a grammatical coreferentiality (*anvaya*), then there must be something distinct from blue and the like.

Even if that which is sublated by the non-perception of the perceptible lacks existence in that form, there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*). Furthermore, even in the position of total destruction without residue (*niranvayanāśapakṣa*), there is no establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasiddhi*). And although one might avoid the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) by relying on the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) consisting of mere exclusions (*vyavacchedamātra*) therein, this still does not serve the purpose at hand. Now, if it is argued that this very perceived illumination (*prakāśa*) is the subject (*dharmin*), [we reply: surely "perceived" means appearing (*pratibhāsamāna*).

And that [light] is indeed blue; it is nothing other than that. If it is asked: "Is this not an effort precisely for the sake of proving something distinct from that? Why, then, is there such a request at the very outset?
[The reply is: Let whatever be your thesis to be proven; however, if there is such a thing as light, its established nature must be shown as the substratum for that proof.

[380,1] A subject (*dharmin*) that is a real entity (*vasturūpa*) is possible. However, if the subject were a non-entity or one whose status as a real entity is doubtful, merely out of deference to the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) between the probandum and the probans, then this rule would not apply; and the establishment of the matter at hand would be far off. Alternatively, if, in deference to the establishment of the matter at hand, the subject is light (*prakāśa*) as a real entity, then, being accepted as having a well-defined nature, it would necessarily be blue itself. In that case—

It follows that form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; nevertheless, the point at issue is not established. Nor can there be a persistence [of form] by means of a voidness that is other than it, for there is no hope for the absence of [intrinsic] characteristics (*anākāra*). Lest there be the suspicion of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*)—that one thing is established as empty of another form—even so, the purpose of the term "by that" (*tena*) is fulfilled.

Alternatively, according to the theory of cognition with aspects (*sākāravāda*), this is a negation of the external object as it is apprehended, just as there is a negation of the form of two moons in the case of one suffering from ophthalmia who sees two moons.

For everywhere it is only that which is superimposed (*āropita*) that is negated, and for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is always only the superimposition of externality upon their own internal aspect; otherwise, reality (*tattva*) would be lost. Therefore, the proof of the subject (*dharmin*) under discussion does not hold in the case of blue. Now, what is the point of this insistence on a specific qualification?

That which is called "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is considered, in general, to be the subject (*dharmin*). For if it were restricted to a particular [instance], there would follow the undesirable consequence of obstructing the presentation of the proof (*sādhana*), since the probandum (*sādhya*) would already be excluded.

Furthermore, no one employs a proof without having intended the probandum; nor is a subject ever presented with its probandum already discarded, as that would be equivalent to proving what is already established. Therefore, the emphasis is not placed on a restriction to a particular instance.
Or let it be so.

This very thing is that which is called "prior manifestation," regarding whose separation from blue you were in doubt; let there be an end to this longing. And the relationship between property and property-bearer (dharmadharmibhāva) is observed through a distinction in exclusion (vyāvṛtti), just as in the case of the essential nature as a reason (svabhāvahetu), where they are one and the same.
[380,16] "The property is characterized by exclusion; since the probandum is the state of being distinct from another, there is no fault whatsoever. That too is incoherent.
[380,17] Because:
[380,18] "The establishment of the probandum and the probans is tenable through mere exclusion."
But the nature of the substratum (dharmin) is indeed useful only when perceived through its differentiation.

For, since it is impossible to understand the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) without a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*), the establishment of reality for the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), which exist as fluctuating forms, depends solely upon their being grounded in the essential nature of the subject (*dharmin*). It does not depend on the subject’s own form also being a fluctuating entity, nor on mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); for this [reality] is not cognized through words such as "tree" unless the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is presented, [since] the distinction of exclusions...

However, it is required for the purpose of conventional linguistic distinction (*bhedavyavahāra*), not for the sake of establishing the existence of the subject (*dharmisattā*); for if it were not perceived as residing in a specific individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that very subject being unestablished. And just as, even when the subject—the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as "this object possessing branches" or "the word 'jar' perceived by the ear"—is perceived, there is no contradiction and thus one proceeds with the proof (*sādhana*) when there is doubt regarding the tree's momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and so forth, so too is it here.
There is no room for the present argument here.

For, as soon as this subject (*dharmin*)—which is capable of being pointed out by the index finger—is presented as blue, at that very moment the doubt regarding its difference is eliminated; it is not the introduction of a formal proof (*sādhana*). This is because, without that blue form, it is impossible for the manifestation to be established as having a specific form.

For the acquisition of its own nature occurs when the mere exclusion of non-manifestation reaches its culmination in a particular manifestation, as in the case of the exclusion of non-wordhood, but not in each individual exclusion (*apoha*). Therefore, because of the suspicion that it might be a non-entity, a real substratum (*dharmin*) is not established. Consequently, since every universal possesses causal efficacy only in the form of a particular, and thus has the nature of a real entity, the substratum is simply "blue."

The procedure for determining difference and non-difference has reached its conclusion in the introduction. However, the nature of momentariness and so forth would remain a subject of doubt, since it has not been rejected.
But here, this very same subject (*dharmin*) is manifested; since it has been shown by the proponent himself in the form of blue, what now—?
Should this be understood by the members of the assembly? Or is there no fault in subsequently applying the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? There is indeed a fault;

for even if it is stated later that "illumination is neither one nor many," since it is concluded that this illumination is nothing other than the very nature of blue, it is impossible to demonstrate any other distinction. Furthermore, when no specific difference is perceived, it is impossible to establish the existence of the subject (*dharmin*).

And although, in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), both entities are indeed excluded from what is not that nature, nevertheless, it is not only "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth that is such;
rather, this too is so. Therefore, because it is common to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*) and not the specific form of the subject (*dharmirūpa*).
This is because it must be relied upon for the sake of engagement or withdrawal precisely through its non-common form, in the sense of "this is thus."

For this very reason, even regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), the desire for further particulars is eliminated by means of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Let it not be that non-existence follows from being devoid of all individuals;

for ultimately, even in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no absence of individuals because it possesses that very definition. Even in the case of momentariness and so forth, these are precisely the distinctions among individuals.

However, by relying on an imagined distinction, the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) holds even when there is a factual separation through exclusion (*vyatireka*). Likewise...

If the status of being a subject (*dharmin*) were to exist through an imagined distinction, then let its reality (*vastutva*) be established by that very form; what effort would there be to refute it if one has accepted it oneself? Or how could another person respect something else that has already been refuted by the very determination of the subject's form? For this very reason, just as one makes an effort for the sake of proving that [subject], so too does the other, who likewise desires to prove his own point.

[381,21] The investigation of the nature of the subject (*dharmin*). This person, like one who is grandly indifferent toward that [subject], does not perceive the requirement for a demonstration when seeking its production. Therefore, enough with that inference which results in a contradiction precisely through the determination of the specific nature of the subject of the probandum (*sādhya*).
[381,22–23] Only a property (*dharma*) that is doubtful once the subject is established deserves to be the means of proof (*sādhana*).
But when the ultimate limit of the specific nature of the substratum is reached, it is truly destroyed, truly destroyed.
For this very reason,
even the rebuttal of the distinction established by convention regarding the subject (*dharmin*) is impossible,
because the subject is thus [defined] only when its particularity is established by valid cognition (*pramā*).
Even when [the object] is established through inference, the form is postulated as specific in accordance with that [inference], depending upon the knowledge of the relationship.
Likewise, even if it were possible, because one is unable to say that "this manifestation is also such," the fault of abandoning the subject matter (*prakṛtahāni*) remains as before;
there is sublation of what was accepted regarding the blue subject.
[382,6] It is established that nothing other than the existent is accepted as real, and [the claim of its existence] is in vain.
[382,7] Just as it was stated regarding the proof of a peacock's cry, [382,8] when a form is possible, there is only one [conclusion] concerning reality.

Furthermore, in the formulation beginning with "in whatever form," if the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) is that "it is neither one nor many by means of the cognition of blue and so forth," then what fault is there? And thus, it can indeed be stated as follows:
"In whatever form something is neither one nor many, in that form it is not real."
Just as pleasure is obscured by pain, so too is light obscured by darkness.
[382,13] Just as in the case of blue, who can prevent the fact that illumination (*prakāśa*)—which likewise pervades such a spatial extent—is devoid of the nature of gross or subtle atoms?

[382,14] Therefore, blue exists, but not in the form of illumination. Consequently, the establishment of their forms as having distinct essences follows. However, the essence of illumination is false. [382,15] And this is logical.
A light resembling a flash of lightning appears somewhere to someone at some time;
in relation to that, external light is considered stable, and therefore its unreality [is established].
Just as the capacity of cognition is considered to produce an unreal blue,
so too the intellect is considered to have the capacity to produce an unreal awareness.
"You cannot say, 'This is not desired by you either,' because my lack of desire for this arose from not knowing such a proof."
Nor has pure luminosity ever been perceived by anyone anywhere.
Furthermore, pleasure and the like are forms of the object to be known; therefore, the intellect is superior to them.
Pleasure is the recognition of a manifestation, and that exists even for one who is cold.
Even in the case of a manifestation, there is a manifestation without distinction even for coldness.

[383,1] Now, if you argue that it is impossible to introduce the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) in that case, then in that event, suffering (*duḥkha*) would also consist of the nature of manifestation itself, and thus it could never be abandoned. Furthermore, because this would lead to the resurrection of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth, everything would be shattered from the very beginning. Therefore, where there is no appearance of non-difference, difference is not established. For this very reason, everyone...
It has been stated that the cause of differentiation is the means for establishing conventional usage.

As for those who say that the subject (dharmin) appearing as duality— because it is an error— is necessarily unreal, like the appearance of two lunar discs to one suffering from ophthalmia, and is thus "as it is seen," their hope is based on the assumption that an error is defined as the manifestation of the non-existent.
And that [notion of permanence] is refuted by this very [argument]. In the same way, the claim that "the manifestation called illusion is unreal," and so forth, is also refuted.
Furthermore, no so-called "illusion-maker" is established as distinct from the self-luminous form [of cognition]; for one cognition is held to arise from another cognition.

Even those who claim that there is a distinction based on the nature of the inclusive and the exclusive, for them too this is a mere conceptual construction, because— as was already largely stated in the discussion on cloth and water— there is no establishment by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a universal (*sāmānya*). Thus,
this [cognition] "blue light" is based upon distinct limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
Just as the cognition of "one with curly hair" [arises] by way of being a specific cognition.

Such is the conclusion of this discussion. Therefore, with respect to the various manifestations such as blue, yellow, and so forth, which arise from their respective immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*),

that which is called "manifestation" (*prakāśa*)— whose nature is established merely through the exclusion of others (*parāpoha*)— is a mere conceptualized property (*kalpita-dharmamātra*) belonging to them.
[383,] The notion that it is "unimpaired even in the case of a fallacy" is a gross delusion.

[383,17] Furthermore, if the relationship between property and property-bearer is established as the reverse, even in that case there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for there is only a misconception (*viparyaya*). [383,18]
The subject (dharmin) is that which possesses experience, while the property (dharma) is that which is conceptually constructed as genus and so forth.
Why, then, is the reverse desired in the case of the credible and the blue?

[383,21] It is merely because this world, weak in discernment, relies upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and posits a distinction—just as in the case of clay and its shape—that it employs conventional designations such as "difference" and the "reversal of property and subject" (*dharmidharmitā-viparyaya*). Therefore, one should not be dogmatic here. Nor is it possible to accept that these two possess a separate status as subjects (*dharmin*).
If blue and so forth are luminous, what need have they for another luminosity?
If blue and so forth are not luminous, what need have they for another luminosity?

Indeed, that which is not luminous by itself cannot be made manifest by another, according to the statement beginning with, "for whatever is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of something... Now, if you think that this is not the case because those who take pride in the unreal (alīka) lack any other intrinsic nature, then—precisely because of the absence of any other intrinsic nature—its intrinsic nature is merely luminosity; so what is the use of another luminosity? Where could that unreality be established?

To say that it "appears as an object" (ābhāsatām) is equivalent to the doctrine that the self is the substratum of cognition and so forth. However, this is the distinction: for one who holds that the self—the object of knowledge—is established as non-luminous, its existence is not contradictory and thus requires another blow [to refute it]; but for one who holds that the self is luminous by nature, even the mere utterance [of such a position] is untenable—so what is the use of these heavy labors of conceptual proliferation? Let there be no exclusion of self-luminosity in the case of unreality; therefore, for that which is not the self...
What kind of offense has been committed by the external object in its manifestation?
If it has the power over the false, how could it not have it over the real thing? Therefore, Dharmottara’s desire is established without any obstacle.
If that [cognition], depending on assistance, manifests only with respect to a real entity,
then it is logical that the real entity alone is the fit object for the conceptualization of identity (*tādātmya*).
And when there is the manifestation of a false distinction, the form does not have a basis as it appears;
likewise, when an external distinction is revealed, what is the purpose of the form?

Now, if it is not accepted that the external and the other (the internal) share the same security and well-being, then let the sublation belong only to the external; how, then, can there be falsity [of the internal]?
Just as the establishment of the external world is brought about by the intellect, so too is its sublation;
this is what is appropriate, and it has been observed repeatedly.
Just as there is no establishment of another's intellect by one's own intellect, so too there is none.
Even sublation does not destroy its own nature, even when it is considered external.
Thus is the intermediate verse.

Furthermore, because that which is false has the nature of non-existence, it possesses no causal capacity whatsoever; thus, even the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*), which depends upon being the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*), is shattered without effort despite having been laboriously established. This sequence is accepted for the purpose of introducing one to the system of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*). And therefore, it is as follows:

Furthermore, regarding the proof of the dual nature [of cognition], there is a persistent insistence in the *Pramāṇavārttika*. Therefore, if it is maintained that, in reality, cognition is indeed formless (*nirākāra*), then let alone the establishment of the causal status of the form; since the external object, like the form itself, cannot be denied as being experienced, how can the proof of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) be established? Thus, the attempt to prove that forms are false is like raising a weapon for one's own destruction.

[384,26] It follows that this occurs "with effort. However, when the form is undivided, because of the capacity of the determination that "blue is seen, not yellow" based on the specific nature of its own-form (*svarūpa*), the conventional establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyavasthā*)—though it is merely based on conceit (*ābhimānikī*) regarding external existence—is nonetheless established.

[385,1] Consequently, for the investigation already undertaken, since there is an absence of any defining characteristic of an object to be grasped (*grāhyalakṣaṇābhāva*), the proof of mere self-awareness (*svavedanamātra*) remains unimpeded. For this very reason: [385,2]

At the end of that [passage], one might think it would be appropriate for someone to say: "This [cognition] has blue and so forth as its form, and it is that very thing which is the experience" (PV III 328; NBhūṣ 139,27), and so on. Yet, even so, because there is subsequently an absence of a pervader, the external form or the [external] object lacks reality.

Do you intend to set aside mere illumination and establish [something else]? Then why this elaborate effort from the very beginning to propitiate the demon of "forms"? Just as it is your own view that this cognition is formless while the external correspondence possesses form, so too, let the accomplishment of the task proceed by introducing the non-perception of such a fixed state. Why, then, concern yourself with the definition of the apprehended object? It is not necessary.

Alternatively, two reasons must be stated for the simultaneous perception of the manifestation [of the object] and [the cognition], because of the fault [inherent] in establishing the form [of the object] by way of its own means, and because the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) must necessarily be relied upon;
thus, it is well established according to the intention of Dharmottara.
And we see that this very threefold method is the direct proof of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) for the Master in all cases.

The intent of the demonstration lies precisely here; however, regarding the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) discussed by the former masters, it is merely inferred, like something gross, because there is no refutation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Therefore, if Dharmottara were inattentive to the rebuttal of atoms, we would see that his position is established as primary and effortless, since he states that "their form is neither one nor many. Thus, everything is in disorder.
In this matter, the view of the Teacher (Ācārya) is as follows: there is no harm whatsoever in this position, provided it possesses even a trace of logic (*nyāyagandha*).

On that point, something has already been said. Furthermore, do not think that because an external object is false—being knowable only through manifestation—the status of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhaka*) is established by some other means.
For if [the object] were not manifested, the consequence would be that self-manifestation (*svaprakāśatā*) would have to be admitted; so what is the use of another manifestation?

Therefore, forms, sounds, and so forth are established as being of the nature of cognition by virtue of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because we have already demonstrated in the refutation of external objects that their uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) is also established. Here too, one need not fear the "terror of fools," for it is not the case that mere self-awareness is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) or that its reality is unestablished; rather, it is precisely the real [self-awareness] that is under discussion, since a conceptualized [one] is untenable.

Since this has already been established, there is no room for the two-fold conceptual alternative. For this very reason, when one proves the falsity of consciousness as well—on the grounds that it does not exceed its own forms—neither the charge of "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) nor the charge of "inconclusiveness" (*anaikānta*) can be leveled. Furthermore, as it is stated by way of a counter-argument: the nature of whatever thing is that form which is not sublated; for example, [the heat of fire].

[385,25] "The essence of awakening (*bodhātman*) belongs to all phenomena; and the nature of the essence of awakening is an uncontradictable form"—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
[385,26] That too has been refuted by this very [argument]: because a distinct subject (*dharmin*) is not established, and because blue is contradicted.
Therefore,
there is no functioning of cognitions apart from the distinction of their forms; thus, victory belongs to the glorious Middle Way, which is powerful in refuting that [position].
If this faultless, non-dual, and manifold [reality] does not exist,
then what room is there for one who maintains that the mind is devoid of form?
The first chapter, the Refutation of the Formless [Cognition], in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.
The Second Chapter [387]:

If, then, the non-existence of a formless consciousness (*cetas*) were [the case] in reality, there would be a collapse of the established order of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*). For the collection of forms is a mere delusion (*bhrānti*), arising from grasping at that which is not [as it appears]; thus, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is that very delusion.
