When the mass of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) produced by that [delusion] is eradicated, because the delusion has vanished, only stainless, non-manifesting luminosity remains—this is *nirvāṇa*. Thus, there is no fault. Otherwise, if a consciousness possessing forms were refuted, the state of purification would be untenable.
But if there were no sublation (*abādhā*), the difficulty would arise regarding the establishment of affliction (*saṅkleśa*).

For, since sentient beings themselves would perceive their own nature without error through their very manifestations, delusion (*bhrānti*) would be absolutely non-existent. Consequently, all sentient beings would be eternally liberated and eternally perfectly awakened Buddhas. If it is argued that "delusion is conceptual cognition (*vikalpikā buddhiḥ*), because it superimposes an object onto its own manifestation, which is not an actual object," [we ask]: how is it that the object being determined by that [cognition] does not manifest? Or, if it is manifesting, how is it that the object does not manifest within that [cognition]?

If, on the other hand, it were indeed manifest, then it would follow that the object is identical with it; furthermore, that [manifestation] would not exist when the object is absent. Moreover, there would be a certainty in every respect regarding such cases as "Māndhātṛ existed," "Śaṅkha will exist," "the self exists," and "sound is eternal. And it would be manifested through its own distinct characteristic as "cow"; and since a convention is impossible regarding a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that cognition would not be conceptual at all.

Therefore, one must accept that the cognition of a cow appears through a distortion consisting of a false, verbalized [concept]—namely, "cowness" (gotva) which is common to all individual cows—such that this manifestation is the determination of the object "cow. For in this way, these faults would not arise, since there is a mistaken determination of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) even though it does not appear [in the cognition].

Just as the unreal universal *gotva* (cowness) appears in the cognition of a cow and is identical with it—and because it is not distinct from that [cognition], it possesses reality or is non-superimposed—so too, in the manifestation of blue and so forth, the identity of the unreal blue and so forth is established by the very fact that their manifestation is established; for there is no contradiction between unreality and non-unreality residing in various forms even within a single entity. Furthermore, if that identity alone were the reason (*hetu*) when reality or non-superimposition is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), then it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to cases such as *gotva*.
If, on the other hand, "non-superimposed identity" is the reason, then that is unestablished (*asiddha*). To this, it is replied:
If it is universally accepted that "grasping at something as what it is not" is indeed an error,
then it is not tenable [to claim] that this occurs even with respect to a false mental image, as if it were real.

[388] In the world, the perception of water where there is no water in a mirage is known as an error (*bhrānti*); and in the treatises, it is stated in many ways that inference is erroneous because it proceeds by determining an object (*artha*) in what is merely its own internal appearance (*svapratibhāsa*), which is not the actual object. Thus, the apprehension of something as being what it is not is recognized as error. If this [error] is untenable in the theory of "images with form" (*sākāravāda*), then consider how it could possibly be tenable in the case of a purely false image (*alīkākāra*).

For knowledge indeed arises with some aspect, whether real or false; however, as for the superimposition of an external object upon that aspect, it may be produced either by that [knowledge] itself or by something else. If it were produced by that [knowledge] itself, then at that very moment another operation would have to be experienced—so how could there be such a superimposition? And at a later time, being non-existent by its own nature, whose operation could it be?

In the second case as well, even another cognition does not perform any function whatsoever toward anything else through any other operation, except by way of an arising that involves the coloring of its own form. Thus, even when this [subsequent] cognition takes the form of the earlier cognition as its object, it does not touch upon any further operation of superimposing the external, apart from merely imitating a fraction of that [external] form; for even the form of the word is included within its own essential nature.

And if another operation were also possible for the sake of superimposition (*āropa*)—rather than [the mere appearance of] a form—one would have to state that [that other operation] is the means of proof even in inference. If it is argued that its function is for the sake of comprehension (*adhigati*) and not for superimposition, we say no; because the manifestation of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) is rejected in inference, this [manifestation] is indeed a superimposition. If it is argued that "superimposition" means having an unreal object, then surely there would be the comprehension of the actual form of fire once it has been established through inference. Therefore, "superimposition," "ascertainment" (*avasāya*), and "conceit" (*abhimāna*) are synonymous.
However, there is a distinction based on correspondence and its opposite, because it would follow that conceptual construction alone is not a means of valid cognition.

Therefore, there is no operation of cognition other than its own form (*ākāra*). And if that external object being superimposed appears in that cognition in its own nature, then this is simply a true perception; what, then, would be the purpose of the superimposition? Furthermore, if it were to appear, there would be the consequence of perceiving a second form. If it is argued that "the appearance of that [external] form is itself the appearance of that [object]," we say no, because that [external object] is the object of the superimposition. For the appearance of a mirage is not itself the appearance of water, even if the two are identified with one another. If it is argued [that they are identified]...

What is this meaning of "unification"? If it means being the cause for the attainment of oneness, then that is impossible, because there is never any actual unification between the object of superimposition and its locus; for instance, there is no cause whatsoever for a rabbit's horn. Nor is it tenable for a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) to claim that what was previously manifold attains oneness, for that would merely be the arising of a different entity, and even that is not within the range of perception apart from the locus of superimposition. Furthermore, since the object itself undergoes no change by that much, how could there be any superimposition upon it?

Now, "single cognition" means unification. Even so, it does not apply to two things, because there is no experience of the object being superimposed. Nor is mere cognition of two things itself a superimposition, as in the case of blue and yellow; furthermore, the claim that there is a cognition of them as one due to the absence of even a trace of awareness of the object to be superimposed must also be rejected. For if an external object were to appear, it would be logical to speak of a cognition of it as one or many, or as existent or non-existent.

If it is argued that this cognition is a "single cognition" because it occurs through the concealment of the true nature of all its aspects, then, if that true nature is concealed, there would be no manifestation of it at all. If it is argued that this is not so because some part [of it] does manifest, we say no; for since a real entity is partless, it must either manifest in its entirety or not manifest at all. This very point has been explained in detail in the treatise regarding the opponent's position.

If it is argued that this is due to "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), it has already been stated that this too—being synonymous with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—does not know even a report of the external object without its own internal form. Furthermore, if it is an apprehension as non-different (*abheda*), then even under the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), what is being asserted is simply an apprehension of identity, which has already been refuted. Even if one merely denies an apprehension as different (*bheda*), no apprehension of the external object has been stated; so how can there be a superimposition (*āropa*) of it?

It is useless to define [the relation] as "not by way of difference," because there is an absence of any established cognition of identity through non-difference, and because it is impossible to deny the mere cognition of the object of superimposition itself; for one who merely restates that much has not stated any specific distinction at all.

Therefore, as long as something is being reflected upon, there is no such thing as "superimposition" (āropa), because there is an absence of contact with that which is to be superimposed. Even when the status of an error is established through some manner of conceptual designation for its appearance and by means of that superimposition—just as if it were false, despite the form being real—there is still an obstruction [to its reality]. However, by that much alone, its ontological reality is not asserted. If that is so, then since there would be even more clearly no error when its own nature appears, how can there be the establishment of an illusion? It cannot be established in any way, provided one respects critical inquiry.

Relying upon conventional discourse—which is pleasing when not subjected to analysis and is established even among children—we employ designations such as "person" (pudgala) and so forth; yet, when analyzed, these utterly fall apart.
Just as the self [is established], so too is external [reality] established through consistency with verbal testimony;
thus, the two types of error, though engaged in worldly transaction, are manifold.
In this regard, as long as there is non-investigation, so long is there saṃsāra; and as long as there is the culmination of the discernment of one's own nature, so long is there nirvāṇa.
Full comprehension of existence itself is said to be nirvāṇa.

Such is the logical principle. How, then, is there a full comprehension of existence (*bhava-parijñāna*), or how can there be activity and so forth through delusion regarding that which is non-existent in reality? We shall explain this later. For now, let us consider how the proponent of formless cognition (*nirākāravādin*) establishes the status of delusion in terms of ultimate reality. In that case, let it be granted that for him as well, delusion does not consist in the imposition of something external (*parāropa*). What is incorrect about the view that delusion is simply the association with unreal forms (*alīkākāra-yoga*), its removal being liberation (*kṣema*)?

First of all, there is the transgression of both worldly convention and scientific treatises. For a person employs the term "error" (*bhrama*) regarding a rope due to the superimposition (*āropa*) of a snake; it is not that knowledge touches the person in any particular form. And as for this superimposition of a snake, when it is investigated, there is no effort [to reach its limit], nor does another have the power to carry it to its conclusion. Thus, it is established that one employs this error characterized by such [superimposition].

In the treatise as well, activity based on the determination of an object within one’s own internal appearance is called an error; it is not, however, because the internal appearance itself is devoid of an object. Likewise, the meaning of "the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized" and so forth is precisely this:
it is not that the conceptualized object is unreal in itself, but rather that it is so because of the superimposition of the perceived upon it.

Even in the case of non-conceptual [perception], where two moons are seen, it would be "delightful only so long as it is not investigated" because the conceptualization superimposes its own operation onto that very [appearance].
Error exists even in the non-conceptual because of conceptualization; there is nothing beyond that.
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] rests upon conceptualization, even though it is non-conceptual.

Therefore, since the persistence of error occurs everywhere solely through the imposition [of something] by another, what is improper about this being merely a different technical term (*paribhāṣā*) that has not been established? If it is argued that there is no fault because the resolution follows from the very impossibility [of the imposition], for you have admitted the incapacity to provide a justification; if that is so, there certainly exists an error established by worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), and there is an investigation that contradicts it. Since the desired point is proven by this much alone, any further distinction is merely a trace of dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*).

For that conventional delusion is indistinguishable from the positions of either truth or falsity; since I have merely accepted the falsity of even the mental aspect (*ākāra*), let there be no insistence that it must persist in the ultimate end. To establish its status as a delusion is a mere dogmatic attachment, because both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) can be established otherwise. As long as the fall of delusion occurs through investigation, that is excellent;
but to say it is "non-existent in every respect" is even more excellent than the excellent.
Therefore, it is appropriate to apply effort toward investigation;
for even among the wise, suspicion may occasionally arise regarding the removal of what truly exists.
These are the two intermediate verses.

Therefore, what is the point of this claim that "error is the appearance of the unreal"? Even for one who does not accept that [definition], this is merely a failure to adopt the opponent's position; it is a transgression of the logic observed therein. As for what is said—that "the avoidance of that [unreal] occurs because of its impossibility"—for one who perceives that impossibility, what kind of "logical vision" (*yogadṛṣṭi*) could there be regarding the view that "error is the manifestation of the non-existent"? For instance, when it is said "appearance of the non-existent," is it intended to mean that there is a manifestation of something non-existent such as God (*īśvara*), or that the appearing form itself is non-existent, or that some existent thing simply does not appear? Regarding these points:
[391] How could that which has the manifestation of its own nature be non-existent?
If it is because of sublation, then is that sublation not likewise one of either perception or inference?
If there is no trust in perception in one instance, what recourse is there in another?
How then can inference, which is preceded by that [perception], be an object of trust?
Perceptuality consists in the direct realization of its own nature, and there is no other [perceptuality].
In the treatise as well, perception is defined precisely as the direct realization of the thing's own nature;
for this very reason, its status as a ground for conceptual construction or error is refuted.
If it were not perceived, there would be no manifestation of its form at all;
therefore, the claim that God and so forth appear [to consciousness] while being non-existent is incoherent.
If its form were to appear, then that [form] would indeed exist;
but since it appears as non-existent, for you it is simply the non-existent that appears.
(These three verses may also be found at RNA2 133,17–22.

By this, the second position also should be understood as refuted; for since existence is established by mere appearance, there is no room for sublation. [Objection: But is it not observed that even in the case of the appearance of two moons and so forth, there is indeed sublation?
It is not the case that there is any lack of logical consistency regarding what has been seen; thus, even that which was previously stated is invalid.
That too is incorrect; for that which is sublated does not appear [in consciousness], while that which appears is not subject to sublation. To explain:
The appearance of the form of cognition is the sublation of the external object;
for just as there is the appearance of color-form, there is likewise the sublation of touch and so forth.
(Cf. RNA1 125, RNA2 133,14f, where the second half reads:
"Even when there is manifestation, if there is no trust, where is trust? Thus it is proclaimed.")

For that which appears as mere form is determined as a specific aggregate of color, taste, smell, and touch. Precisely for this reason, the possibility of actions such as grasping with the hand occurs in relation to [an object like] hair; and even when there is a sublation of what exists, it is only of the form associated with those [other qualities], not of form alone. For one who desires a particular kind of causal efficiency attends only to the establishment or sublation of its means, not to just anything.
What is the use of examining the beauty or ugliness of the form of a eunuch to a lustful woman?

[392] However, it is precisely those who contemplate reality (*tattvacintaka*) who, out of consideration for other purposes, examine even universals (*sāmānya*) and the like. In that regard, there is the mere form (*rūpamātra*) which appears, and the four concomitants which are determined (*adhyavasīyante*) as being of the nature of a composite whole; because people lack discernment, they falsely imagine non-difference between these two and employ the conventional designations "this is unreal" or "this is false."

Therefore, due to that very conceit (*abhimāna*), whatever injunction or prohibition exists here all culminates in what is determined (*adhyavasita*), because its true nature is concealed by the superimposition of something else. Consequently, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of it in reality, just as in the case of the meaning of a word. And it is established that for whichever complex [of factors] there is sublation, there is no appearance (*pratibhāsa*) of it.

Therefore, even if there were an affliction caused by mere conceit regarding that which appears—if it were reality, let it be; if not, let it not be—there is no harm, for such diverse conventionalities are indeed experienced in the world. For this very reason, one enters into the investigation of reality (*tattva*). However, since it does not appear according to the aforementioned method, how can there be a determination of it? Thus, it follows that there is the manifestation of the non-existent.

Likewise, regarding the conceit of non-difference (*abhedābhimāna*), there is the appearance of a non-existent non-difference; and even the "concealment" (*pracchādana*) through the superimposition of something else cannot occur without the manifestation of that other thing—otherwise, one would have to open one's mouth wide in laughter. In this regard, if one were to close one's eyes and reflect upon it, one would only laugh at oneself. For it has been said: even for a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), there is no other mode of superimposition apart from the vivid delineation of a specific form; nor is there a perception of what is not-self (*anātman*).

Furthermore, the negation of its own form is neither intended by people nor possible, because it contradicts the negation of that which appears in its own nature. Therefore, what was asserted in the theory of "having forms" (*sākāravāda*)—namely, that permanent entities and so forth must exist—has fallen back upon [the proponent] himself.
"If there is sublation even when there is an appearance, then non-existence is not considered [to apply] to things that are non-existent;
for there is no negation of perceptions that have not been negated. (81b)
If that whose own nature appears [as real] is not real because of a sublater,
then what confidence can there be even in the sublater, since it too appears as having another nature?
The exclusion of its own nature occurs through the introduction of another nature;
yet even there, doubt arises because of the perception of prior sublation.
If this very [cognition] is the sublation regarding the grasping [of the object], and no other for that which is born of the senses, then let the former alone be the sublation;
for the manifestation of the form is identical in both cases.
You have no proof whatsoever for the claim that [cognition] does not manifest anything other [than itself],
since even when its own nature is manifest, there may be a sublation [of it].
Therefore,
when there is no manifestation of its own nature due to the failure of the purification of the cause, [393]...
If this were so even when there is no appearance of a suspicion of sublation, then there would be a great confusion.
(Quoted in RNA1 129,
RNA2 137) These are the intermediate verses. Therefore,

what further cause for derision is there than this frantic effort to revive— in every way refuted— the theory that the non-existent is manifested, merely by means of hearing words when there is no determination of an object?
The resurrection from the word of one who has been refuted by valid cognition is as wondrous as the revival of one bitten by a snake through the power of a mantra.

Therefore, just as in the case of the employment of words such as "self" (*ātman*) or "cowness" (*gotva*), it is correct that the wise pay heed—whether from their own side or through another—to the mere investigation of the determination and its expression. This, then, is the ultimate truth here: due to the power of various beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), arising in a certain form in dependence upon specific awakening conditions, produces a continuous stream of purposeful action, memory, and verbal expression conducive to outward-directed activity.

Consequently, for a person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), there arise activities and abstentions that correspond to external objects. Such is the cause of the moments of cognition within the mental continuum of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), because the nature of things is determinate. Even at the time of conceptualizing an object whose relation [to reality] is uncertain, there arises the production of activity based on the determination of existence, non-existence, and so forth.

In this regard, that capacity of the means of proof which functions in both ways—attained through the power of its own cause—is precisely this superimposition (*āropa*) of the object upon the domain of activity, which has the alternative name "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*). For example, whether it be an erroneous cognition such as [the perception] of the moon or a non-erroneous one, its very function of grasping consists in generating an ascertainment of that [object] which is seen.

According to the principle that "this [cognition] must be seen as having the object itself as its content through its functional effect (*kārya*) even in some cases," so too, for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in a form such as "there is fire here," its very capacity to impel activity (*pravṛtti-ākṣepakatva*) constitutes the determination of the external object (*bāhya-adhyavasāya*). Just as for non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa*), the very fact of its having the form of the moon and so forth is what establishes its determination, so too for conceptual determination, it is precisely its possessing such a form that establishes the impulse toward activity directed away from other objects.

Consequently, although the appearance of that form does not have the status of being the cause for the apprehension of an unapprehended object, it is established as if distinct by virtue of being the object of superimposition, as is the cognition of the superimposed. If it is argued: "In that case, those very three are established as non-existent, and since establishment is a cognition, there is no escape from the cognition of the non-existent," this is merely shifting the burden within the same stream. For it has been said that superimposition is simply the implication of an activity corresponding to that [superimposed object], and not what is called a [real] cognition.

[394] Therefore, even today, since there is a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that which is non-existent, there is no fault whatsoever: for, according to the theory of the cognition of the non-existent (*asatpratītivāda*), the result is merely a corresponding linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), and the cognition itself has the form "this is non-existent," characterized by a beginningless state (*anādyavasthā*).

In this same way, one should infer [the presence of] such minor disturbances elsewhere as well. This kind of error—consisting in the apprehension of something as what it is not—is the basis for all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); it follows from direct experience. This very process is designated as the "unification of the perceived and the conceptualized. It is the capacity to engage with another object based solely on the awareness of one's own internal representation, and it exists through the concealment of its own nature by means of the form of that other object.

However, with respect to the appearance (*pratibhāsa*), it is said that the form of another is concealed by its own form, because only that [own-form] is manifested. Even though the external exists, it is in reality objectless precisely because of this manifestation. Furthermore, because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) has the nature of the self and because there is no conceptual determination (*anadhyavasāya*), for these very reasons, the threefold establishment of exclusion (*apoha*) occurs: according to conceptual determination, according to appearance, and according to reality.

If that which is excluded from other classes is what is denoted by words, then let it be so in external conceptualization; however, my friend, since this has been established as a limb [of the system], both [the universal and the exclusion] now consist of exclusion (*apoha*) through the determination of appearance (*bhāsādhyavasiti*).

If it is argued that because of the non-existence of the external object there is an absence of appearance, and because there is an absence of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an aspect (*ākāra*) resembling a real entity excluded from heterogeneous things produced by sound, then nothing at all would be denotable; in that case, what in reality would be the referent of exclusion (*apoha*)? [The response is: "This exclusion is clearly that which is nothing at all. The connection [of the words] is "it is not denotable," just as in the preceding sentence. The meaning is this: if exclusion is said to be the denotable, then in reality it is the very denotable that is negated by the exclusion; such is the sense.

Just as "non-existence comes to be" means that "existence does not come to be," it is therefore established that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of words. As for the Sūtra passage beginning with "by whichever property," let as many "twigs" as there may be appear upon this root; we have no insistence on this point for the proponents of Apoha. And since the property of conceptual thought called "ascertainment of the external"—which is characterized by being the reality that causes activity directed toward the external—is established, then the ascertainment of all aspects, if it were to follow [from that], would necessarily have its essence established through the utility of a corresponding subsequent transformation.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the capacity of a conceptual cognition—which delineates a single form—to operate with respect to another form is beyond the scope of experience; therefore, it is logical to ask: how could there be a dependence on other means of valid cognition, such as verbal testimony?

In this regard, although non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is erroneous, it is established as a means of apprehension by virtue of its vivid appearance. Conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), however, because its nature consists of reflective deliberation (*vimarśa*), is the locus of conventional usage such as "superimposition" (*āropa*), even though it functions independently of anything else, because it delineates a single, indistinct exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Every conceptual cognition is called "erroneous" because, while not touching the external object at all—whether that external object exists or not—it serves as the cause for engagement with it. But when the external object does not exist, it is established that the error of non-conceptual cognition consists in its connection with a form containing within it the capacity to produce such a conceptual cognition.

Every conceptual cognition is indeed devoid of an external object; yet, following the distinctions of its own exclusions (vyāvṛtti) and fashioned by its own internal form, it produces recollections of perceived results and so forth.
Thus, like direct perception, it incites the activity of people toward other objects without depending on them.
The superimposition of an object is said to be like the superimposition of water upon a mirage, as in the case of [mistaking] waters for water.
Thus is the summary.

This being the case, that which was determined to have an external form, brought to a state of readiness for engagement by the aforementioned process, and yet sublated—of that there is no appearance; and it is established that there is no sublation of the aspect that actually appears.

For there is indeed no dispute regarding its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). It is simply a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) arising after the perception of that which is endowed with causal efficiency, and there is no impairment of that efficiency. Impairment, however, applies only to that [causal efficiency] which is to be accomplished by a specific collection of conditions; thus, it is only that [specific efficiency] which is absent. Therefore, how can it be said that there is sublation (*bādhā*) of what is appearing? And when one relies on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), everything previously stated recurs.
When considering the absence of a pervader, there is neither a boat nor an ant;
yet, apart from this, there is the examination of defilement and so forth within the system of "having aspects" (*sākāra*).

It has begun. In that regard, even when there is the self-awareness of the true nature [of cognition], no impairment of the afflictions occurs by relying on the state of error—which, though established in worldly convention for all cognitions, is produced by beginningless time. And just as the status of error is established in some cases when an external object exists, so it is everywhere in the case of determinate judgment (*nirṇaya*). It is merely said that, with respect to activity directed toward the external, there is no error whatsoever regarding the self;
for "in whatever way a cognition appears, that indeed is its form."

Thus, because there is a determination toward the external through the association with a word, conceptualization and lack of clarity reside in that very [cognition]; for, in relation to another cognition, that same object remains solitary and clear. However, since such a form [of the object] deviates from the nature of the self (ātman), how could there be such a determination of that cognition, which is born from a specific causal complex?

Even when this very [cognition] is intended to be connected with another object by means of a word without making that other object its own objective domain, even then the connection occurs only with respect to the other and not with respect to itself; this is what must be considered according to the treatise. Therefore, it would not be purely conceptual from its own perspective—this being a case of proving what is already established—but with respect to the other, it is indeed conceptual by virtue of the force of the determination (*adhyavasāya*).

Now, if it is argued that this is said solely by the force of the appearance of the thing's own nature (*vastusvarūpa*), then even to state this in the context of the theory of "cognition with forms" (*sākāravāda*) is a great boldness. If it is claimed that [the external object] is drawn forth by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), we say no; for that [determination] has been established otherwise. Indeed, when that [object] flashes forth, there is no such thing as "determination," because only the manifestation itself is obtained. Therefore, the argument that—although the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear [in cognition]—it is nevertheless determined therein through error (*bhrānti*) is not tenable.

When there is contact with the cognition of that [object] through a determination (*avasāya*), what other appearance could there be? To say "because of its indistinctness" is not tenable; for if that form is being cognized, that very [indistinctness] is unestablished.
One should recall such [verses] as: "A different basis indeed arises" (PV III 235a).

And it cannot be that there is an error at that time, because what appears is precisely the form of a real entity (*vasturūpa*), [and not] a false cognition (*alīkavitti*). If this is argued, then let that very [cognition] be the determination of the object (*arthādhyavasāya*); how so? If you say "it is that very same thing," no; for one who knows "this is false" lacks the established determination of an external object. If you say that it is not a verbalization of a false [object], but rather the awareness of that [false object] is the determination of the external, even so, there would be a mere difference in terminology, and not the manifestation of the intended object.

For as long as there is an absence of contact with an external nature, the term "cognition of a false form" (*alīkākārajñāna*) is synonymous with what is called "ascertainment" (*avasāya*). Consequently, no distinction whatsoever has been stated. And this being the case, just as "the cognition of a false form" cannot bear the relation "of the external," so too "ascertainment of the external" would not be a valid relation. For the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) depends on the conceit of cognizing that [external object]; in its absence, how could it exist?
If that [cognition] is false because it has come down through a tradition, then an error exists for that reason alone; however, this does not apply in the case of what is not false.

Therefore, that which was stated—that "this determination of an object by the intellect is merely a particular appearance capable of association with verbal expression"—is refuted, because the connection with the phrase "of the object" is untenable, and because there can be no error regarding cognition itself. Furthermore, let the determination simply be that the appearance is false; what is the use of the qualification "capable of association with verbal expression"? If it is argued that this is for the purpose of excluding non-conceptual [cognition], [we reply:]...

If this is so, then even in the case of non-false (analīka) discourse, it is only knowledge qualified by that specific [condition] which is an error, not all [knowledge]; thus, there is no total absence of affliction and purification. For even when an error ceases, it is only a particular species of cognition that is relinquished. Furthermore, in both systems, the connection with verbal expression is dependent upon something else, so there is no harm. The only fault is that if that [expression] is not perceived, the determination of its conceptual ascertainment (*avasāya*) is difficult; and that [fault] is common to us both.

Therefore, even for one who pursues [the object] to a great distance, it must be accepted that the determination of the external [object] occurs by resorting to the metaphorical designation of "grasping" it—projecting an external function solely through a specific capacity even in the absence of actual cognition—and thus it rests upon a function that establishes a connection. At that time, there is no difference whether the mental forms (ākāra) are unreal or real.

Thus, having attributed to the object the state of being manifested by way of its being determined as the object of determination, [you argue that] the identity of the object with [its cognition], its non-existence when the object is absent, and so forth, are logical; however, all of that is untenable. That the cognition functions toward an object without having seen it—this alone is the error (*viplava*). Therefore, since there is no contact with the object even when the exclusion (*apoha*) in the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the denotatum, where is the fault of the consequence that [the cognition] would grasp all aspects?
Thus he says: "And the delusion regarding the cognition of the universal is therefore not a flaw. (PV I 169)

Thus, because it implies activity toward that very [object] by way of having the form of the exclusion of others (*ekavyāvṛtti*), and because a person attains satisfaction with just that much and does not investigate further; however, regarding the non-attainment of that alone, he states the contradiction: "That which, despite being existent, has no manifestation in conceptual cognition—of that which is non-existent, this is merely a name; this is far removed from reason. Nor can there be non-existence for that which is manifesting. Therefore, how can blue be manifested as non-existent by means of the example of "cowness," and how can there be a postulation of identity between them?

By this, the argument beginning with "of those two which abide in different forms" and so forth is also refuted. Furthermore, the claim that there is a contradiction between the non-existent and the manifest is incorrect because of the assertion that they reside in a single entity; for there is no entity of manifestation distinct from the blue [object], and there is no purpose in postulating such a distinction, since what is intended is merely the negation of one of two things. And that [negation] would apply when one thing is appearing and the other is imagined, as in the case of "pot-ness" in relation to a cloth, or even when both appear distinctly, as in the case of a hare and a gnat.
Furthermore, this principle is nowhere established for two things that have an identical appearance but whose difference is merely posited through the exclusion of what they are not (*atadvyāvṛtti*).

If it is argued that even when color and shape appear identically, the shape is non-existent, we say no; for in that case too, what is denied is a shape that is distinct [from color], imagined as being "connected with the arrangement of parts. How could one deny the essence of color which is denoted by the word "square" and arises as the exclusion of states that fall within the scope of conventional usage such as "circular"?

Likewise here as well, there is a negation only of that which is distinct and imagined; it is impossible to negate the blue—whether as having the nature of blue or the nature of manifestation—because it appears as non-distinct [from its nature]. Consequently, if "being a real entity" or "not being superimposed" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), [the reason] exists in the case of blue.

Furthermore, with respect to the manifestation of the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*), there is no absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*). For the manifestation of the form of "cowness" (*gotvākāra*) cannot be a superimposition by anyone, because there is no superimposer distinct from existence itself; moreover, the manifestation of the very form of "cowness" is produced by its own cause. Nor is there a superimposition of something upon itself, nor a superimposition of one thing by another; rather, there would merely be the application of a name (*nāmakaraṇa*). Consequently, since the nature of manifestation is never superimposed in any case, there is not even a trace of the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Furthermore, that which is superimposed ought to be indistinct, like water and such; however, the luminosity (*prakāśatā*) of the blue is experienced as being most distinct. It is not, however, like a separate luminosity [superimposed] upon a separate blueness. Or else, if it were distinct, it would follow that luminosity, being existent, would appear just like the blue.

Thus, wherever in reasoning (*tarka*) or scripture (*āgama*) there is the cognition that something is non-existent (*asad*) or false (*alīka*), this is so either with respect to what has been determined (*adhyavasita*)—apart from the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra—or from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyāvahārika*). For he employs the term "false" and so forth merely on the basis of the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for an external object to be accomplished, which is imagined by way of its form (*ākṛti*). Following that [conventional] discourse, this is merely a negation of the external. But in reality (*tattvataḥ*), the non-existent is simply another kind of existent; and it is called "false" because it is other than what is intended. Nevertheless, it might be argued:

When cognition has a permanent form (*nityākāra*), then, because it arises as pervading multiple times, it would follow that—possessing that form—it must be eternally existent; however, this is also trivial. For its having that form is merely by way of imitation (*anukāramātra*), and not through identity (*tādātmya*), since otherwise there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of burning from the mere conceptualization of fire. Therefore, just as a banyan tree, which pervades a vast space, is imitated by a reflection on the surface of a mirror that can be contained within a mere leaf due to some difference in form, so too is the eternal [nature] [imitated] by a momentary form.

And here the experience is this: at the time of conceptualizing a permanent self and so forth, there is a resemblance to that [object] even without an all-pervading duration that would otherwise obstruct the opportunity for other cognitions.

For even though it is false, it need not be a falsehood that pervades all time by way of a permanent form; otherwise, it would lack the capacity to necessitate the engagement in investigations such as its existence or non-existence in accordance with that [form]. Therefore, it is logical that there is a slight resemblance to it even without a pervasion of time, just as when a representation of a vertical staff or similar object is attended to at some particular time.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that for an eternal entity, a production in all its states would occur within a single [moment] by means of the upper, lower, and intermediate parts—which serve to characterize the forms of the past, future, and present—it follows that there is no contradiction in the arising of even a cognition in a single moment when it assumes that form. Therefore, that which is non-existent does not manifest; it may, however, be merely determined (*adhyavasita*), as was stated previously. And it is established that whatever manifests by its own nature, that is not non-existent.

Consequently, there is no such thing as the appearance of the non-existent, for that is impossible by definition. For this very reason, the third alternative—that what exists does not manifest—is also untenable, because existence is pervaded by manifestation; indeed, that which does not manifest is swallowed up by non-existence. (The meaning of *vyāpteḥ* is "because of pervasion.")

[Objection: Is it not the case that what is called "manifestation" (prakāśa) is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes an object? And yet, the absence of a means of valid cognition does not entail the non-existence of the object. Furthermore, the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā-śakti) is the reality of an object, and this is not contradicted even by something unmanifested. [Response: This is true, provided one accepts the doctrine of external objects (bahirarthavāda), since even an unmanifested object is admitted there. However, in the case of the appearance of hair and the like, the object as determined lacks the capacity for causal efficiency.

[399] For in this way, non-existence is established. But if there is an absolute absence of external objects, since cognition is invariably accompanied by manifestation (*prakāśa*), its existence is accounted for by that alone; what then is the use of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? If it is argued that its existence is not established by manifestation alone because it belongs to another's mind, then causal efficiency is likewise not established, for if it does not manifest to anyone at all, how could it exist?
Moreover,
even with regard to an external object, its existence is asserted in reality by means of manifestation.
The classification of sentient beings is established according to the intention of the practitioner and their capacity.
Since even a capacity cannot be established as existing without manifestation,
if one were to claim that it exists by the power of another capacity, there would be an infinite regress.
Power is known through its effect, and being an effect consists in dependence upon something else;
even if the power itself is not certain, it exists if there is a distinct exclusion from others.
If its capacity is not ascertained, how indeed can it have the status of being an effect?
For the nature of a thing as an effect, though it partakes of distinct exclusions, remains its very essence.
Otherwise, why is it that hair and the like do not possess the status of being an effect?
If you say they indeed have the status of an effect, then let their existence simply be their manifestation, since there is no deviation [between the two].
If [you argue that] superimposed things have no causal function, why is it not the same for manifestation?
If manifestation [is established] through unification, how can it be the same for being an effect?
Just as there is no member [of a causal complex] due to the absence of the result, so too there is no result due to the absence of the members;
therefore, when the reality of the thing is in doubt, there is doubt regarding its being an effect and so forth.
Therefore, the determination of its capacity arises from the power of practice;
for luminosity itself is existence, and either that [luminosity] is its effect, or it is simply the cognition itself.
Nor does its existence depend on another effect; rather, it is established through self-awareness (svasaṃvit). For cognition never deviates from its own object.
If there is doubt regarding something in that case, certainty arises from repeated practice;
therefore, even external existence is in reality nothing other than manifestation itself.
[400] Nor is there any loss of momentariness in this way, because cognition grasps [the object] in a single moment;
and that cognition occurs only occasionally, serving as the inferential mark when the force of certainty has been exhausted.
And it is stated in the treatise: "Cognition is the existence of the perceptible, while non-cognition is its non-existence;
these are independent of the loss of designation, purposeful action, and so forth."
Even incapacity in that regard does not constitute a sublation;
moreover, this much distinction has been stated: visibility and invisibility correspond respectively to existence and non-existence.
Sometimes, for someone, there is illumination somewhere by means of inference;
however, the absence of such illumination should be understood as false when one attends to external objects.
Even in the absence of inferential cognition, there is manifestation as mere conceptual construction;
let manifestation be of such a kind as the existence of those things is.
Everyone seeking purposeful action attains the status of a real entity (*vastu*) precisely through its result;
and it is upon that very [result] that one projects the appearance, making it the locus of activity.
And thus there is no impairment of the conventional pride that has been undertaken;
therefore, power, existence, and intrinsic nature are indeed pure.

Therefore, even in the theory of external objects (bāhyārthavāda), although from the perspective of conventional usage there is a twofold status— namely, that power (śakti) is [conventional] existence (sattā) while manifestation (prakāśa) is the ultimate reality (tāttvika).
These are the intermediate verses.

Now, if it is argued that existence (*sattva*) should not be denied to the appearing form (*ākāra*) because it lacks causal capacity (*śakti*), and that for this reason existence is defined as causal capacity—then even so, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [capacity] being distinct from that [form], what kind of desired proof is this? Furthermore, it is not possible to deny that the form possesses causal efficiency (*arthakāritva*), because it has been demonstrated that the moment of the material cause (*upādeyakṣaṇa*), the determination (*adhyavasāya*), and the continuous series (*prabandha*) initiated by it—which consists of the ongoing, uninterrupted ascertainment of existence, non-existence, and so forth—are invariably antecedent to their own production.
Otherwise, the causal relationship would not be established anywhere at all. If it is argued that the cause in that case is a distinct, pure luminosity, [we reply:
"The form is seen to possess causal power through positive and negative concomitance;
another thing attains causality"—this is the established principle of the royal court.
[401] If its status as a cause is not denied even in the case of the mental aspect (ākāra),
then fire does not deny its status as a cause with respect to smoke.

Furthermore, the agency of the other [the self] is dependent upon the one; thus, agency belongs to both, due to the capacity for the persistence of their existence, just as in the case of fire and fuel.
If it is determined that a distinct illumination dependent on blue produces [the cognition],
then it follows that a *piśāca* (demon) dependent on fire is a constituent part of smoke.
For this very reason, ignorance alone cannot be established as a member [of dependent origination];
for the dependence upon a perceived totality of conditions is never denied anywhere.
Otherwise, the entire diversity [of the world] would be produced by karma alone;
there would be an elimination of other causes, and human effort would bear no fruit.
If existence and non-existence do not follow one another, there is no relation of cause and effect anywhere;
and if they do follow one another, there is likewise no relation of cause and effect anywhere.
And the determination of a blue perception does not arise from the seeing of a non-blue form;
for the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl occurs despite the absence of a deviation in color.
When there is a distortion in the apprehension of the distinction from a similar class of material things,
there is the superimposition of "materiality" upon the perception of a limb, because that [distinction] is not perceived.
Or let there be a perception otherwise, even by chance or through fate; in that case, the distinction between castes is to be inferred from it, like smoke produced by a yogi.
Just as in the case of an external seed, when it is joined with the cause that is the sentient being,
so too [is it] when the cognition in the form of the seed gives rise to the form of the sprout.
Thus, setting aside the external object and designating cognition in its place, he declared:
"It is conditions that arise and cease."
If its property (dharma) were pervasive, then luminosity would also exist as a cause such as "earthiness" and so forth; yet it is not a manifestation—this is a sound conclusion.
[402] Therefore, since only the result of an external blue object is observed,
that which is seen in cognitions such as those of [illusory] hair and the like lacks reality due to the absence of such a [corresponding external] object.
In that case, let its very reality be negated due to the absence of that activity;
it is not the mere status of being a real entity that is excluded for something endowed with other activities.
When one emerges from the interior of a mountain cave, mistaking a waterfall for a whirlpool,
does that which is actually real truly become real simply by the transgression of its own activity?
Because the activity of determination has ceased, a person seeking that object would again describe the form of the cognition as non-existent through the appearance of existence in that very place.
Therefore, in accordance with that [convention], when a cognition is intended to be non-erroneous,
statements such as "it appears as non-existent" are made for the purpose of negating what is merely imagined.
For that [universal] is not self-cognized by that cognition; rather, it is something else, and that [other thing] is certainly not real.
Therefore, the "cowness" and so forth are indeed non-existent, because the form does not manifest.
Just as a pair of moons is not even a single moon, so too here, the absence of an apprehended self-nature is to be understood; this is the general direction of the argument.
This arrangement is established according to conventional determination; however, in reality, place and so forth are not universals, because they lack any objective basis for such adherence.
Thus he said, "But not because of being a non-object," and furthermore:
"The appearance of clarity [occurs] because, by virtue of having the nature of cognition, it is an object; however, the notion [of it being hair and so forth]..."

That which has a universal as its object, which appears as hair, and which is devoid of external reality, is reckoned as sensory cognition; it is non-existent because it is a determination of something external.
Likewise,
if it follows that the universal is an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition,
there is no fault, because that is accepted; for [the universal] is identical [to the cognition] by virtue of having the nature of the object.
And it has been stated more than once that the referent of a word is a property-bearer (*dharmin*) that cannot be rejected.
Therefore,
this referent of a word, which is described according to how it is conventionally understood, is [in reality] non-existent.
And it has been stated by [the author] himself in the *Bhāṣya* that [cognition] is of the nature of knowledge;
if existence were according to appearance, then appearance would have to be manifestation.
That very existence [of the object] does not constitute a contradiction even when it is within cognition as if it were external;
there is no sublation because of the absence of a pervader, whereas incapacity and so forth are considered [obstacles] in the case of an external object.
The meaning of a word is connected with dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), because that very form appears in verbal cognition;
and for embodied beings, there is a determination of their own internal aspect precisely as something external.
Therefore, just as the expression "sentient being" is firmly established as the reality even though there are no sentient beings,
so too is that [expression] considered diverse when it is understood that the three realms are merely mind.
The effort expended regarding words such as "all-empty" is exactly the same:
that very mind, possessing its own form, is said to appear as an object.
For the negation of the external object as it is conceptualized has indeed been established by oneself;
moreover, its being afflicted by latent impressions (vāsanā) is held to be due to the arising of forms that are undesirable.
Because it contains within it the capacity to give birth to the volitions projected by worldly activity,
there is neither engagement nor cessation when one has ascended to the pinnacle of non-duality.
How could those very [states] be accepted as saṃsāra for one who knows them,
except through the misconception of the ignorant that "a form is seen in a mirror"?
Just as one removes the attribution of reality to the form of a sensation,
so too must one remove the notion of externality from the forms of cognition regarding existing things.
Just as the moonhood of two moons seen by one with cataracts is unreal,
and because it lacks depth, there is no oneness with the external object in the mirror.
The nature of consciousness is not perceived as distinct from the appearances that have entered within it,
nor through entities characterized by forms or names.

The universal is reckoned as cognition; for this very reason, it is spoken of separately. In common worldly usage, cognition—which is like a mirror—is treated as if it were distinct [from its objects].
The aspects appear as reflections; that which is imagined in both cases is not real.
There is no identity between consciousness and external objects, because it has attained a state devoid of their own intrinsic nature.
There is no otherness because it is not perceived as distinct, nor is there existence for that which does not manifest;
and by the logic of the king’s sequence, it is devoid of both unity and plurality in the mirror.
Thus, it is either appropriate or not that phenomena are joined as being like a mirror;
the yogi abides in the non-manifest, for manifestation is considered to be conceptual construction.

That which appears slightly as external through the exclusion of others within that [consciousness] is an appearance due to its universal manifestation, or it is a proliferation like a Kadamba flower.
That which has ascended upon the form of manifold conceptualization is to be abandoned, even in a mind that is variegated.
The rest is the same. Alternatively:
even when there is the abandonment of the external object of apprehension, one must prevent the persistence of the act of apprehending;
likewise, by abiding in suchness (*tathatā*), one transcends mind-only.
As he said:
"Because even one of those is absent" (PV III 213), and so forth.
"Lest, upon the removal of the superimposition, there should also be the removal of the object of that superimposition—
like the fall of a glance upon a painting that destroys it— there is the warding off of non-appearance."
And so,
just as variegated things remain in the world exactly as they are, in this way the wise lead others to the truth. (In this way the wise lead others to the truth.)
And so forth. And the venerable Ārya-Nāgārjuna says:
"The great elements and so forth are said to be well-established within consciousness;
when that consciousness is known, they vanish. Indeed, they are falsely conceptualized."
In that regard, there is the conviction of non-existence, the obstruction of objects, and [the state] consisting of reflection in the heart;
and "in the knowledge of that" refers to the direct realization of the nature of knowledge, wherein [ignorance] is exhausted.
Even when [the object] is sublated, there is no harm to the names, the causes [of cognition], or their forms;
let the phenomena of the Sage be mere names, whether they exist by way of an imagined nature or not.
In this manner, other cases as well should be inferred.
Then, through the destruction of adventitious impurities, it is like the surface of space;
its equality with the object of knowledge is manifest by virtue of its non-distinction from that object.
This [consciousness] is mere luminosity, resembling the continuum of a lamp-flame;
it is not [luminous] because of a lack of non-luminous parts, but rather through the manifestation of its own form.
Even for that which possesses not even a particle of luminosity, there was no possibility of existence even previously;
rather, the state of being stained or stainless depends upon the determination of error.
In that very [dependent nature], which consists of various forms dependent upon causes, that which is imagined— the act of grasping and the grasper— is non-existent.
For one who discerns the distinction between those two, its single nature is revealed.
"That very [reality], which is of a single nature for one who discerns that duality— [it is] perfected," said the King of Princes on all sides.

Therefore, in the theory of cognitions with aspects (*sākāravāda*), there is no contradiction whatsoever with the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or with the scriptures (*āgama*). Nor is it the case that the aspects are unreal (*alīka*), because the causal efficacy of objects has been established. Or, even if they were unreal, or even if they were merely designated as "error," there is nonetheless no connection to affliction (*saṃkleśa*) in reality, because there is no loss of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and because there is an absence of any establishment based on the imposition of something else.

The notion that "all embodied beings are always already liberated" is an obstruction resulting from a long-continued habituation. For once something has arisen from its own cause in the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it cannot be altered by anything else, not even by something possessing power, much less by what is considered false. Furthermore, when [consciousness] arises as a unity with its own cause, let its nature be non-differentiated cognition; why resort here to the forced twisting of limbs? That entities arise from their own causes and are cognized as having that very nature—this oneness accepted by things themselves is a great affliction for [those] disputants.
[406] If it is argued that because they arise and appear in such a way due to ignorance, they are not reality, that too is not substantial. For:
"Let there be birth from some cause or other; what is the use of a considered cause?
Even if born from something undesirable, it remains exactly as it is, regardless."
Thus, one must with effort offer a final libation to the proponents of non-aspectarianism (anākāravāda),
if they maintain that the ultimate is accessible through faith alone, thinking that some distinction [between them] might eventually arise.
If it is argued that there is a grasping of oneness like that of milk and water even when [the entities] arise separately, [we reply:
no, because there is no grasping of what is distinct; nor is there a misapprehension of the self through something other than itself.
For just as the grasping of a self is by means of the self, so too is that self itself;
the notion of a single conceptualization regarding the manifestation of cognition is dependent upon something else.
If there were no sublation even in another [cognition], the occurrence of error would be impossible;
how much less so in the self-awareness where not even a trace of sublation exists?
If there is a subsequent determination of non-difference, there is no harm by that either;
for, like indeterminate cognition, this too is merely false from the perspective of self-awareness.
And there is no superimposition of another [subject] there, for that [cognition] is false yet self-cognized;
what other peace is there than the cessation of engagement with and withdrawal from it?
That which is merely false, even if it exists, does not act as an obstacle anywhere;
for if it were to act as an obstacle, it would follow that its falsity is abandoned.
Movement to another sphere of experience is certainly not desired; where, then, could bondage be produced?
Furthermore, in its self-awareness, it cannot be bound even by a hundred [means].
For if the knot and its manifestation arise from their own causes within one's own consciousness,
then it is logically untenable that they could be known even through their own distinctness.

For it is not logical that self-awareness, arising from its own cause as something luminous by nature, should possess a dullness brought about by an obstacle through the power of false forms. Therefore, it is also impossible to claim that such a false [form] would make itself known as distinct from itself, precisely because of the contradiction involved. Indeed, for that which is being produced as pure self-awareness, any alteration from that state is contradictory when it arises with a nature that is either that [awareness] or not that [awareness].
If there is an obstacle to the realization of that which consists of nothing more than this, it is actually a merit;
for if that [obstacle] were not itself non-existent, it would have to assume a formal appearance as a disciple.
If [the two] exist in an undifferentiated form, then their identity is unshakable;
even if they are differentiated, provided that which is differentiated is unreal, there is no harm whatsoever.

If it is not maintained that there is a superimposition of the external—whether one reflects in such a way or otherwise—upon the two, namely the false and the non-false, as they have been understood through their distinction; [then what follows?]
For one who maintains that external objects are the object [of cognition], the occurrence of activity and so forth is not possible.
The mind is necessarily fixed upon its own cognition; therefore, since the unreal is permeated by unreality, there is no engagement with or withdrawal from other superimpositions.
Thus, for embodied beings, what need is there for direct exertions toward liberation? For what loss is there even if one abides in the form of the daughter of Śravaṇa?

Consequently, because all sentient beings would always be in a state of liberation, there would be no need even for the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha (*samyaksambuddha*); thus, no one would ever undertake the practice of skillful means (*upāya*). Therefore, this delusion—characterized by the apprehension of that which is not [the case] as being that—is, in its own nature, devoid of rational investigation. If it were not established as having the capacity to impel such activity, then there would be no fault even if it were merely a false appearance; thus, the rebuttal of the aforementioned objection would not hold. "If that false thing exists without impelling activity, then see the audacity displayed by the incapacity of the unreal! // 1653 // [Note: The verse cited here is from Śāntarakṣita’s *Tattvasaṃgraha*, Verse 1653.]
Its engagement occurs through false appearances and qualities of existence, and not otherwise;
this Yogācāra practitioner is one who delights in the perverted, and is not [a follower of] the ultimate truth.

Therefore, [408] it is not merely the false that is useful in existence, for the nature of error does not exist elsewhere than in the determination of that [object], which is elegant when subjected to investigation.

However, the conceptual construction of external objects suitable for worldly transaction is equal in both cases—whether one holds the view that cognition possesses an image (*sākāra*) or that it is imageless (*nirākāra*). Thus, how can the minds of the wise be so habituated to an adherence to the imageless alone by abandoning the possessed-of-image, out of fear of losing the established distinction between affliction and purification?

But if the application [of the means] is directed toward the mental apprehension (*parāmarśa*), then the establishment of the connection with powers and so forth is logical according to the doctrine of those who maintain that cognition possesses a form (*sākāravāda*).
However, according to the doctrine of those who maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākāravāda*), it applies rather to internal affliction and purification.

Thus, there is a great difference. For instance, if the form (*ākāra*) were a real entity, then experience, by perceiving a particularity either through identity with it or through connection with it, would produce a corresponding determination (*adhyavasāya*); and that determination, in turn, would give rise to an activity directed toward a specific object. In this way, there is no confusion of activities. This is because a certain object, due to the utility of a particularity inherent in its own nature, [induces activity], like a blue lotus held in the hand.

Consequently, identity and causal co-operation are established as being dependent upon real entities (*vastu*). Furthermore, if the mental image (*ākāra*) were not a real entity, there would be no distinction between the mind perceiving water and the mind perceiving fire; thus, it would follow that even from the experience of water, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of fire would arise.

In this way, from the conceptualization of fire, there would be an inclination toward one who desires to drink or bathe. Yet, one who thinks "there is no fire here" does not act out of a desire for a drink. What difference is there between [the cognition of fire] and an experience that, due to its transparency, surpasses even the rays of a crystal gem, yet possesses an unreal form? For the crystal itself is not the cause of the distinction in the activity of cognition once it has abandoned the assistance of objects such as blue or yellow. If it is argued that there is a distinction in capacity due to contact with that which partakes of the designation "light" because of the manifestation of an unreal form, that is incorrect; for: [The
