svapna-saṃkalpa-māyā-gandharvanagara-marīcikā-timiraka-candra-dvaya-pītaśaṅkha-vaṃśoraga-rāgādy-upapluta-yogijñāna-deśāntara-viparyaya-smṛti-tarkānumāneṣu vināpy arthena vividhākāra-pratibhāsaḥ ||* *evam ihāpi syāt ||* *na ca tatra bāhyo 'rtho 'sti ||* *tasmād asaty api bāhye 'rthe vijñānasyaivāyam ākāraviśeṣaḥ ||* *na ca tatrānyathā-khyātiḥ, asatkhyātir vā, kintu vijñānam eva tad-ākāram utpadyate ||* *iti siddham ||* And even when an external object is non-existent, there is some example here: just as the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, and the appearance of tawny hairs in a tuft of hair; just as the appearance of horses, palaces, and so forth through the power of illusory mantras; just as the appearance of elephants, horses, cities, and so forth in a dream; just as the appearance of a city and so forth in a city of Gandharvas; just as the appearance of clusters of hair and so forth to one with ophthalmia; just as the appearance of two moons and so forth; just as the appearance of water on dry land like a mirage; just as the appearance of a yellow conch and so forth; just as the appearance of a snake in a bamboo and so forth; just as the appearance of things otherwise even to one whose mind is afflicted by passion and so forth; just as the appearance of unreal objects to yogis; just as there is a reversal of place even in direct perception; just as there is an unreal form even in memory regarding a past object; just as there is the appearance of unreal objects in inference based on reasoning—thus, even here, it may be so. And in those cases, no external object exists. Therefore, even in the absence of an external object, this is merely a specific form of consciousness itself. Nor is it "apprehension of something else" (anyathākhyāti) or "apprehension of the non-existent" (asatkhyāti); rather, consciousness itself arises in that form. Thus it is established.
If you claim that there is non-existence even when there is an appearance, what kind of meaning could "conjunction" have here? Even the designation "unreal" is not capable of denying existence.

Therefore, for one who speaks thus, it would indeed have to be believed that an entity whose nature is entirely undifferentiated becomes capable of immersion and so forth through contact with a sky-lotus, or becomes a giver of burning pain through the proximity of an unpricked thorn or the son of a barren woman. If it is argued that there is a distinction because those two [the sky-lotus and the barren woman’s son] are not perceived despite being non-existent, whereas the form [of the entity] is perceived, we say: no, for even when it is perceived, its non-existence—which is incompatible with providing assistance or exertion—is not brought away.

Furthermore, for that which is non-existent and incapable of having any excellence added to it, no distinction whatsoever can arise from anything; nor does any distinction belong to that [non-existent thing], nor even to the manifestation [of it]. Moreover, the claim that "the form is merely an indicator" (upalakṣaṇa) is also incoherent, because the status of being an indicator is only possible in the case of a real entity, as in the case of a crest-lock and so forth.

Furthermore, even if illumination (*prakāśa*) is thus characterized, it cannot by itself—given its lack of differentiation—be instrumental in producing a distinction in activity. If it is argued that such a power belongs to it due to the efficacy of the object (*karman*), we say no; for a power is not observed to exist in something without depending on a perceived means (*dṛṣṭasādhana*). Nor is such a distinction in activity observed without a distinction in form (*ākāra*). Even so, if one were to merely postulate its status as a witness (*sākṣitva*), it would follow that one could likewise postulate such a status for the cook and others in the case of cooking and similar acts.

Consequently, the capacity of the form (*ākāra*) therein cannot be denied. Nor is there anyone for whom the determination [of objects] is not based on distinct experiences. Therefore, that which "shines forth" (*prakāśate*) is the manifestation (*prakāśa*), which is the form itself. As for the statement that "manifestation is the act of shining forth," this is merely a property (*dharma*) of that [form], intended to exclude other distinct entities; such is the established position.

For external activity is indeed restricted to the form itself; how could there be a state of error in its absence? Therefore, since the doctrine of formlessness is thoroughly refuted, this [theory of] the accomplishment of what was begun is established as the doctrine of the existence of forms (sākāravāda) alone.

If that were the case, then as long as there is cognition, there is an aspect (*ākāra*), and as long as there is an aspect, there is the persistence of an external object—a state of delusion established by the function [of consciousness]. Thus, purification would never occur. However, if the aspects are unreal, then through the total destruction of the mass of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) from which they arise, when they have utterly ceased, nothing but pure luminosity remains—devoid of appearances and resembling space; this is called purification. If it is argued that this is difficult to achieve under the view that aspects are real, let it be so; what can such a person do about it?

For one who is greedy for the destruction of the *saṃbhogakāya* through great undertakings, and who does not eradicate false speech, let there be no false conceptualization at all, nor any outward activity; or rather, let even the mental form (*ākāra*) be undesirable. But what fault is there in the arising of a desired specific mental form through the power of cultivating a particular mental aspect and the application toward the accumulation of merit?

Nor is there ever a constant restriction to that [pure] form due to the removal of defects, because an absolute difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is possible; otherwise, even the occurrence of the false would be eternal. Therefore, the mind—variegated by the splendor of the primary and secondary marks—has reached a certain pinnacle of transformation through the abundance of practice characterized by the full blossoming of hundreds of virtues.
The self is connected [to the world], a treasury of qualities, bound by the impressions of the unreal;
it is devoid of a multitude of pure forms, yet not formless at all.
If conventional reality were to cease, there would be the destruction of the Dharma-body;
and if its forms were to cease, there would be the ruin of the Enjoyment-body.
[410] For one who dwells on the ten stages, that state exists because of the mental aspect of the Buddha;
yet, having abandoned the mass, this licking of the hand is clearly such [an error].
When even the lords of the earth, who are like fully awakened Buddhas, have their inner minds rendered utterly formless,
then those wretched ones who perceive only emanations would find it better to emaciate themselves or lick their own hands.
Through the sovereign power of the Buddha, such awakening for the ten worlds is the supreme gain;
whereas for those wandering like atoms, the burden of delusion brings no happiness, even more so than contact with filth.

If it is argued that because of the direct realization of those dharmas, there is the vision of the Dharma-body, then while the vision of the Dharma-body follows as a consequence, the vision of the Enjoyment-body is not established for him.
Because it possesses that form, the intellect arises with that very form;
this enjoyment of it, which arises from the accumulation of merit, belongs to those dwelling on all stages.
The clear teaching of the Dharma arises from the manifestation of pure worldly conceptualization;
or else, through the ripening of elevated vows, there is even the cognition of all things according to their respective objects.

Even in the absence of an external object to be grasped and so forth, because it is possible for those seeking various objects to have a correspondence with those respective objects, the establishment of omniscience is also merely the play of the forms within one's own cognition. Alternatively,
just as the state of experience for all embodied beings is manifold throughout the three times, so too does [the omniscient one] manifest in every form that conforms to them.

Through the ripening of his resolve, the All-pervading Lord, by the very splendor of his own nature at the time of manifestation, assumes a single form through the intermingling of various appearances.
Covered by a veil of exceedingly subtle clouds, those who perceive the formless understand this entire world as its true nature.

And therein they desire that which is motionless and peerless in every part to be the portion within the range of the body; thus, though it is entirely the remainder, it is [perceived]. Why is this rule established—that the manifold is one? Why is this rule established—that this king is one?

If that state [of the world] exists upon reaching conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) in this way, then this great excellence arises from the vast burden of pure knowledge. And there can be no subversion— despite the efforts of the intellect— of this mass of diverse forms, which has the nature of reality free from affliction, because the intellect itself leans toward that side.
For it is thus: (PV II 212–213, also quoted in NKan 107,22f., with *bādho 'yatnavattve* in the second half). To explain:

Born from the practice of the accumulations, this [ground] is the domain of unsurpassed delight; it is the ground of light like the expanse of space, familiarized by the diminution of adventitious conceptual proliferation through its abiding in the singular awareness of its own object;
it is that which manifests as a multitude of various emanations, never ceasing its mass of activities for the sake of the world. This is the tenth [ground].
By whom should that [duality] be abandoned, for which, at best, only conceptualization is appropriate as its emergence?
Thus ends the second chapter, the "Establishment of Defilement and Purification," in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great paṇḍita Jñānaśrīmitra.
[412] [The Third Chapter]

But how, while abiding solely in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), can the relationship between cause and effect be established, so that the sequence of causes and effects under discussion may become an object of attention? For indeed, neither a cognition belonging to the past, nor one belonging to the future, nor even one consisting of a synthesis produced by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of both, is capable of entering into the conventional experience of the relationship between cause and effect—which is inseparable from the apprehension of distinction in the form "this [effect] arises from that [cause]"—because all cognitions consist solely of self-awareness, and thus it is impossible for them to have any acquaintance with the affairs of another.

Even if today a mere limit (*avadhi*) has been apprehended by the intellect, it is not that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*); and by a subsequent [cognition], it is indeed that which possesses the limit, not the limit itself. Yet, even by a single synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-dhī*), neither is [apprehended]; so who else could be the cognizer? Even the notions of "the limit" and "that which possesses the limit" arise solely through the power of those [cognitions], for not even one of them is the object; rather, the object of both is their own pure intrinsic nature (*śuddha-svarūpa*).

By this, the relation of priority and posteriority (*pūrvāparabhāva*) is rejected, because priority and posteriority are apprehended in some way [even when things are simultaneous]; thus, the fulfillment of the desire that the causal relation (*hetuphalabhāva*) consists precisely of that [priority and posteriority] is achieved. For perception has no operation here, since priority, posteriority, and so forth are excluded when there is a state of distinct cognition. Nevertheless, it might be argued: "Since they arise in succession, priority and posteriority certainly exist; therefore, the cognition of priority and posteriority itself makes its own nature, as prior and posterior, the object of experience."

However, because it lacks the form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it is merely the word that has been set in motion. Yet, by that much, there is no loss of the experience of the object; for indeed, the name is not the essence of things, yet even that proceeds subsequently through a synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-buddhi*). Nor is its self-awareness impaired by that much; for it is precisely as something self-experienced that it presents itself as a sublater (*bādhaka*) in another instance. Furthermore, the cognition of cause and effect is simply the awareness of a fixed sequence of prior and posterior states, occurring by way of the specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by each preceding moment. At the time of the conceit of non-self-awareness, all this is fit for conventional usage;
but when one is intent upon the awareness of one's own true nature, where is there any connection with the prior and posterior states characterized by duality?
Just as it is fit to be perceived by a divided intellect as external, so too is its mutual difference;
likewise, there is also priority and posteriority. If this were not so, the external would not exist at all, yet that which is being measured as external does indeed exist.
Just as there is priority and posteriority in external objects, so too is there the grasping of cognitions themselves;
yet memory is consistent in both cases. Otherwise, experience would be incapable of producing any result whatsoever.
Therefore, that which was established by the intellect through synthesis is indeed self-evident even for one who lacks valid cognition;
yet, when it comes to the descent of valid cognition regarding what is not known by another, such a state is clearly like painting a picture in the sky.
Nor can such a state be established even by the purity of the internal organ (*koṣṭha*), since it has never been within the scope of direct realization;
for if it were ever seen by anyone at another time, it might perhaps tolerate an uncontradicted doubt.
Therefore, even sequential order cannot be determined without a method of apprehension; like a blind man, it too is incapable of perceiving anything else.
Consequently, that which is externally disordered is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), yet it is not disordered with respect to itself; thus, in that [self-awareness], there is no sequence.
Likewise, sound itself is not established; thus, that which is unreal—though perceived as being both prior and posterior—is not [the object].
There is no cognition of another, nor is there delusion regarding oneself; even in the case of delusion, one's own [nature] is not intended in that way.

But how can you yourself establish the negation of the relation between cause and effect, given the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For perception is not determinative, because it is non-conceptual; nor is mere conceptualization [determinative], because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If you argue that a determination—whether born of perception or born of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—is determinative of its own cause, the object, due to an invariable connection (*pratibandha*), then the causal relationship is established by a means of valid cognition; how, then, could it be sublated?

That is incorrect. For in this way, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not demonstrated; because when the apprehension of the causal relationship (*hetuphalabhāva*) by perception is negated, it entails the negation of its operation. If there is dependence on what is accepted by another, there is no independent establishment, since a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is not a proof. This presentation would merely bring about an obstruction to the opponent's negation.
[414] If the cause were to be sublated by something whatsoever, then the status of cause and effect would be undermined.
But if that very cause does not exist, then the status of cause and effect is not established.

And likewise, [the opponent] says, "There is no cause," while [the proponent] states, "[The world] has a cause" (*sahetuka*), and so forth. Nor is there an establishment of one's own conventional usage of existence simply by having performed a negation that obstructs the other's [position]. If it is argued that for the other party as well, there is merely an obstruction to the establishment of their own conceptual apprehension (*parāmarśa*), and that the causal relationship is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus there is no establishment of the conventional usage of non-existence—[we reply: no, because the other party has initiated only that much [i.e., the negation].

For even the conventional usage of "existence" is established as dependent upon a validating means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, if there were some means of cognition regarding the relation of cause and effect, that relation would exist; in its absence, how could it be so? Thus, this relation of cause and effect—when devoid of the possibility of perception at any time or place—brings about a flawless friendship with the external object.
If it is argued that this is not equal [to the case of consciousness] because other defects are possible in the case of the external, [we reply:
another refutation has been stated here by the author of the *Bhāṣya* accordingly.
Even though there was no mention of the *Vinaya* in the words of the *Sūtra* and the *Vārttika*,
the *Bhāṣya* nevertheless forcefully reflects its own independence [by including it].
Or rather, why is this fault not considered to apply exclusively to the external as well?
For otherwise, how could there be such an effort [in the argument] beginning with "if the external were experienced"?

Therefore, let this rule or prohibition established by his benevolence be heeded by the wise; what is the use of anything else? But even so, for one who concludes that "this follows from that logical ground," the reason (*hetu*) has already been discarded; moreover, one must ultimately resort even to non-perception (*anupalambha*). Thus, how can there be any presentation of reasoning (*yuktinyāsa*) without a reason? For in such a context, it is not possible to remain silent.
When one speaks, something must necessarily be either established or refuted;
in that case, how can there be a cognition for one who asserts [the existence of] a non-cause that pervades itself?
Therefore, this grasping of causes by an existent is indeed difficult to abandon.

Furthermore, this position is also contradicted by its own words; for if one says, "From this statement, there shall be a comprehension of the meaning," then the utterance of that statement is directly inseparable from the acceptance of the relation between cause and effect—so how could one deny it? Moreover, since all established conventions are produced by the relation of cause and effect, the very life-force of this doctrine has departed. This too is inconsistent.

For it is not that the relationship between cause and effect does not exist even when established through conventional determination in every respect; rather, [it does not exist] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). Therefore, as long as there is no interruption of conventional practice which is by nature delusive, the adoption of causes in such and such a manner is not faulty.
Just as one accepts a reason for the sake of establishing merely one's own cognition,
so too does one accept its two inseparable concomitants when denying cause and effect.
If it is established by worldly convention, let the relationship between cause and effect remain; but if it is established by direct perception, then let self-awareness be accepted.

Indeed, it is not a matter for the respect of the wise that self-awareness—which is incompatible with the apprehension of a distinction pervading the states of prior and posterior—should simultaneously abide in that state and cognize the nature of cause and effect as being sequential; rather, it is more appropriate to simply accept the direct apprehension of cause and effect and abandon this obsession with the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*).

Therefore, just as the proofs for [the existence of] light and so forth, which establish the absence of an external object (*nirālambana*), are useful for reminding one of conventional usage by relying upon the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), so too the statements of valid cognition that establish causal capacity (*śakti*) are not contradictory. Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect is known by the person engaged in worldly convention (*sāṃvyavahārika*) as being preceded by the apprehension of difference. Once direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that grasps non-difference has arisen, that [conventional notion] dissolves of its own accord; at times, it might not even grasp difference.

In this regard, as long as the operation of the reason (*hetu*) is manifest for both disputants, so long is it well, because the dispute occurs only between those abiding in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). And in that context, where could there be talk of proof without a reason? If that were so, the meaning would be that the reason negates itself by proving the absence of a reason. This is not a contradiction, because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the reason simply does not exist.
Thus, even the dissolution of all established conventions is not a sublation, since it is precisely the gradual subsiding of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that is auspicious (*śiva*).
For all connections between entities proceed by way of cause and effect; [in reality],
there is only that which has arisen dependently, which is impartite and realized through self-cognition.

In the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), however, even that which is the cause establishes that which is to be established, and the established order itself remains intact. Where, then, is there any charge of self-contradiction?
Just as the external object of apprehension exists together with its preceding state, so too does it extend the memory that apprehends it.
When one strives to investigate the root of these distressed states, how can this manifold world endure such a denial?
Thus is the summary.

How, then, is the non-existence of a cause established by means of a cause? This is its meaning: in a conceptual construction that conforms to the form of ultimate reality as it has entered through the gateway of the cause, there is an appearance devoid of preceding and succeeding forms; this very [appearance] is the absence of the apprehension of the relation between cause and effect. Therefore, because it is perceived as possessing activity, even though it is itself devoid of activity, this self-appearance appears as if it were active. Consequently, it manifests as "the cause" and "the cause of the non-existence of a cause."

And there is no means for the realization of reality other than the specific transformation of the forms of conceptual construction. However, once one has reached the ultimate reality characterized by self-awareness alone, there can be no dispute regarding anything anywhere, nor any application of proof or refutation. Even when that [ultimate reality] is far removed within the conventional realm, the mere manifestation of its form in some way remains the only recourse.

Therefore, for one who knows that the comprehension of meaning arises from this very statement, the formulation "there is no cause" is indeed dependent upon the qualification "in reality. Thus, there is no contradiction; however, this fault would occur if there were a total denial [of conventional reality], as in the cases: "the word is non-expressive" or "inference is not a means of valid cognition. Even in those instances, because of the qualification "in reality," there is no contradiction anywhere. For inference, like sensory perception, is a means of valid cognition only from the standpoint of conventional practice (*saṃvyavahāra*), not in reality.

Because it depends upon the apprehension of a relationship (*sambandha*) and so forth; nor can mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-mātra*) accomplish that by means of this [inference], since even in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) must be established through distinct cognitions. Furthermore, validity (*prāmāṇya*) arises from correspondence (*saṃvāda*), and there is no correspondence with respect to any distinct object. Therefore, the validity of anything beyond self-awareness is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*); likewise, the conventional discourse of cause and effect (*hetu-phala-vyavahāra*) is also merely conventional, because both share the same single cognition. It is not the case that as there is a means of valid cognition (*māna*) toward another [object], so too are there cause and effect.
And just as there is the relation of cause and effect in this world, so too is there valid cognition in the other world.
Upon what, then, can one rely for the establishment of the mind in this context?
Since, in reality, no other grasping is established, [if it were argued from] the conventional perspective, it would be a proof of what is already proven.
Conventional reality is the cognition that is pleasing so long as it is not investigated;
reality is that which is apprehended by each successive cognition, up until the non-dual.
And as for the notion that "this has arisen from that," the emergence of this conceptual construction occurs through the mark (*liṅga*) for one who knows the other;
thus, this is merely conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), and here there is no activity for one who knows [reality] itself.
Likewise, even the cognition that performs the synthesis would be a mere conceit;
therefore, whatever is established from that mere conceit is merely conventional.
As long as there is conventional reality, the determination of causes and so forth remains stable;
and by avoiding what is undesirable, one's engagement [with the world] is not at fault.

Now, if [the object] could not exist without causal capacity (*śakti*), then when that very capacity exists, the talk of its being "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*) is false; what is the point of this difference in terminology?
It is not merely that externality is compatible with cause and effect;
rather, from a cognition in the form of a seed, there arises this cognition in the form of a sprout.
In that case, for one who knows the causal relationship between those two cognitions,
what is the point of a verbal distinction, since he already possesses knowledge of the difference external to them?
In the case of non-difference, there can be no establishment of the relation between cause and effect due to the absence of duality;
or else, those two cognitions themselves would be mutually contradictory as being distinct from one another.
There is no prior cognition, nor a subsequent one; there is no self, nor any other grasper.
Later, the conceptualization that acts as a grasper will be the arrow that shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas.
If the apprehension of the word’s power is [admitted], let there also be the apprehension of the external object; what is the use of shame here?
Or, if you delight in logic, then by that very logic, the apprehension of the power must also be released.

If it is argued that the determination "it is seen" exists even with respect to the external object, then the sublation of the external object is actually grounded solely in self-cognition; that [self-cognition] alone constitutes the result and the means.
And thus says the Sūtra:
"The cessation of causes and conditions, the negation of a [substantial] cause, and the establishment of Mind-only—this I call non-arising. (***).

[418] "Non-arising" is the negation of the fruit. The mere existence of mind alone is the explicit negation of cause and fruit. If your activity occurs solely through a cause, it lasts only as long as there is external conceptual determination; as long as the notion of a self persists due to lack of realization, there is no engagement with anything beyond that, unlike the case [of the external world].
There is no certain conclusion apart from inference, and there is no inference without supreme knowledge;
just as that [knowledge] destroys both oneself and others, so too do my reasons destroy both myself and others.

What logic is there in this: that those who, by means of an inference produced from a proof purified by the determination of the three marks—which by its very nature functions through an outward orientation—employ it as a means for establishing the cognition of another (even though it is invariably concomitant with the cognition of oneself), yet in some context raise an objection against the restatement of that very meaning by means of a refutation based on contradiction? What kind of principle is this?

Just as an ordinary person is unable to live without relying on the validity of inference due to their adherence to duality, so too [the yogin] cannot abandon the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the truth established in that state. Furthermore, that very conviction in the truth which consists in the mere realization of one's own self-awakened nature is itself a disregard for external inference; yet it is not possible to remain in such a state [without it], because otherwise there would follow the absurdity of abandoning the exertion characterized by practice, since the goal would have been accomplished at that very moment.

Therefore, when those very [cognitions] proceed from the power of delusion as if through an inclination toward a self, and when direct realization is attained, the all-pervading *dharmadhātu* is established; thus, there is no returning to the denial of inference, just as ashes remain even after the extinction of a fire whose fuel is spent. For this very reason, the meaning is that the conceptual cognition designated as "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) bows down, being without a support. And this very point is reiterated in the context of the investigation into cause and effect; nothing further is prescribed.

To the extent that there is external mental inference, this alone constitutes the acceptance of cause and effect; for at that very time, it is the mark (*liṅga*) which serves as the basis, since it makes known what is imperceptible and acts as the producer upon the cognition thereof. As for the subsequent sublation [of that] when one abides in mere self-awareness—that itself is the relation of cause and effect. What is the point of attachment here? How, then, is the distinction between the producer and the indicator established by the author of the *Vārttika* within the Vijñānavāda? True, this is merely a provisional internal arrangement.
For this very reason, the method of expression is that "it should be postulated by relying upon the intellect" (*buddhi*). However, when the ultimate reality is being extracted, it is said:

"Everything is incapable" (*aśaktaṃ sarvam*, PV III 4), and so forth. This is the meaning: prior to non-duality (*advaita*), a systematic arrangement may be made in whatever way suits the differences in the dull, middling, or superior intellects of those to be instructed; through the gradual sharpening of the mind, one eventually gains conviction in non-duality itself, which is not fixed in any particular stage.

Therefore, although conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) possesses a plurality of levels corresponding to progressively higher ultimate realities (*paramārtha*), the entry into the relationship between cause and effect—which depends upon it—is itself the reality (*tattva*) consisting precisely in the occurrence of the three types of perception and non-perception. Lest there be deception even regarding one's own intended object, this very convention must be adopted over another convention; it is not, however, inferior simply because it lacks adherence to the ultimate, for the distinction lies in the correspondence or lack thereof with one's intention.

Therefore, this is not even a subject for inquiry: how can there be the establishment of an object (*arthasiddhi*) from a mere cognition that lacks a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), much less from one that is sublated by investigation? For in that case, there is no establishment of an object whatsoever, other than the mere satisfaction of the person [involved]. Whatever kind of cognition it may be, it is simply a cognition; likewise, the non-establishment of an object is itself the "establishment of an object"—this is a "sacrificial offering corresponding to the spirit" (*yakṣānurūpo baliḥ*).

If one follows the perspective of the noble ones (*ārya*), then nothing exists from the perspective of our own [worldly] hearts; however, a discerning cognizer should understand things in such a way that they would not be deceived even by mere worldly satisfaction. For this very reason, he says:
"And this has been stated as the nature of conventional means of valid cognition" (*PVin* I 100,20), and so forth.

Therefore, there is no fault of following a specific means of proof for the conventional [cognizer], so where could there be dissatisfaction for anyone else? Now, according to our view, everything indeed exists, but for those who have directly realized reality (*tattvasākṣātkārin*), it does not exist—so what is the final conclusion?
It is true that to one who has realized the truth, this world is like matted hair, a madman, or a ghost;
and even though he has realized the truth, he appears to the world like one with matted hair, a madman, or a ghost.
Therefore, in this regard, sovereignty belongs to will.
If the world were a manifestation of what is non-existent, let its determination proceed from that [will] and not directly.
For there is no manifestation of causes and the like other than through the conceptualization of its own appearance.

Therefore, although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*) there is no relation of cause and effect, how could it be disregarded since it is impossible to avoid within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*)? The production of the intended result arises from the accumulation of causes; for one who seeks its accomplishment follows that [conventional process] precisely because it pertains to the conventional domain. However, for one who has directly realized ultimate reality, just as the relation of cause and effect is not established anywhere, so too is there no performance of such actions anywhere.

If it is asked, "How can that which performs no purposeful action possess existence (*sattva*)? We reply: No, because from our perspective, its continuity of activity for the sake of others is uninterrupted throughout its own moments. However, in reality, luminosity alone is established as true existence; thus it remains settled that this belongs to the manifold form itself.
But even so, if it is argued, "That manifold is one," then this is even more manifold than that! (PV III 200cd)
And then there is this most extraordinary thing: their mutual division.

For a variegated (*citra*) thing is defined as having manifold forms (*nānākāra*); therefore, how could there be non-difference among these forms which are superimposed with mutually contradictory properties? But if that is so, how can there be difference [among them], since those contained within a single cognition do not cognize one another—like distinct mental continua—and because it would follow that only some single [form] would manifest? That is incorrect, because the superimposition of contradictory properties remains as it was.

Therefore, this [cognition] is indeed manifold; however, because it is produced from a non-different material cause (*upādāna*), its nature consists in mutual perceptibility and the appearance of simultaneity. There is no over-extension [of the definition] to cognitions arising in other mental continua, as they lack the state of having a non-different material cause. Here it is considered: does their unity of material cause remove their plurality?
And precisely because of their distinctness, mutual cognition among them is not admitted.

For one consciousness does not enter into another consciousness; rather, the denial of mutual cognition between one's own and another's cognitions occurs solely through the removal of the bolt of a single consciousness. And since that [denial] remains unshaken even in the present case, there is no distinction. Now, if the appearance of coexistence (*sāhitya*) is to be established, what is the use of the entry into a single consciousness? For there is no harm [to the argument] even without it, as it would contradict the probandum. But surely "coexistence" is merely known by the definition of concomitance restricted to the same place and time.

Furthermore, since their manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) consists in the direct realization of their own respective natures, it has not been established that there is mutual cognition [of one another], just as in the case of several men who are present but not all together. Therefore, it is precisely the penetration into a single mutual consciousness (*paraspara-saṃvid-āveśa*) that is useful for the conventional usage of "mutual cognition"; what is the point here of mere association (*sāhitya*)? If, on the other hand, the term "manifestation of association" is intended to mean the manifestation of all [objects] everywhere, then even when the "manifestation of association" is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason "penetration into a single consciousness everywhere" is contradictory (*viruddha*). Thus, this verbal formulation is empty. For if that were its meaning, this would merely be an auxiliary factor (*sahāya*).

If there is no mutual cognition within a single consciousness, then when that [consciousness] is denied, there is no mutual perception at all; in this case, the fault regarding the object is insurmountable.

Or rather, let there be no mutual assistance; however, if the appearance of coexistence (*sāhitya*) consists in the appearance of one another, then even if they share a non-different substratum (*abhinnopādānatva*), their difference cannot be denied. For we do not understand what answer has been given to the objection that "one's own consciousness does not enter into another's consciousness," since this merely restates a synonym without nourishing any specific distinction.

For even when they share a single object of appropriation, those [cognitions], though occurring together, do not enter into one another's awareness; otherwise, what indeed would constitute their difference?
Immersed solely in their own consciousness, they do not touch the consciousness of another;
yet they perceive one another—this is truly a great marvel!
Moreover,

if it is argued that there is a complete familiarity [of the object] due to the non-difference of its appropriation (*upādāna*), then it would be better for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) itself to be non-different; for even when [the nature] is different, there is no such experience.

Likewise, if a single causal complex were to produce a cognition capable of apprehending a restricted object, what fear would there be? For in either case, the defining characteristic [of perception] would be destroyed.

This being so, there is no fear whatsoever regarding the refutation of that which possesses the characteristic of being an object (*grāhya*) by means of [the arguments of] its simultaneous arising and its similarity [to the cognition]; for for one who maintains the existence of external objects (*bahirarthavādin*), the relationship between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) is easily established in quite another way. In that case, because there is no difference in their material cause (*upādāna*), there would be mutual experience, since all things have the nature of experience. However, if they were produced by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrījanyatva*), then the experience of matted hair and the experience [of the cognition itself] would possess their respective restricted states of being the object known (*vedyatva*) and the knower (*vedakatva*). And due to that restriction, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, since the *jaṭa* (the mental organ) also vibrates at that time, how can there be a fixed rule? If it is argued that "only that which has the *jaṭa* as its material cause (*upādāna*) is the object (*grāhya*), while anything else is the subject (*grāhaka*)," [we reply: no, for this would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the sense-faculties. It is not so, because by the very power of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), blue alone arises as the state of being cognized.
There is a mutual lack of assistance due to their simultaneous existence, and both of you alike suffer from the failure to recognize identity (*tādātmya*).

Now, if it is argued that there is the fault of commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) because manifestation (*prakāśa*) arises [in a way that would apply to all], we reply: its arising is as "being cognizable" (*vedyatva*), not as "manifestation" itself. If it is asked, "What is this 'being cognizable'?", then it is the same [problem]: for two things that are self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), what is this "mutual cognition"? Now, if it is argued that "being cognizable" is nothing other than the arising of manifestation, even so, the fault of commonality will be avoided precisely by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Now, since an entity possesses a single nature, just like its blueness, it must necessarily exist in a non-common way through both manifestation and non-manifestation; for it is indeed possible [for it to do so] by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), so let this matter rest.

[422] Now, since this object is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), where could the capacity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) be applied? Furthermore, regarding that which does not even require entry into the determination of its own nature and dissolves of its own accord—how can there be a designation of non-difference in terms of material cause (*upādāna*) in such a case? For when two illuminations have arisen, it is not the case that one is illuminated by the other, nor does one appear to the other, nor is there any logical consistency in saying "in one."

For just as the self-illumination of a lamp is somehow known and understood by following that [knowledge], so too no mutual illumination between lamps has ever been perceived. Therefore, just as the notion that "one lamp is illuminated by another lamp" is an error, so too is the notion that "one cognition is illuminated by another cognition. Thus, for what purpose should there be an answer consisting of a single substratum? By this, even the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) regarding "the cognition of itself" is refuted.

If it is argued that even for the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), the avoidance of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is simply the non-denial [of the definition], this too is refuted as being easily dismissed, because the very object of another's cognition is not established. If it is argued that the illumination of another is indeed observed, we reply: even that occurs only by way of generating a subsequent moment of illumination from a material cause that was previously unilluminated; thus, there is no room for such an objection in the case of cognitions, lamps, and the like.

But he who maintains that even there the light co-arising [with the object] is the illuminator of the cloth—his position is also untenable. For the determination of reality does not occur through mere worldly convention (*lokādhyavasāya*); rather, it depends upon inference based on the grounds for establishing the relation "this belongs to that. If one were to rely on the production of that cognition [as the ground], then since the object co-arising with the cognition would be admitted as its illuminator, the established order would collapse, as [the object] would no longer exist [at the time of cognition]. Alternatively, if it is argued that here too there is parity by reference to a subsequent conceptualizing cognition (*pṛṣṭhajavikalpajñāna*), then this very [subsequent cognition] would be the grasper and not the former one; and since this [subsequent cognition] is simultaneous [with the object], this is the entry into the Sautrāntika doctrine.

Now, if it is argued that light does not possess the quality of being an illuminator merely by generating cognition—even though cognition itself arises simultaneously with it, and that this is due to their mere co-arising from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—then it would follow that the sense organs existing at that time are also illuminators, since they too are not of the nature of light. To this we reply: let light indeed be light; but how can it be an illuminator? For a blue object cannot become yellow merely by being simultaneous with something yellow.

Therefore, nothing that is ineffective can occupy the path of a relationship [with anything]. However, by way of causal assistance, a lamp is seen to participate in the conventional usage [of "illumination"] with respect to objects such as jars, which are not of the nature of light; thus, when it is understood that the cognition of that [lamp] has another cognition as its illumination, one might indeed refrain from employing the genitive case where there is a single shared material cause (*ekopādānabhāva*).

It is not, however, in consideration of perceptibility; for example, in the case of "Maitra is more beautiful than Caitra," this is in consideration of the beauty as it is being understood (*gamyamāna-saundaryatā*), but perceptibility is not in consideration of beauty, because both beauties reside in a single substrate.

If it is argued that no one would employ [such a reason] in this way, [we reply: even if he were a scorner, how could he employ it? For the logic is the same. Thus, by means of the absence of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper, the proof of non-duality through the "logic of the leader" has been established according to the maxim of the blind man milking a cow. And this is not a mere logical quibble; so why this futile trampling upon Śubhagupta out of hatred for the author of the *Vārttika*?

If it is argued that cognitions then appear as both conjoined and distinct—just like multiple lamps—and thus what is the purpose of [the concept of] "awareness" (*vedana*), we say: no. For the conventional usage that they "appear conjoined" is made in relation to a cognizer who is distinct [from them]. But surely, even in the absence of such a cognizer, the manifestation of the conjoined [cognitions] is not exhausted? This is true; however, [it is not so in the ultimate sense].

[423] It may be argued that even a single [consciousness] can be the illuminator of another; however, since the nature of self-illumination exists even for those things obstructed by an iron vessel (*ayoghaṭī*), the point under discussion is not established. Therefore, the establishment of the conventional usage of "mutual cognition" occurs only through the inclusion of one consciousness within the other. For there is not even a rumor that lamps originating from a single source illuminate one another.
If, in that case, the atoms are indeed distinct, then life (*jīva*) is all the more dear [to you];
yet, because such a cause is never observed anywhere, its uniqueness is clearly evident.
If it is argued that, just as a lamp is seen to be self-luminous and manifold,
so too are these appearances [manifold] because they are not distinct from the seed-consciousness, then this would indeed be correct.

Thus, this arising from a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīsambhava*) may, by way of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), enable the inference of one thing upon the perception of another in certain cases; it does not, however, lead to the direct perception (*adhyakṣatva*) of the other, as is the case with taste, color, and so forth. Likewise, sharing a single material cause (*ekopādānatā*) would establish a further degree of homogeneity (*sajāyīyatā*), but not the manifestation of another [quality] that is to be proven through the commingling of intrinsic natures (*svabhāvasaṅkara*). Otherwise, it might even follow that in some instances, one thing could be the "tangle" (*jaṭa*) of another.

By this, the conceptualization that mutual manifestation consists precisely in having a non-different material cause (*abhinnopādānatva*) is also refuted; for it would follow as an absurd consequence that even matted locks, which share a single material cause, would be mutually entangled. For their state of being entangled exists insofar as they possess their own respective forms, and the same applies to their state of being manifest.
Moreover,
just as the existence of a thing is not established by way of producing a form,
so too let it be by way of a single substratum, according to conventional designation.

For just as, according to the Sautrāntika, being an object of cognition consists solely in the production of a form similar [to itself], and not even in its manifestation, so too the manifestation of one thing would be the manifestation of another, and there would be no perception of a variegated [form]. Furthermore, this [notion of] having a single material cause (*ekopādānatva*) is also to be understood purely [in this sense], because it is determined that in both the states of dreaming and waking, the cause is precisely the variegated form; for even at a time of confusion, conceptualization manifests as multiple forms, and even when conceptualizing a single object, the form is variegated due to differences in spatial location.

If it is argued that a cluster arises from a cluster, and that the capacity for production belongs to only one of them, then the fact that multiple things act as producers—conforming to the presence or absence [of the effect]—is the same [as our position]. Furthermore, since we observe the emergence of a blue form even from a fragmented blue form, there is no answer for one who claims that a variegated [effect] arises from a non-variegated [cause]. Moreover, because it is impossible to count [the constituent parts], there can be no deficiency or excess. Furthermore, even if there were deficiency or excess—as in the case of a banyan tree (*vaṭa*)—something single might still produce many;
however, there would be no state of oneness in what is deficient, or if there were oneness, the variegated would be non-dual.

That cognition is like that; likewise, even in other cases, following states such as deep sleep, from the *ālayavijñāna* itself—due to a differentiation of its aspects (*pradeśabheda*)—the arising of one variegated state from another variegated state occurs. Or, let it be that from a single, coagulated form, there sometimes and in some place arises a variegated state, either successively or simultaneously.

First of all, as long as [the mind] remains unobstructed by torpor (*middha*) and so forth immediately after waking, there would be no mutual experience of moments other than those belonging to the first instant, because their material causes (*upādāna*) are distinct. If it is argued that this is due to their being awakened from that same [initial] state through a continuous succession, then, to whatever extent there is an interval, to that same extent there would be a gradual loss of mutual illumination due to the increasing degree of dullness, and this would occur even after some small interval.

Furthermore, the non-destruction of the manifold luminosity is experienced through states such as waking for many days, nor is there any gradation in its intensity. If you argue that this cannot be so in the case of the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), we ask: how can it be possible to perceive what is distinct from a single uniform perception? Even if there were no difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), the distinction or non-distinction inherent in the object itself would be the determining factor. Moreover, in the case of a reductio (*prasaṅga*), the conclusion must be the opposite of the premise; it does not establish the very point [the opponent] intends.
Furthermore, if the apprehension of the effect (*upādeya*) occurs because of its connection with the material cause, [then the same should apply here].
The connection [of the word] "not" with "appropriation" (upādāna) is not the operative factor.

For cognition is inherently remote from one another; yet, by transcending that boundary, proximity reveals its own power, and since that [proximity] is primary only in relation to the material cause (*upādāna*), the experience of a distinct co-existent entity would have to occur solely through the medium of the apprehension of the cause, just like an inference dependent on a single causal complex. If it is argued that this is not so because [the object] is past, there is no difference between remoteness of nature and remoteness of time.

Now, both of these [distinctions] apply to the *upādāna* (the material cause), whereas for co-existent things, there is merely a remoteness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*). In that case, proximity (*sannikṛṣṭatva*) is also diminished; yet, in the case of the *upādāna*, it is predominant—this is the "lizard-and-rabbit" logic (*godhā-śaśa-nyāya*). Furthermore, the persistence of perception occurs by the power of proximity. If, then, there were a manifestation of the past, it would have to be present; how could it be past? Therefore, there is no manifestation of the past.

If such a vision of reality were perceived by another through a consciousness that has become his own self, then the other would be nothing but one's own essential nature; how, then, could there be the cognition of another?

In that case, let the proclamation of "proximity" (sannikarṣa) apply even to one whose eyes are not opened; likewise, there might be the grasping of what is past, as in the case of a yogi. Thus, if this process were to proceed continuously, it would entail the consequence of perceiving every preceding moment, either until reaching a single material cause (*upādāna*) or without limit. Just as there is a gradation in the degree of intervention (*vyavadhi*), so too there is a gradation in the intensity of proximity. Consequently, if it follows that even one's own effect (*svopādeya*) would appear [to consciousness], then everything would be like that.

Moreover, if there were indeed a difference between the various appearances [within a single cognition], then as in the case of blue and yellow, the same would apply to a blue and a brown pillar. Consequently, because one perceives things down to the level of atoms, there would be nothing whatsoever perceived as a single entity that could serve as the single material cause for another; thus, the entire world would fall into an unimpeded blindness. Or rather, this doctrine culminates in the conclusion that "nothing exists at all."

[425] Therefore, if this is precisely what you intend to say, why this trivial wrangling? It should simply be stated directly that even the multiplicity of entities does not exist. If it is argued that the unreality of forms (ākāra) is already accepted, even so, why resort to this which fails to withstand logical scrutiny?
Furthermore, because forms are unreal, a single material cause (upādāna) is impossible;
however, for mere luminosity (prakāśa), there is no harm even in the absence of differentiation.
Furthermore, if a distinction were admitted, one could not tolerate their mutual manifestation;
for if mutual manifestation were tolerated, the state of being grasped object and grasping subject would follow.

Thus, there is a subversion of the established tenet (*siddhānta*). Therefore, even if this non-difference of the material cause (*upādāna*) is explained independently of the Teacher, it does not—failing to imply a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—have the power to bring about the mutual experience and manifestation of these forms (*ākāra*).
If it is seen that such is the case, let it be seen; however, one must investigate whether this [non-difference] belongs to the forms or to the seed’s own self. This is what deserves to be examined.
If [the mind] were a single unity, there could be no variety; if it were manifold, this [variety] would be even more impossible.
Thus, neither unity nor plurality is logically tenable for cognitions.
What, then, is the ultimate truth here? For instance:
if the various forms are indeed the very nature of the mind, how can it be manifold?
Or if the mind itself is manifold, then upon what basis do you maintain its unity?
The intellect, bearing the form of atoms, is neither capable of nor able to perceive them individually; yet they appear when combined, mutually intermingling—what a mysterious process this is!
Therefore, this follows from the force of reality itself, as the wise declare: "In whatever way objects are analyzed, in that very way they fall apart. (PV III 209)
That form by which entities are determined does not exist in reality,
because neither a single nor a manifold form is found in them.
[426] These [entities], being defiled by the investigation [of their parts], do not maintain their constituent members;
for it is better to regard things while closing one's eyes like an elephant.

Thus, it is established by logic that the emptiness of all phenomena is precisely like a dream, an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a reflection; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, one might object: "The present investigation was undertaken with reference to the Blessed One; so now, is even the Buddha, the Blessed One, like an illusion or like a dream?"

Who, then, can here offer a critique? For the Blessed One himself has proclaimed it thus, and the Noble Ones have illuminated that utterance with joy; furthermore, because he accepted that there is no distinction between a *tathāgata* and an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) in terms of suchness (*tathatā*), and because of its unique profundity and magnificence celebrated in the scriptures—where else [could one find it]? [Objection: But surely, since it is sublated by the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) and because the aspects (*ākāra*) such as the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are unreal, where is the magnificence? Moreover, this leads to the consequence of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*).
Since its nature is a cognition in which the non-existent appears, it is erroneous; so where is the profundity? [Reply: That is incorrect.
The grasping of that [object] in what is not that is error; other types of error have been refuted.
Furthermore, one does not perceive the unreal through an unreal form.
Just as this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) exists, so does the Tathāgata exist through knowledge;
even from the standpoint of conventional designation, there is no delusion regarding him, because the seed [of such delusion] is absent.
Since engagement and withdrawal arise from conceptual construction, which in turn arises from latent predispositions,
the state of abiding in the immutable is achieved by uprooting both of these along with their roots.

And in this system, the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti) is not undesirable, because everything that appears here does so as something non-existent in its true nature; nor is there anything else that remains uncontradicted.

This has already been refuted in detail previously. Nevertheless, due to its association with the path that transcends phenomena (*dharmottara-mārga*), this very [mind]— which is devoid of forms such as 'da' and so forth, yet internally flashes with suffering, pleasure, and the like— is accepted as a constituent part [of the path].
"It is said that there is no possibility of sublation here because of the spatial extension [of the cognition]; but even that is erroneous. For:

internal sensation has pleasure and so forth as its object, while external sensation has cold and so forth as its domain; each such cognition, assuming its respective form, is indeed seized by sublation."

[427] For we know that the form of cognition is indeed a particular individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*). And the absence of spatial extension would mean either a smallness of space or its total absence. In that regard, if the fault [of contradiction] applies even to a space the size of an atom, how could it be obstructed by such a small amount? Thus, the first position is not tenable. As for the second, however, it is impossible; for that which is possible must necessarily exist somewhere. If it does not exist anywhere at all, then its non-existence is established.

Furthermore, states such as physical discomfort and mental unease are experienced within the body, manifesting through the exclusion of external locations. Otherwise, if there were no distinction from blue and other objects—as there is none with respect to their luminosity—the same fault would apply. In that case, what is the point of asking how much space they occupy within the body? Or what is "having spatial extension" (*sadeśatā*), since even in the case of color, nothing distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*) designated as "space" is ever perceived anywhere? Nor is the locus itself the space, for if it were, it would follow that wind and sunlight would also lack spatial extension. Moreover, the application of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) does not occur in relation to that [locus], but rather in relation to the object's own nature.

Just as the essential nature (*svarūpa*), though devoid of parts, appears in the conceptualizing intellect as if surrounded by distinct attributes, so too "space" (*deśa*)—which is constructed by a cognition opposed to the reflective awareness of time and form in the manner of "this is here"—enters into linguistic usage only as the counterpart to the movement through space. And it has already been stated that this movement is not remote from the internal experience of pleasure, mental well-being, and so forth, just as it is not remote from the experience of touch.

Now, if you think that whereas in the case of blue and other [objects] a state of having clearly distinct parts such as upper and lower, as well as being delimited by measurements such as a *vitasti*, a *hasta*, an elephant, or a man, is perceived, this is not the case for pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth—then what follows from that? It would merely mean that they are not known to possess spatial extension. For if that were so, it would follow that even odors, tastes, sounds, and the like—which are perceived by non-tactile senses—would lack spatial location. Furthermore, it is impossible to establish a fixed spatial location even for fire and other things that are beyond direct perception.

Now, if it is argued that those two [smell and taste] can be inferred as existing in a restricted location to the extent that smell and taste are produced in the fruit, and that at the time of perception they are grasped by the sense organ according to its remaining size—along with the portion of what preceded it—then why can pleasure and so forth not also be apprehended through their spatial dimension, given that their experience occurs within the body? However, a lack of pervasion is observed in the case of smell and taste within the fruit. If it is argued that the enjoyer is perceived in a restricted location, [we reply:]...

That [cognition] as well, being a gross apprehension, is not capable of determining a location with atomic precision. Therefore, in this case too, it is the same: it exists by pervading some extent of space. Likewise, at the time of perception, there is indeed a determination of the specific restriction of that which is measured by the location of the sense organ. This same principle applies even to pleasure and the like; for that which is produced by seeing or hearing also follows this rule. Indeed, the eye itself, scorched by the sight of the unpleasant, is experienced as becoming cool upon seeing the pleasant.

In the case of plunging into a pond heated by the hot-rayed sun, there is indeed a manifest distinction of magnitude or of the upper and lower parts. Even if one were to imagine the rising [of the sun] in another location, that very same location would remain [the locus of the experience]. A restriction of magnitude is appropriate for kings upon their respective lands; and this alone is human happiness, namely, verbal cognition—thus there is no proof of a difference, either because of the clear manifestation or otherwise.

However, because mental satisfaction (*saumanasya*) is mental in nature, even when its manifestation is indistinct, it is possible—by following from that—to establish it in a general sense as existing somewhere in this very place; thus, there is no obstacle [to such a conclusion]. Nor is insistence useful in that regard, for it would entail the undesirable consequence that the probandum (*sādhya*) itself would be conceptual.

Furthermore, if there were no determination of a fixed measure, and if there were a negation of spatial location in some cases, let there be no negation of temporal location for anything, since it is impossible to determine the measure of a single moment. It is only the coarse intellect that establishes a restriction to specific times, thinking "it did not exist before" and "it will not exist after. In this case as well, the certainty remains established: "It is not outside the body; rather, it is right here, such as in the form of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth."

Furthermore, the connection with time is indeed accepted for mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and the like; otherwise, the fact that they never occur at all would constitute a valid subverting argument (*bādhakayukti*). Moreover, that very [connection with time] establishes their possession of spatial location, because what does not exist anywhere can only occasionally come into existence. Wherever it exists, that is its location; as for whether that [location] is gross or subtle, what does that matter? As for time, the establishment of a restriction is made in view of other requirements.
Just as having a fixed time is clearly evident, so too is having a fixed location;
however, this restriction to a specific place occurs either through atomicity or through a superior [magnitude].
In both cases, however, there is no cessation of the contradiction regarding pleasure and the like.
Therefore, what is the use of a specific refutation when the [opponent's] position has already been rejected by a general negation?

Thus, since spatial extension is necessarily concomitant with existence just like temporal duration, it cannot dispel the fear that the non-perception of a pervader might occur anywhere; nor should you say so, for how could the conventional usage of "existence" itself be established in cases such as pleasure? Just as for you, the proof of its being neither one nor many is not established, so too for me, having set aside the light of my own cognition—like a measured portion—of either oneness or otherness.

For just as, because pleasure and the like do not appear with a form situated in front [of the observer] in the same way that blue does, it is impossible to ascertain their exclusion from being either one or many; likewise, for that very reason, the possibility of either of those two [being one or many] is also [impossible], since the determination "this is one" or "this is many" is perceived only when it is manifesting in front.

Even regarding an imperceptible object, if its status were established according to what is seen [in the perceptible], then even for a form not manifesting in front, its non-existence could be established—due to the restriction of location following the form manifesting in front—just as in the case of sparks of fire produced by intense friction.

If it is argued that "that which exists must necessarily be of one nature [either eternal or non-eternal]," we say no; because those two [categories] are mutually exclusive, there is doubt regarding existence itself whenever there is doubt about either one of them. As for self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), cast away its efficacy just as you have cast away [the efficacy of] white and so forth; do not remain here with hope for it. Furthermore, even for one who points out the "doubtful unestablished" (*saṃdigdhāsiddhi*) fallacy of another by claiming that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no personal conventional usage of "existence," because when there is an absence of both a proof and a refutation, doubt is logically established.

Furthermore, regarding the mass of the nature of cognitions such as "blue" which is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), the very non-observation of sublation (*bādhā*) is its powerful basis. If it is argued: "In that case, let there be invalidity for self-cognition precisely because of that [non-observation]; however, in the absence of sublation, let there be validity," this is not so, because non-existence is not established by mere non-observation. Since everything external is habitually experienced and there is the possibility of a prover for the absence of a sublater, there is no other [means of establishing non-existence] than the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*). However, this doctrine of non-sublation has already been considered in the *Śāstra*; let it rest for now. In this same way, even stories and the like produced by the Vedas would possess the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*).
The claim that validity is established through presumption (utsarga) is also refuted by those who follow.
Wherever there is validity even by itself, the wise know that to be the fruit of repeated practice; for while everything external is practiced, that which is internal is what is truly contemplated.

If it is argued that the appearance of the mass of the apprehended aspect—even though it is unreal—cannot be denied because of the power of the apprehending aspect, such as pleasure and so forth, we say no;
for both parts possess the nature of self-luminosity.
What then would be the apprehended and what the apprehender? Nor can one thing appear through another.

This is because it has already been established [in the previous section] that the external object is refuted; furthermore, the nature of reality does not arise from mere conceit. Moreover, in this view, if the entire host of afflictions—attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, and so forth—is innate insofar as they are of the nature of formless cognition, just like suffering and the rest, then, my dear, what distinction could there be between the pleasant and the unpleasant? And how could there be detachment in the view that [cognition] possesses forms?

For you, the association with the aspect of light (*ālokākāra*) is an error. In the absence of that [error], ignorance and the other [afflictions] would exist as the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those subject to existence; for if they were unreal merely by way of their objective support (*ālambana*), it would follow that pleasure and so forth would also be unreal. Therefore, the statement that "some are to be abandoned because they are undesirable, while others are to be adopted" is nothing but the position of the Aspectarians (*sākāravāda*) expressed in different words. As for the disagreement regarding whether the circle of aspects culminates in what is seen and touched, this is of no consequence.

Just as something may be abandoned by some because it is undesirable even though it is an error, so too, let a particular aspect (ākāra) remain because it is desirable even though it is unreal; thus, the thesis is undermined. Furthermore, these mental factors such as pleasure and so forth are accepted [as real], whereas the mind, being the nature of the aspect insofar as it grasps the object, is to be abandoned; and since the mental factor is what persists, this [aspect] would not be a "concomitant dharma" (samprayukta-dharma), which contradicts scripture.

Moreover, if there is no difference [between the aspect and the mind], they must be unreal just like the mind, or else the mind itself must be real just like them; how then can the thesis of a mind without aspects (anākāra) be established?

[Objection: Surely, whatever is meditated upon in whatever form becomes manifest as such; therefore, even if the mind is meditated upon as having the form of space, it will become manifest as such. Furthermore, since it lacks any established form, that very mind is formless. Thus, how can there be the establishment of the thesis? [Reply: No, because there is no purpose [in such a meditation]. For it is said:

"If you desire to abandon this physical body—which is untouched by the defects of saṃsāra and radiant with the primary and secondary marks—and instead ascend into the sky," [then one must cultivate the form of the Buddha].
Is it not the case that this enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is indeed accepted by the sons of the Arhats?
One who desires to attain the dharma-body (dharmakāya) should resort to a form comparable to space.

If this is argued, then that [cognition] is not first of all the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven), because the intended [proof] is completed precisely as previously stated. Nor is it the *sādhana* (the means of proof) for any object, because the establishment of an object from something formless is unestablished. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the establishment of an object for another is necessarily bound to a specific form. Now, who—other than a proponent of *syādvāda*—would accept that the establishment of an object arises from form itself, whereas for another [cognition] it arises from the formless? If it is argued that this is so on the basis of scripture (*āgama*), [we reply:]...

Where an object is contradicted by reasoning, what refuge can scripture provide? (93b) The capacity of an object, which is distinguished by a specific mode conjoined with merit and knowledge, must itself reach its own ultimate limit at the very point where that [capacity] reaches its ultimate limit; how then could it be severed from that, or how could it possibly arise from anything else?

For whom could comprehension ever be impossible? Nor does the scripture itself have such a primary literal meaning; rather, recourse to another interpretation might occur through the boldness of reasoning, and that [reasoning] has been shown to be exhausted. Even so, out of fear of contradiction, its form must indeed be accepted; and since it is free from contradiction, let it also be established that it alone is capable of conveying the meaning. And if it is argued that for this very reason, even previously, the power of the meaning resided only in that which serves as its means—[we reply:
there is no kind of convention whatsoever wherein contradiction, once established, does not destroy it.
For instance: since this sky has the form of fire, if it were as pervasive as space, its refutation would be exactly like that of space—
even when compared to the moonlight, rivers, jewels, flames, sparks, and so forth.

The connection is "in exactly that same way. For how could there be a comparison by anyone regarding the very nature of those things which are to be proven, whether they have been perceived in their own form or through the medium of an example?

It will come to pass. For one who is dispassionate toward form, that knowledge arises through the very cultivation of the Noble Path by means of the cognition of purity; it does not arise from the mere meditation on that [purity] alone, as it would otherwise be subject to the fear of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) and the collapse [of the object]. Furthermore: "In that which has parts, there is the fault as in the case of a composite whole; in that which is partless, there is the fault as in the case of an atom.
There is no other entity here, for emptiness devours everything."

Therefore, even one who predicts the collapse due to the fear of sublation must accept that [the teaching contains such things], and yet it is impossible [to accept them as true]. If you argue that it must be accepted because it was spoken in the *pravacana* (scripture), then why now drink the salty water of a "father's well"? Or is it that the paths of the elements, the destinies, the wombs, the *śrāvakas*, and so forth were not taught by him? Furthermore, even that which is indicated here as something to be abandoned (*heya*) is not abandoned out of ignorance; rather, it is abandoned because of the inclinations and desires of those to be trained (*vineya*). For the Blessed One is an authority precisely because he provides instruction on attaining heaven.

Therefore, since there is an absence of the cognition of utility therein, and because there is no demonstration of a means for transcending sublation when [the object] is not itself visible, how could there be any accomplishment consisting of meditative cultivation? Thus, the culmination of the operation lies in enjoyment alone; the qualities are restricted to that alone, the taste is restricted to that alone, and the measure is restricted to that alone—anything else is equal only to sublation.
Alas, those for whom the Victor is merely an external object have lost even their own Teacher—
He who was grasped through the direct sequence and who shines with the characteristics derived from the scriptures.
Emptiness is nothing other than consciousness, and profundity resides within that;
it has been deliberated whether this [profundity] pertains to all imagined phenomena.
Even in scripture, it is not heard in his own words that a formless substratum possesses the nature of the *dharmakāya*; nor has any other [authoritative] commentary been made to this effect.
If you maintain that the mind is partless because it serves as its own illustrative example, then let it indeed be empty in every respect.
If it is not so in every respect, then why is the abandonment of partlessness not also dear to your beloved?

Indeed, it was shown previously that the resemblance to space (*vihāyas*) arises precisely through the departure from the conceptual proliferation of adventitious stains. For this very reason, the analogy to space is applied everywhere according to the similarity pointed out in the *Mahāyānottaratantra*, such as "free from conceptual construction like the sky," and so forth. Therefore, it is not by way of being devoid of form (*ākāra*). As for the statement:
"through the departure from the conceptual proliferation of adventitious stains..."
In that which is without proliferation,
without appearance, without support, and without basis; which,
though transcending the eye, is formless and invisible.
Just as depressions and elevations are seen in the sky, yet they do not exist there in that way;
so too, everything is seen even among the Buddhas, yet it does not exist there in that way.

Thus [it is said].
