In this context, the qualification "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*) and so forth is clearly intended to demonstrate the non-existence of even that which appears as high and low—caused by dust, mist, and the like—in the case of space itself. By using the general term "among the Buddhas" (*buddheṣu*) rather than saying "in the Perfectly Awakened One" (*sambuddhe*), there is an effort to employ a plural number that serves as a refutation. However, regarding the Blessed Sugata, the intention is merely this: that even when there is the appearance of high and low, characterized by denial (*apavāda*) and superimposition (*samāropa*), there is no existence of such [faults] in the Blessed One who possesses the aforementioned nature.

Or rather, let there be an application [of these terms] to the Blessed One as well by means of a transformation of the words. Just as it was analyzed by the venerable teacher Vasubandhu in the *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga*, in the section concerning the definition of non-conceptual knowledge—that it is "formless" (*arūpi*) because it cannot be determined by way of the duality of apprehended object and apprehending subject, and "without appearance" (*anābhāsa*) because it possesses an object—let it be so here too when the term "Buddha" is employed. Furthermore, its "possessing nothing" (*akiñcanatva*) should be understood as the departure of adventitious passion and the like. The rest is not contradictory.
For this very reason, in that same *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga*:
Since error is established as being either the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) or non-appearance (*akhyāti*),
it should be understood without confusion that "appearance" has the sense of "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*).

"How do you see it? It appears and shines forth in this way"—just as in such cases, the statement that [an object] "appears" (khyāti) even in the case of conceptual construction (vikalpa) is not contradictory.
And because this is very clear in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*:
"If, however, manifestation were intended to be the appearance of a non-existent form,
then the enjoyment [body] of the Sage— whether as a crown prince or as a king— would be non-existent."
Why did he not state that its manifestation as something else occurs through its predominance?
For he has clearly distinguished the meaning of "eternal" and "pervasive" just as they are manifested.
Therefore, this determination is said to be the manifestation of the non-existent;
hence, out of fear of losing your wealth, do not cast away this heap of jewels.
Is this not the same principle even when abandoning the *dharmakāya* as taught by him?
Indeed, who would have gone for refuge to the Buddha by way of such a denial?
The universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of a thing (*vastu*), which is of the nature of its essential reality (*dharmirūpa*),
is considered to be the *dharmakāya* called emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which rescues those who are timid.
This nature, known as the "essential nature" (svābhāvika), is proclaimed by such terms as emptiness, suchness, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the peak of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
[433] According to the Yogācāra school, the perfected nature is also proclaimed;
as the absence of duality, it is the emptiness of all things on the Middle Way.
The transformation of the outflows is itself the untainted realm;
it is reality and the ultimate truth, and one is called a Buddha because of the awakening to that.
When there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose fruit is the ascertainment of that [object], the qualities that depend upon its power cannot be denied,
just as one cannot deny a distinct subject (*dharmin*).

For this manifold [world], which necessarily appears, must be directly realized as emptiness; by that alone is the perfection of awakening achieved, so what is the use of anything else? Nor is there any direct realization other than self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And since that suchness (*tathatā*) is a mental quality (*cittadharma*) common to both the states of affliction and purification, it is designated as "natural," "innate," and "the fundamental nature" (*prakṛti*); yet, with respect to purification, it is the domain of the discourse regarding the *dharmakāya*.

In that regard, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*), when cultivated independently of specific forms (*ākāra-viśeṣa*), penetrates whichever form happens to be present; thus, it takes as its basis that very final form brought about by the auxiliary cause of the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*) which produces the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth of that particular substratum (*dharmin*). In its prior state, that [consciousness] which is dependent on those [forms] is said to be variegated (*citram*); it is also called "unreal imagination" (*abhūta-parikalpa*) and "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).

At the ultimate limit, however, it is precisely the *citra* [the variegated] that is not so described, because it is not the cause for false conceptualization (*vitathakalpanā*). Rather, that which is devoid of such form is so described. Furthermore, even if there is the mere occurrence of dependence on causes (*hetupāratantrya*), if there is an absence of dependence on unreal latencies (*asadvāsanāpāratantrya*), it is not called "dependent" (*paratantra*), but rather "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*), both because of the enjoyment of the Dharma and because it is enjoyed by those on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Or, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), since there is no relation of cause and effect, where is there dependence?
Therefore, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is indeed the very nature of the Dharma. But is it not the case that...
The nature of the qualities that have attained purity in all its aspects and are free from outflows is the essential body (svābhāvikakāya) of the Sage, characterized by their intrinsic nature.

Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). How then can it be said that the nature called emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is a property (*dharma*) of the form described by others? That is incorrect. Indeed, no nature of phenomena other than emptiness is found within the path of the scriptures (*āgama*). It should be understood according to one's inclination (*adhimukti*) through a distinction in presentation. For instance, some understand selflessness (*nairātmya*) as the absence of a creator god (*īśvara*) and so forth; some understand it as the absence of an eternal self;
and some understand it as the absence of even an inexpressible self, as well as the absence of the conjunction of matted hair and luminosity.

[434] Furthermore, others maintain that because even the external subtle body has vanished, that [consciousness], like a dream, is incapable of being defined as having form, even in its own self-awareness.
And because, through the process of reasoning and reflection, the mind gradually becomes inclined toward that alone.
For the establishment of entities does not occur through either perception or inference;
rather, it is by means of these two alone that they are sublated, because their primary purpose lies therein.

Nor do we say that *dharma* consists merely of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth; rather, it is the nourishment and sustenance of all those modes of mind (*cittaprakāra*) that bear their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are reckoned as body and intellect. Even that [nourishment] is a secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), and it is abandoned for the sake of awakening to enlightenment (*bodhi*). And in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
"The nature (*prakṛti*) of those phenomena (*dharmas*) which have attained purity in every aspect..."

Because it is thus indicated in general terms, there is no abandonment of the *sambhoga* [body]; rather, it is established as a distinct body (*kāya*). Since it is enumerated up to the limit of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is enumerated separately. Therefore, by dividing them according to the relationship between property and its possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*), these two bodies are established. Thus, its relationship with the Blessed One is one of identity (*tādātmya*), whereas that of the *nirmāṇa* [body] is one of origination from it (*tadutpatti*). However, when that eternal nature is intended to be described in the form of all pure qualities (*śukladharma*), then even in that case, it is simply an origination from it. As it has been said:
"Qualities are manifested by the *dharmakāya*.

This being so, although that [the *dharmakāya*] is indeed the means (*sādhana*), nevertheless, one does not pay regard to it merely as such; rather, one regards it solely as the reality (*tattva*). If it is asked why there is no distinction between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), it is because the direct realization of reality itself is the goal, and the cultivation of that [realization] alone is the means; for in its absence, or if it were uncertain, it would be impossible to eliminate those two [categories].

Since its purpose is fulfilled by the appearing subject (*dharmin*) alone, only the search for the validating cognition (*niścāyaka-pramāṇa*) remains; thus, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is accomplished. And that [object] must be cultivated as having a universal form (*sāmānya-rūpa*), like momentariness and so forth; thus, another essential nature (*svabhāva*) is established. Since the designation "Buddha" depends upon the realization of that [nature], that alone is the primary form of a Buddha, or he alone is called "Buddha," just as in the expression "the king is valor itself."

For the *Uttaratantra* states that the variegated nature of the marks and so forth constitutes the state of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*). Yet, even if some other entity were to exist in this way, it would serve no purpose whatsoever. Consequently, even the designation "Dharmakāya" for this [entity] is merely a borrowed ornament; thus, there is no adherence whatsoever to a vision of formlessness. For this very reason: "In the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha, distinguished by its specific body, enjoyments, and abode, situated above the Pure Abodes—there the Perfect Buddhas awaken. Otherwise, why [would they do so] in the Formless Realm?"
Therefore, the Protector, having directly realized the Dharmakāya through his own awareness, abides precisely as the Saṃbhogakāya.
For if there were a difference between the two states, that very goal would be sublated; otherwise, various efforts would be in vain.
And this being so,
consciousness is ultimately real because it is devoid of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject;
yet, due to its separation from being either one or many, even consciousness is empty.
Even conventionally, that form does not belong to those who revolve within the three realms;
nor is such vastness accepted [for them], because it would transcend the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If you can endure momentariness, why should its falsity not be endured? Or, if momentariness is indeed endured, how can death not be endured?
For one who has no fear of death, how could there be fear of anything else?
Indeed, every form of abuse is terrifying only because it culminates in death.
Better than death is perpetual weakness, for that alone is dear to us;
better is the non-attainment of a desired object than its attainment followed by its loss.
Therefore, this very nature is not intended to be transgressed;
nevertheless, it is the established position that some excellence is desired to be attained.

And since this [reasoning] is common to both the momentary and the unreal, there is no fault whatsoever. Just as with momentariness, dependence on causes and so forth should also be understood in the same way. Therefore, enough of this misplaced timidity! Furthermore:
Let the sky itself be devoid of its unreal stains in order to remove them from the surface of the sky; let it be free from movement in order to pacify motion.
If there is no transgression of the nature of things by means of valid cognition, then this is the same even for the doctrine of unreality (*alīka*).
The third chapter, the Entry into the Middle Way, from the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.

[437] [The Fourth Chapter] Alternatively, what is this "falsity" even for that which has the nature of experience? If you say it is due to sublation (*bādhaka*), then by what is what sublated? [If you say it is] the aggregate of variegated forms by means of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), then this is like "protecting a cow after it has already been sold," because you have established a relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) as merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
Because in the Bhāṣya, the contradiction of the theory of "apprehension of the real" (satkhyāti), which is pervaded by that [theory], has been established.

Furthermore, cognition does not subvert itself, because self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) is inherently powerful. Subversion could occur by another [cognition], whether it has the same object or a different object, and whether it is simultaneous or non-simultaneous. In that regard, the claim that "it subverts one which has the same object" is incoherent. What kind of subversion could there be even by one with a different object? If you say it is merely the presentation of its own object, then why would this not constitute a subversion of the former by that very [latter]? Nor can there be subversion by a simultaneous [cognition].

When many things—whether of the same class or of different classes—appear simultaneously, what could invalidate what? But if there is a difference in time, there is even less room for such invalidation, as this would lead to the absurd consequence that Mahāsammata could invalidate Śrīharṣa and vice versa.

Now, if the demonstration that one cognition is devoid of an object by means of another cognition is for the purpose of sublation (*bādha*), and that sublation is not contradictory when occurring between two cognitions at different times: if that object appears in that cognition, then it exists; how, then, could there be sublation? But if it does not appear, it is non-existent by its very nature—what need is there for a further negation? Nor, in that case, can it be said that the sublation has that [object] as its domain. If it is argued that it is the negation of what was superimposed (*āropita*):

Since it has been demonstrated that even superimposition (*āropa*) is established as a mere conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra*), the sublation (*bādhā*) which depends upon it likewise does not transcend the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Now, just as error—characterized merely by the production of another cognition—is based on a specific distinction within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), so too will sublation consist simply in the arising of a cognitive form such as, "This is thus and not otherwise."

If this is so, then it is established that [the cognition] does not sublate [its object] in reality. This cognition has arisen by way of assuming a certain form, but nothing whatsoever has been sublated or established by it, just as when a sweet-tasting cognition follows immediately after a cognition of blue. If it is argued that there is a distinction because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of sublation elsewhere, we reply: that which is established merely through determination is called "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*). Therefore, the demonstration of the emptiness of the objective support (*ālambana-śūnyatā*) does not have sublation as its purpose.

Furthermore, this [distinction between] sublation might occur in a dualistic system through the division between that which has an object and that which does not; however, in a non-dualistic system, it is a great rashness to claim that cognitions—which abide as experiences culminating solely in their own essential nature—could mutually sublate one another. And it has been said: "Just as there is no establishment of another's cognition, so too there is no sublation. (**)

[Objection: But surely the proof of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is also [established] only from another [source], and likewise there will be sublation (*bādhā*). [Response: This is without substance. For one established in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is not able to remain without relying on inference (*anumāna*); otherwise, one would not engage in any activity such as proceeding or desisting. And when inference is relied upon, the proof of consciousness-only follows by force. However, there is no room for inference in the final determination of ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Likewise, if the acceptance of sublation occurs only within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), then since this [object] is determined as being external while it is appearing, the sublation would have to occur in that very [external object]. Whether it be some slight thing or a mass of hair, the establishment of sublation must occur right there; even then, the operation of the proof does not bypass the external form. Now, what is the use of this conceptualization? If one takes the variegated mental form itself as the subject (*dharmin*) and makes it the basis, then the operation of the proof does not apply to the external.
This [position] resembles the story of the man on horseback who forgot his own horse.
With reference to any sensation whatsoever, that which is external is indeed merely external;
and whether that cognition is entangled or not is a useless reflection.
Thus it is established that, in every respect, the sublation [of an object] is inseparable from the determination of the external apprehended object.
Now, if it is argued: "This very [sublation] is considered the object of the sublation of blue and so forth;
therefore, the inquiry as to whether that cognition is manifold or unitary is useless."
Nor does the fear that "this is the form of cognition" disturb the sublater therein;
nor, subsequently, would there be an unblocking of the capacity in that knowledge.
Furthermore, there is no rule of dependence regarding the establishment of external objects and their apprehension;
for this [cognition] of blue is sublated regardless of whether it exists externally or is merely mental.
Or let that distinction exist; nevertheless, there is still sublation of this [distinction]:
does a blow delivered with a mind of enmity not cause death even to one's own kinsman?

If this is argued, we reply once more: it is our established position that there is no room for a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the proof of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only). In that case, when the subverting argument—which is inseparable from the determination of the grasped and the grasper—is established, nothing undesirable is entailed; for just as there is a distortion (*viplava*) regarding that [determination], so too is there a distortion regarding the subverting argument itself, and thus the thesis is proven. Furthermore, it is impossible to avoid its being inseparable from that [determination]. Nor can there be a subversion of what has not been made an object of cognition, because the determination of subversion occurs in the form: "this is subverted by that."

Furthermore, regarding the objectification of that which is to be sublated, there are the following alternatives: it may be objectified by something other than the sublater; by the sublater itself; or by something other than the sublater, either by itself or by another. First, if it is objectified by something other than the sublater, then it is simply not sublatable at all.

Even if it were made an object by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), what room would there be for subversion? For making something an object consists in the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*). If it is argued that the nature manifests precisely as being subverted, this is contradictory: "manifestation of nature" implies the existence of the nature, whereas "being subverted" implies non-existence. If it is argued that both occur sequentially, it is not so; for subversion cannot occur first, because the related term (*sambandhin*) has not yet been cognized.

Now, if it is the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), then since the existence [of the object] is drawn forth by that alone, where is there any sublation? Indeed, even if [the sublation] were to occur at a later time, it could not affect that [manifestation], because at that time the manifestation itself has ceased to exist. Or, if it were still present, nothing would matter even with a hundred sublaters. But if both [the cognition and the sublater] take it as their object, then there is simply the establishment of correspondence; what trace of sublation could there be? Furthermore, it is not logically possible for one thing to be made an object of another—whether by that [cognition] or by something else—since we have already begun this inquiry on the basis of the establishment of consciousness. Nor does making it an object of itself leave any room for sublation.
When that which is manifesting by itself is made an object by another,
its own head must be struck down by that stronger opponent who acts as the sublater.

Furthermore, the conceptual construction—which functions by terminating in its own mere form, thinking "this blue has been sublated by me through this reasoning"—does not even touch upon the matter of difference; nor is it a rash claim that, even in the case of non-difference, it sublates that very self. Moreover, regarding the cognition of both itself and the other, there is simply consistency as before. However, if one were to sublate what has not been made an object, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). But if there is an inclination toward grasping the external, then even when a cognition arises that does not touch that [external object], there might be the hope for the conventional usage of "sublation" based on what was established therein.

And since that [notion] is a distortion regarding resolve (*adhimokṣa*), the affliction caused by it is likewise a distortion. For when the establishment of external objects is overcome, everything is submerged in self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*); thus, what action could there be, for whom, or by what means? Even then, it is impossible to say, "This is exactly this. If that were the case, duality would arise once more—as they have said:
"Even the thought 'this is indeed consciousness-only' does not abide in that state of 'only,' because one still places something before oneself based on perception."
(Thakur adds *triṃśikāyām* in the corrigenda) thus [it is said].

Now, if it is argued that even when there is certainty regarding reality (*tattva*), for one who has not yet attained direct realization (*asākṣātkaraṇa*), a sublation (*bādhaka*) might find scope—just as in the case of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth—even then there is no fault. For just as activity and the like proceed solely through the external domain of innate ignorance (*sahajāvidyā*), thinking "this is to be known from this" or "this is to be attained," so too would the sublation fall upon that very summit. But when there is consideration of pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*), there is the cessation of all activity.

Thus, this relationship between the sublated and the sublator is merely conventional; it finds no occasion during the time when the nature of reality is being revealed. And at that time, while it is true that the means of proof (*sādhana*) likewise has no application, its non-application does not constitute a sublation, because the object to be proven (*sādhya*) has already been established.

If that [reason] is unestablished, the other [refutation] cannot even enter; what purpose does it serve except for the mere satisfaction of another? If, then, the application of the refutation depends upon the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes that [reason], then this fault indeed follows. But who would delay in such a manner? Let the application of the refutation be made right from the beginning. This [objection] is merely like the ritual rinsing of the mouth by one who is already terrified.

For when it is established that there is no entry [of a subverting cognition] upon the realization of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), then, since that application [of the reason] depends precisely on the absence of its identity [with external objects], once consciousness-ness is established through the very [fact of] being perceived—given the requirement for such a determination—the entry of a subverting cognition is dispelled; or, even if it were to occur, it would have to do so in the form "this is not consciousness. Therefore, as long as there is subversion, it is established that [the object] exists only externally and does not have the nature of consciousness. If it is asked, "What, then, is the fault in this proof? [the answer follows].

No, for since inference itself cannot even arise in the proof of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only), what opportunity is there for proof or refutation? For it is said: "Inference and other means of knowledge apply to external cognition, not to one's own singular self-awareness;
but when one's own singular self-awareness is established, that [external object] exists only because of its apprehension therein."
Nevertheless, if satisfaction is found in stating these faults, then since the nature of the other [the probandum]— namely, the subject and the reason— is unestablished,
there is neither establishment nor pervasion; what, then, is not a refutation?

Furthermore, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) or any other subverting argument (*bādhaka*) known as "investigation" (*vicāra*) and so forth is not something distinct from inference that could serve as an object of possibility. For every statement made by one entrenched in a dispute must, in order to be relevant to the subject at hand, necessarily imply an inference through the manifestation of the thesis (*sādhya*), the reason (*sādhana*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). It is for this very reason that we have demonstrated in the *Advaitabindu* that one must necessarily accept the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*).

Otherwise, by mere restatement in whatever manner, what purpose could be established for anyone? Nor can inference, having disparaged perception, be considered "in accordance with reality" (*yathārtha*), because it is produced by that very [perception] through its necessary utility in the apprehension of relations and so forth, even if only indirectly. To claim that this [inference] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it is not a means of valid cognition regarding that [object] is like aspiring to noble birth while one's progenitor is of low birth.
Furthermore, since this awareness of the form [of the object] in its own nature is perception—being free from error and conceptual construction—how could there be any occasion for sublation?
If self-awareness alone is not a means of valid cognition because it is not produced by another [means], then what here is a means of valid cognition?
Therefore, regarding those things established or sublated by that [self-awareness], no other [means] has the power to either sublate or establish them.

[441] Now, if it is asked: "At the time of proving [the existence of] representation (*vijñapti*), how can there be a self-defeat regarding one's own source of proof? It is not so; for when the thesis is established, there is a defeat even for oneself.

Just as a fire that consumes its own support burns the tree from which it was produced by friction against its own mass of branches, if even this "defeat by the other" (*paravitti*) were to destroy itself, who here would be at fault?

Indeed, the proof of representation (*vijñapti*) does not hope for its own validity by refuting another cognition that perceives an external object; rather, the investigation is prompted in such a way by the commonality of perceiving an external object—just as fire is a burner for everyone and thus the fault belongs to no one in particular. However, it is not logical that the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) should seek its validity merely by disregarding perception. For the proof of representation possesses a validity that is even superior to the validity of other cognitions that perceive external objects.

Furthermore, when one does not engage in such conventional usage because the object is not perceived without reflective awareness (*avimarśa*), despite its existence being established by the cognition of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*), then there is no fault in the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). This is because there is no sublation from one's own side, and from the perspective of another, the stick [of punishment] is applied equally. For indeed, there is no manifestation of causal capacity within self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

But when the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) itself is the leading factor, then it is not even capable of undermining the validity of another form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), let alone that of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which by its very nature has cast far away the stain of the suspicion of error and conceptual construction. Therefore, there can be no injury from any source to that which is protected by self-awareness.
[Objection: But surely, if there is invalidity for the sense organ, there can be no validity for inference.
Likewise, it can also be argued that if inference were not a valid means of knowledge, the sense organ would not be one either.

When an inference is refuted on the grounds of a logical mark (liṅga) whose constituent parts have been grasped, the fault lies in that very mark; for if it is not a fault, what purpose is served by refuting what arises from it?
Therefore, even if both [the cognition and its object] possess validity, nevertheless,
let consciousness manifest its own stability within itself, since error is impossible therein;
yet how can this cruel [opponent's] denial of both unity and plurality be prevented?

Who knows whose power is more exalted— the direct perception or the inference, both of which possess equal majesty and glory, since the existence of one is dependent upon the establishment of the other?

[442] That too is not a valid means [of proof]. For let there be parity between the non-perception of the pervader—which is restricted solely to the cognition of another—and the direct perception that grasps the pervasion and so forth, since the validity of the one is necessarily concomitant with the validity of the other. But self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the substratum for both, whereas the other two are not its substratum; so how can it be weighed against them?

Furthermore, because inference has a remote object as its domain, whereas perception does not apply to that same object due to the difference in their respective spheres, what occasion is there for considering their relative strength? For this very reason, it is stated that the thesis (pakṣa) must not be contradicted by perception and the other means of valid cognition.

But surely, even in the case of perception, inference is indeed accepted in order to bring into linguistic usage another nature that was not previously so used. Furthermore, neither affirmation nor negation applies to the mere appearance itself. For the application of words such as "cow" occurs with respect to a specific configuration of dewlap, horns, and limbs when that appears; and the conventional usage of negating a jar occurs when only the bare ground is perceived. Likewise, in the case of the form of two moons within cognition, there is the negation of an external pair of moons.

But affirmation and negation do not apply solely to that which appears. Likewise here, in the context of negation, let as many imagined properties (*kalpita-dharma*) as there are of the appearing form of blue and so forth be negated.

For example: self and other, the grasped and the grasper, the made known and the maker known, permanence and momentariness, unity and plurality; or [the categories of] substance, quality, and being composed of the three *guṇas*; or even down to the nature of atoms accompanied by other forms characterized by touch and so on, causal efficiency, and power—these are all denoted by the term "proliferation" (*prapañca*), because they are all merely imagined.

Therefore, when a subject (*dharmin*) is manifest, the negation or affirmation of another property (*dharmāntara*) that is not itself manifest occurs by relying on conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). This is because even in the absence of verbal or other such usage, the capacity for it remains present in that which is suitable for it, yet this capacity exists in a hidden form. However, there is never a negation of what is manifest. As stated in the *Nyāyabindu*: "When that [subject] is to be proven as being devoid of a certain entity, its non-perception is the reason; it is not the non-existence of that very [entity], because of the employment of words. (PV I 208)
Thus [it is said]: "A reason that is isolated is without a locus" (PV IV 91).

If, then, affirmation and negation regarding that which appears are both useless and incapable, and negation regarding that which does not appear is likewise both incapable and useless, where, then, is the operation of words? Nowhere in reality; this is merely a conventional discourse based on dependent origination, wherein by means of words something is either affirmed or negated.

For just as the affirmation of the existence of a tree by means of a word—such as "the tree exists"—is simply the production of a conceptual construction that projects an activity corresponding to it by virtue of convention; likewise, the negation of it—such as "the tree does not exist"—is simply the production of a conceptual construction that projects the exclusion of those who seek it. However, when neither the negative particle (*nañ*) nor the verb "to exist" (*asti*) is employed, there is merely the production of a conceptual construction of an aspect possessing branches and so forth, which is incapable of either engaging in or withdrawing from activity.

This is what is meant by the non-performance of injunctions and prohibitions. In the proximity of a word, that very same tree appears as if augmented by its existence; thus, compared to the previous [perception], there is merely the delineation of a specific form. Even when joined with the negative particle (*nañ*), it appears as if diminished; thus, in relation to the experience of a positive injunction, there is only the delineation of a diminished form. From that follows activity and so forth, corresponding to that [delimited form].

The same applies to the inferential mark (*liṅga*): although it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpavivartin*) of fire, as in the case of seeing smoke or clouds, there is a distinction based on whether it is invariably concomitant with a corresponding reality or not. Thus, neither affirmation nor negation applies to the manifest form of cognition itself, nor to an external object that does not manifest, whether it exists or not in reality. Nevertheless, through the gateway of the arising of conceptual construction, the conventional practice of affirmation and negation pertains solely to the external object—though only in its imagined form—for that which manifests vividly before one cannot be negated even by a hundred "nots."

And conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is distinct from external apprehension, because it involves the suspension of the state of intent toward determining existence or non-existence when there is a mere conceptual construction of a tree. For this very reason, the form (*ākāra*)—superimposed as an external reality—is called "exclusion" (*apoha*), since it is that alone which appears in verbal cognition. However, due to determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), it is previously explained that [the object] is "external" as being excluded from other classes. Therefore, there is no negation of the form or of the external in reality;
for it is only the external that is [negated] conventionally, but not the form even conventionally.
(See JNA 229; RNA2 65.20: *vidhisādhanam*:

*pratiṣedhanam*) Because of a lack of interest in that [negation] on the part of the world, and because the world is by nature extroverted (*bahirmukhatva*), when there is no room for negation even regarding external objects as they manifest, how much less so regarding one's own self? Therefore, there is no possibility of protection through logical reasons against what has been refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that which is established by self-awareness is indeed established in reality.

Although the relationship between the probandum and the probans is indeed merely conventional (*saṃvṛta*), nevertheless, it must be based upon a valid convention (*sat-saṃvṛti*). For if the establishment of each means of proof and so forth were different for every individual, everything would be established for everyone. Furthermore, there is no possibility of rescue by those who abide by other conventions when their reasons have been refuted. If others should harbor doubt regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), even in that case, it is not possible to live by means of [other] instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) apart from self-awareness;
this has been determined in the treatise just as it was by the world itself when the means of knowledge were lost.

Therefore, since [existence] is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), any inference—such as that based on the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)—has no scope; thus, the thesis is sublated by direct perception. Alternatively, what kind of existence (*sattā*) is intended to be refuted by these proofs? In this regard, if it is an existence well-known in other systems—characterized by its connection with "Being" (*sattā*), its own-nature existence (*svarūpasattva*), the three marks of a valid reason (*trirūpa*), and so forth—or some existence imagined by oneself, then there is no dispute.

[444] Now, that which is established by worldly convention is also characterized by capacity and characterized by manifestation. For it is thus that people say "it does not exist" when they do not perceive something that would otherwise be perceived under appropriate conditions.

In that regard, if the definition [of existence] as "capacity" (*śakti*) is sublated, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). The same logic applies to the sublation of the definition as "manifestation" (*pratibhāsa*) for that which lacks capacity. Alternatively, at that time, manifestation is not the defining characteristic; rather, it is capacity itself, so there is no harm. However, how can existence (*sattā*) in forms and other phenomena be denied, given that their nature is mere luminosity free from adventitious conditions such as imagined capacities? This is because it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*); thus, the thesis is sublated by direct perception. In this way, these entities are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Thus, even though there is a difference in formulation, if the object denoted by the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is something other than manifestation (*prakāśa*) as previously described, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, it should be understood that there is simply no capacity for such a thing to appear. However, the absence of being both one and many is indeed intended, because the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is what is sought to be expressed. For if it were otherwise, that [absence] would be undesirable due to the fear of abandoning intrinsic nature. Moreover, since existence is established through manifestation, what is the point of this [argument]?
Is this not contradictory? If it is asked, "How then can there be non-duality in the variegated?

[the answer is: This is non-dual because of the abandonment of the grasped and the grasper; or else, because of the passing away of the matted hair (jaṭa), because of the destruction of unity and plurality, because of having a form, and because of its being variegated and wonderful.
It is known as "variegated non-duality," and like the word for "king," it is a conventional single sound;
multiplicity does not exist in reality, and thus there is no fruit [arising from it], for that which exists is conventional.

The word "wondrous" (*citra*) has the sense of a marvel, since existence (*sattva*) persists even in the absence of being one or many. The Blessed One is "one" according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), as was stated previously; nor is there any utility in the conventional usage of "many. For just as that Blessed One is to be taken as my refuge, and I too must become exactly like him—such activity, which determines oneness, is purposeful; likewise, nothing is achieved by [determining] multiplicity.

[444,19] We consider the result: because activity toward a distinct substratum is unestablished, therefore, since both are in fact untenable, oneness is conventionally designated with respect to the result and nothing else, just as impermanence is [designated] by virtue of its conformity to tranquility. But surely even this [is so]:

for you, the variegated circle of cognitions—consisting of similar and dissimilar [moments] extending to the periphery of the interval between blue [patches]—is conventionally designated as one and the same; that [is your position].
How is it said?
To the very extent that there is external conceptual attachment, to that same extent this and that appear as distinct.
But his mind is all-encompassing;
for he is indeed that very one who possesses the hands, feet, and so forth of primordial wisdom.

Indeed, Caitra is not merely his hands and other limbs apart from the mental transformations (*manovivarta*). Therefore, just as with other transformations, because they are included within what is denoted by the term "Caitra," there is a single conventional usage (*ekavyavahāra*) solely when one reflects upon the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Even in that case, it should be remembered that a distinction regarding the portion of the objective sphere (*gocarabhāga*) has been stated, just as in the case of the Blessed Lady. Or, in reality, the word "one" (*eka*) refers merely to the exclusion of the manifold (*anekavyāvṛtti*), just like the word "non-dual" (*advaita*).
Therefore, the summary is this: blue and so forth exist precisely as luminosity, yet they are devoid of being either one or many.

[PV III 220] In a variegated cognition, blue and so forth are adjuncts of the cognition and do not appear as anything other than that; for if one were to discern them separately, one would fall into the realm of external objects.

In this context, "variegated" (*citra*) is the negation of unity. "Cognition" (*vijñāna*) refers to a single perceiver. Because it is included within a single consciousness by virtue of appearing as such, there is a negation of multiplicity. The phrase "having cognition as its limiting adjunct" (*jñānopādhi*) means that, through its exclusion from matted hair and the like, there is no sublation [of its existence] because it has cognition as its nature. By the statement "it is impossible to perceive another form, such as yellow, without partaking in it," [it is shown that] there is no purpose for the conventional usage of difference.

He says: For if that [one] could be apprehended even as separate from those [many], and if the accomplishment of what is to be established by them were possible from that [one], then—as in the case of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth—a conventional usage of "many" would be appropriate. But this is not the case; therefore, only "one" is appropriate.

By the words beginning with "for that" (*taṃ hi*), he states the meaning starting with "externally" (*bahir*) and so forth. For when there is a reflective awareness of the nature of cognition within the complex of cognition and so forth, the single word "Caitra" and so on is applied.

In that case as well, one should proceed in the same manner. While discerning and analyzing, one would instead fall back upon the object itself, or rather, it is the birth and apprehension of the object alone that occurs separately, not that of the cognition. For:
"In whatever way a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way."

[445,16] Thus, there would be a single nature even in a mind possessing variegated forms. [445,18] "Name" (*nāman*) means a word that expresses a designation (*saṃjñā*). That single nature is not real. "Appears" (*bhāsate*) means "is produced" (*jāyate*), because the intention is that birth belongs only to that which is manifesting. Therefore, it is indeed devoid of both a unitary and a manifold intrinsic nature. (98b)

Knowledge is a non-dual manifold, free from contradiction; and it has been shown that even within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), it is indeed the object of a single linguistic convention, just like momentariness and so forth.
But even so, since that [knowledge] does not exist while its pervader does exist, how can it be an object of cognition? Moreover, there is no such confidence anywhere in this manner.
Furthermore, when one thing is negated by the affirmation of another, because there is no third category (*rāśyantara*), why would there be "neither" among entities, as in the case of the two sides?

[445,23] How could there be such a possibility? Therefore, at the very time of establishing the definition, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by both modes. But for the opponent, the absence of both [modes] due to the nature of the thing (*vastu-svabhāva*) does not constitute a sublation; thus, this [objection] is irrelevant. [446,1] True, it is irrelevant, because existence cannot be established even without those two, since pervasion itself would be impossible. Where?
And is it thus? Is it not right here, in this very body of cognition (*buddhi*)? Then why now [claim] a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) based on that which has itself become the subject (*pakṣa*)?

Or what fault is there if the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*) involves deviation? For even in another locus of properties (*dharmyantara*), by that same [operation], it is made "inconclusive due to being common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
And if there is protection here merely by making it the subject, then what is the obstacle in that case as well? And when...

Even if the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is directly perceived, there is no impairment of the probandum (*sādhya*); at that time, mere doubt is ineffective, and thus the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*) does not apply for now.

Nor is there a fault such as unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), because [the reason] is established from some cause or other, out of respect for the sublation by direct perception (*adhyakṣabādhana*). And so it is:

Even if there is no confidence in a reason (*hetu*) whose probandum is refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no harm; for what room is there for doubt in other cases? For that very reason, even at the time of defining [the reason], pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established. When one thing is negated and another is affirmed, the negation of a third category occurs only externally.
Indeed, even in that case, it is impossible to demonstrate a sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), because this [third category] is neither different nor non-different from those two.

Because it is impossible to say so; and self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is inherently difficult to traverse, for if there were an absence of difference and non-difference regarding external objects, it would follow that conventional practice (*saṃvyavahāra*) would be abolished.
As it has been said: "For one does not see fire... (*na hy analaṃ paśyan*).

And so forth. Therefore, this principle is restricted to the external alone; however, if the intellect (*buddhi*) is also established in accordance with that, let it be a mere conventional establishment (*vyavasthāmātra*). As it has been said:
"Just as the external is the object of apprehension..."
And so forth. However, even then, it is not direct (*āñjasah*).

As for what was stated in the *Buddhi-adhikāra* [of the *Pramāṇavārttika*], beginning with "Otherwise, of a single entity" (*anyathaikasya bhāvasya*, PV III 358), that was intended from the perspective of a specific Mādhyamika.

This is for the purpose of clarifying the statement: "In whatever way objects are conceived" (PV III 209). If that were so, one might argue: "Just as it is neither one nor many, so too it should be neither luminous (*prakāśa*) nor non-luminous.
This is not the case, because the negation of luminosity is itself sublated by luminosity. Such a thing is impossible regarding oneness and manifoldness for the opponent.
Furthermore, there is no utility in what has been introduced by the words "but" (*tu*) and so forth.
For the loss of both unity and plurality is preserved by their being non-entities (*avastutva*).
But who could preserve a thing from being devoured if it were already being consumed as a non-entity by its own cognition?

Therefore, one who distinguishes between the "one" and the "many" has no authority over the cognition for the purpose of proving non-existence, because the establishment of pervasion depends upon a specific object; thus, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). Furthermore, if you maintain that the determination of the establishment of pervasion occurs through generality alone, then since existence—the pervaded—is established, there must be either oneness or manyness by means of a single [entity], and not manyness.
[447,6] Let it be that "tolerable" is one and the same. For if there were multiplicity, then until the atom is split, there ought to be an appearance of atoms.
[447,7] But this is not so; therefore, [447,8] in whatever manner a cognition appears, [it is so].
The meaning is: by way of the exclusion of many [factors], because it does not possess the nature of an atom (*anaṇurūpatayā*).
That is experienced exactly in that manner;
it is followed—that is to say, it is accepted—because it has the sense of being attained (*prāptyarthatvāt*).

[447,12] Thus, there would be a single nature even in a mind possessing variegated forms. [447,14] The particle *nāma* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "admittedly" (*upagame*). And this [objection] was shown by the word *jñāna* [in the verse], because for the [opponent] who holds that cognition is [unitary], consciousness itself is non-existent. However, when even the atom of cognition is untenable due to the distinction of spatial directions, and a composite whole cannot be produced from partless [atoms], [then...]
[447,16] In the view of manifoldness (*nānātva*), the very commencement of an appearance would be non-manifestation; therefore, this manifestation comes to rest only in unity (*ekatva*).

[447,17] In whatever manner and from whatever kind of non-dual characteristic (*abheda-lakṣaṇa*) knowledge appears, it is experienced exactly in that way; it exists precisely as non-dual, according to the principle that "experience is existence" (*anubhavaḥ sattā*). Thus, the passage beginning with "by name" (*iti nāma*) is easy to understand. The word "name" (*nāma*) is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). By this—
[447,19] Consequently, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it follows from that very admission.

[447,20] But is it not contrary to experience to say that a variegated thing (*citram*) is one, since blue, yellow, and so forth appear only as distinct? Furthermore, [447,21] "variegated" is synonymous with "not manifold," and that [term] is established by the exclusion of oneness; how then can a variegated thing be one? Otherwise, [it would be a contradiction].

If it is argued that light (*prakāśa*) must be manifold, we say no; for the function of cognition pertains to the blue and so forth, not to their difference. The determination of difference or non-difference, however, must follow its basis. If it is asked: "Is this blue and this yellow" is itself a cognition of difference, occurring precisely through their mutual identity?

This is indeed so in the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*). However, by the force of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is superimposed upon the cognition as well. In the case of cognition...

One ought to consider whether these forms are distinct or non-distinct. If it is argued that even in the case of cognition, its determination follows precisely that [distinction or non-distinction], we say no; for certainly not all [cognitions are so determined]. To explain:
by the opponent, the state of being permanent or otherwise is necessarily [determined].
That which is to be manifested exists externally through causal efficiency;
because of the difference in form, it is entirely of a different nature.
Internally, however, it is not necessarily the opposite due to the force of habituation.

The term "internal" refers to the mind (*citta*), which is the opposite of that [external object]. Furthermore, how is it that the nature of cognition (*buddhi*) is not determined as being either stable or otherwise? In reality, because neither priority nor posteriority is perceived; for if priority and posteriority were known, there would necessarily be either permanence or motion.
Because that [duality] does not exist through the resolve upon the one or the many, the two are non-existent.

In that case, if there were differentiation, the consequence would be the non-existence of the appearance of gross objects, and the consequence of the absence of any appearance whatsoever would be difficult to avoid.
Alternatively, if there were unity, blue would be identical to yellow. As it has been said:
"Even in the absence of differentiation, unity would contradict variegation. (* * *)
And yet, it does not appear in that way. Nevertheless:

"In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is accepted as being exactly so; thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the mind possessing variegated forms. (PV III 221) — this corresponds to Prajñākaragupta’s version.

The word "nāma" is used in the sense of concession (*aṅgīkāre*). This is the meaning: it is true that there would be no unity for that which is manifold; however, let there be no denial of the existence of that which is manifest—thus, nothing undesirable follows. This is the intended point:
if consciousness were real, its manifoldness would be established and its [alleged] contradiction would be sublated.
And in the case of identity, your own position would be undermined; for us, however, neither alternative is problematic.

If existence is established, we have not failed in anything even by virtue of its multiplicity; we merely teach unity in accordance with logic. For, because they share the same acquisition and preservation (*sāmānayogakṣematvāt*), there is no impairment of unity within existence.
But multiplicity is its opposite; therefore, that [multiplicity] is excluded from it.

As for what is said—that if there were identity, blue would be yellow—that is a fault only from an external perspective, because those who seek the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of that object would still engage with it, and because the [undesired] consequence of such activity would follow. If you ask, "Even if one does not seek the causal efficiency, how could that which is blue possibly be yellow?", then why should it be deprived of its own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*)? It is better to accept this [distinction].

If you ask why, it would be so if there were invisibility (*parokṣatā*). Therefore, if they were external, there would indeed be a plurality between blue and yellow, lest there be a confusion of activity and the like. But if they are cognitions, there is only oneness. However, due to the long-standing habit of external conventional usage, this position is as difficult to endure as the midday sun facing one directly; what can we do about that? Thus, here there are contradictions with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth.

Even these [conceptions] float away. This is because the conceptual construction that "blue is other than yellow" proceeds by disregarding the operation of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), since there is a natural flow of a single [cognition] following the operation of sensory perception. For this very reason, there is no contradiction in saying that the variegated is one; for it is variegated by way of being blue, yellow, and so forth, but not by way of being manifold. It is only due to the conceit of pervasion by way of manifoldness [that such a notion arises].

Thus it is said: pervasion exists only in the external world. Alternatively, the statement that "the variegated is merely a restatement" means that which you accept as manifold is, in its nature as cognition, actually one; thus there is no fault, like the case of a man mounted on a horse.
[Objection: But surely, the superimposition of contradictory properties is called difference, and it is not restricted here to whether it belongs to the external object or to the cognition.
If you ask why, it is because of necessity itself. For if there were no distinction between external objects, there would be no specific determination of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*);

and if that were disregarded, since there would be nothing more than mere appearance, there would be no distinction at all, and thus that very [causal efficiency] would be absent. In the case of cognition, however, if there were a distinction, its own nature would be lost; for when it is independent of causal efficiency, its existence consists solely in its manifestation. Furthermore, if there were a distinction, it would follow that manifestation is absent in that state. Even if this were so...

Furthermore, if one insists on a distinction between the two, both would suffer a loss of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Nevertheless, without going too far, it is said that the external object—though composed of atoms—is able to withstand analysis; even in the absence of a distinct delineation of atomic forms, it maintains its status as an object of apprehension due to a slight degree of correspondence with cognition in the form of a single, solid, gross appearance. Cognition, however, is not like that; nor is there even a loss of the external object.

It crushes [the object], because it is established merely through overestimation (*abhimāna*); or rather, it might proceed outward solely from overestimation. But as for cognition (*buddhi*) established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could those two [crushing and proceeding outward] possibly exist? For, upon reaching the reflective awareness of an external form, there is a necessary collapse of its own nature in the case of a distinction [between subject and object]. As it has been said:
"For one who discriminates that [appearance] falls upon the object" (PV III 220).
Just as an appearance devoid of causal capacity with respect to an object is like [an illusion of] hair and so forth,
so too the discrimination "this is other than that" occurs only with respect to the external object.

This is not a consequence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), but rather merely the manifestation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from external habituation. Therefore, it is logical that just as the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of cognition is unique to the external world by virtue of properties such as being independent of other cognitions, so too is its differentiation established through the sublation of distinctions created by the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), by the force of reasoning (*nyāyasāmarthya*). If, then, [it exists] only externally...

[450,2] Since difference is produced by contradictory properties and non-difference is not the form of experience, what is the recourse? Furthermore, even in that case, the conventional establishment of "the Blessed One is one" is accepted. For if there were no basis for restriction, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-difference even with respect to another continuum. Thus he says:
"Blue and so forth in variegated cognition" (PV III 220).
And so forth.

The "oneness" of cognition (*buddhi*) would mean that its nature is indivisible, not its multiplicity. Alternatively, this name "cognition" might apply to the intellect itself, but not to the jar. When the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is incapable [of being perceived], the word "name" (*nāma*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). And in whatever way a variegated thing appears...

Even if [the cognition] is contained within a single consciousness, it is experienced in that very same way; thus, there might be a unity of the mind which is the object of the designation "single continuum. However, this kind of impossibility of being distinguished (aśakyavivecanatva) does not belong to that which is intended by the opponent; therefore, there is no fault. Thus, in this independent [argument], the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi) is unestablished, because the unity of the forms of cognition (buddhyākāra) is indeed established. Furthermore, [The text continues: ...api ca, [450,11] etc.

[450,12] What is this unity or plurality, and where do they reside? What is the pervasion of these two with respect to being a real entity (*vastutva*)? [450,13] To this, the answer is: that very same thing is both partless and unitary, and yet it is a plurality when aggregated. Furthermore, in the world, the status of a real entity is established precisely through its unity and plurality. [450,14] Now, if it is argued that what is observed by oneself is useful in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), [we reply that this applies] within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) which is the basis of investigation.

[450,15] "Is there no fault in saying that it was perceived by itself in that very way? To this it is replied: even in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), only that which is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) is said to be seen. And nowhere is a partless entity within the range of perception by these two. Therefore, even though it is manifold, a form consisting of the aggregation of those parts is not perceived either. How, then, could the pervasion of real entities (*vastu-vyāpti*) be established by these two? Nor does anything [partless] exist at all.

[450,18] As for the entity (*vastu*), however, the admission by another (*paropagama*) is not employed as an independent reason (*svatantra-hetu*). And since a *prasaṅga* proof results in a reversal (*viparyaya-paryavasāna*), there would be a contradiction with the probandum (*sādhyavirodha*). Let this be a punishment for one who maintains that an entity is pervaded by unity and plurality; but for one for whom being an entity consists merely in being manifest (*prakāśamātra*), what need is there for such conformity?

Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be established by oneself. Furthermore, if the cognition of a relation between an entity and its being either one or many occurs somewhere, then that very thing is not empty; thus, the proof of the emptiness of pervasion is undermined. Now, it may be argued: "The actual state of things—the conventional usage of 'one' and 'many,' and the determination based on the establishment of valid cognition—indeed exists in the world; however, it does not exist under critical investigation. This is precisely what [we maintain].

If it is argued, "How can that which is to be proven (sādhya) by us possibly constitute a sublation?", we say no; for what you must prove is the absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāvābhāva), since it is precisely the absence of unity and plurality that is put forward as the reason (sādhana). Nor is this a mere pointing out of an unestablished reason (asiddha); rather, it is the lack of pervasion (vyāptyasiddhi) that is being stated. And the pervasion of the contrapositive (viparyayavyāpti) relies upon the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalambha) and so forth, and that [pervasion]—

In some cases, because the pervaded and the pervader are unestablished, the reason is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*), since they are not made objects even by conventional valid cognition (*sāṃvṛta-pramāṇa*). Nor is mere worldly convention (*vyavahāra-mātra*) a valid cognition, nor is it a separate definition. Even in the case of what is not a valid cognition, there is no fixed rule for the establishment of valid cognition.
If you claim that this pride is accepted in the conventional sense, then this very analysis is also conventional.
If it is not even accepted in the conventional sense, then one who speaks thus is a victor in every way.
This is an intermediate verse.

Therefore, if you maintain that the non-existence of entities everywhere follows from the absence of a certain nature—which is itself refuted by valid cognition—then the separation from the son of a barren woman would also be a valid means for proving that [non-existence], since such a separation likewise does not exist. Thus, [your argument] is sound.

The hope for the probandum [is thus fulfilled]. Therefore, when the perception—either in the form of direct sensory experience (*adhyakṣa*) based on the apprehension of the pervasion between the pervaded and the pervader, or in the form of inference designated as a "sublater of the contrary" (*viparyayabādhaka*)—has occurred, it is logical that there is a determination of the absence of one thing due to the absence of the other in some instance. Likewise, the proof of the pervasion of existence by momentariness is necessarily concomitant with the determination of the existence of momentary things.

Thus, that very perception belongs to this [subject]. However, in the present case, if existence were implied for those two in a general sense, the reason—which is invariably concomitant with that [existence]—would be a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) because it would subvert the intended [property]. Even if existence is not implied, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*);
therefore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

[451,14] Therefore, from what [source] does the negation of the cognition of variegated forms follow? If it is asked, "Then from what [source] does the external [object] also [not exist]? [The answer is: Precisely because it does not manifest in reality (*tattvataḥ*). For it is well-established that non-existence is nothing other than non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Nor is there a single characteristic consisting of partlessness (*niraṃśatā*); so what connection is there between the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) and the external object? Furthermore, what is this characteristic of oneness (*ekatā*), by virtue of which—
Is it not the case that no such objection can arise? For it is impossible to demonstrate a distinction [between parts]; yet this is not the case for an external object.

Since that [external object] does not exist, its composite form—though consisting of many parts—also does not exist. If you argue that there will be a plurality of things that *are* capable of being distinguished, then if there were some final constituent that was incapable of being distinguished, only in relation to that would the others possess the quality of being distinguishable from one another; otherwise, they would not.

And it is thus, because even an atom would lead to an infinite regress. However, in the case of a variegated cognition occurring within one's own continuum (*svasantāna*), there is an impossibility of its being analyzed into parts;

he shows that this is not the case when it is together with another continuum. By this, it is clearly stated that the establishment of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader occurs in the cognition, whereas elsewhere it functions as the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

For this very reason, even by the venerable teacher Vasubandhu, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) was set forth solely with reference to external objects, not with reference to cognition. If it is argued that, by virtue of the same logic, [the objection] remains applicable there as well and is therefore difficult to ward off, we say no; for it has already been refuted through the same logic in the passage beginning with "This is consciousness-only" (*vijñānamātram eva*). Precisely for this reason, due to the non-existence of the duality of the grasped and the grasper...

[451,26] Furthermore, by means of the existence of the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), which has as its characteristic the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) of the three realms, the cessation of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) has been accomplished; it was not stated that there is the non-existence of other entities. If it is argued that it was not stated because it could be inferred from that, then the refutation of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) has been stated directly; therefore, its mere absence is not what is to be expressed. Consequently, it is precisely that [unreal imagination] which has been refuted.

Thus, enough with this elaboration. Likewise, having analyzed the matter, the very fact of being incapable of being perceived as either one or many is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) because it is observed in the essential nature (*svabhāva*) by virtue of being defined by mutual exclusion (*anyonyaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatayā*). It is not the state of being a partless mass; rather, the consideration of parts is undertaken merely out of deference to others. Alternatively, it should be understood that through that means, the absence of the impossibility of analysis is what is actually manifested.
[452,5] "Like another continuum. But surely for one who maintains that self-cognition is a single reality, there is no basis for a manifold arrangement;

[452,6] if this existence of another continuum is not established, it is like a factor of a result [that is unproven]. [452,7] Is the establishment of another continuum then merely conventional, in whatever way that may be?

[452,8] What is the point of insisting on this matter? For even in this way, let there not be a plurality of cognitions; since the non-perception of a pervader would remain unestablished even by means of a single [cognition] through its unity. And the word "one" will apply to the exclusion of imagined plurality for as long as conventional usage persists. Therefore, cognition is not distinct from external objects due to a difference created by the superimposition of contradictory properties.

[452,11] Let it be so; what, however, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that? And what is the means of valid cognition even for their unity? [452,12] It is perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself. If it is argued that it is not so because it is followed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), this is merely the fault of conceptual construction. Why is it not the fault of perception itself? No, because the appearance occurs precisely within the mutual awareness (*saṃvit*). Furthermore, blue, yellow, and so forth have been seen by me.

[452,14] Thus is the apprehension of a single agent. And there is the thought, "This variegated appearance is mine," which pertains to a single related entity. This very conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of a single direct perception possesses the form of experience as non-different from a cloth. In this way, is the intellect itself singular, or is its conceptualization—the conceptualization of the three worlds—singular? Even the statement that "there is a variegated appearance within a single intellect" is like the body of a stone-son (*śilāputra*); for [the concept of a body] applies to the body...

Or, it is like the case of hands, feet, and so forth. This is indeed a single determination (*ekāvasāya*); however, due to the conceit (*abhimāna*) that they exist externally, it is merely called a "collection" (*samuccaya*).

In the absence of that [external existence], this very oneness (*ekatva*) is delineated. Thus, even in the case of trees, mountains, and so forth, when they are merely cognitions (*dhīmātratva*), the conventional usage of "one" applies to both cases alike.

Therefore, there is no fault in perception; nor is it established that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is itself a real entity. Thus, it is proven that direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) grasps non-difference.

If it is argued that even in the case of difference, direct perception alone is the refuge, [we reply: in cases such as "the cognition of a single mountain," there is no lack of conformity with conceptualization because of its contrary arising, since it has been observed many times. Why, then, should both be accepted? Therefore, due to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), there is a cognitive distortion (*viplava*).

Thus, by attempting to establish emptiness through the negation of both [existence and non-existence], he has set out to illuminate the *syādvāda* (doctrine of manifoldness) by means of establishing both; this is a "blow" [to his own position]. Now, if the establishment of each one is intended merely to refute the other and not as a definitive statement of its own status—since even that is subsequently refuted in turn—then, when oneness is established by perception, at that very moment the refutation of the second [non-existence] has already occurred.

How can there be a sublation of another based on that [substratum]? For there is no revival from anything of what has already been sublated. If such were the case, and if there were a possibility of revival for that which is being sublated by this [second cognition], what kind of fulfillment of one's desires would that be? Furthermore, because of the lack of cessation in the succession of sublation and revival by the other, the substratum (dharmin), being accompanied by each [cognition] in turn, would never [be established].
The possibility of the non-perception of the pervader [is as follows]:
This is the meaning: it is said that consciousness is not, first of all, a single form, because blue, yellow, and so forth appear without being intermingled;

nor is it manifold, because that would entail the consequence of their mutual non-cognition. In this regard, when the difference in appearance is cited as a refutation to negate its unity, [it is as follows].

In that case, if this [unity] is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), by what means could it be negated? If that [self-awareness] were not firm, from where would there be a sublation even of unity? The same should be said regarding the claim that it is "not manifold" either. Furthermore, if the defeat of the opponent were brought about by another proof independent of the possibility of a counter-position (*pratiyogin*), then there would be no fault; but [here], it is [an attempt to negate] that which is itself accepted as established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[453,8] To say "it is a refutation" is incoherent. Furthermore, there exists no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts [the notion of] unity and plurality. Even if one has the conceit that such [subversion] is possible, there is not even the slightest removal of that which is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Because it is not a real entity, it is not even a single thing; thus, [the concepts of] "one" and "many" are mutually dependent. Since two contradictory things cannot coexist in one place, there is no negation of both. Therefore, in this case, let that very thing for which non-cognition can be demonstrated be considered non-existent.
[453,11] "But if there is no cognition of either [subject or object], that would imply a total absence of cognition; and that is unestablished.

(101b) [453,12] Furthermore, one might argue: "This is merely the attribution of an undesirable consequence to the proponent of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*); therefore, this fault belongs only to him, not to us, since we do not accept that [self-cognition].
[453,13] If you say this?
This great avoidance by the wise is indeed called "undesirable";
for if this were the case regarding all attachments to misfortune, one would have achieved one's purpose.

[453,16] For it has been stated that for one who asserts the acceptance of a pervader, the acceptance of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) follows by necessity. Therefore, [453,17] if, as in the case of non-difference, direct perception were established even in the case of difference, then the avoidance of the doctrine of "maybe" (*syādvāda*) would not be possible. And if no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted, then even if everything could be established according to one's whim, what would be the avoidance of that [doctrine]? If this is so, then:

If both difference and non-difference were established, the doctrine of "maybe" (syādvāda) would be fully attained; however, the Vedānta doctrine, which maintains absolute unity, is a difficult-to-abandon distortion of reality.
To this it is replied:
Although this wheel of the mind is a single self,
it is nonetheless not all-pervasive like space or the wind.
If it were to manifest for the Tathāgata in that way,
then the excellence of mental concentration would not be reality.
Indeed, such pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is not the very essence (*tattva*) of cognition itself, because at one time it is one thing and at another time it is absent.

However, this is a specific established quality (*siddhiviśeṣa*) of the Blessed One. But since there is contact with prior and subsequent forms through direct experience (*saṃvedana*), how can there be permanence?
By this, the objection regarding its own nature (*svatāntaparihāra*—[corrected from *hrasvatāntaparihāra*]) is refuted; for self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) never experiences itself as ceasing.

[454,2] However, the avoidance of the extremes of eternalism and nihilism by means of the continuity [of the stream of consciousness], with respect to intermediate states, is indeed accepted as the abandonment of the extreme of nihilism.

[454,3] It is a gross delusion on the part of the world that the author of the Commentary [holds] non-difference even with respect to the past and so forth; for he negates only the conceptualization of the past and so forth regarding that which is manifest. [454,4] Therefore, mere [non-difference] does not constitute unity, as it would entail the defect of being as all-pervasive as space; nor is there any perception of permanence.

Thus, how can there be any doubt regarding the established doctrine of the Vedānta? Furthermore, how could there even be the cognition that "this extends over such a space" or "this is otherwise"?
