If this were the case, then just as with time, there would be no perception of spatial extension; much less, therefore, could there be eternal omnipresence. As for the claim that both [time and space] are proven, it belongs only to one who is truly shameless.

[454,8] But surely the Digambara also maintains that there is an external [world]; and even in that case, there is in some way both difference and non-difference, and things are neither exclusively external nor exclusively internal. Thus, even if such objections are avoided, what relevance does the Digambara doctrine have here, given that we are concerned merely with the unity and multiplicity of the cognition established by perception? Indeed, it is impossible to avoid every point of similarity; however, their mutual contradiction has been refuted.
[454,11] This is due to the appearance [of objects] by virtue of the predominance of cognition. Therefore, [454,12] in whatever manner a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way;
[454,13] since it appears as having a dual nature, its state always remains exactly so.

By the mention of "cognition" (*jñāna*), this is what is meant: there is no manifestation anywhere as a single entity possessing a dual nature, because even an error is possible—just like the appearance of two moons and so forth—since it is observed that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) subsequently applies. Therefore, how can there be unity for a variegated form (*citrākāra*)?
It is said in reply:
[454,17] Because you lack a sense of shame, there is no liberation for you when examining the meaning of the subject at hand.
[454,18] That which ought to be practiced by us has been practiced by you.

If even one of the two—oneness or manyness—is established, then whatever is desired [as the other] follows; what need is there to speak of both being established? Even a single [entity] would be difficult to maintain.
[454,21] Regarding the objection concerning the unity of the variegated, the reply is: [454,22] Since both unity and plurality are established, that unity is indeed established;
[454,23] thus, there may well be a state of oneness even in a mind possessing variegated forms.

This is also the meaning: regarding form (*rūpa*) which has variegated aspects—that is, aspects that are both one and many—it might be said that even when it is not yet produced in the mind, there is a state of oneness, yet it is not merely a state of oneness. For it is not logical to say that what is blue and square is not blue. Alternatively, [the verse says: "In the mind, it would be as if unproduced... [and so forth].
A single [entity] is not variegated because of contradiction, and there is no contradiction because it is so perceived;
thus, the mind that has a variegated form would indeed be a single entity.
[455,3] In that case, there would also be multiple conventional designations. If there is a purpose, who can prevent it?
For just as the Blessed One is called "one," so too are the four fearlessnesses, the thirty-two marks, and so forth seen to exist;
what harm is there for us? But for you, this is like raising a weapon against yourself. Well then, let this be a refutation of the opponent's reason.

But how can the establishment of your own desired non-dualism of the variegated (*citrādvaita*) be achieved, given that unity is refuted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since there is a confusion of appearances between blue and yellow? Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the impossibility of distinguishing [the parts], that too is a cause of difference based on the absence of deviation due to being produced by a common causal complex (*samānasāmagrījanyatva*); since, however, neither the whole nor its parts are objects for the opponent because they consist of the nature of cognition (*buddhirūpatva*), what is this "unity"?
[455,9] Let it be so.
[455,10] If oneness is merely figurative due to the inability to distinguish [them],
[455,11] how could the non-perception of the pervader truly be unestablished?
As for this claim that the appearance is inseparable from unity, that too is untenable: "For an appearance characterized by spatial extension could not belong to a single thing;
why then do you not accept that the appearance is also inseparable from its diversity?"
Just as the inseparability from the appearance is observed, so too is its dependence on blue, yellow, and so forth; and that very [dependence] is itself differentiation.
Therefore,
why does this teaching of the identity of caustic alkali and curd— which causes both distress and shame— not likewise apply to you, who produce curd from cow's milk?

To this it is replied: If difference is also stated to exist by this much, what is the harm? By the exclusion of non-connection, identity has been stated immediately thereafter. (By the exclusion of this, identity has been stated immediately thereafter.)
In the same way, it has also been shown that variegated non-duality (*citrādvaita*) is the primary [reality];
for otherwise, there would be only oneness, and variegation would not be logically possible.
For one who fears the confusion of forms due to their mutual contradiction, unity must necessarily be asserted; therefore, let the distinction be abandoned on account of the appearance.
When there is a manifestation, there is either difference or non-difference according to its form.
Since there is no manifestation in multiplicity, therefore unity alone is real.
The pervasion of space is possible only for a plurality of things, such as matted hair;
but how could it occur for that which is self-cognized, given that it appears as a single unit?
Let it be that blue, yellow, and so forth possess causal dependence; yet they are not identical, because that which is accepted as a single entity arises in such a manner from its own causes.
Just as oneness is accepted, so too is difference not accepted;
because a second [entity] does not appear, it is indeed mastered as non-different.
And in the position of mutual contradiction, there is no support for a second [element];
even when contradiction is not admitted, non-dualism in its variegated form (*citrādvaita*) has been established.
Therefore, that which consists in the impossibility of distinguishing [cognitions] from one another is not the proof for the non-duality of cognitions;
rather, once this [non-distinction] is established through a single cognition, it is precisely that which is called "oneness."
In this context, what is the meaning of the phrase "there would be a single nature"? It means that oneness is the impossibility of distinguishing [the parts]. Thus:
"In this way, its being a single entity is indeed one thing, while the cognition [of it] is otherwise.
Where is there any use for a lack of conviction regarding this matter, which is established by the force of reality?"
When an external object exists, the white appears as if distinct from the cognition of whiteness;
therefore, one who asserts their identity while seeking the external must be refuted due to the confusion regarding the external.
By this non-distinction, the rejection of direct perception is employed.
Furthermore:
If it is argued that perception itself divides the white from the cold,
then does that which is being divided divide something already divided, or does it divide what is not yet divided?
Since there is not even a trace of another in the case of difference, how could one differentiate? And who would be able to say, "The mind is undifferentiated," if it were to be differentiated?

For even externally, it is precisely the cognition that, while being differentiated itself, differentiates the objects; and in this case, there is no room for other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the nature of the cognition itself, since that is nothing other than self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And thus, to say that "it is one and yet differentiates" is a contradiction. However, in the external world, according to the view that [cognition] is formless (*nirākāra*), although cognition is not differentiated, it is established as having a differentiated nature through the differentiation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, due to the conceit of grasping a differentiated nature.

One might distinguish between objects; however, consciousness itself, whose very nature consists of its own attributes, does not differ between blue and yellow. To claim that it distinguishes these two is a great audacity. If it were to distinguish them by being differentiated within each individual instance of cognition, then—since there is merely an absence of communication between one and another—a variegated appearance would be impossible at that time; so how could there be an established distinction? Or rather, from what source [could it arise]?

[Objection: Does it differentiate [itself] because its limit (*avadhi*) is not perceived? [Response: And what is to be done here by the perception of a limit, since it is precisely because that [limit] is not perceived that its differentiation from that [limit] is established? Furthermore, even when another is apprehended, an entity does not become differentiated by way of the other's form;
rather, the very perception [of it] as identical [to itself] is the perception of its difference from the other, and that occurs even when the other is unperceived.
[457,10] "If it is not incomplete, there is no damage to the cognition of difference.

[457,11] To this, the reply is: if this is stated with reference to the position that even what is not being perceived exists, then this is appropriate only within the framework of the externalist (bāhyavāda) doctrine, not in the system of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā). For instance:
That existence is beyond the senses and that it abides in its own self-cognition—
this which is asserted by others as pleasing, at this I am truly amazed.

Therefore, because it is unmanifest and non-existent, there can be no establishment of difference through dependence upon it. Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot even be an object of dependence; for instance, there is no establishment of non-difference for anything based on a rabbit’s horn. There could, at most, be a mere negation of unity, and that is precisely what is accepted. If one asks, "If it is not excluded from that, what then would it be?"—it is simply a negation of unity.

We reply: Is it not the case that "existent" (*sat*) is defined as that which is excluded from the non-existent (*asat*)? And that which is excluded from the non-existent is also excluded from the son of a barren woman;

yet it is not logical to say that what is excluded from a tree is not excluded from a *plakṣa* tree. Therefore, how could a jar not be excluded from a donkey’s horn? If this is so, then the distinction of even a sky-flower from jars and the like is all the more difficult to deny. For that which is not [excluded] from something...

That which is excluded from something is itself characterized by exclusion. Consequently, it cannot be said that for the son of a barren woman there is neither difference nor non-difference from the Vindhya mountains;
for since the negation of both is necessarily restricted to non-existence, it cannot be adduced as a proof for the non-existence of a universal (*sāmānya*), a person (*pudgala*), or the like.
For the phrase "it is excluded from that" has a common meaning—whether as the sense of the nominative or the ablative—as it is a property of real entities (*vastu*).

Or, it may be by way of their imagined nature (*kalpitadharmatā*). This is the actual reality of the matter here: if the speaker’s intention is merely to negate a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāvatā*) such that "this is distinct from that," then let there be a mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) between a jar and a horse's horn; what harm is done?

Likewise, if the existence of "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*) were intended to be established as real entities (*vastu-rūpa-sthiti*), then that would apply only to things such as pots and cloths, and not to a human and a donkey's horn, nor to a human and a donkey's horn together, because only one of these two would possess the status of a real entity. And this being the case, the intention is simply that the person (*pudgala*) is not distinct from the aggregates (*skandhas*), and thus neither of these two exists in the form of a self or what belongs to a self; nor are they identical.

There is no fault in saying that it experiences a state equal to that of the son of a barren woman. However, regarding existence and non-existence, it is said that they have characteristics established through mutual exclusion by relying on the imagined form (*kalpita-rūpa*) of non-existence; it is not that both possess the nature of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*). For this very reason, it was stated that there is the establishment of the nature of entities such as "self" and "mine. Therefore, as long as something does not appear [as a conceptual construct], it does not transcend the status of being a real entity.

[458,5] Thus, it might be thought that even from non-perception, there is the apprehension of difference when things are mutually unmixed; this is the case when existence (*sattā*) is being established.

[458,6] Otherwise, however, even then there would be only doubt. But that which is perceived as having the nature of light alone (*prakāśaikasvabhāva*) is neither one nor many. As for the appearing entity, since it is not a non-entity, its meaning as "difference" is indeed intended. And that is expressed by means of the convention of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti*).

But there is no mention of the aspect of non-existence (abhāvāṃśa) as a negation therein; for if it were mentioned, its identity [with existence] could not be avoided, so how could there be non-existence? For this very reason, even by way of being both existence and non-existence, duality is not attained. Therefore, since there is no cognition of even a trace of what is intended to be other, it is rightly said: "How could it be distinct from non-existence itself? For this very reason, regarding the preceding and succeeding [moments]...

[458,11] Even if there is non-perception [of the object], the distinction [between them] is nonetheless established; thus, this is clearly nothing more than self-deception. For priority and posteriority are not manifested, and manifestation cannot be associated with priority and posteriority. Therefore, because they do not exist, there is no such thing as the cognition of the past and so forth, since only manifestation exists. And thus:
[458,14] In this delusion, the conceptualizations and imaginings—
such as pleasure, pain, blue, and so forth— which arise from all the sense faculties,
[458,15] are cognitions that are non-different from one another because they are perceived simultaneously.
But priority and posteriority are simply not cognizable at all.
Thus is the summary.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "From what could it be divided?"—since the limit of division does not even appear, what is the use here of considering existence or non-existence? For instance:
"If this [notion] 'it is different from that' refers to the intrinsic nature of the object to be apprehended..."
The appearance of this [object], which has a limit, may or may not exist; it cannot be apprehended in its own nature.
If it is argued that even when another related entity does not appear, there is still a cognition of a related entity such as a father, we reply:

in that case too, we know that being a "related entity" is merely conceptual (*kālpānika*), because if it were a real entity (*vasturūpa*), every related entity would depend upon the cognition [of its counterpart].
For even a limit (*avadhi*) is simply a particular kind of related entity. Therefore, the cognition of one among cause and effect is devoid of the cognition of the other.

Being directed toward objects that possess a pure intrinsic nature, it merely establishes what is constructed by the artisan of conceptualization—the delusion regarding the relationship characterized by mutual dependence.

Therefore, the notion that "the cognition of the delimited object arises when the limit itself is not cognized" is nothing but a misconception; how could perception, which grasps difference, apprehend that which does not appear? Surely, blue must necessarily be accepted as distinct from non-blue, and by that which grasps it...

[459,3] It is not apprehended by perception in that manner; thus, blue is indeed not apprehended. We too say this: if there is no apprehension of non-blue, then since it is not apprehended as distinct from that [non-blue], how is blue itself apprehended? If you argue: "Precisely because there is no apprehension of it, there is the apprehension of its distinction from that; otherwise, both apprehension and non-apprehension would not be established," then [we reply]: just as...

In that case, since there is no apprehension of that [entity], how can there be an apprehension of the difference that has it as its limit? Consequently, what is called the "grasping of that" contradicts its unity just as much as it contradicts the grasping of the difference delimited by it. If it is argued that the very cognition of this form is itself the cognition of difference, then this remains the same even when the cognition of difference is denied.
For how can that which is perceived as distinct without a limit of distinction be considered a distinction?
If it is argued that the word itself should not be so [perceived], let it appear in that way.
For when both appear, it is said that its very nature (*svabhāva*), which depends upon them, does not manifest; this is not a mere rejection of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, just as the appearance of a form unmixed with others is called the manifestation of difference (*bhedapratibhāsa*), so too, a perception independent of such [other forms] is called the disappearance of the manifestation of difference, because only its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) manifests. If this is so, [then...]
[459,14] A thing is not known through the appearance of difference because of a limit, nor through non-difference because of confusion;
[459,15] and since there is nothing other than difference and non-difference, how can there be a cognition of a real entity?
If this is correctly considered, it is as follows:

for if there is no distinction in the object, how could there be a distinction even from the cognition? And if there were a distinction, then even when the cognition is limited, everything would be within the range of everyone.
[459,19] This reflection is merely made under the compulsion of an external dogmatic adherence; and in that regard, this same refutation applies equally.

[459,20] For just as there is no apprehension of difference for one [cognition] when the grasping of difference is not admitted, so too there is none for a second [cognition] in the absence of the apprehension of a limit (*avadhi*), which is the basis for the grasping of difference.

[459,21] In that case, if the establishment of the apprehension of difference for one [cognition] occurs even without the apprehension of a limit—just as the apprehension of an external object occurs with the eyes closed—then [the eyes]...

[459,22] Why should another not have the established determination of grasping a real entity even when there is an absence of the apprehension of difference, just as in the case of the non-apprehension of the form of atoms [459,23]?

For there is no real entity other than the atoms; therefore, in that case too, for one whose eyes are closed, even though there is no apprehension of them, there is the established determination of grasping the real entity. Thus, there is no fault even in the non-perception of difference.

How, then, is there the apprehension of difference? Not in any way whatsoever. Rather, the mere establishment of the apprehension of difference would exist in dependence upon a subsequent determination (*niścaya*). For that [determination], by dividing blue and the mass of non-blue—which have been made objects of appearance corresponding to itself—into their mutual opposition, casts its own activity right into perception itself, such that one thinks: "This blue has been seen, not the non-blue."

With reference to that, it is established that perception itself grasps the exclusion of others, or else that [perception] is a memory—just as a subsequent cognition in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhika-jñāna) is considered to grasp what has already been grasped, with respect to the determination of unity even when [the object] was not previously grasped.

By this, the lack of contradiction in such statements as "it delimits that" is explained. Therefore, by means of this mere internal distinction, there is no involvement of perception in either the grasping or the non-grasping of identity.

In that case, should there now be an identity between perception and non-perception? No, because what is intended is merely the negation of the apprehension of difference. However, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whether it apprehends a counter-correlative simultaneously or successively, or whether it involves a mental synthesis (*saṅkalpa*), may conventionally designate either difference or non-difference; yet, with respect to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that which does not appear is neither one nor many.

If it is asked, "What is the status of that which appears?"—in that case as well, if there were a distinction between the two apprehenders, then, because no other object is delineated, it would be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) grasping at distinction, just as before. If there is no distinction, the doctrine of variegated non-duality (*citrādvaitavāda*) is established; moreover, it is also the case that cognition itself (*buddhirūpa*), as the apprehender of non-distinction, is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is the summary (*saṃgraha*).
Whether an external object exists or does not exist, there is no perception of its difference;
rather, the perception of non-difference occurs within cognition solely by way of its own appearing nature.
Therefore, difference is solely dependent upon conventional usage.

[460,14] But surely, how can another deny that which appears as a manifest form, superimposed with contradictory properties such as blue, yellow, and so forth? This is not denied; for this very reason, it is called "variegated" (*citra*). Regarding that which is denoted by the word "variegated"—namely, the blue, yellow, and so on—it cannot withstand analysis into its own individual distinctions in terms of ultimate reality; this is what is called "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvitti*). And therein lies the superimposition of contradictory properties.

Are they two contradictory properties, or are they [properties] residing in two contradictory things? Even in the first case, is it by way of their substratum (*āśraya*) or by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*)? If it is the position of the substratum, then because the status of being a locus is established through cognition itself, the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is unestablished; for there is no room for the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that which is accepted through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). If, on the other hand, it is by way of their own nature, then mere [contradiction of nature] does not cause distress, since [the two properties] appear within a single, non-different substratum.
For one who brings about loving-kindness (*maitrī*), opposition is destroyed, just like the case of the produced (*kṛtaka*) and the eternal (*nitya*).

If it is argued that while the distinction between those two is merely conceptual (*kalpanākṛta*), here it is produced by appearance (*pratibhāsakṛta*), [we reply: this is an illustration based merely on the difference of their substrata (*āśraya*). If it is then argued that in that case there is no difference of substratum because there is no difference of appearance, [we reply that] the same applies here as well.
Because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is non-different. If it is asked, "In that case, why is there not indeed a difference due to the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*)?", we say no.

For regarding external objects, appearance—also called the "aspect" (*ākāra*)—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); but in the absence of that [external object], the object is merely the manifestation itself. Self-awareness, however, is the means of valid cognition; how could that which is unified with it by that [self-awareness] be differentiated? As for the claim that these are two contradictory properties (*dharma*), that has been cast far aside.
Since difference itself does not exist, where is there contradiction? Therefore, there is no means whatsoever for establishing difference.

On the contrary, it is established that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the means for establishing non-difference and subverting difference; as for external conventional practice, it merely presents [the appearance of difference].
This too has been stated:

"In a variegated cognition, blue and so forth are attributes of the cognition that do not share in another [nature]. For it is impossible to perceive them while they remain within the variegated cognition; rather, one falls [into error] by discerning them as objects. (PV III 220) The phrase "not sharing in another" (*ananyabhāk*) means not sharing in another nature (*ananyasvabhāvabhāk*). Blue and so forth, not partaking in the nature of yellow and so forth, cannot appear [distinctly] while situated within a variegated cognition.
[461,7] It may be possible to perceive [the object] as solitary, because the appearance—which has acquired that property—is restricted to each individual [aspect], such as yellow and so forth.

[461,8] The meaning is that only by relinquishing its mutual nature can it be possible to appear [as such]. For, by discerning and separating that [nature], one would necessarily accept that the appearance has not acquired that property; thus, one would fall into the very position of the proponent of external objects (*bahirarthavāda*). Moreover, this is a qualification of cognition (*jñānopādhi*).
[Blue and so forth]; therefore:
"In whatever manner a cognition appears" (PV III 121).
Because it appears as blue, yellow, and so on, it is experienced in that very way—as yellow and so forth—through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), since they possess a mutually identical nature.
This is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand. Therefore, the author of the *Bhāṣya* rightly says:
"Or rather, that is not surprising, because it is impossible to establish [it] as distinct from what is non-variegated" (PVA 290).

For here, there is no establishment of [the variegated] as distinct from the non-variegated—that is, from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which is of a non-multiple nature—due to their non-difference.

The intended establishment [of the object] culminates in a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), and that has already been proven by [the author] himself. Previously, "oneness" was described as having the characteristic of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) due to the impossibility of its being analytically separated; however, now it is simply the state of being contained within a single cognition—this is the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*).

Therefore, even the possession of variegated forms is said to exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*); in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, there is only non-duality (*advaita*)—having thus conceived the meaning.

That was stated with the intention of merely negating the cognition of difference; however, if it is argued that "in this way it is not non-dual, because it does not appear as distinct from duality," or "in this way it is not knowledge, nor is it self-awareness," that is refuted. For duality is indeed difference. And where is its appearance? Therefore, even if there is no appearance of difference from that [non-duality], how can there be unity, given that unity is included within a single cognition?

Because it has already been established? Likewise for the rest: for if there were an appearance of everything, there would be the consequence of the destruction of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all error.

Nor is it tenable to say that, by way of the conventional reality of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti*), even a distinction like that of a variegated painting is fit for systematic establishment, because of experience.

Because it establishes arising through the contradiction of difference, the statement of non-duality regarding the variegated (*citra*)—by means of mere blue, yellow, and so forth—is indeed a conventional disclosure (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*), not a statement of actual difference. However, for one who has not yet realized reality, the statement of difference cultivated through repeated practice does not obstruct reality.
In fact, these expressive syllables are merely a non-implicative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*); the notion that they serve to establish oneness is an error.

[Regarding] the world: this is the meaning. Alternatively, that which is considered the apprehended and the apprehender—such as blue, yellow, and so forth, or what is denoted by the word "variegated"—is not variegated, nor is it manifold. Because it is not established as distinct from the non-variegated self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the mere negation of manifoldness is intended; and since the opponent's negation of unity is also based on perception itself, manifestation is indeed free from both.
Momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is said to be as if existing; that is what is meant, just as we have previously explained.

For this very reason, because there is no other entity—neither a knower nor a known object—the word "non-duality" (*advaita*) has the meaning of "alone" (*kevala*), and does not signify a mere negation of duality (*dvaitaparyudāsa*). Demonstrating this, he says:
Therefore, self-awareness alone is the absolute non-duality, because of the absence of anything else.

Thus, that which was previously stated by way of an objection—"Now, how is it that what appears does not exist simply because of the conceptualization of it as one or many?"—is addressed here: even while being conceptualized, it indeed appears. If it were non-existent, how could there be an appearance? If there is an appearance, how can it be non-existent?

Thus? And here, the *Ṭīkā* states that because there is perception by way of the nature of perception even for that which is devoid of the forms of unity and plurality, according to the principle that "existence is perception," it is indeed existent (*sad eva*). That very point has been clarified as another established tenet (*siddhāntāntara*). Thus, the doctrine of variegated non-duality (*citrādvaitavāda*) characterized by the attribute of unity is perceived as the primary view of the author of the *Vārttika*; however, for the author of the *Bhāṣya*, it is characterized by the exclusion of both. In reality, however, for both of them, it is one.
This is the intended meaning: however, the distinction between the primary and the secondary is established based on the difference in the manner of manifestation.

[462,19] Therefore, having failed to consider the manifold establishment of non-dual diversity, for whom would the refutation of the Teacher based on the pretext of a commentary be an ornament? [462,20]

If the Master’s intention is one thing, yet the commentator’s intention regarding the literal explanation of the words is another, then it is not possible [to claim otherwise]; alas, this is a manifest error! Thus, since unity alone is established even in the case of a variegated form of cognition, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished. As for the claim that "there is no utility for the non-duality of the variegated for those engaged in worldly transaction," this does not constitute a subverting argument (*bādhaka*).
Because it is the domain of the Buddhas, like emptiness.
If you argue that there is indeed a fault because there is no distinction between the realization of reality and its opposite,
then the owl lives happily without even looking at its own face!
For thus,
there is no contradiction regarding the mind being with form,
because the mind as something manifest is unestablished.
But it is non-existent by its very conceptualized nature, even though it is manifest; this is the distinction.
And by what nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is this wheel of cognitions ever liberated?
Nor is there an experience of its own form,
because that would entail the over-extension of the consequence that it lacks the nature of mind.
And therefore, there was no certainty regarding that at all;
even that [certainty] was distinguished by a difference in form. Nor is this [certainty] accessible through either ultimate reality (*tattva*) or conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
There is a distinction in the absence of dependence on another.
And indeed, there is no cognition of another anywhere;
moreover, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is equal for both.
Therefore, it is not the case that one is conventional while the other is not.
By what means is this distinction established even for you?
Alternatively,
there is never an absence of emptiness,
nor is there any other supreme realization whatsoever.
There is neither the destruction of defects nor the arising of virtues;
when conventional reality is investigated through the lens of causal efficacy, it is not found.
Therefore, in this regard, as long as there is no possibility of analytical investigation,
this method holds that "this existence is one thing and peace is another";
however, when the mind is stirred by the play of analysis, [the distinction between them vanishes].
Tell me, what is existence or peace here? Let it be explained.
And likewise in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: "In this world,
there is no difference whatsoever between these two—
the state of peace and the arising of birth— when considered in terms of their actual mode of existence."
Nevertheless, for those who perform virtuous deeds, the attainment of peace is ordained through the exhaustion of birth.

By way of the existence of the true object (*sad-artha-vṛtti*), that is, by way of the ultimate mode of being (*paramārtha-vṛtti*); the remainder is by way of the conventional (*saṃvṛtti*). Also in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
"Because phenomena are like a dream, there is no conceptualization of existence or peace" (AA 440), and so forth. Therefore, this is established by the very nature of things (*jāti-siddha*).
“Both nirvāṇa and existence—these two do not exist. The thorough understanding of existence itself is called nirvāṇa. (By Nāgārjuna).
The refutation of this is like the murder of one’s own innocent mother; such is the meaning of this treatise.
Whether distinction or non-distinction, whether dual or non-dual—let it be as it may regarding the nature of cognition;
there can be no falsity in manifestation, for that is opposed even to the mere scent of sublation.

"Consciousness is that which cognizes"—thus, the emptiness of all imagined conceptual proliferation exists everywhere. And so it is said: "Those phenomena do not exist in their own-being in the manner in which unlearned, ordinary worldlings are attached," and so forth in detail.
For even mental factors (buddhidharma) exist only by way of forms imagined through another cognition; they do not exist merely by virtue of being self-cognized.

By this, the Blessed One’s being like a dream or an illusion is explained. For even in the case of examples, it is only that which is conceptually determined (*adhyavasita*) that is negated, not that which is appearing (*pratibhāsamāna*). Therefore, it is established that the proof of the Blessed One as possessing form (*sākāra*) is inseparable from its non-sublation. And thus, the meaning of the verse of homage is established.
That which has attained magnificence by its own nature through the characteristics of food and condiments;
which is profound because it is not the domain of others, being empty of the waves of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
and from which the rays of gnosis radiate toward the world through emanations—that [Reality] is not unreal.
Therefore, O Blessed One, the body of the Sage is auspicious on all sides, being free from any stain.
Furthermore:
Just as gold, endowed with the perfection of qualities and form, reaches the ultimate limit of excellence and is inexhaustible;
Just as the body of embodied beings is liberated from the suspicion of the stain of falsehood, so too is the Buddha-body.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the Non-duality of the Variegated, in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great paṇḍita Jñānaśrīmitra.
[Chapter Five] Now,
is not this entire preceding elaboration merely the play of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? And as for this so-called "self-awareness," it simply does not exist,
because it is refuted by both reasoning and scripture.
In the absence of that, from what source could the manifold establishment of non-duality arise?
Nor would there be the state of Samantabhadra, due to the failure to abandon falsity.
Here is the question:
Is it that cognition itself does not exist? Or, even if it exists, how can there be a manifestation [of objects] when it destroys its own object of cognition (*prameya*) by itself?
Whether it be with respect to the cognition of itself or the cognition of another,
this entire [argument] does not hold when subjected to rigorous analysis.
For indeed:
"This consciousness is not mine"—it cannot be made manifest by distinct pieces of clay;
nor does it arise from another anywhere, and even when it appears clearly, this [object] is not real.
If it is argued that manifestation itself is not real, then from what source would reality arise when it is known by another?
Since reality cannot be established in either way, it is improper to claim that this [manifestation] exists by its own nature.
This is the meaning:
even one devoid of consciousness—would he not say that "consciousness itself does not exist"?
If there were neither speaker nor listener, this [cognition] would nonetheless still appear to itself.

As for the claim that "there is cognition of another," it has been refuted elsewhere; so let that matter rest for now. Now, if self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is not denied in every respect, but is rather said to be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛtī*), then, since there is no total rejection of it, its status as conventional must depend upon a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

And this subversion would consist either in the cognition being distinct from the object of cognition (*prameya*) or in the failure to experience it; however, by the very fact of the object of cognition being subverted, the existence of that [self-cognition] is not established.
In that regard:
If there is experience through differentiation, how could there be self-experience because of that differentiation?
Furthermore, the sublation of the object of cognition cannot be accomplished even by Śakra himself.

For it is not possible to determine that the very nature of what is manifest does not exist. Now, if there is no negation of the manifest in every respect, let it be that it is not self-cognized; but let it be cognized by another. This is not so;
for if there is no confidence even in self-cognition, what can be said of cognition by another?
For if self-awareness is absent, awareness of another is also non-existent.

If that which is perceived by another were to exist as something other, how could that "other" itself exist? Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot be the cause for the conventional usage of the existence of another.

If it were to exist while being perceived by another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If you argue that the existence of the other is likewise established in this very way, then let it be the same for the object of cognition (*prameya*) as well.
And if existence were self-evident, then illumination too would be self-existent for the blind;
for the contradiction regarding their own activity is equal for both of these.

[467,11] Now, if it is argued: "Let the fault belong only to him who has accepted even the cognition of another; as for me, there is nothing that is self-cognized, nor anything cognized by another," [467,12] one who possesses intelligence ought not to speak thus. For it is not possible to negate an object—whether it manifests from itself or from another—merely by means of an undesirable position or by words alone. [467,13] If one were to follow valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then...

[467,14] Having first established perception (*pratyakṣa*), one enumerates the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the rejection of what is seen occurs in the case of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth, but not in the case of perception. [467,15] And regarding objects that are beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), the remainder—whether it be total or partial—is not capable of either affirming or negating that object. [467,16] And it is precisely that which is established by perception which is designated as such, wherein there is the direct manifestation of its own nature. Whether that [manifestation] occurs through itself or through another—what does this matter?
If its own nature is not known even in the absence of any activity by another, then that very loss of its own nature occurs; what further need is there for other subverting factors?
Precisely because it appears as a self, it is not sublated;
precisely because it manifests its own object, even the sublater is itself sublated.
Therefore, let it be understood that he too is a merchant by virtue of that very same vessel;
hence, for that which is manifesting, there is no such thing as sublation.

[467,23] But surely protection would come from that very external illumination; self-manifestation, being helpless, would be sublated by another possessing power. To this it has been said: even the other is useful only through the manifestation of its own nature, not by its mere existence, nor by warding off a blow by stretching out an arm. If that manifestation of its own nature were possible for the [object's] own nature as well, nothing else would be required.
On the contrary,
he who is strong by his own power alone is weak in the face of another;
just as one who is intent on guarding himself is, in that regard, merely an "other" to the other.

Likewise, theories such as the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), erroneous appearance (*viparītakhyāti*), the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*), and the deception of perception (*dṛṣṭimoṣa*)—
these various conceptualizations of error are seen by others through external light;
they do not, however, have the power to bring about the manifestation of their own cause.
In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is established exactly in that way;
a cognition does not appear otherwise by superimposing a different form upon it.
Whenever whatever form manifests, it is indeed that very [form] which,
through being made one with its own internal aspect, is called an "error" even though it exists externally.

But when, through repeated practice, cognition—which manifests its own nature—becomes an object of experience even externally, free from any suspicion of error, then where is the possibility of sublation? How much less so in the case of self-awareness (*svānubhava*)? Only this remains: how could such a cognition arise, or how could it be ascertained?

Just as birth occurs by way of its own nature as blue through the essence of cognition, so too does it occur for the intellect from its own cause, just as a lamp occurs by way of its own nature as yellow light.

But how is it that this is only self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) and not cognition by another? It has been stated elsewhere: "The point at issue is simply that a form appearing as either self-cognizable or cognizable by another is indeed non-sublated (*abādhya*). And that is established, for there is no sublation of one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by another means of valid cognition."
How much more so, then, for self-awareness, which is of the nature of direct perception?

Even for inference, which arises from the awakening to the purity of the three marks (*trairūpya*), it is impossible for there to be a sublation by another means of valid cognition (*māna*), or by verbal testimony (*śabda*) and so forth, as the case may be. For it is almost self-evident that two properties capable of establishing two mutually contradictory states cannot possibly exist simultaneously in one and the same subject (*dharmin*). However, the relationship of the sublated and the sublater (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) would occur when one of them lacks firmness regarding its own object.

Regarding its own object, whether there is firmness or lack of firmness in the two extremes belongs to perception alone, through its erring or otherwise. And the erring of perception with respect to its object is nothing but delusion (*bhrama*). Since delusion is restricted to the cognition of another, what rival can there be for self-awareness (*saṃvedana*)?
If there is no sublation even externally for that which has cast aside the suspicion of delusion, how could it be sublated by an inference of non-duality arising from itself?

[Objection: Is there not a contradiction here? [Response: It has been stated in this regard that this is a distortion (*viplava*) of the cognition of another; thus, it cannot be said that even when there is a non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), this is a distortion of self-cognition (*svavitti*), because [self-cognition] does not conform to the operation [of the object] through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognition of another.

Even then, to claim that an entity exists merely by its presence (*sattāmātreṇa*) is a power of great delusion (*mahāmoha*), like the washing away of impressions (*saṃskāra*) by one who possesses impressions through hearing [the scriptures].

If it is argued that there can be a lapse even in the absence of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), then, since there is no lapse in the absence of life, death itself would be the remedy for the lapse; this is a truly excellent Buddhist position! Furthermore, since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is all-pervasive, its absence is impossible to perceive; thus, for one who asserts that even this distortion arises from beginningless ignorance, the [remedy] must be established through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Even with respect to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), errors such as the superimposition of intrinsic nature or passion are not far removed; however, the state of having a contrary form is common to both.

Therefore, utility is not established by mere existence; nor, even if there is utility, does the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)—which is produced by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that does not conform to its operation—have power over it. For one who lacks such power, while failing to regard the grasper of the relation and so forth as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [is not refuted].

Therefore, by virtue of having a single object, it would be only the cognition of another that would be touched by the fault, not self-cognition, because their objects are entirely distinct. Consequently, just as in that proof, if one were to accept the validity of the cognition of another, one would also have to accept inference as a valid means of knowledge even though it contradicts oneself; yet if one does not, then the object to be established by inference is nonetheless proven, and thus it belongs to that very [cognition].

The error becomes manifest through the arising of an inference; it does not do so through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) regarding self-awareness (*svavitteḥ*), because it is impossible to state that which has already been stated by implication. However, if one were to proceed according to one's own whim, one might even take self-awareness as the subject (*pakṣa*); yet, the principle is that no effort is made toward the proof because it is sublated by a specific perception (*pratyakṣaviśeṣabādhitatvāt*).

[469,18] In that case, this logic applies only once the proof of *vijñaptimātra* (representation-only) is established; however, prior to the arising of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), the very proof of that [absence of intrinsic nature] would have no scope. [469,19] It is not so. For as soon as one asserts the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the blue, it is simultaneously rejected by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of self-awareness (*svavedana*) according to the sequence already stated. [469,20] If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the blue] would be devoid of the proof of its being manifest (*prakāśamānatā*) and so forth. This too is not the case.

[469,21] Because it serves merely for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of cognition. Now, even so, if self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*) is being established by negating the state of being illuminated by another, would that not establish the conventional usage of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)? Furthermore, if there is an absolute absence of being cognizable by another, or if there is a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there can be no such thing as a proof or a probandum;
how then can even the establishment of conventional usage occur?

That is incorrect. For the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) exists only at the level of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*). At that time, neither of the two realities is established.

In that context, for one who—despite blue being manifest through other adventitious conditions—still harbors doubt regarding its being manifested by another due to the power of innate formative ignorance (*avidyā*), the presentation of a proof capable of withstanding logical reasoning (*nyāya*) is offered to awaken him. And at that time, it is precisely that [proof] which [is subject to] sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) and so forth.
He will examine this. And when that has been established, there is the conventional usage of "representation" (*vijñapti*).

By this much alone, the task of the Proponent of Cognition (*Vijñānavādin*) is completed. As for the opponent, however, the very fact of perceptual sublation (*pratyakṣabādha*) precludes their application of a formal proof (*sādhana*).
Nor does the operation of perception ever depend upon the non-arising of inference; rather, inference always functions precisely where perception has no scope.
Therefore, it is established that even if [the object] were sublated, just as if it were proven, no opportunity for such a claim arises.

Consequently, self-awareness does not become merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) by virtue of the sublation of its object. Likewise, this objection should not even be raised: "If blue is established through self-awareness, then that self-awareness must also be established through another self-awareness, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is because...
If blue is established by itself, what would be the purpose of its self-cognition? For indeed, one who asserts that even blue must have cognition asks, "What is the use of its self-cognition?
and thus intends that cognition itself should be self-evident. This alone is the doctrine of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), following the maxim of the man mounted on a horse.
However, if that [cognition] were distinct [from the object], then one would not transcend an infinite regress, nor...

Regarding the statement "the doctrine of self-cognition is contact": if, then, it is not distinct and exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), and if that very thing is merely a phenomenon (*dharmamātra*), then when that [designation] is sublated, it cannot remain neutral by itself; how, then, could it be capable of protecting another?
That too is of no consequence.
The blue possesses luminosity, and luminosity also possesses blueness;
the establishment of the distinction between property and its possessor is not considered to be restricted to a single essence.
Protection is indeed non-differentiation; differentiation in this regard is purposeless.
For the protection of others is either inseparable from the protection of oneself, or it does not exist at all.
Precisely because it shines by itself, it is not sublated;
thus the reality of the object is communicated by whatever means of expression.
Furthermore, as for that which is stated out of pride in one's own logical reasoning— that there is no self-cognition because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself,
just as a fingertip cannot be touched by that very same fingertip— in that case too: if the fingertip were not to be touched by its own tip, how could it be smooth?
If this [body] is itself smooth, why is there no contradiction now?
Why does the intellect not itself shine forth? Or rather, why is it that this [object] is perceived as being smooth, or as having arisen by itself?

Since the meaning of the sentence culminates in such a cognition, a contradiction regarding causal efficiency (*kāritra*) arises. Consequently, statements such as "it goes by itself" or "it is white by itself" must not be asserted by proponents of such views in any way whatsoever, either independently or in the presence of those [who hold such views], because they involve the rejection of [the object's] dependence on instigation, coloring, and so forth.
To say "by another" would result in a great confusion. Furthermore, in an action that possesses an object (*sakarmikā*), it is not appropriate for there to be both a single object and a subject;
yet the action of cognition is indeed one with an object, as in "Caitra cognizes blue.
If that is so, then let us remain silent regarding such statements as "consciousness illuminates itself."

Furthermore, regarding the expression "it is perceived" (*vedyate*) and so forth, which others employ with the intention of expressing an object and an agent (*karmakartṛ*), we have merely assigned the conventional term "it appears" (*bhāsate*) to that very same meaning; thus, there is no difference whatsoever. Now, by the passage beginning "the Blessed One is self-existent" (*svayambhūr bhagavān*), there is simply a demonstration that such a nature arises from its own causes alone, through the exclusion of the activity of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), a Lord (*īśvara*), and so on; it is not, however, a perception of duality.

It is said that here the conventional usage of action and agent is intended; if so, then why this hostility toward the consensus that cognition also arises from its own cause in the form of luminosity and is not illuminated by another?
This very nature of being of the nature of light is what constitutes its self-awareness.
However, its self-cognition does not occur through the relationship of action and agent.
This is an intermediate verse.

Furthermore, as for what was said here—that those who speak thus will be contradicted by the world itself—that is refuted by this very point, because such an intention is observed in the world. Even if it is not observed in the case of the object of cognition (*buddhi*), it is nonetheless observed in the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*).

[471,12] Because it is observed that there is a desire to express both self-illumination and other-illumination, as in the case of a lamp and a jar; [471,13] although a duality is seen in external objects,

[471,13] with respect to the nature of cognition (*buddhi*), since other-illumination is sublated, self-illumination alone is established, but not in every respect [471,14] such that conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) itself does not exist.
Indeed, it is known through cognition that "the lamp illuminates," but by what friend is it said that "cognition illuminates"?
Whether manifest or unmanifest, when it is not perceived by anyone,
it is as futile as describing the dance of a barren woman’s daughter.
If this is so, is this not without foundation? For it has been established that this very blue and so forth is cognition whose nature is self-luminous;

how then can it be said by a well-wisher, "By what means is this [established]? Instruction from another is of no weight regarding an object that is self-cognized; otherwise, who could establish the subject (*dharmin*) through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpaka-anupalambha*) and so forth? If that is the case, then in the instance of a lamp as well, how is it that it is nothing but cognition?

[471,23] What is the example? True; it is intended to dismiss the objection that, from the perspective of the world, the world itself will be the subverter. This is merely a place of rest for one whose reasoning has failed, providing no protection; otherwise, if everything were empty, what would the world even be able to subvert?

[471,24–25] If you argue that this is because everything is accepted conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), then the very point that "nothing exists in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is precisely what the world cannot tolerate.

If it is argued: "Let it be that [the object] does not exist conventionally; however, even if it does not exist ultimately, what is there for us to establish? For we intend to transcend both existence and non-existence," [we reply]: No, because the negation of existence is itself the meaning of "non-existent.
If blue and so forth are not entities, who can prevent them from being non-entities?
And in the doctrine that "it is non-existence," existence itself remains established.
Because for those things established through mutual exclusion, the negation of one is the affirmation of the other; it is not otherwise, merely by virtue of a lack of desire.
Alternatively, a third possibility must be stated here regarding these two:
for the wise, they must be established in one and the same place; there is no other way.

It might be argued as follows: "We do not establish the affirmation or negation of anything; rather, it is demonstrated that for those who maintain the positions of existence, non-existence, both, or neither, the respective definitions of their own tenets are untenable. In that case, if the prior absence of existence follows from the very untenability of the definition of existence, then what could we possibly have removed?"

And when, through the impossibility of a characteristic of non-existence, there is an absence of non-existence even prior [to an entity], then how could there be what is called "existence" for anyone by means of the absence of that absence? For just as a maiden experiences joy or dejection through the birth or loss of a son.
Due to the conceptualization of a son in a dream, it does not exist for one who is awake.

If that [statement] does not bring about the falsity of its continuity in order to dispel her remaining grief, then what has been done by it—has an affirmation of the non-existence of a son or the like been made, or a negation of the existence of a son or the like? Or, by the negation of the arising of a son, has the non-existence of something been established;
or, by the negation of death, has the affirmation of existence been established? For from the very beginning, there was simply no son at all.

[472,19] But for one who is awake, there is merely a restatement of that. In this same way, it should be inferred for both the noble and the non-noble. And this very state of being primordially peaceful (*ādiśāntatva*) and natural purity (*prakṛtipariśuddhi*) is proclaimed in the scriptures (*āgama*).
[472,20–21] To this, it is said: What kind of injunctions and prohibitions are being avoided by you—those characterized by arising and destruction?

Is it by grasping with the hand that you intend to bring about the nature of bringing near or removing? Or is it an affirmation characterized by proof, or a negation characterized by sublation, regarding some dharma that has become the subject of dispute?
In this regard, first of all, even for another [opponent], the first two positions do not exist.
But even by you, the third [alternative] cannot be avoided.

For others also maintain that it is not the case that the Blessed One’s authority, which was already established, is later removed, nor that something non-existent, such as Īśvara, is subsequently attributed to him. Likewise, it is not that duality, which was already established, is removed, nor that non-duality is now attributed;
rather, an already established intrinsic nature is restated by another and demonstrated through some form of reasoning.
Thus there is universal consensus. And since this [capacity for speech] exists for you as well, what excellence has been stated [by us]?

This very process of affirmation and negation—namely, the demonstration that "this exists" and "this does not exist"—has necessarily come to one who is engaged in speech, especially for one who has entered into debate out of a desire for victory or a disposition toward the welfare of others. But for one who remains silent, this [process] does not occur.

This would constitute a formal objection (*paryanuyoga*). The analogy of the dream is also universally applicable: for when a property of an object is esteemed by one person and denied by another, there is joy due to its establishment or the attribution of its qualities; yet, when another demonstrates its absence, there is despondency. Consequently, for one intent on diverting that mind, it is merely a restatement from the very beginning that "it does not exist in such a way."
The point that "it has been accomplished" is the same.

In that regard, the example of a dream is under one's own control only for that person who is capable of understanding it. Likewise, even in the doctrine of non-duality (*advayavāda*), just as at the time of waking one superimposes the result of a son—consisting merely of one's own mental image—and experiences joy and so forth, so it is here.

Even in the waking state, there is no harm, because it is merely the form of cognition that is superimposed as being external. It has been stated that in both of those states, although the appearance of non-conceptual perception terminates in its own nature alone, the superimposition of the unreal by conceptualization obscures it;
and that [conceptualization], having concealed its own nature, joins it with the form of another through the act of seeing, which is precisely why it occurs thus: "Today, my son..."

Regarding the thought, "I saw this in a dream," upon reflection, there is no such thing as the seeing of a son; rather, it is simply that a certain cognition arose in me in that manner. Therefore, with respect to the determination of that [cognition], one speaks of "seeing a son born and dead" and so forth; but in reality, where is there any seeing of a son? It is merely the arising of a cognition possessing a specific form capable of producing an attachment to that [son], due to the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

[473,19] Otherwise? What is the true nature of reality here? [473,20] For one who is obsessed with investigation, what is the use of manual examination? [473,21] Let the application of effort be made with joy toward the *Kīrtivārtika* and the *Bhāṣya*.
Even if one is under the power of faith, it is better to rely on the way of the crown prince,
wherein even the noble Nāgārjuna and others are established.
This will be demonstrated below. Furthermore, scriptural passages are causes for the production of mere merit only for one who is not skilled in investigation (*avicāracatura*).

In the course of investigation, however, the affirmation of the second follows by implication when there is a statement negating one of the two—existence or non-existence; thus, it cannot be avoided merely by a lack of desire. For instance, the statement "In a dream, there was no such thing as a son" expresses the non-existence of a son.

Since existence has indeed been established and negation refuted, how is it that for one who is awake neither affirmation nor negation is performed? However, the fact that the Noble One does not have such a vision means simply that a cognition with a contrary aspect arises in opposition to the perception of that [worldly] form; it is not a total destruction of consciousness.
Let this matter rest for now.
Now, if the intended meaning is the negation of the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence, there is by no means an abolition of mere appearance;

this is precisely what we accept, because conceptual construction is inherently erroneous (*prakṛtibhrānta*). Alternatively, if the meaning of emptiness is simply the inability to withstand analysis, then analysis itself relies upon the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); and in that case, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) necessarily enters into it, there is nothing other than self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).

It is neither another perception nor inference, because that would entail the consequence of its being devoid of its own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*). Nor is there the apprehension of a subject (*dharmin*), a property (*dharma*), and so forth;

for, since self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) possesses a determined form within the conventional (*saṃvṛtti*), and because—just as in the case of other objects of cognition (*prameya*) and means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)—no sublation (*bādhā*) is possible, it remains established. Thus, there is no occasion for the qualification "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*).
In whatever way objects are contemplated and analyzed,
in that very way self-cognition rushes forth like a shadow, difficult to escape.
And therefore, what kind of incapacity for analysis could there be in that which is of the nature of self-cognition? For how many analyses can possibly be applied?

Indeed, the luminosity of the manifestation of blue, or its blueness, is not a mere passing away, nor is it another non-luminous property that could be the object of familiarization. And that which is...
The experience of the mere intrinsic nature is the defeat of imagined things;
that itself is it.
And therefore, one should know the equality of non-perception and perception. (Madhyāntavibhāga I.8)
Such is the principle.
This very state of being primordially peaceful and naturally pure,
however, is the purity of stainlessness, which is the exhaustion of all unreal conceptual constructions.

This has already been stated. As for the claim that, by the very acceptance of that [position], the definition of that [object] is untenable—even by that much, there is no disparagement of the nature of experience. For: "Even if the definitions imagined by the foolish are refuted, there is no injury to the true nature of the object, which is devoid of all adventitious conditions. (The same verse is also quoted in ATV p. 530)
Having observed an elephant at the king’s gate,
he said to the cloud-like water-pot of his urine: "With its tusk, it has uprooted the darkness from the very foundation."
Someone [might see] a door with four pillars and a polished archway, made from excrement that resembles a ball of food offering.
"He who stands at the king's gate or in the cremation ground is a kinsman"— thinking thus, the fool, contrary to the profound teaching of mindfulness, regards even such a person as a kinsman.
Therefore, let even those intrinsic natures imagined by others, like the elements (*bhūta*), dissolve away; what harm comes to that which reveals the ultimate? Consequently:
"If this very position is established, then there is no difference between us two."
But if there were sublation in every respect, how could there be non-sublation by the world?
If it is said that even out of regard for the world, wisdom does not exist in its true form,
then why is the distress [caused by] the fact that it does not exist at all in reality not taken into account?
Therefore, whether the world is terrified or not, how can the exposition of reality—which is useful for human goals—be avoided?

If this is your own intention, why do you, O opponent, confound us with falsehood? For who would believe that there is an obstruction to your power even when a valid response exists? Moreover, since the conventional usage of "self-luminous" (svaprakāśa) exists in the world as well, where is the contradiction with worldly experience?

[475,17] Since it is not directly perceived within the scope of cognition itself, what is the use of this? Even though an entity is self-luminous, there is no contradiction with its causal activity, because the example has already been established by relying on the universal (sāmānya). Furthermore:
[475,19] Why is it that such a thought as "this cognition is manifesting to me" does not arise?
And here, in this resolve that touches upon your virtues, I have my own direct experience.
Therefore, enough of this deception of foolish people.

Furthermore, as for the objection that one might suspect the existence of experience is established through memory, and thus claim that memory and experience both pertain to the object itself and are called "cognition"—even in that case, it is simply the cognition bearing the form of the object that is being recollected, and since that [cognition] is remembered as having manifested of its own accord, there is no harm. Moreover, regarding the statement that "memory concerns the object," memory cannot occur with respect to what has not been experienced, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And if the object has been experienced, yet there is no experience of that experience...
Thus, how is this understood here by the heart?
If there is no awareness of cognition, there can certainly be no linguistic usage based on its limiting conditions; if it were perceived by another, an unavoidable infinite regress would ensue.
By this very [reasoning], even when [the object] is set aside, there is an absence of a logical mark (liṅga) for one who infers;
nor is an unperceived mark [sufficient], and there is no disagreement regarding the establishment of its comprehension.
Thus is the intermediate verse.
How then is this cognition, which is being experienced, not designated by way of its limits (*antatayā*)? Is it not indeed already designated:
"Internal is the object such as pleasure and so forth; external is the sphere such as cold and so forth. Perception has those respective forms; there is nothing else beyond that."
This phenomenon called "vibration" (sphurattā) is personally experienced and cannot be denied.
Thus, that very capacity is the means of knowledge, the self is the object of knowledge, and self-awareness is the fruit.

Therefore, while there would indeed be a fault in the position that [cognition] is formless (*nirākāra*), there is not even a suspicion of one in the position that it possesses form (*sākāra*). Indeed, the position that [cognition] possesses form is the one favored by the venerable Śāntideva. As he said:
"That which is seen, heard, and known is not here negated."
"Therefore, it is conceptual construction regarding this that is prevented as the cause of suffering" (BA 9.26).

Here, by the mention of actions such as "seeing" and so forth, it is stated that what is manifest— such as blue or softness— is impossible to deny, for it is not denied in reality (*satyataḥ*) or in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*).

To the question, "Whose is this selflessness? he replies: "It is the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of non-existent things, such as the grasped and the grasper, cause and effect, and so forth"—this is the meaning.

Conceptual construction arises from words alone. For conceptual construction occurs only with respect to that which is not seen; and since that which is not seen cannot exist in reality precisely because it is unseen, this [reason] is also connected here. Therefore, even in statements such as "all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is a negation of a conceptually constructed form in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).
Such is the sense. But for what purpose is there the warding off of unreal conceptualization? Because it is the cause of suffering.

For that very [conceptualization] projects *saṃsāra*, which is characterized by engagement, withdrawal, and so forth; since, in its absence, the mere arising of its form would be of no consequence therein.
As for those who connect the phrase "as real" (*satyataḥ*) with "the conceptualization as reality" (*satyatvena yā kalpanā*), if even in that case...
Even if [the object] were real, the purpose would be to prevent the conceptual construction that "this is real. What fault is there in its being *pariniṣpanna* (perfected)?

Alternatively, if the meaning is that even now one prevents the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that it is real in order to prevent liberation—on the grounds that it is non-existent—then it is contradictory to say that "seeing and so forth are not negated," for while seeing and so forth are rendered unreal, they are nonetheless not negated; this is precisely what constitutes the induction of unreality.

Because it has the sense of negation. Now, if it is not negated conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), then there is a prohibition from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvatas*). But even that is not established by the literal meaning of the words.

The word "truth" (*satya*) is applied otherwise, as a qualifier for "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*); yet in that case, the word "conceptual construction" is not appropriate, because it is precisely a single thing—such as what is perceived—that is intended as the object of affirmation and negation in relation to both the conventional and the ultimate.
For it is thus:
that which is seen, heard, and known is not at all negated here;
rather, from the perspective of conventional reality, this cause of suffering is prevented from the standpoint of ultimate truth.

Thus it is appropriate to say. Therefore, in this context, why do the great ones obscure the literal meaning—[for there is] the repetition of the word "word" (*śabda*), the ellipsis of the word "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*), and the word "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) having a different sense? It is clear that the aspects (*ākāra*) accepted as the domain of the six sensory consciousnesses are not negated because they are self-cognized; rather, it is only the conceptualized [aspect] that is negated.
[Regarding the term] "negation": how then is there a negation of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) for these [cognitions]? It is as it is for the Blessed One. How is it for the Blessed One?

Because of the negation of distinct objects. Even in a single variegated form, the state of grasped and grasper exists directly, even in the subtle [moment], with the intention of [denying] the relationship between action and agent. And this is not a subject for doubt, nor is it a matter for an effort at refutation in every respect.
It should be understood as follows: for just as the conceptualization of cause and effect occurs even with respect to a single entity,
so too would the cognition of the grasped and the grasper occur within a single consciousness.
Just as it was for the Blessed One:
"And this sprout is not self-made," so too for the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna.
By means of the negation beginning with "Not from self, nor from another" (MK I.1), and likewise:
"The mind does not perceive the omnipresent. (*MK I.8*)

And so forth. This is logical. For an imputation that is without limits—such as the imputation that "the aggregates alone are the self" regarding the worldly state—must not be neglected by one who possesses compassion, because the imputation of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject is the primary fault.
Therefore, its negation by way of the relationship between action and agent is appropriate.
But the arising of that which has the nature of self-cognition is indeed praised.

As it is said in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*: "Maitreya, there is indeed no one there who discerns any phenomenon; rather, that mind has arisen in such a way that it appears as such. Even the statement that "the mind proceeds as the appearance of an object" indicates nothing other than self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because the perceived and the perceiver are unified. Likewise, when a person possesses the cognition of blue, it is said that "he knows the blue."
Because the root *ag* has the sense of "going," it carries the sense of "knowing. By the phrase "being one who experiences the cognition of blue," it is clearly stated:
"For one whose apprehension is not perceived, the seeing of the object is not established" (PVin I 55cd). "One who experiences that" means, in short, "one who experiences blue."

And in the *Uttaratantra*, there is this very syllable: "The Dharma is to be personally realized" (UT 10). For one who asserts that the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) exists, there is no refuge other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, it is not...
When one's own realization is established through both reasoning and scripture, there is no obstruction.
Let it be granted that there is self-cognition; however, let it be understood that the object itself is false.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the two means of valid cognition, just as in the case of perceiving a momentary blue object.

[478,17] There is no contradiction between the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even when there is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of that which is qualified by another exclusion established through inference, [478,18] because, just as in the case of momentariness, no certain cognition (*niścayapratyaya*) arises regarding its falsity; moreover, the difference in their objects is evident. That too is trivial. [478,19] For since the proof of momentary destruction is merely a proof of a particularity of existence for the perception that grasps the existence of blue, there is no contradiction. [The proof of] the sublation of existence...

However, to claim that knowability (*prameyatva*) is like a tortoise’s hair is indeed contradictory; furthermore, it is sublated by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), and likewise by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). For instance, what object could possibly cognize itself as being false?
The meaning is that it is the existent intrinsic nature (or the non-existent intrinsic nature) that manifests. Since its very existence has been stated to be nothing other than this manifestation,
how can there be both a negation and an affirmation of it?

By this, the claim that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpannatva*)— like a reflection— is intended as a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*) for the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is also refuted. Furthermore,
what is called "dependently originated" refers merely to the state of being an effect (*kāryatāmātra*).
And since that [impermanence] is eternally opposed [to permanence], let it subvert permanence itself.
