[479,6] "For intrinsic nature is non-artificial and independent of anything else"—
[479,7] according to this intended meaning, it is precisely such an intrinsic nature that is being negated.
Therefore, when such a form is superimposed upon a real entity,
the sublation of that very [superimposition] is unimpeded, as it is established through momentary destruction.
In this way, it follows that a Sautrāntika is indeed a Mādhyamika; this is a great feat!

Furthermore, where an unconditioned nature (akṛtrimarūpa) is accepted, as in the case of space and so forth, there is no arising through dependence (pratītyodaya) established by valid cognition (pramāṇa) in any way whatsoever.
Pots and other such things are perceived as being capable of performing their desired functions;
however, there is no cognition whatsoever that "the self and so forth do not exist" or that they "exist in the opposite manner."
If you argue that they do not exist precisely because they are not perceived, then perception must be the proof of existence;

how then could mountains and the like be non-existent? If you claim that neither perception nor non-perception is a proof of existence, this is merely a counter-argument against others. In response to what, then, is it produced? If you say that by this [non-perception] non-existence is proven, then existence would never be established in any way at any time.

Non-existence is indeed established. This non-apprehension of mine is not the reason for non-existence; rather, it is presented because it has been accepted as such by the opponent himself. If it is argued that existence is not established through non-apprehension, we reply: no, for the proponent of the Self (Ātmavādin) does not accept non-existence based on mere non-apprehension. Even if another person accepts it, the fault is not stated by virtue of one's own admission; therefore, this [reason] remains independent.
Non-apprehension is to be established as the logical reason.
Existence is established by cognition; non-cognition, however, is sublated.
And since that [non-cognition] does not depend on qualifiers, this is a succession of logical impossibilities.

Furthermore, there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) that establishes a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the state of being an effect and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) through their contrapositives;

nor is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) established merely by observing both [the reason and the probandum] in some single instance. Moreover, the absence of intrinsic nature as conceived by [the opponent] is not possible in the case of a reflection, because its appearance cannot be denied. This is because, once the probandum has been established, there is no other means of proof to avoid the charge of the probandum being empty.

[480,2] There would be an infinite regress; furthermore, since the pervasion of appearing things is established by that very [negation] when demonstrating the negation of what has been determined, it is a case of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*). Moreover, since the causal relationship is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) anywhere, the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanaśūnyatā*). If it is argued that the reason, as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), is established by relying on the world, then [the establishment of the reason] must rely on the world.

One must offer a final farewell to emptiness. For one cannot adopt the "half-old-woman" approach, whereby the world is relied upon as the basis for the means of proof (*sādhana*) but not for the object to be proven (*sādhya*).
If it is argued that emptiness is perceived even in a reflection by relying on the world, then it is not so in the case of the original object (*bimba*), because of the perception of its opposite.

[480,8] This is the proof. And it is a logical principle that one cannot take as a thesis (pakṣa) what has been refuted by valid cognition (pramāṇa). If you argue that this is merely a conceit of seeing when there is no perception of the opposite, then even in the case of a reflection, you have a conceit of seeing despite not perceiving its lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva).

It is only the world that relies on valid cognition; regarding the opposite case of the original object (bimba), the world itself is the authority, whereas regarding the reflection, it is not an authority.

[480,11] How could there be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) even with respect to a reflection (*pratibimba*)? If it is argued that the very absence of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) is the means of valid cognition regarding a reflection, then in cases where correspondence does exist—such as with trees and the like—the absence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) would be unavoidable. If it is argued that this is merely a conceit of correspondence, then one must state what the object of correspondence is, since in the case of a reflection, it is different from what is commonly established.
Its absence is cognized.

If it is argued that [the absence of the object] consists in the mountain and so forth being incapable of withstanding the scrutiny of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and being non-concordant [with experience], then at the outset of this inquiry, by which valid cognition do you follow such scrutiny? You must state whether it is perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), or something other than those.

However, since not even a single thing is established without self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), one would fall into a great delusion. Therefore, even when other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are set aside, mountains, oceans, and so forth are established through self-awareness alone. Furthermore, if there were an apprehension of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) through the investigation of some means of valid cognition, then [the object] might be negated by its absence; but that does not exist. Again:

[480,20] What logic is there in the claim that "service to another's feet alone is the refuge," given that the requirement for accepting that [refuge] is satisfied by the mere possibility [of such service]? Furthermore, it is not the case that there is always only a possibility. For the application of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is intended precisely for the sake of the opposite [conclusion], and it is never permissible to present these [reasons] independently as a formal probans (*hetu*). Or, if they were permissible, would it be a conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) or an ultimate (*tāttvika*) means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

The phrase "to be relied upon" does not establish a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with things such as mountains; however, for anything else, there is merely the conventional usage of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), but no establishment of a necessary connection with the appearance of a form. Furthermore, if the inability to withstand analysis in the case of mountains and so forth constitutes their lack of correspondence (*asaṃvāda*), then that itself is their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); what, then, is the use of dependent origination (*pratītyotpāda*)?

Furthermore, dependent origination is inseparable from causal capacity (*śakti*), and causal capacity itself is existence; thus, in the proof of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there is the fault of contradiction. If it is argued that there is no fault because empty phenomena arise precisely from empty phenomena, then is the avoidance of this fault now achieved merely by reciting the established tenet (*siddhānta*)? For if so, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It might be so;
for that very thing which is capable of producing a result is indeed that [result] itself.
What use is there in imagining a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) even in that which is capable?
But for another, the very absence of a prior and subsequent state is the cause for obstructing that conceptual construction; thus, this is faultless. Furthermore:
Because it is the foundation of all cognition, the law of the stability of cause and effect is the basis;
yet for those who long for emptiness, this method is, through effort, the opposite.
Therefore, this so-called dependent origination is in fact no cause at all for the absence of intrinsic nature.

[481,9] Now, if dependent origination itself were the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), and if it were merely established as a conventional designation (*vyavahāra-mātra*), then even so, emptiness would be stated as being merely the state of being an effect; thus, it would result in falling back into the lower position. Or, for one who establishes it as a mere convention, there is no obstacle whatsoever—so what is the use of this? Or else, having oneself imagined that there is intrinsic nature in what is artificial, [one would then negate it] by means of its non-existence.

For one who asserts the loss of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even by means of a horn, one might conceive of the state of being a horse; yet, due to the absence of that [horn], one would also have to conclude that it is not a horse. How then [is it so]?
That which is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), that very thing is considered by you to be emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

this abbreviation is not explained in JNA) [481,16] Such passages as these are connected [to the context]. With reference to the entry into emptiness by means of those very limbs in relation to a lower state of existence, such proofs as these may, in some cases, not possess utility for the proponent of the subject at hand, just like the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

It is established that self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), being devoid of the capacity for objective apprehension, does not serve to define a factor (*aṅga*). Therefore, the claim that self-cognition is established in any way whatsoever by virtue of its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is refuted; for there is no scope for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove it, and because there is an absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and so forth with respect to perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, if establishment were possible without a means of proof, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, in the case of that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśin*):
The state of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not simply the establishment of something as such without depending on anything else.

As for what is also said—that the nature of being "without a net" (*ajaṭasvabhāvatā*) is not established for anyone against the proponent of the Madhyamaka, such that self-awareness would be "without a net" by virtue of being excluded from that—it is merely a slip of the tongue and does not provide protection. For it is thus:
For the practitioner of yoga, there is neither ignorance nor is the middle way non-empty for one who possesses knowledge;
nevertheless, the conventional usage of terms such as "knowledge" and "emptiness" is not contradicted.

If there is a negation of the word that serves as the basis for the exclusion [of something] on the grounds that it does not exist in any way whatsoever, then alas! from the very beginning, by uprooting words such as "momentary," "selfless," "not created by God," "not consisting of primordial matter" (*aprakṛtimaya*), and so forth, one arrives at a state of total non-communication.
One who asserts that there is no employment of a negative particle (*nañ*) without an object [to negate],...
How could one who is himself disregarded by his own words awaken another?
An intermediate verse:
Let this, which is so utterly loathsome, be set aside for now. Therefore, not even a grain of a fault is possible regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Consequently, by removing the qualification "conventional," the establishment that self-awareness indeed exists is consistent with reason; provided, however, that the mind is not possessed by the obsession of dogmatic attachment.
If there is the operation of a sublater even with respect to cognition itself,
then what kind of satisfaction do you have regarding the specific [cognition] presented by that [sublater]?
Or, if somehow it does not apply there, why is it not [perceived] directly?
In experience, there is no sublation of that; self-awareness is the foundation of awakening.
But as for the cognition of another, although it does not exist in reality, even if it is sublated by another inference while established merely through conceit, let it be sublated;
however, since perception—which terminates in its own nature—is incapable of protecting itself, it is simply not capable at all.
Therefore, every investigation here is appropriate only within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
In some cases, sublation by experience is not permissible even within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*).
Nor is there anything experienced that could be sublated by a cognition of that [ultimate reality].
Let this [conflict] be destroyed like Kali by Kāli; let there be peace.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Self-Cognition, in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.
[Chapter Six] Now, one might ask:

"Having begun with the Madhyamaka, which is the locus of such praise, why is this correct Yogācāra view presented as being fully established? This is not a fault, for even this [Yogācāra] was taught by the Blessed One himself, and it is presented here for the purpose of distinguishing between the definitive (*nītārtha*) and the provisional (*neyārtha*).

Because it has been accepted by the Noble Ones who have received its prediction—beginning with the Bodhisattvas and ending with the Crown Prince—and because it has been established by the Teachers as being sound and praiseworthy, this *Sākārasiddhi* (Proof of the Manifestation of Forms) has been undertaken. [Objection: Even so, would not both of these mutually contradictory positions be unreal? In that case, even though the Blessed One, the Teacher himself, was of one heart [with them], he might have taught this [position] out of consideration for those to be trained (*vineya*). But how could those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) and seen the truth [accept such a view]?
Is it because they each fall into one side, teaching only their own respective views? For if this were taught as something distinct and superior, it might be considered so out of deference to others.

Moreover, since the commitment (*samaya*) of the Mantra system is supremely profound, how can there be peace of mind—even for one who is *Samantabhadra*—given that such a great contradiction exists between those two positions? It is said in reply:
In this case, there is a contradiction regarding a single entity existing in two ways;
for the teaching of the Sage has stated that it is the extreme of superimposition and denial.
For here, within this mass of variegated luminosity, neither the superimposition of even a particle of non-luminosity is tolerable, nor is the denial of even a trace of luminosity;
just as when a thorn has entered the body or when a limb is being cut off.
[483,15] Likewise, in this case, with respect to the manifest form, there is suffering due to superimposition and denial.
If negation does not exist conventionally and superimposition does not exist ultimately,
and if neither of those two exists in reality, then what contradiction is there?
Likewise, in the *Sadasallakṣaṇanirdeśa*, the noble master [Maitreya] says:
“Unreal imagination exists; duality is not found there.
But emptiness is found here, and within that, it [unreal imagination] is also found. (Madhyāntavibhāga I.2)

"But the unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms" (MV I.9). By stating this, he expresses the negation of denial regarding that which appears, while simultaneously establishing the negation of the superimposition of the grasped and the grasper. In this context, "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*) refers to that by means of which, or in which, the duality of the grasped and the grasper is imagined, through the gateway of the subsequent conceptualization. That very thing—
Demonstrating it in detail along with its commentary, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* states:
"Just as an illusion is described, so is unreal imagination;
just as that which is produced by illusion is described, so is the delusion of duality."
Just as the cause of delusion— such as wood, clods of earth, and so forth— is encompassed by the mantras of illusion,

so should the construction of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*) be understood within the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*). Just as the forms of elephants, horses, gold, and so forth produced by that illusion appear within the illusion itself despite their non-existence, so too within that construction of the unreal, the delusion of duality appears as the grasped and the grasper.

The nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) should be understood as follows. In this commentary, the phrase "wood, clods of earth, and so forth" refers to forms such as elephants fashioned by skilled artisans, as well as painted images; these are correctly cited as examples. A "clod of earth" (loṣṭa), through the influence of mantras and the like, is surrounded by the appearance of phenomena such as distorted sensory cognitions or yellow colors. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), earthenware, stones, and other such things are included. This is just like that which is produced by illusion (māyā).

This is an explanatory restatement (*vyākhyeyānuvāda*). "In that illusion" refers to the magically created elephant and so forth. This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication), including the clod of earth mentioned previously. The "form" (*ākṛti*) of the elephant and so forth is their color and configuration. By way of that—that is, by way of being an elephant and so forth—it is manifested and determined (*adhyavasita*), because there is no experience of what is non-existent. It is merely a determination (*adhyavasāna-mātra*), like the determination of water in a mirage.
The meaning is that what was stated there regarding elephants and so forth is that they are merely produced by illusion (*māyāmātra*). Thus, it is connected with the phrase "the error of duality.

Its explanation is as follows: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is precisely the grasped and the grasper; its very form (*ākāra*) or delineation (*ullekha*) belongs to this unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), because of the appearance of two parts. Its existence (*bhāva*) or suchness (*tattā*) is the conceptual determination (*adhyavasita*) based on the appearance as the grasped and the grasper.

Just as there is the determination of an elephant and so forth in relation to illusions and the like, so too is there the determination of duality in relation to the imagination of the unreal; such is the meaning.
And thus: "Just as that thing does not exist in it, so is the ultimate reality intended."
Just as there is the perception of that [object], so too is there conventional truth.

Just as there is no reality of that [elephant] in what is produced by magic—namely, the absence of elephant-ness and so forth—in that same way, the ultimate truth is held to exist in that dependent nature (*paratantra*): it is the absence of the imagined characteristic of duality. Just as that magical creation is perceived in the form of an elephant and so forth, in the same way, that unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is perceived through the knowledge of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). In this context, "magical creation" refers to...

It should be understood as something fashioned by illusion (*māyā*). The meaning is that cognition (*jñāna*) is the apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) of things such as elephants and so forth. Conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) consists of the grasped and the grasper; apprehension and determination occur in the form of those two. By this root object, the indication of the subject is shown.
Just as the manifestation of its cause is perceived when that [cause] is absent,
so too is the manifestation of the unreal imagination perceived upon the revolution of the basis.
Just as when a magical creation has ceased to exist, the real object consisting of wood or other materials that served as its cause is perceived,

so too, upon the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because of the absence of the delusion of duality, the real object of the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is perceived. In the root text, "unreal imagination" refers to the *abhūtaparikalpa*, while the "real object" is the separation from duality.
Just as one who is undeluded might act at will in the world with respect to its signs,
so too the ascetic, having undergone transformation and being free from inversion, acts according to his will.

Just as the world, being unerring regarding its cause—such as wood and so forth—acts according to its desire and independently, so too, upon the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), the noble one (*ārya*), free from error, acts according to his desire and becomes independent. And in this regard, it should be understood that this is merely a mechanical device made of wood and so forth, or simply the form of a deluded cognition;
for there is the certainty that "this is not an elephant, nor is it gold."
Its form exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of illusions and the like.
This verse has its meaning already explained:
"In that [state], there is neither existence nor non-existence, and neither non-existence nor indeed existence;
and the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in relation to illusions and the like."
Therein, existence is not non-existence; that which is the existence of its form is not a non-existence. And non-existence is indeed existence;
that which is the non-existence of the elephant and so forth is not a non-existence. Furthermore, no distinction is established between existence and non-existence in illusions and the like:
that very existence of its form therein is itself the non-existence of the elephant and so forth; and that very non-existence of the elephant and so forth is itself [the existence of its form].
There is the existence of its appearance;
likewise, there is the manifestation of non-duality, yet its substantial reality is not found.
Therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other aggregates.

Likewise, here in this unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), there is the appearance of non-duality and the absence of duality. Therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other [objects], which have the nature of unreal imagination. And in this context, "appearance as duality" means that it appears as if it were dual;
its "state" (*bhāva*) is the nature that manifests as internal and external forms.
Therein, existence is not non-existence, and non-existence is indeed not existence;
yet a distinction between existence and non-existence is predicated of form and the other aggregates.

Therein, existence is not non-existence, which is the appearance of duality; nor is non-existence existence, which is the non-existence of the cultivation of duality (*dvayabhāvanāstitā*). Furthermore, the distinction between existence and non-existence is established with respect to form and the other aggregates. For that very thing which exists as the appearance of duality is itself the non-existence of duality.
It is intended for the purpose of negating the extremes of superimposition and denial,
and likewise for the purpose of negating the vehicle of the Hīnayāna.

But for what purpose, then, is the absolute nature and the lack of distinction between existence and non-existence asserted here, respectively? It is asserted for the sake of refuting the extremes of superimposition and denial, and for the sake of preventing one’s departure via the Lesser Vehicle. For, having understood the non-existence of non-existence, one does not engage in superimposition; having understood the existence of existence, one does not engage in denial; and having understood the lack of distinction between the two, [one avoids both extremes].
One does not tremble at existence; therefore, one does not depart by means of the Hīnayāna—such is the detailed explanation. Likewise, the intended meaning in the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* is as follows:
"The existence of phenomena and the exhaustion of obscurations regarding the objects of knowledge."
"I am amazed at what others say regarding the Teacher in this matter"—

having thus spoken with the intention of negating imagined phenomena (*parikalpita-dharma*), as in other contexts, he says the following in order to restrict the doubt that the negation of illumination might apply to the general statement:
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added.
Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated.
Thus, in this context, "from this" (*ataḥ*) refers to that which appears as manifold, which—considering the time of affliction—is designated by the term "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Because it is self-cognized, nothing can be removed from it.
If you ask, "What has been removed by us here, since it was non-existent even previously?"—
what kind of denial could there be other than the establishment of its non-existence?

Nothing whatsoever—whether the non-manifest, the grasped or the grasper, the formless, or the self and so forth—is to be added; rather, that which is real must be apprehended as real alone, and not as unreal: this is the negation of denial (*apavāda*). Furthermore, that which is real must be resolved upon as being real, and not as unreal: this is the negation of superimposition (*samāropa*). However, in order to lead toward a definitive conclusion regarding the specific nature of whether that is real or unreal, [it is explained] in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.

Following the characteristics of existence and non-existence, one understands that duality is unreal, while the substratum (*dharmin*) which is the emptiness of duality is real, because they share a single agent. Furthermore, in this context, the term "from this" (*ataḥ*) refers to the consideration of direct perception; since the collection of modes is not subject to rejection, it possesses reality. However, the other [duality] is unreal because it is merely imagined (*kalpita-mātra*). Consequently, the reality of its emptiness is also clearly indicated. Therefore—

One who has direct realization of reality (bhūta-sākṣātkārī) is liberated, as is one who grasps reality (bhūta-grāhī). The meaning is that one is liberated through the sequence of practice consisting of hearing and reflection.

Furthermore, the middle way (madhyamā sthiti) is free from both superimposition (samāropa) and denial (apavāda); this very thing is the Yogācāra view, so there is no difference in substance (vastu-bheda). For it has been stated that appearance itself is not superimposition, nor is it the case that one denies the object of experience. As for those who [claim] that even here, although it appears...

Those who superimpose the person (*pudgala*), formlessness, sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth, as well as the state of being an object (*grāhyatā*) and so on, and those who deny everything—even that which does not appear—whether in its entirety or in part: the contradiction based on these two types of persons, which consists in their mutual refutation, leads to ruin. Therefore, this alone is the method of emptiness (*śūnyatānaya*), as stated in the *Uttaratantra* (UT 75):

In this regard, those whose thoughts are distracted by emptiness are described as follows: they are not the bodhisattvas who have set out upon the vehicle, but rather those who are deluded regarding the principle of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*. These are those who, for the sake of destroying existing entities, desire the bliss of the liberation of emptiness, thinking that the subsequent annihilation and destruction of an existing state of well-being is *parinirvāṇa*; or again, those who, through the apprehension of emptiness, resort to emptiness, thinking: "There exists some dharma called emptiness, distinct from form and so forth, which we shall realize and cultivate."
Thus it is said. In that regard, what is this method of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha* called?
Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything to be added. Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated. (UT 1.154; AA 499)

[487,19] Such is the detailed exposition. In this regard, because one maintains that the very aspect which exists is unreal, and because one does not subsequently admit annihilation, there is no first deception concerning the meaning of emptiness. Nor is there a second, because—unlike formless sensation and so forth—it is perceived as distinct [from the substrate].
[487,21] Indeed, in this case, nothing whatsoever is to be removed from the *tathāgatadhātu* as a cause of affliction, nor is anything whatsoever to be added to it as a cause of purification.

Thus it has been explained. True; however, because a phenomenon is indicated by means of another phenomenon, by the term "tathāgata-element" (*tathāgatadhātu*), only those phenomena of emptiness that are graspable as the transformation of the mind are to be grasped. This is because there is no room for the suspicion of adding anything else to the mere emptiness established by conceptual construction. Consequently, through the negation of the cessation of the non-existent and the arising of the existent—namely, the signs of affliction and purification—[the meaning is established].

It is precisely the negation of the aforementioned denial (apavāda) and superimposition (samāropa) that is intended; for immediately thereafter it says: "Thus, one sees that whatever is not present in a certain place, that [place] is empty of that. Furthermore, whatever remains there, one understands as it truly is that it exists here as a reality.
By this, the characteristic of non-erroneous emptiness is elucidated through the complete avoidance of both superimposition and denial.
Therefore, there is no negation of the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*). This indeed is the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamārtha*).
Alternatively: "Empty, yet not non-empty; therefore everything is established.
Because of existence, because of non-existence, and because of existence again—this is the Middle Way. (Madhyāntavibhāga I.3)
By this, he stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*: "And that very same thing is called the Middle Way."
[488,9] Directly non-conceptual is the crown of the crown prince; [488,10] what is the use here of the exertion of scholarship?
[488,11] Therefore, this very state is the Middle Way, and it is the Yogācāra system in reality.
And with reference to this very point, the venerable Ārya-Nāgārjuna also said:

"The teaching of the aggregates, elements, and so forth, was given for the purpose of ceasing the grasping at a self; that too has been demolished by the Greatly Fortunate Ones through the establishment of mere representation. (*Madhyamakakārikā* 18.6)

Thus is the praise. However, because of the rejection of other directions, that teaching of the Sage which states, "All this is a mere illusion," is for the purpose of removing the fear of fools; it is not [the truth] in reality. (*** )

Thus it has been said: "For the most part, people have come to regard even the mind as having existence through the power of external objects themselves; and thus, until this very day, despite the efforts of the authors of the *Vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya*, they do not attain awakening, but rather proceed by attacking the intentions of others.
The general statement "mere representation" (*citramātra*) is for the most part intended to indicate that [external objects] are not established, but it is not an absolute negation in every respect.

Because it would follow that praise would have no scope; nor is the possibility of praise found in these things apart from their being mere appearances that are unarisen and unceasing, like a dream. No phenomenon whatsoever arises, nor does any whatsoever cease.
"Only conditions arise and cease.

Because of this statement, their system is indeed one that maintains the existence of mental aspects (*sākāra*), as evidenced by the description of the *saṃbhogakāya* and because others do not describe [the Buddha] through such means as conventional designations (*upacāra*).
How, then, is it so?

Was it not stated that "He is neither red, nor green, nor madder-colored" (*rakto harinmāñjiṣṭaḥ*) and so forth? This was said with reference to the *dharmakāya*. And likewise, immediately thereafter:
"Homage be to You, the non-dual. (*advayāya namo 'stu te*)

Thus it has been stated by relying on the *prasajya* mode of negation. Furthermore, even when paying respect to self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) by saying, "I bow to the *dharmakāya*, which is to be personally realized," there is a misconception; shame on such independence! For self-cognition comes to rest in nothing other than the manifestation of variegated forms. And since that has been firmly established, there is no point in the lamentations of those who deny the *dharmakāya* and so forth. Therefore, the view favored by the Crown Prince alone is the one accepted by the Noble Ones.
It is established as the Middle Way.
By this, those who also maintain that, based upon the form-body (*rūpakāya*), because of the state of natural delusion,
the cessation of mind and mental factors is asserted as the attainment of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); (***).
[489,16] It has been demonstrated that their systematic establishment is also difficult to maintain. For instance:
[489,17] Where could there be a basis consisting of mere form, since it is established everywhere as being of the nature of self-cognition, which is incompatible with the existence of error? [489,18]

Therefore, even knowledge is not able to withstand analysis from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). However, since conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) all five aggregates (*skandha*) exist, one should not say: "Why is there the negation of one and the establishment of another? Furthermore, what is this so-called "convention" (*saṃvṛti*)? If it is a cognition that is pleasing only when not analyzed, alas, since conventions are infinite, why is there a restriction to only five aggregates? [The same would apply to] cognitions of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśvara*), the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), and so forth.

Furthermore, various [cognitions] involving innate or produced delusions—even in a child—would, at their limit, apprehend objects such as the lunar disc through the reach of the hand, being inferable from gestures like stretching out a hand; these would thus cause one to grasp them as conventional truths of those respective entities.
If you say, "Let it be so," then what is the use of now seeking the path for the sake of cessation, since even the Vedas, Īśvara, and so forth would have to be sought?
[489,25] (114a) Now, if even within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), one does not rely on [the existence of] entities because satisfaction is found in some specific [limited] cases, then in that case,

the conventional must be relied upon precisely in the form of perception and inference as defined by their respective characteristics. And this being so, the designation "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) is merely a provisional internal classification.

Neither through direct perception nor through inference is there any proof for the existence of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); rather, by those very same means, it is sublated. Therefore, all cognition is indeed nothing but consciousness.

[490,5] It is said that even in that case, inference alone is the subverter; thus, indeed, there is no stability even there. That being so, [490,6] consciousness alone is conventionally real, not form. Therefore, it is logical that consciousness alone persists throughout the cycle of existence by way of convention, [490,7] because it continues to manifest even when subverted, whereas the other does not. Or, let all five aggregates exist by way of convention.

Would it be through the cessation of cognition itself, or by means of an effort toward its cessation? It cannot be the first position, because the continuity of the mind has been established as having a stable nature. If you argue that it ceases when it is without an object, [we reply: surely "peace" (*śānti*) is said to mean being free from affliction;
so what fault is there in this? If you intend [by "cessation"] destruction, even then, if the object is the sense-field (*viṣaya*), it exists even now.

[490,11] How can that which is truly without an object proceed as a continuous stream? Conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), however, there is never an exclusion of an object. [490,12] Now, what about its support (*ādhāra*)? It has no support whatsoever, because it lacks weight (*gaurava*). Now, what about its cause (*kāraṇa*)? Even now, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the cause; even then, it is not interrupted, especially when accompanied by compassion for the entire world. Because of the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*), it does not [cease].
If it is argued that there is an attachment to rebirth, then let there simply be no cyclic existence characterized by the desire for welfare and happiness and the falling into impure states;

however, who can prevent its occurrence as a mere continuity, especially for one who is compassionate? Therefore, cessation does not occur spontaneously; rather, effort toward the prevention of one or the establishment of the other would belong to one who perceives their respective virtues and faults.

In that regard, what kind of quality belongs to the aggregate of the stomach that does not belong to consciousness? Or what kind of defect belongs to this [consciousness] that does not belong to the aggregate of the stomach?

If you argue that it is because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are inherently deluded, then why is it not said that it is because matter (*rūpa*) is the nature of the aggregate of the stomach? And if you have such great respect for that [inherent delusion], then clods of earth, bricks, and the like would be better for you than these.

What further must be done beyond this? And what indeed is this so-called "error"? It cannot be that unreality belongs only to you, for it would follow by implication that it applies to form (*rūpa*) as well. If you argue that even though it is unreal, the designation of error does not apply to form but only to consciousness (*vijñāna*), then in that case, this is merely a technical convention. Furthermore, the distinction between rejection and acceptance is made solely in accordance with one's own linguistic conventions. This being the case:

Having likewise refuted form, its abandonment would follow. However, if—contrary to the Blessed One’s doctrine of consciousness-only—the cessation of that very [consciousness] is intended and not that of form, even so, what is the point of fostering delusion? Let there be no possibility of error due to the proximity of the form of the matted hair.

If it is argued that error (*viparyāsa*) is perceived in consciousness, but not in a single form such as matted hair, [we reply]: Is it not the case that "error" and "delusion" (*bhrama*) have one and the same meaning? Since this [definition] is merely a determination of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), how does this answer apply here? Alternatively, if the meaning of "delusion" is established according to convention as the apprehension of something as what it is not (*atasmims tadgraha*), then by its opposite, non-delusion (*abhrānti*) is likewise indeed perceived in consciousness.
It might be argued: "The error is indeed an error, as it is established for both parties; yet, in my analysis, even this [error] is merely an error.

If that is the case, then everything is an error, and thus even the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) is an error. If you say, "But surely there is no such thing as the knowledge of emptiness in reality," then let it be that it does not exist in reality; however, the claim that the knowledge of emptiness is an error is some kind of arbitrary convention. Furthermore, [491,2] It might be argued: "The error is indeed an error, as it is established for both parties; yet, in my analysis, even this [error] is merely an error. If that is the case, then everything is an error, and thus even the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) is an error. If you say, "But surely there is no such thing as the knowledge of emptiness in reality," then let it be that it does not exist in reality; however, the claim that the knowledge of emptiness is an error is some kind of arbitrary convention. Furthermore,
In reality, nothing exists; this is what is called emptiness.
In reality alone, there is only delusion here—there is no non-delusion; such is the direction of the teaching.
Since the state of all delusion arises from conceptual investigation,
is that very investigation itself a delusion or is it non-delusory? If it were a delusion, how could all this be a delusion?
If not, then that very thing is devoid of the nature of error.

If it is argued that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is neither delusion nor non-delusion, this is indeed logical. However, within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), just as there are the five aggregates (*skandha*), one must necessarily admit that some things are delusions and others are not. For even then, the cognition of blue in what is blue is not a delusion, whereas it would be a delusion in the case of what is white. Likewise, cognitions such as that of silver must be described in these two ways; otherwise, [the distinction between delusion and non-delusion would collapse].

There is no such thing as a "form aggregate" (rūpaskandha) in reality; it is intended [only] that, conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) constitutes the persistence of the form aggregate.
Yet, regarding this, there is only delusion. There is no correct awakening (*samyagbodha*) to that [delusion], for all undertakings are precisely for the sake of that [awakening].
Conventionally both exist, but in reality (*tattvataḥ*) both are non-existent.
Since everything is nothing but an illusion, to what could this statement possibly refer?

[491,19] Now, if it is argued that error is sometimes observed in cognition alone and not in form, then one might as well say that it is observed in the aggregates (*skandha*) alone. Or, if one perceives faults even in those things accepted by the Teacher, it would lead to the abandonment of the Blessed One as well. However, internal distinctions are common to all. Furthermore, if by "error by nature" you intend to mean that it does not apply to every individual instance, then for that very reason—

This has already been answered. Now, if the meaning is that even when an error occurs somewhere, it is indeed a transformation (*vikṛti*), even so, how can this certainty be reached, given that both states are observed? Regarding this, scripture repeatedly declares that the mind is pure by nature (*prakṛtipariśuddha*) while defects are adventitious (*āgantuka*); furthermore, it is experienced that the mind is oppressed by the suspicion of error until there is correct thorough knowledge.
And that it is "obstructed" has been analyzed in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*.
Nor can this be stated with reference to either the conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or the non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) cognition, since both are observed in both cases.
Alternatively, if such a state exists in one case, let there be the abandonment of that very [distinction]; or, if no difference is perceived, another treatise must be sought for its comprehension.

Therefore, this is a groundless objection: that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are inherently deluded. Furthermore, it is contradictory to claim both the cessation of the mind and mental factors and the realization of the *dharmakāya*, because realization is a property of the mind. If you argue that this is a metaphorical usage of "realization," from what source does that derive? If you say it is because there is no other possible way, then in that case, there must be the abiding of a mind that realizes.

Let it be so; but what is the point of the effort to refute [this], since there is no other possible way [to go]? This attempt to amuse oneself with the curiosity of seeing while plucking out one's own eyes is not acceptable to the discerning.
Or, if you argue that clods of earth and the like are those who directly realize the *dharmakāya* because they lack any superior power (*prabhāvātiśaya*)?

Indeed, the direct realization of the *dharmakāya* does not occur merely by that much, but rather through a specific excellence of realization; otherwise, since mantras and the like would also be identical [to it], they too would possess Buddhahood. If this is so, what is to be accomplished by direct realization when an excellence of non-existence is possible, as in the case of a jewel and so forth? If this is so, what is to be accomplished even by the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*)? [It is for the sake of] a specific capacity.

Since it is possible otherwise—as in the case of jewels, mantras, and so forth—there is neither the *dharmakāya* nor the *sambhogakāya*; thus, the state of the Buddha is utterly pure. Alternatively, since even in the case of realization there is seen a superior radiance of the fruit, just as with form (*rūpa*), let form alone be that which is to be removed, or that which is to be established;
for both are established by someone through something for the sake of a particular purpose.

If it is argued that all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) can be attributed only to form (*rūpa*), then let the opposite be the case—that it can be attributed only to consciousness (*vijñāna*). "No" is not a valid proof; rather, it is like drinking from the sacred vessel (*kośapāna*). Even so, if one were to establish [causal capacity] in only one thing, it might belong only to the mental portion (*cittabhāga*); thus, there would be no restriction to form alone. Furthermore, because we observe that the power of knowledge (*jñānasāmarthya*) is greater than the power of form.

In that very context, the entrusting of the burden is appropriate. Otherwise, how could it be understood that the world is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)? Therefore, even from the perspective of the conventional truth of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhaka*), the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) is not tenable; nor is that same conventional truth [tenable] from the perspective of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*).
[492,19] It is not logical to speak of the final conventional reality as being conventional;
[492,20] for the final [reality] is of the very nature of gnosis, otherwise even substance, quality, and so forth would be [conventional].
Therefore, the abiding of the mind with its mental aspects is itself the Dharmakāya, established through self-reflexive awareness.

If this is so, since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) has real entities as its object, how can the designation "emptiness" be merely a conceptual construct (*prajñaptisat*), and how can it be the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Blessed One? Therefore,
the knowledge other than the enjoyment-body (*sambhogakāya*) is indeed formless.
Others, the wise, understand that the *dharmakāya* has emptiness as its objective support.
In this case as well, since it is distinct from what is designated as the "Buddha" in terms of the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhoga-kāya),
how could it possibly be suitable to be its intrinsic nature?
If that too were of the nature of a Buddha, there would be two Buddhas with distinct characteristics;
yet, if that very thing is of the nature of a Buddha, then the Dharmakāya is something else entirely.
If this very Buddha is the Dharma, then there is no possession (samanvaya) expressed by "his";
it does not exist through the relation of property and property-bearer (dharmidharmabhāva), nor by way of universal and particular (sāmānyaviśeṣataḥ).
If the Buddha were the dharma of enjoyment, the Buddha would be merely a conceptual construct.
Furthermore, if the self-nature of the dharma were something other than that, and if it were a substantial entity, then there would be an infinite regress.
If the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) were not consciousness, then, like blueness and so forth, it would exist within consciousness.
If it were formless, how could it be the true nature of that which lacks enjoyment (or the enjoyment of others)?

[493,11] But then, what is shown in the *Uttaratantra* (UT 40f) by the statement: "Due to the increase, decrease, and ultimate exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*), this very *dharmakāya* is called the *sattvadhātu*, the *bodhisattva*, and the *buddha*"? That which is stated in that very same work: [493,13] "The *dharmakāya* is to be known as twofold: the utterly stainless *dharmadhātu*..."
[493,14] "And its outflow is the teaching of the profound and manifold methods.
[493,16] Thus, by this [verse], the *dharmadhātu* is mentioned; however, that which is under discussion here is not the teaching of the profound and manifold methods known as its outflow.
[493,17] What, then, is the *dharmadhātu*? Study the *Madhyāntavibhāga* itself for this purpose. That which...

"Suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*animitta*), the ultimate truth (*paramārthatā*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—these, in brief, are synonyms of emptiness.

(Madhyāntavibhāga I.15) Thus it has been stated in order to dispel such delusion. Likewise, if there is a misconception even regarding this point—that emptiness is merely a phenomenon (*dharmamātra*)—then [it must be clarified].

"The non-existence of duality is indeed the existence of that non-existence; this is the characteristic of emptiness" (Madhyāntavibhāga I.14). Following such various formulations as these, one might claim that within that very [emptiness], by way of excluding those [dualities], there exists some formless entity denoted by the term *dharmakāya*; this is an arbitrary assertion. But surely, mere phenomena (*dharmamātra*) are conventionally real; how [can they be the *dharmakāya*]?
Is it the object of self-awareness?
Or how is its perpetual absence from the preceding moment established?
In such cases, is there not some positive conceptual determination (*vidhirūpa-parāmarśa*)? It is said in reply:

The existence of all things occurs in two ways, through negation (prasajya) and exclusion (paryudāsa). In every case, even when there is an absence [of a property], the cognition of the substratum (dharmin) is accepted as a means of valid cognition (māna).

First, when it is a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), as it has been said: "For that very existence which is the absence of duality is itself the absence of duality," then there is no suspicion of the absence of apprehension by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
"Duality does not exist therein" (Madhyāntavibhāga I.2).

And so forth; even in the case of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapakṣa*), there is no cognition of the absence of duality other than the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) itself that produces the conceptualization of the absence of duality.

Therefore, in the treatise, one must consider the discussion regarding the negation of identity and the negation of being the locus of a jar in a particular place. In either case—whether by way of non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) or exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—it is merely a matter of linguistic convention that this very same single form of the entity is established.

[494,15] This is the insistence. Or, just as the entry into the Digambara doctrine was refuted by the author of the *Ṭīkā* even when both absolute difference and non-difference were denied on the basis of mere existence (*bhāvamātra*), so too must it be denied in the case of that which has a positive form appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because even that—such as the form of "eternal" and so forth—is not a real entity (*avastu*). And this systematic arrangement is for the sake of that [denial], as was stated previously. Or, just as that very same [author]...
Regarding the term *dharmakāya*: otherwise, there would be no purpose for considering it as being with stains, without stains, all-pervading, and so forth.

Having introduced the commentary on the supreme meaning of the outflow (*niṣyanda*)—on the grounds that the word of the Buddha is characterized by the *dharmadhātu*—it states that this proceeds through the sovereignty of the *dharmadhātu*, which is called the *dharmakāya* and is pure in every aspect. Therefore, it exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*).

The *dharmakāya* is not an object of fear for those possessed of intelligence, because it is established in that very way through both reasoning and scripture. Alternatively, where there is the ultimate negation, that which is its finality in the form of a positive affirmation is indeed a real entity (*vastusan*) in relation to its substratum (*dharmin*).
Thus, "the Blessed One is the *dharmakāya*"—let fear be abandoned. For just as the absence of a jar in a certain location is true, so too is the solitary [negation].
"Region" (*pradeśa*) means the culmination of the object; likewise, "the absence of duality here" means that the nature of cognition is devoid of duality or the state of being dual.

It is with this very intention that the exclusion of duality (*dvidhāpoha*) is established, and its culmination lies in the form of the real entity (*vastu*). Furthermore, the treatise concludes: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is that which apprehends the property (*dharma*). Therefore, regarding the property and the property-bearer...
Relying upon the imagined distinction, both the Buddha and the Dharma are established;
the Saṃgha is the manifestation of the transformation body—such is the abiding of the Three Jewels.
In reality, however, there is indeed identity (*tādātmya*) between the Buddha and his qualities (*dharmas*). By this, that which is the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* with its commentary states:
"The essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) is considered equal, subtle, and connected.
The essential body of all Buddhas is equal because it is without distinction."

It is subtle because it is difficult to know; thus, it is connected with that body characterized by effortful application (*sābhogika*). In this context, one should understand that the actual relationship is one of identity (*tādātmya*). If it is argued: "In that case, since there is the statement that it is the cause of the *saṃbhoga*-buddhahood, let it be simply its production," [the answer is:

no, because in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (116a) it is said that the *dharmadhātu* is the cause of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*), since the noble qualities arise from having that as their objective support (*ālambana*).

By this statement, because the power to bring that [object] into manifestation exists therein, the meaning—that such conventional usage occurs—is made clear. Likewise, in the *Ṭīkā* on the occasion of the discussion regarding the intrinsic nature of emptiness, it is stated that the purpose of the cultivation of emptiness begins with the attainment of the two states and extends up to the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha; the excellence of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) for oneself and others results from the cultivation of emptiness.

Thus it is; the same applies to other cases as well. Alternatively, the establishment of the predominance (*adhipatya*) of that factor (*aṅga*) therein is with respect to its prior state, as in the cases:

"His valor accomplishes all aims," and "momentariness" [is the cause of destruction]. Furthermore, no purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is ever perceived apart from a form (*ākāra*), since its very capacity is observed in the production of all white and non-white dharmas, and in the manifestation of reality (*tattva*) during the arising of white dharmas.

[495,15] [The opponent claims: "There is a state of cooperation. Therefore, everything arises from that very formless [consciousness]. [Response: It has already been shown that there is no scriptural authority (*āgama*) for this, nor is there any logical reasoning (*yukti*).
Furthermore, even though this world arises through the power of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), [people still perceive objects].
One relies on an action performed by another that functions as if it were present before one's eyes.
What kind of darkness is this, such that, failing to see clearly, one perceives both the existent and the non-existent?

[495,21] From the root *kṛ*, when there is a desire to express the agent or the object, the suffix *ṇic* is applied; the meaning is "caused by another" or "the action performed by another. [495,22] It is better that one does not perceive the existing relationship between cause and fruit, which is merely a slight appearance (*ākāraleśa*), than that one perceives what is non-existent and belongs to another domain. [495,23] But is this not a verse from the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* concerning the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*)? Is there any doctrine of self other than this? [It concerns] permanence and omnipresence.
If it is argued that this is not so because [the self] is not admitted [by us], we say no, because the proponents of the self (ātmavādins) are diverse. For:
The agent and the enjoyer, distinct from the perceived objects, is the domain of the *ahaṃkāra*;
it is stainless, and liberation for yogins consists in its remaining as the sole residue.

Furthermore, since you do not experience any utility in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) when there is no manifestation of a distinct intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), you would certainly not accept its momentariness. Therefore, this [entity] is the object of such statements as: "It is incapable even of performing the function of mere cognition, like that which is non-conceptual by nature. However, when the *dharmakāya* is established in scripture as being both eternal and omnipresent, then—

What is the answer? It is not the permanence of a continuum (*pravāha-nityatā*), because it is precisely the permanence of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-nityatā*) that is being taught. And so it is said in that very same place: "Permanence exists both by way of the non-lapse of the fundamental nature and by way of continuity.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "The permanence of the fundamental nature belongs to the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), because it is permanent by its very nature."

The enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika*) is non-ceasing because the enjoyment of the Dharma is uninterrupted; the emanation body (*nairmāṇika*) is non-ceasing by way of continuity, because even after vanishing, it repeatedly manifests emanations. And its mastery has already been explained according to the *Uttaratantra*: "Just as space, being non-conceptual, pervades everywhere."
The element of the purity of the nature of mind is likewise all-pervasive.
(I.49) What does this demonstrate?
It is the universal characteristic that pervades its defects, its qualities, and its ultimate state.
“In the inferior, mediocre, and superior [objects], like space in those things that have taken form” (UT I.50).

Regarding the phrase “in those things that have taken form,” the commentary states: “in vessels made of clay, silver, and gold. Furthermore, the word *gata* should be understood as having the sense of *prakāra* (type or variety). Patañjali [states in the Mahābhāṣya regarding the rule *harateḥ gatatācchīlye*]: “[The suffix *kta* is used after the root *hṛ* when it denotes a habitual state of having gone (*gatatācchīlya*). This is the intention of Patañjali as explained by Kaiyaṭa and others (see *Pradīpa* on *Pāṇini* 1.3.21). Thus, *gata*, *vidha*, and *prakāra* are synonymous.
Thus, there is a conventional usage for the suffix *-tā* in the sense of habitual action (*tacchīlya*). The instrumental case in *nirvikalpatayā* is used in the sense of "being in such a state.

The element (*dhātu*) of the mind’s natural state of non-depression is suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, its eternal pervasiveness is stated in its primary sense. Consequently, if the *dharmakāya* were a substantial entity (*dravya*) itself, how could the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*) be avoided?
[496,21] However, the permanence, omnipresence, and so forth of the *dharmatā* are conventional;
even though it possesses intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*), they are established according to conceptual construction, just like momentariness and the like.

Here too, the specification of the subject (*dharmin*) is "among those that are inferior, middling, and superior. Nor is it a doctrine of no-self (*anātmavāda*) due to a lack of pervasiveness, like the Digambaras; nor is there any insistence on a doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*), for one who does not see clearly perceives both the existent and the non-existent.

Thus, because the fault remains unrefuted in that very same way; even if there were such a thing, the portion consisting of the aspect (*ākārabhāga*) of that which is to be trusted would still be true, and this is difficult to avoid. This is merely a designation of existence (*sattāprajñaptimātra*); however, that which is to be trusted is indeed substantially real (*vastusat*). For this very reason, the nature of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogātmā*) is not false, nor is it distinct [from the Reality Body], because it is the manifestation of its basis; and because it is not unrelated [to it], this is mere poetry devoid of scripture and reasoning. And that—

The meaning of the name "Buddha" is unreal, while that which is its *dharmakāya* is real; such is the correct position. Furthermore, if the Buddha were merely subordinate by virtue of being simply dependent [upon the *dharma*], then the direct designation "the Buddha is the *dharma*" would imply that the Buddha is the master (*prabhu*) of the *dharma*. Alternatively, if both [the *dharma* and the *dharmakāya*] together constitute the Buddha, then in the alternative analysis of whether this refers to each individually or to their aggregate, there is only one [consistent conclusion].

It is also well said that the Buddhas are unreal, false, and delusive, because of the contradiction between delusion and awakening. And how can that which is unreal be accepted as the cause of the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) within the nature of the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? As the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* states:
"The fulfillment of the two purposes for the two [bodies] is established in all its aspects."

Thus [it is said]. Regarding this, the commentary states: "The enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) is characterized by the fulfillment of one's own welfare; the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*) is characterized by the fulfillment of the welfare of others. This fulfillment of the welfare of others is established, respectively, in the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and the enjoyment body. And this being so, it is the fruit of the *dharmakāya* and the cause of the emanation body for the fulfillment of the welfare of others. Furthermore, this fulfillment of one's own welfare appears even while being non-existent."

All of this is a delusion. Therefore, this claim that the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is the perfection of one's own welfare subverts the thesis of its unreality regarding the mental aspects (*ākāra*).
By this, the conceptualization that the enjoyment body is respected for the sake of a purpose—even though the Buddha is trustworthy or even real—is also refuted.
Because, by that [delusion], there is not even an atom of a fruit, and because it is of the nature of a blemish.
Someone, disregarding a minor fault, persists in an action out of regard for a greater purpose; yet that [action],
being devoid of its intended object, becomes a swarm of bees of primary faults.
How could one who is more senior pay heed?

It is not tenable to say that its arising occurs through the power of karma; for karma alone is the cause of that which must be abandoned absolutely, and it does not merit being undertaken, just like other transgressions. It has also been well said that the Tathāgata’s error arises from a lapse in karma; thus, it follows that his [error] must have ceased in every respect. Furthermore, what need is there for those designated as Bodhisattvas?

If [the cognition] were entirely devoid of form, it would be unfit for human beings to cultivate in any way whatsoever; if one admits that it possesses a form, this would be like a "bathing of an elephant" (a futile effort).
The assertion of formlessness is for the sake of establishing formlessness;
yet to accept a form is its own refutation—what else could there be beyond that?
These are the intermediate verses.
Regarding that which is to be prevented through a longing for an object, what obstruction to its power can there be for one who is worthy of trust?
If it possesses power in any one instance, let it be proclaimed as possessing power everywhere.
For positive and negative concomitance are not the refuge for establishing the existence of a cause.
Therefore, for those who maintain that there are no mental aspects (*nirākāravādin*), the form [of reality] must be established as possessing all powers, resembling a pure, infinite, and empty sky;

let this be another system—what is the use of further attachment to other views? For if one departs from the method of the leader, the noble Maitreya, what kind of establishment of Buddhist reality could there be?
In brief, he indeed [says]:
Regarding the mind within the three realms, he declared it to be manifold; here, the duality of the perceived and the perceiver is indeed false.
Thus, dispelling [that duality], he drove away [the view] that is fixed upon superimposition and denial.
The glory of one's own welfare, which has as its cause the benefit of others through the enjoyment [of the Dharma].

Furthermore, in no discussion concerning the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) or secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), has it been shown that this form of a Buddha does not exist in reality, or that it is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). Even when the conventional designation "Buddha" is introduced with the emphasis on the *dharmakāya*, non-existence or mere figurativeness is not established;
for it is observed that the primary marks and so forth belong to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) as well. This is also stated in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:
[498,14] "His body is adorned with all the various marks" (MSA***).

Regarding this, the commentary states: "The mention of 'various' is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the marks of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and others"—this is merely a confirmation.

Furthermore, even though this has been written, because the Blessed One has abandoned the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), error is impossible for him, and he is of the nature of mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśanajñāna*).

Because the images of all objects of knowledge arise within it at every moment, its nature is that of a single wheel of cognition (*ekajñānacakra*). For this very reason, it is marked by the symbol of the wheel.

The direct experience of the reflections of all objects of knowledge is itself its awakening to all objects of knowledge. Consequently, because he possesses an excellence of intelligence (*buddhi*) through the realization of the true nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), he is called "Buddha. Therefore, his own and others' [dualistic notions] are extinguished, and even the mental aspect (*ākāra*) itself is lost.

Because of the establishment of error, where could there be the application of a praiseworthy cognition, or where could there be the abandonment of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)? Since one perceives the unreal as being precisely unreal, there follows the consequence of the doctrine of error consisting in the apprehension of that [unreal] in what is not that. This has been refuted in the case of the cognition of a form (*ākṛti*).
There is neither the method of mantra nor the system of the perfections;
let that very state remain, free from fault,
delightful, and adorned with the jewels of the qualities of heaven.
Thus is the intermediate verse.

Now, if it is maintained that the *saṃbhogakāya* indeed exists—even though it is unreal—and is capable of accomplishing that purpose; or even if it possesses such capacity, because of its very purity, there is another state resembling space, characterized by the direct realization of the *dharmakāya* through the withdrawal of that [body].

Is there no fault? No, because even so, one has not avoided the transgression of the non-eternality of non-decay (*aśraṃsana*). Furthermore, it follows that the Blessed One, being thus devoid of the *dharmakāya*, would act for the sake of the world; and that contradicts what the *Uttaratantra* states:
"Having beheld the entire world with great compassion, the Knower of the World..."
"Without wavering from the *dharmakāya*, through emanations of various forms...
(UT II 53). The connection is explained in detail as follows: "He displays [the Buddha's deeds], beginning with the *jātakas* and ending with *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore:
"In every celestial realm, without wavering from the state of Brahmā..."
Just as Brahmā displays his manifestation without effort, so too does he appear.

In the same way, the Sage, without effort, through emanations within the realms of sentient beings, appears to those who are worthy without wavering from the *dharmakāya*. (UT IV 53–4) This and more is explained at length. Now, if it is said that there is no wavering from the *dharmakāya* with respect to its natural purity (*prakṛtipariśuddhi*), then...
[499,15] Since this is equal for every living being, what excellence is expressed by the Blessed One in speaking thus in this continuous sequence?

[499,16] Therefore, this distinction is made solely with regard to purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalyaviśuddhi*); it is simply that at the time of the direct realization of the *dharmakāya*, the performance of the welfare of the world does not depend on mental effort (*ābhoga*) and so forth. Consequently, this effort is intended to dispel the doubt that such [activity] occurs only upon arising from meditative absorption (*samādhivyutthāna*). Likewise...

And it has been stated that this occurs through effortless emanations (*anābhoga-nirmāṇa*). Thus, by the abandonment of the body, the refutation of the proponents of a self who claim to have attained reality (*tattva*) is established.
Furthermore, even if "movement" is intended to mean the repeated emergence from and re-entry into meditative absorption (*samādhi*), even so, what is the point of this?
Is it through exertion? Indeed, [it is said]:
"The *sambhogakāya* is supreme for the sake of purity, and from that, the *sambhogakāya* exists for the accomplishment of the goal."
When will the Sage attain such composure as mine, whose body is so habituated to sinking and rising?
And thus, the welfare of others would not have its injunctions unimpaired, nor would there be eternal purity; let this matter rest for now.

Let there be no recollection of the story of Tundi. Furthermore, as for what was said—that the Dharma is itself the Buddha—since even in that case there is an absence of any conceptual distinction, and because [the terms] are sufficient [to function] even when their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are distinct, like [the words] *ina*, *muni*, and *indriya*, how [could there be a problem]?

[500,4] What is the establishment of a different body? Furthermore, that statement regarding the Victor and the Dharma—which is not contradictory to their being synonymous—begins with "not wavering from the *dharmakāya*," and so forth.
For it is not logical to say that one is a Sugata by not wavering from a Buddha; however, it is indeed logical to say it is because of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*). Of the one...
And he speaks of the establishment of designations (*prajñapti-sthiti*), and that is the statement, as illustrated by the example: "Just as Brahmā does not move from his Brahma-state.

For in that case, Brahmā alone is ultimately real (*paramārtha-sat*); however, that state (*pada*) is merely conventionally real (*prajñapti-sat*), for it is not some other distinct entity, since the designation of a "state" refers to a particularity of the basis, the requisites, and the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
Even when the very intrinsic nature (svarūpa), depending on specific limiting conditions (upādhi-viśeṣa), is denoted by the word *pada*— just as in the case of the term *ācāryapada*— nevertheless,

that which is indicated as if it were separate from the substratum (dharmin) through conceptual construction (kalpanā) exists only as a designation (prajñaptisat). Likewise, in this case as well, it follows that one of the two things denoted by the terms "Sage" (muni) and "Dharma-body" (dharmakāya) exists only as a designation.

[500,13] Let it be so for the Dharma alone, but not for the Sage, because of the absence of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). [500,14] If that existence is also devoid of form, how can the arising of the *saṃbhogakāya* be spoken of? (***) Thus, there is a contradiction with one's own words. Furthermore, in this way, even the "Sage" would be entirely formless; and consequently, from the *dharmakāya*...
[500,17] To say that "it does not move" would imply the misconception that the *sambhogakāya* itself, as a mere conceptual designation, is what is expressed by the term *dharmakāya*.

[500,18] If you argue that the *dharmakāya* is the emptiness of duality (*dvayaśūnyatā*) for that [sambhogakāya], even then, how can the birth of the *sambhogakāya* be spoken of? For it has already been established that the purpose is fully accomplished by that much alone.
[500,19] Thus it is concluded.

[500,20] Now, if it is argued that there is some distinction such that the sphere of activity (*kāryakoṭi*) of the *sambhogakāya* is one thing and that of the formless [Dharmakāya] is another; [500,21] then, because of this distinction, the absence of activity cannot be maintained as a formal establishment, since for both [bodies], being equally manifest, the analogy of the Brahman and the word "That" (*tatpadadṛṣṭānta*) is untenable, [500,22] and because even in the various treatises there is no such presentation regarding the *sambhogakāya*, whereas in the case of the Dharmakāya it is as follows: (118a) just as the Dharmakāya...

The reason has been stated, and it has already been demonstrated accordingly. Let it be that there is some activity of the formless [cognition] toward the enjoyment-body (*sambhoga*), or toward another group of effects; however, the existence of the enjoyment-body itself is indeed established. Consequently, both must be admitted as non-illusory (*analīka*); this is how the connection must be made.
So then, how can the illusoriness of the enjoyment-body, or the proof of supramundane non-manifesting cognition (*nirābhāsajñāna*), be proclaimed? Because of the subverting [evidence].
If it is argued that [the enjoyment body] is unreal—[we reply:

if, by means of the analogy of Brahman, one sets aside reflections and the like, then the unreality of the enjoyment body would be established; however, the power of sublation has already been considered.
[501,3] Through the uninterrupted continuity of appearance and causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), the previously mentioned status of being subordinate is thereby refuted. Furthermore,

[501,4] when both [appearance and efficacy] are established as having functional capacity, if one should desire the emptiness of duality itself to be the *dharmadhātu*, which has another name, the *dharmakāya*— either out of deference to the Crown Prince as shown previously, or now by means of the analogy of the station of Brahmā (*brahmapada*)— then:

And the body would be the fourth, precisely because the emanation (nirmāṇa) is distinct [from the other three]. Furthermore, that twofold emptiness belongs specifically to the enjoyment body (sambhoga), since it is designated as being connected [to it], and because it is taught as the uninterrupted enjoyment of the Dharma belonging to that very [body]. Indeed, there is no enjoyment other than self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).
Also in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:
In some places he displays the wheel of Dharma through hundreds of diverse gateways;
in some places he manifests birth, and in others, the wondrous and supreme disappearance.
In some places he manifests complete enlightenment, and in others, repeatedly with his emanations;
yet he does not move from that state, and he performs all these deeds.
Thus, the *Bhāṣya* states: "From the state of the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). And that untainted realm is the *dharmakāya*.
The meaning is the same as "the stability of its direct realization" for the purpose of immovability. Alternatively, it may be the fourth body (*kāya*).

Thus, a fourth nature would follow from the three natures—such as the formless, the with-form, and the imagined—because it would be distinct from the manifold wheel of mind known as unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*). If it is argued that this very mind is itself unreal imagination, we say no;
for this point has not been disclosed even by the masters of the means (*upāyakāra*), nor can a non-luminous mind or a non-mind ever be luminous.

And it was stated previously: "in form and so forth, which have the nature of unreal imagination. Thus, the discussion regarding form and so forth as the imagined, the conceptualized, and the true nature (*dharmatā*) should be followed in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*. If it is argued that the explanation is otherwise, let it be; however, it is said that it does not conform to the logical words [of the text]. Furthermore, even in this way, the aggregate of forms alone would be a distinct nature called "unreal."

[501,23] It might be argued: "It is included within the imagined (*kalpita*). If so, where and of what is there an imagination? If it is said that the form (*ākāra*) is imagined in that which is formless, [we reply: the view of an effect is that what appears in that which does not appear is imagined or superimposed (*āropita*). However, in the case of luminosity (*prakāśa*), that which is non-luminous, or in the case of a form, that which is formless, is superimposed as if it were something else; thus, it is precisely that which is included within the imagined. Therefore, [501,25]...
That which is free from difference and identity, appearing as the body of conceptualization through its nature as *dharmatā*,
