[532,1] Furthermore, the imagined duality is not even blue, because it does not appear [as such].
[532,2] Therefore, that which is the intrinsic nature must also be stated regarding the imagined and the other [natures]. //36//
To claim that the imagined is indeed manifesting—what could be more reckless than this?
Even in the case of a mirage, let it be that the imagined water is what is manifesting; what else could it be? (37)
If it is accepted in that way, let it be stated that milk is the effect of that [curd].
If you say, "It is not so because it does not exist," then how can that which is non-existent be milk? (38)
If it is argued that it is due to superimposition (*āropa*), then let it be a mere superimposition;
however, it is not the manifestation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because if there were such a manifestation, the activity of that [nature] would necessarily follow. (39)
[532,9] Reality itself would follow as a consequence, and likewise, sublation would be rendered powerless.
[532,10] For if its activity were lost through sublation, it would no longer be milk; for that [milk] possesses that activity. //40//
How is it said that the reading of that [text] flashes forth in superimposition?
Thus, the superimposition consists in the flashing forth of the grasped and the grasper, but not [in the grasped and grasper themselves]. (41)
Since both parts have the nature of self-luminosity, what could be the grasped object and what the grasper? For that would entail the loss of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). (42)

Therefore, let the very form that is manifesting be the fourth nature; for the notion that "there is a conceptualization of the visible within the invisible self" is merely some kind of mental construction. (43)
Therefore, the dependent nature is manifold; thus, cognition consists of the imagined and the conceptualized.
This is clearly observed in the determination of the form of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). //44//
Since both superimposition and denial regarding the imagined duality—which appears as the dependent nature—have been refuted, they are eliminated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*. (45)
Contemplate the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, the noble commentary along with its sub-commentary, wherein form and the other aggregates are explained as being clearly manifest as the dependent nature. (46)
Its appearance exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, existence and non-existence are attributed to illusions and the like. (47)
Therein, existence is not non-existence, nor is non-existence simply existence;
moreover, the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in the case of illusions and the like.
Likewise, the appearance as non-dual exists, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other aggregates. ||49||
Therein, existence is not non-existence, nor is non-existence simply existence;
moreover, the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in respect to form and the other [sensory objects]. (50)
It is intended for the purpose of negating the extremes of superimposition and denial, and also for the purpose of negating the vehicle of the Hīnayāna. //51//
"And regarding 'in form and so forth,' this means 'in those things whose nature is unreal imagination.
Look at the commentary's explanation, or its detailed exposition, for that. [52]
Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is, and he who sees reality is liberated. //53//

If it is maintained that this deliberation has as its object a thing perceived by direct perception, then there is no direct perception other than the variegated [cognition]; such is the effort made in both philosophical systems.
In the statement analyzing the *dharmadhātu*, the subject (*dharmin*) is expressed by the term "phenomena" (*dharma*);
likewise, this has been clearly stated by the immediately preceding words. (55)
For this very reason, the cessation of phenomena afterwards is indeed Nirvana;
yet this fault has been accepted by those who, under false names, long for the destruction of mental forms.

[533,19] "There exists a dharma called emptiness, distinct from form and the rest; this is that which is to be cultivated"—this is the reproach encountered by those who deny the existence of mental aspects (anākāravādins). [57]
Having realized that objects are merely mental chatter,
he abides in mind-only which appears as those objects;
thus it is said regarding the path of penetration and the vision.
Indeed, it is the attainment of direct perception of the dharmadhātu. ||58||
"That which is devoid of duality in the form of the grasped and the grasper"—thus is its distinction; it is not, however, anywhere a destruction of its aspect. //59//
The abandonment of the two characteristics is clearly evident everywhere;
for this very reason, there is no state of grasped object and grasping subject among the forms [of phenomena]. //60//
The appearances of duality proceed, yet they are not conceptual constructions; furthermore, for the sake of purification, here too there is both appearance and the state of determination. (61)
"It is not deluded regarding all objects of knowledge, yet it is never directed toward them"—the reason for this explanation is that [the mind] is "without mental aspect" (*anākāratā*). (62)
The meaning is "by way of the absence of the modes of the apprehended object," for even when the reflection arises;
this will become clear immediately hereafter upon examining the root text and the commentary. (63)

Thus, in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-mūla* and likewise in its commentary (*bhāṣya*), the meaning of the phrase "due to the excellence of the beginning and the end" has been correctly analyzed by means of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*). //64//

And likewise, in the *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga*, when the author of its commentary himself proceeds to explain the characteristic of non-conceptual cognition through the method of the investigation of phenomena (*dharma*) and their true nature (*dharmatā*): // 65 //
The term "formless" (arūpin) is used because it cannot be defined in terms of the grasped or the grasper;
and this term "without appearance" (anābhāsa) is described as being beyond the range of the cognitive domain.

But if it is so by way of the absence of appearance and the absence of an object of apprehension, then what is the use of this effort? It would be more appropriate to state the primary [position] directly. (67)
"Nothing whatsoever that is considered an object of perception appears within this"—this is the etymological derivation intended here, and it is likewise accepted in the *Uttara-tantra*. (68)
In that which is nothingness, without appearance, without support, and without basis;
which has transcended the range of vision, is formless, and is invisible. (69)
Just as depressions and elevations are seen in the sky, yet they do not exist there in that way;
so too, everything is seen even among the Buddhas, yet it does not exist there in that way. //70//

In this case as well, if the excellence of the qualification of the example resides in the omnipresent [subject], then it must necessarily be applied [to the subject], for its nature is indeed non-manifestation, just like that [example]. //71//
The abandonment of both the objective support and the basis is equal, by comparison, to the upper half;
it is "nothingness" because of being free from all adventitious defects. (72)
But the first verse has fulfilled its purpose through its own mere qualification;
thus, the plural number in the word "buddheṣu" (in the Buddhas) serves as a differentiator from that [previous case]. (73)
Because of their equality in being empty, there is no lack of nature, nor is there a lack of intrinsic nature;
rather, they are equal through the abandonment of the high and low positions of superimposition and denial. //74//
In the case of things that have the nature of real entities, there may arise the perception of high or low status;
however, in the case of that which has the nature of a non-entity, even suspicion does not exist—thus it is said to be like space. //75//

And if non-conceptual cognition is non-erroneous, while conceptual form is erroneous, then the conventional discourse of the three bodies would cease, because the enjoyment body would be utterly destroyed. //76//
As long as there is this delusion, which is a mere heap of forms, so long there is no Buddhahood;
since awakening is the antithesis of delusion, how could it be the nature of a Buddha? (77)

Nor is this merely conventional reality, for conventional reality is indeed conceptual construction; nor can it be called a "body" through metaphorical designation, because it is logically established as being nothing but relinquishment. //78//
[535,17] Due to the sovereign power of the Buddha, it is not possible for those who are fortunate to have even a mere appearance of that [Buddha];
[535,18] for they are more devoid of form, whereas the Buddha is superior by virtue of his manifestations. ||79||
[535,19] The sovereignty of the Buddha and their blessedness in various stations [are evident], since for those wandering in error, such a massive delusion arises. [80]
And just as pervasion and eternity have been described according to his own intention, the explanation regarding the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga*) is not like that; this is his great sovereignty. (81)
Because his self is adorned with all the various marks, he is called Citravāk (the One of Varied Speech);
the author of the Commentary states that this is because he is distinguished from the multitude of marks belonging to the Lord of the Wheel. 82.

In order to demonstrate that the dharmakāya is primary, the subsequent [verse] states that it belongs even to the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśa); thus, he did not describe it as being unreal or the like. [83]
And this *Sūtrālaṃkāra* would be contradicted if there were falsity:
"The perfection of the two purposes for both is established in all its aspects. (84)
The Enjoyment Body is the perfection of one's own welfare, while the Emanation Body is the glory of the welfare of others;
these two are established in the Nature Body—such is the teaching of the Commentary. (85)
Thus, the body of the *dharmakāya* is the cause for the *nirmāṇakāya*; the claim that the *saṃbhogakāya* is the perfection of one's own welfare is an error. //86//
[536,9] In the doctrine of space, because it possesses the nature of a body, there is no plurality for the Sage;
[536,10] for plurality is not pervaded by form, as is the case with the mind, mental factors, and the self. ||87||

But the *Ṭīkā* says that because the Sage lacks the grasping at a self and has abandoned both himself and others, he does not speak of "the earth" [as a self]; rather, it clearly states that the body is the grasping at a self. (88)
One's own welfare, the welfare of others, the nature of the ultimate body (*paramārthakāyatā*),
and the conventional body (*saṃvṛttikāyatā*) which is based upon that;
the fruit consists of the state of dissociation and maturation.
Thus, in the supreme tantra that follows, what is the meaning? ||89||
The self-benefit body is considered by us to be the essential nature (svābhāvika), while the other-benefit body is the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga).
However, in this context, it is the establishment of their ultimate reality that is intended. (90)
Whether indirectly or directly, the Emanation Body (nirmāṇakāya) relies upon those two conventionalities; and it is taught that emanation is the conventional fruit. (91)
While speaking of the qualities of the Tathāgata, how could one possibly abandon the emanation body?
Thus, having referred to those two bodies in the commentary as being ultimate, [it is said: 92.
And the rule regarding the basis of self-perfection is not contradicted;
self-perfection is twofold: through the accomplishment of form and through worldly prosperity. (93)
In the first [verse], having established the beginning, [he speaks] of the second in the second [verse], with many qualifiers such as "inconceivable" and "transcending the world. (94)
Alternatively, the power of those two resides in the self and in the enjoyment of perfection;
the pure essential body (svābhāvikakāya) is to be known as being like a statue made of jewels. //95//

Because its nature is unconditioned, because it is the locus of the jewels of the qualities, and because it possesses supreme sovereignty over the Great Dharma, the Enjoyment Body is like a universal monarch. //96//
Because its nature is that of a reflection, the emanation is like a golden image;
thus has it been asserted by those who take pleasure in their own position regarding the Teacher. (97)
The enjoyment body is conventional, excluding the emanation body; fie upon its independence!
Having illuminated the entire world with great compassion, the Knower of the World [acts]. //98//
"Without wavering from the *dharmakāya*, through emanations of diverse forms"—by such a continuous passage as this, that which is demonstrated right here [is shown]. (99)
Furthermore, it has been stated regarding the Jātakas and other tales ending with Nirvāṇa:
"In every celestial abode, he never wavered from his Brahma-like state. (100)
Just as Brahmā might manifest his appearance without effort, so too does the Sage, through effortless spontaneity, manifest emanations throughout the world-systems. //101//
"Without wavering from the *dharmakāya*, he comes into the sight of those who are worthy.
Thus, and so forth, it is explained at length there that [the manifestation] is distinct from the *dharmakāya* by means of speech. (102)
If the self of enjoyment does not exist, what other sage could bear the burden of activity? (103)
In some places he displays the wheel of Dharma through hundreds of diverse forms;
in some places the disappearance of his birth, and in others the wondrous rite of collyrium; in some places the entirety of enlightenment, and in others, repeatedly, with emanations.
And yet, he does not waver from that state, and he accomplishes everything. //104//
Thus it is said in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: "In this regard, the locus is the untainted realm (anāśrava-dhātu) as proclaimed in the commentary; that is indeed the immovability of the Dharma-body. (105)
Nevertheless, it is held that the self and its form are indeed false and an error;
yet, to claim that the burden of causal efficiency arises from something other than these is truly a shame to shame itself. (106)
Furthermore, even if error exists by way of an unreal nature, it would be pointless with respect to the gross object;
for if it were accepted, the burden of mental aspects would necessarily have to be abandoned. //107//
Because it remains like the form of a cloudless sky, this supreme state has arisen, having cast off the attainment of the three bodies. //108//
If the enjoyment body were to perish, its property—the dharma-body—would not exist;
nor would its effect, the emanation body. This would be a flawed conclusion regarding the nature of Buddhahood. (109)
[538,9] Let it be that the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) has set; let the dharma-body (dharmakāya) be formless.
[538,10] And from that very [dharma-body], let there be the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya); thus, the Buddhist conclusion is excellent. //110//
Precisely because it is an error, having abandoned the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya), it takes recourse in the state of being bodiless (anaṅgadaśā).
For that is indeed the ultimate limit of purification; why then would there not be a union of those three? 111.
[538,13] It has been demonstrated that this is contradictory according to the method of the Crown Prince;
nevertheless, if there is some curiosity regarding the investigation, it shall be stated. [538,14] ||112||
If the *dharmakāya* is defined as the manifestation without mental aspects (*anākāra*), then what is the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya*, which is not suitable to be abandoned? (113)
Even if he remains for the sake of a purpose, how can he be a Sugata because of his being subject to error?
If he were useful for a purpose, it would only foster falsehood and unreality. (114)

And that being so, there is neither delusion nor the abandonment of non-delusion; consequently, for one who is not deluded, there is the establishment of equality and the refutation of dogmatic tenets. ||115||
Therefore, that which is the cause of this [defilement], which must necessarily be abandoned, does not deserve to be undertaken.
Consequently, even for that reason, he is not the Sugata; if it were only the Dharma that is the Victor.
The conventional expression "the Dharmakāya of the Jina" is not established, because even by way of different exclusions (vyāvṛtti), it is a designation for that which is one and the same. ||117||
Otherwise, there would be a hundred bodies for the Jinas and so forth due to their non-differentiation;
moreover, the conventional expression "the Buddha of the Jina" does not exist anywhere. //118//

However, the term expressing the property of the substratum is indeed distinct as it participates in linguistic convention; for example, one says "the wood-apple tree" or "the tree's wood-apple," but not "the wood-apple is the tree. (119)
If the Buddha is considered to be mere phenomena (dharmamātra), then it is logical for the Buddha to possess the Dharma;
for if the Buddha's body is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), then the Dharma is his quality.
That being so, your body is formless and equal to the fourth state; the triad of bodies is not to be counted as distinct from the enjoyment body, because of its non-differentiation. (121)
"The essential body (svābhāvikakāya) is considered equal, subtle, and connected"—if one explains the word "connected" in this way, it would contradict the objection [stated above]. //122//
It is said that it is "connected" with the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogika-kāya*);
since the enjoyment exists, its quality deserves to be connected with it. //123//
In its absence, there is no identity; even if it exists, there is no identity due to absolute difference.
This is because it is proclaimed therein that [the dharmakāya] is the cause of the enjoyment-buddhahood (saṃbhogabuddhatā). ||124||
If it is argued that there is a causal relationship, then the effect cannot be a non-entity belonging to anything.
If it is asked, "How then can the cause also be merely characterized by the nature of a non-entity? [125]
In the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, it is stated that [the *ālayavijñāna*] arises by having that as its object;
and in various places, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) likewise states that it is the cause of all phenomena. (126)
Or, having separated that part [of the self], it is likewise said to exist even previously, just as the valor of this king alone accomplishes all his aims. (127)
It has never been stated that anything arises from a formless self;
however, the refutation set forth in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* applies equally here as well. (128)

Even though this person arises from the occurrence of dependent existence (*pratītyabhāva*), they rely on what is produced by another as being manifest before them; [the phrase] "arising from that" is found in the *Mātṛkā*.
What kind of darkness is this, of such a nature, that through it one perceives both the existent and the non-existent? ||129||
The agent and the enjoyer, distinct from what is perceived, is the object of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);
it is stainless, and liberation for yogins consists in its being the sole remainder. (130)

Thus, this is merely the doctrine of a self, and it is neither eternal nor characterized by inactivity; furthermore, its nature would result in being eternal by virtue of being the *dharmakāya*. (131)
[540,7] Even through the non-lapse of its intrinsic nature, there is no permanence in the continuum;
[540,8] for here, in this case of the intrinsic nature, that meaning is joined with the commentary. //132//
In the determination of the delusion regarding effects, that which is indeed intrinsic is proclaimed as the *dharmakāya* with reference to purification. (133)
The nature is emptiness, the phenomenon; the Sugata himself is the enjoyment body. By dividing its internal and mutual qualities, there is the fourfold body. (134)

The mention of the *dharmakāya* within the three bodies expresses the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*); the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is included within the fourfold enjoyment aspect, and the remainder is also contained herein. (135)
Just as space, by virtue of its non-conceptuality, is omnipresent everywhere, so too is the element of the stainless nature of the mind all-pervading. (136)
Thus, by means of the *Uttaratantra*, the primary all-pervasiveness has been proclaimed;
this doctrine of the Self is fully evident as that of the Vedāntins. (137)
[540,19] However, the permanence, pervasiveness, and so forth of the *dharmatā* are conventional;
even though it possesses intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*), they are established according to conceptual construction, just like momentariness and the like. [138]
Without a distinction, there is no logical justification; for this [distinction] is lost from the perspective of the actual nature of things (*vastutva*).
Therefore, in the context of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), that doubt is excluded by the All-pervasive One. (139)
Thus, because of the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervading;
and because of the non-interruption of that very [activity], he is also said to be eternal. ||140||
That which is to be applied here is not itself declared to be eternal by its very nature;
for since it exists within the sphere of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika-adhikāra*), it is therefore not the true form of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*). //141//

When there is the performance of universal activity in the state of enjoyment, purity exists; yet when that is absent, as before, there is contradiction, for both complete purification and the welfare of sentient beings are not eternal. (142)
"If there is no formless [reality], and its identity with the self [is not established], then this very one is the Dharmakāya"—thus the King began. (143)

[Haru – 26/08/08] Very close to [541,7]: Through the destruction of the accumulation of afflictions and their absolute destruction, who is revealed in the Tantra as the essence of sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and Victors? [541,8] //144//
The Dharma-body is to be known as twofold: the utterly stainless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and its natural outflow, which is the teaching of the profound and manifold methods. (145)

Thus, the explanation is also found in that very same place; however, while the subject is expressed by means of its attribute, the *dharmakāya* under discussion is the utterly stainless *dharmadhātu*. (146)
Suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate truth, and the realm of phenomena—these, in brief, are synonyms for emptiness. (147)
Thus, in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, the dharmadhātu has been described:
"The perfected nature, the untainted realm, is to be known as reality. (148)

Emptiness is said to be twofold; therein, due to the state of affliction, the quality of the dependent nature is to be known as existing when the stains of the enjoyment body have been eliminated. (149)
Those untainted dharmas which have attained purity in all its aspects constitute the essential body (svābhāvika-kāya) of the Sage, characterized by their intrinsic nature. ||150||
In this regard as well, it is not contradicted by the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, because intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is established as the cause and as reality (*tattva*). (151)
Alternatively, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is their very emptiness; and this is held by all, yet it is called "pure speech" because it is introduced by the Buddha. (152)
Even though the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga) is not included within the pure [realm], it is reckoned among the assembly;
for that must be called a distinct body—how then could it be the Dharma-body at that time? (153)
Because it is primary, however, nothing else is its subordinate equipment;
for, since they consist of a single cognition, it is apprehended precisely by the apprehension of that [primary object]. ||154||

Although enjoyment, the locus, and the form are not distinct from that [consciousness], nevertheless, the conventional distinction between them—such as "the person"—is like other [conventional] designations. (155)
Thus ends the second chapter, the definitive exposition of the words of the noble Asaṅga, the Crown Prince, concerning the investigation of the essential nature of the Dharmakāya.
[Chapter Three] If one is liberated by isolating the mere nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as either "the Buddha" or "the Dharma," how can there be self-cognition in the absence of duality? (1)
Because of awakening to that, he is called "Buddha," and not because of the blazing marks and so forth;
for one who loves all pure qualities does not abandon that objective support.
The realization of that is common to all Buddhas; it belongs to no other.
Recollection of that is the worship of the Protectors; its fruit is the certainty regarding the object of knowledge. //3//

Therefore, the Buddha is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and the Dharma is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Since Buddhahood consists in the predominance of these two, how could there be a distinct heap [of dharmas] from this? ||4||
For this very reason it is said that the Buddha is indeed the Dharma, just as it is said that the king is indeed his majesty; in reality, there is an identity between the two. (5)
And as it was said by the venerable master: "The object of the word 'Buddha' is the purified continuum of mind; this is also what is called the 'Dharma' of the Great Sage. (6)
In that regard as well, through the direct realization of the *dharmakāya*, that sound is the Dharma itself, just as the Victor is the Dharma; and likewise, he is indeed the Victor. (7)
In the *Āryeśanītivivṛti*, which describes the manner in which formless things do not appear and proclaims the abandonment of the mere duality, there is no doubt regarding that which is formless. (8)
Even when there is effort toward the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), that very consciousness is not eliminated;
otherwise, how could its cessation be said to occur at the stage of Arhatship? (9)
If there is a turning away [from the world], there is no difference in the ten stages; it is without appearance, and the goal to be proven is accomplished.
For it is said that perfect awakening occurs in Akaniṣṭha, not born from the formless realm. (10)
The commentary also states: "Nowhere in the scripture is it said that there is no cognition of the form [of the object];
this follows the scripture as established by the renowned teacher Sthiramati. (11)
If it is argued that this has been stated as being indeed formless (*nirākāra*), then certainty is destroyed;
for what is the use of other considerations for us, since the subject at hand has already been established? (12)

Let some systematic arrangement be established in the scriptures by the Victors in some way, or by the First Teacher; it is not the case that everything has been introduced here [in this work] at present. (13)
Because the mode of equanimity (upekṣākāra) truly exists, there is no destruction of form even in the formless realm (ārūpya);
for a mental aspect (ākāra) is a transformation of cognition, since some kind of form persists.
If the manifestation of the genus of cognition is its form, why is it not like space?
Or rather, when cognition arises, what is there to be excluded? Nothing at all. (15)
But in the case of blue and so forth, a cognition distinct from that form is denied;
for even in a dream, no such other cognition is observed to exist otherwise. (16)
In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is established exactly in that way;
if one desires that it should possess such-and-such a form, then this very [cognition] is presented as its object. (17)
The formless realm arises from detachment from the form of delusion and from the disposition toward tranquility;
therefore, for the Buddhas, blue and so forth are themselves the self, and duality does not exist at all. //18//
The establishment of the non-existence of all things occurs in two ways, through the negation of implication (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and the negation by exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Here, the negation by exclusion consists of the two: the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) and its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). (19)
[544,17] First of all, its status as a real entity is not contradicted by self-awareness;
[544,18] for the cognition that establishes the absence of another is indeed a direct perception of the locus (dharmin). //20//
The absence of a jar on the ground is established by the perception of the ground;
likewise, the absence of duality in the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga) is established by the perception of that enjoyment body. ||21||
The Noble One, considering that other [view], said: "Homage be to You for this non-duality!
You did not describe [the self as] 'red,' 'green,' 'mañjiṣṭha-colored,' and so forth. (22)
"It is to be personally realized"—thus it is taught by its own voice;
for even when that conceptual construction is excluded, one has reached the final resting place because the basis [of duality] has been eliminated. //23//
The finality of that which is to be determined has also been made clear by Saṃbhoga;
for this very reason, they have elucidated the acceptance of the "aspect" (sākāra). //24//
No phenomenon whatsoever arises, nor does anything whatsoever cease;
it is only conditions that arise and cease. (25)
Thus, because the intellect is applied to the place of the sprout, the seed, and so forth, there arises a clear appearance of them, which is the imagined destruction of the continuum. (26)
The great elements and so forth are said to be fully contained within consciousness;
when that [consciousness] is known, they vanish. Is it not indeed falsely conceptualized? //27//
In that regard, the conviction of non-existence is the comprehension of the meaning through hearing and reflection;
"the knowledge thereof" refers to the exhaustion [of obscurations] upon the direct realization of the nature of that knowledge. //28//

The teaching on the aggregates, elements, and so forth is for the purpose of ceasing the grasping at a self; that too has been discarded by the fortunate ones through the establishment of [everything as] mere representation. (29)
Thus, from the removal of praise, there is certainty even regarding inclination (*ruci*).
If this distinction is made in view of the two states, it is as has been stated. (30)
The teaching of the Sage that "all this is mind-only" is for the purpose of removing the fear of the ignorant; it is not [the truth] in its ultimate sense. //31//
This inclusion is made by granting the wish of those who are attached to annihilationism; it is not so because of the removal of fear, for in reality there is no such cutting off. //32//
[545,19] Otherwise, the fear of fools and the loss [of purpose] would be equal in both positions.
[545,20] What difference is there here, such that there could be praise or rejection in such a manner? ||33||
And regarding the statement beginning with "Nothing is to be removed from this," since it has already been explained, why should it be further explained by oneself? What could be more than this? (34)

"An element is to be seen as an element by means of the self that is an element, and likewise by means of the self that is an element"—is this not the meaning of the statement being proclaimed here? (35)
For in the doctrine that everything is non-existent, there would have to be some unreal thing that is to be seen as having a real form; this is the extreme of denial (apavādānta). //36//
[546,3] "The same applies to you regarding superimposition (samāropa)," because for you, conceptual construction (kalpanā) is not superimposition.
[546,4] In that which manifests non-conceptually, superimposition is indeed the conceptualization of duality. //37//
If negation does not exist conventionally and superimposition does not exist in reality, and if neither of those two exists in reality, then what contradiction is there? (38)
Conventionally, there is no denial; for in reality, it is indeed a denial.
Thus, the doctrine of the non-existence of everything follows, and its refutation has already been stated. (39)

If emptiness is real, it is well said that whatever is absent from something makes that thing empty by virtue of its absence—just as a house is empty of men; thus there is no contradiction between the subject (dharmin) and the property (dharma). //40//
Unreal imagination exists; duality is not found there.
But emptiness exists here, and this [unreal imagination] also exists in it. //41//

The doctrine of universal non-existence, however, is indeed to be refuted on the strength of valid cognition (*mīti*). For this very reason, the Noble Ones will consider [the matter], and thus it is not the case that they do not perceive anything at all. (42)

Or else, this negation is similar [to that of external objects] when there is conceptualization regarding observation, based on the imagined relationship between the object of cognition and the cognizer. (43)
Just as their power of merit arises from variegated cognition, so it is said by those engaged in conventional discourse: "They see this and that. (44)
We perform a negation of existence, but not an affirmation of non-existence;
for that too is something to be negated—this is a grand ambition indeed! (45)
The very negation of existence is designated as non-existence;
since the negative particle lacks another referent, it does not constitute a positive injunction nor a sublation of a single entity. (46)
Of two things whose natures consist in mutual exclusion, the negation of one is not capable of persisting for even a moment without the affirmation of the other. (47)
When the intrinsic natures of things imagined by the naive are non-existent, there is no harm to the nature of reality which is free from all adventitious adjuncts. //48//
Therefore, the finality regarding the two aspects does not reside in either affirmation or negation alone.
Consequently, let the denial of appearance and the superimposition upon non-appearance be abandoned. (49)
Just as there is pain when a thorn enters the body or when it is being cut out,
so too here, in this flickering form, there is suffering through both exaggeration and depreciation.
Therefore, the pure primordial state does not differ from the Yogācāra;
for liberation from the extremes of superimposition and denial is indeed the Middle Way. //51//
Neither empty nor non-empty, therefore everything is so designated; because of existence, non-existence, and existence again, that is the middle way. (52)
[547,11] This statement regarding emptiness is based on the meaning of non-existence according to the views of others;
this effort of the Noble King has been rendered futile by those consumed by dogmatic views. [53]

Therefore, regarding the removal of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) from sentient beings through these very dharmas, there is no cause for astonishment, because this has been proclaimed repeatedly in the treatises with reference to the imagined nature (*parikalpita*). //54//
The Vijñānavādin himself might raise this objection using the word "other";
what greater calamity than this could there be for the Vijñānavādin? //55//
If he who is to become a perfectly awakened Buddha were a deceiver, where would there be liberation?
Even those deceived by him alone, the wise, partake in splendor.
The method of knowledge [arises] from the intention of others; likewise, O Protector, why would there not be other teachings for the Noble One?
Indeed, it is according to those who are to be trained by him.
Even those like you are his disciples in that same way. //57//
He extended praise for the noble lord of the earth, who had not expressed his own private intention nor any common sentiment even toward another man.
But effort is the middle way, and that is it. ||58||
Even if there is equality in the attainment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no further fault regarding the purpose of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
If, then, with respect to a single truth that is similar, it were twofold—
Better is entry into the mouth of a lord of the earth than [into that of a lowly man]. ||59||

If you are a follower of the Dharma through reasoning (*dharmānusārin*), then let your praise be solely devoted to the authoritative treatises (*pramāṇa-śāstra*); but if you are a follower through faith (*śraddhānusārin*), then let it be for the sake of the great multitude.
The crown prince is worthy of being honored by the assembly. ||60||
Alas, even regarding the person (pudgala), there is nothing more than the mere word of the Victor;
there is no attainment of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) through the release from the *Saṃdhinirmocana*. But if one disregards that, [the definitive meaning is attained].
[548,14] When the Buddha himself is the speaker, what is the distinction? ||61||
Intermediate verses: [548,15] antarāślokāḥ ||

By dividing the single [teaching] according to the differences among those to be trained, through its profundity and ultimate meaning, and by way of affirmation and negation, its fourfold establishment is proclaimed. (62)
For some are intent on denial, while others are intent on superimposition;
with reference to the former, the first [extreme] was taught, and the latter, the final one, with reference to the others. (63)
Having refuted attachment to those who are themselves intent on negation, those who establish the existence of thought through reasoning abide by the system of Yogācāra. (64)
Furthermore, regarding those things colored by superimposition, the middle way functions by way of sublation;
and through that, there is frequent expression of negation that is free from qualifications.
Like a lame man supported by a staff, they will stand by themselves upon the wall of the expressed meaning;
why would the identity of meaning between the words "similarity" and "dissimilarity" not be a distinction? (66)
The pure Middle Way does not differ in reality from the Yogācāra;
therefore, it is excellent that even the Noble One is established in the Noble Way. (67)

Because one observes a distinguished capacity [in the disciple], and because of drawing others [toward the teaching] through that means, as well as through encouragement, a description full of enthusiasm is not contradictory. //68//

Therefore, even according to their system, as long as there is a negation of what has been stated, that should be understood as referring only to the imagined nature, just like the second master’s doctrine. //69//
This is the summary view: "This is the negation of the imagined.
Every form established as an object of cognition is considered imagined within the mind. (70)
The aspect mounted upon cognition is conceptualized as having the form of the object of knowledge; it is also characterized, in some respects, by its nature as cognition. //71//
Let the negation of the imagined nature be grasped as its being apprehended as the object and so forth;
just as it has been analyzed in the commentary, because that [imagined nature] does not exist, that [negation] is also non-existent. //72//
Since that which appears is indeed non-existent, it is produced by ignorance; for that power which manifests the non-existent is called "ignorance. (73)
Alternatively, manifestation has the sense of determination when it flashes forth in conceptual construction;
it is considered to be produced by that [conceptualization], which abides in a state of imagination brought about by the latencies of ignorance. //74//
For the teaching in the Prajñāpāramitā relies upon three [natures]:
the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected. (75)
By all such terms as "it does not exist" and so forth, that which is imagined is refuted;
through similes such as "like an illusion," the dependent nature is taught. //76//
The perfected nature is proclaimed through fourfold purification;
for in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there is no teaching other than this. (77)
Thus, because the sequence of meanings in the system of the *pāramitās* is inexhaustible, the stainless doctrine of *sākāravāda* shines forth within that very context. (78)
Therefore, if another meaning alone is primary and real, then it is a reasonable statement that this very meaning should also be accepted according to the system of the Noble Ones (ārya). //79//
[550,3] Now, if there is a distinction regarding the part "from that," even so, what is gained? [550,4] By the mere negation of both, has the goal been accomplished by the wise man? //80//
Even the negation of appearance must be expressed as appearance itself; it is not a duality.
Because of the absence of defining characteristics, the fact that there is no sublation when [appearance] exists was indicated previously. (81)
Furthermore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga-kāya) and its metaphorical designations and so forth are described in clear syllables;
this is because it is the primary meaning according to the Noble One, or because it is revealed in his own realization. //82//

For what has not been accomplished by the Blessed One through the employment of words whose meaning is condensed, by means of speech that makes easy the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted? (83)
Or is it self-praise by means of the excellence of its qualities and form? Or otherwise, what is the point of this commentary (*vārtika*) which is a mirror for that system, as seen by others? (84)

In this regard, the author of the Vārttika has diligently established that even with respect to external objects, cognition possesses a form; having done so, he leaves only that [cognition] as the remainder, because of the sublation of the apprehended object. (85)
That experience belongs to that [consciousness] as its very self, and it does not belong to anything else;
even its being known through direct perception consists in its having that as its nature. (86)
Thus speaking, the Noble Lord, while the author of the *Vārttika* speaks in this manner, even though he is face-to-face, he does not become an object of conviction if he acts otherwise. (87)
If, even after entering into the mental aspect, the mind within the mind is formless, then what is the fruit of this internal placement of the aspect as being desired to be false? (88)

The mind is established as being without form for both parties—the proponent of self-cognition and the opponent—because even when external objects are superimposed upon cognition, the refutation of the mental image is the same. (89)
Therefore, why such exertion? Is it not simply that after washing [the mind], one should abandon [it]?
For the continuity of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) in false manifestations is established without effort. (90)
When the form [of the cognition] has been refuted by accepting that it is the apprehended object, then the proof of the form is logical only upon the conclusion that the mind possesses a form. (91)

Having established that the mind possesses a form, on the grounds that it is perceived as nothing other than light acting as the instrument in the act of apprehension—which serves as the support for hundreds of conflicting views—[it follows that it is not momentary]. (92)

Having established with persistence the logic of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their result, one still remains unsatisfied; for even at the end, the effort expended toward that purpose remains great. //93//
For one who vainly establishes a presently unreal form, that very beginningless proximity to perception would be the illustration. //94//

Therefore, since the mind is established by its very nature as possessing the power to manifest itself as non-self, the consideration regarding the destruction of the characteristics of the apprehended object is fruitless. //95//
Enough with the two reasons expressed through the phrase "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*);
let it be stated, as Dharmottara did, that [the opponent] is under the sway of a second teacher. //96//
Furthermore, this refutation of being neither one nor many is not intended for the ignorant;
even regarding external objects, it is not a refutation at all, since it does not refute the atom. (97)
Having remained with the object of cognition refuted while its aspect was established through effort, the Sautrāntika is described as being closer to reality than the Vaibhāṣika. (98)

Therefore, regarding everything that is invariably determined as "false" or "non-existent," it is not apprehended in its own essential form as an aspect (ākāra), but rather as something external. //99//
That pair of moons was seen, yet the statement "it does not exist" does not negate the cognition;
nor is it that the perceived form is false while the two moons themselves are real. (100)
Because of the fault arising from the superimposition of water, the form of the mind is indeed logical;
however, a manifestation that appears uniquely to oneself cannot belong to another. (101)
This establishment according to conventional determination is not, however, from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for things such as hair-locks and the like are not universals, because they lack objective referents upon which one could fixate.
"In some cases" refers to the *mātṛkā*.
Thus he says: "But not because of being non-objects," and furthermore, "the appearance as something clear;
since it is an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition, the notion [of it being an object] regarding hair-tufts and the like is again [addressed]. (103)

The appearance of hair, which has a universal (sāmānya) as its object, is devoid of external reality; it is classified as sensory cognition because it determines what is non-existent as being external. //104//
If it is argued that [the universal] is an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition, then it follows that it is a universal;
since this is accepted, there is no fault, for its commonality consists in its having the nature of an object.
And it has been stated more than once that the referent of a word is a property-bearer (*dharmin*) that cannot be rejected.
Therefore, this referent of a word is said to be as it is conventionally perceived, even though it does not exist [ultimately]. (106)
Even though the object of a word does not exist, there is the determination that "this is the object of a word";
this has been shown because, when a word is heard, it appears as a form within cognition. //107//

However, there is the determination that the external object of a word exists according to its conceptual determination, because it is established as the mere thing excluded from what does not possess that form. //108//
If existence were according to how it is perceived, there would be no determination here;
rather, that very appearance is the existence of the object, while the dependence on external power is merely a matter of convention. (109)
Therefore, it is established that the form is said to be the object precisely because it is cognition;
and as for what was explained by the author of the Commentary, what is the point of laboring over that? (110)
If the mind possesses only an aspect, then even at the limit there is no excess;
thus, defilement and purification would be one, and not two. (111)
Defilement is simply the aspect (ākāra), while purification is its cessation;
thus, in the doctrine of the absence of aspects (anākāravāda), there is the establishment of both. 112.
Delusion is the grasping at that which is not [the object] as being that; conceptual construction is its destruction, which is equal.
If conceptual construction were also equal, how could it be an error, given that it possesses the form of truth? (113)
In the act of ascertainment there is the state of being manifest, and in manifestation there is identity with that [ascertainment].
Furthermore, if the object were lost, there would be no such cognition as "it is called a name" and so forth. (114)
There would be certainty regarding the entire essence, and the object would be clearly manifest as "cow";
moreover, since there is no convention regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), cognition would be purely conceptual. (115)
Therefore, the cognition shines forth through the universal of all individual cows; its manifestation as such is by way of the unreal "cowness" accompanied by verbal expression. //116//

Let it be that there is a determination of "cow"; therefore, these faults do not arise, because even in the absence of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is a determination of it through error. (117)

Just as there is the manifestation of a false "cowness" (gotva) in the cognition of a cow, so too there is identity, non-distinction, the absence of superimposition, and even substantial reality. [118]

Likewise, when there is the appearance of blue and so forth, the identity of the unreal white and so forth with that manifestation is established simply by the establishment of its state as manifest; let this be accepted. (119)
When there is no superimposition upon the reality of the thing itself, the logical mark (liṅga) belongs to that same nature (tādātmya) or to its lineage (gotra).
Any superimposition based on the non-exclusion of [other properties] such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth is unestablished. ||120||
All of this is trivial, because for those who maintain that cognition possesses a form (sākāravādins), even an existing object does not appear; how much less so could one that is non-existent? (121)
Because it is the very nature [of the cognition] that appears, even a fool has this certainty;
indeed, the faults that would follow for him based on the appearance of an external object are not applicable here. (122)
[553,17] Where is the application of convention for a word that is expressive? [553,18] Of what is the word expressive, wherein the act of convention-making occurs? ||123||
What kind of verbal artifice is this that you perceive? Show me, too, where there is ever any relationship between the signified and the signifier. (124)
If its form is false, how is that [cognition] any different? If the convention applies to what is false, why does it not apply to a true form as well? (125)
The result does not truly exist even when the aspect is present, for it is unreal.
If [the result is denied] because of the superimposition of an object upon the unreal, by what means is it denied when it is real? ||126||

What is the superimposition of an object? And if it pertains to reality, what is its nature even in the case of falsity? Is the form real or false? Furthermore, by what is the superimposition of a real entity produced? (127)
For since there is no appearance of a real cow-nature, why is there not an appearance of a real form?
If the form is real even though it appears, then the form must be unreal even though it is real. (128)
Since superimposition is possible because of the appearance of what is non-existent, how could it occur in the case of the real?
But surely, even regarding the non-real, how can there be a convention if the non-reality itself is not determined? (129)

Therefore, because it consists in the superimposition of a thing capable of causal efficiency upon the body [of the word], the making of a convention does not differ whether [the object] is real or unreal. //130//
In the state of suchness, no determination of the word exists; nor is there any appearance of an object. Therefore, in reality, what could possibly be denotable? ||131||
Whether there is non-appearance or appearance, there is no superimposition of anything whatsoever;
such a thing is merely a conventional designation established through the distinction of dependent origination. //132//
When conceptualization arises from the non-conceptual, following a mere trace, it occurs due to the words of one who employs conventions, directed toward a specific mental image. (133)

The conviction that "a convention has been established" arises again regarding the persistence of such words; furthermore, the determination of the denotable object occurs within the nature of the cognition that projects activity. (134)
Thus, when the arising of a conceptual form that projects such activity occurs, there is the superimposition of water and so forth; and this is equal to both the real and the unreal. (135)
Therefore, although in reality there is no superimposition of anything upon anything anywhere, this [superimposition], being established by conventional usage, cannot be denied. (136)
As long as there is the conceptualization of a self in what is not-self, like water in a mirage, that very delusion is saṃsāra; nirvāṇa is the abiding in reality. //137//
Therefore, in this matter, as long as critical inquiry has not yet arisen, this is the principle: "this is cyclic existence, and that is peace.
But when the mind is stirred by the play of inquiry, tell me: what here remains as either cyclic existence or peace? (138)
And thus:
"In this world, from the perspective of the operation of ultimate reality, there is not the slightest difference between these two—tranquility and birth.
Nevertheless, the attainment of tranquility is established through the destruction of birth."
[It is for those] who perform virtuous deeds. ||139||
Likewise: "Both nirvāṇa and existence—these two do not exist.
The thorough understanding of existence itself is called nirvāṇa. (140)
In the cognition of water, the falsity of the form is not the cause;
likewise, in the establishment of error, there is the confusion of the grasped and the grasper. (141)
Whether the form is real or unreal, there is no fault on the part of the mind, provided that an external superimposition which would impel activity does not arise. (142)
Even knowledge that possesses the aspect of truth is conceptual with respect to its object;
it is therefore defective because it projects activity, since activity is what constitutes cyclic existence.

If it is argued that activity occurs neither in the absence of conceptual construction nor in its presence, then why is this not also the case regarding the recollection of specific qualities? Therefore, there is no difference.

Just as something may be capable of performing a certain function in some place due to practice beginningless in time, so too this capacity of conceptual construction is established as the means for proof. (145)
For this very reason, the afflictions exist within the conceptual constructions of Bodhisattvas;
therefore, effort must be applied to destroy those latencies as long as the state of cause and effect persists. //146//
The manifestation of the unreal form of "cowness" is not established for one who possesses the cognition of a cow;
for even a conceptual construction with a real form is a determination because it leads to engagement. //147//
Just as the real form of "cowness" appears in the cognition of a cow, so too its identity, its non-separateness, its non-superimposition, and its reality [are established]. (148)
Likewise, when there is the appearance of blue and so forth, the manifestation of the real white and so forth is established; therefore, let their identity be accepted as real. (149)
Whatever is the nature of an object, that object appears as a form in the conceptualization of a cow;
and blue, being of the nature of a manifest object, does not appear otherwise than as such. (150)
Since identity and difference have been eliminated, sublation is established as being real;
moreover, nothing other than the white [color] perceives it, and thus there is no proof of superimposition.

But how could a false form—which is capable of neither benefiting nor harming, which appears only occasionally, and which either flashes forth or is capable of purposeful action—be considered unreal? (152)
For when its own nature is thus understood, even an opponent becomes its servant;
therefore, it is self-luminous by nature, whether pure or indeed afflicted. (153)
That which is merely false, even if it exists, does not act as an obstacle anywhere; for if it were to act as an obstacle, its falsity would result in its being truly real. (154)
Movement to another object-domain is certainly not accepted as being where bondage occurs;
moreover, even with a hundred [arguments], there is no bondage for that [consciousness] in self-awareness. //155//

For if it were the case that the knower and the manifestation both arise from their own causes within the bond of self-awareness, this would be illogical; therefore, cognition is impossible even through identity with itself. (156)
Arising in that manner from its own cause and being experienced as having that nature—[if] identity were accepted by entities, it would be a great affliction for proponents. (157)
Therefore, this hollow form does not touch it, even though it vibrates;
yet, by that much alone, why would there not be defilement for it through another continuum? (158)
Even though the distinction between mental continua exists as a real entity (*vastu*), it does not contradict that [cognition].
However, since the aspect (*ākāra*) is unreal, it is something that can be contradicted; what else could this possibly be? (159)
Apart from the occurrence and cessation of that, there is no other such thing as saṃsāra.
[556,22] When the obstruction regarding the various determinations of reality has been established, ||160||
Furthermore, there is no distinction among determinations other than their mental aspect;
because of the conceptual construction of the aspect of water, one proceeds toward water itself. (161)
Even the conceptualization of the form of water does not arise from the mere form of water, for while it exists, it is accompanied by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). //162//

When those latencies have been completely eradicated, there is no longer conceptualization of the unreal—such as the state of grasped object and grasping subject—from that which is non-conceptual and solitary. //163//

Even if non-conceptual knowledge is the cause because it is the basis for the latent impressions, then upon the destruction of that [knowledge], there would be the cessation of the arising of the aspect as it has proceeded. ||164||
From the moment of taking up the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), through the gradual practice of generosity and the other perfections,
there arises the manifestation of the forms of the universal body, enjoyments, and abodes.

For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others and one's own welfare without resting until the end of saṃsāra, because of the singular devotion to that alone, the exertion for its cause is peerless. (166)

[557,11] Finally, through the glory of merit and wisdom endowed with great compassion, [he is] the one who accomplishes the stability of the continuity of the bonds of purified latent impressions. ||167||
In that regard, non-existent conceptualization is time; it is affliction, and purification is subsequent. Since consciousness possesses aspects, this systematic arrangement is established. ||168||
This form is the wheel of adornment consisting of the essence of the common substratum— the hundredfold fullness gathered from the manifold qualities of non-duality;
and even the succession of moments has no substance apart from that which is to be accomplished.
The principle of "possessing aspects" (sākāra) is the life-force of the group of principles. ||169||
It is observed that even for women and others who are drawn by the flavor of pleasure, a cultivation arises in such a way that it depends upon the means for achieving a superior state of well-being;
and likewise, upon its completion, it takes on a form that is to be celebrated as a continuous flow of bliss.
In the process of establishing what is sublated and what is not, let there be the single remainder of bliss through the abandonment of both; what need is there for anything else? (170)
[557.23] Two intermediate verses:

Thus ends the third chapter, which is a definitive exposition on the complete contemplation of the *dharmakāya*, beginning from its entirety and extending to the limits of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*), establishing the consensus among other authors of the treatises.
[Chapter Four] Let it be that there is no other [external object]; let the establishment of the proven and the opposite consist in having a mental form (*sākāra*) alone.
But by whom can its falsity be prevented, given its exclusion from being either one or many? (1)
[558,4] Let there be the exclusion of being one or many, but not the unreality of that which is manifest.
[558,5] For sublation occurs only when a form has been determined, never within the domain of direct perception. (2)
Even in the case of a double moon, the appearance of mere form is not sublated;
however, there is sublation of touch and so forth, as well as of the form that accompanies them. (3)
Likewise, even in a dream, a son or the like is imagined though non-existent, yet it does not possess the body of cognition;
due to the sovereign power of mantras, there is no physical harm from yellow appearances in clods of earth and such. //4//
[558,10] Gold and so forth are imagined and are sublated; however, there is no appearance of a clod of earth and the like.
[558,11] Nor is there a determinate cognition [of it]; therefore, for this [clod], there is neither affirmation nor sublation. //5//
The theory that "this is a misapprehension of something else" is flawed because such a misapprehension is impossible;
however, the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti) is well known, being conceived in relation to the existent.
[558,14] Is it not also the case that, according to the intention [of our opponents], it is the clod itself that appears otherwise?
[558,15] One should not insist on conventional usage; for in reality, those two do not exist. //7//
"Even when devoid of that form, they appear in quite another way"—because of this statement, the actual meaning here should be understood as it has been explained. (8)
Likewise, because those [errors] are not seen by one whose eyes are unimpaired, the nature of the imagined is stated by this [analogy] regarding the appearance of gold and so forth. (9)
There is no sublation of anything in reality; however, there is sublation of that which is imagined within conventional reality.
If even that which is manifest were subject to sublation, how could there be any confidence even when it is sublated? (10)
If it is argued that the invalidating cognition of inference does not have a real entity as its object, [we reply:
it must necessarily be grounded in the nature of a real entity; otherwise, it would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).
Even when a previously perceived object is determined within a positive operation, even a negation ultimately results in the nature of that very object. (12)
[559,3] Two intermediate verses:
It is held that another [cognition] simultaneously makes known the absence of an object;
how, then, could a cognition that is active toward its own object bring about the knowledge of that absence? (13)

If [the cognition] is invalidated by another object through the presentation of its own domain, why is it not also invalidated by that [other object], since its own domain is established by it as well? //14//

If purposeful causal efficiency is distinct because it lacks that specific purposeful action, then why would the loss of one thing entail the loss of another? Yet, if there is no difference between them, how can this [distinction] appear?
Having observed that color (rūpa), there is the sublation of touch (sparśa) due to the cessation of burning and so forth;
yet touch does not manifest here [in the cognition of color]. That very sublation belongs to it—what is the use of others? ||16||

If that which is first made an object of cognition, or something else, were to be sublated, how could it be sublated while it is still manifest? And if it is not manifest, what would there be for the sublater to do? (17)
There is no sublation when there is a difference in time, because each thing manifests at its own respective time;
likewise, even when there is no difference in time, as in the case of blue, yellow, white, and so forth. (18)
Therefore, sublation, like superimposition, occurs through the distinction of dependent origination;
it is conceptually constructed and not real in its true nature. But what need is there to speak of that which is merely one's own self-awareness?

If it is argued that as long as the non-establishment of self-cognition has not been proven, there may be a sublation [of the thesis], then let sublation proceed only after the non-establishment of self-cognition has been thoroughly examined. (20)
If, at the outset of the undertaking, one were to say that the contradiction of one's own thesis has not been incurred, [thinking]:
"In the negation of another's cognition, my own cognition is established," [21]
In whatever way objects are contemplated and analyzed,
in that very way self-cognition remains like a shadow, never departing even from one who runs.
For this very reason, even though he was engaged in a negation, the Teacher declared:
"If this is pleasing to objects themselves, then who are we in that matter? (23)
If there is no sublation by another, let there likewise be no establishment by another.
How, then, can even the establishment of self-awareness come about through a further means of proof? (24)
The establishment of anything from something else occurs not in reality (*tattva*), but rather in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*);
this is just as the establishment of fire and so forth from smoke and so forth is accepted. (25)

If self-awareness is established as non-reality, then for as long as the establishment of the factors of the proof persists, that alone is reality which is established by the power of the means of proof. //26//

Once that which is to be proven is established through the power of its own means of proof as mere self-cognition, there is no longer any possibility whatsoever for further establishment or sublation. (27)
One who does not awaken to anything else is incapable of abandoning what is under discussion;
nor is one who abandons what is under discussion capable of apprehending something else from something else. ||28||

For this very reason, when the cognition of another is apprehended, it undermines itself, because there is also room for the cognition of the three features (trairūpya) that serve as the cause for one's own self-awareness. //29//
But the fact that those forms have been abandoned does not constitute a contradiction even if they are not cognized;
for the manifestation of the probandum exists through another [means], and not otherwise. //30//
If it is argued that [the appearance] should not exist even by itself, provided that the appearance is not [real] in every respect—this may be correct;
however, since the illumination exists, why should it not exist by itself? (31)
There is illumination, but it does not arise from itself; how could it not arise from something other?
Otherwise, just as there would be a subverting argument [against that], so too there is no such subversion regarding cognition arising from itself. (32)
[560,19] Furthermore, there is no obstruction of an action within its own self by means of two streams through their own interruption;
[560,20] why is it not said by the wise man that even a sharp stream is [sharp] by itself? //33//
If that [capacity] is produced as sharp from its own cause alone and not from anything else, then knowledge whose nature is luminosity is also produced from its own cause alone. (34)
Let it not be that manifestation is produced by the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary;
rather, the form itself, which arises as having that nature, is designated by the word "manifestation. (35)
Just as illumination is seen to result from the mutual assistance between a lamp and a cloth, why is it not likewise observed that the lamp illuminates itself? 36.
If the lamp depends on the sense organ, why does that dependence not also exist in the jar?
Even when that [organ] is present, the jar does not depend on the lamp, nor does the lamp depend on anything else. //37//

Just as, even when effort and so forth are present, the statement that there is "coming of its own accord" serves to exclude being impelled by another, so too does it serve to exclude what is produced by that [effort] in the case of self-manifestation. (38)
Even in scripture, that which appears as self-cognition despite contradiction is the negation of that subtle state of the grasped and the grasper. (39)

Just as the state of being both cause and fruit in a single entity was refuted after being raised as a doubt, so too has the state of being both grasped object and grasping subject in a single entity been refuted after being raised as a doubt. (40)

Therefore, it is held that the mind is self-luminous, not by way of being an object and an agent; rather, having arisen from its own causes, the mind shines forth independently of other things. //41//
[561,13] It is made clear in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* because its meaning is demonstrated there;
[561,14] it is also indicated by such statements as "the arising of the appearance of objects" (*arthābhāsa*). ||42||
Therefore, self-awareness is not contradicted by either reasoning or scripture;
that very same defect which contradicts the cognition of another is like fire to a tree. //43//

Nor is it desired that the apprehension of another’s cognition involve the operation of one’s own cognition; for it is through the qualities or defects of that [other’s] cognition that one’s own cognition is either uplifted or disparaged. (44)
The fault does not lie in mere existence, but rather in its functional activity;
for earth and the other elements are not to be censured when they remain at a time when they are not performing their causal function. (45)

Therefore, there is no fault regarding self-awareness; however, because of the extensive nature of its manifestation, luminosity is itself determined as being excluded from awareness of anything other than that.
If there is no appearance either from itself or from another, then there is no appearance at all;
and it is not appropriate to say this of something that is like a clod of earth and so forth. (47)

If it is maintained that there is an appearance even when there is exclusion from both itself and others, then let there be for you the existence of a thing despite its being devoid of both unity and plurality. (48)
If a thing is held to be real even when it is devoid of being one or many, then why do you not accept the existence of an appearance even in the absence of both self-nature and other-nature? 49.
Nevertheless, even while appearing thus, these entities cannot be denied;
because they appear in a non-common way, they will also possess the nature of cognition.
The appearance as form also possesses a real nature of direct perception;
and since there is no fault in self-cognition, nothing at all is undermined. //51//
But how could it be that there is such a thing as "the self-cognition of blue"?
For this [blue] does not know itself, by virtue of which it could be said to have self-awareness. //52//

Since internal forms such as pleasure and so forth, and external forms such as cold and heat and so forth, appear, for whom, by what, and how could there be cognition? Nor can there be oneness [between them]. //53//
To begin with, these [cognitions] do possess luminosity; therefore, it is impossible to deny it.
If that [luminosity] were not possible in the case of distinct [cognitions], then let there be non-distinctness among the cognitions. (54)
How could there be non-difference among these things which possess distinct forms?
Therefore, is it intended that there is an absence of duality, or rather that duality itself is a real entity? //55//

Whether distinction or non-distinction, whether in two ways or not in two ways—let it be as it may regarding the nature of cognition; there is no unreality in manifestation, for it is opposed even to the scent of sublation.
For there is no sublation of one's own experience by any logical arguments;
for that [experience] alone is their source, and they find their finality in it alone. //57//
Let it be that difference and so forth belong only to thought; there is no exclusion of luminosity.
Wherever there is repose in luminosity—whether it be one's own or another—that alone is real.
When the self-cognizing subject is established as existing in sentient beings, what is the use of investigating whether it is one or many?
For it is said that its establishment as a result follows from its non-existence [as such]. (59)
Even if mere manifestation is established, how can self-awareness be asserted? And if the object is established by that much alone, what need have we for the term "self-awareness"? (60)
For the opponent's intended thesis is indeed sublated by perception;
and that [thesis] is established even when its own nature is revealed by the opponent.
Perceptuality arises from the direct realization of its own nature, and there is no other;
even by another, that very form of illumination first shines forth. (62)
Nevertheless, self-awareness certainly exists; however, it is not "its own" [awareness], and thus there is no self-awareness [in that sense].
Since sublation is unestablished, there is no harm even in the doctrine that cognition is known by another.
Neither the cognition of another nor self-cognition is established;
therefore, what kind of thing is this so-called "perceptuality" by which [the opponent's position] could be sublated? (64)
The perceptual nature of that which has the character of direct realization has been declared;
there is no impairment even to its specific definition in the case of non-ascertainment. //65//
Just as there is a pervasion of particulars by the universal, so too is this [universal] established by them;
when the particular is established, the universal follows, and when the universal is established, that [particular] follows.
Whether it be a hero or someone else, one must cultivate certainty regarding being human;
yet, there is no defeat for a human being in the doubt concerning those two.
If that non-duality were established, there would be a loss of humanity;
however, whether humanity is unestablished or established, there is no loss of duality. (68)

Therefore, regarding an object that is beyond the senses, when there is a state of dual appearance, let the impairment of the appearance be determined; however, regarding the appearance itself, both [the subject and the object] abide as one.
There is no doubt regarding manifestation; rather, doubt concerns difference and non-difference.
Of these two—difference and non-difference—one must necessarily be concomitant with manifestation. (70)
Just as the persistence of difference and non-difference depends upon logical justification, light is not like that; for if it depended on something else, how could it be called "light"? (71)

If the pervasion of light were to occur by means of two [objects], there would be a coexistence of the two; yet pervasion is never established anywhere, and nevertheless, no impairment has been asserted. //72//
Since one does not know by means of a sensation that is either non-different or different, how can there be sublation by perception? This [argument] is sufficient for the pervasion itself. //73//

If it is argued that perceptibility must be established by the opponent who asserts the sublation, then what kind of perception could there be for one who has accepted a means of valid cognition? (74)

Even when there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), upon the determination of the three forms [of the reason], perceptual cognition must necessarily be involved, whether mediately or immediately. (75)
In that case, what kind of direct perception do you have if it does not exist for us?
If that [perception] is conventional, then let the sublation also be from the conventional, just like the proof.

[564,11] When form is apprehended, conventional cognition is capable; what sequence is there for non-sublation? [564,12] And whatever kind of thing is established, let that very kind be the sublater. //77//
If the conventional nature of both the means of cognition and the object of cognition is due to conventionality, then that very conventionality must still be investigated;
since it is not yet established, how can it serve as a proof? (78)

If the apprehension of the pervasion (vyāpti) of the final [cognition], which lacks awareness [of itself], were to depend on another [cognition], then let that other grasper be erroneous; what loss is there for self-awareness? (79)
For one who lacks valid means of knowledge, silence is indeed better;
for by speaking, one must necessarily either refute something or establish something. (80)
If you claim that pride is accepted as conventional, then this very analysis is also conventional.
If it is not accepted even conventionally, then one who speaks thus is a victor, just as [the Buddha was]. (81)
Nor is there such a possibility of sublation even in the case of causes such as light, because the reversal of the unique appearance has not been established. (82)
By this direct perception as well, there is merely the act of making it an object;
there is no establishment of its existence. Is this not, then, an occasion for sublation? (83)
Because it is made an object by a means of cognition that establishes a positive entity, there is nowhere any capacity to establish existence; rather, existence is merely worldly. //84//
In all cases, it is logical to establish a distinction in existence for that which is produced by human effort;
however, that which contradicts existence—such as destruction—is a sublater of existence. (85)
Therefore, whether it be itself or something else, that which possesses the manifestation of the object's own form is alone the domain of direct perception. 86.
Even when there is doubt regarding whether something has that form or not, the nature of the object of awakening remains stable;
for it is only through the presentation of knowledge and the object of knowledge that there can be proof or refutation. //87//
Form should not be sought in its own intrinsic nature for the sake of pacifying delusion; and when form appears as a mere manifestation, there is no possibility for delusion to exist.

[565,11] Let it be simply "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha); what then is the purpose of the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta)? [565,12] If it is argued that even the insistence on establishing the two types of error is futile; //89//
[565,13] It is true that this was indeed composed by the venerable teacher Dignāga;
[565,14] however, it was done in the *Vārttika* by superimposing externality upon the form of the world. ||90||
If people were to perceive the aspect as being merely an aspect, and the mother-of-pearl as being merely mother-of-pearl, how could there ever be delusion for anyone anywhere? (91)
