At that time, the determination of identity with respect to two things that do not possess that nature is rightly to be set aside precisely by means of abandoning conceptual construction. //92//
But when the apprehension of an object by all embodied beings is observed specifically within the form of cognition as a very clear and distinct manifestation, [93]
Then, the apprehension of a false object would be perception because it is free from conceptual construction;
thus, that second qualification [of perception] becomes redundant, like the apprehension of what has already been apprehended. //94//
It is said that this [cognition] is "accompanied by obscurity" only in consideration of worldly understanding;
furthermore, another [type of cognition] is taught for the sake of removing the delusion regarding the conceptual nature of this [cognition] which appears clearly. (95)

At the time of investigating reality, that determination of error occurs only in relation to the imagined [object], when there is a clear appearance; it does not occur in relation to the reflection of its own form. 96.
Even though it is non-conceptual, it possesses the nature of error because of conceptualization; there is nothing beyond that.
Therefore, although it rests in the non-conceptual, it is said to be "resting in conceptualization. (97)
If conceptualization were erroneous, there would either be another error or none at all;
if conceptualization were non-erroneous, then error itself would not exist. //98//
[566,7] Two intermediate verses:
The fact that something appears directly excludes its unreality;
therefore, falsity belongs to the object alone, not to the cognition or the person. //99//

Therefore, even amidst disputes regarding difference and non-difference within the means of cognition, the state of being an object of perception is established for that which is manifest; and that alone is existence.

This non-duality is considered variegated because it is devoid of the grasped and so forth; the conventional designation of a "single" entity for what is manifold is as futile as the notion of a person. (101)
As long as there is external attachment, so long does this appear as distinct from that;
but when the mind encompasses it all, then that very thing becomes his hands, feet, and so forth, for he is indeed knowledge itself.
In a variegated cognition, the blue and other colors are attributes of the cognition itself and do not belong to anything else;
for it is impossible to perceive them as such, since one who attempts to distinguish them falls back upon the external object. //103//
In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way;
thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the mind, even though it possesses variegated forms. (104)
Summary verses: [566.20] [The following are] summary verses: [566.20]

By these two [arguments], "variegated cognition" and so forth, the contradiction of being both one and many is established respectively; for it is sublated by its nature as a cognition and because it cannot be perceived as distinct [from its parts]. (105)
The inclusion of the remaining cases is by means of the passage beginning with "For that [is] in vain through various sounds" (mudhānekadhvanis taṃ hi).
By the passage beginning with "Whatever [is] as [it is]" (yad yatheti), the logical proof is established: the identity of a single designation is the oneness of that [object]. (106)
Nor is there any doubt regarding the capacity [of inference] when there is a contradiction between perception and inference;
for inference always depends upon the senses, whereas that which is born of the senses never depends upon inference. (107)
Just as you avoid contradiction with direct perception when accepting inference, so too, without avoiding contradiction with inference, there can be no occurrence of sensory perception. (108)
And when inference applies elsewhere regarding what is beyond the senses, what kind of contradiction could there be?
What object is sublated by the sense-faculty? This [inference] is not a means of valid cognition within its own specific domain.
In the case of the persistence of its own existence, a further quality [is established] through perception and inference;
for it is not apprehended by direct perception, and thus its status as being beyond the senses is established. ||110||
Therefore, there is no need for inference by means of another perception anywhere;
as for that which is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), what kind of inquiry could there even be regarding it? (111)
If self-awareness alone is not a means of valid cognition because it is not produced by another [means], then what is a means of valid cognition here?
Therefore, regarding those things established or sublated by it, no other [means of cognition] has the power to either sublate or establish them. (112)
An intermediate verse:
[567,14] Since it manifests even when both unity and plurality are excluded, by what means could it be prevented?
[567,15] Nor is there a pervasion between existence and those two, because that is sublated by direct perception itself. ||113||
At the time of the operation of a characteristic, its pervasion is refuted by this [reasoning];
this restriction exists only externally by virtue of its functional capacity. (114)
Even in the case of duality, not every external object is common to all cognitions;
this would be like the cases of permanence and impermanence. If it were not so even in the case of non-duality, there would be no harm.
Stability and the like, being pervaded by the relation of priority and posteriority, do not exist in the absence of that [momentariness].
Stability is not pervaded by oneness or manifoldness; therefore, it does not exist in cognition, nor does consciousness [possess such stability]. (116)
[567,22] Furthermore, there is pervasion; moreover, because that too exists, these two are one.
[567,23] For indeed, the determination of all aspects does not occur even regarding an object that is directly perceived. //117//
When blue and so forth appear, the appearance itself is the direct cognition;
therefore, there is no distinction [between them], nor is there any suspicion of a difference from yellow and the like. (118)

Even in that case, the establishment of non-difference is due solely to the appearance of a pervasive unity; for if there were difference, there would be no manifestation, just as in the case of cognitions belonging to a different continuum. (119)
If it is argued that the distinctions such as the appropriated [aggregates] and so forth are mutually manifest, this is incorrect;
for even the designation "appropriated" does not eliminate their distinction. (120)
Even if there is proximity, what could be the purpose of apprehension? If that very [proximity] were the direct manifestation, it would indeed be the manifestation itself. (121)
And by virtue of that power, why is there no perception of the cause and effect within the grasping?
However, the gradation of proximity exists therein only in relation to that very [grasping]. //122//
If, in this context, the manifestation of coexistence is intended to mean mutual apprehension, then why is there not also a manifestation of proximity even when there is no mutual apprehension? (123)

Therefore, there can be no variegated appearance, for consciousness cannot tolerate differentiation, because it is characterized by the non-difference of its own nature due to the mutual penetration of cognitions. (124)
If [the effect] always arises from the variegated [cause] alone, what need is there for a single material cause?
Furthermore, even during the state of contraction, there is no absolute certainty regarding the variegated nature [of the cause]. (125)

As long as the birth of a variegated [effect] is perceived from a variegated [cause] itself, so long is it not tenable for there to be a distinct material cause for each part, nor can they be established independently of one another. (126)

If even that which is diverse, such as the act of grasping (*upādāna*), is established as a unity, why should that which is grasped (*upādeya*) not be so? Thus, the non-duality of the manifold (*citradvaita*) remains unrefuted.
Or how could even a single blue object appear as atoms?
Therefore, when the existence of many [atoms] is subverted, by what means could there be stability and unity for anything? (128)
If it is thought that the absence of both unity and plurality follows for this very reason, let it be so; however, it has already been explained that the negation of existence is impossible. (129)
But this is the case regarding difference: mutual manifestation is not logical, because there is no power in the subsequent [cognition] to differentiate its own material cause. (130)
Therefore:
"Because they are necessarily perceived together, blue and yellow are non-different. For their very nature is consciousness, which is non-different; so how could there be any distinction? (131)
There is no restriction of simultaneous cognition for two distinct things, such as blue and yellow; for in this manner, each one may be perceived by the two persons individually. (132)
Regarding this, it is said:
"In a variegated cognition, the blue and other colors are attributes of the cognition itself and do not belong to anything else.
Indeed, that which is impossible to perceive falls upon the external object when one attempts to distinguish them. (133)
"In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way;
thus, there would indeed be a single nature even in a mind possessing variegated forms. (134)
For even when there is sublation, as in the case of external objects, there is no perception of a single [nature] by persons;
because since it is apprehended otherwise, the restriction [of the object's nature] is destroyed. (135)
Whatever appears as a single entity is like the white form in a painting;
and the entire variegated picture appears as yellow, cold, pleasure, and so forth. (136)
This has been stated with reference to a single intended cognizer;
therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason] on account of what appears to another mental continuum. (137)
In the example, there is no lack of the probandum (sādhya-śūnyatva), because there is no sublation by the contrary;
for appearance is pervaded by grossness, since it does not break down into atoms.
Because each atom is submerged [within its own particularity], there is no mutual cognition of them;
nor is there any manifestation of a single atom, for it is only the gross [object] that appears. //139//
The appearance of external atoms is a single, more massive cognition; but what will the appearance of the atoms of consciousness itself be? (140)

Even in the case of a whole composed of many parts, there is a single cognition of a variegated form; this is sufficient for conventional usage. But what is the status of that [cognition] in the case of the intellect? (141)
In one case as well, the cognition of a single part has been established as having a form;
since conventional practice cannot be otherwise, the grossness of cognition is difficult to abandon. //142//
Therefore, since the appearance is pervaded by grossness, when that [grossness] is withdrawn, for you who maintain the unity of the mind, it is withdrawn from being manifold. (143)
Just as there is the exclusion of difference from a homogeneous conceptualization due to the consequence of non-appearance, so too is it from a heterogeneous conceptualization. (144)
Therefore, let there be no probandum, no example, and no doubt or misconception;
nor can there be sublation of the probandum by perception, because perception itself lacks a firm foundation. (145)
There is no conceit, no apprehension of another, and self-cognition does not grasp at difference;
the conceptual construction that "this is different from that" follows from latent predispositions.
Just as this [subject] independently imagines the external to be distinct from itself, so too does it itself imagine the external to be distinct from the internal. 147.
Even though external objects exist, direct perception does not cognize their difference from anything else;
for if it did, there would be the apprehension of everything else as well, since they are apprehended as being qualified by that [difference].
If this "distinct from that" is the very nature of the object to be apprehended, then that object would either appear with its limit or it would not be apprehended in its own form. (149)
For if difference is perceived even without a formal rule [of differentiation], why would non-difference not be so?
Consequently, there would be a mere metaphorical application of difference; therefore, difference does not exist in reality.
The apprehension of a form that is not mixed with others is indeed the cognition of difference.
That which is unmixed with others is distinct from them; such is a single object. (151)
But when one thing is mixed with another, the apprehension of the other is not appropriate;
for if the other is not apprehended, how can that which is unmixed be apprehended as a solitary entity? (152)
Since this [object] shines forth as something solitary, it is not conjoined with anything else;
for how could the manifestation of another thing be apprehended as solitary? (153)

Just as there can be no apprehension of something isolated when another thing is manifesting, so too, even when another thing is not manifesting, that which is "isolated" is indeed mixed with another. (154)
Just as the mental transformation [appears] such that "this is unmixed with another," if experience were likewise [unmixed], by whom could the primary intellect (*pradhī*) be prevented? //155//

Just as, my dear father, having excluded the other, the apprehension of a mixture does not exist; so too, my dear father, having excluded the other, the apprehension of a distinct entity does not exist. (156)
Therefore, it is logical that perception grasps only the thing-in-itself;
by means of it, neither a distinct nor a non-distinct entity can be grasped. (157)
An object is not known through the appearance of difference because of a limit, nor through the suspicion of non-difference;
nor is it anything other than difference and non-difference. How, then, can there be a cognition of a real entity? (158)

If everything is indistinguishable from its object, how could there be any distinction even from cognition? And if there were such a distinction, then even when there is a limited measure, everything would be within the range of everyone. (159)
[571,13] However, when there is an adherence to external apprehension, the refutation is equal in the case of reflection;
[571,14] just as it is when the apprehension of difference is not accepted, so it is when there is the apprehension of a real limit. (160)
Therefore, let the apprehension of external objects be set aside by closing one's eyes, however one wishes;
but how can one who knows reality be refuted when he merely describes the non-apprehension of difference? (161)
Perception does not create differentiation; rather, conceptual construction is the thief that creates it here.
That [conceptual construction] casts its own fault upon perception—such is the established nature of differentiation. (162)
If it is argued that this [cognition] is one, just like the blue [object], how could this be consistent? For how could it be coherent that the blue and its other parts are one? (163)
If that [atom] is not one either, then how can there be an appearance when there is a division of the atom?
Furthermore, since an atom cannot withstand analysis, how and of what could there be a division at that time? (164)
Or, if it were not a real entity, then even that would be undermined by the refutation of oneness.
Since oneness is established through manifestation, the reality of self-awareness is firmly established.
Furthermore, for that which is devoid of another name, there can be no attainment of spatial extension; nor, when the manifestation of space is lost, can it even be called a "manifestation. (166)
One's own nature is not different from another's nature; that [distinction] is applicable only to external objects.
For consciousness, which culminates in self-cognition, what recourse is there for that which is "other"? (167)

Even though an external object is perceived by the intellect as divided by spatial location, by what means does the intellect itself—though divided by spatial distinctions—become the basis for conventional usage? 168.
Even though it occupies a large space, cognition cannot admit of differentiation because of its identity with that [object];
just as there is no differentiation within it despite its non-difference [from the object], so too it is with the form (ākṛti). //169//
If it is argued that "that single thing is variegated," then this is even more variegated than that;
and this is most variegated of all: that there is a mutual perception of difference. (170)
If there is a manifestation of a single cognition as variegated, it may or may not be external;
otherwise, in the consequence of its non-manifestation, there would be neither external objects nor cognitions. (171)
Whether atoms exist or do not exist, there can be no correspondence with the appearance in cognition;
therefore, the appearance of cognition is contradictory to both atomicity and its absence. (172)
Regarding this, it is said:
In a variegated cognition, blue and other such colors are attributes of the cognition itself and do not belong to anything else.
Indeed, they cannot be perceived [as external]; for one who attempts to distinguish them falls upon the object [itself]. (173)
In whatever way a cognition appears, it is followed as being exactly thus;
in this way, there would indeed be a single nature for the mind that possesses variegated forms. (174)
In the experience of a variegated [cognition], this blue and so forth is distinguished by its nature as cognition;
since it does not assume the form of the others, being non-bulky, it cannot be perceived. (175)

Because the distinction [of atoms] would apply to every single atom, or else there would be only a heap of blue and so forth; for it is impossible to perceive each individual [atom] as it has been described, since they are apprehended by the intellect one by one. (176)
Therefore, a single experience must be admitted as having manifold aspects, from which the mind born of subsequent reflection constructs the notion: "This is distinct from that. (177)

For this very reason, when one distinguishes an object such as blue and so forth, one would be distinguishing the object itself; it would not be the form of the cognition, because if that were distinct [from the object], there would be neither cognition nor an object of experience.
Therefore, in whatever manner and by whatever means the cognition shines forth,
it is accepted as being qualified by that very same gross unity.

Furthermore, the superimposition of contradictory properties serves to establish difference in that case where difference is established by perception for the sake of accomplishing conventional usage. (180)
In this context, self-awareness alone is direct perception, and it is not differentiated;
when there is the state of being blue and so forth, conceptualization follows it, but for us, it is not differentiated. (181)
If it is argued that there is a distinction [of cognition] due to a distinction in its manifestation, then that very [manifestation] is called the "aspect" (ākāra).
When the object of knowledge is external, that [cognition] is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); with respect to that object, self-awareness (svavid) is the valid cognition (pramā).
[573,13] Since this [object] has been made one with self-cognition, how could it be differentiated externally by means of differentiation?
[573,14] Just as the apprehension of cognitions occurs through the sense organ, so too does their differentiation occur through self-cognition. (183)
If manifestation is appearance, that [appearance] is not found in itself; the determination of difference produced by the form of the object of cognition is destroyed by knowledge. (184)

For if the white [snow] were to split the cold [ice] by its very presence, then that which is being split would either be distinct from it or not distinct; if there is no distinction whatsoever, how could it split it?
If there is a distinction, since there is not even a trace of another [entity], how could it split it?
Who could possibly say, "The mind has been split," or even "It was not split"? [185]

The external object does not perish, whether through division into atoms or through non-difference; for in the latter case, there would be a confusion resulting from the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). However, the cognition perishes precisely through its differentiation, because its existence consists solely in being manifest (*vida*).
Therefore, even the variegated does not undergo differentiation; what can we do about this? //186//

[574,1] Even so, if you claim that there is a distinction merely out of conformity with the cognition of the ignorant, [574,2] even by this much your reason remains unestablished. [574,3] Furthermore, there would be the loss of oneness, or else the contradiction of conformity with cognition.
"But even that [substantiality] does not exist for us; this is what has been stated by the opponent. [574.4] /187/
Intermediate verses:

If the pervasion of entities by unity and plurality were established anywhere, then at the time of the proof of universal emptiness, that reason would result in the subversion of what is intended. (188)

Furthermore, even if something is established by worldly consensus, not everything imagined by the world is accepted as the determination of reality; rather, it must be consistent with valid cognition. (189)
Neither through perception nor through inference has anything partless ever been observed anywhere;
for that which would be a manifold aggregate is not a single entity whatsoever. (190)
[574,12] Each gross object is perceived as neither one nor many.
[574,13] But in reality, what could be one? Nor is there any such thing as a real entity at all. //191//
For the wise, the acceptance of another's position is not valid when establishing an independent proof;
nor does the primary meaning apply in a reductio ad absurdum, for if it did, it would result in the destruction of one's own tenet. (192)
Let that person who maintains that existence is pervaded by either one or both of these [modes of being] be refuted;
however, the proponent of existence by means of mere non-erroneous cognition is victorious. (193)
In every case, however, pervasion in respect to the reason depends upon the establishment of valid cognition;
and that [pervasion] is to be known through the non-perception of the pervader and so forth in the contrapositive. (194)
When the means of knowledge is established, neither the pervasion nor the pervaded is admitted by oneself;
it is proclaimed that what is known by another is sublated only by the cognition of another. (195)
Furthermore, the acceptance of intrinsic nature does not necessarily entail being the sole attractor [of the effect];
for its pervasion remains unestablished even now, and it is moreover contradicted by valid cognition. (196)

If, by taking up the pervasion through the exclusion of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyastarūpeṇa*), one negates that [existence], why would things not be devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*), just like the absence of a donkey’s horn? (197)
[575,1] In that case, how is the external object also refuted by the negation of being one or many?
[575,2] Because, in reality, it is not perceived, and thus its characteristic as an object of apprehension is lost. ||198||
Nor is there a partless unity; rather, it is the perception of distinct things that is not designated by the word [“one”].
And that [perception] does not exist externally because of the non-existence of that [external object]; therefore, their collection [is likewise non-existent]. //199//
Even in the case of an atom, unity is impossible to demonstrate through analysis;
since that [difficulty] remains unabated even in the case of variegated cognition, where is the use for your aversion? (200)
But in a cognition that has a variegated form, it is impossible to perceive a single [element] as distinct;
through the distinction from other minds, that [cognition] possesses the characteristic of being both one and many. (201)
Regarding this, it is said: "The distinctness of a cognition from blue and so forth is evident;
from what [source] is that [distinctness] inferred? If [it is argued that it is from inference], let it be so conventionally, however that may be. (202)

Nevertheless, just as momentary things are conceived in dependence upon an imagined permanence, so too do cognitions depend upon a single object that is a firm mental construction distinct from others. (203)

In that case, even if there is no single entity whose distinction is impossible, [a plurality] would arise from it as something else; thus, even in the external world, there would be a manifold of distinguishable things—what need is there for a single accumulation? (204)
It is not the case that when a composite whole is destroyed, a single atom remains;
therefore, a multiplicity consisting of an accumulation of those atoms is refuted by that very same fault. ||205||

Likewise, when this semblance of that [self], which is neither one nor many, has been refuted, then this collection of many atoms, which is accepted by the proponents [of the self], is likewise refuted. (206)
It can also be explained in this way from the perspective of external objects;
however, the investigation into the whole and the atom was undertaken because of the intentions of others.

And when, by the very cognition of variety, there is the sublation of both unity and plurality due to the removal of other sublaters, why is their establishment not likewise accomplished by that same cognition? (208)
If there were oneness, there would be an absence of variety; if there were plurality, it would be even more so.
Just as there is no oneness due to its variegated nature, so too is the status of being one or many.
Without the introduction of a contradictory [reason], there is no sublation of the counter-entity;
likewise, since many [entities] are destroyed within the cognition of a single self, speak! [210]
And in that case, there would be a collapse of the pervader’s absence due to the persistence of the [opponent's] position;
however, for us, this fault does not apply if both are established by valid cognition. (211)
If all aspects are abandoned, how could there not be something uniform anywhere?
That [reality] is endowed with both unity and multiplicity, as well as with their two modes of manifestation. (212)
Granted that there may be identity within that variegated painting consisting of both difference and non-difference;
nevertheless, the proof is for the sake of establishing one thing, not for the sake of subverting another. (213)
Even for that [opponent], after the sublation, such a great hope remains:
"If the single entity is established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), how could there be a subsequent sublation? (214)
If a single entity is not established by means of valid cognition, how could there be the sublation of another?
If contradiction were inherent in itself, the negation of one would not be the affirmation of another. (215)
And a positive cognition, being diverse, would negate the other by way of introducing a contradiction;
if it is capable while being expressed, oh, what a state for those who rely on valid cognition! //216//
[576,15] At times there is no loss of either, yet it remains established as each one;
[576,16] at times that [reality] appears as unity, and at times as multiplicity. (217)
Nevertheless, the existence [of the reason] in one [instance] is unestablished, because of the absence of the pervader. ||218||
If existence in the form of causal efficiency and so forth is what is being negated, what harm is done? For that which has the nature of mere appearance is not sublated even by Brahmā.
Even if there were a sublation of that subject, it would not constitute a sublation of the [thesis] itself;
for example, "this is blue"—it may appear as such, yet it may or may not be true. (220)
If it is argued that when there is doubt regarding the substratum (dharmin), there is doubt regarding its property (dharma), from what source [is this known]?
If it is because of identity (tādātmya) in reality, then this is the same as [the case of] the non-momentary and so forth. ||221||

[576,24] Now, if it is argued that certainty regarding one thing destroys doubt even when it has arisen with respect to another, [576,25] that too is the same in the case at hand, because of the distinction between exclusions (vyāvṛtti). ||222||
When even external existence is in reality nothing but cognition, then where is there sublation and where is there doubt regarding the appearing subject? (223)

If something seen by someone at one time were to become an object of inference at another time, then nothing would ever be unfit for perception; for what could possibly remain an object of perception? (224)
Even in the absence of inference, there is the manifestation of conceptual construction itself;
for those things, whatever their mode of existence may be, their cognition is likewise. (225)

Making clear that existence is nothing but cognition, the skillful author of the *Vārttika* established that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), without depending at all upon an external object.
The status of substances and so forth as appearing is vain, insofar as they appear merely in the form of that appearance.
In a variegated [cognition], there would be only the state of being a single appearance, and no proliferation through qualities and the like. (227)
For in the Vijñānavāda system, stability is both real and a constituent part of the fruit;
oh, what shamelessness! Or rather, everything is indeed great for the great. (228)

The apprehension of that [object] occurs when there is full knowledge of the preceding and succeeding [moments] and when there is knowledge of another; for how could it occur when self-cognition is the final limit, since both [of those conditions] are impossible? (229)

In the absence of appearance, there is no cognition of priority and posteriority, because that would entail the loss of cognition; nor is there cognition of priority and posteriority in the presence of appearance, due to its conformity with non-duality. //230//

Because the two do not exist within the single nature of the self, there is no state of being a fruit or a factor for either the self or the other; nor is it twofold due to the exclusion of what is other. (231)
Therefore, just as there is the knowledge of another, so is the establishment of cause and effect;
just as there is the repose of self-awareness, so is this conventional truth.
Therefore, they say that the establishment of "mind-only" is without production;
for this reason, even dependent origination is not established, and thus it cannot serve as a proof. //233//
Dependent origination itself is not what is to be expressed as emptiness;
because of the pair of lower abidings, there is no such distinction, so this is a vain exertion. //234//
Let non-arising itself be the cause, for there is no fault in the previous [position].
Even if cause and effect were abandoned, where could the manifest form go? (235)
Therefore, every phenomenon is empty of its very own imagined forms; there is not even the slightest part that appears as something real.
This is the manifold non-duality, this very wheel of variety.
That which is to be cultivated should be cultivated by means of those things to be cultivated, free from conceptual proliferation, for the sake of auspiciousness.
Direct realization does not occur for those who bear existence as long as there is a lack of thorough familiarity with what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted within this state;
therefore, it remains unshakable until the perfection of the cultivation of the two accumulations through the qualities of both body and mind.
That yogi, the lord of yogis, having attained awakening in the incomparable abode, is renowned. ||237||
Just as gold, endowed with the perfection of qualities and form, reaches the ultimate limit of excellence and is inexhaustible,
being free from even the suspicion of the stain of falsehood.
In that very same way, may the body of a Buddha belong to all embodied beings. ||238||
[578,15] Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Determination of the Non-duality of the Variegated.
[578,16] Thus ends the Sākārasaṃgraha-sūtra.
[578,17] This work is by the great scholar and master, the venerable Jñānaśrīmitra.
